title: UPDATE 1-Indian officials pour balm over troubled rupee
text:
* Rupee rebounds from record low hit on Tuesday

* Policy adviser says cenbank intervened on Tuesday

* Econ affairs secretary says govt considering measures (Updates with quotes, details, background)

By Neha Dasgupta and Suvashree Dey Choudhury

MUMBAI, June 12 (Reuters) - India said on Wednesday it was considering measures that would help stabilise the rupee after it hit an all-time low but the assurances are unlikely to be enough unless backed by concrete steps to revive inflows into the slowing economy.

The government may issue an overseas bond to raise capital for infrastructure, economic affairs secretary Arvind Mayaram said a day after another official said the government may target overseas Indians for a debt issue.

Mayaram, however, said the government had no plans to moderate gold imports which have been a key reason for a large current account deficit that is putting pressure on the rupee.

The rupee rebounded on Wednesday to trade at 58.00/01 per dollar from Tuesday's record low of 58.98 but trimmed gains after a higher-than-expected consumer price inflation reading for May.

On Tuesday as the currency hit the buffers the Reserve Bank of Indiaintervened, the deputy chairman of the Planning Commission Montek Singh Ahluwalia said, confirming suspicions that the rupee rebounded from RBI dollar sales.

The RBI late on Tuesday also asked exporters at special economic zones to realise their dollar earnings and get them back into the country within one year in a bid to increase the supply of dollars in the market.

The central bank also hastened the process of dollar inflows through online payment channels by increasing the amount that exporters can bring back to $10,000 from $3000.

"The government talking up the rupee has had an impact on the sentiment. Going ahead, if the macros remain weak, the government will have to take steps to further attract inflows," said Anjali Verma, economist at PhilipCapital in Mumbai.

SELLOFF IN EMERGING MARKETS

The downward pressure on Indian assets has been exacerbated by the recent selloff across emerging markets and Indian officials have pointed to a broad rally in the dollar as the trigger for the latest falls.

The rupee has fallen more than 8 percent since the beginning of May, and although that is the worst performance in Asia, other currencies are also being hit.

"We'll keep looking at different instruments, and bonds are one of the instruments we are looking at for raising resources for long-term infrastructure financing," said Mayaram on the sidelines of a conference in Mumbai on Wednesday.

Policymakers are also trying to comfort investors by focusing on measures to help narrow the current account deficit, including easing foreign direct investment rules.

Tackling India's current account deficit, which hit a record 6.7 percent of gross domestic product in October-December, is seen as key to preventing continued weakness in the rupee.

"It will be a totality of our efforts to convey the impression that the current account deficit is being brought under control and the economy is going to rebound," Ahluwalia told CNBC-TV 18 in an interview.

For now, the rupee is likely to remain dependant on global movements of the dollar, ahead of key data this week including wholesale inflation and trade data and the Reserve Bank of India's policy review on Monday.

"They (RBI) did intervene yesterday which would suggest that they felt market pressures were pushing the currency to an unnecessary low point," said Ahluwalia. (Additional reporting by Subhadip Sircar and Swati Bhat; Editing by Rafael Nam and Sanjeev Miglani)

title: Indian Rupee at New Record Low; Falls on Broad Dollar Strength
text:
MUMBAI--The Indian rupee weakened to a new record low against the dollar on Tuesday, in line with strength in the U.S. currency against a number of Asian counterparts.

Around 0410 GMT, the dollar was valued at 58.47 rupees compared with 58.15 rupees in late Asian trade Monday.

The dollar is in favor with investors in the region, with the notable exception of Japan, following a string of better-than-expected U.S. economic data over the past few weeks. On Monday, Standard & Poor's revised its U.S. credit outlook to stable from negative.

India's yawning current-account gap has hit the rupee hardest among depreciating Asian currencies. Oil and gold imports contributed to a deficit equivalent to 6.7% of gross domestic product in the October-December quarter.

A currency dealer at a state-run bank in Mumbai said the dollar has been "overbought," but "there now appears room for the rupee to breathe."

Radhika Rao, an economist at DBS in Singapore said in a note that while the key trigger for the rupee's fall to a record lows has been broad dollar strength, "the domestic negative macroeconomic backdrop serves to hasten the bear-run."

Ms. Rao said she doesn't expect the Reserve Bank of India to intervene in the currency market in a large way, but the central bank may help prevent a one-sided and volatile move in the exchange rate.

title: UPDATE 3-RBI's hidden hand pulls Indian rupee off record low
text:
* Rupee hits life low of 58.98 to the dollar, ends at 58.39/40

* Cbank likely sold dlrs via state-run banks, say dealers

* Comments from chief econ advisor to the govt also aid sentiment (Updates close, adds economic advisor's comments, NDF market movements)

By Swati Bhat

MUMBAI, June 11 (Reuters) - Suspected central bank intervention hauled the rupee off a record low struck on Tuesday afternoon, reassuring a market worried by the Reserve Bank of India's earlier inaction as the currency's fall gathered pace.

Striking 58.98 per dollar at its weakest, the rupee had plunged 3.25 percent this week, notching record lows for two consecutive days.

Dollar-selling by state banks, believed to be acting at the behest of the central bank, prevented a fall though the 59 per dollar level, though intermittent bouts of dollar selling by exporters had also slowed the fall.

The partially convertible rupee recovered to close at 58.39/40 per dollar, but it was still 0.4 percent weaker than Monday's close of 58.15/16.

"Finally the central bank stepped in. The selling was not huge, but enough to cause a rebound in the rupee," said a senior dealer with a state-run bank, who declined to be identified given the sensitivity of the matter.

Comments from senior government officials had offered little comfort to investors until stronger comments came on Tuesday, immediately following the talk of central bank intervention.

India's government, central bank and the securities markets regulator will take "warranted" action to stall a sharp fall in the rupee, the Finance Ministry's chief economic adviser Raghuram Rajan said on Tuesday.

He also added that oil companies had agreed to stagger dollar purchases as much as possible to reduce pressure on the rupee, which would mark an important move, considering these firms are the biggest domestic buyers of the greenback.

However, the market continues to remain jittery.

"The rupee has rebounded today, but the market continues to remain nervous," said Vikas Babu Chittiprolu, a senior foreign exchange dealer with state-run Andhra Bank.

"There is not much exporter selling even now. I expect 57.70 to 59.30 range for the rest of the week," he added.

Analysts believe pressure on the currency had intensified after comments on the limitations of currency intervention by Reserve Bank of India Governor Duvvuri Subbarao on Friday.

Subbarao said a failed defence of rupee can be worse than no defence, and reiterated that the central bank intervenes in the market only to manage volatility.

"Fundamentally, INR will continue to depreciate because of CAD (current account deficit), but this move has happened too soon and too fast," said Samir Lodha, managing director at QuantArt Market Solutions.

Analysts noted that while foreign institutional investors (FIIS) were still net buyers of debt and equity so far in 2013, the risk that they could turn sellers could force the central bank to intervene to at least moderate the volatility.

"Technically, the rupee has made a short term low of 58.98 levels, from these levels, we expect a correction till 57.50-57.25 levels but the overall view still remains bearish," said Abhishek Goenka, chief executive at India Forex Advisors.

The weakness in the rupee has prompted investors to exit their positions in the debt market while the domestic equity market is also under selling pressure.

The rupee has dropped in 16 of the last 18 trading sessions and is down 7.9 percent since the start of May. The currency has been the worst performer in Asia since the start of May.

The fall in the spot rupee was also exacerbated by the large long dollar positions being built in the offshore non-deliverable forwards market, traders said. Indian rupee NDFs were pricing the rupee at 61.89 in a year's time, 5.7 percent weaker than the spot rate of 58.39.

"Any respite for the INR from some possible bunched up FII debt and FDI inflows this month will be temporary," said Rajeev Malik, senior economist at CLSA in Singapore.

"Barring volatility, the INR will eventually weaken to cross 60/USD in a sustained manner. Admittedly, this is playing out sooner than we expected because of the earlier change in the global backdrop," he added. (Reporting by Swati Bhat; Editing by Tony Munroe/Simon Cameron-Moore)

title: India Central Bank  Seen  Intervening  to Help Rupee
text:
MUMBAI--India's central bank likely sold U.S. dollars in the foreign exchange market Tuesday, creating a temporary respite for the battered rupee currency after it plumbed to new lows for the second straight day.

Deep concerns over India's economic direction, however, mean the currency is likely to remain under pressure, traders said.

Dealers said the Reserve Bank of India appeared to sell dollars to stop the U.S. currency breaching 59 rupees. The bank doesn't comment on intervention but large orders put through state banks--as seen Tuesday--typically point toward central bank activity, dealers said.

The action brought some relief to the rupee, which is one of the worst-performing emerging market currencies this year due to concerns about India's slowing economy and large current account deficit.

After trading just short of 59 per rupee, the U.S. dollar retreated to 58.40 on Tuesday afternoon following the suspected intervention. It was still trading higher than 58.15 late Monday and off 8% against the dollar since early May.

Analysts say central bank action may slow the rupee's decline but it is unlikely to change the currency's fortunes.

"They've done well to intervene," said Marc Ostwald, a foreign exchange strategist at Monument Securities Ltd., a brokerage in London. "Does it turn around the rupee? Definitely not."

Investors are worried about India's large current account deficit, which was equal to 6.7% of gross domestic product in the final quarter of 2012. India's exports have stagnated amid weak global demand, while imports of gold and oil have remained high, widening the deficit.

The government relies on foreign investment flows to bridge the gap. But foreign investors have pulled out $2.5 billion since late May. That compares with inflows of $4.49 billion for the first five months of 2013.

In part, the outflows reflect a selloff across emerging markets as investors move more money into dollar-denominated assets. But India's currency has underperformed others in Asia, signaling investor frustration with the country's failure to follow through on promises to allow more foreign investment in its ailing economy.

On Tuesday, Raghuram Rajan, the government's chief economic adviser, said he believed the slump in the currency had outweighed the economy's fundamentals.

Mr. Rajan said recent efforts the government has taken to reduce demand for gold imports, which include raising import taxes on gold, are starting to bear fruit.

"With the steps which the government has taken we will see a significant drop in gold imports in June," he said.

These steps fall short of economic overhauls that could unleash a wave of foreign investment in sectors ranging from retail to insurance, analysts say.

Radhika Rao, an economist at DBS Group in Singapore, said in a note that while broad dollar strength has triggered the rupee's fall to record lows, "the domestic negative macroeconomic backdrop serves to hasten the bear-run." The weak currency is dampening expectations the central bank will cut rates when it meets June 17. Businesses have been calling for a sharp cut to give a boost to economic growth, which has slowed to 5%, much below annual rates of 9% a few years ago.

Inflation also has moderated recently, raising hopes of a rate cut. The next set of inflation data, due Friday, is expected to show that wholesale prices, the benchmark in India, remained below 5% in May.

That would have made a stronger case for rate cuts. But the rupee's slump has raised the specter of higher inflation down the road as imports become more costly.

"We were expecting a rate cut in May," said Deepak Panjwani, head of fixed income at GEPL Securities, a Mumbai-based brokerage. "But given what's happening with the rupee, a rate cut looks difficult."

title: Selloff in Emerging Market  Currencies  Accelerates as US Treasury Yields Rise
text:
--Emerging market currencies plunge as selloff accelerates

--Yen rises sharply as demand for perceived safe-haven currencies soars

--South African rand at fresh four-year low against dollar

--India's central bank suspected of intervention after rupee falls to record low

--Turkish lira bucks the trend as central bank sells dollars at three separate auctions


 
   By Clare Connaghan 
 

Emerging-market currencies came under intense selling pressure Tuesday, with the Indian rupee slumping to a fresh record low and the South African rand falling to a new four-year low against the dollar, as fresh expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve will unwind its monetary stimulus in the coming months pushed up U.S. Treasury yields.

The rand once again felt the brunt of the selloff, losing more than 1% in European trading hours, as the dollar rose to as high as ZAR10.3610 at one point, marking the South African currency's weakest level since mid-March 2009. The Mexican peso also felt the pain, slumping to its weakest level this year, as a jump in U.S. 10-year Treasury yields to a 14-month high drove traders and investors away from emerging-market currencies.

"The widening in U.S. Treasury yields has triggered a sharp repricing among emerging market assets," said Societe Generale in a note to clients.

The drop in Treasury bond prices lacked a clear immediate trigger. But upbeat labor-market data Friday, the move by ratings firm Standard & Poor's to upgrade its outlook on the U.S. Monday, combined with a fresh reminder by Fed official James Bullard that the central bank is watching economic data carefully to pick its time to change policy, all contributed to the decline. In addition, $66 billion of new Treasury bonds are due to hit the market this week. Typically, investors sell older bonds to make space for new debt.

The plunge in emerging market currencies Tuesday is nothing new as these markets have experienced bouts of heavy selling pressure ever since U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke and minutes from a recent Fed policy meeting in May suggested the Fed might start pulling back on its bond purchases some time this year. That made investors fear that the tide of money flowing into emerging markets might soon diminish.

The selloff has been so severe in some currencies that it has prompted action from authorities, with Brazil and Poland's central bank both intervening in the past week to support their currencies. India's central bank is suspected of joining that club Tuesday, with local dealers reporting the bank sold U.S. dollars in the foreign-exchange market to support the battered rupee, after the dollar pushed as high as INR58.98.

Only the Turkish lira managed to buck the overall trend, stabilizing after an early dive, but only because the central bank warned it would start additional short-term monetary tightening if needed to stabilize the currency. As protests in the country continued Tuesday, the lira fell to TRY1.9098, its weakest level against the buck since December 2011. However, the currency rebounded when the central bank made its announcement and then subsequently conducted three separate dollar sales of $50 million each.

Outside emerging markets, the dollar's performance was mixed against other major currencies, rising sharply against the commodity currencies of Australia, New Zealand and Canada, while falling against the euro.

The Australian dollar fell below $0.9350 against the greenback for the first time since September 2010, while the New Zealand dollar slumped to a one-year low against the buck.

Like emerging market currencies, the so-called commodity-bloc has come under pressure because of concerns the Fed will reel in its bond purchases, while the slowdown in China has also weighed on sentiment. Also, there's less liquidity in these currencies, so when investors "rush for the exits, the move is more pronounced," said Daragh Maher, a currencies strategist at HSBC in London.

The yen and Swiss franc were the other big movers in Tuesday's trading session as demand for perceived safe-haven currencies rose. Disappointment from the lack of extra action by the Bank of Japan overnight also contributed to the move, participants said.

"For the market, we're in a situation where we need something new to feed this yen bear market and when you don't get it and you've got a market positioned for yen weakness, you get pullback's like this," said Mr. Maher.

Meanwhile, news is awaited from the German Constitutional Court hearing in Karlsruhe, which is expected to rule on a complaint about the European Central Bank's as-yet unused outright monetary transaction bond-buying program. They will also keep a close eye on the U.S. Treasury yields.

At 1153 GMT, the euro was trading at $1.3283 against the dollar, compared with $1.3258, late Monday in New York, according to trading system EBS. The dollar was at Y96.98 against the yen, compared with Y98.76, while the euro was at Y128.845, compared with Y130.92. The pound was trading at $1.5546 against the dollar, compared with $1.5570 late Monday in New York.

title: DJ Stocks, Dollar Slump Amid Fed Worries
text:
U.S. stocks fell and the dollar slumped, extending a bout of market turmoil as investors puzzled out the implications of a possible tightening of central-bank easy-money policies.

The sharp moves appeared to be a resumption of the volatility seen overnight as investors fretted that the U.S. Federal Reserve would soon move to cut back on the money it's been pumping into the economy.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 79 points to 15160.30, while the dollar traded down 2.7% at 96.12 yen, on track for one of its biggest percentage declines in the last three years. Treasurys, which had slumped earlier Tuesday, pushed higher as investors shed riskier assets.

The afternoon selling marked the second reversal for financial markets on Tuesday. Earlier, stocks, bonds and currencies from the Philippines to Spain to the U.S. came under pressure. A selloff in government-bond markets across Europe led to higher yields from Greece to Germany.

Financial markets had stabilized during New York trading hours, but turned south again in the afternoon, underscoring how a lack of clarity about the Fed's thinking has made markets more volatile.

"People are less certain today than they have been in the last two years," said Peter Gorra, head of G10 currency trading at BNP Paribas in New York. "They're looking over the edge and they're not sure what's on the other side."

Traders pinned the blame for the market's ups and downs on sensitivity to signals from central bankers, in particular the Bank of Japan and the Federal Reserve.

In the U.S., investors have been rattled by Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke's suggestion last month that the central bank is considering a move to wind down its bond purchases.

While officials have tried to send signals in recent weeks that any changes will be gradual, traders are increasingly convinced the U.S. central bank's next move will be to begin tapering the pace of its bond buying program, removing a key source of support for asset prices even as concerns about a slowdown in global growth are mounting.

"The recent uptick in volatility across financial markets looks increasingly as if it might be to do with a growing loss of confidence in Western central bankers' great monetary policy experiment," said Jeremy Batstone-Carr at Charles Stanley.

The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note, which rises as bond prices fall, rose as high as 2.291% earlier in the session-the highest level in more than a year, according to Tradeweb. Treasurys later rebounded, pulling the yield back to 2.195%.

Meantime, in Japan, investors looking to see whether the BOJ would ramp up its asset-buying program were disappointed after the central bank refrained from introducing new measures<http://online.wsj.com/article/SB10001424127887324634304578538661580938482.html("http://online.wsj.com/article/SB10001424127887324634304578538661580938482.html")>, citing signs of economic recovery.

Stocks saw their steepest declines in Asia, with shares off 4.6% in the Philippines-the biggest drop since September 2011-and 3.1% in Indonesia. European and Japanese stocks also traded lower. Japan's Nikkei Stock Average fell 1.5%, after rallying 4.9% in the previous session.

Emerging-markets currencies from Brazil's real to South Africa's rand also gained ground after being hammered earlier in the day along with global stock markets. Both currencies had hit four-year lows earlier.

The Indian rupee traded at a record low as the dollar strengthened to nearly 59 rupees before the Reserve Bank of Indiaintervened, while central banks in Brazil and Turkey also stepped into the market to stabilize their exchange rates. The Australian dollar, another high-yielding currency that has fallen sharply in recent weeks, dropped as low at US$0.9325, its weakest level since September 2010.

The yield on Greece's 10-year benchmark government bond rose 0.90 percentage point to 10.35% Tuesday, hitting its highest level since early May, according to Tradeweb. The yield on the corresponding Portuguese government bond surged 0.34 percentage point to 6.52%, a two-month peak. Italian and Spanish bond yields also rose. Haven German Bund yields climbed, albeit more modestly than their lower-rated euro-zone peers.

Market watchers said they expect the volatility to continue until the Fed lays out how and when it will end its stimulus. The Fed next meets on June 18 and 19.

"Whether it's six months down the line or 12 months down the line, it's going to be tapering," said Geoffrey Yu, chief currency strategist at UBS. "Once that happens, we're going to find a base in different asset classes."

title: DJ UPDATE: Indian Rupee Hits Fresh Low Against the Dollar
text:
MUMBAI--India's currency hit a fresh record low against the dollar Tuesday on rising concerns over a widening trade imbalance and the pace of promised economic steps.

The rupee was trading at 58.85 rupees to the U.S. dollar compared with 58.15 rupees in late Asian trade Monday, its previous lowest level.

Asian currencies broadly have been declining as investors move money into U.S. assets. The dollar is in favor following a string of better-than-expected U.S. economic data over the past few weeks. On Monday, Standard & Poor's revised its U.S. credit outlook to stable from negative.

But the rupee is among the most battered regional currencies due to concerns over its current-account gap. Oil and gold imports contributed to a deficit equal to 6.7% of gross domestic product in the final quarter of 2012.

Radhika Rao, an economist at DBS Group in Singapore, said in a note that while broad dollar strength has triggered the rupee's fall to record lows, "the domestic negative macroeconomic backdrop serves to hasten the bear-run."

Ms. Rao said she doesn't expect the Reserve Bank of India -- the central bank - to intervene in the currency market in a large way but it may sell dollars in an attempt to reduce volatility.

While a rise in the dollar has hurt the rupee, emerging-market investors attributed the broader weakness in the Indian rupee to the country's ballooning current-account deficit. They say the deficit has become emblematic of the troubles in Asia's second-largest economy, which is suffering from slowing growth and high inflation. India's exports remain sluggish because global demand is weak, while a run-up in gold purchases is keeping imports elevated.

India for months has relied on inflows from foreign investment funds to bridge this gap and stabilize its markets.

That support is ebbing, however, as some money managers lose patience with a government that they say has been slow to implement new rules aimed at attracting foreign investment and spurring growth.

"India's fundamentals aren't robust," says David Robbins, a managing director with TCW Group Inc. who oversees the fund manager's $7.4 billion emerging-markets portfolio. "Clearly, the government has to do more."

Foreign investors have pulled $1.59 billion from India's bond market this month, according to the Securities and Exchange Board of India. That compares with inflows of $4.49 billion for the first five months of 2013.

The downward pressure on Indian assets has been exacerbated by the recent selloff across emerging markets.

But the rupee has underperformed other Asian currencies, which some investors say underscores the greater challenges facing India. The rupee has weakened 7.5% against the dollar since the start of May. Over the same period, the Thai baht has dropped 5.1% and the Philippine peso is down 4%.

The experience of IKEA shows India's bumpy road to reform. In 2012, India amended its laws to allow foreign retailers to have 100% ownership of their stores. But government agencies delayed the approval of the Swedish furniture retailer's $1.95 billion investment plan, which was approved in May, nearly 10 months after it was submitted.

Indian officials also pledged to raise fuel prices, which are heavily regulated, to reduce government spending on subsidies and to encourage drivers to cut consumption. But fuel prices remain well below prices on the world market, and the cost of oil imports remains high. This continues to cause a drag on the current account, which hit a record deficit of $32.6 billion in the three months ended Dec. 31, 2012.

"Given the situation, we expect the rupee to remain under pressure, at least for the next three months," said Mahendra Kumar Jajoo, chief investment officer at Pramerica Asset Managers Pvt. Ltd., which oversees about $447 million of assets.

To be sure, some investors say India's economy will gain from the government's efforts, even if progress has been uneven so far.

"India has been taking the right steps in the right direction," says Teresa Kong, portfolio manager of the $68 million Matthews Asia Strategic Income Fund. She has been buying the rupee recently, and is looking to add exposure after Monday's sharp fall. "It's not clear to me that India is worse off today than it was six months ago or a year ago." She adds that the fall in world oil prices since the start of the year could translate into a positive surprise, in terms of a narrowing of the current-account deficit, later this year.

As well, some Indians based in the Middle East are capitalizing on the rupee's fall by bringing money back to India, said N.S. Venkatesh, the head of treasury at state-run IDBI Bank Ltd.

The selling of dollars could lift the rupee in the near term.

title: DJ  Indian Rupee Sinks to Fresh All-Time Low
text:
MUMBAI--The Indian rupee sank to a fresh all-time low against the dollar Monday, hurt by broad strength in the U.S. currency.

Investors rushed to the dollar after the world's largest economy reported better-than-expected economic data, triggering fears that the U.S. Federal Reserve could taper its monetary stimulus sooner than expected.

U.S. employers added 175,000 jobs in May, topping economists' expectations slightly.

The rupee's previous all-time low was 57.33, recorded on June 22, 2012.

It has depreciated 7% against the dollar since the start of May, in line with a decline in many Asian and international currencies as investors shift positions to reflect a stronger dollar and an increase in U.S. Treasury rates.

Concerns over India's gaping current-account deficit also weakened the rupee, accelerating its decline.

"The rupee, of late, has been hit more than other currencies," said Pradeep Khanna, managing director and head of FX trading at the Indian unit of HSBC PLC in Mumbai.

"Foreign institutional investors in India have been pulling out money, mainly from the debt market."

As the market is still volatile, currency dealers are watchful for any Reserve Bank of Indiaintervention, Mr. Khanna said.

India's central bank neither confirms or denies its presence in the market. It has a stated policy of stepping into currency markets only to ease volatility. It doesn't defend a specific exchange rate.

title: UPDATE 1-Indian rupee recovers from near 1-yr low; cbank watched
text:
* Rupee ends at 56.84/85 per dlr vs 56.7250/7350 on Wed

* Some stability seen as chances of cbank intervention rise

* Rupee seen trading in 56.70-57.10 range on Friday-traders

By Swati Bhat

MUMBAI, June 6 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee recovered after touching the key psychological level of 57 to the dollar on Thursday, helped by dollar selling by some foreign and custodian banks, but sentiment remains cautious ahead of key U.S. data on Friday.

The initial fall pushed the rupee frighteningly close to a record low hit nearly a year earlier as fears of an end to the U.S. Federal Reserve's monetary stimulus sent the dollar higher.

Recent U.S. economic data has been mixed, which has left investors caught between fears the Fed will reduce its stimulus and worries the U.S. economy is still weak.

"The U.S. data has been weak past few times and if that continues tomorrow, expectations of Fed withdrawing the stimulus will be hampered," said Pramod Patil, assistant vice-president, forex and money markets, at United Overseas Bank.

The rupee is not far off the record low of 57.32 hit in late June last year, raising the prospect of a potential intervention from the Reserve Bank of India, although most analysts do not expect bold actions given that the rupee weakness is tracking global factors.

Still, further falls are bound to revive concerns about funding India's current account deficit. The government on Wednesday increased import duty on gold, and the finance ministry is looking at raising the cap on foreign investment in sovereign debt.

"The psychological level of 57 has been hit and thus it invites fears of some intervention. The market is a bit cautious at these levels," said Paresh Nayar, head of fixed income and foreign exchange trading at First Rand Bank.

The partially convertible rupee closed at 56.84/85 per dollar, after earlier touching 57, its weakest since June 28, 2012. The rupee had closed at 56.7250/7350 on Wednesday.

Domestic shares fell on worries about the Fed stimulus programme, tracking Asian indexes that slipped to new 2013 lows. The benchmark BSE index closed down 0.25 percent.

Traders also cited heavy dollar demand from oil refiners, the largest buyers of the greenback in the domestic currency market in early trade but dollar selling by foreign and custodian banks helped the unit recover.

Comments from a senior government official hurt the rupee as well. Propping up the rupee "artificially" is not the right thing to do, said Montek Singh Ahluwalia, the deputy chairman of the country's Planning Commision.

The rupee is expected to hold in a 56.70-57.10 range until the U.S. non-farm payroll data, traders said. The data is due after India market close on Friday and the reaction would be seen on Monday.

Domestically, investors are expected to focus on inflation, trade, and industrial output data, all of which are expected ahead of the Reserve Bank of India's policy review on June 17.

Expectations that the central bank would cut interest rates a fourth time this year have been recently dashed after Governor Duvvuri Subbarao expressed concern over retail inflation and the current account deficit.

In the offshore non-deliverable forwards, the one-month contract was at 57.20, while the three-month was at 57.78.

In the currency futures market, the most-traded near-month dollar/rupee contracts on the National Stock Exchange, the MCX-SX and the United Stock Exchange all closed around 56.99 with a total traded volume of $5.3 billion. (Editing by Prateek Chatterjee and Jijo Jacob)

By Romit Guha

NEW DELHI--India's central bank is concerned about the country's wide current-account deficit and still-high retail inflation, Governor Duvvuri Subbarao said Thursday, damping hopes that it would continue to lower interest rates to support economic growth.

The local currency hit a 10-month low and bond prices fell to its lowest in two weeks as the markets were expecting the Reserve Bank of India would cut its policy lending rate at its June 17 meeting to help boost economic growth that has slowed to its weakest pace in a decade.

Mr. Subbarao, while speaking at an event in the western Indian city of Ahmedabad, said the RBI will factor in the current-account gap while formulating its monetary policy. He said the wide deficit is weakening the local currency and may fan inflation that has slowed in recent months.

The bank is concerned about the size of the deficit as well as the way India funds it, he said.

India's current-account deficit is estimated to be around 5% of gross domestic product in the last fiscal year ended March 31, compared with the previous year's 4.2%. The gap widened to a record 6.7% of GDP in the October-December quarter, the latest period for which the number is available.

The big deficit underscores the impact of the weak global markets on India's exports of goods and services. India's imports, especially of oil and gold, remain high. The country funds much of the deficit with foreign investments in its stock and bond markets, which authorities and analysts say could become tricky as these investments are usually short term.

"The result of the high current-account deficit has been the depreciation of the rupee," he said. "Rupee depreciation is a problem because it pushes up the cost of our imports, it increases debt servicing, it causes inflation and it erodes our external payment situation," he added.

Thursday, the Indian rupee fell to 56.38 to a dollar, a level not seen since July 25. The local currency is hit by concerns that the U.S. may reduce its bond-purchase program, which has emerged as a key source of funds for investments in emerging markets such as India.

Mr. Subbarao said India's retail inflation is still a concern. Sacrificing growth in the short term is "inevitable" as the RBI strives to rein in inflation, he added.

Consumer inflation slowed to 9.39% in April from 10.39% a month earlier, but is still high. However, the wholesale-price inflation, the main gauge of inflation in India, eased in April to below 5%, a level the central bank says it is comfortable with.

The RBI cut its key lending rate thrice this year, all by a quarter of a percentage point, and markets were hoping it to further reduce the rate at its next policy meeting.

The yield on the benchmark 8.15% bond due in 2022 rose to 7.45% in late trade, a two-week high, before closing at 7.44%, compared with 7.39% on Wednesday.

  By Sudeep Jain and Khushita Vasant 
 

MUMBAI--India's central bank is ready to intervene in the currency markets to check any sharp fall in the rupee, apart from its stated position of getting into the market to reduce exchange rate volatility, a top official said Monday.

Any steep currency fall has a tendency to fuel expectations of further depreciation, Reserve Bank of India Deputy Governor Subir Gokarn said at a conference on capital flows.

"Therefore, the intervention policy not only aims at quelling the excessive volatility, but also attempts to moderate speculative one-way downward movement of the India rupee," according to a presentation he made at the conference.

The rupee has fallen nearly 3% against the U.S. dollar over the past one month as global risk aversion has increased due to concerns over the approaching U.S. fiscal cliff.

The RBI doesn't say whether it intervened in the currency markets and publishes data on its foreign-exchange transactions with a lag of more than a month.

Mr. Gokarn said the drivers of currency volatility become more dominant if the current account deficit is high, as is the case with India.

The country's current account deficit, as a proportion of gross domestic product, slipped to 3.9% in the April-June period from 4.5% in the January-March quarter. But it still remains outside the central bank's comfort zone of 2%-3%.

Mr. Gokarn said that addressing domestic drivers of currency dynamics is key to exchange rate stability.

By Sudeep Jain

MUMBAI--India's foreign-exchange reserves fell sharply in the week to July 6, central bank data showed Friday, magnifying concerns over the sufficiency of the reserves amid the recent fall in the Indian rupee.

Foreign-exchange reserves fell by $2.37 billion to $287.62 billion in the week ended July 6, mainly due to a $2.3 billion drop in foreign-currency assets, the Reserve Bank of India said in a press statement.

But, direct central bank intervention in the currency market may not have been the cause for the fall in reserves, said analysts.

The RBI may have supplied foreign currency to state-owned oil refiners to pay for crude-oil imports, said Moses Harding, senior vice president at IndusInd Bank.

Last month, oil importers said the central bank had asked them to route half their dollar purchases through a single state-run bank.

This was seen as a move that would allow the central bank to supply dollars to oil companies when required and isolate a key source of dollar demand from the broad market to reduce the pressure on the Indian rupee.

The rupee hit a record low of 57.22 to the dollar on June 22 as investors fled risk-sensitive assets amid the deepening sovereign debt crisis in the euro zone.

The local currency has borne the brunt of global risk aversion due to concerns over India's large current-account and fiscal deficits and the government's failure to boost investment. The dollar was quoted at 55.14 rupees late Friday in Asia.

The dollar's recent rally against major currencies due to rising concerns over global growth may have also reduced the value of the non-dollar assets in India's reserves, Mr. Harding said.

The RBI doesn't provide any reasons for the changes in foreign-currency assets. It also doesn't say whether it intervened in the currency market.

India's precarious external position is seen as a key risk for the economy, which is facing the combination of a sharp slowdown and high inflation.

The current-account deficit widened to 4.2% of gross domestic product in the fiscal year that ended March 31, after remaining below 3% since 1991, as exports slowed while imports remained high.

India's dwindling foreign-exchange reserves are a concern because, unlike most emerging economies, the country imports much more than it exports.

(Adds analyst's comment in 10th-11th paragraphs, background)


 
   By Sudeep Jain 
 

MUMBAI--India's central bank intervened heavily in May to support the local currency -- mainly through forward contracts rather than selling dollars in the spot market, central bank data showed Tuesday.

The Reserve Bank of India's choice to intervene more in the forwards market may have been prompted by concerns that selling dollars and buying rupees on the spot would exacerbate the local currency's shortage in the domestic banking system, said analysts.

The RBI sold a net $485 million of foreign exchange from its reserves in May, compared with $275 million in April. But, the net value of outstanding forward contracts to sell foreign currency at a future date rose to $10.31 billion in May from $3.45 billion in April.

The latest RBI data covers the period when the Indian rupee lost almost 7% against the dollar as risk aversion emanating from Europe's sovereign debt crisis magnified concerns over India's high fiscal and current account deficits and the government's failure to boost investment.

The dollar, which it a record high of 57.33 rupees on June 22, was quoted at 55.39 rupees late Tuesday in Asia.

The RBI doesn't say whether it intervened in the foreign-exchange market and has a stated policy of intervening only to curb volatility.

The central bank intervened heavily on the spot market in November and December, selling more than $15 billion over the two months to protect the rupee.

In recent months, however, its spot interventions have become muted, while intervention in the forwards market has picked up since March.

India's banking system until recently has been facing an acute shortage of cash, partly as a result of currency-market intervention, say analysts.

Given that liquidity conditions are tight, forwards intervention is the better approach since it is as effective as spot intervention, he added.

"The dollar-rupee should trade in a narrow range next week, with intervention at higher levels and good amount of buying at lower levels," said Ashtosh Raina, head of forex trading at HDFC Bank, in comments made before the data.

By Subhadip Sircar

MUMBAI, June 22 (Reuters) - India's benchmark federal bond yield ended marginally higher on Friday because of profit-taking, but hopes of a sustained fall in global crude oil prices and more central bank bond purchases are likely to keep debt prices supported.

The slump in oil prices is helping ease some of the concerns about inflationary pressures that were cited by the Reserve Bank of India as the main reason for keeping interest rates on hold on Monday, a decision that stunned markets.

Though yields initially surged after the decision, benchmark 10-year yields have closed up only up 1 basis point for the week, helped as well by expectations the RBI will step up bond purchases via open market operations.

The spike in global risk aversion has sent the rupee

to a record low against the dollar for a second consecutive session on Friday.

That has forced the RBI to intervene in foreign exchange markets, and is thus raising expectations of more OMOs to offset the impact on rupee liquidity.

"Signals of weak global demand is pushing down crude, and in turn reining in inflation expectations in India, supporting bonds," said Harish Agarwal, a dealer with First Rand Bank in Mumbai.

"Hopes of continuation of OMOs is also helping sentiment."

India's 10-year benchmark bond yield rose 1 bp to 8.35 percent on Friday. Total volumes on the central bank's electronic trading platform were at a high 221.20 billion rupees.

The yield on the new 8.15 percent 2022 paper ended at 8.08 percent, up 3 basis points.

Though the gains for the week were mild, the RBI decision snapped seven consecutive weeks of falling yields, and have put into doubt potential near-term rate cuts, especially after Governor Duvvuri Subbarao followed up with hawkish comments on inflation.

The 1-year overnight indexed swap surged 18 basis points for the week, after falling 3 basis points to 7.75 percent on Friday.

The longer-end 5-year rate dropped 5 bps to 7.19 percent, ending up 3 bps for the week.

Analysts don't expect a rally in bond prices, but at least they expect yields to be capped should the RBI continue to buy bonds via OMOs or in secondary markets.

The RBI bought 112.88 billion rupees in government bonds via open market operations on Friday, lower than the notified 120 billion rupees.

A Reuters poll this week showed traders expect 1 trillion rupees in additional OMOs for the rest of the fiscal year ending in March 2013, both to counter FX interventions and to inject enough liquidity to allow the government to sell a record 5.3 trillion rupees in bonds.

The government sold 150 billion rupees of debt in session, including 70 billion rupees of the most traded 9.15 percent 2024 bond at bullish cutoffs.

The rupee slid despite suspected intervention by the central bank. Traders said the Reserve Bank of India carried out soft intervention, or selling smaller dollar amounts, through the day.

Strategists say the rupee will be a troubled currency for some more time.

Westpac strategist Jonathan Cavenagh said in a note that the rupee hasn't been able to find much support despite improved risk appetite in recent days, even though the broader backdrop for Asian currencies has been reasonably supportive.

India's poor domestic situation--fiscal and current-account deficits, and sluggishness on reforms--coupled with poor news from ratings firms continue to outweigh any broader improvement in risk appetite, he said.

The RBI's decision to keep interest rates unchanged hasn't helped either.

"We still feel dollar-rupee will have a meaningful correction lower at some stage but it's likely we need to see more action on the domestic policy front before this transpires," Mr. Cavenagh said.

In the sovereign-debt market, bonds finished higher as global oil prices declined significantly.

The new benchmark 8.15% 2022 bond finished at INR100.64, compared with INR100.25 at Wednesday's close. The 8.79% 2021 note was at INR102.85 compared with INR102.56.

Lower oil prices are positive for an import-dependent country like India. Further, it translates into softer inflation and lends more room for interest rate cuts.

title: UPDATE: JP Morgan Economist Says  India Central Bank  Should Relook  FX Intervention  Strategy
text:
-- Rupee's 15% depreciation since March equals to monetary easing, says economist

-- More interest rate cuts will hurt rupee

-- Govt should raise foreign investment cap in local bonds, cut withholding tax

By Khushita Vasant

MUMBAI--India's central bank needs to have another look at the way in which it intervenes in the currency markets because its recent dollar sales haven't been able to stop the rupee's slide, a senior economist said Wednesday.

"Intervention is a legitimate instrument, but the Reserve Bank of India didn't do it the right way," Jahangir Aziz, J.P. Morgan senior Asia economist, told Dow Jones Newswires.

"The RBI could have intervened in a more strategic manner when the market was willing to accept it as a signal that the RBI is coming out and defending the currency."

The central bank is suspected of having intervened heavily in recent weeks, but the rupee slumped to a series of record lows, with its worst being 56.51 against the U.S. dollar on May 31.

Other corrective policy steps didn't help much either.

The frequent dollar sales have been eating into India's foreign exchange reserves, which fell for a fourth consecutive week to $288.26 billion as at May 25. This is a sharp decline from $306.775 billion in early December.

While the reserves are at a relatively comfortable level for now, it would be a cause for concern if the RBI keeps up the intervention pace over the next few months, said Mr. Aziz, a former top adviser to India's finance ministry.

He believes the RBI shouldn't cut interest rates at this point. The rupee's depreciation of 15% since March and subsequent weakening against trading partner countries has made exports competitive. "That, in itself, is effectively equivalent to about 100-150 basis points of monetary easing."

Further rate cuts at a time when the rupee has been declining, when capital inflows are fairly sluggish and there is uncertainty overseas ahead of polls in Greece will only hurt the currency more.

The clamour for rate cuts has grown shriller in the past week after India reported a 5.3% gross domestic product growth for the January-March quarter -- the slowest pace in nearly 10 years.

Mr. Aziz said also that the government should raise the ceiling on foreign investments in local bonds to $50 billion from $15 billion. It could slash the withholding tax on bonds for investors to encourage participation from overseas investors.

Mr. Aziz thinks the greenback's rally is overshot, and it may correct 5%-6% in the near-term.

Whether the Reserve Bank of Indiaintervened generated split views among traders, and any dollars sales were likely to have been mild, they added.

title: MARKET EYE FOCUS-Indian CD rates to rise on liquidity squeeze
text:
MUMBAI, May 29 (Reuters) - Short-term borrowing rates in India are expected to rise further in the next few weeks as companies pay advance taxes, exacerbating a severe cash shortage in the financial system.

 Rates on 3-month certificates of deposit were at 9.70 percent on May 28, h igher than any of the first quarters in at least the previous three years, while borrowing rates for three-month commercial paper surged to 10.23 percent.  

 Bankers expect 3-month CDs to go as high as 10.25 percent in June and the one-year CD as much as 10.30 percent.

 Unlike years past, cash conditions have not improved significantly in April and May, as government spending that usually kicks in at the start of a new financial year has failed to have the usual impact given the structural deficit in liquidity in India's inter-bank system, analysts said.

 Traders are now bracing for worse liquidity conditions as companies are expected to pay as much as 300 billion rupees ($5.41 billion)in advance taxes starting in mid-June.

 That's especially the case given the Reserve Bank of India has been intervening frequently in currency markets, though it has offset some of the impact on rupee liquidity by purchasing bonds via open market operations.

 "Inter-bank liquidity is seen tightening more in June because of further forex interventions, keeping an upward pressure on short-term CD rates," said N.S. Venkatesh, treasurer at IDBI Bank. 

 The severe cash shortage in the banking system is clearly shown by banks' repo borrowings, which has averaged about 1 trillion rupees a day in the current quarter, well above the 650 billion rupees levels the central bank considers normal.

 The RBI's bond purchases via OMOs as well as in secondary markets has also not been big enough to offset this liquidity deficit.

 The RBI has bought 320.87 billion rupees via OMOs over the previous three weeks, and traders are waiting to see whether it will announce a fourth consecutive action this week.

 Apart from fresh borrowing, banks are already refinancing existing CDs that mature towards the end of the quarter. 

 Dealers estimate that up to 1.4 trillion rupees of CDs will be rolled over by the end of June, mostly at the short-end, all of which is expected to further worsen liquidity.

 "Redemption and rollover pressure of CDs up to June, especially in three-month segment, will add to the pressure on short term rates," IDBIs Venkatesh said. ($1 = 55.4050 Indian rupees)

title: WSJ BLOG/India Real Time: Rupee's Likely Defender: Bond, India Bond
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's India Real Time Report blog at http://blogs.wsj.com/indiarealtime.)

By Shefali Anand

As the Indian rupee hovers near its lowest levels against the U.S. dollar, investors and analysts have been calling for a special bond sale to strengthen the currency.

On Monday, the local currency was up from its nadir, trading at 55.36 rupees to the dollar. Last week, it had hit an all-time low of 56.37 rupees.

The rupee's recent strength was partly because of some intervention by India's central bank on Friday.

But there are only so many rupees that the central bank can buy.

To get fresh money into India, some economists suggest issuing a special type of bond targeted toward Indians who live abroad. Such bonds have been issued only three times in India's history, and have been a huge success in the past.

In 1991, they were called "India Development Bonds" and they raised $1.6 billion. In 1998, so-called "Resurgent India Bonds" raised $4.2 billion, and in 2000, India Millennium Deposits raised $5.5.billion. The proceeds from these sales were primarily meant to boost India's foreign currency reserves and ultimately help India's balance of payments.

These were five-year bonds, issued in foreign currencies like the dollar or the British pound, and repaid in the foreign currency. So, the investor didn't have to worry about exchange rate risk. But it did ensure that the government got a lot of foreign money which it could hold for five years which added to India's foreign currency reserves. These bonds have historically been issued by India's largest bank, State Bank of India, which is majority-owned by the government and thus carried an implicit government guarantee.

Economists say such bonds could come in handy now, at a time when foreign investors are skeptical of putting fresh money into India. They would be attractive if the bonds pay a better interest rate than whatever the non-resident Indians can get in their own countries.

These NRI bonds "can provide some kind of chunky inflows," says Siddhartha Sanyal, India economist at Barclays Capital. "Eventually, our sense is that (RBI) would go for something like this."

But the size of such a bond issue would need to be much larger than the ones issued in the past, and its timing would have to be thought through.

"Will this be seen as a sign of a very, very difficult time for India?" says Sonal Varma, economist at Nomura in India. If so, the costs of issuing the bonds -- the interest rate the government pays on them -- could go up.

Another option to attract foreign capital quickly would be something that India has toyed with for a long time -- a sovereign bond issue. These would be bonds issued by the Indian government in dollars or another foreign currency, available to foreign investors and traded in foreign markets.

At the moment, only foreign investors who are registered in India can buy Indian government bonds and these are rupee-denominated and can be traded only in India. Also, there are restrictions on how much Indian government debt foreigners can buy.

"RBI is always worried that too much of external debt is not a good thing," says Samiran Chakraborty, head of research for South Asia at Standard Chartered Bank.

Mr. Chakraborty notes that a decision to issue sovereign bonds would ultimately have to come from the government. Also, this may not be the best time to issue such bonds because India's weakening economic growth could force it to pay a higher interest rate to attract global investors. India's credit rating is at risk of losing its standing as high quality, which makes it less attractive to foreign investors.

RBI Governor Duvvuri Subbarao said last week that a bond sale is not on the cards right now.

Even if these bond sales happen, economists say they would only be a temporary help. The only sure way to boost the rupee is to address the major concerns for its decline, which include a widening current account deficit and lack of large foreign capital inflows.

"For a more sustained reversal in the currency, you need Delhi to act as well," says Mr. Chakraborty.

text:
MUMBAI, May 24 (Reuters) - Indian overnight cash rates fell on Thursday as demand waned from banks which had already borrowed heavily over the last few sessions, traders said.

However, liquidity continues to stay tight given the lack of fresh debt redemptions or interest payments, which is likely to keep the cash rate above the repo rate of 8 percent in the near-term, say traders.

Expectations the Reserve Bank of India could step up its interventions in currency markets as the rupee continues to hit record lows are also expected to keep rupee liquidity tight.

The rupee has shed 12.7 percent against the dollar since its 2012 peak in early February and is the worst performer in Asia so far this year.

After intervening aggressively earlier this month, traders say the RBI has appeared to hold back in recent days, reluctant to fight the intense global risk aversion that is pushing up the dollar.

However, the central bank was seen selling dollars on Wednesday, and some saw signs of action on Thursday.

"There was a lot of selling from state-run banks as well today, which could probably have been on behalf of the RBI but custodian flows were also very good," a senior trader at a Japanese Bank said.

title: DJ 2nd UPDATE: India Not Looking At Direct Dollar Sales To Oil Firms - Official
text:
-- Comments likely to put more pressure on rupee

-- Oil companies account for 10% of dollar deals, with $2 billion-$3 billion weekly demand

-- Official says oil companies have enough money, and crude prices falling

(Rewrites throughout, adds finance ministry official's comments, updates currency level, adds context and background all through)

By Prasanta Sahu and Sudeep Jain

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--The Indian government Wednesday dampened market expectations that the central bank would sell dollars directly to oil importers at a fixed daily rate, with a senior finance ministry official saying there're no such plans to support the battered rupee.

The comment could hurt the rupee because oil importers -- which account for about one of every $10 transacted in the market -- are a significant reason for the recent surge in demand for the greenback.

Most analysts believe that the direct selling of the greenback to oil importers -- a mechanism referred to as a "dollar window" -- would isolate a key source of demand from the broader market.

This would ease pressure on the rupee as India's oil companies alone buy $2 billion-$3 billion of the greenback every week.

The finance ministry official's comments to reporters were out of sync with a statement earlier Wednesday by C. Rangarajan, chairman of the influential Prime Minister's Economic Advisory Council. Rangarajan had said that selling dollars directly to oil companies could be an option to limit the rupee's fall.

The Indian rupee has been in a furious downward spiral over the past week, with the dollar punching through key barriers every day to continue notching up all-time highs.

Since the middle of March, the local unit has fallen more than 10% and is now more than 22% lower than a year earlier. At 1108 GMT Wednesday, the dollar was trading at INR56.08 after touching a record high of INR56.22.

The central bank is believed to have been in the market heavily in recent days -- including on Wednesday -- but with little effect.

While a weak rupee helps India's exporters by making their products and services cheaper, it makes imports -- especially that of oil -- more expensive and drives up already high inflation.

The rupee's latest slide began after the federal budget in March shook investor confidence and led to a large outflow of cash.

The budget unveiled proposals which many believe are detrimental to foreign investor sentiment, including tax proposals giving authorities sweeping powers to examine deals they feel are structured solely to avoid taxes.

The pain is aggravated by India's yawning fiscal and current account deficits.

The rupee's fall picked up pace recently, with the dollar rising against most currencies in a flight to safety sparked by the possibility of Greece leaving the euro zone.

Asian markets and commodities fell across the region Wednesday after a former Greek prime minister said preparations for an exit from the euro zone are being considered.

The comments sent investors to the U.S. dollar in overnight trading, with the euro stabilizing in Asia at $1.2669.

The rush to the greenback symbolized a diminishing risk appetite, which has pushed down commodity prices as well.

Foreign exchange traders in India are refusing to stick their necks out and put a bottom to the rupee.

But they agree that a dollar window for oil companies would help.

"The impact would depend on how many dollars they [the RBI] provide, but it would be much more effective than direct intervention," said Vivek Rajpal, a strategist with Nomura India.

But the finance ministry official who said there are no plans for direct sales added that the oil companies have enough cash at the moment, and that global crude prices are falling anyway.

He said also that reforms on foreign direct investment in multi-brand retail and civil aviation are expected soon, which will bring in overseas funds and provide support to the rupee.

title: DJ Emerging-Market  Currencies  Suffer As Euro-zone Fears Build
text:
-- Forint, rupee, real among biggest fallers as safety of dollars sought

-- Intervention by emerging-market policy makers so far deemed inadequate

-- Market nerves likely to persist, sparking some speculation about a possible emerging-market crisis 


 
   By Laura Clarke 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

LONDON (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market currencies came under the cosh Wednesday as investors lost confidence in the ability of policy makers to resolve euro-zone tensions and support flagging growth, prompting a flight of capital out of less liquid markets and into the safety of the dollar.

The Indian rupee was a standout decliner as the dollar hit an all-time record high above INR56.20. The Korean won fell to a five-month low and the Brazilian real hit its worst level since May 2009 as worries about the ramifications of a possible Greek exit from the euro zone intensified, with Greek elections increasingly seen as a referendum on the issue due June 17.

In Europe, the Hungarian forint sank to its weakest level in about four months against even the unloved euro, which rose to as high as HUF303.35, almost 6% higher than it was at the start of the month. The Polish zloty also hit a four-month low against the dollar.

"This is now a massive global markets issue," said Societe Generale emerging-market analyst Benoit Anne, ahead of an informal gathering of European leaders to discuss measures to boost growth and reassure frazzled markets.

Emerging-market currencies typically are a sensitive barometer of broader market sentiment. They tend to fare better than major currencies when optimism is high but worse when markets are running scared as global investors cancel non-core bets, repatriate capital and seek out the safety of the dollar or yen.

Efforts by local central banks to staunch the sell-off have so far offered little relief. In the case of Brazil, the weaker real has also been welcomed as a boon to exporters even as the pace of depreciation has threatened to become disorderly, creating some policy confusion, while suspected intervention by India's central bank to defend the rupee has been inadequate and barely made a dent, analysts said.

"We are guaranteed more weeks of severe stress and interventions can't be patchy; authorities must show their teeth," Anne said.

Meanwhile, accusations the Hungarian government has been dragging its feet continued to dog the forint even as prospects improved Wednesday for a financing agreement between it, the European Union and International Monetary Fund.

"The forint is finally paying the price for the lack of clarity on financing. What level does the forint have to go to for the government to get really serious about cutting a deal with the IMF?" asked Timothy Ash, head of emerging-markets research at the Royal Bank of Scotland.

However, with the euro-zone crisis threatening to spill out of control and the global economy in a fragile state as Chinese growth slows and the U.S. recovery stutters, governments from emerging markets could be left powerless to contain further weakness in their currencies, according to some market observers.

As Stephen Jen of SLJ Macro Partners said Monday: "Though I'm unsure if this is indeed the beginning of an emerging-markets currency crisis, I think there is a high likelihood that such a crisis will take place...this year."

At 1506 GMT the Hungarian forint traded at HUF303.25 and HUF240.75 against the euro and dollar respectively. Against the dollar, the Indian rupee was at INR56.01, the Brazilian real was at BRL2.0915 and the Korean won was at 1,175.3.

title: UPDATE 3-Indian rupee skids to new low; more falls seen
text:
* Rupee hits record low; more falls seen ahead

* Policymakers lack of response seen worsening falls

* RBI hands seen tied; oil dollar sales would help

By Swati Bhat

MUMBAI, May 23 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee slumped to another record low against the dollar on Wednesday, ratcheting up pressure on policymakers to restore confidence in the currency at a time when appetite for risky assets is ebbing around the world.

After the markets closed, the government announced that it will allow state-run companies to raise gasoline prices, a measure that on its own will have negligible fiscal impact but that is at least seen as a signal that India could begin to look at fuel reform - a key concern for investors.

But without government action, analysts saw no near-term catalysts to revive the rupee, which on Wednesday fell beyond the symbolically significant level of 56 to hit a record low of 56.225 to the dollar.

Traders said it could weaken further to 57, extending a drop of more than 13 percent from its yearly peak in February.

"This step is just a flash in the pan and does not change the fiscal figures," said Indranil Pan, chief economist at Kotak Mahindra Bank.

"So I don't see any positive impact on rupee from this development. Only if diesel, LPG, kerosene prices are increased it will have implications on the fiscal figures,"

Global risk aversion due to the crisis in the euro zone has exposed India's vulnerabilities, most prominently a current account deficit that reached 4.3 percent of GDP in the December quarter. The economy depends on capital flows to bridge the gap.

Worries about the government's ability to fix its finances have also weighed heavily on the rupee, as investors worry the government will overshoot its deficit target of 5.1 percent of gross domestic product for the fiscal year ending in March 2013.

Easing the government's fuel subsidy burden has been seen as a key step, despite the potential inflationary impact.

Other factors that have made the rupee Asia's weakest-performing currency this year have included sluggish policy reforms and a recent controversial tax proposal on foreign investment.

"India is one of those odd cases where the bottom-up corporate environment is very strong, but it is challenged by poor politics and macroeconomic policies," said Pranay Gupta, Asia chief investment officer for Lombard Odier.

The political will to take tough steps to put Asia's third largest economy back on a firm growth path was lacking, he said.

'TIME TO PANIC'?

Wednesday marked the sixth consecutive session in which the rupee has hit a record low against the dollar. It recovered slightly to close the day at 55.9950/56.0050.

Non-deliverable forwards are pricing in more weakness, implying levels of 56.46 in a month's time and 57.25 in three months. Citing technical chart analysis, Standard Chartered said in a report on Tuesday the rupee could fall to as low as 58.62.

Given the absence of government measures, traders have focused on steps the Reserve Bank of India could take.

However, after intervening earlier this month, the central bank has turned cautious on selling dollars because global risk aversion is undermining most emerging market currencies.

Traders estimated the RBI sold $100-$250 million earlier on Wednesday in its first intervention in three sessions. But the amount was too small to stem the rupee's fall.

The central bank has taken several measures to try to stem the rupee's slide, including raising deposit rates for non-resident Indians and forcing exporters to convert half of their foreign currency holdings into rupees, but to no major effect.

The RBI could do more, such as selling dollars to state oil importers, which Nomura argues would reduce dollar demand in the currency market by $8.8 billion per month.

However, the central bank is seen mindful that its foreign reserves total nearly $292 billion, enough for roughly six months of imports, down from $320 billion in October.

Instead, analysts say that the best defense for the rupee rests with the Indian government, which they say needs to implement more confidence-boosting measures about its finances and stimulate investment.

"It is the time to press the panic button," said Rupa Rege Nitsure, chief economist at Bank of Baroda.

"The government has to do something right now to reverse investor sentiment, so that India can start attracting capital inflows," she added.

Morgan Stanley downgraded India's economic growth forecast for 2012 to 6.3 percent this week, below the levels of the Lehman crisis, citing the government's propensity for fiscal policies that support consumption at the expense of private investment.

At least for now, foreign investors have not yet staged an exodus from Indian markets. Though they sold a net $930 million in debt and stocks in April, th ey are slight buyers in May as of Tuesday and significant net buyers in the year to date.

The measures helped the rupee start trading higher Tuesday, but steady dollar buying by oil importers soon began to hurt.

This in turn hurts investor confidence and prompts outflows during times of global risk aversion, further denting the currency.

title: WSJ UPDATE: India's Rupee Freefall Hurts Stock Investors
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India's currency continued a freefall Tuesday, propelled to new lows over concerns about the country's economic outlook--a currency decline which is exacerbating losses for foreign investors in India's stock and bond markets.

The Indian rupee fell to a fresh record low Tuesday of 55.47 rupees for one U.S. dollar, making it one of the worst-performing currencies in Asia this year.

The rupee has lost around 12% against the U.S. dollar over the last three months and is 23% lower than a year ago due to a host of economic problems facing India, including high fiscal and current account deficits, slowing economic growth and government paralysis on business reforms. The rupee has fallen to fresh record lows in its past five trading sessions.

Indian stocks also have been losing value, leading to a double-whammy for foreign investors. India's benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange's Sensitive Index is down 13% over the past three months.

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal website, WSJ.com.)

Funds that measure their returns in U.S. dollars have been even more heavily hit. India-focused mutual funds available to U.S. investors have lost 18% on average in the past three months, according to research firm Morningstar Inc.

Hedge funds, too, have been hit, although they have been able to limit losses through buying derivative products that spread their risk. The average India-focused hedge fund has lost 5% over three months through end-April, compared to a 1.7% average gain for Asia funds, excluding Japan, in the same period, said Singapore-based research firm Eurekahedge Pte.

"Regardless of their portfolio performance, if the rupee depreciates then they will take a hit," said Farhan Mumtaz, an analyst at Eurekahedge.

While Asian currencies also have lost some value against the dollar in recent days as globally risk-averse investors have loaded up on the U.S. currency, India is faring worse because of deepening concerns about its macro-economic stability.

The rupee's losses stem from India's widening current account deficit and lack of robust capital inflows amid high inflation and failure to push through much-needed economic reforms. In recent days, global risk aversion caused by uncertainty over the euro-zone debt crisis has added to pressures on the rupee.

For now, foreign investors are generally holding on to their Indian investments, hoping for a rebound. But prolonged local currency weakness could at some point force investors to cut their losses, further weakening the currency. Foreign institutional investors have pulled out $163 million from Indian stocks since April, reversing their optimism during the first three months of the year when they bought Indian stocks worth $8.8 billion.

Analysts are dour on the outlook for the rupee in the near term, particularly because India has taken few steps to correct its fiscal and economic imbalances such as reducing massive fuel subsidies or allowing more foreign investment in India's retail sector.

Meanwhile, recent measures by India's central bank aimed at bolstering the currency, such as forcing exporters to convert their dollar reserves into rupees, have failed to lift the rupee. The bank has been intervening to prop up the currency but without success. There was no sign of intervention Tuesday, traders said.

On Tuesday, India's Finance Minister Pranab Mukherjee said the Reserve Bank of India will continue to intervene. But many analysts believe that the central bank, which has foreign reserves equal to only seven months' worth of imports, may have exhausted its firepower to support the rupee.

The most pessimistic forecasts expect the currency to go as low as 60 rupees per dollar.

"It seems that policy makers lack a coherent plan to stabilize the INR in the short term or to boost growth," wrote Dariusz Kowalczyk, senior economist at Credit Agricole CIB, in a research note Monday.

While money managers who invest in Indian stocks have been prepared for some volatility in the rupee, the losses have been larger and faster than most had expected.

"This month has been painful," said Samir Arora, a hedge fund manager at Helios Capital Management Pte., based in Singapore.

Some money managers have begun to cut back on their allocations for Indian stocks in regional portfolios in recent months.

"In our portfolios, we are currently finding more opportunities in China and Korea," said Andrew Beal, an Asia-focused fund manager at U.K.'s Henderson Global Investors.

He said that the falling rupee is a symptom of the deeper structural malaise in the Indian economy. "The situation may need to get worse before a coalition of pro-reform groups can push ahead with desperately needed measures to open and up and deregulate the economy," Beal said.

In general, foreign money managers are bracing themselves for a tough couple of years ahead for India.

"Many foreign investors are concerned about further deterioration in India's macro-economic condition in combination with policy and political uncertainty," said Seth Freeman, chief investment officer at San Francisco-based EM Capital Management LLC. "These investors are largely taking a wait and see strategy."

To be sure, some long-term India bulls are taking the rupee's losses in their stride and say its part of doing business in India.

"We think there's a possibility that it could get worse, but I don't think it should ring major alarm bells," said Sukumar Rajah, a Indian-based money manager with Franklin Templeton Investments of the U.S. "If the sentiment looks up, there's a chance that rupee would go up," he adds.

-By Shefali Anand, Khushita Vasant and Raghavendra Upadhyaya, The Wall Street Journal; Shefali.Anand@wsj.com [ 05-22-12 0748ET ]

title: MARKET EYE FOCUS-In rupee fall, RBI may target oil next
text:
As the rupee plumbs to record lows against the dollar, traders say the Reserve Bank of India could go beyond interventions and target dollar demand from oil companies, an approach that if done right may just help stem the rout.

 Having proved unable to contain the rupee's falls via its actions in the forex markets, the RBI was widely reported to have met oil companies this week, and a look at the numbers shows why.

Forex dealers estimate average daily demand for dollars from state-run oil refiners at around $400-$500 million, with demand peaking towards the end of the month when they are supposed to make payments.

 Targeting oil could succeed, but it will come down to how the RBI does it, traders say.

 The RBI is widely seen to have two options: it could open a dollar window for oil companies to buy dollars directly from the central bank or it could purchase oil bonds via special market operations. 

 RBI opted for the latter in 2008 and then again in 2009 because oil companies back then were holding illiquid bonds. That helped the central bank both inject dollar liquidity and help the sector monetise its debt. 

 However, 2012 would be different. Oil companies no longer hold much outstanding oil bonds a nd traders see a far more effective approach if the RBI were to sell dollars directly to the sector.

 "The direct dollar window to oil firms can help the rupee recover to around 53.80 per dollar. Oil prices also have come down by 10-15 percent, that will also help the rupee over the next 30-60 days horizon," a dealer in FX and rates at a private bank said. 

(Reporting by Subhadip Sircar, Swati Bhat & Suvashree Dey Choudhury)
