* Domestic equities fall more than 1 percent

* Rupee may face selling pressure before fiscal year end-traders

(Adds quotes, comments, updates to close)

By Aditya Phatak

MUMBAI, March 19 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee fell back on Monday as local stocks dropped for the third straight session and foreign capital inflows dried up during the session amid subdued volumes towards the close of the fiscal year.

The rupee is seen moving in a range of 49.85 to 50.50 to the dollar this week, although some traders did not rule out a bout of selling towards the end of the month as banks close accounts for the 2011/12 fiscal year.

The rupee ended at 50.23/24 to the dollar, after rising to 50.0650 in early trades. It had closed at 50.175/185 on Friday.

Dollar inflows into local debt likely supported the Indian currency early in the session. However, a fall in local equities pulled the rupee lower.

The inflows had came after an auction on Friday of unused limits, which allow foreign institutional investors to buy long-term government and corporate bonds, was oversubscribed.

"49.85 has emerged as a very strong resistance for the rupee and as the year end approaches traders will look to crystallise profits," said Naveen Raghuvanshi, associate vice president of foreign exchange trading at Development Credit Bank.

"It is also the quarter end and the month end, so market could turn biddish (on the dollar)."

The government's budget for 2012/13 was also seen as negative for the currency since it offered no new solutions to address the country's fiscal constraints, traders said.

Rating agency Moody's Investors Service said the budget was credit negative for Asia's third largest economy.

Technical charts also hinted at selling pressure on the rupee if it failed to strengthen past the 50 level soon, b ut most traders expect any sharp slide in the rupee to be cut short by the central bank.

The Reserve Bank of India has been actively intervening in the local foreign exchange market over the past few months to shore up the currency in case of acute selling pressure.

title: DJ UPDATE: India  Central Bank  Acknowledges Govt's Efforts To Lower Fiscal Gap
text:
-- Budget presents significant fiscal consolidation, central bank official says

-- New revenue proposals increase reliability of fiscal consolidation process

-- Liquidity conditions to determine further bond buybacks

(Combines related articles, adds deputy governors' comments in 4th, 10th, 14th, 16th and 17th paragraphs)

By Nupur Acharya and Sudeep Jain

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian central bank Friday applauded the government's plan to lower the fiscal deficit but said it will also consider crude oil prices and economic growth while deciding on interest-rate cuts.

The comments are important because the Reserve Bank of India had recently stepped up its criticism of the government's lax fiscal policies, which are seen as diluting the central bank's effort to curb inflation through a tight monetary policy. The RBI has said that it would be constrained from lowering rates in the absence of credible fiscal consolidation.

The RBI left its lending rate unchanged at 8.50% Thursday, saying the risks to inflation had increased due to higher crude prices, the large fiscal gap and a weakening rupee. The RBI next meets to review monetary policy April 17.

"A significant part of the correction [in the fiscal deficit] is coming from new revenue proposals, particularly indirect tax proposals, so... the reliability of the process goes up," RBI Deputy Governor Subir Gokarn said at a press conference.

India aims to reduce its fiscal deficit to 5.1% of gross domestic product in the next fiscal year that starts April from 5.9% in the current year, Finance Minister Pranab Mukherjee told parliament in his budget speech Friday.

The government is banking on lower subsidies, an economic recovery and an increase in indirect taxes to meet the deficit target.

The government will attempt to keep subsidies below 2% of GDP next fiscal year and try to keep it below 1.7% over the following three years, Mukherjee said.

The central bank can draw comfort from the government's efforts to reduce its fiscal deficit, which appear credible, Ashima Goyal, a member of the RBI's technical advisory committee on monetary policy, told Dow Jones Newswires.

Sudipto Mundle, another member of the committee, said the budget targets are realistic and would help reinforce credibility of the government's projections on the fiscal deficit.

Deputy Governor Gokarn also said that the central bank would decide whether to carry out more bond buybacks depending on the liquidity conditions.

The banking system has been facing an acute liquidity shortage due to the government's over-the-top borrowing program, advance tax payments by companies and the RBI's intervention in the foreign exchange markets to protect the rupee.

India's foreign exchange reserves fell by $1.030 billion to $293.959 billion in the week ended March 9, central bank data showed Friday.

The RBI has bought back government bonds on a large scale and has slashed banks' minimum cash requirement by 125 basis points in less than two months to pump cash into the system.

Separately, RBI Deputy Governor H.R. Khan said it would be difficult to manage the government's huge borrowing program.

The government plans to borrow a net INR4.79 trillion from the market next fiscal year to fund its budget, compared with INR4.4 trillion this year.

Officials from the RBI and India's finance ministry are likely to meet on March 27 or March 28 to decide on the government's borrowing calendar for the first half of the next fiscal year, Khan said.

Khan also said that he expects INR600 billion to flow back into the Indian banking system in the first fortnight of April as the government spends or refunds advance tax payments of companies.

- By Sudeep Jain, Dow Jones Newswires; 91 22 6145 6123; sudeep.jain@dowjones.com

--Anant Vijay Kala in New Delhi contributed to this article.

title: Indian rupee slides to 7-wk low on importers
text:
* Gold, oil importers step up dollar purchases

* Worries over global econ outlook weigh on rupee

* Expectations of RBI intervention seen aiding rupee

(Adds quotes, comments, updates to mid-morning)

MUMBAI, March 7 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee continued to weaken for the fifth consecutive session on Wednesday, sliding to a seven-week low, due to incessant dollar demand from oil refiners and gold importers.

Mounting worries over slowing world economies and renewed uncertainty over Greece's bailout added to the downward pressure on the rupee, traders said.

At 11:01 a.m. (0531 GMT), the rupee was at 50.64/65 to the dollar, after dipping to 50.76, its lowest since Jan. 18, according to Thomson Reuters data. The unit had closed at 50.36/37 on Tuesday.

"There is huge demand in the market. It seems that everybody just wants to buy dollars including most sections of importers," said a foreign exchange dealer with a large state-run bank.

Local oil refiners have been buying dollars aggressively in the past few sessions due to a recent surge in global oil prices, with India importing nearly 80 percent of its oil needs.

Demand for gold in India, the world's largest consumer of the bullion, has climbed amid the festival and wedding season after prices fell 2.8 percent since Feb. 27.

Outlook for foreign inflows has been clouded as expectations of a revival in reforms were jolted after the Congress party's severe losses in crucial state elections on Tuesday.

However, expectations that the Reserve Bank of India may take action and intervene actively in the foreign exchange market to support the rupee is likely to provide some support to the currency, traders said.

"People do remember what happened last time when they tested RBI's resolve so they will be even more careful now. You don't want the central bank to shut you from the market completely," said a senior currency trader with a private sector bank.

The RBI has been intervening in the currency market over the past few months to support the rupee, which touched a record low of 54.30 on Dec. 15, and took numerous steps including slashing of banks' trading limits to cut speculative trades.

were at 51.04.

title: UPDATE: India  Central Bank  Likely To Have Sold Dollars To Protect Rupee
text:
--Intervention likely began when dollar was at INR50.52, dealers say

--RBI likely to stop dollar from appreciating above INR51.00, analyst says

--Wednesday's suspected intervention at least the second this week

(Recasts 1st paragraph, updates currency level in 4th paragraph, analyst's quote in 7th paragraph and background in 8th-13th paragraphs)

By Sourav Mishra and Sudeep Jain

OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India's central bank is likely to have intervened in the foreign exchange markets for at least the second time this week Wednesday to prop up the rupee after the local unit fell to a seven-week low against the U.S. dollar.

The Reserve Bank of India likely started selling dollars when the greenback was trading around INR50.52, five dealers told Dow Jones Newswires.

The suspected intervention helped push the rupee into positive territory after it slumped to a seven-week low of 50.76 to a dollar, according to the dealers who spoke on the customary condition of anonymity.

The dollar was quoted at INR50.28 in late Asian trade Wednesday, down from 50.36 Tuesday.

The RBI's suspected presence in the currency markets comes as the rupee has lost about 3% against the greenback over the past five sessions. Rising concerns over Greece's ability to avoid a sovereign default and jitters about slowing global economic growth have triggered a selloff in riskier assets, including equities and a wide array of regional currencies such as the rupee and Korean won and the Australian dollar.

Analysts expect the RBI to ramp up its intervention if the rupee continues to weaken.

"The Indian central bank may not allow rupee weakness beyond the 51.00 mark and may support the local currency as it approaches this level," said Moses Harding, head of global markets at IndusInd Bank.

The volatility in local debt, equity and currency markets is likely to increase in the run-up to the RBI's rate-setting meeting on Mar. 15, which will be followed a day later by the federal government's budget announcement for the fiscal year starting April 1.

Wednesday's suspected intervention follows a similar move on Monday, when the RBI is believed to have started selling dollars when the greenback was trading around INR49.90.

The RBI didn't comment on the suspected actions, but it's public position is that the central bank intervenes only to dampen exchange-rate volatility and not to protect a particular currency level. It discloses data on its foreign currency transactions with a lag of more than a month.

Data disclosed by the central bank show the RBI intervened heavily to protect the local unit as it fell to a record low of 54.2925 to a dollar in mid-December.

The central bank sold $7.8 billion of foreign currency in December--its highest monthly sale since the peak of the financial crisis in October 2008.

The rupee's recent losses follow gains of much as 9% against the dollar earlier this year on a surge in portfolio capital inflows following measures to ease foreign investment restrictions in capital markets.

title: UPDATE: India  Central Bank  Says Has Room To Cut Cash Reserve Ratio Further
text:
--Open to using all instruments to manage liquidity, official says 
   --Inflation risks emerging with rising oil prices 
   --Growth not sole driver of monetary policy, official says 
   --Reducing statutory liquidity ratio won't ease liquidity crunch 
 

(Adds comments in 6th-8th, 10th and 12th paragraphs, background in 3rd-5th paragraphs)

By Sourav Mishra and Sudeep Jain

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India's central bank has room to reduce banks' minimum cash requirement further, a top official said Monday, adding that it is open to using all instruments to manage liquidity.

"If we think its appropriate to use it [a cash reserve ratio cut] we will, and it is certainly on the table," Reserve Bank of India Deputy Governor Subir Gokarn said on television in comments indicating that a CRR cut may come at the Reserve Bank of India's next policy meeting on March 15.

The comments come against the backdrop of an acute liquidity shortage, which hasn't eased despite frequent bond buybacks and the central bank's move on Jan. 24 to cut the CRR by half a percentage point to 5.50%.

The cash reserve ratio is the minimum percentage of deposits that banks must hold with the central bank.

The cash shortage--brought on by fiscal third-quarter advance tax payments in December and the Reserve Bank of India's intervention in the currency markets to prop up the Indian rupee--is expected to worsen when companies pay advance taxes for the January-March quarter in the middle of March.

A cut in the statutory liquidity ratio--banks' mandatory bond holding requirement--would not be effective as most banks hold bonds in excess of the minimum requirement, Gokarn told reporters separately.

He told the CNBC TV-18 television channel that growth considerations weren't the sole driver of monetary policy, and that some risks to inflation are emerging, such as the recent rise in crude oil prices.

India's gross domestic product growth slowed to a more than two-year low of 6.1% in the October-December quarter, hurt by successive interest rate increases and a weak external environment.

The timing and magnitude of rate cuts would be conditioned by the emerging risks, Gokarn added.

The RBI left its policy rate unchanged at its previous two rate-setting meetings after a staggering 13 increases over the past two years.

Gokarn also said the government's fiscal stance needs to be consistent with the RBI's monetary stance and he expects the government to take some steps in this direction when it presents its next budget on March 16.

In its previous policy statement, the RBI said it would be constrained from lowering rates in the absence of credible fiscal consolidation.

India is expected to widely overshoot its aim of keeping the fiscal deficit within 4.6% of its gross domestic product in the current fiscal year through March.


 
  --By Sudeep Jain, Dow Jones Newswires; 91 22 6145 6123; sudeep.jain@dowjones.com

title: RPT-EXCLUSIVE-Iran defaults on rice payments to India-traders
text:
(Repeats story with no changes to text)

* Payment defaults on about 200,000 tonnes of rice

* Indian rice exporters fear further payment defaults

* Exporters' group asks government to intervene

* India meets about 70 pct of Iran rice needs

By Ratnajyoti Dutta and Mayank Bhardwaj

NEW DELHI, Feb 7 (Reuters) - Iranian buyers have defaulted on payments for about 200,000 tonnes of rice from their top supplier India, exporters and rice millers said on Tuesday, a sign of the mounting pressure on Tehran from a new wave of Western sanctions.

The default prompted the head of the All India Rice Exporters' Association to call on members to stop rice exports to Iran based on credit, which would be a fresh blow to a country where imports of staple foods are already being hampered by sanctions.

"It is a serious issue and we do not rule out further payment defaults by Iran," said Vijay Setia, the association's president.

Indian sources said the Iranian buyers had defaulted on payments worth about $144 million for rice shipments under long-term supply deals. Iran shipped the cargoes from Indian ports in October and November. Most Indian rice exporters allow 90 days credit.

Iran relies on imports for about 45 pct of its annual rice consumption of 2.9 million tonnes, according to U.S. Dept. of Agriculture data.

In other supply disruptions, five deliveries of grain to Iran were diverted to new destinations because payments were held up, ship tracking data showed last week. Other cargoes are sitting offshore Iran because of difficulty with payments.

Under a tightening grip of sanctions, the country of 74 million people is finding it increasingly difficult to repatriate the hard currency from its crude oil exports, its major foreign currency earner, that it needs to pay for shipments of food and other imports.

A sharp drop in the value of the rial is adding to Iran's import costs and the financial sanctions make it difficult for traders in the country to channel import payments through unofficial routes involving middlemen based in Dubai.

India is Iran's top rice supplier, accounting for some 70 percent of its annual requirement of 1-1.2 million tonnes of the grain, mainly the aromatic variety called Basmati.

Traders and officials in Iran could not be immediately reached to comment.

The United States slapped fresh sanctions on Tehran from the start of this year, targeting financial institutions that deal with the central bank, hoping to stem oil revenues and persuade Iran to abandon a suspected nuclear weapons programme.

U.S. President Barack Obama tightened those sanctions on Sunday, again targeting Iran's central bank and giving U.S. banks new powers to freeze assets linked to Tehran.

The European Union has agreed to ban Iranian oil imports, a measure expected to take full effect within six months.

SANCTIONS BITING?

The rice defaults could be the latest sign that those sanctions are biting as Iranian importers find it increasingly difficult to settle payments.

Ukraine's maize exports to Iran dropped 40 percent in January due to payment problems, Ukrainian consultancy ProAgro said last week.

Ukrainian and European traders said they were no longer booking Ukraine grains shipments to Iran because of the payments difficulties, although talks were underway to save the market, the country's farm minister said.

Five ships of grain have been diverted away from Iran to other destinations and about 400,000 tonnes of grains on at least 10 vessels have been held up outside Iranian ports because of payments problems, trade sources said last week.

The Indian rice association's Setia said the group had approached the Indian government to recover their dues.

"As part of efforts to minimise losses, we are asking our colleagues to avoid sending rice on credit," he said, adding they were not calling for a ban on exports to Iran.

A government source acknowledged exporters had sought help.

The rice default is the latest snag in India-Iran trade, which is heavily skewed towards Tehran.

India is Iran's second-largest buyer of crude and it has struggled to settle payments worth some $11 billion annually after New Delhi scrapped a long-standing mechanism in 2010 under pressure from Washington.

While New Delhi has switched to a payment conduit for its Iranian oil using a Turkish bank, Indian rice exporters have been using a loose, unofficial route involving a network of middlemen based in Dubai.

The middlemen receive payments from Iranian importers in rial and pay Indian exporters in U.S. dollars. The consignments are sent directly from India to Iran.

But Indian traders said the defaults started after the rial plunged over the past month, making previous purchases costlier for Iranian importers.

The cost of transactions also went up for the Dubai middlemen as they use U.S. dollars to pay Indian exporters.

On Jan. 26, Iran announced an 8 percent devaluation of the rial and said it would enforce a single exchange rate, aiming to stamp out a black market where the dollar's value has soared due to fears over new sanctions imposed by the West.

Indian traders said about 20 Iranian companies have failed to clear their dues during the past month.

"It threatens to jeopardise the trade with them, hurting both India and Iran," Anil K. Mittal, chairman of KRBL Ltd, a leading Indian rice miller and exporter, told Reuters.

"Due to sanctions on Iran, currently banks are not involved in payments to Indian rice suppliers. The payments are direct and at times on credit, making Indian exporters vulnerable to defaults. Indian traders must avoid supplying on credit."

Setia said India should not send any more rice to Iran on credit, adding suppliers such as those in Thailand, Vietnam and Pakistan had already stopped doing so.

However, the Thai Rice Exporters' Association said Thailand had stopped selling rice to Iran about a decade ago.

Javed Agha, chairman of the Rice Exporters Association of Pakistan acknowledged that sanctions had made traders reluctant in both Pakistan and Iran to do deals.

"Banking if a problem between Pakistan and Iran," he said. "There is no proper system."

BOOSTING EXPORTS TO IRAN

New Delhi will send a delegation to Iran this month to explore boosting exports to smooth use of the restricted rupee currency, which the two sides have agreed to use to settle 45 percent of India's $11 billion a year oil bill.

But this would give Iran large amounts of a currency which is difficult to use for international trade.

An Indian ministerial panel on food exports meets on Tuesday to review rice and sugar shipments. The issue of exports to Iran is not on the agenda, government officials said, seeking to knock down reports that the panel could discuss the possibility of boosting rice and wheat exports to Tehran.

India, is expected to produce 102.75 million tonnes of rice in the crop year to June 2012, a farm ministry forecast said last month. Basmati makes up around 5 percent of India's total rice production.

India's Jan. 1 rice inventory at government warehouses was 29.8 million tonnes against a target of 11.8 million tonnes.

China, Japan, India and South Korea, which together buy about half or Iran's 2.6 million barrels per day of crude exports, are under pressure from U.S. sanctions to cut back their purchases.

China has already cut Iran imports in the first three months of this year over a pricing dispute and a flurry of U.S. diplomats have discussed the sanctions with Asian government officials.

South Korea is paying Iran for crude in its local currency, but difficulty repatriating the funds under the weight of sanctions means won worth an estimated $5 billion has piled up South Korean banks.

($1=48.93 rupees)

(Additional reporting by Qasim Nauman in Islamabad and [20120208 020335 GMT]

title: REFILE-POLL-Indian rupee to hold steady in 2012, portfolio flows key
text:
(Refiles to remove extraneous matter)

* For results click on

* Rupee to fluctuate between 50.0 and 48.8 in 2012, end year flat

* Stimulus abroad, India's ability to attract portfolio flows key to rupee

By Rahul Karunakar

BANGALORE, Feb 3 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is expected to hold steady through much of this year, encumbered by an economy that will struggle to attract the portfolio flows it needs to fund to its balance of payments, a Reuters poll showed.

The currency will not revisit the record lows it hit in mid-December, the poll showed.

But the rapid slowdown in the economy and persistently high inflation make India a relatively less attractive investment destination, even in a year when developed economies are expected to pump massive stimulus into financial markets.

The Reuters poll of 28 strategists and analysts, taken this week, saw the rupee trading at 50.0 against the dollar in a month, 50.5 in three months and strengthening to 48.8 a year from now, which is close to Friday's spot market levels of 49.03. That compared with 52.0, 51.4 and 49.0 in the December poll.

Expectations are already running high for another round of bond purchases from the U.S. Federal Reserve and for the European Central Bank to lend more to its troubled banking system. Analysts expect a lot of that cash will flow towards emerging markets and commodities.

Yet, further strength in the rupee may depend on investor confidence in prospects for a global recovery as well as a snapback in India's domestic economy.

"If we see global risk appetite improve from here then dollar/rupee could fall further," said Nick Verdi, FX strategist at Barclays Capital in Singapore.

"But we think weak fundamentals will limit rupee appreciation from here," he said, making a specific reference to India's weak fiscal position .

After losing 16 percent of its value last year, the rupee recouped about half of those losses on Reserve Bank of Indiaintervention and a general rush back into riskier assets among global investors.

Foreign investors put about $2 billion into Indian markets in January alone, after being net sellers in 2011. The rupee posted its largest monthly gain in over 17 years in January, rising 7.5 percent.

Yet a current account deficit as wide as 3 percent of economic output plus weak foreign direct investment and a pipeline of maturing foreign borrowings make it imperative that India keeps attracting foreign money into its stock and bond markets.

Economists in a separate Reuters poll cut their forecasts for India's economy and now expect it to grow 7.6 percent in the fiscal year to March, its slowest pace in two years. The economy grew 6.9 percent in the quarter ended September 2011.

After 13 rate rises to stamp out inflation in between March 2010 and October 2011, the central bank signalled last month it was shifting its focus to growth by cutting the cash reserve requirements for banks by 50 basis points.

"The fact that inflation is more sticky in India than in most other economies in the rest of the region is limiting the extent to which the RBI can loosen monetary policy," said Verdi.

The RBI also intervened many times in the market late last year, selling dollars in an attempt to prop up the rupee, which fell to a record low of 54.30 against the dollar on Dec. 15.

The central bank also announced a series of measures aimed at cutting out speculative bets on the currency and boosting capital inflows into Asia's third largest economy. .

That intervention stabilised the rupee, and possibly transferred some of the bearish bets into the offshore rupee markets. One-year offshore non-deliverable forward contracts

were at 51.85 earlier on Friday, effectively pricing in a 5 percent depreciation in the next 12 months.

Analysts also noted that, like any central bank intervention, the impact of the RBI measures are not long-lasting.

"Most of these measures are temporary in nature and while they are good for the near term stability of the rupee they are negative for long term sustainability," said Bhupesh Bameta at Quant Capital.

By Sourav Mishra and Sudeep Jain

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of India could reverse its recent curbs on currency trading once markets stabilize as they run counter to its capital account management strategy, a top official said Friday, indicating that the central bank is now more comfortable with the rupee's trading range.

There will be a situation when the restrictions will no longer be necessary and "we will take the situation back to where it was," RBI Deputy Governor Subir Gokarn told reporters after a conference, without disclosing any specific timeline for reversing the measures.

In December, the RBI placed limits on unhedged foreign-currency positions that banks can hold overnight and also banned companies from cancelling and rebooking forward contracts with the same underlying exposure as part of measures to prop up the local currency.

"The whole purpose of our capital management strategy is to bring as much liquidity into the market as possible, as many legitimate participants as possible, and when we impose curbs, we are actually restricting the space," Gokarn said.

The RBI had imposed the curbs after the rupee slumped to a record low of 54.2925 to a U.S. dollar on Dec. 15. The local unit, which dropped 16% versus the greenback in 2011, has jumped more than 11% from its record low and is up about 9% in 2012, thanks to the RBI's curbs and direct intervention as well as improving global risk appetite and India's measures to boost capital inflows.

Friday, the dollar was at INR48.88 at 0808 GMT.

Partha Mukherjee, president of treasury and international banking at Axis Bank, said that, even though the central bank might not reverse those curbs immediately, Gokarn's comments are positive for the markets as they indicate that the RBI is increasingly at ease with the rupee's level.

Separately, Gokarn told the CNBC-TV18 television channel that, unlike in 2008, the RBI doesn't currently have room for aggressive rate cuts as commodity prices remain high.

Slowing economic growth and easing inflation have fuelled hopes that monetary easing is imminent. The RBI had raised rates a staggering 13 times over the past two years, but left rates unchanged at its last two rate-setting meetings.

Gokarn also said the liquidity deficit in the banking system remains above the central bank's comfort zone of INR600 billion, and the RBI would continue to consider open market operations such as bond buybacks to ease the cash crunch.

title: 3rd UPDATE: India  Central Bank  May Consider Rolling Back  Forex  Trading Curbs - Official
text:
-- Deputy governor says trading restrictions are imposing costs on some market participants

-- U.S. dollar falls to its lowest in three months against Indian rupee

-- Central bank asks banks to consider cap on clients' unhedged forex exposure

-- Best to be unpredictable about tactical currency management, says governor

(Recasts the first paragraph, adds details and context in 2nd to 4th paragraphs)

By Nupur Acharya and Sudeep Jain

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of India may consider rolling back recently imposed restrictions on currency trading once markets stabilize, a top central bank official said Thursday, as the rupee surged to a three-month high against the U.S. dollar.

The trading curbs were imposing costs on some market participants and run counter to the central bank's broad strategy of having "robust, vibrant" foreign-exchange markets, RBI Deputy Governor Subir Gokarn told television channel Bloomberg UTV.

In December, the RBI placed limits on unhedged foreign currency positions that banks can hold overnight and also banned firms from cancelling and rebooking forward contracts, as part of measures to prop up the rupee.

Gokarn, however, declined to give a timeline for reversing the measures, saying that would be a matter of "very fine judgement as to whether the situation has stabilized or not."

The comments come as the rupee has risen more than 8% this year against the U.S. dollar after tumbling about 16% in 2011. The local unit has been boosted by a surge in foreign fund flows into local equities and debt, apart from the RBI's intervention and the curbs on speculative trading.

India has taken a series of measures to attract overseas capital such as raising the cap on foreign investment in local bonds and allowing banks to freely set interest rates on deposits received from non-resident Indians.

The dollar was at INR49.15 late Thursday in Asia after dropping to a three-month low of INR48.95 earlier in the day.

However, foreign-currency exposure of Indian firms remains a concern, with the central bank Thursday asking banks to consider framing policies to limit the unhedged foreign-currency exposure of their clients.

Banks should also price the risk arising from unhedged foreign-currency exposure into credit premiums, the RBI said in a statement.

Local media reports have speculated that only 40% of Indian corporations' foreign-currency debt is hedged. That means a sharp fluctuation in the exchange rate could lead to steep credit losses.

Separately, RBI Governor Duvvuri Subbarao Thursday reiterated the bank's policy of keeping mum about intervention in the foreign-exchange market.

"It pays to be a bit unpredictable on when you intervene, how much you intervene, how you are going to move the exchange rate," he said at a conference.

The RBI recently intervened in the currency markets to prop up the rupee, with its dollar sales rising to a 32-month high of $2.9 billion in November.

The central bank data on intervention is published after a lag, and the RBI has a long-stated policy of getting into the market only to manage excessive volatility.

title: UPDATE: RBI Governor Subbarao: Best To Be Unpredictable In  Currency  Management
text:
-- Best to be unpredictable about tactical currency management, says governor

-- Strategic policies on currency management must be clear and stable

-- U.S. dollar falls to its weakest in three months against Indian rupee

(Adds governor's comments in 10th and 11th paragraphs, context in 5th and 12th paragraphs, rupee move in 6th paragraph)


 
  By Nupur Acharya and Sudeep Jain 
  Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India's central bank governor Thursday said it is best to be unpredictable in tactical currency management, reiterating the bank's policy of not disclosing details of intervention in the foreign exchange market.

"It pays to be a bit unpredictable on when you intervene, how much you intervene, how you are going to move the exchange rate," Duvvuri Subbarao said at a conference.

The Reserve Bank of India recently intervened in the currency markets to prop up the rupee, with its dollar sales rising to a 32-month high of $2.9 billion in November.

The central bank data on intervention is published after a lag, and the RBI has a long-stated policy of getting into the market only to manage excessive volatility.

The rupee, Asia's worst-performing major currency in 2011, has risen about 8% in 2012 against the U.S. dollar on the back of foreign fund flows into local equity and debt, apart from the RBI's intervention and imposing of new curbs on speculative trading.

India has taken a series of measures to attract overseas capital such as raising the cap on foreign investments allowed in local bonds, as well as the total costs that companies are permitted to incur to raise overseas loans.

Also, the RBI has allowed banks to freely set interest rates on deposits received from non-resident Indians.

These measures have helped revive capital inflows and boost the rupee.

The dollar fell to INR48.95, a three-month low, intraday Thursday. It was trading at INR49.05 at 0830 GMT.

While the central bank may remain discreet about its market intervention, Subbarao said strategic policies on currency management should be clearly laid out in the public domain and remain stable over time.

Also, it is difficult for the central bank's monetary policy steps--such as rate increases--to control inflation when the fiscal deficit is wide.

India's fiscal deficit is expected to overshoot the government's target of 4.6% of gross domestic product for the current fiscal year through March by as much as one percentage point. While government spending has remained high in the run-up to elections in five states this year, tax revenue has taken a hit due to a slowing economy.

The central bank's policy tightening has helped pull down inflation, but it still remains uncomfortably high because heavy government spending continues to stoke demand.

Besides, rising growth worries have forced the central bank to end the current tightening cycle.

Subbarao added: "It is unrealistic that the Reserve Bank pursue inflation target completely oblivious of other objectives, [of which] most important is growth."

The RBI has aggressively tightened monetary policy since March 2010 to bring spiraling prices under control. But this has choked industrial activity, forcing the central bank to shift to a growth-supportive policy stance.

title: DJ UPDATE: India Official: Rupee's Rise Not A Sign Of Economic Bounceback
text:
--Indian rupee's gain due to capital inflows, steps by authorities, says official 
  --Central bank may not intervene strongly in currency market at current levels, says BNP Paribas 
 
  (Recasts 1st paragraph, updates currency level in 4th paragraph, adds analysts' comments in 6th and 18th paragraph) 
 

By Abhrajit Gangopadhyay and Sudeep Jain

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee's recent surge isn't really a sign of--or even backed by--a strong economic recovery, a top government official cautioned Friday, giving weight to comments from analysts who have warned over the past few weeks that they see little evidence the currency can sustain its rise.

"The Indian rupee is appreciating due to foreign capital inflows, and previous steps taken by the authorities are also helping," the Finance Ministry official, who asked not to be named, told Dow Jones Newswires.

The comments, from one of the country's most senior officials, come at a time when the rupee is at an 11-week high against the U.S. dollar, and traders appear to be bullish on the local currency.

The dollar was trading at INR49.39 at 0921 GMT--its lowest level since Nov. 9, 2011. The greenback has lost nearly 9% from the record high of INR54.2925 reached on Dec. 15, 2011.

Despite this, the Finance Ministry official's views are backed by analysts, who believe that the currency's rise shouldn't be taken to signal a revival of the Indian economy, and that traders should look through the euphoria and study the basics instead.

Investment bank Brown Brothers Harriman said in a recent research note that it doesn't think that the "underlying fundamentals have shifted that much in 2012, so we remain skeptical that the INR [rupee] outperformance can continue."

Watchers attribute the rupee's recent rise to a range of measure taken by the government and the Reserve Bank of India coupled with improved global risk appetite, and outright central bank intervention in the foreign exchange market.

Foreign investors have already put a net $4.8 billion into local debt and stocks in 2012 so far--compared with $8.3 billion in the whole of 2011--following measures to ease foreign investment restrictions in capital markets.

Also, the Reserve Bank of India has actively intervened in the currency markets to prop up the rupee, with its dollar sales rising to a 32-month high of $2.9 billion in November.

Last month, the RBI placed limits on the unhedged currency positions that banks can hold overnight, and banned companies from cancelling and rebooking forwards contracts to clamp down on what it called speculative behavior.

RBI Governor Duvvuri Subbarao Tuesday said the restrictions may not be temporary.

That aside, there is much to be concerned about.

India runs a persistent current account deficit due to a large trade gap, which is likely to increase given the weak global outlook for exports and the non-discretionary nature of India's major imports such as crude oil.

India's July-September current account gap widened to $16.9 billion from $15.8 billion in the April-June quarter.

Another concern is India's fiscal deficit, which is expected to overshoot the government's target of 4.6% of gross domestic product for the current fiscal year through March by as much as 1 percentage point.

While government spending has remained high in the run-up to state elections in five states this year, tax revenue has taken a hit due to a slowing economy.

In the July-September quarter, India's gross domestic product grew 6.9%--the lowest reading in more than two years.

Investors are now watching how the central bank will respond to the rupee's recent rise. It may not intervene strongly at current levels, said Chin Loo Thio, a currency strategist at BNP Paribas.

The bank has a stated policy of not revealing if it has intervened or not, and it says that it will step in only to curb volatility.

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee rose to a near six-week high against the U.S. dollar Friday, driven by capital flows into local debt as a series of measures to attract foreign cash began to pay off.

The rise--which helped to further reverse some of the currency's large selloff last year--came after the central bank was Thursday spotted selling dollars in the foreign exchange market.

The Reserve Bank of India's intervention is whittling down India's foreign exchange reserves, which fell to a more than 12-month low of $293.54 billion in the first week of January, data showed Friday.

The reserves were at record high of $320.80 billion in September.

The dollar was at INR51.53 late Friday in Asia, after falling to an intraday low of INR51.29, its weakest level since Dec. 5 and down from INR51.60 Thursday.

Despite the rupee's recent rise, market analysts warned that the rally is unlikely to continue unless the central bank clearly shows that it has shifted its focus to helping growth rather than fighting inflation.

They added that, if the Reserve Bank cuts rates at its Jan. 24 policy meeting, it would signal to foreign investors that it is supporting the economy, and that would in turn lead to increased capital inflows.

Apart from continuing concerns over a ballooning fiscal deficit and a gaping current account gap which could widen due to India's unfavorable trade balance, steady demand for the greenback to settle bills for oil imports and defense purchases also clouds the rupee's long-term prospects.

Philip Wee, a senior currency economist at DBS Group Holdings, said investors may wait to see what the central bank says on Jan. 24 before pouring in more foreign capital.

The rupee was Asia's worst-performing major currency in 2011, with the dollar gaining about 19% against the rupee. The greenback has lost about 3.3% against the Indian currency so far in 2012.

India recently raised foreign investment limits in government and corporate bonds by $5 billion each to $15 billion and $20 billion, respectively. The time for investing in these government bonds ends Friday.

It also relaxed regulations for overseas investments in shares, and allowed banks to freely set interest rates on deposits from non-resident Indians.

The steps were aimed at attracting foreign capital, which had dried out in the past year due to slowing growth and diminishing risk appetite.

Also, an upgrade of India's ratings by Moody's late December improved appetite for government debt, which offers yields much higher than other major economies.

The effects of the measures were evident in data from the capital markets regulator, which show foreign funds have invested INR101.13 billion in Indian debt so far in 2012, compared with INR17.09 billion a year earlier.

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--India's central bank stands ready to intervene in the currency markets to smooth any sharp move in the rupee, which is expected to stabilize after its recent fall, a Reserve Bank of India deputy governor said Thursday.

"We will respond strongly to any sharp one-way moves" in the currency, Subir Gokarn told Dow Jones in Singapore.

He said recent measures such as freeing for non-resident Indians and putting restrictions on forward hedging contracts have helped stabilize the exchange rate.

The RBI acted after the rupee fell more than 15% against the U.s. dollar between September and mid-December and ended the year down 18.8% against the greenback, making it the worst performer among Asian currencies.

The central bank sold some $4 billion-$5 billion in November to staunch the rupee's fall, according to calculations by Kotak Mahindra Bank . Gokarn said the RBI won't defend any particular rupee level and acts only to curb volatility.

The RBI aims to ensure that currency movements are not being distorted by speculation, but the precise rupee rate "is not something we have a view on," Gokarn said.

"Our whole approach to exchange-rate management has been driven by the need to ensure that our medium-term external situation is secure, while also not allowing the currency to move uncontrollably," Gokarn said.

He said banking-system liquidity is tight but not at crisis levels, noting that money-market rates remain within the Liquidity Adjustment Facility corridor--the gap between the rates at which banks can park funds at the RBI and access money at the central bank's daily liquidity facility.

title: DJ UPDATE: Japan, India Agree To Set Up $15 Billion Swap Line
text:
-The swap line is five times the countries' previous arrangement

-It can help buttress the two economies against euro-zone debt crisis

-The swap line could help the Indian central bank support the weak rupee

(Adds analyst's comment in 6th paragraph, context about rupee in 5th, 7th-8th paragraphs.) 


 
   By Takashi Nakamichi and Prasanta Sahu 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--The Japanese and Indian governments agreed Wednesday to set up a three-year, $15 billion bilateral currency swap line in an effort to buttress their economies against Europe's sovereign debt crisis.

The new swap line--five times the previous arrangement, which expired in early summer--follows a Japan-South Korea deal in October to boost their bilateral swap pact to $70 billion from $13 billion.

The moves signal spreading doubts among Asian economic powerhouses about the ability of European leaders to fix their problems anytime soon.

"At a time when the world economy is unstable, as shown by Europe's sovereign problems and other issues, Japan and India both recognized the need to bolster a Japan-India currency swap line to ensure stability in the financial markets," Japan's Finance Ministry said in a statement.

The swap agreement could help the Reserve Bank of India support the Indian rupee, which has fallen nearly 15% against the U.S. dollar since April, making it the worst performing currency in Asia.

"It will backstop the Indian rupee and reduce the pessimism," said Priyanka Kishore, a foreign exchange strategist at Standard Chartered Bank.

The RBI has frequently said it doesn't want to deplete India's foreign-exchange reserves through regular interventions to steady the rupee, but would only step in to check excess volatility.

The RBI has so far stopped short of aggressively intervening in the market, but had taken a number of small measures to boost capital inflows and curb speculation in the foreign-exchange market.

The swap deal is part of a package of agreements that includes Indian pledges to relax financial regulation so that Japanese companies can make investments more easily.

Concerns have been growing about the damage Europe's debt problems could do to Asia, one of the world's most important growth drivers, if, for example, European banks unwind their investments in Asia to cover losses from their holdings of risky European government debt.

Japan surprised the world over the weekend by announcing a broad set of currency deals with China, the world's second-largest economy after the U.S., but Tokyo sees India as key to its economic future. India's high growth rate, driven by local consumption, offers attractive export prospects. Over the three years through 2010, Japan's exports to India rose 47% to $9 billion, while its imports from the South Asian country climbed 36% to $5.7 billion, the Japanese finance ministry said.

title: Indian rupee closes off lows as shares perk up
text:
* Dollar demand from local oil companies weighs

* Volumes low due to year-end caution, recent RBI steps - traders

* Rupee seen at 53.10-53.15/dlr early next week - Canara Bank

(Updates to close)

By Aditya Phatak

MUMBAI, Dec 22 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee closed weaker but off its intraday low on Thursday as domestic equities turned positive after early losses and on signs that the European Central Bank's massive loans to banks will avert a euro zone credit crunch for now.

Some traders cited dollar sales by foreign banks as a reason for the rupee's rebound, while others speculated about possible intervention by the Reserve Bank of India. Demand from oil importers limited the currency's gains, traders said.

The RBI is widely thought to have sold dollars on Dec. 15 after the rupee hit a record low of 54.30 to the dollar, and traders suspect it has been intervening intermittently ever since.

Earlier in the day, RBI Governor Duvvuri Subbarao said the central bank was monitoring foreign exchange markets hourly and would step in to contain any sharp volatility.

"Who would want to invite the RBI's wrath, when room to manoeuvre in the market has already reduced drastically," said a trader at a private sector bank, referring to recent measures taken by the central bank to curb speculative trading.

This, he said, was the main reason that players cut their long dollar positions once the euro and equities reversed course.

"Everybody is afraid of that phone call (from the RBI)," he said.

(For details on steps taken by the RBI to curb the rupee's volatility and increase inflows see: )

The euro is seen as the main gauge of global risk sentiment, so is closely tracked by traders in emerging markets such as India.

The rupee ended at 52.72/73 to the dollar, down from Wednesday's close of 52.49/50. It hit a low of 52.90.

Demand from oil importers, the largest buyers of dollars in the domestic market, kept the rupee under pressure for most of the session.

"Risk sentiment is still jittery and dollar demand from oil companies has been persistent," said Ravi Kumar, manager foreign dealer at Canara Bank. "Rupee could weaken to around 53.10-53.15 next week as month-end demand from oil companies rises."

Traders said volumes in the dollar-rupee market have fallen sharply due to a combination of the RBI's curbs on trading limits on Dec. 15 and caution ahead of book closures on Dec. 31.

One-month offshore non-deliverable forward contracts were quoted at 53.19, indicating more short-term weakness in the onshore spot rate.

In the currency futures market, the most-traded near-month dollar-rupee contracts on the National Stock Exchange, the MCX-SX and the United Stock Exchange closed around 52.77, with total volume at $3.76 billion.

title: FACTBOX-Steps countries are taking to counter hot money
text:

Nov 5 (Reuters) - More governments around the world are moving to keep their currencies from strengthening as investors, turning their backs on low interest rates in developed economies, pour money into higher-yielding markets.

Below are recent cases of direct or indirect government intervention in the currency markets, compiled by Reuters:

SOUTH AFRICA WANTS WEAKER RAND, ADMITS IT WILL BE DIFFICULT

* New long-term growth plan envisages "a careful balancing of more active monetary policy interventions to achieve growth...through a more competitive exchange rate and a lower cost of capital," government says on Oct. 26.

* Government insists this does not violate G20 agreement, to which South Africa subscribed three days earlier, to avoid competitive currency devaluations.

* Government says it will build up foreign currency reserves to curb rand <ZAR=> appreciation.

* But analysts doubt it has financial muscle to force down rand; finance minister says international cooperation needed.

* Treasury Director General says tax on capital inflows into bond market would not work for South Africa.

TURKEY STEPS UP FOREIGN EXCHANGE BUYING

* Central bank says on Oct. 1 it will raise the amount of foreign exchange that it buys at weekly auctions, as the lira <TRY=> hits its strongest versus the dollar in almost a year.

* Central bank official says it will buy a maximum of $500 million of foreign currency each week; previously, it usually bought $200 million with an option of buying a further $200 million.

* Prime minister recently said Turkey needed to build up its forex reserves.

title: India adviser: 'All options' to handle inflows surge, volatility
text:
* As of now, not in favour of imposing direct controls

* India can absorb present level of inflows

* Current account deficit largely funded by inflows (Adds quotes, background)

By Manoj Kumar

NEW DELHI, Nov 4 (Reuters) - India will keep all options on the table to handle a surge of capital inflows and the attendant volatitily, but is not in favor of direct controls, the Finance Ministry's chief economic adviser said on Thursday.

The comments came a day after the U.S. Federal Reserve committed to buy $600 billion more in government bonds by June 2011, a move many fear will lead to a surge of investment inflows into emerging markets like India, Korea, Brazil and China.

"Part of the money is also coming in because of the confidence in India's ability to grow," Chief Economic Adviser to the Finance Ministry Kaushik Basu said.

"So we have to keep all options on the table about how we handle it in case there is a surge and volatility."

India however faces a huge current account deficit which is nearing almost 3 percent of GDP, a gap which is largely financed by capital inflows. Policymakers therefore say India does not need to impose capital controls right now.

"India is a much stronger economy today and so we should be able to take it," Basu said.

India has already received more than $26 bilion of capital inflows into equities so far this year.

India's response has been measured in comparison to other economies like China, South Korea and Brazil who have vowed to fight the latest round of quantitative easing by the United States. [ID:nTOE6A300V]

Central banks in countries like Japan and South Korea that are faced with a rising local currency have indicated they may take measures to counter the appreciation pressure.

India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, has however maintained it will only intervene in foreign exchange markets if inflows turn 'lumpy' or 'volatile'.

The Indian rupee <INR=IN> has appreciated 5.1 percent in 2010.

However, on the global front, Wednesdays move by the Fed could have negative repercussions for the forthcoming Group of 20 meeting in Seoul.

With many emerging countries willing to retaliate, government officials say a meaningful outcome to the currency and global imbalance debate now looks a little bleak in Seoul. (Editing by Bryson Hull)

title: =DJ UPDATE: India Sept Exports Up 23.2%; High Commodity Prices, Low Base Help
text:
(Adds comments of trade minister, details)

By Prasanta Sahu and Anant Vijay Kala

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--India's September exports rose sharply helped by high global commodity prices and a weak base in the previous year, keeping the country on track to meet its export target despite a strong local currency.

Exports during the month rose 23.2% to $18.02 billion from a year ago, Trade Secretary Rahul Khullar said Monday.

In August, exports were up 22.5% at $16.64 billion.

Exports till September from the start of the fiscal year on April 1 increased 27.6% to $103.3 billion, Khullar told reporters at a conference.

Imports in September rose 26.1% to $27.14 billion, while between April-September they were 29.9% higher at $166.5 billion.

The trade deficit in September narrowed to $9.12 billion from August's $13.06 billion as imports moderated. The trade gap was $63.2 billion in April-Sept.

"In the first six months (of the fiscal year) we have done well," said Minister for Commerce and Industry Anand Sharma. "We are very much on track to meet our target of the 15% increase (in exports) and India's exports to cross $200 billion this (fiscal) year," Sharma added.

India's export growth slowed for the first time in nine months in July after expanding more than 30% each month between November and June largely because of weaker base year levels at the time of the global economic crisis.

Khullar said the favorable base will likely continue for three to four more months, aiding export growth.

Also, global festive demand in November and December will likely raise consumption overseas and could further spur demand for Indian exports.

But a recent spike in the rupee could dampen prospects for Indian exporters.

Trade Secretary Khullar said a strong rupee could hurt exporters with a time lag.

The rupee has risen 1.76% against the U.S. dollar since Sept. 28, driven by heavy foreign fund inflows into local stocks and subscriptions to the almost $3.5 billion initial share sale of state-run miner Coal India Ltd.

Trade Minister Sharma said the exchange rate movement wasn't presently volatile, a sign that the government or the Reserve Bank Of India may not yet intervene to stem the rise and shield Indian exporters.

"We don't see that we have reached a stage where the rupee (appreciation) can be termed as volatile," Sharma said. "The RBI and the finance ministry are keeping a close watch," Sharma added.

India's central bank has reiterated it will intervene in the foreign exchange market only if movements in the rupee are volatile or lumpy.

title: RPT-INTERVIEW-India FinMin: Inflation may have hit plateau
text:
(Repeats story issued on Sunday)

 GYEONGJU, South Korea, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Headline inflation in India, which was at 8.62 percent in September, may have reached a plateau, Indian Finance Minister Pranab Mukherjee said.

 High food prices, which have helped keep broader inflation in India well above the central bank's comfort zone of around 5 to 6 percent, are the result of both supply and demand factors that reflect changing consumption patterns, Mukherjee told Reuters.

 The Reserve Bank of India, which expects headline WPI inflation to ease to 6 percent by the end of March, has raised policy rates five times this year to rein in inflation and is widely expected to raise rates by a further 25 basis points on Nov 2.

 "The direction of the inflation rate movement is consistent with the Reserve Bank's projection made in the July review, though the magnitude could be slightly different. Inflation rates seem to have reached a plateau," Mukherjee said in a written response to questions from Reuters emailed late on Saturday.

 India's wholesale price index (WPI) inflation was in double-digits for six months through July.

 Mukherjee said food inflation, which has been stubbornly high and came in at more than 15 percent in early October on an annualised basis, is both a demand and supply issue.

 "High food inflation reflects both demand and supply factors. Demand factors ... reflect changing consumption patterns," said Mukherjee, who was in South Korea for the Group of 20 meeting of finance ministers.

 Rising incomes fuelled by an economy on track to grow at 8.5 percent this fiscal year have led Indians to consume more food.

 IMF REFORMS

 Mukherjee welcomed a G20 deal on International Monetary Fund reforms that underlines the growing clout of developing economies by giving them a bigger voice.

 "Our complaint was that the quota share should reflect ground reality and economic strengths currently. Otherwise it would have eroded the credibility of the institution. That has now been corrected," Mukherjee said.

 India's finance minister also said further quantitative easing by advanced economies would cause problems, and Indian policymakers will respond depending on the extent of the easing.

 Emerging economies including India are seeing an influx of fund flows from the developing world as investors seek higher returns, pushing up asset prices and putting upward pressure on currencies including the rupee <INR=IN>.

 The U.S. Fed is expected to embark on another round of asset purchases, which would inject more liquidity into markets. [ID:nN21128261]

 Mukherjee reiterated the central bank's stated position that India will intervene only if capital flows are "lumpy" and "volatile".

 Global regulators are still working on a framework for identifying systemically important financial institutions but Mukherjee said Indian banks may be be asked to maintain additional capital and liquidity levels once proposals are finalised at the G20 level.  (Editing by Tony Munroe)

title: Q+A-Will  India intervene  again to curb rising rupee?
text:
MUMBAI/NEW DELHI, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Expectations are growing that India's central bank will continue to intervene in currency markets after its suspected dollar-buying last week to ease upward pressure on the rupee.

A surge of capital inflows have pushed the rupee up 6 percent since the start of September and close to 5 percent on the year, threatening to slow export growth.

The suspected dollar-buying by the central bank, which traders believe was its first such move this year, came days before Coal India kicked-off a $3.5 billion IPO, the country's largest, that is expected to draw billions of additional dollars into India.

More governments around the world are moving to keep their currencies from appreciating or weighing capital controls as investors pour money into higher-yielding markets. [ID:nSGE69503F]

Below are some question and answers on the Reserve Bank of India and intervention in the currency market.

WILL RBI INTERVENE AGAIN?

Possibly. The partially convertible rupee rose to a more-than two-year high beyond 44 per dollar last week.

Persistent U.S. dollar weakness and ultra-low interest rates in developed markets have prompted a surge in flows into faster-growing emerging economies that could prolong the upward pressure.

Asia's third-largest economy has attracted a record $33 billion this year from overseas into stocks and bonds, which are helpful to the extent that they can help fund a current account deficit forecast to reach $42 billion by the end of March.

More U.S. quantitative easing could unleash further flows into emerging markets like India.

Exporters, which are a powerful lobby, have argued for intervention. Margins in key industries including technology services and textiles are being squeezed by a strong rupee.

Central bank Deputy Governor Subir Gokarn said India must manage inflows so it can fund its current account deficit while at the same time not harming exports. [ID:nSGE69E03S]

Export competitiveness is more than a function of a straight two-way quote between the rupee and the dollar. The Real Effective Exchange Rate takes into account the inflation differential between two trading economies and is a better gauge of the effective exchange rate between them.

The rupee's REER based on a trade-weighed basis of six of its major trading partners provisionally moved up to 111.73 on Sept. 9, above 102.45 at the end of 2009. A level of 100 is neutral.

The central bank maintains that it will step in to curb volatility but will not try to protect any particular level in the currency.

HOW WILL RBI MANAGE ADDED LIQUIDITY IF IT INTERVENES AGAIN?

If the central bank keeps intervening in the market it would result in more rupees entering the banking system, adding to the challenge of inflation management. Headline inflation at 8.6 percent in September is well above the central bank's comfort zone of 5-6 percent.

Right now, liquidity in the Indian banking system is relatively tight, due in part to funds flowing into IPO applications as well as slower-than-expected government spending of the proceeds from telecoms spectrum auctions earlier this year, making it an easier time to intervene.

The RBI can also sterilise additional rupees resulting from its dollar purchases -- something it did three years ago through the issuance of market stabilisation scheme bonds (MSS).

However, doing so is expensive given high market yields, and would add to the government's already high fiscal burden.

For 2010/11, the central bank fixed an upper limit of 500 billion rupees ($11.3 billion) for bond sales under MSS.

WHAT OTHER MEASURES CAN INDIA TAKE TO MANAGE INFLOWS?

Indian policymakers say they do not favour capital controls for now, but Finance Minister Pranab Mukherjee last week said he was on the lookout for "toxic assets".

India imposed controls in 2007 when it tightened rules for unregistered foreign investors by clamping down on the issuance of participatory notes, or P-notes, which were a popular vehicle for foreign investors in stocks.

RBI Governor Duvvuri Subbarao said recently that capital controls can be skirted and making frequent policy changes can send the wrong signal to investors.

India occasionally adjusts limits on flows into debt.

For example, it recently increased limits in government and corporate bonds by $5 billion each, to $10 billion and $20 billion, respectively.

The increase came with the caveat that the added limit can only be used to invest in at least 5-year paper. That encourages flows into long-term investments such as infrastructure and discourages a flood of hot money looking for short-end arbitrage.

India could also clamp down on external commercial borrowings (ECBs) by Indian companies looking to access cheaper funds from abroad, especially in a rising domestic interest rate scenario.

India could tighten the ECB tap by reducing sectoral ceilings, more stringently specifying end-uses for ECB funds and perhaps auctioning ECB entitlements. title: FUND VIEW-Aviva favours won, rupee among emerging  currencies
text:
LONDON, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Good yield differentials and a low likelihood of stringent capital controls make the Korean won and Indian rupee among the best emerging currency bets against a weak dollar, a fund manager at Aviva said.

 Kieran Curtis, who helps manage $1.4 billion in local currency emerging debt at UK insurer Aviva, says that based on real effective exchange rate (REER) analysis, the Korean won <KRW=>, the Philippine peso <PHP=> and the Indian rupee <INR=> look the most attractively valued Asian currencies.

 In Latin America, the Mexican peso <MXN=> stands out and in emerging Europe, the Polish zloty <PLN=> and Hungarian forint <HUF=> could have some upside, says Curtis, whose fund gets currency exposure via local emerging debt and also uses forwards as an overlay to optimise FX returns.

 "Basically, positioning and pressure on valuations on these currencies has been weaker than, say, on the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> and Brazilian real <BRL=>," he said. "In theory they have more room to appreciate than most other emerging currencies."

 Expectation of additional large doses of monetary stimulus for the U.S. economy has kicked the dollar to multi-year lows against many emerging currencies, fuelling fears more developing countries will bring in measures to stem currency appreciation.

 Brazil on Monday raised its levy on bond inflows to 6 percent while Thailand has put a 15 percent tax on interest and capital gains on Thai bonds. 

 South Korea's finance minister said on Tuesday the government is preparing measures to deal with problems caused by foreign capital flows, while India's central bank intervened in rupee markets last week for the first time this year.

 But Curtis said investors must learn to deal with FX controls or seek out markets where curbs may be less punitive.

 "The Bank of Korea is active but has never really been successful in controlling the strength or volatility of the won," Curtis said.

 "Inflation in Asia is more stable and currencies still look cheap on (an) absolute basis," he said. "They are not places that really manipulate their currencies much."

 TURKISH BONDS OVERVALUED

Currency appreciation and the collapse in core yields have pushed year-to-date returns on emerging local bonds <.JGEGDCM> to around 17 percent.

 Emerging European currencies should benefit if the German economy continues to improve, Curtis says though he remains underweight the forint <EURHUF=>, citing uncertainty over Hungary's ability to tackle its budget deficit and its relationship with the International Monetary Fund.

 Unlike the Fed and Bank of Japan, the European Central Bank has not embarked on more stimulus, pushing the euro <EUR=> to a recent eight-month high against the greenback. 

 "The risk for the forint and zloty is that they could get a kick from any ECB policy change. But the eurozone can tolerate FX strength in the short term and that is good for currencies that trade high-beta to the euro," Curtis added.

 Curtis is neutral on the Brazilian real, noting that the rise in the inflows tax will affect future flows.

 "You have to be a medium or long-term investor to make it worthwhile ... You have to hold (the bonds) for over a year to realise the value," he said. 

 Curtis acknowleges signs of overvaluation in some emerging local bond curves. He cites Turkey where interest rates are 7 percent despite five-year average inflation at 8.7 percent. 

 "In many countries interest rates ought to be higher and bond curves ought to be a bit higher. They look a bit expensive. But they are still very inexpensive compared with core markets."  (Editing by Susan Fenton)

title: Indian rupee snaps 3-day gains as euro slips
text:
* Euro's losses versus dollar weigh on rupee sentiment

* Early losses in local shares also hurt the local unit

* Rupee to underperform Asian peers in medium term: BarCap

* Rupee seen at 42/dollar by mid-2011: DBS (Updates to close)

By Swati Bhat

MUMBAI, Oct 18 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee on Monday snapped a three-day winning streak as the dollar's gains versus major units overseas weighed, but hopes for capital inflows stayed firm with the launch of the country's largest-ever share sale.

The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> closed at 44.36/37 per dollar, 0.6 percent below 44.10/11 at close on Friday, when the rupee rose as high as 43.95, its highest since Aug. 29, 2008. The rupee traded in a band of 44.1800-44.4150 during the day.

"I was anticipating today's move. Euro also started reversal from $1.4100 and stocks also seem to be heading lower. After the mega flows, there should be some reversal," said Hari Chandramgathan, a foreign exchange dealer with Federal Bank.

The U.S. dollar bounced from a 10-month low against a basket of currencies on Monday, as investors uncertain about the extent of monetary easing by the Federal Reserve trimmed bearish bets against the greenback. [USD/]

The index of the dollar <.DXY> against six majors was down 0.4 percent when the rupee market closed.

"We think room for further appreciation of the INR is limited, as short USD positions are showing signs of being overstretched and the RBI is likely to join other Asian central banks in trying to limit currency appreciation," analysts at Barclays Capital wrote in a daily note.

On Friday, the Reserve Bank of India governor Duvvuri Subbarao said the central bank will intervene in the forex market if inflows turn lumpy. [ID:nSGE69E0CM]

Traders said they will continue to closely watch the central bank this week, which bought dollars on Thursday in a move they believe was the first intervention this year. [ID:nSGE69D0EX]

"It is highly likely that the Coal India IPO will be highly oversubscribed and we could see some FII repatriation once the IPO allocation is finalised," analysts at Barclays Capital said.

"We look for USD/INR to move in a range of 43.90 to 44.50 for the week with an upside bias. In the medium term, we think the rising current account deficit and weaker fundamentals are likely to result in INR underperforming against other Asian currencies".

The world's largest coal miner Coal India's $3.5 billion initial public offering is currently underway and is expected to see a flood of foreign capital inflows. [ID:nSGE68T06Y]

"Globally, USD was stronger today, so a bit of that's rubbed off on INR," said Ananth Narayan G., head of fixed income, currencies and commodities, South Asia at Standard Chartered Bank in Mumbai.

Early losses in local shares also hurt the rupee. Shares <.BSESN> reversed early losses and eked out a 0.2 percent gain on Monday, as robust foreign fund interest and strong September quarter earnings overshadowed the pressure from the launch of country's biggest-ever initial share offer. [.BO]

For the year to date, the rupee is up 4.9 percent on record $23.3 billion foreign fund inflows into shares.

"We are looking generally for Asian currencies to appreciate against the dollar about 5-6 percent per year for next five years," said David W. Carbon, managing director of economic and currency research at DBS.

He said DBS expects the rupee to be at 42 to the dollar by mid-2011.

One-month offshore non-deliverable forward contracts <PNDF> were quoted at 44.73, weaker than the onshore spot rate.

In the currency futures market <INRFUTURES>, the most traded near-month dollar-rupee contracts on the National Stock Exchange, MCX-SX and United Stock Exchange closed at 44.4675, 44.4625 and 44.4625 respectively, with the total traded volume on the three exchanges at about an average $7.4 billion. title: UPDATE 1- India  cbank head says will  intervene  if flows lumpy
text:
* India cbank will intervene if flows lumpy, volatile-head

* Cbank will take steps to ease liquidity situation: deputy (Updates with quotes, details, background, deputy comments)

By Rajesh Kumar Singh

CHANDIGARH, India, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of India will intervene in the forex market if inflows turn lumpy and volatile, its governor said on Friday.

The central bank on Thursday bought dollars to stem the rupee's strength, traders had said -- a move which they believe was the RBI's first intervention in 2010. [ID:nSGE69D0EX]

"We are watching the exchange rate situation. Our policy is quite clear, which we have said a number of times that we will intervene if flows are lumpy or volatile or if it disrupts the macro-economic situation," Duvvuri Subbarao said.

"That remains our policy," he told reporters at a press conference after the RBI's board meeting in the northern Indian state, but declined comment when asked if the central bank had indeed intervened in the market on Thursday.

Subbarao said he would not elaborate on when the central bank will or will not intervene.

India has attracted a record $22.5 billion in inflows into stocks this year, which have put an upward pressure on the rupee.

Since the start of September, the rupee <INR=IN> has appreciated 6.8 percent on foreign equity inflows of more than $9.5 billion, pushing the currency to a more than 25-month high.

India must manage capital inflows so that it can fund its current account deficit while at the same time not harming exports, Deputy Governor Subir Gokarn had said on Thursday. [ID:nSGE69E03S]

TEMPORARY LIQUIDITY SQUEEZE

Outflows towards state-run Coal India's initial public offering to raise up to $3.5 billion in the country's biggest initial public offering (IPO) have been squeezing liquidity in the banking system.

The world's largest coal miner's IPO will open on Monday.

"This IPO may add pressure (on liquidity) at least temporarily, so it is something that we will look at and if the circumstances warrant, we will think about responding," deputy governor Subir Gokarn said at the press conference.

The Reserve Bank of India has been reluctant to intervene in currency markets, but may be forced to in coming weeks as foreign investors are expected to pour in billions of dollars to buy shares in the country's largest-ever IPO. [ID:nSGE69A09L]

Traders said an intervention at current levels would serve two purposes -- infuse liquidity into the system, which has a deficit of over 800 billion rupees according to the liquidity adjustment auction, and prevent sharp appreciation of the rupee.

Another deputy governor Shyamala Gopinath also said on Friday the central bank was closely monitoring the liquidity situation and would take appropriate actions as and when needed. (Writing by Swati Bhat; editing by Malini Menon)
