title: RPT-RBI FOCUS-IPO flows may force cbank to  intervene  in  FX
text:
(Repeats story issued late on Wednesday)

 * India cbank reluctant to intervene in forex market

 * Coal India's $3.5 bln IPO to trigger more inflows

 * RBI typically intervenes only to manage volatility

 * Cbank not seen favouring capital controls

 By Suvashree Dey Choudhury and Tony Munroe

 MUMBAI, Oct 13 (Reuters) - India's central bank is reluctant to intervene in currency markets but may be forced to in coming weeks as foreign investors pour in billions of dollars to buy shares in the country's largest ever IPO.

 Foreign investment in Indian stocks stands at a record $21.8 billion and more than a third of that flowed in since the start of September, pushing the rupee to a two-year high last week.

Coal India's $3.5 billion share sale next week could prove the tipping point for intervention if, as expected, it generates heavy demand, although Reserve Bank of India sources downplayed any intention to manage inflows and ease pressure on the rupee.

 "We are not traders. We don't buy dollars and sell dollars alternately. The volatility will be temporary and exporters and importers will take care of the levels," said an official, who is directly involved in currency management.

 The central bank won't entirely dismiss intervention though. Officials said the RBI, as always, stands ready to manage any currency volatility and Governor Duvvuri Subbarao indicated in Washington over the weekend that the central bank will intervene if inflows are "lumpy and volatile".

 That's exactly what India may get from the Coal India IPO, which is expected to be popular given the company's dominant market position and because a lower-then-expected price band for the share offer could result in heavy oversubscription.

 "As of now, we don't intend to intervene as this is just a temporary issue of flows coming in and going out," the RBI official said, declining to be identified.

 "The governor's statement was a weapon to calm down markets and ensure there is no panic. It doesn't necessarily mean we will intervene. Intervention by us is a big thing," the source said.

 <^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Coal India's IPO                            [ID:nSGE69C09B]

 Breakingviews column on IPO flows           [ID:nLDE69B0V2]

 ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^>

 Half the Coal India shares will be sold to institutions, with the majority of such demand expected to come from overseas.

 Under new rules introduced this year, institutional investors must prefund in full the IPO shares they want to buy. Previously, they had to provide 10 percent up front.

 If the institutional part of the IPO is five times subscribed and foreign funds account for 70 percent of such demand, it would draw more than $6 billion in additional funds into India -- or the equivalent of more than a quarter of the record overseas funds that have already invested in stocks this year.

 The Coal India offer will open to institutions from Oct 18-20 and shares will be allocated within 12 working days of the closing. Refunds of unallocated funds are expected to head back out of India, while IPO proceeds will go into government coffers.

 "Given we will likely see lumpy U.S. dollar inflows first, followed by a part of that going back, we should have RBI watching the market very carefully. Will not be surprised if RBI does come in to smooth the flows out," said Ananth Narayan G, head of fixed income, currencies, commodities-South Asia at Standard Chartered.

 YIELD QUEST

 Sluggish economies and ultra-low interest rates in developed countries have sent a flood of return-hungry funds to emerging markets, putting upward pressure on currencies and prompting many central banks to step in to brake the appreciation.

 Brazil's Petrobras   last month raised $70 billion in the world's largest share sale, adding to inflows already chasing double-digit interest rates and pushing the real <BRL=> to two year peaks.

 Last week, Brazil doubled a tax on foreign investment in bonds to 4 percent, and the central bank has been stepping up buying of dollars.

 Subbarao indicated in Washington, where he attended a meeting of the International Monetary Fund, that he did not support capital controls.

 "Capital controls can be gamed or circumvented. Also stop-go policies send wrong signals to potential investors," he said.

 In 2009, the RBI sold a net $5.8 billion to prevent the rupee from falling below a record low of 52.2, but traders believe it has refrained from intervening this year.

 "There are costs associated with intervention, because we will have to also sterilise the money," the RBI source said.

 The rupee is up 5.3 percent since September. Last year, record inflows of $17.5 billion pushed it up by 4.7 percent.

 More state share sales will further test India's tolerance for inflows. Power Grid Corp  and Hindustan Copper  aim to raise a combined $2.8 billion by year-end.

 On the face of it, India would welcome inflows -- if they are stable. The April-June current account showed a record deficit and on the capital account, foreign direct investment is down this year.

 "Our absorptive capacity for inflows has risen as our current account deficit is growing," a second central bank official, who declined to be identified, told Reuters.  (Editing by Neil Fullick)

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee climbed against the U.S. dollar Thursday for the second straight session as foreign investors bought into local assets ahead of the country's largest-ever share sale next week.

The local unit was also boosted by a rally across the region after the Monetary Authority of Singapore said it will guide its currency higher at a slightly faster pace in a bid to contain inflation.

The dollar slipped to a fresh 25-month low against the rupee before finding heavy support from oil importers as local stocks fell.

The U.S. dollar was at INR44.11 late Thursday, lower than INR44.52 late Wednesday.

"We saw pretty heavy inflows today (Thursday), but we expect this to continue and maybe even intensify over the next two to three days," said the trading head at a foreign bank.

State-run Coal India Ltd.'s upcoming $3.5 billion initial share sale has stoked the appetite of overseas investors, who seek high returns in a fast-expanding economy. The issue, which opens Oct. 18, is expected to trigger a deluge of foreign capital inflows, which could further push the rupee up.

The bank executive expects the dollar to slip to INR43.50 in coming sessions as inflows pick up pace.

But importers continue to buy the greenback heavily at lower levels, slowing the rupee's rise, taking cues from a volatile share market wobbling amid global uncertainty.

The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark 30-share Sensex closed down 190.24 points, or 0.9%, at 20,497.64. The index had gained 2.4% Wednesday.

Besides, speculation on possible central bank intervention may also limit the rupee's rise. But many participants argue that the Reserve Bank of India is unlikely to intervene in the currency market anytime soon.

"The rupee's volatility is unlikely to last beyond a few days, so I don't see the RBI drawn away from its recent stance of avoiding intervention unless it has to," the bank executive said.

The RBI hasn't intervened in the foreign exchange market since November, according to the central bank's data up to August.

In the bond market, Indian government bonds ended flat as traders avoided directional bets ahead of the key September inflation print and an INR110 billion debt sale Friday.

The benchmark 2020 bond ended at INR98.54, a tad lower than INR98.58 last close. The most-traded 8.13% 2022 bond ended at INR100.52, inching up from INR100.47 at Wednesday's close.

Traders expects the monthly wholesale price index for September to provide clarity on the central bank's next move at its forthcoming rate-setting meeting on Nov. 2.

India's inflation likely accelerated 8.55% from a year earlier in September, quicker than the 8.51% rise in August, according to the median estimate in a Dow Jones Newswires poll of 19 economists.

(Repeats story issued on Sunday)

 MUMBAI, Oct 10 (Reuters) - India would intervene in the foreign exchange markets if needed to maintain stability, the central bank's governor said during a panel discussion at the International Monetary Fund in Washington on Saturday.

 Foreign institutional investors have pumped a record $21.3 billion into Indian equities so far this year, helping push the rupee <INR=IN> to a 25-month high last week.

 The Reserve Bank of India, whose official view on the level of the rupee is uncertain and typically intervenes only to soften sharp moves in the partially convertible currency, has refrained from intervention during the recent rupee rally.

 "If the inflows are lumpy and volatile or if they disrupt the macroeconomic situation, we will do so," RBI Governor Duvvuri Subbarao said of intervention.

 A surge in fund flows into faster-growing emerging economies has prompted several to intervene to head off appreciation and protect exports.

 "Our intervention will be to keep liquidity conditions consistent with activity in the real economy and to maintain financial stability and not to stand against developments driven by changing economic fundamentals," Subbarao said according to a text of his remarks published on the RBI website on Sunday.

 He said India has not intervened because its absorption of inflows has increased as the current account deficit widens on a surge in imports on an upbeat outlook for growth and investment.

 "Economies that have current account surpluses or only small deficits have intervened. That does not mean we won't intervene," Subbarao said.

 He said the Indian central bank would continue to use macro-prudential instruments in order to maintain stability, noting for example a recent move to tighten rules for bank lending against stocks.  (Reporting by Tony Munroe; Editing by Greg Mahlich)

title: India 's  Central Bank  To  Intervene  In  FX  Mkt If Flows Lumpy -Gov
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India will intervene in the foreign exchange market if capital inflows become volatile or lumpy, Reserve Bank of India Governor Duvvuri Subbarao said Saturday, in what may be a sign of the central bank's growing concern on a sharp rupee rise. "If the inflows are lumpy and volatile or if they disrupt the macroeconomic situation, we will do so (intervene)," Subbarao said in an address to global central bankers at the International Monetary Fund in Washington, posted on the central bank's website.

"Our intervention will be to keep liquidity conditions consistent with activity in the real economy and to maintain financial stability, and not to stand against developments driven by changing economic fundamentals," he said.

The comments acquire significance ahead of a host of initial share sales by companies. Coal India Ltd's initial public offering, which is slated to garner between $3 billion and $3.5 billion, will open on Oct. 18. It will be India's largest ever IPO.

The issue is expected to generate huge foreign fund interest and foreign exchange dealers expect a sharp appreciation pressure on the rupee due to lumpy inflows in the offering.

Subbarao, however, said that the RBI has stayed away so far from the currency markets in spite of record portfolio inflows for a single month in September.

India has so far been swamped with capital inflows in recent months as foreign funds invest in emerging market economies seeking higher returns, resulting in the rupee's appreciation against the U.S. dollar.

Foreign funds have pumped in $5.43 billion in September alone, topping over $20 billion for 2010. The rupee has gained 3.3% in the July-September quarter.

On Thursday, the Indian rupee rose to a 25-month high against the U.S. dollar. The dollar plummeted to an intraday low of INR44.12, a level not seen since Sept. 8, 2008.

Despite a recent surge in capital inflows, India's central bank, unlike many of its counterparts in Asia, has stayed away from intervening in its foreign exchange markets.

"The reason why we did not feel the need to intervene is because our absorption, driven by a widening current account deficit as imports have surged on the back of a positive outlook on growth and investment, has also increased," Subbarao said.

Japan on Friday said it will monitor the yen's ascent with "greater interest" and could foresee another intervention in the currency market if deemed necessary.

Japan intervened in the currency market for the first time in more than six years in September, dumping around Y2 trillion to tame the yen's upward trend, which hurt exports and the overall economy.

Several emerging market economies including Brazil and South Korea have been perturbed on the surging capital inflows ands have taken action to hold the value of their currencies down.

Subbarao said the RBI has avoided flip-flops in its policy actions and that the use of controls should be prudent.

"We already do and will continue to use them (macroprudential regulations). But the operative word here is prudential."

The central bank recently tightened rules for bank lending against stocks.

Subbarao said that adequate forex reserves act as a buffer or self-insurance.

India, being a current account deficit country, the "reserves comprise essentially borrowed resources, and we are therefore more vulnerable to sudden stops and reversals as compared with countries with current account surpluses," Subbarao said.

India's April-June current account deficit widened to $13.7 billion from $4.5 billion a year ago.

Implementing Basel III A Challenge

Subbarao said growing economies such as India will face a challenge in the implementation of new global banking rules, or Basel III norms, which may require lenders to have more capital and liquidity.

That may raise lending costs for banks and reduce overall lending when credit demand begins to pick up, Subbarao said.

In July, the Basel committee put out a paper indicating the broad agreement reached on the Basel III proposals.

The proposed reforms will require banks to hold more and better-quality capital and to carry more liquid assets, which will limit their leverage and mandate them to build up capital buffers in good times that can be drawn down in periods of stress.

A Bank of International Settlements study shows that countries may have to lose about 0.2% of gross domestic product over a four-year period if the new capital regulations come into effect.

The implementations of the Basel III norms come at a time when Indian banks are witnessing loan growth. India may be the second-fastest growing economy in Asia but non-bank sources of credit and internal savings have kept bank credit growth low.

"Our credit demand will see rapid expansion because of the investment needs of infrastructure, the 'catch up' of the manufacturing sector, and most importantly, because of the credit demand that financial inclusion will bring," Subbarao said.

title: =DJ MONEY TALKS: Rising Rupee Won't Force  India Intervention
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India's central bank is unlikely to intervene in the near term to kneecap a sharply rising rupee.

Despite some noise from policy makers about hot-money flows, the Reserve Bank of India appears content to let the dollar slide against the rupee as long as the move isn't disorderly or one-sided.

That leaves India and Australia as the most prominent exceptions to the Asia-Pacific trend of central banks intervening to sell their own currencies in a bid to protect their exports.

RBI Deputy Gov. Subir Gokarn said Tuesday that capital inflows were emerging as a "potential threat" and the central bank was thinking of ways to deal with it. The comments sparked off speculation the RBI may be preparing to intervene in the currency market for the first time since November to curb the rupee's rise.

However, there are valid reasons for the bank to stay on the sidelines.

The rupee has been a laggard in Asia for most of the year--falling 1.1% against the dollar between January and August. Recently though it has surged higher and is up around 6.7% since the beginning of September: the dollar fell to a 25-month low Thursday at INR44.12.

Foreign funds have made a beeline for Indian equities, pumping in over $20 billion so far in 2010, already exceeding all of last year's investment. Of that, $5.43 billion flowed in during September alone.

While policymakers have zeroed in on such inflows and the potential threat of asset-price bubbles down the road, intervention or any form of capital controls to rein in the rupee appears to be off the radar for now.

With the rupee's gains largely reflecting a broadly weakening dollar, intervention would likely prove ineffective at this stage.

Moreover, the rupee's rise, as measured by the real effective exchange rate, has lagged those of its South Asian and North Asian export competitors in the January-August period, according to Bank of International Settlements data.

Talk of possible capital controls has also been knocked down by Finance Minister Pranab Mukherjee, who said Thursday capital inflows have not distorted market sentiment.

Inflation is another reason why the RBI may take it easy on the rupee. Consumer prices remain high, with headline inflation at 8.5% on-year in August; a higher rupee will provide some relief to policymakers as it cuts into imported inflation.

The government wouldn't want to harm foreign investor sentiment, especially at a time when it needs the inflows to bridge the current-account deficit. The April-June gap was $13.7 billion; it is forecast above 3% of gross domestic product for the fiscal year that ends March.

All of this means policy makers in India can leave the rupee alone for now.

title: AT A GLANCE: Officials Warn  Currency  Fight Can Undermine Global Economy
text:
THE NEWS: A number of high-ranking officials spoke out Thursday on the currency battles that have spurred tensions around the globe, with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Dominique Strauss-Kahn warning that such conflict can undermine the world economy.

A day after U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner essentially accused China of sparking a global currency war, Strauss-Kahn said the IMF needs to launch a "systemic stability initiative" to build international consensus on global currency policies.

Also Thursday, European Central Bank President Jean-Claude Trichet stressed that currency levels should reflect economic fundamentals, while World Bank head Robert Zoellick said multilateral bodies have a role to play in resolving currency tensions but that, ultimately, countries must tackle the issue by rebalancing their economies.

COUNTRIES ON CURRENCY: China is committed to moving toward a flexible exchange rate regime, but the pace currency reform has to be gradual, a People's Bank of China official said Thursday.

India's central bank may move to cap gains in the rupee if it rises to 43-42 against the U.S. dollar, though intervention is unlikely at current levels, a senior finance ministry official said after the local currency hit a 25-month high against the greenback.

Meanwhile, Brazilian central bank President Henrique de Campos Meirelles said that a combination of U.S. policies, European economics and China's fixed exchange rate has led to major distortions in currency markets.

THE MARKETS: The U.S. dollar recovered from a broad slump against most of its rivals as investors pared bets on riskier assets ahead of Friday's reading on the U.S. employment situation.

Thursday afternoon, the euro was at $1.3877 from $1.3929 late Wednesday, according to EBS via CQG. The common currency rose as high as $1.4030. The dollar was at Y82.43 from Y82.96, after falling as low as Y82.11, while the euro was at Y114.40 from Y115.55. The U.K. pound was at $1.5872 from $1.5885. The dollar was at CHF0.9690 from CHF0.9618.

The ICE Dollar Index was at 77.587 from 77.435, rebounding from a dip below 77, its lowest level since January.

WHAT THEY'RE SAYING: "Many do consider their currency as a weapon, and that's certainly not for the good of the global economy," the IMF's Strauss-Kahn said.

"The current policies of the developed countries is leading to very significant capital flows into some of the emerging countries. This is putting upward pressure on exchange rates," said South African Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan, who heads the Group of 24 emerging and developing countries.

"More than ever, I think that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals," the ECB's Trichet said. "Excess volatility ... [has] adverse implications for economic and financial stability."

title: UPDATE:  India  Official: RBI May  Intervene  If Rupee-Dollar Hits INR43-INR42
text:
(Adds comments from official, analyst) 
 
   By Prasanta Sahu 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--India's central bank may move to cap gains in the rupee if it rises to 43-42 against the U.S. dollar, though intervention is unlikely at current levels, a senior finance ministry official said Thursday after the local currency hit a 25-month high against the greenback.

"At the moment, foreign institutional investments have not reached a point where the government and the Reserve Bank of India need to lose sleep," the official told Dow Jones Newswires on condition of anonymity.

But he added that authorities are monitoring the rupee's movements "very carefully."

The dollar was changing hands at INR44.19 in late trade Thursday after hitting INR44.12 in session, a level not seen since September 2008.

Unlike many of its Asian peers, the RBI has stayed away from intervening in its foreign exchange market, despite a recent surge in capital inflows. Foreign funds pumped in $5.43 billion in September alone, and the rupee gained 3.3% in the July-September quarter.

"The (down) move in the USD/INR has been rapid and, if it persists, could increase central bank concerns regarding volatility and competitiveness (of exports)," said Priyanka Chakravarty, a foreign currency strategist at Standard Chartered Bank.

The finance ministry official added that a fresh rush of foreign capital inflows could push the rupee up further, hurting exporters.

Coal India's $3 billion-$3.5 billion share sale, the country's biggest ever initial public offering, is likely to attract foreign investors when it opens on Oct. 18, resulting in large dollar inflows.

"(The) export sector has to be protected and it (impact on exporters) will definitely be a factor that will be at the back of the mind of the RBI governor while he takes a decision," the official said.

RBI Governor D.Subbarao has prioritized taming inflation in the world's second-most populous country, where more than 70% of residents live on less than $2 a day. The relative strength of the rupee, Asia's second best-performer in September, helps curb imported inflation.

India's foreign currency reserves rose 0.4% in the past year, the least among Asia's 10 biggest economies. China's holdings rose by 15%, Japan's 2% and South Korea's 16%.

"RBI intervention, as of now, looks unlikely because the central bank may end up boosting liquidity, which it doesn't want," a senior trader with a German bank said.

Finance Secretary Ashok Chawla, who is in the U.S. ahead of the International Monetary Fund meeting in Washington this weekend, said Wednesday strengthening currencies across the developing world is likely to be a hot topic at the meeting.

But he downplayed concerns over the strength of the rupee, saying that while it may weigh on exporters, it also helps the purchasing power of importers.

title: UPDATE: India  Finance Minister: Don't Think RBI Needs To  Intervene  Now On Rupee Rise
text:
MUMBAI -(Dow Jones)- India's central bank doesn't need to intervene now to moderate the rupee's rise, the country's finance minister said Monday, even as huge capital inflows led to a 3.3% rise in the local unit in the September quarter.

"The Reserve Bank is watching it. I do not think just now it (the rupee strengthening) is a cause for any intervention," Pranab Mukherjee told local television channel ET Now.

"As and when intervention is called for, Reserve Bank will be doing it."

Mukherjee's comments come amid increasing speculation in the foreign exchange market that the central bank may act to slow the rupee's rise even as the Reserve Bank of India has been adopting a hands-off attitude on the local unit.

Lagged RBI data shows that the central bank hasn't intervened in the foreign currency market for eight months to July 31.

This differs from the approaches of other central banks in Asia.

Japan, for example, stepped in heavily on Sept. 15 to cut off a yen rally that threatened to hamper the competitiveness of its exports, dumping a massive Y2 trillion in the market.

The central banks of Malaysia and Korea have both stepped in intermittently to smoothen the movements of their local units.

Traders have been fleeing the greenback, putting in money in riskier currencies, including that of India, the second-fastest growing major economy in the world.

The RBI has intervened around INR43-INR44 to a dollar on previous occasions and the possibility of intervention remains quite strong if the rupee gains more, said local bond house IDBI Gilts in a note.

"As RBI follows the policy of managed float, if the appreciation of INR (rupee) is continued, (an) intervention by RBI becomes quite likely."

Mukherjee also told the news channel that there was no need for the government to consider putting a limit on foreign fund inflows.

"There is (a) stable policy regime. We do not change our policy with some sort of knee-jerk reaction," he said.

India in fact liberalized its foreign fund rules in September, allowing foreigners to invest more in the country's debt markets.

Large capital inflows into the country's stocks have pushed the benchmark 30-share Sensitive Index to a 33-month high. Foreigners pumped in $5.43 billion in September alone.

These portfolio flows are crucial to meet the country's gaping current account deficit, but at the same time they could pose a difficulty for the central bank if they turn out to be hot money, or short-term flows, chasing returns.

But Mukherjee said he doesn't expect any substantial outflows that would create uncertainty as India's economy is growing robustly.

He also said that the central bank wasn't behind the curve in raising interest rates, although he said that persistently high food inflation was a cause of worry.

Mukherjee expects food prices to moderate after the festive season and said that the central bank must strike a balance between growth and inflation.

Food prices in India rose for the fifth-straight week with the food articles index, rising 0.8% to 179.9 in the week ended Sept. 18, latest data showed.

Deepak Mohanty, an executive director with the RBI said last week in a speech that food price inflation may acquire a structural character, unless supply-side measures were taken.

The central bank has already raised the key borrowing rate by 125 basis points, and the key lending rate by 175 basis points so far in 2010 in a bid to anchor inflationary expectations.

-By Bijou George, Dow Jones Newswires; +91-22-6145-6111; bijou.george@dowjones.com [ 10-04-10 0725ET ]

title: HEARD ON THE STREET:  India  Unruffled By Rupee Swing
text:
Intervention is the latest buzz in Asia's currency markets. India remains an outlier.

It's not for a lack of volatility in the rupee: The currency has jumped 3.4% against the greenback so far in September -- most of that in the last week alone. The gains have come during a surge in investment into India's capital markets. Foreigners have bought $3 billion worth of Indian shares already in September alone , nearly a fifth of their total buying for the year so far.

The steep gain has currency traders looking for signs the Reserve Bank of India might step in and slow things down. There's good reason, though, to think it won't.

For one, intervening against a rising rupee will add capital to India's banking system -- undermining the central bank's own fight against inflation. The inflation problem has forced the RBI to raise banks' reserve requirements, for example, to ensure that they have less to lend.

True, the RBI can offset the additional liquidity by selling so-called sterilization bonds to Indian banks -- again with the intention of tying their capital up, but that's not without a cost. India typically invests its reserves in U.S. Treasurys, where yields are lower than what the RBI will pay those banks, creating a situation called negative carry in which the central bank loses money as those sterilization bonds stack up. Recent rate hikes in India mean the difference in yields between two-year Indian bonds and U.S. Treasurys has widened to 5.87 percentage points from 3.5 percentage points eight months ago, the Royal Bank of Scotland says.

Anyway, over the long-term, India's economic fundamentals take care of the RBI's job here. India imports more than it exports, and as the country's importers busily convert their rupees into dollars they also offset the inflow of global investor funds. Widening current account deficit, meanwhile, is a good reason for the RBI to stay away from blocking the inflow of dollars.

Unlike for its peers in the region, intervention is one task off the RBI's desk.

(Harsh Joshi is a Heard on the Street columnist in Mumbai. He has been with Dow Jones Newswires since 2007 and covered the central bank, money and foreign exchange markets, and the banking sector. He can be reached at harsh.joshi@dowjones.com or at +91-22-6145-6101. )

By Bharghavi Nagaraju

BANGALORE, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Indian shares reset 32-month highs for the fourth straight session on Wednesday driven by continued robust foreign fund inflows and a catch-up rally in index-heavyweight Reliance Industries Ltd .

India's top software services exporters, which derive more than half their revenue from the United States, joined the party as promising U.S. retail sales data boosted optimism over recovery in the world's largest economy.

The market took in its stride India's widening trade gap, which stood at a 23-month high in August, and a higher deficit outlook for the financial year ending March 2011. But, the trade secretary said the bulging deficit was not yet a problem and could be financed. [ID:nSGE68E0AH].

The 30-share BSE index <.BSESN> ended up 0.8 percent at 19,502.11 points, with 17 of its components advancing. It hit a high of 19,554.50 points, its highest since January 2008.

"Foreign institutional investor money is what is driving the market as of now and will continue to drive as long as there is no major upheaval in the international markets," said Ambareesh Baliga, vice president at Karvy Stock Broking.

"When money is chasing growth, it is difficult for us to fix a valuation for the market. It is the money that decides the valuation."

India, Asia's third-largest economy, is expected to surpass government estimates for an 8.5 percent growth in 2010/11 boosted by a surprise 13.8 percent jump in factory output in July.

Foreigners have poured in $14.3 billion into Indian stocks so far this year helping the benchmark index rise 11.7 percent. In 2009, a record foreign fund inflow of $17.6 billion led to an 81-percent surge in the index.

Reliance Industries, which was down 9.3 percent this year until Tuesday on concerns over diversification into non-core businesses and delay in ramp-up of gas production, surged up 2.3 percent to close at 1,010.45 rupees.

Tata Consultancy Services and Infosys Technologies , India's top two technology firms, scaled new highs earlier in the day. TCS closed up 2.2 percent, while Infosys and No. 3 ranked Wipro rose 2.5 percent and 2.3 percent respectively.

Financials closed mixed ahead of the central bank's mid-quarter policy review on Thursday, when the bank is widely expected to raise key interest rates by 25 basis points. [nSGE68E09E].

Top lenders State Bank of India and ICICI Bank closed down 1.7 percent and 0.1 percent respectively. HDFC Bank and mortgage lender Housing Development Finance Corp bucked the trend notching up 1.8 percent and 1.3 precent gains respectively.

Vehicles maker Tata Motors hit a new high in at least 20 years for the second straight session before a lower-than-expected 29-percent rise in August global vehicle sales pushed the shares down 2.9 percent at close.

Top utility vehicle Mahindra & Mahindra also scaled a record high and ended up 0.95 percent. Leading car maker Maruti Suzuki gained 1.8 percent.

In the broader market, losers led gainers in a ratio of 1.4:1 on volume of 558.2 million shares.

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee Monday rose to its highest level against the U.S. dollar in a month, in line with other Asian peers as China's decision to ease the yuan's peg to the greenback boosted local stocks and encouraged investors to buy currencies perceived riskier.

The dollar was at INR45.76 in late trade, down from INR46.17 in late Friday trade. This was the dollar's lowest level since May 18, when it touched INR45.51.

Currencies across Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea gained after the People's Bank of China said Saturday it would allow the yuan to gradually rise against the dollar. Beijing had pegged the yuan at CNY6.83 to a dollar since July 2008 to protect its export sector amid the global financial crisis.

China's decision buoyed stock markets across Asia, with the Bombay Stock Exchange's Sensitive Index rising 1.7% to close at 17,876.55.

While the central banks in South Korea and Thailand are suspected to have intervened to cap their currencies' gains, the Reserve Bank of India stayed away from the market.

"The RBI's absence from the foreign exchange market may also make the rupee particularly well placed to gain from the yuan de-pegging," Standard Chartered Bank said in a report.

"Given that the USD/INR (pair) is likely to convincingly breach INR46.00, the market will now focus on the 100-day moving average, which is at 45.70," it added.

Top Indian policy makers said it is too early to judge the impact of China's currency move on the rupee.

"What happens to the exchange rate, we are evaluating the impact and that in turn will have an impact on trade and capital flows. So I think we have got to wait for some time and see how this plays out," RBI Deputy Governor Subir Gokarn said.

Finance Secretary Ashok Chawla said the government will "wait and watch" the impact of the currency move on the economy. China is one of India's largest trading partners, enjoying a $15.2 billion trade surplus during April-December 2009, according to latest data.

In the bond market, government bonds ended mixed as strong demand for funds to pay for Internet bandwidth licenses strained liquidity.

The benchmark 7.80% 2020 bond closed at INR101.58, down from INR101.64 at Friday's close. However, the second-most traded 8.20% 2022 bond finished higher at INR102.00 from INR101.81 at last close.

The market didn't draw any comfort from Gokarn's comments that the central bank could consider additional measures to ease liquidity.

"What I want to emphasise is that this (tight liquidity) is temporary. This is money that is accruing in government accounts, which will be spent, which will find its way back into the system. (It is) not a permanent structural change in the system," he said.

text:
MUMBAI, June 3 (Reuters) - India's trade minister said on Thursday the stage has not come for the central bank to intervene in the currency market, after the rupee fell 4.3 percent against the dollar in May on the back of euro zone debt problems.

"Currency fluctuations are a reality. Depreciation is there and it is an impact of what is happening in the world," Anand Sharma told reporters on the sidelines of a business conference.

"I don't see the stage has come for intervention by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India)," he said, adding he will ask the finance minister to ensure adequate dollar credit availability by banks for companies. (Reporting by Suvashree Dey Choudhary)

title: RPT-SCENARIOS-India rupee may rise despite interim hurdles
text:
(Repeats story issued late on Tuesday)

MUMBAI, June 1 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is getting battered alongside regional peers and is likely to remain volatile until the euro zone uncertainty draws to a close but it is still expected to gain over fiscal year 2010/11.

The partially convertible rupee is among Asia's five worst-performing currencies in 2010 having shed 6.3 percent from the year's high of 44.18, after out-performing rivals last year.

The unit shed 4.3 percent in May largely weighed by foreign funds withdrawing around $2 billion from the local stock market, in their biggest single-month pullout since October 2008.

India is far less dependant on exports than some of its Asian peers, which insulates it somewhat from external shocks.

Analysts and traders believe the rupee will continue to remain volatile and there is a possibility that it may even revisit record low levels of 52.2 per dollar touched in early March 2009 on the back of a sustained risk aversion.

Here are some scenarios on the rupee's outlook:

RUPEE WEAKENS FURTHER IN THE NEAR-TERM

The most likely scenario. Almost all emerging market currencies are under pressure amid the global flight to safety and the rupee is unlikely to be an exception.

It is seen closely tracking moves in domestic equities and the euro in the near-term with the bias clearly towards further weakness. A widening current-account deficit adds to downside risk.

"There is no strong momentum for sustainability of near term gains in EUR/USD and in domestic bourses into the short/medium term," said J.Moses Harding, head of global markets at IndusInd Bank.

He said importers should stay hedged on possible near term rupee gains towards 46.00-46.10 and 45.75-45.85, while exporters should sell at 46.55-46.65 and then at 46.75-46.85.

If the current bout of global risk aversion persists, the rupee may drop towards record lows before heading back to a path of longer-term appreciation based on capital inflows and the economy's growth prospects, analysts said.

RBI INTERVENES TO PREVENT SHARP SWINGS IN RUPEE

Only if the rupee is an outlier. The Reserve Bank of India is unlikely to intervene if the unit falls or rises sharply on any single-day as long as it moves in line with fundamentals, but it will step in to curb speculative flows from fueling volatility.

The RBI's official view is that it is agnostic on the value of the rupee.

A weak rupee would help exporters and as long as the unit moves on fundamental factors and not hot money flows, the RBI is unlikely to step in.

Hence the central bank will only intervene to smoothen flows but will not be influencing the rupee's moves in any way.

RUPEE GAINS TOWARDS 43.50-44.00 BY END OF FY11

A likely scenario, assuming a normal summer monsoon helps growth and attracts foreign capital, boosting the rupee.

Europe is the wild card. If the situation there settles down, risk-appetite may return with India attracting foreign investment thanks to robust economic growth, which is forecast this year to reach 8.5 percent.

Foreigners, despite the large sales of Indian stocks in May, are still net buyers of $4.6 billion worth of shares in 2010, adding to last year's record inflows of $17.5 billion.

India's economy grew at its fastest in six months in the quarter through March thanks to government and consumer spending, which was roughly in line with expectations and likely to keep the central bank on its path of gradual monetary tightening.

Policy tightening would in turn support the rupee as rate differentials between India and developed economies could rise and attract more foreign funds, with most economists expecting the rupee to end the fiscal year 2010/11 at around 43.5 to 44 levels against the dollar.

"Fundamentally nothing has changed for India. So when the dust settles and investors re-focus on local fundamentals, we are likely to witness a clearer acceleration in INR gains," said Priyanka Chakravarty, a forex strategist at Standard Chartered.

RUPEE DEPRECIATES ON BROAD DOLLAR RALLY

A possibility given safe-haven buying of dollar assets amid Europe's woes and a recovering U.S. economy. If U.S. recovery gains momentum, the dollar may see a broad rally versus majors and emerging market currencies.

A sustained crisis in the eurozone would also boost the dollar's appreciation prospects.

This could weigh on the rupee, pushing it towards 48-49 per dollar levels by end-March 2011.

One could look to trade this view by buying dollar on dips to 45.90, and adding on a move towards 45.45, with stop-loss below 44.75, looking for a move to 48.09 and possibly 49.05.

One-year onshore forward rates <INR1Y=> suggest a 2.3 percent depreciation in the rupee from current levels, but those expectations were much higher at 2.9 percent at the end of March, suggesting the market is becoming less bearish about the rupee. (Additional reporting by Reuters FX analyst Krishna Kumar in Sydney; Editing by Jason Webb, Ron Askew)

title: UPDATE 1- India FX intervention  may be called for-adviser
text:
(Updates to recast lede, adds details, quote, background)

KOLKATA, May 14 (Reuters) - India's chief economic adviser to the finance ministry on Friday called for some intervention by the central bank to counter the rupee's appreciation against the U.S. dollar.

"I am not in favour of increasing capital controls. May be this is the kind of situation where some open market action to counter the exchange rate appreciation is called for. But this is something we have to think about," Kaushik Basu said in the eastern Indian city of Kolkata.

Basu said the rupee's sharp rise against the U.S. dollar is putting huge pressure on exporters, adding that in the 2009/10 financial year ended March 31, the rupee has strengthened 12.6 percent against the dollar and 8.3 percent against the euro year-on-year.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has not interevened in the foreign exchange market from December to March, the longest hiatus since mid-2006, triggering views of greater tolerance level for larger gyrations of the Indian unit by the central bank. [ID:nSGE64D01P]

So far in 2010, the rupee has risen by 3.1 percent against the dollar on the back of nearly $6 billion net capital inflows.

"RBI's policy is (the) right kind of policy, it is not to try to buck the trend if it is a permanent change taking place," Basu said.

"But here, there is a change which seems like fluctuation there is a reason to believe right now what is happening is a bit of fluctuation. So some attempt that market place action to correct this is indeed called for."

The rupee <INR=IN> touched a record low of 52.2 per dollar in early March 2009, and since then has gained 15.6 percent. It currently trades at 45.15 to the dollar.

Basu also said he expects India's headline inflation to ease in coming months and food inflation to ease gradually.

"It is very very unlikely that inflation will go back to double digits. In June, it might increase slightly due to base effect," he said.

India's wholesale price index <INWPI=ECI> rose an annual 9.59 percent in April, driven by high food and fuel prices, government data showed on Friday, lower than March's annual rise of 9.90 percent. title: India  cbank says did not  intervene  in  FX  mkt in March
text:
MUMBAI, May 12 (Reuters) - India's central bank did not buy or sell dollars in the foreign exchange market for the fourth straight month in March, the central bank's monthly bulletin showed on Wednesday.

The rupee moved from around 46.09 per dollar levels at the start of March to 44.88 levels towards the end, helped by robust capital inflows of a net $4.4 billion.

The rupee's fortunes are closely linked to capital flows. So far in 2010, foreigners have purchased a net $6 billion worth of local shares, adding to record inflows of $17.5 billion in 2009.

In 2009, the central bank sold a net $5.8 billion to prevent the rupee from depreciating sharply. For the 2009/10 fiscal year the central bank has been a net seller of $2.6 billion.

The rupee had dropped to a record low of 52.2 per dollar in early March 2009, but it ended the fiscal year 2009/10 up 4.7 percent boosted by large foreign fund inflows and periodic central bank intervention.

On Wednesday, the partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> was trading at 45.27/28 per dollar, marginally stronger from its previous close of 45.30/31. (Reporting by Swati Bhat; editing by Surojit Gupta)

title: UPDATE 1-No MSS bond issuance in near term-India finmin source
text:
(Adds details)

NEW DELHI, April 21 (Reuters) - India's central bank may not issue market stabilisation scheme (MSS) bonds in the near term as there is no excess liquidity in the market, a senior finance ministry official said on Wednesday.

"There is sufficient liquidity in the market. But we can't say that there is excessive liquidity," the official, who declined to be named, told Reuters.

A strengthening rupee on foreign inflows has fuelled market speculation that the central bank may start issuing the market intervention bonds.

The central bank can issue intervention bonds of upto 500 billion rupees ($11.3 billion) in the 2010/11 fiscal year that started on April 1.

Earlier on Wednesday, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Duvvuri Subbarao said issuance of intervention bonds would be more difficult in the current fiscal year given the low market appetite. [ID:nBMA007382]

The Indian rupee, which has gained about 4.7 percent in 2010, rose to a 19-month peak this month on foreign fund inflows into the equity market. Foreigners have bought shares of about $5.7 billion so far in 2010.

A Reuters poll conducted last week showed the local currency is expected to appreciate about 1.2 percent against the dollar between now and end-December.[ID:nSGE63E01W]

The official said the finance ministry and the RBI are yet to decide on the timing and the maturity date of the new 10-year benchmark bond.

Early this month, sources had told Reuters that the issuance of a new 10-year benchmark bond could be delayed as the government and the RBI want to increase volumes in the existing benchmark paper and avoid volatility. [ID:nSGE6360EA]

Traders in the bond market were expecting the government to sell a new 10-year bond in the first week of this month, but the bond on offer, instead, was the current benchmark -- the 6.35 percent 2020 maturity bond.

Traders had been concerned the central bank may issue a fresh 10-year bond, which would have pushed them to sell the 6.35 percent 2020 bond in order to make room for the new issue.

The official also said the government has no plans currently to issue cash management bills (CMBs). The government uses CMBs to meet temporary mismatches in its finances. ($1=44.42 Indian rupees)

(Reporting by Rajesh Kumar Singh and Manoj Kumar; editing by Malini Menon)

Traders and analysts say suspected moves likely due to either desire to slow (but not reverse) INR's rise, or as warning to those tempted to think INR's movements will only be one way - and plan trading strategies accordingly. title: Indian rupee firm but off fresh 19-mth high
text:
* Profit-booking expected; rupee seen easing to 44.80

 * No central bank intervention currently: traders  (Updates to mid-morning)

 MUMBAI, April 7 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee was trading firm on Wednesday but off a 19-month-high as mild profit-booking offset a rise in local shares, and traders said state-run banks were not actively buying the dollar.

 At 10:25 a.m. (0455 GMT), the partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> was at 44.37/38 per dollar after hitting 44.31, its strongest since Sept. 8, 2008. It had ended at 44.45/46 on Tuesday.

 "The rupee movement seems flow specific ... the market seems oversold to me and over the next two days you should see a pullback to 44.80," said a trader with a foreign bank.

 Dealers said state-run banks were not actively buying the dollar, implying the central bank was not currently looking to intervene to prevent further appreciation despite the rupee's recent rally.

 The rupee climbed 2.7 percent in March, its biggest monthly gain since May 2009, on the back of foreign portfolio inflows of about $4.4 billion, and has strengthened a further 1.3 percent since then.

 Latest data from the Reserve Bank of India showed it had not intervened in foreign exchange market in December and January.

 Stronger Asian currencies also supported the rupee. For a snapshot on Asian currencies, see [EMRG/FRX].

 India's main stock index <.BSESN> climbed above 18,000 points for the first time since February 2008 and rupee traders said they were positive on stocks in the near term, indicating they expected foreign portfolio inflows to remain robust.

 One-month offshore non-deliverable forward contracts <PNDF> were at 44.37/47, near the onshore spot rate.

 In the currency futures market <INRFUTURES>, the most traded near-month dollar-rupee contracts on the National Stock Exchange and MCX-SX were both quoting at 44.4675.

 Meanwhile the index of the dollar <.DXY> against six major currencies was up 0.1 percent.

 The euro struggled, plagued by fresh worries about debt-laden Greece, while commodity currencies like the Australian and Canadian dollars held gains on the back of expectations of higher interest rates. [USD/]  (Reporting by Jeanette Rodrigues; Editing by Ranjit Gangadharan)

title: WSJ BLOG/ India  Real Time: The Meaning of  Intervention
text:
(This story has been posted on The Wall Street Journal Online's India Real Time Report blog at blogs.wsj.com/indiarealtime.)

Posted by Abhrajit Gangopadhyay

It must be some law of finance akin to Murphy's Law that says whenever officials aren't predicted to intervene in the currency markets, they do.

Sure enough, the Reserve Bank of India was reported by Dow Jones Newswires to be suspected of intervening in the foreign exchange markets Tuesday morning, buying dollars at 44.35 rupees.

But that's not to say the broader point has changed. Traders and analysts say the central bank's interventions may have been caused either by a desire to slow (but not reverse) the rupee's rise, or as a warning to those who might be tempted to think that the rupee's movements will only be one way - and plan their trading strategies accordingly - that the RBI retains the power to surprise.

"The RBI was probably a bit uncomfortable with the speed of the rally, so it probably moved in to smooth things out a bit," one trader with a foreign bank told Dow Jones.

In other words, the RBI's actions are mostly aimed at smoothing the rupee-dollar volatility and not pegging the rupee to any specific level. Only if the dollar weakens towards 43 rupees is the bank expected to intervene more aggressively, analysts say.

The RBI neither confirms nor denies interventions, but its actions are reflected in data that come out with a month's lag.

Pure coincidence, we're sure, that the bank's efforts to buy dollars came just as U.S. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner touched down in Delhi for an official visit to India.

title: Reserve Bank of India - DRG Study on ‘Exchange Rate Policy and Modelling in India’
text:
The Reserve Bank of India released a DRG Study entitled, ‘Exchange Rate Policy and Modelling in India’.

The Study is co-authored by Prof. Pami Dua, Professor in the Department of Economics of Delhi School of Economics along with Dr. Rajiv Ranjan, Director in the Department of Economic Analysis and Policy of the Reserve Bank of India. The study covers two main topics: first, various aspects of economic policy with respect to the exchange rate and second, modelling and forecasting the exchange rate.

The study analyses India’s exchange rate policy and discusses the structure of the foreign exchange market in India in terms of participants, instruments and trading platform, as also, turnover in the Indian foreign exchange market and forward premia. The study then attempts to develop a model for the rupee-dollar exchange rate taking into account variables from monetary and micro structure models as well as other variables including intervention by the central bank. The focus is on the exchange rate of the Indian rupee vis-à-vis the US dollar, i.e., the Re/$ rate.

The study also covers the exchange rate policy of India in the background of large capital flows. The movement of the Indian rupee is largely influenced by the capital flow movements rather than traditional determinants like trade flows. Though capital flows are generally seen to be beneficial to an economy, a large surge in flows over a short span of time in excess of the domestic absorptive capacity can be a source of stress to the economy giving rise to upward pressures on the exchange rate, overheating of the economy, and possible asset price bubbles.

The study notes that an important aspect of the policy response in India to the various episodes of volatility has been market intervention combined with monetary and administrative measures to meet the threats to financial stability while complementary or parallel recourse has been taken to communication through speeches and press releases. In line with the exchange rate policy, it has also been observed that the Indian rupee is moving along with the economic fundamentals in the post-reform period. Moving forward, as India progresses towards full capital account convertibility and gets more and more integrated with the rest of the world, managing periods of volatility is bound to pose greater challenges in view of the impossible trinity of independent monetary policy, open capital account and exchange rate management. Preserving stability in the market would require more flexibility, adaptability and innovations with regard to the strategy for liquidity management as well as exchange rate management. With the likely turnover in the foreign exchange market rising in future, further development of the foreign exchange market will be crucial to manage the associated risks.

After studying various aspects of economic policy with respect to the exchange rate, the study attempts to gauge the forecasting ability of economic models with respect to exchange rates with the difference that this is done in the context of a developing country that follows a managed floating (as opposed to flexible) exchange rate regime. Starting from the naïve model, the study examines the forecasting performance of the monetary model and various extensions of it in the vector autoregressive (VAR) and Bayesian vector autoregressive (BVAR) framework. The study examines, first, whether the monetary model can beat a random walk. Second, it investigates if the forecasting performance of the monetary model can be improved by extending it. Third, the study evaluates the forecasting performance of a VAR model vs a BVAR model. Lastly, it considers if information on intervention by the central bank can improve forecast accuracy. The main findings are :

The monetary model generally outperforms the naïve model. This negates the findings of the seminal study by Meese and Rogoff (1983) that finds that models which are based on economic fundamentals cannot outperform a naive random walk model.

The result that it is possible to beat the naïve model may be due to the fact that the intervention by the central bank may help to curb volatility arising due to demand-supply mismatch and stabilise the exchange rate. The exchange rate policy of the Reserve Bank is guided by the need to reduce excess volatility.

Forecast accuracy can be improved by extending the monetary model to include forward premium, volatility of capital inflows and order flow.

Information on intervention by the central bank helps to improve forecasts at the longer end.

Bayesian vector autoregressive models generally outperform their corresponding VAR variants.

Thus, the availability of information on certain key variables at regular intervals that affect the exchange rate can lead to a more informed view about the behavior of the future exchange rates which may allow the market participants to plan their foreign exchange exposure better by hedging them appropriately. Such key variables could include past data on exchange rates, forward premia, capital flows, turnover and intervention by central banks. As regards availability of data on key variables relating to the Indian foreign exchange market, most of the data are available in public domain and can easily be accessed by market participants, academicians and professional researchers. Skilful use of these variables will help them gain sound insight into future exchange rate movements.

[Note: Development Research Group (DRG) is constituted in the Reserve Bank’s Department of Economic Analysis and Policy for undertaking effective policy-oriented research backed by strong analytical and empirical basis on subjects of current interests. The views expressed in these studies are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of the Reserve Bank.]

title: UPDATE:  India  Adviser: Large Capital Flows Give New Dimension To  Intervention
text:
(Adds more comments from Rangarajan, RBI's Subbarao, background)

By Nupur Acharya & Bijou George

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Capital inflows into India have begun to dominate the balance of payments, giving a new dimension to the central bank's interventions in the foreign exchange market, a top adviser to the Prime Minister said Tuesday.

"The extent of accumulation of reserves, and the degree of sterilization, influence the growth of money supply," C. Rangarajan, chairman of the Prime Minister's Economic Advisory Council said in a speech.

"The monetary authority has to take a view on the permissible expansion of money supply in the context of large capital inflows," he said.

Rangarajan said if there were limits to sterilization, the accumulation of reserves would have to be limited.

Sterilization, in terms of RBI operations, is the process in which the bank drains excess rupees from the market by selling special intervention bonds. The excess rupees arise when the RBI intervenes in the foreign exchange market, buying dollars.

The government has to pay interest to investors to subscribe to the special intervention debt, which adds to its fiscal burden.

"Capital inflows have come to dominate the balance of payments and the exchange rate may begin to appreciate even if there is a significant current account deficit because of large capital flows," Rangarajan said.

India has historically run a deficit on its current account, which has been mostly financed by large capital inflows into India, the world's second-fastest-growing major economy.

Rangarajan said that no monetary authority can afford to ignore prolonged volatility or misalignment in the forex market.

"However, the framework evolved is such that intervention to stabilize the exchange rate has to be an exception than the rule."

Double Digit Inflation Unlikely

Rangarajan said that an inflation rate of 5%-6% may be considered appropriate. "I don't see the prospect of double-digit inflation," he said.

Most analysts are predicting wholesale inflation to reach double digits by the end of the fiscal year to March 31.

Wholesale price growth is already above the RBI's revised estimate of 8.5% for the fiscal year, with inflation hitting a 15-month high of 8.56% in January, preliminary data showed Monday.

"It is possible that if the rabi [winter-sown] crop is good, and there is every prospect that the rabi crop is going to be good, then it may have a moderating influence [on inflation]," Rangarajan said.

RBI Governor Subbarao, speaking at the same event, said growth was as important as price stability for a developing economy like India.

"In the Reserve Bank, we cannot be pure inflation-targeters to the exclusion of growth concerns. So we have to keep both price stability and growth in view and now increasingly as a result of the crisis --financial stability."

-By Bijou George & Nupur Acharya, Dow Jones Newswires; 91 22 61456113; djn.in@dowjones.com [ 16-02-10 1530GMT ]

* Fiscal consolidation easier in period of price stability (Updates with quotes, details, background)

By Suvashree Dey Choudhury and Neha D'silva

MUMBAI, Feb 16 (Reuters) - Despite a significant current account shortfall the Indian rupee may rise on the back of large capital inflows, the prime minister's economic advisory panel chairman said on Tuesday.

"Capital inflows have come to dominate the balance of payments and exchange rate may begin to appreciate, even if there is a significant current account deficit because of capital flows," C. Rangarajan said in a prepared speech that was circulated ahead of an event.

So far in 2010 foreigners have been net sellers of about $500 million of equities, after they moved in $17.5 billion in 2009 and analysts expect India to attract inflows going ahead.

The rupee <INR=IN> is up 0.7 percent so far this year, after having risen 4.7 percent in 2009.

Rangarajan said central bank intervention in the foreign exchange market must be an exception and not a rule.

"No monetary authority can afford to ignore prolonged volatility or mis-alignment in the foreign exchange market," said Rangarajan, who once headed the central bank.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has said it intervenes in the foreign exchange market to prevent excessive volatility but does not target any specific level on the currency.

"The extent of accumulation of reserves and degree of sterilisation influences the growth of money supply and the monetary authority has to take a view on the permissible expansion of money supply in the context of large capital inflows," Rangarajan said.

India is set to unveil the national budget on Feb. 26 and economists are expecting the government will start its move towards fiscal consolidation by withdrawing some of its stimulus measures introduced to help the economy during the global crisis.

Rangarajan said fiscal consolidation becomes easier in an environment of reasonable price stability.

Headline inflation in January accelerated to its fastest pace in more than a year, vaulting above the central bank's end-March forecast and putting more pressure on the RBI to raise borrowing rates. [ID:nnSGE61E06Z]

"Tying central banks to a specific target of inflation may be too restrictive and may even be counter-productive," he said.

RBI Governor Duvvuri Subbarao had said last week the central bank cannot just focus on inflation while formulating the monetary policy as growth was also a concern for a developing country like India. [ID:nBMA006986]

Rangarajan said asset prices should also be a key input while framing the monetary policy. (Writing by Swati Bhat; Editing by Ranjit Gangadharan)

title: FUND VIEW- India, Korea attractive ,Indonesia a crowded trade
text:
* Rupee, won good currency picks on fundamentals - Aberdeen

* Buying Indonesian bonds is a crowded trade - Aberdeen

By Saikat Chatterjee

HONG KONG, Feb 11 (Reuters) - Markets may be pricing in too much policy tightening in countries such as South Korea and India, creating opportunities for bond investors, a fund manager at Aberdeen Asset Management said on Thursday.

Central banks will also start withdrawing stimulus by draining excess liquidity, which meant less aggressive intervention to limit currency gains, making some of them, including the Indian rupee <INR=>, a good pick, Adam McCabe told Reuters in an interview.

"We still think policymakers will go gradually and will focus on domestic demand and will keep in mind their vulnerabilities," said McCabe, who manages $4.4 billion in assets in Asia-focused funds.

He added that India and Korea were some of his favourites.

The Bank of Korea had once been tipped to be among the first G20 central banks to start tightening policy but the government's opposition to such a move and heightened uncertainty about the global outlook has scaled back those expectations. It left rates unchanged at a review on Thursday. [ID:nTOE61A00S].

McCabe said India could ill-afford to keep intervening to keep its currency down as it would flood the banking system with rupees, adding fuel to an already high inflation unless it mopped up excess cash, which in turn would add to borrowing costs.

Singapore-based McCabe, who moved to Aberdeen from Credit Suisse in 2009, said his fund had a long-duration strategy on Korea and was underweight Thailand, where the market has been underpricing the extent of tightening by the central bank.

McCabe was also bullish on Malaysia, expecting it to lag the rest of Asia in raising interest rates and said he favoured the Korean won <KRW=> against the Japanese yen <JPY=> given that South Korean companies were gaining the share of China's market at the expense of their Japanese rivals.

Latest data showed South Korea's exports to China in January nearly doubled from a year-ago period. [ID:nSEW002162].

CROWDED TRADES

But unlike some of his counterparts, McCabe is cautious on Indonesian bonds and has in fact cut positions recently as foreign investors made a beeline for its high-yielding debt.

Latest data showed foreigners owned a record 117.5 trillion rupiah worth of federal debt early in February after boosting their holdings by $2.2 billion or nearly a fifth last year.

McCabe said that even though the medium term outlook for the economy was positive, a risk of a spike in inflation if the central bank kept rates on hold for too long or a lack of progress in reforms could shatter investor confidence.

"Foreigners love the place and it worries me when a trade is so crowded as all it needs is a policy mistake for the herd to head to the door," McCabe said. (Editing by Tomasz Janowski)

title: WRAPUP 1-Asian c.banks scramble to contain  currency  strength
text:
* Intervention seen in S.Korea, Indonesia, India, Singapore

* Korean official vows further action on won, if necessary

* Concerns that rapid currency gains may hurt recovery

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Jan 11 (Reuters) - Several Asian central banks intervened on Monday in an effort to temper the rally in their currencies as the dollar weakened broadly, highlighting fears that rapid currency rises may hurt economic recovery.

Central banks in South Korea, Indonesia, India and Singapore were spotted buying U.S. dollars to contain their currencies, driven up by the dollar's weakness and expectations that China's strong exports data may prod Beijing to allow the yuan to rise.

"I think Asian central banks are watching the pace of currency appreciation," said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist at BNP Paribas in Singapore. "They are cautiously optimistic about the economy and don't want to prick the nascent recovery."

In a sign that concerns over strengthening currencies were not unique for emerging markets, the head of Swiss National Bank said on Monday that the central bank will fight any excessive rise of the Swiss franc against the euro, hinting at a possible intervention.

In Seoul, a senior finance ministry official, speaking after the authorities were seen buying dollars, warned that the authorities would act further to temper the won if necessary.

"We are worried that the foreign exchange market is leaning excessively one way," Kim Ik-joo, head of the ministry's international finance bureau, told Reuters.

"We are closely watching foreign exchange rates and we will take proper measures if necessary," Kim said.

Dealers said, the authorities tried to prevent the won from rising past the 1,200-per dollar level, though the currency briefly hit 1,114.9 per dollar, its strongest in more than 15 months, and closed on the stronger side of the 1,200 mark.

The won has gained 4 percent against the dollar so far this month, making it the top performer among nine emerging Asian currencies tracked by Reuters.

The rising won also intensified purchases of Korean bonds by foreigners, along with the view that rate rises will be slower coming in the year ahead, with the buying, in turn, pushing the won further up.

Confronted with a steady stream of investment funds betting that Asia will continue to lead the global economic upturn, the region's authorities have been using both verbal and market intervention to cool of the pressure on their currencies.

Taiwan went a step further last week, unveiling new controls to curb speculative inflows, giving foreign short-term investors betting on currency gains a week to invest their funds in stocks or pull out.

In Indonesia, the authorities were also spotted trying to stem the rise of the high-yielding rupiah, which jumped as much as 1 percent on Monday, and the central bank said it would keep on buying dollars to rein in its currency.

In Singapore, the central bank was also seen buying dollars as the Singapore dollar hit a one-month high and in India, state-run banks were spotted buying the U.S. currency after the rupee rose 1 percent to its highest in more than 15 months.

The rupiah has gained 3 percent against the dollar so far this month, making it the second best performer in Asia. (Additional reporting by Vidya Ranganathan in SINGAPORE, Lee Soo-jung in SEOUL and Swati Bhat in MUMBAI; Editing by Tomasz Janowski)

title: Reuters Summit-UPDATE 1-BofA-Merrill fears India reform delays
text:
(For other news from the Reuters India Investment Summit, click on http://www.reuters.com/summit/IndiaInvestment09?pid=500)

* Conservative regulations may delay financial reforms

* Volatile fund flows worrying but taxing them not a solution

* India should step up domestic participation in stk mkt (Adds details, more quotes)

By Nishant Kumar and Pratish Narayanan

MUMBAI, Nov 23 (Reuters) - India, whose protected financial sector helped insulate it from the worst of the global economic meltdown, should not be complacent in its push for financial sector reforms, a top Bank of America-Merrill Lynch executive said on Monday.

"One thing that does worry me is that the conservative nature of Indian regulation. That may persist longer than it would otherwise have done because of the financial crisis," said Kevan Watts, who heads the combined Indian operations of Bank of America and Merrill Lynch.

The rousing re-election of the Congress party-led government in May, which freed it from dependence on communist allies, lifted hopes of an acceleration in long-delayed financial reforms.

But the global financial meltdown has dampened Indian appetite for financial liberalisation, especially as limits on foreign banks and active regulation of the financial sector were seen as sheltering it from the worst of the downturn.

"The danger is, that if you like, India will rest on its laurels of having circumvented the crisis well," Watts told the Reuters India Investment Summit in Mumbai.

India has for years talked about allowing a greater role for foreign banks and giving equal voting rights to foreigners in private-sector banks, currently limited to 10 percent irrespective of their actual holding.

No foreign firm is allowed to operate in the pension sector and private Indian players have only a limited presence.

The life insurance market was opened nine years ago, but companies are not allowed to raise debt or go public in their first decade of operation, putting the onus on shareholders to fund costlier growth.

Foreign ownership in the life insurance sector is capped at 26 percent.

Watts said financial reforms could help India's large savings to make its way into productive investments.

India has about $400 billion in domestic savings, but little is funnelled through the banking channel currently to fund, for example, the country's huge requirements to build infrastructure.

CAPITAL FLOWS

Watts, who has spent nearly three decades with Merrill Lynch and has been based in India for about 18 months, said swings in foreign capital flows were a concern, but taxing them was not a solution.

"I think volatility of fund flows is certainly something I would be worrying about if I was advising the government," said Watts, who early in his career worked for the British treasury.

"When you start taxing things, there are a lot of unintended consequences," the Oxford alumnus said, adding, "Critically for India, any unilateral move of that kind would really damage its reputation globally."

He said India should instead use existing mechanisms, such as sterilising inflows by issuing special bonds. India's central bank has in the past used market intervention bonds to absorb excess liquidity generated by large foreign capital inflows.

Foreign investors have so far bought more than $15 billion of local equities in 2009, after selling $13 billion in 2008, helping send Indian stocks up about 75 percent and lifting the rupee to its highest in more than a year.

The capital inflows are part of a trend globally that is seeing investors chasing faster growing emerging markets, given sluggish recovery and low interest rates in developed economies.

This has raised concerns inflows may create asset price bubbles and drive currencies to uncompetitive levels. That has prompted some economies, including Brazil and Taiwan, to impose controls and others, such as Russia, to say they were considering such steps.

Watts said India should also encourage more domestic participation in its equity markets to counter the impact of foreign investment flows.

Indian institutional investors lack muscle to counter rapid fund flows. For instance, government pension funds are not allowed to invest in equities, while investment by private pension funds is limited to just 5 percent of their assets.

Financial reform is "not about whether foreigners can own 49 percent of life insurance joint ventures or 26 percent," he said. "Perhaps the most important thing that the Indian government can do is to encourage the further development of domestic Indian institutional investors," he said. title: MONEY TALKS: Why The RBI May Let The Rupee Rise
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--"The day before yesterday's volatility is today's flexibility." So quipped then-Reserve Bank of India chief Yaga Venugopal Reddy during the rupee's sharp rise of 2007.

Once again, the rupee is on a roll, hitting over one year-highs against the U.S. dollar and breaching key technical levels. It has finally broken free after trailing its Asian peers and has gained nearly 4% so far this month, while the Philippine peso has risen 2.2%, the Korean won 1.2% and Indonesian rupiah 2.7%. Yet the Reserve Bank of India has looked away.

This is at variance with their counterparts in places like South Korea, Taiwan and Thailand who have been active in their market, buying dollars to protect their exports.

Going by analysts forecasts, the rupee is set to rise further from here. Standard Chartered Bank has a dollar/rupee forecast of INR45 by end-March and INR42 by the end of the fiscal 2010-2011 year, while ING Vysya Bank has a one-year forecast of INR43. Currently it is trading at INR46.24.

There are seven reasons the RBI may let the rupee gain, only stepping in to iron out the moves if they become too sharp.

For one thing, the imperative to protect exports is less for India, which is largely a domestic consumption-driven economy.

Secondly, the rupee is to a large extent playing catch up to other Asian currencies; the RBI has never indicated it likes an undervalued currency and may not hold the rupee back if the U.S. dollar collapses against its key trading partner currencies.

Thirdly, the central bank has traditionally shied away from intervention as long as the dollar's decline has been broad based, which is the case now.

Fourthly, top government policy makers are increasingly getting vocal about the need to continue stimulus until growth takes hold.

The RBI is expected to be one of the first major Asian central banks to raise interest rates as it battles inflation pressures, but allowing the rupee to rise would temper imported inflation and could allow the RBI to push back the hikes a bit. Global crude oil prices have climbed to one-year highs and comprise two-third of India's import costs.

Fifthly, what worries the RBI is the quality of capital inflows, less so the quantity.

While portfolio inflows have may a comeback on the back of a global risk appetite revival, the current capital inflows also include a healthy dose of foreign direct investment, overseas borrowing and remittances from abroad. The RBI can live with that.

Sixthly, Westpac says that the cost of intervention in India is among the highest in Asia. The government would have to bear an interest cost for the special bonds the RBI would have to issue to soak up liquidity. Given the government's stretched finances, this would be an added burden.

Seventhly, top policy makers seem increasingly comfortable with a rising rupee as long as volatility is kept in check, going by their recent comments at least.

(Subhadip Sircar is Senior Correspondent for Dow Jones Newswires covering central banking, fixed income and currency markets in India. He can be contacted on 91-022-61456113 or by email: subhadip.sircar@dowjones.com)
