title: Indian rupee hits 1-yr high as dlr slides, stx rise
text:
* Dollar index <.DXY> drops to 14-mnth lows; euro gains

* Rise in shares raise expectations of increased cap inflows (Updates to mid-morning)

MUMBAI, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee climbed to one-year highs on Wednesday buoyed by the dollar's broad-based fall and a stronger start to the stock market that could trigger more capital inflows.

By 10:35 a.m. (0505 GMT), the partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> was at 46.15/16 per dollar, off a high of 46.0950, its strongest since Sept. 26, 2008 and 0.8 percent above its Monday's close of 46.48/49.

Financial markets were shut on Tuesday for a local holiday.

"Weaker dollar overseas is fuelling selling, it is a sell uptick story," said Ashtosh Raina, head of foreign exchange trading at HDFC Bank.

The dollar slid to its weakest level in 14 months against a basket of currencies on Wednesday, under pressure from expectations of continued low U.S. interest rates and investor bets on commodity currencies. [USD/]

Indian shares rose <.BSESN> 1 percent early, tracking mostly firmer Asian markets, but gains are expected to be limited by concern the market may have moved ahead of valuations. [.BO]

Foreign fund investments into local shares are key factor determining the direction for the rupee. Foreigners have bought a net $12.8 billion worth of shares this year, almost reversing net outflows of more than $13 billion in 2008.

At the day's high, the rupee has gained 13.3 percent from its record low of 52.2 hit in early March and is up 5.7 percent in 2009.

One-month offshore non-deliverable forward contracts <PNDF> were quoting at 46.03/13, stronger than the onshore spot rate, suggesting a bullish outlook for the rupee.

"The rupee is mostly likely to breach the 46/dollar mark, if the Reserve Bank of India doesn't intervene," Raina said.

The central bank has previously said it buys or sells dollars in the spot market to prevent volatility in the local currency. Dealers said they would watch out for any RBI action to limit the sharp rise in the rupee.

India's central bank bought a net $181 million in intervention in August, when the rupee had risen to a two-month high, its bulletin showed on Monday. [ID:nBOM308873]

"Given the state of USD sentiment, it may just be a matter of time before targets such as 42 appear on the horizon," Sean Callow, forex strategist at Westpac, said in a Wednesday note.

"The modest amounts reported for intervention from May to August indicate strongly that the range-bound price action on the rupee at a time of sizeable gains for other Asian currencies was not due to large scale central bank USD purchases. We would be surprised if the data for October aren't more eye-catching." (Reporting by Swati Bhat; Editing by Jarshad Kakkrakandy)

title: Telkom, miners lift S.African bourse; rand gains
text:
* Stocks up, led by telecoms group Telkom

* Rand gains, flirts with 14-month high vs dollar

JOHANNESBURG, Oct 12 (Reuters) - South African stocks rose on Monday, boosted by higher global markets and with telecoms group Telkom jumping on reports the government plans to force down the interconnect costs charged by cell phone operators.

The rand rallied, flirting with a 14-month high against the dollar, as the greenback slipped and metal prices gained.

The JSE Top-40 index of blue chips <.JTOPI> added 0.92 percent to 22,936.15 points, also buoyed by above-forecast corporate earnings that lifted investor sentiment globally and the strong metal prices that bolstered miners.

The broader All-share index <.JALSH> added 0.99 percent to 25,630.16 points.

"Everyone is looking at the earnings season in America and Europe for signs of a sustained recovery in the global economy," said Michael Carlsson, a trader at Consilium Securities.

"So far so good. But the big heavyweights are coming out this week and we'll see how it goes."

On the bourse, Telkom was among the winners on news that the government may force cell phone companies to cut interconnect fees. [ID:nLF553811]

Shares in Africa's biggest fixed phone line operator rose 3.15 percent to 42.86 rand.

"Telkom stands to gain from lower interconnect fees and the mobile operators will battle. I think we are seeing that sort of being reflected in the shares," said Jan Meintjes, an analyst at Gryphon Asset Management.

The rand <ZAR=D3> was trading at 7.3410 to the dollar at 1550 GMT, 0.9 percent stronger than its previous close in New York after touching 7.30 earlier in the session.

Traders said a weak dollar helped propel metals, sending the price of gold -- a key South African export that is often seen as an alternative to holding the greenback -- above $1,050 an ounce and towards Friday's record high.

The dollar fell as investors positioned ahead of U.S. corporate earnings his week on expectations that better-than-forecast results will drive up risk appetite.

"Gold is flying higher, oil is up, those things will drive commodity currencies like the rand stronger," Bidvest Bank chief trader Ion de Vleeschauwer said.

"The dollar is very weak, so again its the normal factors influencing the rand that is in play."

The rand has surged almost 30 percent against the greenback this year, but moves have lost momentum around 7.30 -- it hit a 13-month high of 7.2925 last month.

It has recovered all the losses sparked by the collapse of merger talks between mobile phone group MTN and India's Bharti Airtel <BRTI>BO> and despite repeated verbal intervention from the central bank, warning it is too strong.

Analysts say dollar and commodity price moves continue to drive the market, although some traders suggest the central bank has upped buying dollars and that importers tend to come in around 7.30 to the dollar, capping gains.

"The flavour of the week, of the month, or the year really, is the weak dollar and it looks to be continuing," de Vleeschauwer said. Government bonds were relatively steady, with investors nervous about a big increase in government and utility supply, as well fear expectations electricity prices will rise sharply for a number of years, spurring inflation.

The yield, which moves inversely to the price, on the 2015 issue <ZAR157=> up 1 basis point at 8.43 percent while the 2036 <ZAR209=> yield rose 3 basis points to 8.62 percent.

On the bourse, Old Mutual jumped 3.92 percent to 12.73 rand, making it the top gainer among blue chips, after it said it planned to issue a seven-year sterling benchmark bond.

Miners also gained as commodity prices cruised higher with Anglo Platinum up 3.05 percent to 710 rand and rival Impala Platinum tacked on 1.75 percent to 174.50 rand.

But Sasol shed 0.28 percent to 288 rand after broker Goldman Sachs cut the petrochemical group's profit forecast and its 12-month price target. (Reporting by Gordon Bell, Vuyani Ndaba and Tiisetso Motsoeneng)

title: FUND VIEW-AXA bets on Indian commodity, tech firms
text:
* Hopes for 15-20 percent rise in domestic shares in 2009/10

* Sees earnings boost to commod firms on capacity utilisation

* Expects weak currency, order flow pick-up to help software

By Nishant Kumar

MUMBAI, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Indian shares may add another 15 to 20 percent to their blistering rise in 2009/10, led by global themes such as software and commodities as world economy bounces back from its worst recession in decades, a fund manager said.

Prateek Agrawal, head of equity at Indian fund arm of French insurer AXA , said his main bet was on commodity firms with spare capacity who might see earnings surge as inventories start to build back in three to four months on demand revival.

"As growth returns to a larger part of the world, they may see higher capacity utilisation, they may see slight uptick in prices," Agrawal said on Tuesday.

Shares of Tata Steel , the world's No. 8 steelmaker by output, Sterlite Industries , a subsidiary of London-listed Vedanta Resources , and Jindal Steel & Power were part of Agrawal's portfolio at July-end.

The fund manager, who oversees about 900 million rupees, is also overweight on Indian software exporters given their better-than-expected June quarter results and signs of revival in demand from developed world, their main market.

"As we go deeper into the year and as the concerns that are around companies in the developed world reduce, you will see higher degree of order books for Indian firms," he said.

A weaker rupee against the dollar should also help technology firms, he said, adding rupee might not go beyond 47.5 rupees in the next at least three to four months as India's fiscal situation remained under stress.

Even a torrent of foreign inflows was unlikely to strengthen the currency as the central bank would intervene, said the fund manager who holds Aptech and India's No. 2 software exporter Infosys Technologies which announced outsourcing deal from oil and gas firm BP last week.

"We really believe that this space could deliver some amount of outperformance till between now and at the end of the year," the Mumbai based-executive said.

SEES MARKET UP, SHUN TELECOM

Agrawal, who remains fully invested, said chances of earnings growth in 2009/10 was reasonably higher.

He expected two to three percent earnings growth for firms part of India's benchmark index <.BSESN> in FY10 and a robust 20 percent the next financial year as economic growth revives.

That would translate into 18,000-19,000 level for the index, up 16-22 percent from its Tuesday close, by April next year considering Indian shares have historically traded at 15 times their 12-month forward earnings, he said.

"We believe next three-four months is the sweet spot in the market," the fund manager said, adding a poor monsoon suppressing rural consumption and hurting India's nascent growth revival was not as bad as many feared.

He said market is not factoring in increased support prices for crops which may offset decline in produce for farmers.

"Except for a small part of the population which may actually see their produce down by more than 20 odd percent, most of the guys will be better off," Agrawal said.

"Versus the fear in the street, the reality on the ground is not as bad," he said, adding his portfolios were underweight telecom firms given their pricy valuations and large capital requirement as they bid for 3G licences later in the year. (Reporting by Nishant Kumar; editing by Ramya Venugopal)

title: India  cbank bought $1.04 bln in June  intervention
text:
MUMBAI, Aug 12 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) bought a net $1.04 billion in intervention in June, marking the biggest monthly purchase of dollars by the central bank since April last year, its bulletin showed on Wednesday.

The RBI bought $1.28 billion and sold $235 million, the data showed. The central bank had purchased a net $4.3 billion in April 2008.

The dollar purchases were probably to rein in the rupee, which climbed to a seven-month peak of 46.75 per dollar in early June. The central bank often intervenes in the currency market to smoothen volatility in the rupee.

The rupee <INR=IN>, however, reversed gains and touched a five-week low of 48.90 later in the month because of a fall in local equities.

It shed 1.65 percent in June, its steepest drop since February, as foreigners pulled out about $650 million over the last two weeks during the month.

The June intervention lowered the central bank's net sales in 2009 to $6.07 billion from $7.11 billion in the previous month. In March, when the rupee fell to record low of 52.20 per dollar, the RBI had sold $3.4 billion.

India's foreign exchange reserves <INFXR=ECI> were at $271.641 billion on July 31, from a peak of $316 billion in May 2008. (Reporting by Anurag Joshi; Editing by Ranjit Gangadharan)

title: India cbank says sold $1.44 billion in May
text:
MUMBAI, July 10 (Reuters) - India's central bank sold a net $1.44 billion in May, even though the rupee rose more than six percent on the government's strong re-election and a surging sharemarket, the bank's monthly bulletin showed on Friday.

The Reserve Bank of India's dollar sales in May were 42 percent below April's $2.48 billion, and were likely to have been concentrated in the first half of the month, when the rupee was trading between 50 and 49 per dollar

On May 16, the Congress-led coalition won national elections by a huge margin, sparking a rally in equity and currency markets. The rupee rose more than 3 percent on the result.

The May intervention took the central bank's net sales in 2009 to $7.11 billion. In March, when the rupee fell to record low of 52.20 per dollar, the RBI sold $3.4 billion.

The Bombay Stock Exchange's 30-stock benchmark index, the Sensitive Index, is likely to recover some lost ground Thursday, but charts indicate it will struggle to move past its major resistance of 14,800.

The index slipped below the lower end of the 14,550-15,600 range Wednesday - falling 2.9% to end at 14,522.84 - which is a major sign of weakness.

Considering the oversold condition in the hourly charts, there is a case for an intra-day rally up to 14,800.

The index is likely to drop to 14,300 once the anticipated short-term bounce is over. The Sensex has to close above 15,030 to indicate a reversal of the short-term downtrend.

Most U.S. stocks fell amid weakness in commodity and financial stocks, although strength in consumer and technology stocks helped the Nasdaq stay in the black.

The financial sector is dividing itself into strong and weak players. Even as some large banks repaid the government, Standard & Poor's cut ratings on 18 regional banks and pushed five into junk territory, saying their business looks less profitable going forward.

JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley all said they have bought back the preferred shares they issued to the government under last fall's bailout effort.

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee fell to its lowest level in more than a month against the U.S. dollar Wednesday, hurt by a sharp slide in the local stock market.

The dollar ended at INR48.13, up from Tuesday's close of INR47.75. It last closed higher May 15.

The rupee's fall came despite a moderate intervention by the Reserve Bank of India in the foreign exchange market to support the local currency.

"The dollar was strong on weak stocks and global cues, but the RBI stepped in and sold the dollar at INR47.95," said a dealer with a private bank.

Traders said the central bank likely sold between $200 million and $400 million.

The central bank's latest move was in contrast to its recent interventions when it was believed to have supported the dollar, which fell sharply following the reelection of the Congress party-led federal government last month.

Custodial banks sold dollars heavily. Dealers said these could be on behalf of foreign investors who were pulling out investments from local shares.

The Bombay Stock Exchange's Sensitive Index fell 2.9% to 14,522.84.

"We're looking at short-term strength in the dollar as the month-end and quarter-end demand (from crude oil importers) will come into play," said R.K. Gurumoorthy, head of foreign currency trading at ING Vysya Bank.

Also, advance tax payment for the first fiscal quarter indicates earnings at companies could be weak. As a result, stock markets may slip and "the dollar can target INR48.50 by end-June," Gurumoorthy said.

Meanwhile, government bonds ended up as the market took comfort from former RBI governor Bimal Jalan's view that there was room to lower interest rates further.

The 6.07% 2014 bond, the most traded paper in recent sessions, closed at INR97.75, up from INR97.50 Tuesday, while the 7.59% 2016 bond ended up at INR103.78 from its previous close of INR103.55.

"Interest rates should be lower in an economy which is reviving. If interest rates could be lower by 50 basis points, that would be good," Jalan told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview.

Dealers are now awaiting a bond buyback auction by the RBI Thursday for further cues.

title: Indian rupee falls to 1-month low as shares drop
text:
* Hits 48.16 against dollar, lowest since May 18

* Main share index falls 2.9 percent on profit-taking

* Rupee down 2 pct this month, but up 8.5 pct from March low (Updates to close)

By Anurag Joshi

MUMBAI, June 17 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee weakened to a one-month low on Wednesday, weighed down by an almost 3 percent drop in the local stock market that could trigger profit-taking by foreign portfolio investors.

The partially convertible rupee ended at 48.13/14 per dollar after hitting 48.16, which was its lowest since May 18, and about 0.8 percent weaker than Tuesday's close of 47.75/76.

It has lost almost 2 percent this month, but is up 8.5 percent from a record low of 52.2 hit on March 3 as foreigners bought Indian shares worth nearly $8 billion over three months.

"The fall in the stock market was the primary factor, which pulled the rupee lower," a senior trader with a foreign bank, said.

"With the rupee now beyond 48 to the dollar, there is more likelihood of the RBI intervening," he said, referring to the Reserve Bank of India.

The central bank buys or sells dollars through a clutch of state-run banks to check volatility in the local unit.

India's main stock index <.BSESN> fell 2.9 percent to their lowest close in three weeks, as doubts about the health of the global economy dampened sentiment worldwide and sparked profit-taking on an 86 percent rally since early March. [.BO]

Despite the rupee's losses in June, analysts expect the currency to appreciate by the end of December.

A victory for the ruling coalition in national elections last month has raised hopes for economic reforms such as opening up the insurance and pension sectors and stake sales in state companies.

"The recent election outcome, the revival in global risk appetite and pick-up in capital inflows into India positively affect the balance of payments," Macquarie analyst Rajeev Malik wrote in a note.

"We reiterate our INR/USD (rupee-dollar) forecast of 46 by end-2009, strengthening further to 43 by end-June 2010."

title: Rising India rupee hits resistance; more gains seen
text:
* Up 10 pct from March record lows, stalling at 47/dlr

* Rising rupee extra burden for faltering export sector

* Intervention to check pace of gains rather than weaken it

By Swati Bhat

MUMBAI, June 9 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee has surged as cash floods into India as investors turn optimistic on the global outlook, but traders say authorities are trying to temper the rise so it does not disrupt an emerging economic pick-up.

The rupee is not at historic highs, indeed it is rising from a record low of 52.2 per dollar in early March, but its rapid 10 percent rise is causing difficulties for exporters just as the government and central bank are working to boost industry.

Traders say the Reserve Bank of India has intervened to slow its rise, half of which came in two days after the unexpectedly strong re-election of the Congress-led coalition last month, and they see 47 per dollar as its tolerance limit for now.

"The Reserve Bank of India is stemming the fast pace of appreciation in the rupee as it hurts exports, which are crucial for manufacturing sector revival and therefore important for GDP sustainability," said Shubhada Rao, chief economist at Yes Bank.

Following the rupee's gains of as much as 4.5 percent in the two days after the election results, the central bank stepped in to buy dollars -- just months after it had been selling them to support the rupee -- and traders estimate it has bought $4 billion to $5 billion in intervention since then.

The rupee has made a couple of ventures through 47 per dollar since then, hitting a seven-month peak of 46.75 on June 3, at which point its was up 11.7 percent in three months, but has been unable to sustain the moves against the intervention.

"I suspect they are uncomfortable with the pace of appreciation that has come through, especially post-elections," said Robert Prior-Wandesforde, an economist with HSBC in Singapore.

"It's not a particular level, but just the magnitude of the recent move."

A Reuters poll after the election results found the rupee was expected to end 2009 at 46.25 per dollar. It was trading around 47.6 per dollar on Friday afternoon.

FOREIGN MONEY

Since mid-March, foreign funds have pumped in about $7.5 billion into a stock market that has rallied over 90 percent from its early March lows as investors regain their appetite for risk.

"We cannot yet say to what extent the current inflows are sustainable. If the RBI allows the currency to appreciate very fast, tomorrow when funds dry up it will also depreciate equally fast, and they want to avoid this sharp variation," said Rupa Rege Nitsure, chief economist at Bank of Baroda.

Foreign fund flows play a substantial role in driving the rupee. In 2007, record inflows of $17.4 billion helped the rupee gain more than 12 percent and the following year, net outflows of more than $13 billion saw it tumble by one-fifth.

Nitsure said falling exports and large trade deficits pointed at a small overvaluation of the rupee in the last month.

Exports have fallen in annual terms in the seven months to April, and the government expects them to keep falling until late 2009.

While not as export-driven as other Asian economies, exports account for about 15 percent of India's economy and are a key component of industrial output, which fell in three of the four months to March but beat expectations in April. [ID:nBOM501117]

Other trade-weighted measures suggest the rupee may still be a little undervalued despite its rapid rise against the dollar.

title: India Rupee Likely Soft In Forwards Mkt On Oil, Export Woes
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee is likely to weaken in the forwards market as declining exports and rising crude-oil prices are expected to subdue the currency's recent surge induced by the federal-election results, analysts said.

Refiners are expected to take cover on their likely higher import bill as crude has been moving up in the past few months. However, cover on the receivables for India's exporters may decline, leading to a demand-supply mismatch in the over-the-counter forwards market.

The dollar premium on the most-traded one-year contract could rise to INR1.25 in about a month and INR1.50 by July, said Moses Harding, head of global markets group at IndusInd Bank.

The one-year forward premium over the spot price closed at INR1.08 Wednesday.

Dealers said the central bank has been intervening in the spot and forwards markets to prevent a sharp rise in the rupee as a stronger local currency could render India's already dwindling exports less competitive. The market intervention could further boost premiums, they said.

"There is still demand for forward dollars and the rupee outlook seems bearish," IndusInd Bank's Harding said. "If the rupee actually goes for a toss, then there will be more demand for forward dollars."

One of the main threats to the rupee is from India's shrinking exports, which contracted 33% from a year earlier in April to record their seventh straight month of decline.

Trade deficit had narrowed from a year earlier in March - the latest month for which data is available - as import cost also fell because of lower oil prices.

But, that trend is expected to change with the recent gains in crude-oil prices. Crude oil accounts for about two-thirds of India's import bill.

The premium on rupee forward contracts had been locked in a narrow range over the past month, tracking the currency in the spot market and because of uncertainty over the composition of the new federal government.

But, a decisive mandate in favor of the Congress party-led alliance in the elections has bolstered hopes of bold economic reforms and improved foreign investor sentiment, sending the rupee more than 3% up Monday - its steepest intraday rise since 1998.

The rupee closed at INR47.49 to a dollar Wednesday.

Ravindra Babu, a senior dealer at Andhra Bank, said a stable government and investments from abroad are the factors that could ease the pressure on the rupee.

But, dealers cautioned the sharp spike in the rupee this week was overdone with a high probability of a retreat to the near-INR50 levels it had been confined to in the recent past.

HSBC is also bearish on the rupee and expects it to hit INR54 to a dollar by the end of 2009.

Royal Bank of Canada, in a recent research note, said the rupee is expected to underperform most other currencies in Asia's emerging markets, citing India's "horrible fiscal accounts and debt levels."

The government expects India's fiscal deficit at 5.5% of gross domestic product in the current fiscal year ending March 31, but analysts peg the gap at more than 10%, taking into account the deficits of state governments and off-budget items.

The threat of global rating agencies downgrading India to junk also looms large, which is a huge negative for the local currency.

Also, interest rates in India are unlikely to be further lowered soon, offering significant arbitrage opportunities over western markets which have near-zero interest rates. This could also boost forward premiums.

Generally, premiums are determined by interest-rate differentials between currencies, but the demand-supply situation also plays a role in countries such as India where the capital account is not fully convertible.

"Government bond yields are only going up and at this moment nobody is expecting a rate cut. So I don't think forward premium will come down drastically unless there is a substantial inflow and export booking," Andhra Bank's Babu said.

Premium on the one-year forward contract could rise to INR1.40 in the next couple of months and may go even higher if investment inflows aren't revived, Babu added.

title: =DJ UPDATE:RBI's Gopinath:No Change In  Forex Intervention  Policy
text:
(This article was originally published Tuesday) 


 
   By Anant Vijay Kala & Subhadip Sircar 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India's central bank hasn't changed its policy on foreign exchange market intervention and will continue to curb volatility, Reserve Bank of India Deputy Governor Shyamala Gopinath said Tuesday.

"We are closely monitoring the situation," Gopinath said on the sidelines of an event, when asked about the recent sharp fall in the rupee.

The comments come on a day when the rupee hit a fresh all-time low, breaching INR52 against the dollar.

The rupee has lost 6.2% against the dollar so far this year on top of a 19% fall in 2008.

The RBI has sold net $31.7 billion in the foreign exchange market to stem the rupee's fall in the current fiscal year till December.

Dealers said the RBI's recent intervention has been intermittent even as the local currency has posted sharp falls over the past several sessions.

"As we know the dollar has strengthened against other majors. Our policy on the rupee has not changed," Gopinath said.

She said the central bank will ensure that the government's bond market borrowing program is conducted in a smooth manner.

"RBI as a debt manager to the government would ensure that we conduct the borrowing in a smooth and non disruptive way," Gopinath said.

The government has upped its borrowing program four times this fiscal year to INR3.06 trillion from the INR1.45 trillion originally budgeted in February 2008.

It plans to borrow INR3.62 trillion in the next fiscal year.

The RBI is conducting open market operations to buy back bonds and also buying back market stabilization scheme bonds, issued earlier to cushion the market from supply concerns by ensuring comfortable liquidity.

"All I can say is that we monitor all developments closely and take actions as appropriate, necessary," Gopinath said when asked about the possibility of further interest rate cuts by the central bank.

Analysts are widely expecting the RBI to slash rates after economic growth was at its slowest pace in nearly six years during October-December.

The economy expanded 5.3% during the period under review, compared with 7.6% during the July-September quarter.

Last Friday RBI Governor Duvvuri Subbarao met banks chiefs and asked them to lower lending and deposit rates.

"Banks have to take their (interest rate) decisions based on their asset and liability profiles. It is a commercial decision but yes we have seen them starting to respond," Gopinath said.

India's largest state-run lender State Bank of India Monday slashed the interest rates it offers on some deposits by 40-50 basis points.

title: UPDATE 1- India  to use  intervention  bonds to fund deficit
text:
(Updates with details, background)

MUMBAI, Feb 27 (Reuters) - India's central bank said on Friday it will convert 450 billion rupees ($8.8 bln) of intervention bonds into federal bonds in instalments by the end of March, helping the government plug a budget funding hole.

The government had indicated last week it would seek the transfer of the funds to avoid overburdening the market with bond issues and causing a spike in yields before the fiscal year ends in March.

The government estimated this month its fiscal deficit would be 6.0 percent of gross domestic product in 2008/09, well above its intital estimate of 2.5 percent.

Accordingly, it sharply revised up its gross borrowing target for 2008/09 to 3.06 trillion rupees, more than double the initial estimate of 1.45 trillion rupees.

The extra borrowing will be made up of 1.16 trillion rupees of bonds and the remainder funded by the conversion of MSS bonds.

Concerns over swelling bond supplies have pushed up bond yields in recent weeks, with the benchmark 8.24 percent 2018 bond <IN082418G=CC> rising 109 basis points so far in 2009.

The central bank is expected to step up its purchases of federal bonds in coming weeks to prevent a potential spike in volatility. [ID:nBOM115800]

Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) debt was introduced in 2004, mainly to absorb surplus cash generated due to the central bank's dollar-buying intervention in the foreign exchange market. For factbox, double click [ID:nBOM435887].

Since excess cash in the banking system would have fuelled inflation, the liquidity absorbed via MSS bonds were kept in a separate account. Although the government paid the interest on the bonds, it was not able to use the funds for expenditure.

"The situation has reversed in the recent period primarily on account of change in the external accounts resulting in attendant draining of primary liquidity reflecting the impact of Reserve Bank's operations in the foreign exchange market," the central bank said in a statement.

"Consequently, the sterilised liquidity in the MSS cash account can be reversed by transferring the amount to the normal cash account of the government," it said.

The central bank issued large amounts of MSS debt in 2007 and early 2008 as the rupee was rallying. But as foreign flows have turned, the rupee has slumped to record lows and the central bank has been buying back MSS bonds in recent months to support market liquidity. title: India Rupee, Bonds Fall; Trade Resumes After Mumbai Attacks
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India's currency was lower Friday while bonds slipped after the terrorist attacks on Mumbai, with expectations that risk-averse foreign investors would pull funds out, at least for the short term.

Trading resumed in financial markets after Thursday's halt, with attacks on hotels and other areas frequented by tourists and business travelers leaving 130 people dead; sporadic violence was continuing on Friday.

This "is probably the worst terrorist attack India has faced in its audacity, choice of locations, reported hostage taking and apparent targeting of Westerners," said analysts at the Eurasia Group.

"It seems likely that foreign investors for a long time will attach a higher political/security risk premium to their operations in India."

The U.S. dollar was recently around INR49.71, up from INR49.49 on Wednesday and expected by dealers to trade in a INR49.50-INR49.75 range; the rupee, which has fallen over 20% this year, has been one of the worst-performing currencies in Asia given foreigners have sold over $13.46 billion in India stocks.

"The bid/ask spreads are very wide and trading is quite thin as there is a lot of uncertainty in the market," said one currency market dealer.

Government bonds were lower despite a drop in weekly inflation and an assurance from rating agencies that the attacks were unlikely to have a material impact on the economy; the benchmark 8.24% bond was recently at INR107.60, from INR107.75 on Wednesday.

Dealers said the rupee's fall may be limited by potential central bank's intervention.

Also, "foreign investors will return to India once the markets stabilize. That should happen very soon with easing inflation and interest rates steadily coming down," said R.K. Gurumoorthy, head of currency trading at ING Vysya Bank, who expected the dollar to fall to INR46 by the end of March.

A dealer with a private bank added that markets had to some extent already carried a risk premium; "this is not the first time such an incident has happened. There may be some early panic in the market but it should be a short-lived setback and we could see the rupee stabilize very soon."

The main driver going forward for markets would be how much impact the attacks might have on the broader economy, given growth has already been showing signs of cooling, analysts said.

Growth slowed to 7.9% for the fiscal first quarter ended June 30 and is expected to slow further to 7.3% in the second quarter, according to a Dow Jones poll of 13 economists, with the data out at 0630 GMT.

Still, many economists doubted there would be a major, or prolonged, economic impact from the attacks.

Stocks were expected to open lower with the benchmark Sensex called down about 200 points, with declines likely in airline, hotel and other tourism-related shares; the expiry of monthly derivatives contracts Friday could exacerbate the early weakness.

Wednesday, the Sensex ended up 3.8% at 9,026.72.

Some however said the impact on stocks could also be short-lived: "It's hard to see how the tragic events will have anything but a negative impact on the market over the next five to 10 days. However, to the extent that a lurch down will make the market unquestionably cheap on valuation grounds, it could well lead to value investors looking afresh at this market in 2009," said Saurabh Mukherjea, head of equities at UK-based investment bank Noble.

Credit premiums were steady with the five-year credit default swap on State Bank of India, a proxy for India's sovereign credit, holding at 390-425 basis points after widening around 20 basis points Thursday.

title: WSJA: Asian Shares Drop,  Currencies  Sharply Lower
text:
OF THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA 
 

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Asian stocks were sold off heavily Thursday, knocking many of the region's currencies sharply lower and prompting governments to intervene.

Markets in Tokyo, Hong Kong and South Korea fell in response to a broad selloff overnight in the U.S. Tokyo's benchmark index fell 6.9%, while Hong Kong and Seoul were down 4% and 6.7% respectively. Australia's major benchmark dropped 4.2% and Shanghai fell 1.7%. Mumbai and Singapore were down 4.1% and 2.8% late Thursday. Jakarta was down 2.8% late.

The selling continued in Europe, where the DJ Stoxx 600 index was 3% lower. U.S. stock futures were down 1% to 1.5% in screen trade.

The stock hits reflect fears of deflation in the U.S., a major market for Asia-made goods, and the impact of a slowdown on commodity-rich nations like Australia and Indonesia.

That has led to a flight to safer investments typically denominated in U.S. dollars and the Japanese yen, taking money out of Asian markets and contributing to a drop in local currencies.

"It's part of the wholesale destruction of wealth across the planet," said Patrick Bennett, a strategist with Societe Generale in Hong Kong. "With asset and equity prices tumbling, investors are being encouraged to cut exposure completely."

Weaker currencies can boost big exporting nations because it makes their goods cheaper to sell in other markets. But declining currencies also hit countries with extensive foreign borrowing needs, can drive up inflation by making imports more expensive and can scare off foreign investment.

Among the hardest hit, Indonesia's rupiah and South Korea's won fell to their lowest level against the U.S. dollar since the Asian financial crisis a decade ago.

Thailand's baht fell to its weakest level since March 2007, while Taiwan's dollar hit a three-week low and the New Zealand and Australian dollars also weakened further.

The central banks of South Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore and India intervened to defend their currencies, local traders said. Australia's central bank issued data that showed it plowed A$3.15 billion into currency markets last month to defend the Australian dollar against a sharp decline.

Japan and Hong Kong have defied the trend, the former because its currency is seen as a safe haven and the latter because it is pegged to the value of the appreciating U.S. dollar. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city's de facto central bank, put roughly HK$15 billion into the market Thursday to bring the currency's value within its trading band with the U.S. dollar.

Economists cautioned that the current environment hasn't reached the point of the Asian currency crisis, when domestic funds followed foreign investors as they ran for the exits. Most governments have moved to back bank deposits to reassure consumers. Regional financial institutions have cleaner balance sheets than a decade ago, and bad loans have so far had only a minor effect on regional banks.

Still, continuing hits to currencies continue could erode consumer confidence, leading locals to consider moving their money elsewhere. "The impact on confidence could become a much bigger problem," said Sim Moh Siong, an economist at Citigroup in Singapore. "If this goes beyond how much money foreigners remove from Asia, the situation could broaden out."

In Tokyo, the Nikkei Stock Average of 225 companies ended down 6.9% at 7703.04. Shares of major banks and brokerages were hammered, with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group tumbling 10% to Y281,500 and Nomura Holdings ending down 11% at Y666.

Shares of nonlife insurers dropped after sector companies reported dismal fiscal first half results Wednesday and sharply reduced their earnings forecasts for the full fiscal year ending March.

Although most of the bad news had already been factored in by investors, forecast revisions confirmed the grim outlook. Tokio Marine Holdings went limit-down at Y2,220, and Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance Group Holdings also went limit-down at Y2,035.

Real estate stocks also sank, dogged by credit concerns, with Mitsui Fudosan skidding 14% to Y1,070, and Mitsubishi Estate falling 13% to Y1,077.

In Seoul, the Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, finished down 68.13 points, or 6.7%, at 948.69, based on skepticism over conditions in the U.S., particularly among financials.

Shinhan Financial Group declined 9.7% to KRW26,400, and KB Financial Group plunged by the daily limit of 15% to KRW24,550. Among builders, Hyundai Engineering & Construction and GS Engineering & Construction both dropped by the daily 15% limit to KRW42,100 and KRW45,200, respectively.

In Shanghai, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index, which tracks both A and B shares, ended down 1.7%, or 33.71 points, at 1983.76. Railway companies and insurance companies fell on profit-taking.

China Railway Group Ltd. dropped 4.1% to CNY5.82 after gaining 4.7% Wednesday, while China Life Insurance Co. fell 4.0% to CNY20.24 after rising 6.1% in the previous session.

-By Carlos Tejada, The Wall Street Journal; carlos. tejada@wsj.com

title: 4th UPDATE: Asian Shares Slump On US Woes; Nikkei Falls 6.9%
text:
(Adds information, quotes, updates/adds market levels)

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian share markets fell Thursday - some of them to multiyear lows - after a late-day slump on Wall Street, with the health of the banking and auto sectors still cause for much concern.

"We haven't seen bargain hunting because nobody knows whether anything is a bargain anymore - value is disappearing overnight," said Najeeb Jarhom, senior vice president of research at AmFraser in Singapore.

Falls accelerated as the day wore on: Australia's S&P/ASX 200 ended down 4.2% at its lowest level since early 2004, with Japan's Nikkei shedding 6.9%, hurt in part by a surprise trade deficit in October; Korea's Kospi ended with a 6.7% decline with Taiwan's market down 4.5% at a more than six-year trough.

Margin lenders "are flat out with their margin calls," said Chris Blair, head of retail at Patersons Securities in Sydney; analysts elsewhere noted some redemption activity, though others said the continued slide in markets might prove attractive for braver, longer-term investors.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was recently down 6.2% with India's Sensex off 5.1%.

Light trading volume showed the level of caution among investors; "the market continues to trade on fear. Fundamentals are going to take a back seat for a while. It's like (watching) a terminal patient," said broker David Price of Forsyth Barr in New Zealand.

Japan's yen was notably higher with central banks intervening in several markets in Asia to keep a lid on the U.S. dollar; risk aversion was showing up in wider credit spreads while crude oil futures came in for some selling on demand-related concerns.

U.S. stock futures were down 1%-1.5% in screen trade and European spreadbetting firms were calling stocks there to fall; CMC Markets tipped London's FTSE-100 to drop 93 points.

Asia's declines came after the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed under 8000 for the first time in more than five-and-a-half years as investors worried about the future of U.S. auto makers and banks; it declined 5.1% while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 6.5%.

There were ongoing concerns about the U.S. economy with poor data Wednesday on the housing market and gloomy minutes from the recent meeting of the Federal Open Markets Committee.

Some were starting to talk about the risk of a global deflationary spiral: "Faced with this prospect, central banks (in Asia, ex Japan) are loosening monetary conditions and will continue to do so well into 2009," said analysts at Standard Chartered.

Technology stocks suffered with the Semiconductor Industry Association forecasting global chip sales for 2009 to decline 5.6%; Hynix Semi shed 15% in Seoul with Powerchip Semi down 6.9% in Taiwan and Elpida Memory off 3.7% in Tokyo.

"As dramatic declines in consumer and industrial confidence began developing in late summer, order cancellations began to grow and in many cases, slowing orders degenerated into a complete stop in orders as players across the supply chain moved to extremely cautious positions," said iSuppli senior vice president, market intelligence services, Dale Ford.

Shipping stocks were hit with Divay Goel, director and head of operations for Drewry Maritime Services, telling Dow Jones Newswires Wednesday he expected around 20% of orders for building new dry bulk shipping vessels may be canceled in 2009; Korea's Hyundai Heavy Industries sank 14.4%.

Japan's main index traded under 8000 for the first time since Oct. 29; banks were hit with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial tumbling 10% and Nomura Holdings 11% while insurer Tokio Marine Holdings shed 15% after reporting poor first half results and terminating its plan for a share buyback.

Miners and financials fell in Australia with BHP Billiton down 9.1% and Rio Tinto down 13%; ANZ Bank lost 5.9% with Commonwealth Bank 5.2%.

Hong Kong property stocks were hit with that subindex down 7% and Cheung Kong down 5.9%; HSBC fell 4.2% on worries about the outlook for business in Europe and the U.S.

The Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.6% after a 6.1% rally Wednesday; Singapore's Straits Times Index was down 4.1% with Malaysia's main index falling 2.0%, Indonesian shares 3.5% and Thai shares 4.0%.

New Zealand's NZX-50 closed with a 2.3% fall to its lowest level since June 2004, while Philippine shares ended down 3.5% decline.

In currency markets, the U.S. dollar fell to Y95.15 with the euro at Y118.80; the euro was around $1.2490 while the Australian dollar slipped back to US$0.6346.

Asian currencies were active: The U.S. dollar rose above S$1.53 against the Singapore dollar and against the Korean won it hit its highest level since March 1998, while it reached a 2008 high against the Malaysian ringgit; against the Thai baht, it touched its best level since March 2007.

The Philippine central bank was suspected of selling U.S. dollars to support the peso, with intervention also spotted in Indonesia, Korea and India; in Hong Kong, authorities again sold Hong Kong dollars to preserve the currency peg.

"Though valuations might look cheap for some currencies, this is typically not the time that investors take on more risk. Given how brutal this year has proved for many investors, we sense this adage may hold particularly true this year," said analysts at Morgan Stanley.

Japanese government bonds rose with futures adding 0.49 to 139.32; credit default swaps widened with the iTraxx Japan Series 10 index at 330 basis points from 290 basis points Wednesday.

Toyota CDS were at 170 basis points, from 135 basis points on Nov. 18 and 55 basis points on Oct. 2; "pretty wide, huh? Toyota used to trade almost the same level as sovereign" CDS, said a credit trader at a Western bank in Tokyo, adding "autos are just taking it on the chin - everyone's keeping an eye on what's happening with the Big Three in Detroit."

The cost of protection in Asia ex-Japan widened, too, with the five-year iTraxx investment grade index quoted at 425-470 basis points versus a 420 basis-point midspread close Wednesday.

U.S. Treasurys nudged up in Tokyo after strong U.S. gains with the 10-year note up 7/32 at 103 14/32, yielding 3.342%; players were betting on a further Fed rate cut in December.

Spot gold was at $735.20, up 30 cents from New York; front-month Nymex crude was down 93 cents at $52.69 a barrel on Globex - a 22-month low - after declining 77 cents in New York.

title: Indian cbank says sells net $3.8 bln in September
text:
MUMBAI, Nov 12 (Reuters) - India's central bank sold a net $3.8 billion in intervention in September, when the rupee dropped past the 47 per dollar level to its weakest in more than 5 years.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) sold $6.48 billion in September and bought $2.7 billion, the central bank's monthly bulletin showed on Wednesday.

In August, it bought $3.8 billion and sold $2.6 billion, while in July the central bank sold $9.9 billion, the highest in a month since the RBI began publishing its currency intervention figures in April 1995, and bought $3.58 billion.

The central bank has bought a net $10.67 billion between January and August, the monthly RBI bulletin showed.

The rupee fell more than 16 percent in the first nine months of 2008, ending September at 46.95/96 per dollar <INR=IN>. Last month, it hit a record low of 50.29 on heavy foreign withdrawals from a slumping stock market.

On Wednesday, the rupee ended at 49.30/32, down 20 percent this year. In 2007, record portfolio inflows of $17.4 billion had helped the rupee rise to a near decade high of 39.16 in November.

Foreign funds are net sellers of $12.7 billion this year. (Reporting by Anurag Joshi, Editing by Mark Williams)

title: UPDATE: Indian Bankers Say Liquidity Remains A Concern
text:
(Adds quotes from State Bank of India, finance ministry.)

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Insufficient liquidity in India is a concern as external credit lines dry up, and the government needs to take proactive steps to ensure that the banking system remains flush with cash, bankers said Thursday.

"Liquidity is a major issue but as far as I know authorities are aware of it and they will continue to provide positive bias towards liquidity from now into the future," O.P. Bhatt, chairman of State Bank of India (500112.BY) said at a banking conference.

With the financial crisis making global credit scarce, Indian corporates are increasingly looking to local banks for funds to meet their requirements.

"Liquidity is also required to continue to meet the (shortfall) in the future as many of the lines of credit that were available globally are not available," said Chanda Kochhar, joint managing director and chief financial officer at ICICI Bank (532174.BY).

Overnight rates in India's interbank market shot up to the 21% level last week on a cash squeeze stemming mainly from heavy rupee-buying foreign exchange market intervention by the central bank. The Reserve Bank of India took a host of measures Saturday to cool lending rates, including a cut in the repo rate by 50 basis points as well as a 100 basis point cut in the cash reserve ratio and statutory liquidity ratio.

Call rates have subsequently eased to around 6%-7% levels.

A senior Finance Ministry official Thursday said that the central bank's moves have been successful.

"Call money rates have come down. It is a sign of success. Money is accessible. My sense is that the call money rate will continue to be calm," the executive, who didn't want to be named, said in New Delhi.

Banks Haven't Asked For Dollar Loans Yet

Bankers said that they haven't approached the central bank yet for dollar-denominated lines of credit for their overseas branches. "We are not asking for dollar loans and we are not asking it for capitalization," said Bhatt.

ICICI Bank's Kochhar also said that ICICI hasn't made such a request to the RBI.

Separately, the government official said that India is currently not facing a shortage of dollars in its cash market.

"The last set of announcements has addressed the dollar liquidity issue. My personal sense is that it (dollar liquidity crunch) is behind us," the official said.

-By Subhadip Sircar, Harsh Joshi, John Satish Kumar & Mukesh Jagota; Dow Jones Newswires; 91 22 22884212; djn.in@dowjones.com [ 06-11-08 0752GMT ]

title: India Yld Curve May Steepen On Special Bonds Buyback By RBI
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of India's buyback program for special intervention bonds is likely to spark demand for shorter-dated paper and lead to a steepening of the yield curve, traders say.

The first buyback of INR100 billion ($2 billion) of the so-called market stabilization bonds is slated Thursday, and banks which hold the bulk of such paper may offload them only at a hefty discount of 15-20 basis points to existing secondary market yields, they add.

"The RBI has clearly said that it will calibrate the buyback with the government bond auctions. So we can expect that the RBI will keep announcing buybacks, which should help boost demand for short-term paper. Naturally, the yield curve should also steepen," said Piyush Wadhwa, vice president of treasury at ICICI Securities Primary Dealership Ltd.

The spread between the one-year and 10-year paper, which currently stands at around 47 basis points, is likely to widen to 100 basis points in the next two to three months, said a bond dealing head with a foreign fund house.

On Saturday, the Indian central bank announced a slew of measures to boost liquidity, including a 50-basis-point cut in the repurchase rate as well as a 100-basis-point cut in the cash reserve ratio as well as banks' statutory liquidity ratio.

It also said it will buy back market stabilization bonds issued earlier to provide more durable liquidity to the system.

The central bank introduced the market stabilization scheme bonds in 2004 to soak up excess liquidity.

The RBI used the instrument extensively in 2007 to suck out excess rupee liquidity generated by its purchase of dollars in the foreign exchange market to prevent a rapid rupee appreciation.

The RBI stopped selling these special bonds from early September as the rupee started losing steam and cash supply tightened.

As of Oct. 24, the outstanding amount of bonds under the market stabilization scheme stands at INR1.65 trillion.

The RBI will buy back INR50 billion of the 6.65% 2009 paper and another INR50 billion of 5.48% 2009 paper Thursday in its first buyback auction.

On Friday, the RBI will sell INR100 billion of bonds under its regular bond auction.

The Indian government is slated to sell INR390 billion of bonds in the fiscal second half as part of its normal borrowing program. Finance Minister P. Chidambaram recently said that the government will overshoot its borrowing program as it spends more on loan waivers to farmers and salaries to employees.

Over half of the fiscal second half borrowing is slated in the 10-year and above segment.

"Given the huge uncertainty all around, shorter-dated securities will be in fashion. Banks may not be willing to part with them," said a bond manager at the fund house.

RBI May Have To Pay A Hefty Yield Discount

Bond dealers say that the RBI will have to offer a hefty discount on the market yields to get a good response.

Most dealers say that the discount will be at least 15 basis points on the secondary market prices.

Currently, the 6.65% bond is yielding 7.13% and the 5.48% paper is yielding 7.19% in secondary market trade.

These paper have been illiquid for most part as banks hold them in their hold-to-maturity portfolio, which doesn't subject them to mark-to-market provisions. Most of these paper were issued when interest rates were low, but subsequently, interest rates hardened in India, eroding the value of the bonds.

Now, with the global financial crisis escalating, the RBI has started easing interest rates with the RBI's benchmark lending rate down by 150 basis points since the beginning of October.

"Banks may prefer to hold on to these paper as interest rates are headed south. The RBI will have to offer at least par rates (face value) for the bonds to make a success of the buyback," said Baljinder Singh, a dealer with Andhra Bank.

However, some dealers say that the lowering of the statutory liquidity ratio by the RBI has led to INR400 billion of excess bonds in the system.

"There will be definitely some interest as banks have an excess of SLR bonds at the moment," said a bond dealer.

Under Indian rules, banks have to maintain a portion of their deposits in gold, cash or approved government securities, which ensures a captive demand for such bonds.

On Saturday, the RBI cut the statutory liquidity ratio by 100 basis points to 24% to boost liquidity in a cash-strapped interbank market.

-By Subhadip Sircar & Anant Vijay Kala; Dow Jones Newswires; 91 22 22884212; djn.in@dowjones.com [ 05-11-08 0740GMT ]

title: 2ndUPDATE:India Stocks,Rupee Rally As Mkt Eyes More RBI Cuts
text:
(Updates with closing stock, bond, rupee levels; adds prime minister's comments)

By Subhadip Sircar & Neelabh Chaturvedi

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Indian stocks and the rupee rose Monday as investors welcomed the latest rate cut from the Reserve Bank of India and speculated that the central bank's focus on spurring economic growth means further easing is likely.

The RBI on Saturday cut its repurchase rate for the second time in as many weeks and injected more cash into the banking system to protect India's slowing economy from a worsening global financial crisis. The central bank also for the first time put ensuring economic growth at the top of its policy agenda, a clear signal that it will chop interest rates further, analysts said.

"We maintain that the RBI is on the path of undertaking the mother-of-all-monetary-easings," said Rajeev Malik, economist at Macquarie Securities.

The RBI's move pulled down the interbank call rate to 7.25% from 21% Friday, and helped India assets continue to claw back some of their losses from a vicious selloff last month.

Stocks soared, with the 30-stock Sensex ending up 5.6% at 10,337.68, a near two-week high. The rupee climbed, pulling the U.S. dollar down to INR48.66 from INR49.45 at Friday's close.

Government bonds, however, fell, ignoring the heavy liquidity infusion as the RBI unexpectedly lowered a key reserve norm, the statutory liquidity ratio, which will cut the proportion of deposits banks must invest in sovereign debt. The 8.24% 2018 bond ended at INR104.54 as against INR104.97 at its close Friday.

Saturday, the RBI cut its repo rate by 50 basis points to 7.5%, adding to an earlier 100 basis point cut in October. It also lowered banks' cash reserve ratio further by another 100 basis points to 5.5%, which will add INR400 billion of liquidity.

Additionally, it cut banks' statutory liquidity ratio by 1 percentage point to 24%, a rate untouched for over a decade.The RBI will also provide refinance to banks for up to 1% of their deposits under a special liquidity adjustment facility valid for 90 days.

The central bank has also allowed banks to borrow up to 1.5% of their deposits to fund non-banking financial companies.

More Cuts Eyed

Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, during a meeting with the heads of India's biggest companies Monday, said the government will protect growth.

"The government will take all necessary monetary and fiscal policy measures on the domestic front to protect our growth rates," Singh said.

" A crisis of this magnitude was bound to affect our economy and it has."

Economists predict additional cuts in the central bank's key lending rate, or repurchase rate, as well as more cuts in the cash reserve ratio.

The slew of measures by RBI comes barely a week after it maintained status quo at its mid-term monetary policy review Oct 24.

Standard Chartered Bank expects the latest moves to infuse INR1.2 trillion of liquidity into India's banking system.

However, heavy central bank intervention to protect the rupee means that liquidity may still become tight going ahead.

India's foreign-exchange reserves fell $15.5 billion in the week ended Oct. 24, the most on record, to $258.4 billion.

"Given the pressure on the rupee due to the maturing of $52.7 billion of foreign-currency loans by June 2009, and the need to intervene in the forex market to prevent any free-fall in the currency, more liquidity-enhancing measures will be needed going forward, in our view," Standard Chartered said in a note.

The Indian rupee has lost nearly 20% against the US dollar so far in 2008 and is one of the worst performers.

Standard Chartered now expects the cash reserve ratio to fall to 4% by end March, while the repo rate may fall to 6% and the reverse repo rate to 5% by end June.

RBI Puts Growth Before Inflation Vigil

In its statement Saturday, the RBI said it cut the repo rate "in view of the ebbing of upside inflation risks as also to address concerns relating to the moderation in the growth momentum."

Analysts said that signaled the central bank less concerned about inflation and is now focused squarely on spurring economic growth.

Tushar Poddar, economist at Goldman Sachs, said: "We think the downturn is spreading rapidly from the financial sector to real activity, and there are serious downside risks to our growth forecast of 7% in the next financial year."

India's economic growth fell to 7.9% in the fiscal first quarter ended June 30 as against 9% for the previous year.

Macquarie expects growth to slip to 7.2% in the current fiscal year.

The RBI revised its current year forecast to 7.5%-8% from 8% previously at its policy review.

Earlier Oct, RBI Governor Duvvuri Subbarao said that growth may moderate more in the next fiscal year if the financial crisis continues.

India's inflation rate has been rapidly easing as global commodity prices tumble on demand concerns as economies across the world slip.

Inflation rate fell for the fifth successive week to 10.68% due to a fall in the prices of manufactured goods, food and fuel in the week ended Oct. 18, from 11.07% a week earlier.

State-Run Banks Take Lead, Others Cautious

Some state-run banks have taken the lead and lowered interest rates after the RBI move.

Union Bank of India Monday cut its prime lending rate by 50 basis points to 13.5%. State Bank of India, the country's biggest bank is yet to act.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said he will ask state-run banks to consider lowering interest rates.

"That (the RBI move) is the signal," Chidambaram told the Press Trust of India Saturday.

But the private sector players including ICICI Bank still want to wait and watch.

"The impact on deposit and lending rates will have to be watched over sometime," said Chanda Kochhar, joint managing director at ICICI Bank.

Analysts say a substantial fall in lending rates remain unlikely.

"In our view, bank lending rates are unlikely to fall substantially and immediately, as liquidity conditions remain tight and credit risk remains elevated," said Poddar.

"We expect banks to gradually lower first the deposit and then the lending rate by only 50-100 basis points, not least due to moral suasion and pressure from the RBI and government, particularly on public-sector banks," he said.

-By Subhadip Sircar & Neelabh Chaturvedi; Dow Jones Newswires; 91 22 22884212; djn.in@dowjones.com [ 03-11-08 1216GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1-India's markets tumble as investors run for cover
text:
(Updates market rates)

MUMBAI, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Indian financial markets were pummelled on Monday as investors ran for cover in the face of the global financial crisis, knocking shares to their weakest level in three years and the rupee to a record low.

Money market rates rose sharply ahead of a holiday and as the central bank intervened in currency markets to support the rupee.

Signs of a looming global recession and slowing corporate earnings heightened investor risk aversion across Asia, helping send India's benchmark index <.BSESN> down as much as 11.5 percent at one point and stoking worries that ebbing foreign capital would drag the rupee <INR=IN> down still further.

Shares in India's biggest bank, State Bank of India , plunged to a 1-½ year low on worries over bad debt provisions.

Its second-quarter net profit beat forecasts by rising 40.4 percent from a year earlier, but its shares ended down 8.6 percent after the bank ramped up its provisions for bad debts almost fourfold compared with the previous quarter. [ID:nBOM79617]

"It seems like a ball has fallen from the top of a tower and is on its way down and is gathering pace but has not yet reached the bottom," said Sanjeev Patkar, head of research at Dolat Capital Markets in Mumbai.

"How much of this is speculative and how much of this is forced liquidation remains to be seen but this selling is having a multiplier effect and we will see some more of this in the coming days before it recovers."

The 30-share index fell below 8,000 points to its lowest level since October 2005 before recovering some ground to end down 2.2 percent.

It has lost 58 percent so far this year, the worst performer in Asia in 2008 after China <.SSEC>, Hong Kong <.HSI> and Vietnam <.VNI>, as foreign investors have sold emerging market assets and repatriated their funds.

The index rose 47 percent in 2007 when foreigners pumped in a record $17.4 billion. Outflows so far this year are $12.6 billion.

RUPEE FORTUNES The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN>, whose fortunes are closely tied to foreign flows in and out of the stock markets, slid to a record low of 50.29 per dollar, even though traders reported central bank intervention to prop it up.

It ended trade a shade stronger at 49.87/88, but Kotak Mahindra Bank said it could fall to 52.5-54.00 per dollar by the end of the year as capital is drained from the country and pressure builds on the trade deficit from falling exports.

Interbank overnight lending rates jumped above 9 percent from 6.00/6.25 percent on Friday, well above the central bank's main short-term lending rate of 8 percent, but below 23 percent hit earlier this month.

Like many central banks around the world, the Reserve Bank of India has been pumping record amounts of liquidity into its money market to try to keep credit flowing.

It has slashed banks' reserve requirements to free up cash and a week ago knocked 1 percentage point off its key lending rate to try to bring stability back to India's markets, strained by capital outflows, intervention and banks' reluctance to lend.

On Monday, it pumped 427.7 billion rupees ($8.6 billion) in via its money market operations to oil the wheels of the credit markets but rates remained elevated as banks borrowed heavily ahead of two market holidays this week.

"Due to the holidays banks are borrowing as much as they can now and also the central bank has been selling dollars, which is squeezing rupee liquidity," a dealer with a foreign bank said.

Bond and money markets are closed on Tuesday for a local holiday. Stocks will trade briefly in the evening.

The central bank opted not to follow last Monday's surprise rate cut with another one at a scheduled review on Friday, a decision which disappointed bonds and sent yields up.

But yields eased again on Monday as expectations rose that falling commodity and oil prices might persuade the central bank it has room to ease policy again.

The 10-year benchmark bond yield <IN082418G=CC> fell 20 basis points to 7.60 percent.

"In the current global and local settings, the RBI should be putting more policy easing in place, because it has that flexibility and because the economy is screaming for it," Rajeev Malik, economist at Macquarie Securities, said in a note. (Editing by Ranjit Gangadharan)

title: Reverse repo to continue as policy tool-India cbank
text:
MUMBAI, Oct 25 (Reuters) - India's central bank will continue to use its reverse repo rate as an active variable in its monetary policy and has not abandoned it, Governor Duvvuri Subbarao said on Saturday.

The reverse repo rate is the rate at which the central bank absorbs excess cash from banks and it has remained unchanged at 6.0 percent since July 2006, even though the repo rate, or key lending rate, has risen six times in the same period before being cut to 8.0 percent last Monday.

"We will continue to use that variable in our monetary policy. At the moment it is 6.0 percent and that's where we decided to leave it," Subbarao told news agencies a day after the central bank's quarterly policy review.

"But it does not mean we have abandoned it. Far from it."

The central bank left all its key rates steady on Friday and said it had to strike an optimal balance between financial stability, price stability, anchoring inflation expectations and sustaining growth.

Subbarao also said the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) would continue with its established policy of intervention in the currency markets.

"There are institutional policies of RBI, how we intervene, how much we intervene and in what markets we intervene and we will continue that policy."

Heavy central bank intervention rescued the Indian rupee from a record low of 50.15 per dollar <INR=IN> on Friday and kept the unit supported through the day even as the stock market plunged 11 percent to three-year lows.

Dealers said the central bank likely sold between $3 billion and $4 billion via state-run banks to defend the currency, and with investors pulling money out of emerging markets the outlook for the rupee was bearish.

Subbarao said the central bank was monitoring the dollar liquidity situation, assessing the impact of recent measures such as easing oversees borrowing rules for corporates.

"For dollar liquidity we have said we are sensitive to maintaining the rupee and forex liquidity. A number of measures have been taken," he said.

"We are monitoring the situation and if something more needs to be done we will do it but I am unable to say at this meeting what precisely we will do." (Reporting by Surojit Gupta and Charlotte Cooper; Editing by Anthony Barker)

title: 3rd UPDATE:Asian Shares Skid Into Weekend; Nikkei Sheds 9.6%
text:
(Adds detail, quotes, closing levels; updates other information)

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian share markets crawled into the weekend on their hands and knees, with selling picking up late on Friday amid concerns the global economy was sliding towards recession as key companies issued cautious earnings outlooks.

"Absolute carnage in Asia as recession fears spread like a wild fire. Risk aversion is happening on a massive scale," was how Knight Equity Markets vice-president Ioan Smith described things.

Markets were looking increasingly disorderly with Korean shares slumping 10.6% by the close and Japan's Nikkei 225 ending down 9.6%; both indexes broke key levels to hit multi-year lows.

There was much caution before the weekend with U.S. stock futures down heavily in screen trade; S&P 500 futures were quoted 4.1% lower, Nasdaq 100 futures down 2.5% and Dow Jones Industrial Average futures down 301 points.

European spreadbetting firms were now calling stocks there well lower. "Volatility and uncertainty seem to be the watch words at the moment," said CMC Markets dealer Matt Buckland.

Key companies around Asia issued cautious earnings or earnings guidance: Japan's Sony and Korea's Samsung Electronics were the most prominent of these.

That deepened concerns about the economic hit from the financial market crisis and spurred risk aversion, which showed up in a large rise in the Japanese yen.

"The theme of weaker global growth has replaced the issue of troubled banks for now and continues to weigh on investor psyches," said analysts at UBS.

Analysts said emerging markets were feeling the contagion from developed markets, where the subprime crisis had begun. Indeed, recent data had shown a decline in emerging market central bank foreign reserves and fund outflows from several key markets.

In Korea the bourse wrapped up the week on a downbeat note, ending at 938.75, under 1000 for the first time since June 29, 2005; it fell 20.5% for the week and was down 35.2% now for October.

Sentiment was hurt by news gross domestic product growth slowed in the third quarter to its lowest quarterly level in four years; "we've just stepped into a dark tunnel," said Citigroup economist Oh Suktae.

Also, Samsung Electronics fell 18.8% with its third quarter net profit of KRW1.219 trillion down from KRW2.191 trillion a year earlier and less than the KRW1.26 trillion forecast in a Dow Jones Newswires poll of analysts; LG Electronics shed 9.8% and Hynix Semiconductor fell its daily limit of 15%. Kia Motors dropped 14.8% after its weaker-than-expected earnings.

Japan's Nikkei 225 ended at its lowest level since April 2004, crimped by electronics shares as Sony's sharp outlook cut for earnings through March 2009 rippled through the sector; Sony shed 14% to a new year-low of Y1,972.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 closed down 2.4% at its lowest level since November 2004 with financials tepid; Perpetual fell 6.8% and Axa Asia Pacific 8.0% after they suspended fund redemptions.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was down 6.6% with HSBC shares falling 6.4% after Morgan Stanley cut its target price on the stock.

Taiwan shares ended 3.2% lower with weakness in chip makers, while New Zealand's market shed 1% and Philippine shares 2.1%.

Singapore's Straits Times Index was down 7.3%; "we are still seeing fund redemptions. The ingredients are there for a rebound but there's just no catalyst," said a dealer at local house in Singapore. Indonesian shares were down 6.6% with Thai shares off 5.4% and India's Sensex down 7.7%.

The euro was the main decliner in currency markets with non-Japanese short-term speculators selling it against the yen on Japanese stock losses.

The U.S. dollar dropped to Y94.93 from a high of Y97.98 with the euro at Y121.05 from Y127.04 earlier, falling to its lowest level since December 2002. The euro was down at $1.2740 from a high of $1.2975.

Australia's currency was under pressure, falling to US$0.6370, as was the British pound.

The recent rise in the yen was starting to cause some concern in Tokyo with finance minister Shoichi Nakagawa quoted by Kyodo as saying the government would closely watch the currency and stock markets and communicate with the Bank of Japan and overseas authorities; still, few would take that as a sign that currency market intervention was a chance anytime soon.

The Korean won was on a roller-coaster ride with the U.S. dollar rising to KRW1,465 from KRW1,408.8 Thursday before suspected intervention from the central bank to sell dollars took it back to KRW1,436.

Malaysia's ringgit hit a new low for 2008 against the U.S. dollar with intervention spotted to sell the dollar in several places, including India and Indonesia.

"Dollar/Asian currency markets are trading with an almost universal bid and though some spot markets are being kept in check by central bank intervention, discounts for Asian currencies priced in the NDF market are deep and widening further," said Societe Generale strategist Patrick Bennett.

Japanese government bonds were higher on safe-haven demand with lead December futures up 0.84 at 137.92; some said the swaps market was staring to price in the chance of a Bank of Japan interest rate cut.

Spot gold erased early gains with the U.S. dollar well bid and on the Nikkei's fall; the metal was at $712.50 an ounce, down $8.60 from New York.

Base metals were tepid with a trader at a global trading house in Shanghai saying buyers "were on strike; if copper prices are dropping 5% per day they are hardly going to buy. It will continue until prices stop falling and a rally looks like it could be sustainable." LME three-month copper was at $3,965 a ton, down $75 since Thursday's kerb.

Front-month Nymex crude gave up early gains despite expectations OPEC at its meeting later Friday would agree to cut output; it was down 27 cents at $67.57 per barrel.

title: Emerging  FX -Asians plumb multi-year lows on growth fears
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 23 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah hit its lowest level in nearly three years as Asian currencies fell to new multi-year lows on Thursday, hit by investor fears over global growth and persistent selling of risky assets.

 A day after Hungary raised rates by a hefty 3 percentage points to defend its currency, risk aversion was elevated in Asia with stock markets in Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines falling between 4 and 7 percent.

 The rupiah <IDR=> hit its lowest in nearly 3 years at 9,950 a dollar, the Philippine peso weakened to its weakest since early 2007 at 49 per dollar while the Malaysian ringgit fell to 3.5771, a nearly 2-year trough.

 The broad selling in emerging markets seemed to have sucked Asia in deep, even though it is backed by better fundamentals, such as ample reserves and growth estimates in higher single digits even in dismal global circumstances.

 "The nasty part is that deleveraging/balance sheet hole-plugging can produce indiscriminate selling, so Asia can be swept up even though its fundamentals are better," said Sean Callow, a strategist at Westpac Bank

 Central banks in India, Indonesia, Korea and the Philippines have been intervening to slow their currencies' decline and some of them were suspected of being in the market on Thursday.

 Analysts reckon policy makers are however merely smoothing the currency depreciation, and are tolerant of the weakness at a time when the risks of recession in Asia's main export markets are as high as that of heavy capital outflows triggered by the credit crisis.

 "Adding liquidity to increasingly thin and volatile markets is a valid policy decision, and note that FX reserves of most economies are ample," Patrick Bennett a strategist at Societe Generale said in a note.

 "We would only become concerned with a central bank attempting to defend a particular level, or one which was clearly acting contrary to economic fundamentals."  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR  Change on the day at 0526 GMT

title: Indian rupee hits record low, cbank  intervenes
text:
* Central bank likely sold $2 bln to lift rupee off low

* Losses in local stocks heighten worries of capital outflows (Updates to close)

By Swati Bhat

MUMBAI, Oct 22 (Reuters) - The rupee slumped to an all-time low on Wednesday before trimming losses on heavy dollar sales by state-run banks, but a slide in the stock market indicated there would be more pressure on the Indian unit.

The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> ended at 49.28/29 per dollar, 0.5 percent weaker than Tuesday's close of 49.04/06. It hit a record trough of 49.50, at which point it was down 20.4 percent in 2008.

Traders said the rupee would have fallen more had the state-run banks not intervened on behalf of the Reserve Bank of India.

"They are likely to have sold nearly $2 billion today," said Agam Gupta, head of forex trading at Standard Chartered Bank. "If they had not we would have been at 50 already."

He said the central bank was trying to smoothen the heavy demand for dollars, but was not trying to defend any particular level.

One-month offshore non-deliverable forward rupee contracts <PNDF> were at 50.79/94, nearly 3 percent weaker than the onshore spot rate, indicating a bearish outlook for the currency in the near term.

Indian shares fell 4.8 percent in a broad-based selloff, erasing the previous sessions gains, as recession fears hammered international equity markets. [.BO]

Foreign funds have sold a net $12.2 billion worth of Indian shares this year, and the stock market is down by half in 2008. Last year, the funds had bought a record net $17.4 billion, and the stock market rose 47 percent.

A stronger dollar overseas was also hurting rupee sentiment, dealers said. The dollar soared to a two-year high against the euro and a basket of currencies as a worsening global economic outlook prompted more investors to liquidate risky assets in favour of the U.S. currency.
