MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee slumped to an all-time low against the U.S. dollar Wednesday as foreign investors continued to pull out of local stock markets caught in a downward spiral.

The dollar ended at INR49.31 Wednesday, up from INR49.00 in the earlier session. It hit an all-time high of INR49.50, breaching the previous INR49.30 high hit earlier this month.

The greenback also drew strength from its gains against global currencies.

"The dollar has been rising against global majors. If the trend continues then it wouldn't take much time for it to reach INR50.50, the next key psychological level," said L. Subramanian, foreign exchange head at ICICI Bank.

The local currency is also expected to depreciate in the next few sessions due to possible order cancellations by exporters.

"With the dollar showing no signs of correction, there is a possibility of export cancellations, which may lead to further depreciation of the rupee," he added.

Demand for the buck also got a boost as several participants who were absent from the market Tuesday, because of a strike by RBI workers, bought heavily to meet customer flows, said a senior dealer with a state-run bank.

The greenback later retreated on suspected intervention by the Reserve Bank Of India that led to a wider selloff by market participants.

Subramanian estimated the central bank has been selling an average of $500 million to $600 million each session as it seeks to slow the rupee's slide.

The Bombay Stock Exchange's Sensex closed down 4.8% at 10,169.90, dragged down by weaker global stock markets.

In the bond market, the 10-year benchmark bond surged for the fourth straight session as it resumed trading after the repo rate cut earlier this week. Trading in the 8.24% 2018 note had been halted for book closure ahead of coupon payments.

The note ended at INR104.25 Wednesday, up from INR103.47 last close. Yield on the paper fell 12 basis points to 7.60%.

"Liquidity has already eased significantly. If it remains at present levels for about a week then we could safely discount an extension in the current bonds rally," said a senior dealer with a state-run bank, who expects yield on the 10-year note to fall to 7.35% in about a week.

Bonds gave up some gains after Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said the government may overshoot its fiscal deficit target for the current fiscal year, cementing market fears that it will likely borrow more.

"The market had for a long time been anticipating this. But it seems to be the first time the government has admitted it," said a dealer with a private bank.

Later in the session, a senior finance ministry official said the government was likely to borrow INR500 billion more in the current fiscal.

Dealers said the market will now watch for the crucial weekly inflation data due Thursday for further cues.

India's wholesale price index-based inflation rate is expected to rise to 11.49% on year in the week ended Oct. 11, from 11.44% in the previous week, according to the median estimate in a Dow Jones Newswires poll of five economists.

title: FX  Asia: Indian Rupee To Weaken Despite Govt, RBI Moves
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee is likely to continue falling against the U.S. dollar in coming months, despite government and the central bank attempts to stem capital outflows from India's stuttering economy. 

The currency has lost nearly 10% of its value against the greenback since September, hitting a lifetime low of INR49.30 on Oct. 10, amid a broad scramble to buy dollars even as the pipeline of foreign money has sputtered.

India's authorities have responded with a slew of measures to bolster the domestic economy and attract capital - the latest being the Reserve Bank of India's surprise 100 basis point cut in its key lending rate Monday.

More steps are likely to follow, but as the likelihood of a global economic slowdown mounts and money is pulled from emerging markets, analysts say further countermeasures will at best only slow the rupee's decline. Some now predict a fall to INR52.00 to the dollar by the end of the year.

The rupee is likely to come under further pressure as India's balance of payments deteriorates.

"The options are clearly limited for both the government and the Reserve Bank of India, beyond frequent intervention to smoothen the volatility and allow a gradual depreciation," said Saugata Bhattacharya, vice president of business and economic research at Axis Bank.

Having relaxed the ceiling on overseas borrowings for local infrastructure companies and doubled the limit for foreign investment in domestic corporate debt to $6 billion, the government is considering a hike in the cap on investment in the insurance sector. It may also allow more foreign direct investment in cash-crunched sectors like retail.

Still, opening a whole number of windows to foreign direct investment is unlikely to change the picture over the next two to three months as capital remains scarce globally.

The world financial crisis has drastically cut investor appetite for emerging market assets. In sharp contrast to 2007, when foreign funds bought over $17 billion of Indian shares, they have pulled out over $11 billion so far this year.

The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark Sensex index has registered huge losses this year. It is currently just above the 10,000 point mark, having hit a lifetime high of 21206.77 points on Jan. 10.

"The rupee's recovery is intimately linked to global economic conditions improving and a return of risk appetite," said Vikas Agarwal, strategist at JP Morgan Bank, who pegs the dollar to cost INR49.00 by end of this year.


 
   The RBI May Have Run Out Of Tools 
 

The RBI seems unable to arrest the rupee's tailspin. Its 100-point cut, aimed at giving a leg-up to local stocks and thereby boosting investor confidence and easing the pressure on the rupee, produced only a modest bounce in the currency.

Indeed, the rupee quickly retreated to near its intrasession lows and then breached the key psychological INR49.00 level late in the Indian day.

"I think they (the RBI) are already doing the maximum. They can't do much more. It's highly unlikely the currency will appreciate in the next three to six months," said Sailesh K. Jha, senior economist at Barclays Capital.

He expects dollar/rupee to touch INR52.00 by the end of 2008.

The RBI has been intervening in the foreign exchange market almost every day of late, by selling dollars from its reserves. It has started special operations for oil refining companies, which often dominate the forex market to procure dollars for their imports.

It has also twice raised interest rates on domestic accounts of Indians living abroad to bring in more dollar remittances.

But sustained intervention, while damping sharp intraday fluctuations, is taking its toll on the country's foreign exchange reserves. Central bank data shows reserves to have fallen from over $300 billion on Aug. 1 to $274 billion in the week ended Oct. 10, a majority of that through dollar selling.


 
   Balance Of Payments Deteriorating 
 

India, which imports nearly two-thirds of its total oil needs, is also feeling the strain in its trade account because of 2008's high oil prices. Oil imports doubled in the fiscal first quarter that ended June 30 versus a year earlier.

The current account deficit widened to $10.724 billion in the fiscal first quarter, compared with $6.301 billion a year earlier.

This almost eclipsed the surplus in India's capital account, and economists are projecting the country may fall into an overall deficit in its balance of payments over coming quarters.

And, whatever relief will come from the sharp cooling in oil prices will be offset by a weaker rupee.

"With dwindling capital flows, it'll be difficult to counter a largely consistent current account deficit. This will naturally put further pressure on the rupee," said Bhattacharya of Axis Bank, who tips the dollar to hover around INR50.00 by end of December.

Traders said the Reserve Bank of India has intervened to sell dollars through state-run banks after the rupee had fallen to 48.62 in early deals.

The main share index <.BSESN> fell more than 4 percent, weighed down by tight cash conditions, which the rupee-buying intervention exacerbates, and worries about the risk of a global recession.

Dealers said dollar demand from oil firms also put downward pressure on the rupee. Oil <CLc1> is India's biggest import, and refiners are the largest buyers of dollars in the currency market. (Reporting by Anurag Joshi; Editing by John Mair)

NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--Indian government bond prices rose Wednesday on expectations of more measures from the central bank to improve liquidity in the banking system.

The benchmark 8.24% 2018-dated bond ended at INR102.20, up from its previous close of INR101.95. Yield on the note fell by three basis points to 7.91%.

Cash in the banking system has dried up in recent weeks as companies made quarterly tax payments and the Reserve Bank of India's intervention in the currency markets drained cash.

Banks remain reluctant to lend to each other, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said, with call money rate spiking to 10.25% Wednesday from 8.75% on Tuesday.

"The government and the Reserve Bank of India are agreed on the measures that have to be taken immediately," Chidambaram told reporters at a press briefing.

The comments bolstered market expectations of more steps by the central bank to soothe shaky markets, after the RBI had last week aggressively slashed the proportion of deposits banks must set aside with it.

"Given that capital inflows have been scarce and it has a lot of headroom to cut the cash reserve ratio at a time when fears of sharp slowdown in growth are emerging, we could see some actions later today (Wednesday)," said Ramya Suryanarayanan, economist at DBS Bank.

However, gains were capped on speculation the central bank measures may include a possible cut in the statutory liquidity ratio, a norm that governs the amount of sovereign debt banks must hold.

Under SLR, Indian banks need to maintain 25% of their deposits in gold, cash and government securities, hence any lowering of the requirement would hurt demand for government paper.

In the currency market, the Indian rupee fell against the U.S. dollar as a slide in local shares raised concerns of more capital outflows from the country.

The dollar ended the day at INR48.53, up from its previous close of INR48.08.

"There was good buying interest on account of firm rates in the non-deliverable forwards market but central bank intervention capped the gains," said a foreign exchange dealer at a state-run bank.

The Bombay Stock Exchange's 30-stock index down 674.28 points, or 5.9%, to end at 10,809.12.

title: Indian cbank bought net $1.2 bln in August
text:
MUMBAI, Oct 13 (Reuters) - India's central bank bought a net $1.2 billion in intervention in August, when the rupee weakened past 44 to the dollar for the first time in nearly 1-½ years, data showed on Monday.

It was the first net purchases by the central bank after being net sellers in the previous two months to slow the rupee's slide.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) bought $3.8 billion in August and sold $2.6 billion.

In July, it had sold $9.9 billion, the highest in a month since the RBI began publishing its currency intervention figures in April 1995, and bought $3.58 billion.

The RBI had sold almost $7 billion and bought $1.77 billion in June.

The central bank has bought a net $14.45 billion between January and August, the monthly RBI bulletin showed.

The rupee fell 10.3 percent in the first eight months of 2008, ending August at 43.935/945 per dollar <INR=IN>.

Last week, it slumped to an all-time low of 49.30 on heavy foreign withdrawals from a sliding stock market.

The RBI is suspected to have intervened actively to halt the fall in the past few weeks. On Monday, the rupee ended at 48.25/27, down 18.3 percent this year.

In 2007, record portfolio inflows of $17.4 billion had helped the rupee climb to a near decade high of 39.16 in November last year. In comparison, foreign funds are net sellers of $10.8 billion so far this year. (Reporting by Anurag Joshi; Editing by Ranjit Gangadharan)

title: Emerging  FX -Asia slides as stocks pounded, won trades wildly
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were battered on Friday as investors dumped stocks amid the financial turmoil despite a round of global interest rate cuts, prompting dollar-selling intervention in South Korea, Indonesia and India.

 The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> fell as far as 9,750 per dollar, down about 1.6 percent from Thursday's close, as trader cited dollar-selling intervention by the central bank to support the local currency.

 "The action keeps players sidelined," said a trader in Jakarta.

 The South Korean won <KRW=> moved wildly, gaining over 12 percent to 1,224.9 per dollar at one point after falling sharply earlier, as the authorities were seen selling dollars to defend the won, which has lost 27 percent against the dollar this year.

 A wave of selling pounded Asian shares amid growing fears of the financial turmoil, with the MSCI index of Asia-Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> falling 7.7 percent to its lowest since January 2005.

 The Indian rupee <INR=IN> hit a record low at 49.25 per dollar, as the central bank said it would cut bank's cash reserve requirements to 7.5 percent to ease a liquidity crunch. [ID:nBOM357479]

 Meanwhile, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell to 1.4865 per U.S dollar, giving up its early gains as investors turned bearish on data showing the economy is in recession.

 "It's due to the GDP figure," said a trader in Singapore.

 The Sing dollar briefly rose to 1.4724 immediately after the central bank announced an easing in monetary policy.

 Some traders said suspected official intervention helped the local unit.

 Singapore's central bank, which sets policy by managing the Singapore dollar in a secret trade-weighted band against a basket of currencies, eased monetary policy for the first time in five years after its economy sank into recession [ID:nSIN389047]

 The central bank said on Friday it was shifting policy from a gradual appreciation bias to a neutral zero-appreciation bias for the trade-weighted currency, in response to slowing growth and expected easing in inflation.

 The central bank maintained the width of the secretive band.

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> lost almost 0.9 percent to 47.8 per dollar, while the Thai baht <THB=TH> was down 0.4 percent to 34.48 per dollar.

 "We see some interest selling from exporters and some from offshore," said a trader in Bangkok. "The bias is that the dollar should go up against the baht, like dollar/regionals."

 Markets in Taiwan are closed for a holiday.

 Meanwhile, the cost of dollar funding remained elevated in Asia on Friday, with overnight dollar funds <USDOND=> quoted between 4 and 7 percent in Singapore, 4.5-5.8 percent in Bangkok and 4-5 percent in Jakarta, traders said.

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee weakened against the U.S. dollar Wednesday to a more than six-year low on persistent worries about capital outflows, but recouped most of its losses after several central banks cut key policy rates, raising hopes of greater stability in global financial markets.

The dollar ended at INR48.01 Wednesday, up from INR47.94 in the previous session. It hit an intraday high of INR48.80, its highest level since July 2002.

The U.S. Federal Reserve cut its target federal funds rate 50 basis points to 1.5% Wednesday and was joined by the Bank of Canada, the Bank of England, the European Central Bank, Sweden's Riksbank and the Swiss National Bank.

"The (rate cut) news will help reverse the downtrend in global equity markets. Sentiment in India will also be lifted, which will be a positive for the rupee," said L. Subramaniam, head of foreign-exchange trading at ICICI Bank.

He said he expects sharp gains for the rupee from now on, driven by a likely recovery in local stock markets and expectations of heavy cancellations in the non-deliverable forward market Monday.

"I think the rupee should rise to the next technical level of INR46.58 on Monday," he said.

Indian financial markets will remain closed Thursday for a religious holiday.

Local dealers said the Reserve Bank of India didn't actively intervene in the foreign-exchange market Wednesday as any move may not have stemmed the rupee's depreciation due to genuine outflows from local stocks amid the prevailing global economic uncertainties.

The RBI also refrained from heavy intervention as the move could sap rupee liquidity from an already strained banking system, said a dealer with a foreign bank.

The Bombay Stock Exchange 30-stock Sensex index ended down 3.1% at 11,328.36, its lowest close in over two years. It had fallen as much as 8.2% to 10740.76 early in the previous session on foreign fund selling and a weak overnight close in the U.S.

In the bond market, government bond prices rose sharply after the global rate cut news raised hopes that the Reserve Bank of India may follow suit.

The 8.24% 2018-dated bond ended at INR101.70, up from INR100.84 in the earlier session. The yield on the benchmark note fell 13 basis points to 7.98%.

"Going by the reaction, it seems traders are discounting a 25-50-basis-point cut in the repo rate (RBI's key lending rate) after the news," said Baljinder Singh, bond dealer at Andhra Bank.

Singh notes, while a repo rate cut looks unlikely as inflation remains high, the central bank could move to infuse liquidity by lowering banks' cash reserve ratio - the portion of deposits that banks need to set aside with the RBI in cash.

Bonds were also helped by a drop in crude oil prices, which fell to an intraday low of $86.05 a barrel. Crude oil later recovered to around $89/bbl.

However, initial gains were capped by a scheduled INR100 billion bond sale Friday that prompted traders to cut positions hoping for better prices to build stock at the auction.

Dealers will now scour the inflation data, industrial output data and bond auction results, all slated for Friday, for further cues.

The annual wholesale price index-based inflation rate is expected at 11.98% in the week ended Sept. 27, compared with 11.99% the previous week, according to the median estimate in a Dow Jones Newswires poll of six economists.

title: INTERVIEW:Dollar May Rise To INR50 By Jan On Global Woes-UBS
text:
NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee may plunge to lifetime lows against the dollar over the next three-four months due to a widening trade deficit and heightened risk aversion, the director of emerging markets foreign exchange strategy at UBS AG said Wednesday. 

The Reserve Bank of India, which is said to have been intervening in the foreign-exchange market sporadically, mightn't be able to stop the rupee's fall as it is legitimately preoccupied with forestalling a liquidity crisis, Nizam Idris told Dow Jones Newswires.

The dollar - now trading around INR48.66, a more-than-six-year high- may shoot up to INR50 by January, Idris said by phone and email from Singapore.

"With sentiment soured by extreme risk aversion and deleveraging, the dollar has remained well-supported against most Asian currencies," Idris said.

In the case of the rupee, the market is concerned by an adverse trade balance and the large amount of foreign investments already sunkin India, which are currently being pulled out, he said.

India's current account deficit widened to a record $10.72 billion in the fiscal first quarter ended June 30, compared with $6.30 billion a year earlier, the Reserve Bank of India said late last month. Idris expects the deficit to continue widening.

Asian currencies from the Korean won to the Indonesian rupiah have been pummeled as the global financial crisis escalates, depriving these countries of the dollars they need to fund their ballooning current-account deficits.

The Indian rupee has lost 19% since January, marking a sharp reversal in fortunes for the unit, which was Asia's second-best performer last year with a 12% rise.

The dollar hit a lifetime high of INR49.07 against the rupee in June 2002.

Foreign investors have been net sellers of local shares worth $9.7 billion so far this year. The country's benchmark Sensex stock index has slid more than 46% since the beginning of 2008.

Idris said the current financial turmoil may make it difficult for the Reserve Bank to intervene aggressively.

"Under such an environment, maintaining liquidity conditions precedes the need to control the exchange rates," he said. "Only when the need for liquidity eases - and this may take a while - would more aggressive intervention become easier."

Earlier this week, the RBI cut the amount of deposits banks have to set aside as cash with it for the first time in five years as overnight borrowing costs rose sharply.

For its part, India's capital markets regulator has said that it will remove a ban imposed last October on the issue of participatory notes with derivatives as underlying assets by foreign institutional investors. However, this move is unlikely to lead to heavy inflows anytime soon as global financial markets remain in a funk, Idris said.

To be sure, he expects the rupee to recover once risk appetite returns, as the central bank would then focus on taming inflation by jacking up interest rates.

Idris expects inflation to stay above the RBI's comfort level of 7% by March 2009.

title: India cash rate spikes after rupee hits 5-yr low
text:
MUMBAI, Oct 1 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee fell to five-year lows and overnight cash rates climbed to 18-month highs on Wednesday on fears foreign investors caught in a global credit crunch and turbulent markets would pull more money out of India.

The rupee slumped in early deals, and intervention by the Reserve Bank of India to prop it up worsened a cash squeeze that has seen record amount of funds pumped into the banking system through the central bank's daily market operations.

The cash rate surged to 17.50 percent, its highest since April 2, 2007, according to Reuters data, and nearly double the central bank's main lending rate of 9 percent, and a morning fund injection of more than 700 billion rupees ($15 billion) could only bring it down to about 15 percent.

"The deleveraging and the credit contraction that is happening in the world markets is having an impact here and that will continue to keep the rupee pressured downwards," said Mohan Shenoi, treasurer at Kotak Mahindra Bank in Mumbai.

The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> fell as low as 47.2350 per dollar, its weakest since early June 2003, before it was propped up by the central bank's dollar-selling intervention and strengthened back past 47 per dollar.

Bond yields fell as banks bought debt to meet their reserve requirements. The benchmark 10-year yield <IN082418G=CC> was at 8.49 percent below a previous close of 8.62 percent.

Analysts think money markets will remain tight for some time as the central bank is expected to keep propping up the rupee.

As well, the central bank is selling 70 billion rupees of bills on Wednesday, and the government said last week it would auction 390 billion rupees of bonds by the end of the year.

"Everybody is rushing to cover their cash requirements, and this is also a holiday-shortened week and nobody wants to take any chances," said G. Bhaskar, a senior dealer with state-run Andhra Bank.

Currency and debt markets were closed on Tuesday due to fiscal half-yearly closing of books by banks. Markets will shut again on Thursday for a national holiday.

And just as record buying of stocks by foreigners last year helped propel the rupee up more than 12 percent towards 10-year highs last year, the withdrawal of foreign funds this year has been a key factor in its fall of more than 16 percent.

Foreigners have sold a net $9.3 billion of Indian shares so far in 2008, including about $2 billion in September, after buying a record $17.4 billion last year. The stock market, which rose 47 percent in 2007, is down by more than a third this year.

There are other worries for the rupee, including widening trade and current account deficits.

"We may see the rupee test 48-49 per dollar in the next 3-6 months due to the deteriorating balance of payments conditions," Kotak Mahindra's Shenoi said.

The current account deficit <INCURA=ECI> widened sharply to $10.72 billion in the June quarter from $1.04 billion three months earlier as a sharp rise in oil prices widened the trade gap. [ID:nBOM201884].

Macquarie Securities expect the current account deficit to widen to $37 billion in 2008/09 from $17 billion in 2007/08. (Editing by John Mair)

title: UPDATE: India MOF Exec: Expect RBI To Hold Rates Steady
text:
NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--India's federal finance ministry expects the Reserve Bank of India to hold key policy rates steady at its Oct. 24 meeting, a senior ministry official said Wednesday.

"There is little scope for cuts in the cash reserve ratio and the statutory liquidity ratio now," the official, who asked not to be named, told reporters.

Under SLR, Indian banks must invest at least 25% of their deposits in gold, cash and government securities, ensuring a captive market for sovereign debt. India's cash reserve ratio, or the proportion of deposits banks have to set aside as cash with the central bank, is 9%. "There is a liquidity problem currently, but the situation will improve once the government pays INR250 billion to banks under the farm loan waiver," the official said.

The Indian government had earlier said it will waive off INR670 billion in small farm loans, and banks will be compensated in cash over the next three years.

The official said the government plans to pay interest to commercial banks on the amount of farm loans that they have already waived off under a government program to boost fresh lending to the agriculture sector.

The first chunk of the loans were waived off on June 30.

On the sharp decline in the value of the Indian rupee against the dollar in recent weeks, he said the Reserve Bank of India is likely to continue intervening in the local currency markets to check volatility.

"The RBI doesn't target any level for the rupee. Their clear policy on the currency is to check volatility," he said.

Since the beginning of the year, the rupee has lost nearly 16% against the dollar, erasing gains of over 12% last year.

The rupee touched an over five-year low of INR47.23 to a dollar in early trade on Wednesday, but later recovered on suspected RBI intervention. At 1110 GMT, the dollar was changing hands at INR46.69.

The official also said the current global financial crisis is likely to slow India's movement toward fuller capital account convertibility as suggested by a government-appointed panel that set a roadmap for easing capital controls last year.

"You can't keep moving at the same pace if things are happening around you," he said.

text:

* Indian rupee seen ending 2008 at 45.50/dlr

* While stronger than now, will end 2008 down 13 pct

* Rupee seen strengthening to 45.00 by end-March 2009

By Swati Bhat

MUMBAI, Sept 17 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is expected to recover from recent two-year lows in coming months, aided by the central bank, but will still finish 2008 more than 13 percent below where it started, a Reuters poll showed on Wednesday.

The rupee hit 46.99 <INR=IN> per dollar on Tuesday, according to Reuters data, its weakest since July 2006 and just short of a five-year low. At the trough, it was down more than 16 percent in 2008.

The rupee recovered ground on Wednesday, closing at 46.33/35.

According to a median forecast in the Reuters poll of 10 economists, the rupee will climb back to 45.50 by the end of this year. That will still leave it 13.4 percent below its 2007 close of 39.41.

Economists said easing oil prices and a statement this week by the central bank that it would continue propping the currency up, after much dollar-selling intervention in recent weeks, were the two main factors likely to help it.

"There is some improvement over time in the current account deficit situation with the oil prices coming off so much, and hopefully if the global financial turmoil settles down, then we may see some capital inflows coming in as well," said A. Prasanna, economist with ICICI Securities.

After appreciating more than 12 percent against the dollar last year, the rupee has faced heavy pressure from rising risk aversion among foreign investors and record oil prices, as India imports about 70 percent of its oil.

Oil <CLc1> has fallen more than $50 per barrel from $147 in July, relieving pressure on the import bill, but market turmoil worldwide and concerns of slowing growth in India have seen foreigners sell a net $8.7 billion in shares so far this year.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said late on Tuesday it would continue to intervene by selling dollars to support the rupee, either directly or through state-run banks. See [ID:nBOM324806].

It also took steps to attract more capital inflows by making interest rates more attractive on some foreign currency and rupee deposits for non-residents.

But not everyone expected capital inflows to rise substantially by the end of this year.

Shubhada Rao, chief economist at Yes Bank, said the renewed financial turmoil stemming from the collapse of Lehman Brothers could dampen or delay inflows.

"We still have some pain left," Rao said.

A wildcard is whether authorities restart special market operations for refiners. Refiners are the largest dollar buyers in the local market and for about two months until July the RBI lent them dollars from reserves in exchange for oil bonds.

If this resumed, the rupee could rise by at least one rupee as a major source of dollar buying would be reduced.

"This facility might recommence if the RBI desires to send a signal that it is uncomfortable with the pace of INR weakness," Vikas Agarwal and Sid Mathur, economists at JP Morgan Chase, wrote in a note.

text:
* Rupee rises more than 1 pct after central bank moves

* Cbank sold dollars around 46.70, traders say (Updates to close)

By Swati Bhat

MUMBAI, Sept 17 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee rose more than 1 percent in volatile trade on Wednesday, boosted by the central bank's move to keep selling dollars and lift deposit rates for non-resident Indians, but stock market losses remained a weight.

The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> ended at 46.33/35 per dollar, off a high of 46.25, and 1.2 percent stronger than 46.89/90 at the close on Tuesday. It fell to a low of 46.99 on Tuesday, its weakest since July 2006, according to Reuters data.

On Wednesday the rupee fell as low as 46.75 due to heavy dollar demand from foreign institutional investors and oil companies, traders said.

They said the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) commitment on Tuesday to continue intervening to support the rupee helped it strengthen in early trade. [ID:nBOM320160]

title: India cbank sold $9.9 bln in  currency  market in July
text:
MUMBAI, Sept 12 (Reuters) - India's central bank sold a gross $9.9 billion in currency market intervention in July, the highest on record, in a volatile month when the rupee hit a 15-month low but then later rose 1.1 percent on the dollar.

The central bank's monthly bulletin showed on Friday the monetary authority sold $6.32 billion on a net basis in July, trimming its net dollar purchases in 2008 to $13.24 billion.

The $9.9 billion gross is the most sold in a month by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) since it began publishing its currency intervention figures in April 1995. It surpasses record dollar sales of almost $7 billion gross in June.

The rupee fell 7.4 percent in the first seven months of 2008, ending July at 42.57/58 per dollar <INR=IN>, in a reversal of its fortunes in 2007 when strong foreign investment inflows drove it to 39.16, its highest in nearly a decade.

This year's fall accelerated sharply in July as crude touched a record above $147 a barrel, the trade deficit widened, and investment outflows weighed.

Traders say that in recent months and days the central bank has continued to support the rupee, which is now at its lowest in two years, has shed nearly 4 percent this month alone and lost 13.9 percent this year. (Reporting by Anurag Joshi; Editing by Charlotte Cooper)

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee fell to a 23-month low Thursday as concerns of fund outflows from local stock markets and the dollar's global strength continued to weigh on the local currency.

The dollar ended at INR45.57, up from INR45.11 in the previous session. It touched an intraday high of INR45.57, last seen early in October 2006.

But dealers said the greenback was stonewalled by suspected massive foreign exchange intervention by the Reserve Bank of India.

Traders estimated the central bank could have sold close to $2 billion in the session as it sought to check the dollar's unrelenting rise.

But despite the cap, strong demand from foreign investors pulling out money from local shares and heavy oil bids lifted the foreign currency close to its intraday high.

"The RBI was holding the dollar back. Had it not been in the market, the dollar would have shot through the roof," said a dealer with a private bank.

Traders said apart from the dollar's infused by the RBI there was no supply of the currency.

"Even exporters are sitting on their cash piles betting on even better levels ahead to sell," said L. Subramanian, chief foreign exchange dealer at ICICI Bank.

Subramanian said the Non Deliverable Forward, or NDF, market had been tracking the surge in the dollar index, which measures the currency's performance against global majors.

But the index seems to have reached its technical top and a correction could be round the corner.

"If the dollar reverses its gains overseas or if big flows hit the market, then we could see a major correction domestically," he said.

The Bombay Stock Exchange's 30-stock Sensitive Index, or Sensex, closed at the lowest in nearly two weeks, falling 338.32 points, or 2.3%, to 14,324.29.

In the bond market, government bond prices surged late in the session after the Chairman of the Indian Prime Minister's Economic Advisory Council said inflation looked to have peaked, leaving little room for further monetary tightening.

The 8.24% 2018-dated bond ended at INR99.75 Thursday, up from INR99.14 in the earlier session. The yield on the note fell nine basis points to 8.28%.

"My gut feeling is that inflation has peaked and will start tapering off. I do not basically see the case for further monetary tightening if inflation tapers off," Suresh Tendulkar told UTVi television news channel in an interview.

The market was also buoyed by speculation that the weekly inflation rate may ease to levels sharply lower than economists' expectations.

India's wholesale price index-based inflation rate was expected to come in at 12.01% on the year in the week ended Aug. 30, easing from 12.34% in the previous week, according to the median forecast of 12 economists in a Dow Jones poll.

However, data released after market hours belied all rumors, showing the inflation rate at 12.10%.

"The numbers seem very disappointing after the rumors that had been doing the rounds. We would have a bad session tomorrow with an opening at least 50-70 paise lower than today's close," said Ashish Vaidya, head of interest rate trading at HDFC Bank.

Vaidya said if stop-losses get triggered then it could mean a nose-dive for the benchmark 10-year government paper.

title: UPDATE 2-Eyes on S.Korea as Asian c.banks defend  currencies
text:
(Updates levels, adds Philippine intervention)

 SINGAPORE, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Central banks in Malaysia, India and elsewhere in Asia defended their weak currencies on Tuesday, but analysts suspected that South Korea's hands-off stance may deter others from standing firmly in the way of their falling currencies.

 The Bank of Thailand said it had sold dollars to put a floor under the baht <THB=TH>, which hit a one-year low of 34.49 per dollar on growing political tensions.

 Thai Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej declared a state of emergency in Bangkok on Tuesday and gave the army control of public order after overnight clashes between pro- and anti-government protesters.

 Market participants also reported interventions in India, Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia as currencies there buckled under the U.S. dollar's broad rally, the latter hitting an 8-month high against a basket of major currencies as oil prices fell.

 "All central banks are trying their best to stop the flood of outflows," a trader in Singapore said.

 In South Korea, where the won <KRW=> has been plumbing multi-year lows, the authorities restricted their efforts to meetings, warnings. Dollar-selling intervention, if any, was light as the volatile currency hit a new 4-year low near 1,134 per dollar.

 No one is sure why the Korean authorities have loosened their grip and let the won weaken, but market participants believe it is either because they want to shore up exports or out of reluctance to spend reserves against an inevitable dollar rally.

 Analysts said Korea's indifference to won weakness could weaken the resolve of other central banks.

 "It's very difficult if one goes, particularly if it's a large and important third-markets competitor for the rest of the region, like Korea," said Simon Flint, a strategist at Lehman Brothers. "It becomes difficult for the others to resist depreciation from a trade-weighted perspective.

 "Secondly, it weakens people's belief in the ability of the central banks to intervene effectively once they have seen one central bank can't do as they have apparently said they will do."

 INDIA ALSO STEPS IN

 The Reserve Bank of India was also spotted selling dollars but the rupee <INR=IN> still continued falling to hit a new 1-½   year low of 44.35 per dollar.

 The Malaysian central bank may have sold dollars at 3.4190 and 3.4180 per dollar, a trader in Kuala Lumpur said, but the ringgit persisted with its decline.

 The rupiah <IDR=> hit a low of 9,196 per dollar, its weakest since Aug. 19. A trader in Jakarta said the central bank sold dollars from 9,190.

 "It's not large. I think they realise that there is no point intervening aggressively in a dollar bull market all over the place," said one trader in Jakarta.

 In the Philippines, the central bank was seen selling dollars as the peso <PHP=> reached 46.60 per dollar, its weakest in almost a year.  (Reporting by Vidya Ranganathan; Editing by Jan Dahinten)

text:
SINGAPORE, July 1 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies traded narrowly on Tuesday as investors warily held back following decade-high inflation rates in Thailand and South Korea, while authorities were suspected to have intervened in some currencies.

Foreign exchange authorities in Indonesia, Malaysia, India and the Philippines were suspected to have intervened to support their currencies.

South Korea's annual inflation in June rose to 5.5 percent from 4.9 percent in May, hitting its highest in almost 10 years.

Subsequently, the Korean won <KRW=> weakened to 1,048.75 per dollar, 0.3 percent lower than its previous close of 1,046 <KRW=KFTC>, while market players kept a look-out for possible dollar-selling intervention.

Earlier on, several currencies in the region were buoyed by a pullback in oil prices <CLc1>, which hit a record high above $143 per barrel on Monday, but these currencies gave up gains as oil prices rebounded to around $141 per barrel on Tuesday.

Still, the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> inched up by 0.1 percent to 9,215 against the dollar and held around those levels throughout the day.

Traders in Jakarta said the authorities had sold dollars everyday for the past few weeks to support the rupiah, and were doing the same on Tuesday.

"The government cannot subsidise our local oil, and this has caused higher inflation, so another way to (support growth) is to maintain the dollar/rupiah pairing at a cozy rate so our industries can run well," an Indonesia-based trader said.

Indonesia's annual inflation rate rose to a 21-month high of 11.03 percent in June, due largely to the lifting of fuel subsidies in the country.

The country's policy setting meeting will take place on Thursday, and Robert Prior-Wandesforde at HSBC said he expected a 25-basis-point hike in the present interest rate of 8.5 percent.

"We are expecting another quarter-point move on Thursday and a total of 125 basis points of hikes by the end of this year, taking the policy rate up to 9.75 percent," the economist said.

Thailand's consumer prices in June rose 8.9 percent from a year earlier, higher than the expected 8.5 percent polled in a Reuters survey. However, markets in Thailand were closed for a mid-year holiday.

MORE INTERVENTION CITED

The Indian rupee <INR=IN> fell to a 15-month low of 43.437 on heightened concerns over the impact of rising oil on the economy's growth. Traders said they suspected the central bank had been selling dollars early in the day.

Traders in Manila also cited intervention by the Philippine central bank to support the peso <PHP=>, which hit a 9-month low of 45.02.

"Seems foreigners are not willing to touch this currency in the short term until political news is gone," a trader in Kuala Lumpur said.

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> briefly dipped to 44.45 per dollar, down 0.7 percent from Friday's close and its weakest level since October.

 Philippine markets were closed on Monday for a holiday.

 A trader attributed the peso's fall to a combination of domestic concerns about high oil prices and the dollar's broad rally, and suspected the central bank was again in the market to limit the peso's decline.

 "I think the concerns locally are the primary driver of the weakening peso," he added.

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell as far as 1.3695 to the U.S. dollar, down 0.6 percent from late Asian trade on Monday.

 "It's due to Bernanke's statement," said a Singapore-based trader, who expected the currency to move between 1.3645 and 1.3720 for the day.

 The dollar jumped to a three-month high against the yen <JPY=> on Tuesday after Bernanke said on Monday that the central bank would strongly resist an erosion in inflation expectations, convincing more investors that rate hikes could come this year.

 Bernanke also highlighted inflation risks from surging energy prices and that the risk of a substantial downturn in the U.S. economy had receded, sparking broad dollar gains and sending U.S. bond yields soaring. [ID:nN09303720]

 Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury Secretary Paulson declined on Monday to rule out intervention in the foreign exchange market  to stabilise the dollar. [ID:nN09578167]

INTERVENTION

 Meanwhile, central banks in South Korea, India and Thailand intervened to prop up their currencies in the face of a broadly stronger dollar, traders said. [ID:nSP101255]

 The South Korean won <KRW=> gained as much as 1 percent to 1,021.75 to the dollar, boosted by suspected dollar sales by the foreign exchange authorities.

 Despite suspected intervention by the Reserve Bank of India to support the rupee, the currency <INR=IN> eased a fifth of a percent to 42.932 per dollar.

 A second trader added: "If the baht breaks 33.50 level, it will move to 34.00. That means depreciation from 32.50 to 34.00 in 2 weeks, which is too fast. So they try to stabilise the baht."

title: TABLE-Asia ex-China's  FX  reserves fall $9 bln in May
text:
SINGAPORE, June 10 (Reuters) - Asian holdings of foreign exchange reserves, excluding those of China's, fell for the second staight month, central bank data showed, as some central banks sold dollars to support their weakening currencies.

 Asia's reserves, excluding China's, in May fell by nearly $9 billion from April to $2.54 trillion, following a $10 billion decline in April from March, the data showed.

 The overall decrease was led by an $6.86 billion dip in Japan's reserves, the second straight monthly decline, as higher U.S. yields cut the value of bonds in Japan's reserves while the euro's fall versus the dollar also dented the stockpile.

title: WRAPUP 1-Indian, Thai, Korean  currencies  fall as oil soars
text:
BANGKOK, June 9 (Reuters) - The Indian and Thai central banks intervened on Monday to stem losses in the rupee <INR=> and baht <THB=> triggered by soaring world oil prices and more foreign selling in their respective stock markets.

The South Korean won <KRW=>, down 9.4 percent so far this year, also fell to a one-week low against the dollar although traders said they had not seen the central bank selling dollars to curb the decline.

The won recovered some of its early losses as investors remained on the lookout for possible government dollar-selling, but is expected to remain under pressure from high oil prices and inflation that is likely to curb demand in Asia's fourth-largest economy.

The Bank of Thailand blamed foreign speculators for pushing the Thai currency to its weakest level in five months, although it is still up 1.35 percent so far this year.

"We've seen some speculation and we are watching it," Assistant Governor Suchada Kirakul told reporters after the central bank intervened for the second time in two days.

The baht closed at 33.23/25 after earlier hitting a five-month low of 33.41.

"The baht has weakened too fast. Our economic fundamentals have not changed overnight," she said.

"We will try to calm the baht's volatility. We don't want to see a move in one direction," she said, reiterating comments she made to Reuters on Friday. [ID:nBKK9980].

Suchada said the baht weakness was triggered by a sell-off in Thai shares last week, while importers of oil and other materials were still buying dollars on Monday.

Foreign investors sold a net 12 billion baht ($360 million) worth of Thai shares last week.

They have sold 27.4 billion baht worth of Thai stocks so far this year as inflation soared to near 10-year highs and anti-government protests renewed fears of political instability.

CURBING INFLATION

Asian central banks have traditionally intervened to prevent currency appreciation, which hurts exports, the main driver of growth for most of the region's economies.

But the focus is now shifting to containing inflation, with oil prices at record highs near $140 a barrel driving up costs and fuelling demands for higher wages.

The Indian rupee, which has dropped more than 8 percent since Jan. 1, fell as low as 42.93 to the dollar from Friday's close of 42.66/67 after a decline of more than 4 percent on the main stock index <.BESN>.

Foreigners dumped $879.1 million of Indian stocks in the four days to Thursday, bringing their net sales so far this year to $4.8 billion.

The central bank was seen selling dollars around 42.93 to the tune of $400-$500 million, three traders said.

"There had been heavy sporadic selling by state-run banks around 42.93 levels and the message seems to have been clear to the rupee shorts: 'Don't take it very far,'" one trader at a foreign bank said.

The central bank usually intervenes via a few state-run banks.

India's economy is highly susceptible to soaring oil prices since it meets 70 percent of its crude oil needs through imports, which are paid for in dollars. When oil refiners buy dollars to meet their commitments, the rupee usually weakens. (Writing by Ed Cropley; Editing by Darren Schuettler and Jacqueline Wong)

title: MONEY TALKS: The Top Eight Themes For  Currencies  In June
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--The comedian Billy Connolly jokes that there are two seasons in Scotland: "June and winter."

Perhaps not, though, for traders. We may find the coming month fails to bring much sunshine even as optimism grows on the U.S. - and global - economy.

Here are the top eight themes for foreign exchange markets in June:

Traders will be closely watching the U.S. economy for signs it is holding up well, all things considered, with some expecting it to soon exhibit renewed strength.

But those hopes may be premature.

Retail and housing data are still showing weakness and consumer sentiment remains a key variable. May nonfarm payrolls due Friday are forecast in a Dow Jones Newswires poll to have fallen a further 70,000, and April payrolls may be revised downward. Hardly an economy in recovery mode, even if it's not as bad as some had expected for this time of the year.

Also, the Institute for Supply Management's May manufacturing index is expected to remain below 50 - contraction territory - as inflation pressures restrict activity. Economists expect a reading of 48.5, from 48.6 in April, while the key services index is likely to print at 51.1, little changed from April's 52.0.

Markets may have gotten a little ahead of themselves in May in predicting a recovery in the U.S. economy within a matter of months - and thus a sustainable recovery in the dollar. Wait until later in the year for that.

Theme No. 2 will be oil prices, which are expected to stay lofty around $115-$130 in June and thus also pressure the dollar.

But oil is not just a negative for the U.S. currency (or a positive for the euro). There are winners and losers in Asia, depending on how much a particularly country is reliant on oil, its current-account position and its fiscal position.

Goldman Sachs recently put the biggest winners from higher oil prices as the Canadian dollar, the Norwegian krone, the Malaysian ringgit, plus the Australian dollar and the euro. The biggest losers, the bank says, are the Korean won, the Taiwan dollar, the Philippine peso and the Thai baht, as well as the Indian rupee and the Chinese yuan (the won, rupee and peso seem to be the favored whipping boys as a whole when it comes to punishing misbehavior on the current-account front).

That's based on the sensitivity of currencies to oil on four counts: energy trade balance, energy reserves, terms-of-trade sensitivity to oil and foreign exchange trade-weighted-index correlation to oil.

Indonesian oil importers also need to buy a lot of dollars, and the rupiah has been feeling the pinch because of that.

The theme of oil naturally feeds into the theme of inflation, as countries like Indonesia and Taiwan look to cut fuel-price subsidies and as Asia as a whole grapples with higher prices, not just for energy but also food and other commodities.

Morgan Stanley's Stephen Jen believes the stagflation risk is highest in emerging markets (food prices make up 30-50% of the consumer-price index basket in many such economies).

The economic damage from high inflation may inflict more pain on Asian currencies than the buffer that some central banks may provide (though slowly) in the form of higher interest rates.

Officials may also tolerate greater currency gains in Asia (theme No. 4), but again this may be outweighed by the broader hit from economic weakness derived from high prices.

So far we've seen limited use of currencies as interest-rate tools (aside from Singapore), and many Asian currencies are still weaker year-to-date. Korea and India in particular may have to embrace more activist intervention policies for their currencies.

Theme No. 5 is the Federal Reserve, which meets later this month on interest rates.

The June meeting is unlikely to be hugely exciting, with Bernanke & Co. most likely to hold rates steady. What will be interesting is whether they signal greater comfort with where the U.S. economy is going, and greater discomfort on prices.

The rate-futures market in the U.S. is still looking at a 56% chance for a rate hike in late October. That may offer some measure of support for the dollar but is a fragile support at best - rate-hike expectations could easily dissolve in the coming weeks.

Theme No. 6 is yield in general. We have several key central bank meetings on the slate in early June, including Australia, New Zealand, the Bank of England and the European Central Bank.

While most of these central banks are expected to hold rates where they are this month, there is the expectation that Australia and the ECB, in particular, won't be showing any inclination to cut rates - the RBA may even have another hike in the pipeline.

The Kiwis have been sounding more dovish of late, but after a pretty stimulatory budget from the government it may be hard to enact any rate cuts before the end of the year. Yield should continue to support the Australian (and New Zealand) currencies and others, especially if stock markets calm further and the Japanese continue to show appetite for the carry trade as a result.

Theme No. 7 will be U.S. and euro-zone rhetoric on the relative strength of the dollar and the euro.

It's doubtful the U.S. and Europe have agreed behind the scenes to welcome gains in the dollar, especially with the U.S. economy still on such shaky footing, and especially with first-quarter earnings season showing how many big U.S. firms are reliant on offshore demand to shore up their bottom lines.

Expect this issue to keep coming up, though, in market chatter with rumors the U.S. has give the green light to a rising dollar.

The yuan again makes it into the top eight. After a quiet April and first half of May, Beijing has loosened its grip a little on the yuan and allowed some fresh gains.

There was much doubt anyway that it had shifted gears on currency policy (i.e., to put the brakes on the yuan), but the comments from officials of late should serve to reassure that they view a strong currency as a part of their inflation-fighting strategy.

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar rose to an over one-year high against the Indian rupee Thursday as oil refining companies bought the greenback in the local currency market, spooked by surging global crude oil prices.

The rupee, the second best performing Asian currency in 2007, is currently in a tailspin as foreign investment in local equities has slowed to a trickle, and analysts expect the currency to get weaker in the near term.

"High oil prices and inflation are not supportive of a stronger rupee in the near term," said Craig Chan, a currency strategist at Lehman Brothers. He expects dollar to trade at INR43.50 by the end of May.

The rupee has lost 8.6% of its value against the dollar so far in 2008.

At 0505 GMT, the dollar was changing hands at INR43.15, after touching an intraday high of INR43.20. It was last this high on April 9, 2007, when it traded at INR43.06.

"Unless there is a sharp jolt to the market - a sudden weakening of dollar globally or some intervention by the central bank - I suppose we'll see INR43.50 level in the near term," said Sundeep Bhandari, managing director and head of global markets, South Asia, at Standard Chartered Bank.

India imports nearly two-thirds of its total oil needs and the spurt in global crude oil prices is widening its trade deficit.

"We have to remember that the current account deficit of countries like India and Korea will weigh much more on their currencies than others in Asia," he added.

The country's trade deficit was $80.4 billion in the fiscal year that ended March 31.

"I don't expect the Reserve Bank of India to intervene aggressively as the rupee is now nearing its equilibrium value. They may step in to control any panic reactions, though," said Rupa Rege Nitsure, chief economist at Bank of Baroda.

Intervention in February was $3.9 billion, and in January it was $13.6 billion.

title: MONEY TALKS: BRIC Tightening Shouldn't Harm Growth Outlooks
text:
By Matthew Cowley 
   A DOW JONES NEWSWIRES COLUMN 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Four of the world's largest developing economies are going in the opposite direction to the Federal Reserve: they are restricting money supply just as the Fed has been opening the tap.

This shouldn't be seen as a contradiction; in fact, it is probably healthy for the global economy.

Inflation is on the rise around the world, driven primarily by higher food and energy prices. Authorities in Brazil, Russia, India and China - the so-called BRIC countries - are all tightening the supply of money in response to the threats.

That could stoke fears about weighing down further a global economy that is already spluttering from the developed-world financial crisis. According to the International Monetary Fund, the BRICs account for about 50% of global economic growth, so the prospect of slower growth in these countries could be significant.

The bigger threat, however, is that the BRIC economies have been growing faster than is probably healthy over the last few years. Export-driven growth has given way to strong domestic consumption, albeit still fueled by a commodities boom. That's more of a worry than any fallout from the global financial crisis, for now.

Economists remain sharply divided over the extent to which the economic slowdown in the U.S. and Europe will harm the developing world. One camp suggests there will be little or no effect, as emerging markets are now strong enough to stand on their own two feet. Another says there is far too much complacency about the risks.

For BRIC central bankers, the argument may be moot. They have to deal with what they can see, and that is inflation.

Stephen Gilmore, global emerging markets strategist at Banque AIG in London, referred to this as a "timing issue." These countries are "tightening because there are inflationary challenges" right now, he said. "If inflationary pressures were to soften, clearly the countries would have more potential" to ease monetary policy, he said.

Gilmore's own base case scenario is that "you get something of a slowdown but it's not too dramatic for the global economy."

For now, most short-term economic forecasts seem to have factored in much of the expected slowdown this year, as the inflation threat had been telegraphed well in advance. An average of the IMF's forecasts for the four BRIC countries indicates gross domestic product is likely to expand 7.2% this year, down from 8.5% in 2007, with a slowdown across all four economies.


 
   A Wide Range Of Policies 
 

There is a broad difference among the four countries' growth rates, reflecting their different stages of development. Brazil, considered a more mature country, is at the low end, with forecast GDP growth of 4.8% for this year, according to the IMF. At the other end is China, which is expected to grow 9.3%. Russia and India are seen growing 6.8% and 7.9%, respectively.

Of the four, Brazil has the least to worry about inflation, thanks to its orthodox monetary policies and hawkish central bank. Earlier this month, the bank raised rates by 50 basis points to 11.75%, the first hike in more than two years. Still, at 4.7%, inflation is above the government's year-end target of 4.5%.

Russia, India and China face more of a challenge. Russia's central bank has raised rates but inflation is likely to come closer to 12% than the government's own forecast of between 9% and 10%.

Fearing social and economic consequences of continually raising interest rates, India and China have resorted to a broader set of tools to control inflation. Both have raised bank reserves and in India's case, levied new taxes, while China has intervened directly in lending markets and introduced price controls.

India's main inflation gauge, the wholesale price index, was up 7.33% on year for the week ended April 12, well above the central bank's non-binding "comfort level" of around 5%. China's annual inflation reached 8.7% at the end of March, well above the target for the year of 4.8%.

Brazil is helped by its floating exchange rate. A sharp influx of foreign currency - to buy its goods or seek out the higher interest rates - have driven the currency to record strong points against the U.S. dollar. That in turn contributes to inflation-busting by making imports less expensive.

The other three get less help from their currencies. Russia's and India's currencies are both managed through capital controls, while China's yuan is tightly pegged to a basket of currencies. The yuan has been allowed to appreciate since 2005, but is still widely viewed as being undervalued.

Given the threat of inflation, slightly slower growth among the BRICs would be healthy for the global economy. Should inflation subside, or the developed-world slowdown become more infectious, then the BRIC governments seem to be well-placed to reverse their course of action and prevent any dramatic slowdown.

(Matthew Cowley, a special writer with Dow Jones Newswires, writes a regular column about the fixed income market. He previously covered emerging markets from New York and before that the Brazilian economy and stock market for Dow Jones in Sao Paulo.)

title: Emerging  FX -Asia loses ground; Singapore dlr, ringgit hit lows
text:
SINGAPORE, April 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies fell on Friday against the broadly stronger dollar, buoyed by positive U.S. labour market data and receding expectations of more Federal Reserve interest rate cuts.

 The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> retreated from a decade high scaled on Wednesday and the Singapore dollar came off its record high hit on the same day as investors bought the U.S. dollar.

 The Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell almost 0.8 percent to 1.3640 to the U.S. dollar, which firmed against the euro and the yen after data released on Thursday suggested the U.S. labour market held up well despite slumping home values. [ID:nN24402636]

 The U.S. dollar gained extra headway against the euro after soft German business sentiment data cast doubt on the outlook for the euro area economy. [ID:nBEB002074]

 "The Singapore dollar is moving in line along with the euro, while the Malaysian ringgit is also getting slightly sold down," a trader in Singapore said.

 "The Singapore dollar took a long time breaking 1.3590, and there are a lot of investors selling at 1.3600," said the trader.

 The Singapore currency peaked at an all-time high of 1.3468 on Wednesday.

 The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> fell as far as 3.16 per dollar, down about 0.5 percent to its lowest level in more than a week.

 Markets still factor in a moderate 25 basis point cut in U.S. interest rates next week, but many investors believe the Fed is ready to take a break after that. Futures markets are now pricing in a 30 percent chance that the Fed will keep its benchmark unchanged at 2.25 percent at its upcoming policy meeting.

 Meanwhile, the Thai baht <THB=TH> touched a two-week low at 31.66 per dollar.

 Thai finance minister Surapong Suebwonglee said on Friday that the authorities did not target any particular baht rate against the U.S. dollar.

 "Our principle is that we will like to have the Thai baht move in line with other Asian currencies," he said.

 The baht, one of Asia's top performing currencies, has gained about 6.5 percent against the dollar so far this year.

 BEARISH ON RUPEE

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> fell 0.3 percent to 42.1 per dollar, as concerns about mounting global and local inflationary pressures dampened investor confidence.

 The Philippine central bank held interest rates steady on Thursday, but warned it would jack up rates if commodity-fuelled inflation spread to the broad economy.

 The Indian rupee <INR=IN> fell to a one-month low at 40.25 per dollar, weighed by dollar buying by oil firms and other importers and fears of a possible dollar-buying intervention by Reserve Bank of India (RBI).

 "In our view, deteriorating current account dynamics, muted portfolio inflows and presence of the RBI's bid will lead to further rupee weakness," analysts at JPMorgan said in a note.

 "Separately, we recommend investors stay paid FX forwards as valuations are still attractive and as the RBI will increasingly rely on forwards to sterilise rupee liquidity," they added.

MUMBAI, April 11 (Reuters) - India's central bank bought $3.88 billion in intervention in February, nearly a quarter of the amount it took in January as a falling stock market dimmed appetite for local assets among foreign investors.

The central bank controls the partially convertible rupee tightly by frequently intervening to discourage wide swings.

In January, it had bought $13.625 billion, which was its largest monthly intervention in 2007/08, as big-ticket IPOs hit the market attracting huge foreign inflows.

Dollar purchases in the first 11 months of the fiscal year 2007/08 were $75.39 billion.

Analysts said intervention has slowed sharply as foreign investors pared their investments in local stocks, reducing the need for the central bank to buy dollars.

The rupee <INR=IN> traded in a broad 39.38-40.03 per dollar band in February.

Data also showed the central bank had a net long forward position of $16.178 billion in February, lower than $16.629 billion on January.

MUMBAI, March 14 (Reuters) - India's central bank bought a record $13.63 billion in intervention in January, when the rupee <INR=IN> fell just short of a 10-year high against the dollar, its monthly bulletin showed.   

In 2007, the central bank bought $74.9 billion in intervention. The Indian currency climbed more than 12 percent against the dollar last year, a gain second only to the Philippine peso <PHP=> among Asian currencies, ending 2007 at 39.42 per dollar. title: India inflation moderate in coming months-ministry
text:
NEW DELHI, Feb 28 (Reuters) - Inflation in India should remain moderate in the coming months due to policy measures taken over the last year, the finance ministry said in its annual economic survey on Thursday.   

Rising incomes, rising commodity prices, and dealing with large capital flows were some of the challenges to be faced in keeping prices under check, the 2007/08 economic survey said.   

"The behaviour of agricultural prices, including essential consumption items, will be critical, given falling poverty and rapidly rising per capita income," it said.   

Supply-side pressures were likely in areas such as the farm sector and infrastructure, and monetary policy needed to address inflationary expectations caused by price rises that were due to supply and demand mismatches, the survey said.   

The ministry survey said containing inflation was a priority, because rising prices hurt the poor, and putting pressure on interest rates hit both savings and investment.   

Annual wholesale price inflation <INWPI=ECI> hit a six-month high of 4.35 percent in early February, although it was still below the central bank's target of close to 5 percent for 2007/08.   

The government said monetary policy had to juggle continued capital flows and their impact on the exchange rate, foreign exchange reserves and market liquidity.   

The central bank bought almost $75 billion in intervention in 2007 trying to contain the rise of the rupee. Such dollar buying adds rupees to the domestic money market, which could be inflationary if left in the system.   

The central bank raised banks' reserve requirement by 250 basis points since December 2006, with the last increase in November, to manage the amount of cash in the banking system. It has also sold special bonds to absorb funds released by its intervention.

title: Indian rupee rises on capital inflow hopes
text:
(Updates to close)   

MUMBAI, Feb 27 (Reuters) - The rupee rose on Wednesday on hopes for another U.S. rate cut, which could attract foreign capital to India, but suspected central bank intervention limited the gains. The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> ended at 39.78/79 per dollar, stronger than Tuesday's close of 39.905/915. During early trade, the currency had hit 39.70, its strongest since Feb. 18.   

The rupee fell to a five-month low of 40.25 last week.   

"Today, we saw the rupee up on the back of the weak dollar," said a senior trader with a private bank.   

The dollar sank to a record low against major currencies on Wednesday, after a U.S. Federal Reserve official on Tuesday suggested interest rates may soon be cut again to fend off a recession in the world's largest economy. See [ID:nL27168912]   

The weakening dollar triggered a rally in commodities, with crude, India's largest import, continuing to hover above $101 per barrel.   

"We didn't see any big inflows from foreign institutional investors today, but sentiment was up due to equities," the trader said.   

India's benchmark share index <.BSESN> ended 0.11 percent higher, shedding early gains of nearly 2 percent, as investors sold shares on news European stock indices had slipped into the red. See [ID:nBOM20600]   

Inflows of overseas capital are a key driver of the local unit, causing it to climb 12 percent against the dollar in 2007.   

Foreigners bought a net $1.3 billion of Indian equities so far this month, after selling about $4.3 billion in January.   

India's central bank has left its key lending rate steady at 7.75 percent for nearly a year, but in January the Fed slashed its federal funds rate by 125 basis points to 3 percent.   

Another U.S. rate cut would widen the interest rate differential between the two countries, increasing the flow of foreign funds into higher yielding Indian assets.   

"Also, we saw corporates liquidating long dollar positions," the trader said.   

Dollar purchases by the central bank once the rupee hit 39.73 largely staved off further gains, the dealer said.   

"For tomorrow, a lot depends on how the dollar does overnight," the trader said. "But I think we'll be seeing a range of 39.70-39.85," he said. (Reporting by Catherine Bosley; Editing by Ranjit Gangadharan)

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee pared some of the last two sessions' losses against the U.S. dollar Thursday as concerns over dollar shortage eased after the central bank stepped in to supply greenbacks to the market, dealers said.   

The dollar ended at INR39.93, down from its previous close of INR40.22 as possible intervention by the Reserve Bank of India neutralized some of the cash crunch.   

"The concerns over the dollar shortage have eased slightly, but we have to wait and see if this is a long lasting effect. But I think the supply (of dollars) should be adequate for rest of the week," a private bank's dealer said.   

The dollar has scored high against the Indian unit recently as foreign capital inflows have trickled to a halt, creating a sudden scarcity of dollars and pushing the dollar-rupee to a five month high Wednesday.   

The shortage, combined with the recently flared up crude oil prices, has resulted in the last year's second best performing currency of the region losing over 1.5% since the beginning of February.   

But some bankers are still positive on the rupee long term.   

"This is a temporary reflection on the fact that there are virtually no foreign institutional investment inflows. But once the sentiment improves, even a little bit of inflows can push the rupee back up," said P. Mukherjee, head of treasury at  Axis Bank.

Mukherjee expects the currency pair to touch INR38.00 by the end of this year, if not sooner.   

In the government bond market, prices rose for the first time in four sessions as high yields attracted buyers.   

The benchmark 7.99% 2017 bond ended at INR102.69, up from INR102.43 last close. Its yield fell by 4 basis points to 7.58%.   

"These levels are a good time to enter the market. Also, cash liquidity showed some signs of improving," said a local fund manager.

title: Indian  central bank  says bought $2.73 bln in Dec
text:
MUMBAI, Feb 13 (Reuters) - India's central bank bought $2.73 billion in intervention in December, taking its dollar purchases in 2007 to $74.9 billion as it tried to temper the pace of rupee's rise <INR=IN>, its monthly bulletin showed on Wednesday.   

The Indian currency climbed more than 12 percent against the dollar last year, a gain second only to the Philippine peso <PHP=> among Asian currencies, ending 2007 at 39.42 per dollar.   

Foreign portfolio flows of $17.4 billion into the stock market <.BSESN> and about $2.3 billion into debt in 2007 were key drivers of the rupees gains last year.   

Intervention in December was substantially lower than the $7.83 billion in November, when the rupee had peaked at 39.16 per dollar, its strongest is nearly a decade.   

Traders said the central bank's dollar purchases so far in 2008 have slowed as risk-averse foreign funds pulled money out of the stock market amid falls in global markets.   

India's currency reserves jumped $98 billion in 2007 to a record of $275.6 billion on Dec. 28. (Reporting by V.Ramakrishnan; Editing by John Mair)

title: Indian rupee at 2-½   month lows on dlr squeeze
text:
(Updates to close)   

 MUMBAI, Feb 13 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee fell to its lowest level in 2-½   months on Wednesday as a dollar shortage in the market and concerns about foreign funds selling stocks prompted banks to sell the local unit.   

 The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> ended at 39.76/77 per dollar after falling as far as 39.8950 in afternoon trade, its lowest since November 27. The rupee had closed at 39.66/67 on Tuesday.   

 "We've seen quite a lot of activity today, with supplies from the stock market reduced and importers buying dollars ... in addition to a lack of dollar supplies," said Rohan Lasrado, head of foreign exchange trading at  HDFC Bank.

 Foreign funds bought more than $17 billion of stocks last year, a key driver of the rupee's rise of more than 12 percent in 2007. But the funds have sold more than $3.5 billion so far this year as weak global markets heighten risk aversion.   

 That has led to a dollar shortage in the banking system, spurring dealers to buy dollars in the spot market and sell them in the forward market, pushing near-term currency forwards into discount.   

 Dollar/rupee forward premiums were quoting at a 0.03-3.20 percent discount for 1-5 months.   

 "That is why exporters are postponing their dollar sales, as they traditionally book their receivables when it is trading at a premium," the head of trading at a foreign bank said.   

 India's benchmark share index <.BSESN> rose 2.05 percent on Wednesday, snapping a five-day fall, but dealers said most of the gains were due to local fund buying rather than foreign buying.   

 Data showed India's central bank bought $2.73 billion in intervention in December, taking its dollar purchases in 2007 to $74.9 billion as it tried to stem the rupee's more than 12 percent rise in 2007.[ID:nBOM181447]. title: Indian rupee up on inflow hopes, cbank hand seen
text:
(Updates to close)   

MUMBAI, Feb 1 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee strengthened on Friday on expectations of capital inflows after the U.S. Federal Reserve's rate cuts, but traders said the gains were checked by suspected central bank intervention.   

The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> ended at 39.35/36 per dollar, slightly weaker than the day's high of 39.33, its highest since Jan. 21, according to Reuters data.   

The rupee ended at 39.38/39 on Thursday and hit a near-decade high of 39.16 percent in November.   

Trading volumes for the day were low at $861 million, data provided by Clearing Corporation of India showed.   

"It's been a very dull day, not much trading," said Rohan Lasrado, head of trading at  HSBC in Mumbai.   

"We've seen capital outflows due to the Reliance (Power) IPO, but these have been offset by capital inflows thanks to the dollar losing ground," he added.   

Foreign funds were net sellers of $841.6 billion on Thursday, taking total sales to about $4.8 billion in the last 12 sessions, after pouring $17.4 billion into Indian equities in 2007.   

The main share index <.BSESN> snapped a four-day fall and rebounded more than 3 percent on Friday. See [ID:nBOM40048].   

Traders expect demand for local assets to gather momentum in the near term, as a result of the Fed's recent rate cuts.   

The U.S. central bank cut rates by a hefty half percentage point on Wednesday, in an attempt to halt a sharp slowdown in the United States.   

Flows of foreign capital into India have been a key driver of the rupee's rise.   

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) limited its intervention in the currency market on Friday, permitting the rupee to gain slightly, dealers said.   

India's central bank aims to check the rupee's rise to ensure Indian exports remain competitive.   

"The central bank has not been intervening in the market to the level we anticipated, so we've seen a bit of appreciation," Lasrado added.

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Indian government bond prices ended down Friday in lower-than-average volume as participants booked profits ahead of the central bank's monetary policy review next Tuesday.   

The 7.99% 2017 bond ended at INR103.80, down from INR104.07 at Thursday's close. Its yield rose to 7.42%, up four percentage points from its previous close.   

"The market will remain thin on Monday, too, and we should see some readjusting of positions before the policy. But, on the whole, the market remains positive and expects some reduction in the rates," said Jayesh Mehta, head of debt markets at DSP Merril Lynch.   

Bond yields touched two-year lows earlier in the week, as some investors upped the odds of a rate cut by the Reserve Bank of India as uncertainty over the health of the global economy increases and the difference between local and U.S. money-market rates widen.   

However, other market participants think the RBI may just hold rates steady as latent inflationary pressures persist and money supply remains high.   

"If the fuel prices are revised upwards in the near future, there exists a huge possibility of inflation rate touching 5% by the end of the fiscal year," said Namrata Padhye, fixed-income research analyst at IDBI Gilts.   

India's wholesale price index-based inflation rate rose 3.83% on year for the week ended Jan. 12, slightly up from 3.79% the week before. The RBI estimates inflation to be around 5% in the current financial year that began Apr. 1, 2007.   

Friday, attendance at trading desks was thin due to a strike by workers at state-run banks who were protesting against mergers among state-owned banks and the outsourcing of business services.   

The Reserve Bank of India said Friday it bought INR4.90 billion of bonds in the secondary market in the week ended Jan. 18, down from INR12.30 billion in the previous week.   

It sold INR900 million of bonds in the same week, compared with no sales the previous week.   

In the currency market, the Indian rupee rose against the dollar, as rejuvenated local stocks brought hopes of more foreign funds into India, although suspected intervention by the RBI likely capped its gains.   

Bombay Stock Exchange's 30-stock Sensitive Index, the Sensex, moved 1,139.92 points higher Friday - its highest intraday gain in terms of points - to close at 18361.66, up 6.6%.   

"The Indian economy, considering the speed at which it is growing, is going to remain a good investment opportunity for western countries for some time to come," Padhye of IDBI Gilts said.   

The dollar ended at INR39.37 Friday, down from INR39.46 at its previous close.   

The RBI is believed to have supported the dollar regularly in the past three sessions, though the support level seems to be shifting progressively lower.   

India's foreign exchange reserves rose by $3.169 billion to $284.898 billion in the week ended Jan. 18, data from the central bank showed Friday.
