title: DJ Asian  Currencies  Surge in Line With Euro, Prompting  Intervention
text:
-- Asian currencies surge as euro climbs on ECB, dollar slumps on budget

-- Intervention spotted in Philippines, Malaysia, Korea, Indonesia, Thailand, India

-- Singapore dollar logs record high, Australian dollar highest since 1983 float, Korean won 2.5-year peak

-- No letup seen for dollar weakness until the Fed ends QE2 in June 


 
   By P.R. Venkat 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian currencies surged Friday as the euro climbed on an interest-rate hike and the dollar languished on a potential U.S. government shutdown, prompting several central banks in the region to intervene to curb their currencies' gains.

Among the sharp gainers, the Singapore dollar broke from its recent stagnancy to pop to a record high against the U.S. currency, the Australian dollar again notched its highest level since being floated in 1983 and the South Korean won hit a two-and-a-half-year high.

Central banks in the Philippines, Malaysia, Korea, Indonesia, Thailand and India apparently bought dollars to keep the advance in their own currencies under control, local traders said.

Traders began the day expecting the dollar might rise against Asian currencies, as investors looked set to take profits on recent dollar declines to square their positions heading into the weekend.

Instead, the U.S. currency remained weak as the euro added to gains from Thursday's rate hike by the European Central Bank, its first tightening since 2008. Many Asian currencies take their cue from the euro, which has acted as a barometer of global risk appetite.

The dollar fell against most major and regional currencies as hopes faded that Republicans and Democrats in Washington could agree on a budget deal before the U.S. government runs out of operating cash at midnight Friday.

"The tightening cycle in Europe has clearly started, and the rate-differential argument is pertinent here," while U.S. budget worries weighed on the dollar, said currency strategist Nizam Idris at UBS in Singapore.

Asian central banks may try to cushion the dollar's fall against their currencies but know they can't stop the trend, and are simply trying to keep their export-reliant economies roughly competitive with their neighbors'. The authorities seldom comment on intervention, but officials at several central banks in recent days have said they will act to prevent excessive volatility.

The region's currencies have surged over the past year as Asia has led the global economic recovery and as low interest rates in the richest countries have spurred a flood of investor capital into Asia seeking higher returns.

Asian currencies also got a boost as the People's Bank of China fixed the tightly controlled yuan higher Friday for a sixth session, setting the dollar's central parity rate at a record low CNY6.5420.

Expectations that Beijing will allow faster yuan gains sent the yuan sharply higher in the market for nondeliverable forwards, an offshore venue where investors can bet on future moves. The 12-month dollar/yuan contract sank to a three-year low bid quote of CNY6.3620, from CNY6.4000.

The region's currency authorities are generally tolerating greater appreciation these days to help them battle rising inflation, said Thomas Harr, head of Asia currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. The dollar will likely remain weak until at least June, when the Federal Reserve is slated to end its "quantitative easing" policy of buying government bonds, he said.

Friday's euro ascent kick-started the Asia rally. The common currency had come off Thursday's highs as the ECB's quarter-percentage-point rate hike was almost universally expected and central bank chief Jean-Claude Trichet said the ECB hadn't decided to embark on a series of rate increases.

Nonetheless, the euro took off in the Asia morning on the view that the ECB may tighten every quarter, and the currency never looked back.

The euro's rise to a 2011 high above $1.44 spurred accelerating gains among Asian currencies, notably the Singapore dollar. The U.S. dollar had been largely holding above support around S$1.26 for the past two weeks, but the euro's climb helped break through that level. At 0945 GMT, the euro was at $1.4399, and the U.S. currency bought S$1.2571.

"Whoever is long dollar will be suffering here," said Idris.

The ICE Dollar Index, a broad measure of the currency's value against the currencies of America's main trading partners, was at 75.185 late in the Asian session. That was down from 75.534 late in New York and threatened a slide to its November 2009 low of 74.17 in coming weeks.

To tame the peso at five-month highs, the Philippine central bank apparently bought $600 million between PHP43.05 and PHP43.00 in heavy trade, defending the U.S. currency around the psychologically important PHP43.00 line, Manila traders said. Bank Negara Malaysia apparently twice sold the ringgit, which has benefited as a proxy for the rising Chinese currency, Kuala Lumpur traders said. They spotted the central bank buying dollars at MYR3.0210 late in the day after a defense at MYR3.0220 failed.

The Bank of Korea apparently bought an estimated $1 billion as the dollar fell to 1,082.00, its lowest since August 2008, when the global financial crisis was escalating, Seoul dealers said.

In a bid to curb the rising rupiah and baht, Bank Indonesia apparently bought an estimated $100 million at IDR8,653, while the Bank of Thailand apparently bought dollars around THB30.03, local dealers said. After the rupee hit a six-month high, the Reserve Bank of India was seen apparently buying dollars at INR43.98, local traders said.

-By P.R. Venkat, Dow Jones Newswires; +65 64154 152; venkat.pr@dowjones.com

By Anant Vijay Kala

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of India is suspected to have intervened in the foreign exchange market Friday after the rupee rose to a near-six-month high against the U.S. dollar, two traders said.

This is the first time since November that the central bank is believed to have intervened in the market as the strengthening rupee threatens to hurt India's rapidly growing exports.

"There was substantial demand from nationalized banks," said a trader with a state-run bank, who didn't wish to be named. "This was believed to be on behalf of the RBI," he added.

Both traders said demand for the dollar was seen from around INR43.98, which was the intraday low for the dollar. The greenback had last fallen below this level in mid-October. It was trading at INR44.07 late Friday.

The dealers, however, declined to give an estimate on how much of the greenback the RBI may have bought.

The local currency had risen sharply early in the session after an interest rate hike by the European Central Bank late Thursday fueled expectations of a similar action in India.

Sudarshana Bhat, head of forex at Corporation Bank, said the dollar's rebound was aided by demand from oil companies and weakening local stock markets.

The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark Sensitive Index ended 0.7% lower at 19,451.40, down for a fourth consecutive session.

"But in the near-term, expectations are that the rupee will continue to strengthen tracking gains in the euro and other major currencies against the dollar," Bhat said.

The next crucial support for the pair will be at INR43.95. "If that is broken, then we could see the rupee gain all the way to INR43.75 or INR43.80 very soon," he added.

The rupee has gained 1.4% against the dollar so far in 2011 after rising about 4.0% the previous year.

The RBI has raised interest rates eight times since March 2010 as it struggles to control inflation. The markets widely expect the central bank would raise its main lending and borrowing rates by another 25 basis points when it next meets to review monetary policy on May 3.

The widening interest rate differential with advanced economies, which are still following loose growth-supportive policies, is attracting capital inflows into Asia's third-largest economy and in turn helping the rupee.

The RBI doesn't set a target level for the rupee and has often said it intervenes in the foreign exchange market only to curb excessive volatility.

 SINGAPORE, April 8 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar hit a record high and the South Korean won rose to a 2-1/2-year high on Friday, leading gains in emerging Asia, as foreign exchange authorities pulled back their defence lines on domestic currency strength in the face of rising capital inflows.

The combination of robust equity flows into Asia and a revived interest in carry trades will probably keep emerging Asian currencies strengthening in the near term, analysts and dealers said.

 "Asian authorities have accepted that much of the gain in their currencies is due to general U.S. dollar weakness whilst many central banks are allowing currencies to do an increasing amount of the work to dampen inflation pressures," said Mitul Kotecha, head of global FX strategy at Credit Agricole in Hong Kong.

 "Capital flows to Asia have strengthened sharply over recent weeks, pointing to ongoing upward momentum," he said, adding there is still risk of intervention to slow currency appreciation rather than reverse it.

 Hedge funds piled on the move higher in Asian currencies, taking particular interest in the Singapore dollar ahead of a policy meeting of the Monetary Authority of Singapore next Thursday. MAS is widely expected to tighten policy, which it manages through exchange rates.

 The Singapore's central bank allowed investors to cross 1.2600 per dollar, which it had been defending. South Korea's currency authorities had not been spotted buying dollars until the won hit a 2-1/2-year high beyond 1,085.00, having moved its intervention levels increasingly lower in the past several weeks, dealers said.

 Asian monetary authorities are facing a rising tide of portfolio investment entering their economies and putting upward pressure on their currencies, and also a risk of quickening inflation. Oil prices hit a 2-1/2-year high on Friday.

 In the week ended Wednesday, emerging market equities enjoyed net inflows of $2.7 billion in fresh cash, the fourth-largest weekly tally since 1992, data from Lipper showed. [ID:nN07259168]

 WON

 The won hit a fresh 2-1/2-year high against the dollar as offshore hedge funds built up short yen/won and euro/won positions  .

 The won strengthened to as firm as 1,082.0 versus the greenback during the local trade, the strongest since Sept. 8, 2008. Hedge funds had left dollar offers around 1,085 won, a U.S. bank dealer said.

 The South Korean currency found further support from demand for exporters' settlements, while the authorities lowered their intervention level to 1,082 per dollar, dealers said.  

 Foreign investors extended their net purchases of Seoul shares to a 18th consecutive session, helping the KOSPI  end up 0.27 percent. That is the longest string of net buying by foreign investors since October 2010.

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR

 The Singapore dollar firmed to a record high of 1.2560 per U.S. dollar on surging demand after the central bank allowed market players to cross the line which it had been defending.

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was seen pulling back dollar bids at 1.2600 per the greenback, although it was spotted buying it around 1.2560 later, dealers said.

 The Singapore dollar has been supported by expectations that the MAS will tighten more on Thursday to fight inflation.

 YUAN NDFS

 Dollar/yuan non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) fell sharply with the one-month NDF hitting a fresh all-time low, as investors rushed to catch up with a series of six consecutive stronger yuan mid point fixings.

 The 1-month dollar/yuan NDF slid to as low as 6.5030 and the 1-year NDF fell to 6.3605, the lowest since April 2008. That implied spot yuan appreciation of 2.4 percent in the next year, slightly more than the 2.2 percent implied by the one-year NDF a week ago.

 Earlier, China's central bank said it will open domestic bond market further to overseas investors. [ID:nB9E7EN01L]

 "PBOC said that they will accelerate opening of its bond market, though acknowledging inflows will add to CNY appreciation. So maybe investors are now betting on a faster CNY appreciation," said Frances Cheung, a strategist at Credit Agricole CIB in Hong Kong.

 RINGGIT

 Demand from interbank speculators and leveraged names lift the ringgit  to a two-week high against the dollar.

 The Malaysian currency strengthened to as firm as 3.0200 per dollar, the strongest since March 25.

 Malaysia's central bank was spotted buying dollars, but it also followed its Asian peers lowering levels of dollar bids.

 The central bank, which had been guarding 3.0250 versus the greenback, intervened around 3.0220, dealers said.

 RUPEE

 The India rupee  hit a five-month high against the dollar on demand from interbank speculators and leveraged accounts.

 The rupee strengthened to as firm as 43.98, the strongest since Oct 15, 2010. If it clearly breaks through 43.97, the high of Oct 15 last year, demand for the Indian currency is seen increasing more.

 The central bank has not been spotted intervening yet, that could attract fast money and funds for catch-up buying.

 The rupee returned to levels of 44 per dollar, but that was mainly because of dollar demand from oil importers.

 The rupee has risen 1.5 percent against the dollar so far this year, the second worst performing currency after the Thai baht among emerging Asian currencies.

title: ADB Official: Expect Indian Rupee To Be Stable This FY
text:
NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee is likely to be stable through the current fiscal year that began April 1, with capital inflows helping to comfortably manage the country's large current account deficit, an Asian Development Bank official said.

"We have a stable outlook for the rupee," Rana Hasan, principal economist at the India office of the Asian Development Bank, told Dow Jones Newswires late Wednesday in an interview.

The local currency gained 1.5% against the U.S. dollar in the last fiscal year. It gained 0.8% so far since April 1 and was last trading at INR44.20 to a dollar.

India's October-December current account deficit sharply narrowed to $9.7 billion from $12.2 billion a year earlier as non-trade payments such as receipts for software services increased, central bank data showed.

But it still remains high compared with its emerging market peers, most of which run a surplus. The wide current account gap has been compounded by a large fiscal deficit.

The ADB expects India's current account deficit to widen to 3.5% in the current fiscal year from about 3% last fiscal year.

Capital inflows--into both equity and debt--amounted to $32.2 billion in the last fiscal year and the government expects them to remain below $40 billion this fiscal year.

Hasan said the rupee's current levels reflect the country's economic fundamentals as the exchange rate remains largely flexible.

"I think one of the benefits of having a flexible exchange rate is that the current exchange rate does reflect economic fundamentals," he said. "I think it [flexible exchange rate] has served India well."

The central bank's policy of intervening in case of too much volatility in the forex market is appropriate for India, he said.

The economy's fundamentals aren't going to change dramatically, he said.

The ADB expects India's economy to grow 8.2% for this fiscal year.

-By Prasanta Sahu; Dow Jones Newswires; 91 11 43563309; subhadip.sircar@dowjones.com [ 07-04-11 0709GMT ]

title: UPDATE: India  Central Bank : Exchange Rates Should Be Aligned To Economic Fundamentals
text:
(Adds comments from RBI chief in 4th, 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, 12th and 13th paragraphs, background in 5th, 6th and 14th paragraph)

By Sourav Mishra

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Foreign exchange rates should move in co-ordination with a country's economic fundamentals to keep tensions in the global currency markets in check, the governor of the Reserve Bank of India said Tuesday.

"Currency interventions should be resorted to not as an instrument of trade policy, but only to manage disruptions to macroeconomic stability," Duvvuri Subbarao said at an event organized by the central bank of Sri Lanka in Colombo.

The speech was posted on the central bank website.

"The question boils down to what can surplus countries do domestically to increase consumption and what can deficit countries do domestically to increase savings."

The U.S. and other advanced economies have long been vocal about the need for China to devalue the yuan. China, on its part, has slammed developed economies for keeping their own currencies weak by practicing loose monetary policies.

But the spirit of co-operation was evident when the G-7 intervened after the yen, counterintuitively surging after the recent earthquake and tsunami, hit an all-time high of JPY76.25 to the dollar.

"The crisis also taught us that given the deepening integration of countries into the global economic and financial system, uncoordinated responses will lead to worse outcomes for everyone," Subbarao said.

He said the spectre of protectionism will rise in the coming years and will take new forms.

Subbarao said that managing capital flows shouldn't be treated as an exclusive problem of emerging market economies, and advanced nations need to share the burden of adjustment.

Capital inflows--according to the central bank chief--should meet two criteria: they should be stable and be roughly equal to the economy's absorptive capacity.

Capital controls, in some cases, can be an acceptable tool to manage capital flows, the governor said.

Subbarao said the global financial crisis has outlined the vulnerabilities of the U.S. dollar as a single reserve currency, but the use of the Special Drawing Right, or SDR, wasn't a feasible option as it had to meet several criteria.

"The SDR has to be accepted as a liability of the IMF, has to be automatically acceptable as a medium of payment in cross-border transactions, be freely tradeable and its price has to be determined by forces of demand and supply."

The SDR is a notional currency that at present has only four constituents: the dollar, the euro, sterling and the yen. There has been demand that the currencies of the four largest emerging economies--Brazil, Russia, India and China--should all be included in the SDR basket.

-By Sourav Mishra and Khushita Vasant, Dow Jones Newswires; 91 22 6145 6115; khushita.vasant@dowjones.com [ 29-03-11 0859GMT ]

title: Indian cbank did not  intervene  in  fx  market in Jan
text:
MUMBAI, March 11 (Reuters) - India's central bank did not buy or sell dollars in the foreign exchange market in January, the second absence since November when it had bought a net $870 million, its monthly bulletin showed.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had bought $1.37 billion and sold $500 million in November, compared with purchases of $450 million in October.

On a net basis, November was the RBI's biggest monthly intervention since June 2009, when it had bought $1.04 billion.

In the current fiscal year that began last April, the bank has so far purchased a net $1.69 billion from the market.

In January, the rupee moved in wide band of 44.60 to 46.01 per dollar, closely mirroring moves in the domestic sharemarket and reducing the need for intervention to curb excessive volatility or movement in either direction.

India's central bank doesn't target a specific level for the rupee and has said it intervenes in the forex market only to prevent excessive volatility.

In 2010, the central bank bought a net $1.85 billion compared with net sales of $5.8 billion in 2009, when it had to intervene to prevent the rupee from depreciating sharply.

The rupee had dropped to a record low of 52.2 per dollar in March 2009, but ended the year 4.7 percent higher, boosted by foreign fund inflows of $17.5 billion. In 2010, the rupee rose 4.1 percent, boosted by record inflows of $29.3 billion.

So far in 2011, however, foreign funds are net sellers of $1.8 billion, pushing the rupee down over 1 percent this year.

title: =DJ 2nd UPDATE: IMF Says India Growth To Stay Strong, Urges Reforms
text:
(Adds comments from IMF official, Credit Suisse economist) 


 
   By Jeffrey Sparshott & Prasanta Sahu 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--India's economy is expected to continue expanding rapidly in coming years, but authorities should raise interest rates to curb inflation and push ahead with fiscal and financial reforms to maintain that growth, the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday.

"Sustaining rapid growth over the medium term will depend on sustaining reforms to facilitate infrastructure investment," the IMF said in a report on India's economy.

India's economic growth was among the strongest in the world last year, making it one of the driving forces of the global recovery.

The IMF forecasts that India's gross domestic product will grow 8.75% this fiscal year, which runs through March. Growth will taper off to about 8% the following year, the IMF said.

But India also is grappling with high inflation, surging inflows of foreign capital and high levels of government debt.

The IMF recommended that India accelerate its plans to end economic stimulus measures adopted during the global economic crisis.

"More substantial current spending adjustment, mainly by further cutting subsidies and improving the targeting of spending, would help achieve social goals along with medium-term fiscal consolidation," the IMF said.

That includes liberalization of diesel and fertilizer prices, the IMF added.

Earlier Wednesday, Oil Minister Murli Deora said the government is trying to prevent further increases in the price of diesel amid rising crude oil costs. Diesel is the main transportation fuel in India, and higher prices mean higher freight costs for essential commodities such as food.

The IMF recommended that India's central bank further increase interest rates to tackle inflation.

The Reserve Bank of India raised interest rates six times in 2010, and is widely expected to hike them again at its Jan. 25 policy meeting.

Real interest rates "are negative now. So rates should be moving to positive territory," Sanjaya Panth, IMF's senior resident representative to India, told reporters Thursday in New Delhi.

"We see room for further rate increases," but it's "something that has to be done gradually and that needs to be looked at continuously," Panth said.

The IMF expects headline inflation to be at 6.5% by end-March. That would be higher than the current policy interest rate, or repurchase rate, which stands at 6.25%.

The RBI's estimate is for 5.5% inflation at the end of March, with an upward risk to the forecast. The inflation rate was at 7.48% on-year in November, according to the most recent data.

Robert Prior-Wandesforde, head of India and South East Asia economics for Credit Suisse, said he endorsed the report's approach.

"A key issue is that real interest rates are negative," Prior-Wandesforde said. Monetary policy in India "is basically too loose for an economy that is growing above its sustainable rate."

Credit Suisse forecasts another 75 basis points of rate hikes in 2011.

The IMF also cautioned Indian authorities on the country's current account deficit, which is expected to reach 3.3% of GDP in 2010-11.

"As the deficit rises, so does the potential impact of a sudden stop or reversal of capital flows. Another risk is that the scale of the inflows could exceed India's capacity to absorb them," the IMF said.

But India doesn't need any new capital controls for now, Panth said. India currently caps the amount of money foreigners can invest in local debt markets.

"We don't think India's absorptive capacity has been reached or exceeded," he said.

India's first line of defense against an oversized deficit is a stronger currency, the IMF said. If the rupee became too strong, the international lender suggested India could intervene in the foreign exchange market or take regulatory measures.

"Over time, deepening the corporate bond market, increasing the supply of shares and further liberalizing foreign direct investment would increase the country's capacity to absorb capital from abroad," the IMF said.

The IMF also said India needs to pursue reforms to encourage private investment in infrastructure development, such as deepening the corporate bond market and lowering the cost of doing business in the country.

"There are several obstacles to achieving set targets. These include availability of financing, land acquisition, multiple clearances, capacity constraints, and governance issues along with various sector-specific concerns," the IMF said.

-By Jeffrey Sparshott, Dow Jones Newswires; 202-862-9291; jeffrey.sparshott@dowjones.com

title: MARKETWATCH VIEW: Rise In The Road Ahead
text:
What a difference a week makes. Just when it seemed that most macro risks were benign, and even the ones overseas had receded somewhat, came China's sudden spurt in inflation, the failure of the Group of 20 countries to hammer out anything substantial, and sovereign risks in Europe back in the spotlight.

India's benchmark Sensex closed 2.1% lower Friday, trading down 4% from the previous Friday's record close of 21,004.96 when it seemed right in the middle of a sweet spot.

The G-20 communique acknowledged that emerging economies could use macro-prudential tools to control capital inflows, pointing to capital controls to keep currency appreciation in check. India is probably the only emerging economy that has openly said that it won't put any caps on foreign-fund inflows, as it banks on these to contain the widening current account deficit.

India's current-account deficit widened to $13.7 billion in the April-June quarter from $4.5 billion a year earlier, with the gap marginally larger than the January-March quarter, when it reached $13 billion.

Global investors focused Friday on China's risks of rapid credit growth, asset bubbles and inflation, sending the Shanghai Composite Index 5.16% lower. But Columbia University's Nobel Prize winning economist Joseph Stiglitz last week argued that India is more vulnerable to an asset bubble than China is at this point.

"Where I do have a worry is countries like India, where they are debating how much intervention in the market we should have. And there are people who say in India we shouldn't have capital controls, even though Brazil's done it, China's done it," Stiglitz warned.

He said that "strong economies that don't yet have capital control become the focal point" for the liquidity injected by the U.S. Federal Reserve. He probably has a point.

New Delhi has been happy with letting dollar inflows continue unabated. After all, along with local consumption, foreign capital inflows are the two engines driving growth in India.

Year-to-date, foreign funds have invested $28.69 billion in equities and $10.26 billion in bonds, according to data with the capital-market regulator.

To put these numbers in perspective, that is 28.3% of all dollar inflows into equities and a whopping 57.9% into bonds from the time India opened its doors to foreign investors back in November 1992.

To be sure, inflows into bonds have also been aided by India's decision in late September to double foreign investment limits in government securities to $10 billion from $5 billion, and increase the limit for corporate bonds to $20 billion from $15 billion.

Still, in a signal of India's growing tolerance for the cash gush that is pushing the local currency and stocks higher, the chairman of the prime minister's Economic Advisory Council said last week that the Indian economy has the capacity to absorb capital inflows of up to $70 billion annually without government intervention.

"The quantitative easing by the U.S. Fed may have implications in terms of capital inflows, but as I had indicated earlier, India's current account deficit will be around 3% of gross domestic product" this fiscal year through March 2011, C. Rangarajan said.

East Asian economies were also happy to let rampant capital inflows into their countries until the Asian crisis emerged in the middle of 1997.

There are other parallels as well: substantial current account deficits, rising inflation, appreciation in both asset prices and exchange rates, and booms in real estate. India's central bank, just a week and a half back, pre-empted a bubble in mortgage lending by tightening lending norms.

What the Reserve Bank of India hasn't done yet is stem the rupee's rise. It did, however, recently warn about intervention if capital flows are volatile. But intervention also brings with it inflation.

Inflation for the month of September was 8.62%, well above the comfort level of the central bank. This, despite hikes in key policy rates six times this year.

The Reserve Bank of India, which was solely focused on inflation so far this year, is now in a conundrum.

Government data Friday showed that India's industrial production in September grew 4.4% from a year earlier, its slowest pace in 16 months. What must have the central bank worried is that this reading was sharply below the 7.0% median estimate in a Dow Jones Newswires poll of 15 economists and far below the 15.2% rise in July.

Deputy Governor Subir Gokarn admitted as much, saying Saturday that industrial production data "may reflect the beginning of a slowing in the growth momentum, but until we see every indicator pointing in the same direction, it's difficult" to get a clear picture.

Adding to his worries is the fact that, despite a good monsoon, food prices haven't come off.

"For the time being, I will set it (food prices) as a risk and challenge to inflation management," he said.

Which now puts the onus back on inflation. Both the RBI and market participants will be closely watching if inflation is cooling in line with expectations.

India will report inflation data for October on Monday. A median poll of 15 economists expect the wholesale prices to be likely up by 8.50% from a year earlier.

So, while external factors will overhang on Indian markets in the near term, the domestic picture has taken a turn as well.

title: INTERVIEW-India doesn't need capital controls on portfolio flows
text:
* Temporary capital flow spikes can be managed - official

* FDI levels not "very volatile"

* Capital flows consistent with current account deficit

By Krittivas Mukherjee

SEOUL, Nov 10 (Reuters) - There is no need for India to introduce capital controls on portfolio flows and foreign direct investment levels are not very volatile, a top Indian policy maker said on Wednesday.

Many fear a U.S. Federal Reserve move to buy $600 billion more in government bonds by June 2011 will lead to a surge of "hot money" inflows to emerging markets such as India, South Korea and Brazil.

The debate could have negative repercussions for this week's Group of 20 meeting in Seoul, and with many emerging countries willing to retaliate, a meaningful outcome to the currency and global imbalance debate now looks a little bleak.

Montek Singh Ahluwalia, deputy chairman of the Planning Commission, which charts India's economic growth path, said he saw no need at the moment to alter policy in India to control capital flows.

"I personally do not think there is any need to alter the present policy for foreign direct investment because I think that's not a very volatile thing, and if we get more of it within the realm of possibility then it's excellent," Ahluwalia told Reuters.

"I also do not think at the present moment there is any need to introduce any capital controls on portfolio flows. We have capital controls on debt and I do not think we should relax those too readily. But yes those are things that you look at on a month by month basis."

Central banks in countries such as Japan and South Korea that are faced with a rising currency have indicated they may take measures to counter the appreciation pressure.

INDIAN SUPPORT FOR QE2?

India's response has been measured in comparison with other economies such as China, South Korea and Brazil who have sharply criticised the latest round of quantitative easing by the United States.

India's central bank, the Reserve Bank of India, has however maintained it will only intervene in foreign exchange markets if inflows turn "lumpy" or "volatile".

The Indian rupee has appreciated 5.1 percent in 2010.

India's prime minister this week offered qualified support for the Federal Reserve's attempt at monetary stimulus, saying anything that stimulates the underlying growth impulses of entrepreneurship in the United States would help the cause of global prosperity.

Ahluwalia said India was running a current account deficit consciously in the belief that it would be able to finance it.

"We are consciously following a strategy in which we want to step up investment in a world in which Indian exports for a while will not do as well as they might otherwise," he said. (Reporting by Krittivas Mukherjee; Editing by Alex Richardson)

title: UPDATE 3-Dubai trades world's first Indian rupee futures
text:
(Adds Indian paper comment, session range, details)   

 DUBAI, June 7 (Reuters) - A Dubai futures bourse began trading the world's first contracts on the Indian rupee on Thursday without the blessing of India's central bank, which may lose some control over the partially convertible currency.   

 The Dubai Gold and Commodities Exchange (DGCX) said it launched the non-deliverable rupee-dollar contract to tap India's burgeoning foreign trade, especially with the United Arab Emirates, New Delhi's third largest trading partner.   

 The DGCX, based in the UAE's commercial hub of Dubai, said it had discussed the contracts with the Reserve Bank of India, which bought $22 billion in the five months to March to check the rupee's rise.   

 "They would not express an opinion one way or the other, which from our point of view is quite satisfactory," David Rutledge, a director at DGCX, told reporters in Dubai on Wednesday. "The market is outside the jurisdiction of India's central bank, which places curbs on trading in the rupee."   

 India's Financial Express said the launch of the contract stemmed from what it described as Indian policy shortcomings.   

 "Rupee currency futures trading on the DGCX in the Gulf emirate symbolises the profound mistakes of Indian economic policy," it said.   

 The rupee has been convertible on the current account since 1994, meaning it can be changed freely into foreign currency for purposes such as trade-related expenses. It cannot be converted freely for activities such as acquiring overseas assets.   

 "With the introduction of rupee futures, the Reserve Bank of India's intervention will also become slightly ineffective," said Srinivas Sribashyam, head of currency trading at  Bank Muscat International, in Oman.   

 "They will be keenly watching the Dubai rupee futures and it will be another source of frustration for the RBI," he said.   

CENTRAL BANK SILENT   

 The central bank, which says it intervenes to smooth volatility, declined to comment.   

 "I don't think they like it really ... I don't think they can do anything about it," A.V. Rajwade, a member of an official panel on capital account convertibility, said in New Delhi.   

 A central bank-appointed panel has recommended a plan to allow fuller rupee convertibility and greater movement of capital in rupees by the end of the 2010/11 fiscal year.   

 Rupee futures were likely to be a preferred hedging and investment mechanism against currency fluctuations over the existing non-deliverable dollar/rupee forward market (NDF), some analysts say.   

 "NDF has counterparty risk exposures and in futures contract traded on exchange there are no counterparty exposure risks because of the margining system," Rajwade said.   

 "Having a platform that provides price discovery of the rupee will actually enhance the NDF market by making those contracts easier to price," said Ben Floyd, general manager of business and product development at DGCX.   

 India's currency climbed around 9 percent this year on increased capital flows as Asia's fourth-biggest economy expanded at the fastest pace in almost two decades.   

 DGCX rupee trading focused on the key June contract <DIRM7>.   

 Settlement price for 100 Indian rupees was $2.4583, with 645 lots having been traded. It hit a high of $2.4615 and a low of 2.4571 during the 12-hour session.   

 "The volume is very good and it is more than what everyone in the market had expected, perhaps far beyond what RBI itself had expected," said a Dubai-based trader.   

 Each non-deliverable rupee-dollar contract represents 2 million Indian rupees ($49,360). The maximum price fluctuation is $2 per contract which will be offered in the current calendar month and the following two, the DGCX said.   

 In case of physical settlement, the euro-equivalent of the settlement price will be calculated, it said.  ($1=40.52 rupees)

title: RPT-UPDATE1-India cbank:developing mkts will help manage flows
text:
(Repeats story issued late on Thursday)   

MUMBAI, May 31 (Reuters) - India is moving towards a fully developed financial system to help it manage rising capital inflows, but needs to guard against risks arising from global imbalances, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said on Thursday.   

Large capital inflows and the changing nature of tax collections had led to large volatility in cash levels in the money markets, which the central bank said had made its task of cash management more difficult.   

"Enhanced integration of financial markets allows risks to be shared more broadly and facilitates the flow of capital to the productive sectors," it said in its annual report on currency and finance for the fiscal year 2005/06 (April/March).   

The report, though largely a historical document, does contain some forward-looking comments.   

The RBI has used market stabilisation scheme (MSS) notes and bonds to remove foreign exchange inflows of a long-term nature from the system, while its daily liquidity operations were intended to manage short-term fund levels.   

But a lack of knowledge of whether market inflows were long- or short-term funds made this difficult to judge properly.   

"There is, therefore, a need to explore further instruments/options to undertake liquidity management, particularly in the context of a move to fuller capital account convertibility," the report said.   

The central bank noted that there was also a limit on its MSS issuance, and it could not sterilise operations indefinitely.   

According to the central bank's Web site, the outstanding balance under the MSS was 888.02 billion rupees as on May 18, below a self-imposed limit of 1.1 trillion rupees.   

The central bank said developing the financial system, which included the introduction of new products in the debt, currency and derivative markets to help manage risks, would be a step towards fuller capital account convertibility.   

Other possible steps included allowing more investments by foreigners in the bond market and the launch of an instrument similar to federal fund futures in the United States.   

"Expansion of access by foreign investors to the Indian government securities market will have to be done carefully, taking into account issues related to opportunities for arbitrage, overall macro economic conditions and the need for financial stability," it said.   

The reforms of financial markets and the path to convertibility were linked processes, and were being managed in tandem, the report said.   

The central bank said that it had become more active in the foreign exchange market to counter massive capital inflows, but the extent of its intervention was relatively low when compared with emerging market economies.   

The rupee hit a nine-year high against the dollar earlier this week, largely driven by foreign inflows.   

"Intervention by the Reserve Bank of India has been effective in reducing the volatility in the Indian foreign exchange market," the central bank said.   

While reaffirming its positive outlook on the economy, the RBI said that a global reversal in risk appetite could trigger a wave of capital outflows.   

"The re-pricing of risks can trigger massive adjustments in portfolio holdings of global investors and this can lead to sharp swings in capital flows out of riskier assets in emerging economies, with implications for foreign exchange markets and other domestic financial segments," it said. The report will be posted on the central bank's Web site:   www.rbi.org.in  ("http://www.rbi.org.in")

Dealers said the RBI intervened heavily to stem the currency's gains, with a dealer estimating the intervention at $300 million-$400 million.

The rupee, however, may still have some strength as foreign fund inflows are expected to remain strong, but all eyes will be on the RBI, the dealer added.

Large-scale intervention will be needed to mop up these flows and may need a complimentary liquidity mop-up exercise, the bank said.

text:
MUMBAI, May 23 (Reuters) - India's central bank is likely to step up dollar buying in the currency market and knock the rupee off a nine-year peak, as slowing inflation gives it more elbow room to intervene,  Kotak Mahindra Bank said on Wednesday.

India's wholesale price index rose 5.44 percent in the 12 months to May 5, lower from the previous week's 5.66 percent, and falling within the central bank's target for the first time in five months.   

Concerned about a widening trade deficit and the potential for a sudden reversal of capital inflows, the RBI has kept the rupee in a broad range of 43.00-47.00 per dollar in the past three years.   

But strong economic growth and a booming stock market have attracted huge capital inflows, spurring the central bank to buy $22 billion in the four months to end-March 2007, in a bid to stem the local currency's rise.

title: INTERVIEW:India  Central Bank  Must Curb Rupee Rise -Tarapore
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India's central bank should intervene immediately to stem the rupee's sharp rise against the U.S. dollar to avoid hurting economic growth, said S.S. Tarapore, a former deputy governor of the Reserve Bank of India.   

The Indian rupee is currently trading at nine-year highs against the dollar helped by overseas borrowings by domestic companies and foreign capital inflows into stocks, local companies and infrastructure development.   

"If you allow the real effective exchange rate to appreciate, you are appreciating against fundamentals. Your interest rate is higher, your inflation rate is higher and you try to be stronger than those currencies (in the basket). It will kill industry," Tarapore, who is also a member of a central bank advisory committee on monetary policy, told Dow Jones Newswires in a recent interview.   

According to the central bank, which looks at a six-currency trade-weighted index, the rupee was overvalued by 12% on April 18. A  JP Morgan index estimates the rupee is overvalued by around 17%.   

The Reserve Bank of India has traditionally intervened when the rupee was overvalued above the 5% level, foreign exchange dealers said.   

Tarapore said the real effective exchange rate appreciation was not a correct instrument for containing inflation.   

"It is the worst possible instrument. Generalized inflation means there is lot of liquidity in the system and the remedial measure is to cut back on monetary expansion," Tarapore said.   

He advocated the Reserve Bank of India's intervention and consequent sterilization through cash reserve ratio hikes and market stabilization scheme bonds.   

"The MSS or sterilization through cash reserve ratio has a cost. But we are not understanding or calculating the cost of non-sterilization as it is in terms of devastation of the economy, higher inflation and REER appreciation," Tarapore added.   

Foreign exchange dealers said the RBI has largely been absent since mid-March to stem the rupee's rise as it wants to tackle inflation. Central bank intervention in the foreign exchange market adds to liquidity fanning inflation.   

He said the RBI can consider incremental cash reserve ratio hikes to counter the criticism the ratio is a blunt instrument.   

The incremental cash reserve ratio immobilizes excess liquidity from where it is lodged rather than the average ratio which impounds equally from banks that are slower growing as well as banks that are faster growing.   

The RBI has raised the cash reserve ratio thrice by 50 basis points each since early December to the current level of 6.5%.   

The federal government has also raised the ceiling for market stabilization scheme bonds to INR1.1 trillion from INR850 billion earlier.   

Tarapore said real interest rates are still low in India and the scope for further monetary tightening still exists as signs of overheating remain visible.   

"Fundamentals do not warrant Indian interest rates going down. Over the recent period of monetary tightening, real interest rates have gone lower," Tarapore said.   

He added that sustaining a higher growth rate would require the current account deficit to rise.   

"Once you reach a 5%-6% current account deficit, all the rating agencies will say India is a dangerous country. It has got an unsustainable current account," he said.   

"If the stock market is booming, India runs a huge current account deficit and the rupee appreciates, the rational thing for a foreign institutional investor will be to take money out," he added.   

India is one of the few emerging economies to run a current account deficit, which stood at $11.8 billion for the April-December period of the last financial year.   

JP Morgan estimates current account deficit at 1.2% of the gross domestic product for the financial year ended March 31. Government data on the deficit for the last fiscal year are due later this month.

title: UPDATE:  India  Mohan: RBI  FX Intervention  Low Vs Mkt Turnover
text:
(Adds more details and bond prices)   

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian central bank's level of intervention in the currency market is insignificant compared with the daily market turnover, the Reserve Bank of India's deputy governor said Wednesday.   

"Even though the central bank does intervene in the foreign exchange market, the volume (the size of RBI's intervention) is low compared to the overall turnover of the market," Rakesh Mohan said at a seminar on European financial markets.   

According to the latest data available, the RBI bought $2.31 billion from the foreign exchange market in March, after mopping up a record $11.86 billion in February.   

The average daily turnover in India's foreign exchange market is around $30 billion, market participants said.   

In the last financial year that ended March 31, the central bank bought around $27 billion from the currency market to stem the rupee's gains against the U.S. dollar.   

Despite the RBI's interventions, the rupee has firmed up against the dollar in recent months largely due to robust foreign fund inflows.   

On May 7, the rupee hit INR40.53 to a dollar, its highest level in nine years. At 00830 GMT, it was trading at INR40.84 to a dollar.   

Change in SLR Depends on Monetary Conditions   

Mohan said the RBI will consider lowering banks' statutory liquidity ratio only after factoring in the underlying monetary conditions.   

Indian rules require banks to keep 25% of their deposits in approved bonds, gold or cash as statutory liquidity ratio.   

"The recent change in legislation enabled the central bank to reduce the ratio, but depending of course on the macro and monetary conditions," Mohan said at the seminar.   

The federal government, which earlier had the power to change the statutory liquidity ratio, recently amended the rules to empower the RBI to decide on the floor of SLR.   

Bond prices fell after Mohan's comments on fears that any cut in the SLR will reduce banks' demand for bonds.   

Banks are the largest buyers of Indian government bonds.   

At 0830GMT, the benchmark 8.07% bond due in 2017 was trading at INR99.75, down from INR99.83 before Mohan's comments.   

"Though Mohan did not say that the SLR will be cut, the market just reacted to his statement as it needed one reason to sell after the rally (of last two sessions)," said a state-run bank's dealer, who didn't wish to be identified.

title: Indian  central bank  says bought $2.3 bln in March
text:
MUMBAI, May 14 (Reuters) - India's central bank bought $2.3 billion in intervention in March, sharply lower than its record dollar purchases in February, the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) monthly bulletin showed on Monday.   

The rupee <INR=IN> began a sharp rally around mid-March that took it to seven-year highs that month. It has since risen to a nine-year high of 40.53 per dollar last week, and on Monday it was trading around 41 per dollar, up about 8 percent this year.   

The March intervention took the RBI's dollar purchases to $22 billion since the start of November 2006. It bought a record $11.9 billion in February alone to check the rupee's rise.   

The rupee's gains have been powered by robust capital inflows, some of which the central bank had tried to absorb. Foreign funds have bought nearly $3 billion of local equities this year, after pouring in nearly $8 billion in 2006.   

However, when it sells the rupee to stem currency gains, it adds rupees to domestic money supply. That meant it was adding to money supply and stoking price pressures at the same time it was tightening policy to rein in credit growth and inflation.   

Firm inflation data prompted the central bank to intervene less aggressively in March, analysts say.   

The central bank is widely believed to have sold rupees less aggressively in April and May too, though traders remain wary of building large currency postions on fears of provoking intervention.   

India's foreign exchange reserves were $204 billion on May 3, rising $26.8 billion in 2007, of which $9.4 billion had come since early March. Traders said a large part of this year's increase was due to the RBI's dollar purchases.   

Before November last year, the RBI had not intervened since May 2006. In the fiscal year that ended on March 31, the central bought a total of $26.8 billion in intervention.   

It bought a $8.14 billion in the financial year to March 2006, down from $20.85 billion in 2004/05.

title: Indian rupee edges toward 9-yr peak; cbank watched
text:
(Updates to open)   

MUMBAI, May 8 (Reuters) - The rupee headed back towards a 9-year high on Tuesday, reclaiming some of the previous session's late losses as traders tested to see whether the central bank had decided to cap the currency's strength.   

At 9:50 a.m. (0420 GMT), the partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> was at 40.755/765 per dollar, up from Monday's close of 40.87/89.   

The rupee had hit 40.53 per dollar on Monday, its highest since May 1998, according to Reuters data, before skidding lower in late trade -- which some traders suspected was due to intervention by the Reserve Bank of India.   

"There was panic when the rupee started falling yesterday, but sanity seems to have been restored, though I'm expecting a volatile session," said a dealer at a private bank.   

"We'll be watching the stock market very closely for an indication about inflows," the trader added.   

The rupee has gained more than 8 percent this year, with most of the gains coming in the last two months, boosted by capital inflows into the fast-growing economy. Foreign funds have bought more than $2.9 billion worth of stocks so far in 2007.   

The central bank bought $19.7 billion in the four months to end-February in a bid to stem the rupee's rise, but is seen as having stayed away from the currency market recently.   

Helping the rupee was weakness in the dollar against major currencies ahead of three central bank meetings this week that may underscore market expectations for U.S. interest rates to fall this year as rates in other major economies rise.

title: India  rupee at 9-yr peak as  intervention  fears ease
text:
MUMBAI, May 7 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee struck a nine-year high against the dollar on Monday as investors felt confident that the central bank would not intervene to limit its gains, with sentiment also boosted by gains in Asian currencies.   

At 10 a.m (0430 GMT), the partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> was at 40.595/605 per dollar, off an early peak of 40.53, its highest level since May 1998, according to Reuters data. It ended at 40.8450/8600 on Friday.   

"The RBI's body language suggests it's not concerned about the rupee's strength at the moment," said the chief dealer at a corporate, referring to the Reserve Bank of India.   

"If they don't, why should the market?" added the dealer, who said the dollar should find some support around the 40.50 level, as traders were likely to book profits.   

The rupee has gained over 9 percent this year, boosted by robust capital inflows into the fast-growing economy.   

The central bank bought $19.7 billion in the four months to end-February in a bid to stem the rupee's rise, but traders said it has not been a major presence in the market recently.   

The heavy intervention had increased money supply and added to price pressures at a time when the RBI was tightening policy to rein in credit growth and lower inflation -- which has led to the market belief that further intervention was unlikely for now.   

The rupee also found support after the dollar slipped against the yen and most Asian currencies after a soft payrolls report reinforced expectations the Federal Reserve would lower interest rates later this year.

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India government bond prices rose Thursday as traders bought securities on hopes that data due Friday will show inflation is falling, dealers said.   

Besides inflation data, dealers also expect a scheduled INR100 billion bond sale and a possible market stabilization scheme auction, which will determine the direction of bonds next week, they said.   

The benchmark 8.07% 2017 bond closed Thursday at INR99.46, up from INR99.32 at Monday's close. Its yield fell by two basis points to 8.14%. Indian financial markets were shut Tuesday and Wednesday due to local holidays.   

"We are seeing some buying in bonds as the market expects the latest inflation data to fall," said Piyush Wadhwa, treasury vice president at ICICI Securities.   

According to a Dow Jones Newswires poll of six analysts, wholesale price inflation for the week ended April 21 is forecast to fall to 5.86% from 6.09% in the week earlier period.   

The commerce ministry will release the data at 0630 GMT Friday.   

"Strong statutory liquidity ratio related demand from banks and a slight ease in liquidity conditions also aided bonds," said a dealer at a primary dealership.   

Under Indian law, banks have to maintain 25% of their deposits in the form of cash, gold, or approved securities, and report this position to the central bank every alternate Friday.   

The overnight call money rate eased marginally to 8.35% from 9.25% at Monday's close on the central's bank's electronic dealing platform due to a slight improvement in system liquidity.   

In the currency market, the Indian rupee rose against the dollar on heavy dollar flows to the market.   

The dollar closed at INR41.11, down from INR41.18 Monday close.   

"As the markets were closed for trading for the last two days, the accumulated dollar funds for the last few days came in to the system today," said a dealer at a private bank.   

The local currency's rise was also aided by strong foreign fund buying of local stocks, dealers said.   

The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark 30-stock Sensex rose 205.84 points, or 1.5%, to 14,078.21.   

However, the dealer at the private bank expects the rupee to weaken in the coming session on fears the Reserve Bank of India may intervene to curb the currency's appreciation.   

"The dollar could rise to about INR41.20 tomorrow as these bunched-up flows dry up and the central bank steps in," he said.   

The federal government has recently raised the ceiling for bond sales under the market stabilization scheme to INR1.1 trillion from INR950 billion previously, a move that will allow it greater flexibility in intervening in the foreign exchange market.

title: UPDATE: Which Indian Stocks To Consider Heading Into Monsoon Season
text:
By Jay Somaney   

PLANO, Texas (Dow Jones) -- "Sell in May," advises the age-old adage, "and go away." This May, though, the adage does not fit, especially as far as Indian stocks are concerned.   

Let me outline the reasons, and then we will examine each one in detail:   

* Anticipation of the monsoons.   

* Most Indian stocks that trade on U.S. exchanges have barely budged, despite very good earnings due to a rising rupee.   

* The weakest quarter for Indian information-technology companies is the March quarter, and that is now behind us.   

* Despite a rising rupee, guidance from most Indian companies for the June quarter and for the fiscal year ending March 2008 was very good, all things considered.   

* The Reserve Bank of India has not intervened in the currency markets, and that is why the rupee has appreciated as much as it has.   

* Interest rates have more than likely peaked in India.   

Rain   

The monsoons are very important to the Indian economy, as a large portion of Indians are still considered rural residents who are very dependent on agriculture for their livelihood. A good rainy season means the power of the rural consumer is unleashed with purchases of farming equipment, motorcycles, automobiles, trucks, cell phones, clothes, jewelry and much else.   

The folks at the weather department have forecast a seasonal monsoon this year. That basically means that the amount of rainfall across India will vary no more than 10% up or down from normal, which is great news.   

For most Indian and quasi-Indian IT companies, the quarter ending in March is the seasonally weakest one, as annual wage hikes and increased visa costs lead to compressed margins.   

We are now entering the sweet spot for these companies, as the September and December quarters are usually the best.   

Buying when no one else is buying is how the easy money is made. By the time we are in the third and fourth quarters, these stocks' levels should be a lot higher than at the moment.   

Markets are currently fixated on the rising rupee, and as a result, despite stellar results and guidance from the Indian and quasi-Indian IT sector, the stocks have done very little. A major reason for the U.S. dollar's drastic decline vis-Ã -vis the Indian rupee has been a lack of intervention by the Reserve Bank of India, which is in a fight against inflation. As a result, the Indian central bank has refrained from buying dollars and weakening the rupee. As soon as inflation comes back in, the RBI will be forced to intervene and start buying dollars in order to keep Indian goods and services competitive in the global marketplace.   

There was also a lot of hand wringing in the media and among the dark siders about how these Indian and quasi-Indian IT companies are facing slowing demand and stagnant pricing for on-site and offshore work.   

Nothing could be further from the truth. Actually, demand is still very strong, and even if the U.S. economy drops into a recession the demand for Indian IT; business-process outsourcing, or BPO; and offshoring will only get stronger as American companies look for ways to decrease costs. Most of these companies are seeing across-the-board increases in prices paid ranging from up 2% to as much as 5%, depending on which company you look at and whether it's for on-site or offshore work.   

Finally, interest rates in India have more than likely peaked after a series of rate hikes strung together by the central bank since the beginning of this year. Between December 2006 and March 2007, Indian interest rates are up almost 250 basis points. Since February 2006, interest rates have been hiked by 400 basis points. More than likely, we have seen the last of these hikes in India, which means a major headwind will be removed from the markets.   

The Indian central bank left interest rates unchanged at its last meeting, April 24. It also revealed its annual policy statement for the year ending March 2008 and forecast GDP growth of around 8.5% and inflation to around 5% for this fiscal year.   

At present the bank rate stands at 6%, the reverse repo rate at 6% as well, the repo rate at 7.75% and the cash reserve ratio at 6.5%, and I don't think they will rise from these levels.   

Five to consider and four to avoid   

So, given the backdrop heading into the month, here are the five Indian and quasi-Indian companies to consider buying in May:   

* Cognizant Technology Solutions .   

* Infosys Technologies .   

* Satyam Computer Services .   

* Icici Bank .   

* Patni Computer Systems .   

These are the four Indian companies to avoid in May, waiting for a better entry point later in the year:   

* Tata Motors Ltd. .   

* Dr Reddys Labs .   

* Rediff Com India Ltd. .   

* Sify Ltd. .   

In summation, the sell-in-May-and-go-away mantra should be applied only selectively this year. And, until next time, happy investing. [ 05-01-07 1620ET ]

title: V. PHANI KUMAR'S THIS WEEK IN INDIA: Have Investors Misread  Tata Tea's Intentions?
text:
By V. Phani Kumar   

MUMBAI (Dow Jones) -- Investors in  Tata Tea Ltd. may have heaved a sigh of relief in the past week after its shares were boosted by an unconfirmed report in U.S. media that  Coca Cola Co. is eyeing an acquisition of enhanced-water brand Glaceau.   

But whether those gains will be sustained is a completely different matter.   

Tata Tea's shares have been depressed ever since its fateful announcement in August of plans to buy a 30% stake for $677 million in Energy Brands, the unlisted firm that owns Glaceau. Over the next few months, the shares lost heavily as investors worried over the steep $2.2 billion valuation of Energy Brands and the impact of the acquisition on its financial profile.   

Against that backdrop, the market read big-and-mighty Coke's (KO) reported interest in buying Glaceau for around $3.5 billion as a compliment to the Tatas' decision to move in early and as a vindication of their investment strategy.   

Even so, the 14% surge in  Tata Tea's shares in the past week may have been overdone. Here's why:   

Some market participants seem to believe, perhaps naively, that the Tatas will cash out smilingly if Coke or someone else makes an attractive offer. I don't see how that's going to happen.   

Glaceau is a rapidly growing brand in the world's largest consumer market, with a product line-up targeted at the every-increasing population of health-conscious individuals. It also complements  Tata Tea's beverages and perfectly suits the Tatas' global ambitions. With just a 30% stake now, the Tatas may not have management control in Energy Brands, but certainly view it as a strategic investment.   

Given that, why anyone would think that the Tatas may behave like a venture fund or private-equity investor and sell out beats me.   

Even if one supposes that  Tata Tea may find any forthcoming offers too much to resist, where will it invest the proceeds? In a similarly strong and growing brand in the U.S. or Western Europe, I would think. Why then, would they exit Glaceau in the first place, nipping the bud before the blossom?   

The man in the hot seat is obviously Gateau's founder and CEO, J. Darius Bikoff, and it all boils down to whether he is attracted to any fresh offers that might come Glaceau's way. The Tatas, meanwhile, will no doubt ponder whether they should exercise the option they have to buy an additional 10% stake in Glaceau. And that brings us back to  Tata Tea's shares.   

If the Tatas do exercise that option or decide to raise their stake further through negotiations, it will mean further cash outflows. And that could bring another round of correction to the shares, especially if the Tatas don't get a majority control.   

There could be myriad other possibilities, including one where Tata agrees to stay on as a minority shareholder while Glaceau's control passes to someone other than the current management. It's difficult to predict the outcome of such an event today, but what is clear to me in the absence of further updates is that  Tata Tea's shares have jumped the gun and may be asking for a pullback.   

Rupee's strength vs. dollar spells doom for small exporters   

With the specter of a strengthening rupee against the U.S. dollar looming large over Indian exporters, investors in some of these companies will continue to be a worried lot in days to come. And it isn't just the software companies, which face little competition from regional peers and are more assured of continued order flows.   

Worse-hit are the hundreds of small-scale companies, especially textile exporters, who typically compete with exporters from other low-cost countries where the currency appreciation hasn't been as much in the past few months.   

The dollar, which could buy around 45.61 rupees in August, is currently worth just 41.10 rupees, due in part to a broad weakness for the greenback against most major currencies of the world and in part to uninterrupted capital and fund inflows.   

What makes matters worse for these small exporters is that the Reserve Bank of India isn't showing any signs it'll intervene and prevent further strengthening of the rupee. The central bank is waging a war of its own against excessive liquidity inflation, and is worried that purchasing dollars to support the greenback will only boost the supply of rupees further. title: RPT-POLL-Indian rupee to peak at 40/dollar in 2007
text:
(Repeats story issued late on Thursday)   

 MUMBAI, April 26 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is likely to peak at 40.00 per dollar in 2007, although its current rally may be running out of steam after a rise of more than 8 percent this year, a Reuters poll showed on Thursday.   

 The partially-convertible rupee hit a nine-year high of 40.60 per dollar <INR=IN> on Thursday, driven by foreign portfolio and direct investment as well as overseas fund raising by Indian firms, and is Asia's best-performing currency so far this year.   

 The median forecast for the rupee among 11 economists surveyed was for a decline to 41.50 by the end of June and to 42.40 by the end of 2007, 4.4 percent above its close for 2006.   

 But continuing strong capital inflows into the robustly growing economy were expected to propel the rupee to the psychological 40 level at some point this year and two economists forecast it would break through that barrier to 39.50.   

 "The appreciation has been much faster than we expected. India is a fairly good bet among emerging economies due to its strong growth, high attractive yields and a hawkish central bank," said Chin Loo Thio, currency strategist at BNP Paribas in Singapore.   

 "The central bank's strategy to cool inflation via rupee appreciation will continue."   

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) spent much of the past six months intervening to keep rupee gains in check but since mid-March the currency has been rising and traders say intervention has been scaled down substantially.   

 Analysts say the reason is its intervention, which pumped billions of rupees into circulation, was adding to cash-fuelled inflation pressures, forcing the central bank to adopt a more hands-off approach.   

 Annual inflation hit a two-year peak of 6.7 percent in early 2007 but has since cooled to about 6 percent and analysts expect a further retreat in headline numbers in the next two months. Once that happens, many see the RBI returning to its old intervening ways.   

 "I think the RBI will intervene once the inflation scenario clears out because this is a very, very sharp appreciation," said D.K. Joshi, chief economist at ratings agency Crisil.   

 The central bank kept its key lending rate steady this week after five successive increases but it raised the limit on bonds it can sell to absorb funds generated by its intervention, giving itself leeway to step in at a later date.   

 "I see one more bout of intervention if the inflows continue to be strong. The REER (a trade weighted) indicator is at unsustainable levels," Indranil Pan of  Kotak Mahindra Bank said.   

 The RBI's six-currency real effective exchange rate index stood at 112 in mid-April, showing the rupee was 12 percent overvalued.   

 The currency's scorching run has forced a number of banks including  JP Morgan, BNP Paribas and  Barclays Capital to revise their rupee forecasts for the year.   

JP Morgan, a long-standing rupee bear, changed its year end forecast to 43 per dollar from 45.

title: UPDATE 1- India  cbank raises ceiling on  intervention  bonds
text:
(Updates with background, analyst reaction, bylines)   

MUMBAI, April 27 (Reuters) - India's central bank increased its firepower for currency intervention for the second time in a week on Friday, raising the ceiling on the amount of bonds it can issue to absorb funds generated when it sells rupees for dollars.   

The rupee has appreciated more than 7.5 percent against the dollar since the start of the year, most of that in April, and hit a nine-year high of 40.60 per dollar <INR=IN> on Thursday.   

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said in a statement it was raising the 2007/08 ceiling for its intervention bonds to 1.1 trillion rupees ($26.8 billion) from 950 billion rupees, and said it would review the limit again if the issuance topped 950 billion rupees.   

The outstanding balance for intervention bonds, known as market stabilisation bonds, is now 780 billion rupees, it said.   

"Now the RBI has adequate ammunition for another round of dollar purchases keeping in view the strength of the rupee," said Indranil Pan, chief economist at  Kotak Mahindra Bank.

The rupee closed at 41.08/10 per dollar on Friday. Its rise has been driven by large inflows of foreign investment capital as well as cheap debt raised abroad by Indian companies.   

The central bank has intervened extensively to try to curb its gains, buying almost $20 billion in the four months to the end of February, although traders say it possibly held off this month as intervention was pumping inflation-fuelling cash into the domestic market.   

The RBI had only just raised the intervention bond issue limit on Tuesday, when it took it to 950 billion from 800 billion, but the rupee has continued to appreciate and the market is nervous it could step in unexpectedly.   

But some analysts said Friday's move did not necessarily mean it was setting itself up for massive rupee-dampening action straight away - although it clearly was arming itself for more rupee selling at some point.   

"This only indicates that they are giving themselves extra elbow room for a future date, and they will watch incoming data such as money supply and bank loan growth before stepping in," said Manoj Rane, country treasurer at BNP Paribas India.   

"If they really wanted to intervene they would have caught the market by surprise, shown dollar bids in the market or even a verbal intervention would have sufficed," he said.   

But the market might read the decision as an intervention precursor and cut back short-dollar positions on Monday, he said.   

The RBI is also concerned that annual credit growth, which has averaged 30 percent for the past three years, and money supply growth in excess of 20 percent, are fuelling inflation, which is hovering above 6 percent annually.   

It has tightened monetary policy aggressively since mid-December, although it opted to leave rates steady this week while it waited to see whether the measures were taking effect.   

One method of tightening has been to increase the cash reserve ratio -- the amount of funds banks have to keep with it on deposit -- a tool it has used three times since December. Many in the market expect it will raise the ratio further this year.   

"It tells you maybe more cash reserve ratio increases are not on the cards now and more intervention is in store," said ICICI Securities analyst A. Prasanna.   

($1=41.1 rupees). ((Writing by Charlotte Cooper, editing by John Mair; Reuters Messaging: saikat.chatterjee@reuters.com@reuters.net; Tel: +91-22 6636-9035))

title: UPDATE 3-India cbank holds rates, acts against high inflows
text:
(Updates with poll, intervention bonds, prices)   

MUMBAI, April 24 (Reuters) - India's central bank took steps to ease the upward pressure on its currency from capital inflows while leaving its key lending rate unchanged at 7.75 percent as expected at a policy review on Tuesday.   

However, the rupee jumped to a nine-year high of 41.04 per dollar <INR=IN>, stocks <.BSESN> ended 1.5 percent up and bond yields fell as the market welcomed the rate pause and reckoned the central bank would not act aggressively to check growth.   

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which has raised the lending rate five times in less than a year, forecast Asia's fourth-largest economy would grow 8.5 percent in the fiscal year ending March 2008, lower than 9.2 percent expected for 2006/07.   

Its last rate increase was at the end of March, and it said its focus was still on the fight against inflation rather than on economic growth at present.   

It aimed for wholesale price inflation, currently above 6 percent on an annual basis, of near 5.0 percent by next March but said rising prices still posed the main risk to the economy.   

Analysts said its main focus was to offset the impact of foreign capital inflows that have complicated its efforts to curb inflation and credit growth, as higher interest rates have simply attracted more capital.   

"Foreign exchange inflows can potentially reduce the efficacy of monetary policy tightening by expanding liquidity," the central bank said in its annual policy review.   

Foreign investors have recently poured billions of dollars into India's booming property and stock markets and into projects to expand production capacity to meet rapidly growing domestic demand.   

This has pushed up the rupee, and the central bank, concerned about a widening trade gap and the risk of a sudden reversal of flows, bought a massive $11.9 billion in February alone to block the rise. But its actions have put more rupees into the domestic money supply, adding to inflation pressures.   

Rob Subbaraman at Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong said many of the new measures addressed the strong capital inflows.   

"(They) seem to be a growing issue or concern for policy makers in India, and will continue to be a big issue," he said.   

Readying for further rupee strength, the RBI said it was also raising the limit on bonds it uses to neutralise intervention.   

EASING THE RULES   

Thailand too has been troubled by strong foreign inflows and slapped on controls last year.   

But, mindful that India needs foreign money to build up its infrastructure, the RBI opted instead to allow more domestic outflows, noting infrastructure bottlenecks were a constraint on the economy.   

It said moves to greater capital account convertibility might accelerate and proposed letting firms repay more foreign debt sooner, as well as raising the aggregate ceiling for overseas investment by mutual funds.   

It raised a limit for firms' portfolio investment abroad and proposed a higher cap on their general overseas investment as well as cutting the rate ceiling on non-resident deposits.   

It aimed to contain money supply growth at 17-17.5 percent in 2007/08, below the actual rate of about 20 percent.   

TIME FOR A BREAK   

Analysts polled by Reuters after the decision expected at least one more tightening, although a pause was possible as inflation and credit growth showed signs of slowing.   

"The RBI has kept the door open for any swift measure, and it could be warranted by anything, but we believe it won't be needed in the near term," said Harish Menon at  ING Vysya Bank.

The RBI kept its key borrowing rate, known as the reverse repo, steady at 6.0 percent and held the bank rate, used to price long-term lending, steady at 6.0 percent.   

There was no change to banks' cash reserve ratio beyond a previously announced increase to 6.5 percent due on April 28. It has raised the ratio three times since mid-December in an attempt to curb credit growth of about 30 percent a year.
