title: FX  ASIA:  Intervention  Fears As  India  Rupee Nears 9-Yr Highs
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--After a rush of capital inflows spiked the Indian rupee to multiyear highs, concerns are rising the country's central bank may take a more aggressive approach in reining in the currency.   

The rupee's surge to near nine-year highs from three-year lows last July is hurting exporter earnings, and with inflation starting to ease, the Reserve Bank of India could have room to resume currency intervention after staying away since February. The central bank could also take steps to counter capital inflows, analysts said.   

Thus, in the near term, the dollar is unlikely to breach the key INR41.00 support, and could instead bounce back up to INR42.50, they said. Over the longer term, the dollar could trend higher toward INR44.00, possibly by year end. Standard Chartered Bank, for instance, expects the dollar to end 2007 around INR43.80.   

"The RBI needs to aggressively intervene as a continuous rupee rise will have a deflationary impact on the economy and slow growth," said A.V.Rajwade, a member of the RBI's committee on fuller capital account convertibility.   

The rupee has risen nearly 9% since it hit a three-year low last July. At 1040 GMT Wednesday, the dollar was trading at INR42.02, near nine-year highs.   

Rupee strength has hit exporter earnings hard, particularly for the country's important software and textile firms, whose earnings are in dollars.   

"Export growth, in terms of the three-month moving average, has dipped to about 7% now from 32.3% in August. Part of this (lower growth) will be a lagged impact of a significant increase in the rupee," said Sujan Hajra, chief economist at Mumbai-based brokerage firm Anand Rathi Securities.   

Analysts reckon that a one-percentage-point gain in the rupee against the dollar shrinks Infosys Technologies' operating margin by 50 basis points and HCL Technologies' margins by 35 basis points. These are among two of India's largest software export firms.   

Likewise for the textile industry. "Operating margins for most apparel manufacturers are likely to fall to 2.5%-3% from around 6% currently due to the rupee rise and rising interest rates," said Vijay Agarwal, chairman at Apparel Exports Promotion Council, an industry body.   

Rupee strength not only hurts earnings but also Indian exporter competitiveness against major rivals such as Indonesia, China, and Bangladesh.   

Latest government data showed India's merchandise exports rose 7.9% on year to $9.70 billion in February while imports grew 25.1% to $14.36 billion in the month. For the April-February period, exports totaled $109.13 billion, suggesting that for the fiscal year ended March 31, exports likely failed to meet the government's target $125 billion.   

With export growth moderating, India's trade deficit for the April-December period was $52.3 billion, higher than the $40.1 billion gap for the previous full fiscal year. The current account, meanwhile, was in deficit of $11.8 billion for the April-December period.   

JP Morgan, which said its Real Effective Exchange Rate Index shows the rupee is overvalued by more than 13%, a record high, expects the current account deficit to widen to $14.3 billion for the last fiscal year and $19.9 billion this year.   

"The RBI should intervene immediately to stem the rupee rise. It is important to remember exports create employment, not imports," said Ajit Ranade, chief economist at AV Birla Group.   

The RBI tried to stem the rupee rise between November and February, buying $19.7 billion of dollars during that period. But when it stopped, the rupee shot higher.   

The RBI may have been keen to allow the rupee to gain as a way of controlling inflation. Rising prices became a hot political potato recently, with the ruling Congress party attributing its defeat in some recent state elections to higher prices.   

But inflation has begun to ease as a favorable statistical base effect comes into play, and recent fiscal and monetary measures start to pull prices lower.   

Inflation was 5.74% on year for the week ended March 31, easing from a two-year high of 6.73% for the week ended Feb. 3, and is expected to slip under 5.00% in the first half of this fiscal year.   

Apart from inflation, the RBI also stopped its interventions since February possibly because it has reached close to the INR800 billion limit on issuance of its market stabilization securities. Without the ability to issue more bonds, the RBI risks leaving its interventions unsterilized, which would contribute to faster money supply growth and potentially higher inflation.   

The RBI and federal government had said a review the ceiling would be made when it breaches the INR700 billion mark. Analysts expect the central bank to review the ceiling when the RBI makes its annual policy review on April 24.   

Speculation has also heightened the RBI could announce measures to counter the heavy capital inflows such as restrictions on commercial borrowings by companies, and cutting interest rates on deposits offered to nonresident Indians.   

"The thrust of the policy will be on addressing structural issues that are causing a surge in capital inflows," said Shubhada Rao, chief economist at Yes Bank.   

Capital Inflows, primarily into India's equity markets but also from foreign direct investment, have helped the rupee rise sharply.   

India recently became the fifth Asian economy to cross the $200 billion level in foreign exchange reserves.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia up,  intervention  fears cap rupee's gains
text:
SINGAPORE, April 18 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose against a weaker dollar on Wednesday, but the Indian rupee retreated amid growing concerns about fresh central bank dollar-buying intervention.   

 The Thai baht <THB=TH> gained nearly 0.3 percent to 34.75 to the dollar. It had hit 34.70 in early onshore trading, its highest level in almost a month.   

 The dollar sank to a 26-year low against sterling <GBP=> and weakened against other major currencies after data showing weaker U.S. core consumer inflation in March, bolstered the view that the Federal Reserve may lean towards a rate cut this year.   

 "The dollar is under pressure. The low consumer prices could be positive for U.S. equities as it helped take some pressure off the Fed, and that was a helpful lead to Asian equity markets," said Sean Callow, currency strategist at Westpac Bank.   

 The rupee <INR=IN> eased back to around 41.95 per dollar surrendering most of its daily gains after briefly hitting 41.80, which was still off its 9-year high of 41.63 hit on Tuesday.   

 Analysts are concerned that the rupee's rapid gains in recent days might push the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to intervene. So far they say the central bank appears to have accepted the strength in the currency, which helps hold down inflation.   

 "Following aggressive intervention in February and March, the central bank appears to have scaled back their dollar buying significantly this week," currency strategists at UBS said in a research note.   

 The RBI bought $1.14 billion of reserves in the first week of April, central bank data shows, implying a slowdown from a record $11.9 billion it bought in February to prevent the rupee's gains.   

INTERVENTION LIKELY   

 But UBS cautioned that the RBI was standing aside to wait for a clearer economic picture, and its dollar-buying intervention will resume if money supply and inflation eased.   

 "We would therefore not be surprised if the RBI returns to the rupee market before the week is up," UBS said, adding they were cautiously shifting their 1-month dollar/rupee forecast to 42.50.   

 The won <KRW=> rose as high as 927.3 per dollar, its highest since early January, despite concerns about intervention by the Bank of Korea, which traders said had stepped into the market this week to cap the currency's gains.   

 The baht has gained about 3.8 percent this year, trailing the rupee's 5.5 percent rise as the best-performing currency in Asia, despite Bangkok's attempts to cap the baht's rise to protect its exporters.

MUMBAI, April 17 (Reuters) - The rupee skidded from fresh nine-year highs against the dollar on Tuesday, as investors squared off short dollar positions on fears the central bank would intervene heavily to stem the rupee's rally.   

The partially convertible rupee ended at 41.97/98 per dollar, falling sharply from an intraday high of 41.62, its strongest since May 1998, according to Reuters data. It had ended at 41.85/86 on Monday.   

"We might be heading into a consolidation phase, or for a bit of a correction," said Pradeep Khanna, director and head of foreign exchange trading, treasury and capital markets at HSBC India.   

The rupee has gained 12 percent from a three-year low of 47.04 in July, including more than 6 percent in 2007 to be Asia's strongest currency against the dollar this year.   

According to a JPMorgan index <JPMREER>, the rupee is overvalued by 14 percent, compared with 8 percent a month ago.   

A stronger rupee hurts the competitiveness of Indian exports, and the country's top software exporter  Tata Consultancy Services told Reuters on Tuesday that the rupee's strength was a major concern, and that it had currency hedges worth $1 billion. Despite no signs of intervention on Tuesday, traders remained concerned the rupee's recent strength may compel the Reserve Bank of India to intervene aggressively in coming sessions, in a bid to maintain exporters' competitiveness.   

The rupee rose sharply in early trade, reflecting a squeeze on cash in the system, with overnight loan rates <INROND=> trading at around 16 percent, compared to 6 percent when cash is ample.   

The rupee's gains have been fueled by domestic deposits by overseas Indians, that increased by $4 billion in 2006/07 while foreign borrowings by companies rose $14 billion, according to JPMorgan. Foreigners have bought more than $2.1 billion worth of shares so far in 2007.

The Reserve Bank of India largely refrained from intervening in the foreign exchange market to support the dollar, which accentuated the rupee's sharp rise.

title: UPDATE:India Is Fifth Asian Econ With Over $200B  FX  Reserves
text:
(Adds details about sources of reserve accretion, analyst comments.) .   

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India's central bank said Friday that the country's foreign exchange reserves have crossed $200 billion, making it only the fifth Asian economy with a level that high.   

Reserves have risen sharply in recent months as the Reserve Bank of India has aggressively intervened in the foreign exchange market to stem a more-than-9% rise in the value of the rupee since July, analysts say.   

The increase in reserves is bound to intensify debate on whether a part of the reserves should be invested in high-yielding assets, the returns on which can then be used fund infrastructure development in the country.   

The reserves are now invested mostly in low yielding U.S. government debt, but there have been recent calls for the reserves to be moved into equities overseas and real estate.   

"The productive use of foreign exchange reserves over and above what the RBI thinks is (the minimum comfort level) necessary in its risk assessment is always an issue," said Samiran Chakraborty, chief economist at ICICI Bank.   

The latest federal budget suggests studying a proposal to set up two overseas entities to borrow foreign exchange from the RBI. These entities could then fund long-term infrastructure projects.   

India's federal government estimates it will need investments of $320 billion during the next five years to improve the quality of infrastructure to match global standards.   

Some economists also feel that India could do with a slower pace of rise in reserves as it adds to inflationary pressures, requiring sterilization measures such as domestic bond issuances.   

"I think it is a number we are increasingly getting worried about. We could do with a slower growth in forex reserves," said Abheek Barua, chief economist at  ABN Amro Bank.

ABN Amro estimates the cost of sterilization at 2% of gross domestic product.   

The RBI said earlier Friday that it bought $19.7 billion in foreign exchange between November and February.   

Its weekly statistical supplement showed reserves rose by $1.141 billion for the week ended April 6 to $200.320 billion from a week earlier. Reserves have risen $46.111 billion in the past 12 months alone.   

China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan are the other Asian economies to have reserves in excess of $200 billion.

title: Indian  central bank  says bought $11.9 bln in Feb
text:
MUMBAI, April 11 (Reuters) - India's central bank bought a record $11.9 billion in February as it tried to rein in the rupee that rose to a 16-month high that month, the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) monthly bulletin showed on Wednesday.   

The intervention, for the fourth month in a row, took dollar purchases to $19.7 billion since November. The central bank often intervenes to ensure a stronger rupee does not hurt exports and to smoothen excess volatility.   

The rupee <INR=IN> closed at 42.8275/8375 a dollar on Wednesday, off an eight-year high of 42.76 hit on Monday. It has gained more than 3 percent in 2007, and is up nearly 10 percent from a three-year low of 47.04 in July.   

Traders were wary of building short positions in the dollar on fears of provoking central bank intervention, although foreign capital inflows have been rising.   

India's foreign exchange reserves climbed to a record $199.2 billion on March 30. They rose $4.5 billion in March, and traders said part of this increase was due to the RBI's buying of dollars.   

In January, the central bank had bought $2.8 billion after buying $1.82 billion the month before and $3.2 billion in November.   

Before that, the central bank had intervened in May, when it bought $504 million. It bought a net $8.14 billion in the financial year to March 2006, down from $20.85 billion in 2004/05.

title: Indian rupee seen losing steam, fall by June
text:
MUMBAI, April 11 (Reuters) - India's rallying rupee, Asia's best performing currency this year, should start losing momentum soon and head lower as the central bank will step in to ensure exports are not hurt, analysts said on Wednesday.   

The rupee <INR=IN>, trading at 42.85 a dollar, has risen more than 3 percent since the end of December to its highest level in nearly eight years, thanks to a spike in interest rates and growing foreign investment.   

The biggest factor, however, for the rupee's climb has been the central bank, which usually keeps a tight control on the unit through heavy market intervention.   

With its priority shifting to fighting stubbornly high inflation, the central bank has stayed away from aggressively buying dollars against rupee sales -- because the intervention boosts money supply and fuels inflation pressures.   

This could change.   

"In my view, inflation has probably peaked. When that shows marked signs of cooling, they will start intervening in the currency markets," said Abheek Barua, chief economist at  ABN AMRO Bank, India.   

"I expect them to start intervening from the second half of the month," he said, adding he expected the rupee at 43.50-44 by June.   

The annual inflation rate has slowed to 6.39 percent from a two-year high of 6.73 percent in early February, but is still above the central bank's comfort level 5-5.5 percent.   

The central bank raised its main lending rate five times in the fiscal year that ended in March, and increased the proportion of funds banks have to deposit with it three times in four months to douse inflation.   

There are concerns the central bank may again tighten policy when it meets on April 24.   

Analysts said the rupee's rise, of nearly 10 percent from a three-year low of 47.04 in July, has increased its overvaluation on a trade-weighted basis posing a threat to exports and a widening trade deficit.   

"The risk of a correction either via market forces or by central bank intervention has increased," said Singapore-based Bank of America strategist Han-Sia Yeo, who expects the rupee to weaken to 44 by end-June.   

India's trade shortfall widened to $52 billion in April-December 2006 from $40 billion in the year-earlier period, and the stronger rupee is expected to squeeze margins of export-focused companies such as software services.   

The rupee is currently overvalued by 11.1 percent against a basket of six currencies of India's top trading partners, according to a JPMorgan index <JPMREER>, up from 8.1 percent a month ago.   

The rupee is on the wrong side of the REER -- real effective exchange rate, privately maintained by the Reserve Bank of India, JPMorgan analysts Claudio Piron and Yen Ping Ho said in a note, raising concern that rupee "valuations have overshot".

title: India rupee in sight of 8-yr high; cbank watched
text:
(Updates to open)   

MUMBAI, April 9 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee inched towards an eight-year high on Monday as the prospect of capital inflows spurred dealers to buy the currency, but they remained wary of intervention by the Reserve Bank of India.   

At 9:50 a.m. (0420 GMT), the rupee was at 42.75/76 per dollar, up from Thursday's finish 42.90/92 and closing in on an 8-year high of 42.63, according to Reuters data. The market was closed on Friday for a holiday.   

"The market's view is that the rupee is going to strengthen ... and that the RBI will most likely stay away," said the chief dealer with a a private bank.   

"I expect the rupee to trade in a 42.65-85 range on today," the dealer added.   

The central bank is suspected of having sold rupees regularly since November in a bid to rein in the local unit, which has risen about 10 percent since last July, when it hit a 3-year low.   

The rupee's gains have been powered by robust capital inflows into Asia's fourth largest economy, and the central bank is thought to be uncomfortable with the pace of its appreciation.   

According to a JP Morgan index, the rupee is overvalued by 10.6 precent, compared with 7.9 percent a month ago.   

The RBI's intervention has fuelled money supply growth and inflation, both running above its target band. With the central bank focused on taming inflation, many dealers believe any further intervention will be muted in the near term.   

The dollar strengthened against some Asian currencies after strong March jobs data on Friday eased concerns about a slowdown in the U.S. economy and dimmed the chances of a rate cut in the near term.

title: Indian rupee pulls back from steep fall; cbank eyed
text:
(Updates to close)   

MUMBAI, March 30 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee ran out of steam on Friday after partly recovering from its largest single-day percentage fall in nearly nine years, as investors shied away from testing the central bank's resolve on the last trading day of the financial year.   

The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> surged in early trade but ran out of momentum to end at 43.45/48 per dollar, recouping some of its losses from Thursday's close of 43.770/785 when it fell 1.7 percent on suspected central bank intervention.   

It had risen to 43.01 on Wednesday, its highest in more than seven years, Reuters data showed.   

The central bank said after market hours on Friday it was raising its short-term lending rate by 25 basis points to 7.75 percent with immediate effect and its cash resere ratio by half a percentage point, a move traders said would strengthen the local currency.   

"We should see dollars flow into the market as a result of the rate hike, which will push the rupee higher, though there should be good support for the dollar around 43.25-30," said the chief dealer at a private bank.   

"What remains to be seen is the central bank's stance. April may not have the strong inflows we saw in March, which will console the RBI, and perhaps they will keep their hands off," he added, referring to the Reserve Bank of India that has intervened regularly since November in a bid to thwart the rupee's rise.   

The central bank said on Friday that foreign exchange reserves had risen by nearly $2 billion on March 23 from a week earlier, an indication of the extent to which it has intervened in the local foreign exchange market recently, analysts said.   

The rupee is about 8 percent above a three-year low hit last July, and traders were wary that the central bank may be worried about its strength and want to cap further gains.   

The rupee was given a fillip after overnight rates soared to as high as 80 percent on Friday, their highest level in more than a decade, due to an acute shortage of funds as banks curbed lending to meet statutory capital adequacy requirements ahead of the financial year-end on March 31.   

Gains in the local unit were capped by strong demand for dollars from oil refiners for month-end payments. India imports about 70 percent of its oil.

title: Indian rupee falls 1.7pct, biggest drop in 9 years
text:
(Updates to close)   

MUMBAI, March 29 (Reuters) - The rupee fell 1.7 percent on Thursday, posting its biggest single-day percentage loss in nearly nine years, on suspected central bank intervention and short-covering of dollar positions after the Indian unit had risen to a 7-year high on Wednesday.   

Traders said month end dollar buying by oil companies also pushed the rupee to its lowest close in more than a week.   

The rupee <INR=IN> ended at 43.770/785 per dollar, weaker than Wednesday's close of 43.04/06. It was the biggest percentage drop since May 14, 1998, when it had dropped 1.9 percent, Reuters data showed.   

The rupee has gained about 7.5 percent since hitting a three-year low last July. It touched a peak of 43.01 during trade on Wednesday, its highest level since November 1999, according to Reuters data.   

"The central bank aggressively sold rupees between 43.30-50, which suggests the rally is over," said a dealer with a private bank.   

"Everyone was expecting a correction to happen, though its speed was a little surprising," added the dealer.   

Traders also said a shift in the settlement date for three-day forward contracts struck on Wednesday due to the end of the fiscal year was another reason behind the fall. India's fiscal year ends on March 31.   

"The premium was built into today's rate as there is no settlement of currency deals on April 2 because of year-end account closing for banks," a foreign bank trader said.   

Call money rates traded at 10-11 percent on Thursday. They touched a decade high of 70 percent last week, as banks faced an acute cash crunch following advance tax outflows of about 300 billion rupees ($6.8 billion).   

Standard Chartered said that while the rupee's near-term strength may persist, it would fall to 45.50 by the end of June.   

"The excessive strength in the rupee has been caused by a liquidity squeeze... as government expenditure seeps back into the system, liquidity is unlikely to tighten much further," it said in a note on Thursday.   

"Finally despite the fact that the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) has so far tolerated rupee appreciation, intervention is still possible," it said.

MUMBAI, March 22 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee slipped from 19-month highs against the dollar on Thursday as tight money market conditions eased, and month-end demand for dollars from oil refiners kicked in, traders said.  

Investors also squared off short positions in the dollar on fears the U.S. currency had been oversold, and that a sharp correction would ensue, possibly triggered by Reserve Bank of India intervention.

"People weren't convinced about the rupee's rally -- it was the pain on call rates that made people sell (dollars)," said a dealer with a private bank.  

"But over the last few years, everytime the market has approached the low 43s it has quickly moved in the other direction... a lot of people have absorbed that trend, and bargained to buy (dollars) today," the dealer added.

Traders also said that month-end demand for the U.S. currency from oil refiners was picking up, putting further pressure on the rupee.  

Goldman Sachs said the rupee's spike was temporary, and expects it to trade at 44.15 within a 3-month target period.  

"We expect the rupee to depreciate as it is over-bought. Banks will likely start re-constituting their dollar assets, and the recent excessive demand for the rupee will moderate on the back of some easing of liquidity," the investment bank said in a note.

title: Indian rupee rises past 43.50 to 19-mnth high
text:
(Updates to close)  

MUMBAI, March 21 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee climbed past 43.50 versus the dollar on Wednesday to a 19-month high as traders dumped dollar holdings to take advantage of interbank rupee rates that rose as high as 70 percent on a cash crunch.  

The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> ended at 43.4450/4550 per dollar, its strongest close since Aug. 1, 2005, according to Reuters data, and taking gains over two days to 1.5 percent. It had closed at 43.85/86 on Tuesday.  

"The cost of carry is heavy, which is keeping people from going long (dollars)... in fact (it) encourages people to go short," said Agam Gupta, head of foreign exchange trading at Standard Chartered Bank.  

"We might visit 43.25 before it bounces back to 43.50/75. I think it will be (caused by) the combination of a natural correction and a bit of RBI intervention," he added, referring to the Reserve Bank of India that is suspected of having sold rupees regularly since November in a bid to preserve exporters' competitiveness.  

The overnight cash rate <INROND=>, the rate at which banks lend funds to each other, jumped to 70 percent on Wednesday -- which bankers said was the highest since 1996, when the rate topped 100 percent.  

Cash in the banking system shrunk sharply due to quarterly tax payments estimated at 300 billion rupees ($6.9 billion).  

In addition, the central bank this month resumed bond sales under the market stabilisation scheme (MSS) after a gap of 18 months.  

Sentiment was also lifted after the benchmark share index <.BSESN> rose 1.9 percent on Wednesday, raising expectations of further capital inflows.  

Still, traders were nervous the central bank may intervene aggressively to prevent the rupee from appreciating further and boost funds in a cash-starved system.  

Data shows the central bank purchased close to $8 billion in the three months to January, and traders widely believe it has played an active role in capping the rupee in February.  

"...the risks are high that the RBI will intervene more aggressively in the foreign exchange market to provide more liquidity and interrupt short dollar/long rupee carry plays that generate 2 bps a day carry," JP Morgan said in a note on Wednesday.

Traders and analysts said the rupee's sharp gains may be temporary, and it could weaken as cash rates ease.

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Indian government bonds fell for the second straight session Friday as higher-than-expected inflation data sparked fears of more monetary tightening by the central bank, market participants said.  

A squeeze in banking system cash due to quarterly advance tax payments by Indian companies is also likely to push bond prices down in the coming sessions, they said.  

The benchmark 8.07% 2017 bond ended at INR100.35, down from INR100.54 on Thursday's close in thin trade.  

"Trading volumes have dried up and there is no activity in the market now because of the lack of clarity on direction," said a foreign bank dealer.  

Wholesale price index-based inflation for the week ended March 3 rose to 6.46% on the year from 6.10% in the previous week. A Dow Jones Newswires poll had forecast inflation at 6.27%.  

The higher-than-expected inflation data prompted Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram to say that the government would continue to take steps to check rising prices.  

"Let me assure the honorable members that government has taken, and will take, fiscal, monetary and supply side measures to moderate inflation," Chidambaram told the lower house of Parliament.  

But despite the efforts by the government and the central bank, headline inflation is likely to remain above 6.0% in the remaining part of the current fiscal year, said D. K. Joshi, principal economist at rating agency Crisil.  

"There will be some moderation (in the inflation rate), but it will be after April," said Joshi.  

In the currency market, the Indian rupee rose to a three-week high against the dollar as banks sold the greenback to generate cash in the face of the tightening liquidity.  

The dollar ended Friday's session at INR44.11, as against INR44.20 late Thursday.  

"The call money rate has shot up and that makes holding long dollar positions costlier," said one foreign bank dealer.  

Traders said the Reserve Bank of India is likely to intervene in the market in the coming sessions to stem further appreciation of the rupee.  

The call money rate nearly doubled to 10% Friday from Thursday, reflecting strong demand for funds in the market.

title: TRADE IDEA-HSBC says buy Indian rupee
text:
MUMBAI, March 12 (Reuters) - HSBC has recommended to buy the Indian rupee <INR=IN> as a jump in foreign direct investment (FDI) in recent months has calmed concerns of funding the country's widening trade deficit.  

 The rupee could rise to 43 per dollar by the end of 2007, a level it hasn't tested since late-July 2005, the London-based investment bank said in a note to clients on Friday.  

 The rupee was trading at 44.24 to the dollar on Monday.  

 India's current account deficit of about $7 billion in July-September was offset by inflows of $9 billion, mainly from FDI and remittances by non-resident Indians.  

 FDI inflows are expected at a record $12 billion in the current fiscal year ending on March 31, against $5.7 billion a year earlier.  

 HSBC said India's central bank, which often intervenes to rein in the rupee to ensure exports are not hurt by a stronger currency, may be forced to let the unit gain.  

 "It is difficult for a central bank to resist currency strength and also face an overwhelming case for tighter monetary policy," it said.  

 India's foreign exchange reserves climbed to a record $195 billion on March 2, up $14.6 billion from a month earlier, helped largely by suspected central bank purchases of dollars to cool the rupee.  

 The intervention, which involves selling rupees, has partly contributed to a spike in annual inflation to above 6 percent against a central bank target of 5-5.5 percent by end-March.  

 HSBC also said the rupee was not vulnerable to equity outflows as a recent stock market correction showed.  

 "Indian rupee is not as highly leveraged to the equity market as the consensus believes. During the recent period, the rupee depreciated by just 1.1 percent and emerged again as one of the best performing emerging market currencies," it said.

MUMBAI, Feb 19 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee hovered near a recent 16-month high on Monday as banks sold dollars to meet funding requirements after a monetary tightening measure took effect over the weekend.  

Only the prospect of central bank intervention kept a lid on the rupee's gains, traders said.  

At 10:10 a.m. (0440 GMT), the partially convertible rupee was at 44.07/08 per dollar, inching toward a 16-month high of 44.03 hit earlier this month, and up from the previous close of 44.10/11. The U.S. and many Asian markets are shut on Monday for local holidays.

The rupee also found support after the dollar stayed at a near six-week low against the euro and a five-week trough versus the yen after a U.S. government report showed on Friday the pace of home construction fell 14.3 percent in January, fuelling expectations for a Fed interest rate cut.  

Reports of two bomb blasts that killed at least 64 passengers aboard a train travelling between New Delhi and the northern Pakistani city of Lahore around midnight on Sunday, had little impact on the rupee, traders said.  

But sentiment for the Indian unit was tempered by the spectre of central bank intervention. The Reserve Bank of India has consistently bought dollars to ensure exports are not hurt by a strengthening domestic currency.  

It bought about $5 billion dollars in November and December, official data showed, and the market widely believes the central bank has played an active role in the currency market this year.

title: ANALYSIS-Frisky rupee sets monetary challenge to India c.bank
text:
MUMBAI, Jan 5 (Reuters) - India's central bank is trying to drain the banking system of excess cash to fight inflationary pressures, but the squeeze on funds has helped send the currency to an 11-month high.  

Now the market is wondering how much more rupee strength the central bank will tolerate, especially as intervention would involve selling rupees into the market -- thereby adding more of that extra cash it is trying to drain out.  

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) says that when it intervenes, it does so to calm rupee volatility.  

It steps in when foreign investment flows into the stock market, for example, drive the currency up more rapidly than it likes, as when it was suspected of toppling the rupee from what was an eight-month peak of 44.35 per dollar <INR=IN> in November.  

However, the currency touched 44.1250 on Jan. 2 with no sign from the monetary authority and is now holding at about 44.30.  

"The rupee has been an underperformer vis-a-vis other Asian currencies," said Gaurav Kapur, senior economist with ABN Amro Bank.  

"You cannot stop the rupee's appreciation, given the kind of capital inflows we are witnessing. Chances of intervention are lower."  

Over 2005 and 2006, net foreign buying of Indian equities reached almost $19 billion.  

The RBI, concerned about 30 percent annual growth in credit fuelling inflationary pressures, raised its key lending rate four times last year and is now staging a two-part increase in the amount of cash banks are required to deposit with it.  

The first leg took place on Dec. 23 and the second is on Saturday. After the first one, the interbank overnight rate spiked 11 percentage points to 21 percent, the highest in nine years, although it has now come back to about 7.50 percent.  

As the rate went up, banks sold or swapped dollars to generate rupee funds, pushing the rupee higher.  

HANDS OFF, PERHAPS  

The RBI does not have an official target for the rupee, which has oscillated between 47.00 and 43.00 for the past three years.  

Analysts say the central bank gets uncomfortable when it estimates the rupee is overvalued by 8 to 10 percent on a trade-weighted basis -- especially when there is a rapid move to that level -- and that it is more prone to intervene to check gains than curb losses.  

Some say that for now, though, with annual inflation near 5.5 percent, the central bank will focus more on interest rates than currency management and may tolerate greater rupee strength.  

"There seems to be some concern at the central bank about overheating in the economy, particularly in certain sectors. Interest rate management, under such a scenario, is likely to take precedence over curbing rupee gains," Kapur said.  

"Technically, the next level to watch for is 44.02, with resistance at 44.65," he said.  

Some analysts see the central bank letting the rupee gain, albeit gradually, with short bouts of intervention to check spikes.  

"We see the rupee at 44 per dollar by the end of March," said Sailesh Jha, senior economist with Credit Suisse in Singapore.  

Others say the strength of capital flows into the stock market plus remittances and foreign direct investment may decide the extent of the central bank's tolerance.  

"They may not be comfortable with the sharp rise in the rupee. They may feel the need to intervene to maintain the export competitiveness," said Yes Bank chief economist Shubhada Rao.  

Others say cash conditions will not be so flush over the coming month. The increase in the cash reserve requirement has taken funds out of the system, says JPMorgan, so the central bank has more leeway to intervene on the currency without worrying unduly about the need to sterilise the rupee flows that result.  

If the rupee continues to appreciate in trade-weighted terms, as shown in JPMorgan's real effective exchange rate <JPMREER>, which suggests it is moving out of the comfort zone, then the RBI may cap it.  

"The RBI retains this option. They would look at how strong inflows are and how strong the pressure on the rupee to appreciate," JPMorgan economist Siddharth Mathur said.

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee rose to its highest closing level against the dollar in over nine months Tuesday, fueled by robust foreign fund flows, but the market is cautious about its further gains, traders said.  

The market will be wary about the Reserve Bank of India, or RBI, intervening to support the dollar in the coming sessions, they said.  

The dollar ended at INR44.45, its lowest finish since March 21, as against INR44.56 on Friday's close.  

"I think the RBI is likely to intervene if the dollar-rupee tries to breach INR44.35 tomorrow," said a dealer with a local bank, who expects the dollar to trade in INR44.35-INR44.50 range Wednesday.  

"Generally the market seems to be bullish on the rupee because foreign fund flows to the stock market should continue at good levels," the dealer said.  

Foreign fund flows into India's stock market have been a major factor that pushed up the rupee in recent times, prompting the central bank to reportedly intervene in the market on a number of occasions.  

The Bombay Stock Exchange's 30-stock Sensitive Index rose 236.60 points, or 1.8% to 13,708.34 Tuesday.  

In the government bond market, prices fell Tuesday amid meager volumes.  

The benchmark 7.59% 2016 bond ended at INR99.74 as compared with INR99.95 on Friday's close.  

Bond market participants said the market is unlikely to recover during this week as liquidity conditions remain tight with banks' cash reserve ratio, or CRR, going up by 25 basis points to 5.25% from Dec. 23.  

The CRR will further rise by another 25 basis points from Jan. 6.  

The RBI raised the CRR, which is the proportion of time and demand deposits a bank must hold in cash with the central bank, to absorb about INR135 billion from the banking system.  

"The bond market doesn't have many cues now. The volumes will stay thin during this week," said a dealer with a local bank.  

Some players expect the current liquidity squeeze to ease by mid-January.  

According to Anindya Dutta, Treasurer at Calyon Bank, more funds are expected to flow into the banking system over the next couple of weeks through government's interest payments to provident funds and likely intervention of the RBI in the foreign exchange market to support the dollar.  

Dutta said he expects the bond market to revive once the liquidity conditions improve.  

"I expect the 10-year bond yield to touch 7.45% by mid-January (from the current 7.62%)," he said.

MUMBAI, Dec 11 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee fell to a 3-week closing low on Monday as dealers said the central bank had continued to intervene in the currency market even after its surprise move last week to tighten monetary policy.  

A 2.9 percent drop in the stock market did not help sentiment either, although traders expect steady foreign flows due to an equity offering by Cairns India and Oracle Corp's bid to lift its stake in Indian banking software provider i-flex solutions Ltd to provide support in the next few weeks.  

The rupee <INR=IN> ended around 0.2 percent lower at 44.8350/8450 per dollar, its lowest close since Nov. 21 when it finished at 44.86/87.  

But it is still nearly 5 percent above a three-year low of 47.04 hit on July 19, with its gains helped by foreign inflows, the bulk of which have been mopped up by the central bank.  

"One thought that after the central bank's move to tighten policy to fight inflation, the authorities would ease their grip on the rupee," said a chief dealer at a company.  

"But no such thing happened. They in fact drove the rupee down to around 44.85 from 44.78 in thin trade towards close."  

When the Reserve Bank of India intervenes to buys dollars, normally through state-run banks, it pumps rupees into the banking system. This can add to inflation pressures and puts upward pressure on money supply growth.  

After markets had shut on Friday, the RBI announced a two-stage increase in the cash reserve ratio, that sets how much banks must keep with it, by 50 basis points to 5.50 percent.  

"The RBI's reluctance to let the rupee appreciate substantially in the light of strong capital inflows will only make conducting monetary policy more challenging for the central bank," Rajeev Malik, senior economist at JP Morgan, Singapore wrote in a note.

MUMBAI, Nov 20 (Reuters) - India's central bank did not intervene in the currency market in September, data released on Monday showed, although dealers say it has been intervening steadily in November to curb rupee strength.

Dealers say the central bank has been intervening this month to drive the rupee <INR=IN> down from a eight-month high of 44.35 hit on Nov. 10. It was trading at 45.01/02 at 1100 GMT.  

India's foreign exchange reserves rose to a record $168.284 billion on Nov. 10 from $167.116 billion a week earlier, and analysts said the gain was mainly due to the central bank buying dollars for rupees.  

It last intervened in May when it bought $504 million, following on from $4.31 billion worth of intervention in April, when it was acting to maintain India's export competitiveness.

text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 16 (Reuters) - The South Korean won recovered some ground it had lost to the dollar over the past couple of days, helped by a large bout of dollar inflows on Thursday for local businesses and by the absence of central bank intervention.  

 Other Asian currencies also stabilised as markets waited for U.S. consumer prices data to give them a sense of direction for Federal Reserve policy.  

 The Japanese yen <JPY=> rallied briefly to 117.75 per dollar on a report that China's central bank had been buying yen for its reserves but soon gave up those gains, pushing the dollar to levels near 118 yen traded overnight after the Fed said in minutes of its October meeting that reducing inflation was its biggest concern.  

 Asian currencies, many of which had hit multi-month and multi-year highs at the start of this week, slipped in early deals but stabilised subsequently.  

 After hitting a six-month high of 927.8 per dollar on Monday, the won <KRW=> had gradually lost ground this week, falling earlier on Thursday to around 944 per dollar, its weakest level since late October.  

 However, by 0730 GMT, it had rebounded slightly to be quoted around 937 per dollar.  

 "The upside in dollar/won changed to downside as the yen rose and offshore markets sold dollars," said Yun Jin Ko, a dealer with Kookmin Bank in Seoul.  

 "Exporters of ships and electronics joined in," she said.  

 Mirza Baig, Deutsche Bank's currency strategist said a surge in export orders for Korean manufacturers of ships, oil platforms and power plants had created a steady stream of strong foreign exchange earnings, putting pressure on the won to appreciate.  

 "The absence of the Bank of Korea makes it easier for spot to fall," he said.  

 Fearing rapid and volatile appreciation in their currencies, central banks in South Korea, Thailand and India are suspected of having sold their currencies this week. Traders estimated Bank of Korea had bought about $1.5 billion on Monday and Tuesday.  

 Baig said only a few exporters seemed to be testing the Bank of Korea's tolerance.  

  "Not all segments of the market play this cat and mouse game with BOK. Exporters generally just want a good level to sell," he said.  

 WON, RUPEE CAPPED?  

 Gerrard Katz, head of currency trading for North Asia at Standard Chartered Bank, said this stream of export earnings will put a floor under the won, despite the Bank of Korea's attempts to rein it in.  

 "Dollar/won will find 945-950 tough resistance. I heard a lot of exporters forecast a 900-940 range for next year so they will be (dollar) sellers," he said.  

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell to 1.5611 per U.S. dollar in early trades, having gradually come off the 9-year highs around 1.5545 hit this week. It then pared back to be traded at 1.5575/80.  

 The Indian rupee <INR=IN> rallied nearly half a percent from Wednesday's close near 45.34 per dollar.  

 JPMorgan Chase said in a note to clients the risk of intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) remained high with the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted level now estimated to be at the top end of the MAS's secret policy band.

text:

MUMBAI, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee rose to its strongest in nearly five months on Friday, underpinned by cheaper oil and propelled by foreign fund inflows which sent stocks soaring to record highs.  

The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> ended at 45.41/42 a dollar after touching its highest since May 19 at 45.40, 0.4 percent firmer than its previous close of 45.61/62.  

"The mood is very, very, very bullish as foreign fund inflows are robust. We may see the rupee establish a (higher) trading band of 45.25-45.55 in the near term," said V. Rajagopal, head of currency trading at Kotak Mahindra Bank.  

The rupee has gained 3.6 percent from a three-year low of 47.04 set in July, with the pace escalating in the past two months on a pick-up in foreign fund inflows.  

But some say the central bank may step in to slow the rise and protect export competitiveness.  

"The rupee's gains have been unmatched by other currencies and that may spur the Reserve Bank of India to intervene to moderate the sharp rise," said Kotak's Rajagopal.  

According to a JP Morgan six-currency real effective exchange rate <JPMREER>, the rupee is overvalued at nearly 7 percent, more than the 5 percent seen a month ago.  

CAPITAL INJECTION  

Recovering from a savage correction in May, the stock market ended at a record on Friday, driven by strong corporate earnings which have boosted hopes foreign funds will increase their investment in India.  

The benchmark 30-share index <.BSESN> has risen about 43 percent from a June low, with foreign funds pumping more than $2.4 billion into Indian equities since August, compared with net investments of $2.8 billion in the first seven months of 2006.  

Big capital inflows have helped fund the widening current account deficit, which for the fiscal year 2005/06 was the highest since the country opened its economy in 1991. It doubled to $10.61 billion from $5.4 billion a year earlier.  

"The capital inflows have been responsible for the rupee rally. It is also benefiting from retreating oil prices, a positive for both fiscal finances and its balance of payments," DBS said in a recent note.  

DBS expects the rupee to rise to 45 per dollar by the end of 2006.  

CHEAPER OIL TO FUEL RISE?  

Lower oil prices help in reducing India's oil import bill and relieve pressure on the current account deficit. The country imports more than two-thirds of its oil.  

"With oil prices having fallen nearly 25 percent over the past eight weeks, the resulting shift in the demand/supply balance in the currency markets is significantly bullish," said JP Morgan in a recent note. It estimates dollar demand from oil importers alone contributes nearly $1 billion per week to overall dollar demand.  

Oil <CLc1> was trading around $58 a barrel, more than 25 percent down from a July peak of $78.40 per barrel.  

Still, some believe the rupee rally may be on its last legs with oil stabilising and as local stocks become expensive.  

"With the year-end nearing, fund managers may take some money off the table, and with oil prices likely stabilising around these levels, the rupee may be nearing the end of the rally," said Shahab Jalinoos, foreign exchange strategist at ABN Amro Singapore.

title: UPDATE: India Rupee Breaks Key Level, May Slip Further
text:
(Updates with comments from the finance minister and an economist.)  

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee broke key psychological levels and fell to a 37-month low of INR47 to the dollar Wednesday on the back of soaring oil prices and a weak stock market, which triggered expectations of continued capital outflows.  

The U.S. currency's broad gains overseas also weighed on the local unit, market participants said.  

Although several analysts believe the currency could extend losses in the coming weeks, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said the local unit is a stable currency in terms of its trade-weighted exchange rate and hinted it may even appreciate depending on market conditions.  

At 0935 GMT, the dollar was trading at INR46.96, off its INR47.02 peak tested earlier in the session, a level last hit on June 4, 2003. It had closed at INR46.70 Tuesday.  

"In terms of the real effective exchange rate (or REER), the value of the rupee is stable," Chidambaram told reporters.  

The rupee's real effective exchange rate, or its value in trade-weighted terms, is around 103, indicating overvaluation of around 3%. The rupee is considered fairly valued when its REER is 100.  

Chidambaram said the movement of the rupee also depends on demand and supply conditions in the market.  

"It is quite likely that the rupee might also appreciate depending on the market conditions," he said.  


 
   Analysts Disagree 
   

Several market-watchers believe the rupee is likely to extend losses in the coming weeks as slowing stock-related capital inflows leave it vulnerable to a further rise in global oil prices and a widening current account deficit.  

Arbitraging by banks between the rupee market and the non-deliverable forward market overseas, and the dollar's broad rally against other major currencies are also weighing the rupee down, analysts said.  

"There are a host of factors that are playing out right now," said Ashit Parekh, head of foreign exchange trading at IndusInd Bank. "There's high global oil, the stock market fall, Middle East tensions, falling Asian currencies and, of course, the current account deficit."  

Parekh expects the local unit to keep weakening, albeit at a slightly slower pace going forward, with the dollar possibly testing INR47.05-INR47.10 over the next couple of weeks and even breaching a multiyear high of INR47.50 over the next few months.  

The rupee has fallen around 2% against the dollar so far in July alone and more than 5% since the beginning of the current fiscal year in April, mainly on the back of a worsening current account deficit and a weak stock market.  

India's current account deficit in the fiscal year ended March 31 nearly doubled to $10.61 billion from $5.40 billion in the previous year.  

Economists expect the current account shortfall to widen further as India's strong economic growth fuels accelerated import growth and high global oil prices inflate the country's oil import bill.  

Investment flows into the local stock market have also slowed in recent weeks. Foreigners have halved their holdings in Indian equities to about $2.6 billion so far this year, compared with nearly $4 billion in portfolio inflows during the January-March quarter alone.  

No Major RBI Intervention So Far  

Despite the rupee's sharp decline, traders say there hasn't been any significant intervention in the market by the Reserve Bank of India so far.  

"While the RBI may be allowing the rupee to find its own level from the (current account) deficit point of view, it's possible they could come in to smooth market fluctuations around current levels if the market remains volatile," said a senior dealer at a local bank.  

Some analysts believe the Reserve Bank of India will tolerate a gradual rupee decline in the coming months, as that could help correct the unit's trade-weighted overvaluation and make Indian exports more competitive in the global markets.  

"It (the rupee's fall) must be within the RBI's comfort zone, or else the central bank would have intervened. The RBI has enough muscle to correct (the fall) if they want to," said D.K. Joshi, principal economist at credit rating firm Crisil.  

The Indian central bank doesn't fix any target level or range for the rupee, but sometimes intervenes in the market to smooth market volatility or to prevent the currency from straying too far from fair valuation.

title: RPT-Indian cbank may keep rupee vigil post float -Mohan
text:
(Repeats story issued late on Saturday)  

 MUMBAI, June 3 (Reuters) - India's central bank is likely to continue its strict vigil over the currency market despite moving towards fuller rupee convertibility, one of its deputy governors said in a speech released on Saturday.  

 A committee appointed by the central bank started work last month to lay down a road map for a fuller float of the rupee, the biggest reform measure in more than a decade. It is expected to submit its report by July-end.  

 "Fuller capital account openness will lead to a confrontation with the impossible trinity of simultaneous attainment of independent monetary policy, open capital account, and managed exchange rate," Rakesh Mohan said in a speech organised by Stanford Center for International Development and Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research.  

 "Only two out of the three would be feasible," Mohan said. "With a more open capital account as a given' and if a choice is made of an anchor' role for monetary policy, exchange rate management will be affected," he said in the speech delivered on Friday.  

 Mohan said a freely floating exchange rate would threaten the independence of monetary policy adding that the impact of exchange rate changes on the real economy could be quite adverse for developing countries like India.  

 He said the more mature and well developed financial markets and economies could absorb the risk associated with exchange rate fluctuations with negligible spillover on the real activity due to greater access to high-end technology.  

 "On the other hand, for the majority of developing countries which specialise in labour-intensive and low and intermediate technology products, profit margins in the intensely competitive markets for these products are very thin and vulnerable to pricing power by large retail chains," he said.  

 "Consequently, exchange rate volatility has significant employment, output and distributional consequences. In this context, managing exchange rate volatility would continue to be an issue requiring attention."  

India's central bank usually intervenes through state-run banks in the foreign exchange market to contain excessive volatility and to maintain export competitiveness.  

 While the rupee is fully convertible on the current account, there are restrictions on free movement of capital.  

 Analysts in JP Morgan say the new committee is likely to link the move towards fuller convertibility to the lowering of the deficit, which a fiscal responsibility law aims to cut to 3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2008-2009.  

 India has progressed in cutting its stubbornly high fiscal deficit to 4.1 percent of GDP last year from 5.9 percent in 2002/03 and is expected at 3.8 percent this year.  

 WORRIED ABOUT FOREIGN BANKS  

 Mohan said fuller capital account convertibility will lead to a greater presence of foreign banks in India over time but a number of regulatory issues would arise.  

 India's banking sector is relatively closed to foreigners and foreign banks have to seek the central bank's permission if they want to pick up more than a 5 percent stake in banks.  

 Mohan said that the presence of large global banks would pose a huge challenge to smaller Indian banks.  

 He also said the attention of top management of foreign banks to operations in countries like India are low since developing countries do not contribute much to their overall business.  

 "Consequently, any market or regulatory transgressions committed in one country by such a bank, which may have a significant impact on banking or financial market of that country, is likely to have negligible impact on the bank's global operations," Mohan said.  

 He added that strong regulatory action against such global banks had negligible market or reputational impact.  

 "Hence there is inevitable tension between the benefits that such global conglomerates bring and some regulatory and market structure and competition issues that may arise."

title: RPT-Indian rupee fall seen adding to case for rate rise
text:
(Repeats story issued late on Thursday)  

 MUMBAI, June 1 (Reuters) - A rapid fall in India's rupee to a three-year low against the dollar <INR=IN> this week adds to pressure on the central bank to raise interest rates, analysts say.  

 The rupee's drop will raise import prices in local currency terms, fuelling inflation that is already being fired up by strong economic growth and a renewed surge in world oil prices.  

 After an emerging markets sell-off that sucked in the rupee, analysts say India's central bank is likely to intervene in the foreign exchange market to check any further sharp losses.  

 But selling dollars and soaking up rupees will put upward pressure on short-term market rates by reducing the supply of the local currency.  

 "If the kind of moves we have seen over the last couple of weeks build into a sustained negative environment, with central bank selling dollars, then the monetary policy will have to be suitably adjusted," said Sanjeet Singh, head of research at ICICI Securities.  

 The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> fell more than three percent in May to touch 46.57 on Wednesday, its lowest since June 2003, as foreign funds pulled money out of the stock market.  

 The three-year low came on the same day data showed the economy grew in January-March at a higher-than-expected annual rate of 9.3 percent, which analysts said cemented expectations for a quarter-point rise in rates when the central bank reviews policy on July 25.  

 India's benchmark short-term rate stands at 5.5 percent and was last raised in January. Since then the rupee has fallen around 5 percent against the dollar and some analysts see it dropping to 47.50 by December if foreign funds continue to see emerging markets as too risky.  

 The Reserve Bank of India left rates unchanged in April but said India could not be out of step with global developments like U.S. interest rates and crude oil prices.  

 RISING TRADE DEFICIT, INFLATION  

 India's annual inflation rate, based on wholesale prices and reported weekly, rose to 4.32 percent on May 13, its highest level since February.  

 Analysts say if an expected rise in domestic fuel prices is factored in, the inflation rate could rise to 5 percent by the end of September.  

 Economists say rising imports reflect the fast pace of the economy's growth but a weaker rupee makes oil imports costlier.  

 Oil is India's biggest import and analysts expect the rising oil bill and strong import demand to widen the trade gap to $59.1 billion in the year ending March 2007 from $55 billion last year.  

 With inflationary pressures building, the Reserve Bank of India is expected to continue raising rates after July, analysts said.  

 "The RBI is on a tightening trajectory and we forecast a further 25-50 basis points in rate hikes during FY07," said Ashish Agrawal, Merrill Lynch's fixed income analyst in Mumbai.  

 Robust foreign fund inflows into the stock market had been cushioning the rupee from the impact of a widening current account deficit, caused mainly by high oil prices.  

 Now that funds are leaving for less risky markets, the current account is under pressure, analysts said.  

 "The core problem is that (India's) current account deficit is funded by volatile capital," said Sanjay Mathur, regional economist with UBS Warburg in Singapore.  

 The current account, which covers trade and services, is estimated to have ended the 2005/06 fiscal year with a deficit equivalent to 3 percent of gross domestic product, a sharp expansion from a year-earlier 0.9 percent.  

 India's benchmark share index <.BSESN> has fallen roughly 20 percent from a record high of 12,671.11 on May 11 as foreign funds cut their investments.  

 Net foreign investment in stocks since the start of the year has dropped to about $2.4 billion from a peak of nearly $5 billion in early May.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rupee thumped again, others mixed
text:
SINGAPORE, May 31 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee dropped to a three-year low and the Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso fell on Wednesday as regional stock weakness renewed concerns about global risk aversion and a deeper sell-off in emerging markets.  

 In contrast, the Thai baht <THB=> and Singapore dollar <SGD=> edged higher, drawing support from a rally in the yen and news that China's central bank has reaffirmed its commitment to deepen foreign exchange reform to make the yuan more flexible.  

 Markets in Hong Kong and Taiwan were closed for a holiday, while South Korea was shut for local elections.  

 The Indian rupee <INR=IN> fell to a three-year low around 46.55 per dollar, but trimmed those losses after suspected central bank intervention and data that showed India's economy grew at a stronger-than-expected annual rate of 9.3 percent in the first quarter.  

 "The focus of weakness in Asian currencies is definitely on the rupee," said Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered.  

 "India has a large current account deficit and although the GDP numbers were better than expected, this will exacerbate the current account deficit."  

 And with some Asian equity markets sharply weaker on Wednesday, dealers said regional currencies were not yet immune to the global risk aversion that has dealt a blow to emerging markets this month.  

 A sharp sell-off on Wall Street on Tuesday helped push India stocks <.BSESN> down more than five percent. Equity markets in Indonesia <.JKSE> and Singapore <.STI> shed more than two percent each.  

 The rupiah <IDR=> eased about 0.9 percent from late Asia levels on Tuesday to 9,252 per dollar, while the peso <PHP=> weakened to 52.91 per dollar -- about 0.6 percent weaker than Tuesday's 1-1/2-week high around 52.58.  

 "Many players yesterday were trying to push dollar/peso through the 52.60 area and as that has failed to hold, we have seen short covering," said a trader in Manila.  

 Other emerging markets were also weak, with the Turkish lira <TRL=> at its lowest since April 2003 and the South African rand <ZAR=> sliding to a near 6-½   month low versus the dollar.  

 However, some Asian currencies were holding up well.  

 The baht <THB=> firmed to a 1-½   week peak at about 38 per dollar, finding support from China central bank comments on yuan flexibility raised expectations for further gains in the yuan <CNY=CFXS> and other Asian currencies.

title: State Bank India Chmn: INR/USD Movement Mkt Determined
text:
NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--The movement of the Indian rupee against the U.S. dollar is being determined by the market, not by intervention, and its recent slide has been driven by the forces of demand and supply, the chairman of the State Bank of India (500112.BY) said Tuesday.   

"We are doing our normal commercial operations. Dealers are taking positions," Arun Kumar Purwar told reporters when asked if the central bank had asked SBI to intervene.   

The rupee has slipped nearly 1.5% against the dollar over the past week on portfolio outflows and steady demand for the dollar from oil importers looking to fulfill month-end payment commitments. [ 30-05-06 0901GMT ]   

The Reserve Bank of India sometimes intervenes in the country's foreign exchange market via state-run banks to protect the country's trade competitiveness and keep the currency's volatility in check.   

Turning to the local stock markets, the chairman of the country's largest bank by assets said the Indian equity market was very attractive for buyers.   

"It's a good opportunity to buy. The fundamentals of the economy remain strong," he said.   

Local stocks have nose-dived in recent weeks, with the benchmark stock index tumbling more than 1,100 points since the beginning of this month, tracking the trend in global equity and commodity markets.   

The government expects the Indian economy to have grown a robust 8.1% during the last fiscal year that ended in March. It is expected to expand around 7.5%-8.0% during the current financial year.

MUMBAI, May 22 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee pulled off its 2006 low on Monday and erased nearly all its losses against the U.S. dollar on the back of suspected central bank intervention and a partial recovery in India's stock market.  

The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> ended at 45.55/57 to a dollar, off the day's low of 45.82, its weakest in 2006. It ended at 45.5550/5650 on Friday.  

Dealers said state-owned banks sold dollars, probably on behalf of the central bank, at various points in the day including below 45.60.  

"It seems that the central bank is alert about movement in the rupee related to the stock market. They are more comfortable if the swings are on account of demand-supply factors," said a dealer with a private bank.

The central bank said it was in touch with major settlement banks and stock exchanges to ensure that payment obligations on the bourses were met smoothly.  

"The central bank's statement soothed sentiments in the foreign exchange market to some extent," said a dealer with a foreign bank.

title: UPDATE 1-India cbank bought $8.15bln from  FX  market in March
text:
(Adds details, trader quote)  

 MUMBAI, May 19 (Reuters) - India's central bank said on Friday it had bought $8.15 billion from the foreign exchange market in March, which dealers said was to check gains in the overvalued rupee and pump liquidity into the banking system. The figures show the monetary authority stepped in for the second month in a row to rein in rupee appreciation and maintain India's export competitiveness, dealers said.  

 "We knew the central bank was intervening in March in a big way and the data just confirms that," said a trader at a private sector bank. "Liquidity in the banking system also came back during that month."  In February the central bank bought $2.61 billion of foreign exchange after staying away the preceding five months.  

 Data in the central bank's bulletin released on Friday showed it bought a net $8.14 billion in the financial year to March 2006, lower than $20.85 in the same period a year earlier.  

 In December, it sold $6.45 billion to meet the redemption of a foreign currency deposit scheme.  

 The recent dollar-buying spree by the central bank has taken its foreign exchange reserves to a record $162.41 billion, an addition of $21 billion in the past 12 months.  

 India is the fifth-largest holder of foreign exchange reserves in Asia after China, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea.  

 On Friday, the rupee headed back towards its lowest level this year as demand for dollars from oil importers and custodial banks compounded dollar gains on the global currency market.  

 Strong foreign fund inflows worth $4.2 billion -- a bulk of which have been absorbed by the central bank -- have helped support the rupee since the start of the year. But the Indian currency has weakened considerably this week, tracking falling stocks and other emerging markets.  

 At 2:45 p.m. (0915 GMT), the rupee was trading at 45.57/59, 1.2 percent down so far in the week and just off its 2006 low of 45.64 hit on Tuesday.

title: UPDATE: US, China, Japan Differ On Imbalances Fix
text:
HYDERABAD, India (Dow Jones)--Finance officials from the U.S., China and Japan agreed Thursday that global imbalances must be fixed, but they continued to disagree on the role that currencies should play in that adjustment.  

Their discussion during a seminar on the sidelines of the Asian Development Bank's annual meeting is the latest in a series of recent public comments that show policy makers around the globe are increasingly worried about the threat to the global economic outlook from these uneven trade and capital flows.  

"We are all on the same boat, no one will escape if this boat sinks," said Li Yong, China's vice finance minister. "Each and every nation should shoulder its own responsibility."  

U.S. Treasury Undersecretary Timothy Adams said during the seminar that China's currency policy is cautious and needs to move faster.  

But China said that a fall of 25% in the U.S. dollar against other major currencies could hurt China's structural adjustment and reform program, while Japan Finance Minister Sadakazu Tanigaki said a weaker dollar shouldn't be the focus of efforts to resolve the global imbalances.  

"Over emphasizing a realignment of exchange rates alone as a means to adjust imbalances could invite market speculation and deal a blow to the global financial market, thus adversely affecting the world economy," Tanigaki told the panel discussion, according to prepared text issued by Japan's Ministry of Finance.  

Tanigaki's comments show that despite the Group of Seven leading nations' call last month for emerging Asian currencies to appreciate versus the dollar, Japan remains wary that such a currency policy may overreach its intended aims.  

The Japanese finance minister said late Wednesday that the G7 call for greater currency flexibility wasn't a call for dollar weakness.  

U.S. Treasury's Adams said that impediments and distortions in financial markets need to be reduced to help adjust global economic imbalances.  

U.S. policymakers have repeatedly urged Beijing to allow the yuan to strengthen in order to reduce China's large trade surplus with the U.S. by making Chinese goods more expensive.  

But China's vice finance minister defended China's decision to gradually allow the yuan's value to rise and said government plans to increase domestic demand would help correct global imbalances.  

"The Chinese government has already started to apply a mix of policy measures including expanding domestic demand,...a floating exchange rate regime, and increasing exports so as to improve the balance of payments situation," said Li.  

China's trade surplus tripled in 2005, reaching a record $102 billion.  

"China has actually now joined the international community in maintaining global stability and growth," said Li.  

Economists have been pondering global imbalances for some time because when a country has large current account, trade and budget surpluses, it relies on excess savings from other parts of the world to finance its growth. On the other hand, countries with large surpluses are diverting their savings to other markets, in some cases depriving their own economies of much-needed investment.  


 
   India Doesn't Plan FX Policy Change 
   

Adams said it is neither likely nor desirable for global imbalances to be unwound quickly and was optimistic that imbalances can be addressed smoothly.  

Adams also conceded that the U.S. "needs to do more" by reducing its fiscal budget deficit.  

The Treasury official called on the International Monetary Fund for its assistance as well.  

"One way the IMF can help is to help our understanding of questions like why emerging Asian economies are exporting capital to the U.S.," he said. "No matter what we say, it's viewed through the prism of self interest, so the IMF can remove this in a way we can't."  

Tanigaki said he couldn't deny that greater flexibility for Asian currencies could play a role in reducing massive current account surpluses and deficits in many countries.  

But he said that to ensure that policy-makers and market forces adjust global imbalances smoothly, macroeconomic reforms should be the "main driver" of this process.  

China should transform itself into an economy led by consumer spending from one driven by "overinvestment, overproduction and brisk exports," he said.  

Other emerging Asian economies should also stimulate domestic demand, while oil producers should invest more in increasing capacity and diversifying their industrial base, Tanigaki said.  

The U.S. should continue to trim its fiscal budget deficits and European countries should pursue more structural reforms, he continued.  

China's vice minister of finance also said that a "relatively smooth" change in the U.S. dollar would help countries with their adjustment programs.  

Referring to China's exchange rate reform, Li said: "We try our best to (reform the exchange rate) as fast as we can."  

He said China's shift to a managed float of its currency, the yuan, "reflects China's willingness for further reforms of the exchange rate regime and cooperation with the international community."  

India's finance minister, P. Chidambaram, signaled that India wouldn't likely alter its currency policy despite the G7's recent call.  

"The exchange rate has been quite flexible in recent years, and this has been useful for us...I don't see any immediate change in the exchange rate policy," he said.  

India doesn't set a target level for its currency, but the central bank often intervenes in the market to smooth excess volatility.  

He said India also wouldn't likely significantly alter its economic policy even if the unwinding of global imbalances hurts the world economy.  

"In case the world economy slows down, India is likely to be less vulnerable as the India growth story is driven by domestic demand," he said.  

-By Stanley White and Rick Carew, Dow Jones Newswires; stanley.white@dowjones.com  

(Anil Varma contributed to this story.) [ 04-05-06 0909GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1-India to stay in c/a deficit in near future-finmin
text:
(Adds details, quotes)  

HYDERABAD, India, May 4 (Reuters) - India's current account position is likely to remain in deficit in the near future and the government will not change its exchange rate policy, Finance Minister Palaniappan Chidambaram said on Thursday.  

The shortfall in the October-December quarter stood at $3.85 billion, narrower than $5.06 billion deficit in the July-September quarter.  

"Going by the current indication and projections ... India's current account is likely to remain in deficit in the near future," Chidambaram said at the annual meeting of the Asian Development Bank in Hyderabad, southern India.  

The current account registered a $5.4 billion deficit -- or nearly 0.9 percent of gross domestic product -- for the full fiscal year ended in March 2005, the first shortfall in four years.  

Analysts estimate the deficit to have widened to about 3 percent of GDP in 2005/06 as the trade gap widened on the back of a rising oil bill and as imports outpaced exports in a robustly growing economy.  

"For India, current account surplus has been a minor source of reserve accretion," Chidambaram said. "In our case capital flows as opposed top current account surpluses played an increasingly important role in the accumulation of reserves."  

He said India's central bank will continue to intervene in the foreign exchange market without any fixed target for the rupee.  

"We feel that our approach aimed at exchange rate flexibility ... along with market intervention essentially to manage volatililty and ebb in capital flows seems to have served us well," he said.  

India's central bank intervenes through state-run banks to curb excessive swings in the currency market. Most of the recent inflows into the booming stock market have been absorbed by the central bank to rein in the rupee and keep exports competitive.  

Foreign funds have bought Indian equities worth more than $4 billion this year, adding to nearly $10.7 billion inflow last year.  

Data from India's central bank released last week showed foreign exchange reserves rose to a record $157.26 billion on April 21 from $155.196 billion a week earlier.

By Anirban Nag  

MUMBAI, April 28 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves jumped by more than $2 billion in the week to April 21, an increase which economists said reflected further central bank purchases of dollars to stem the rise in the rupee.  

Data from the central bank released on Friday showed the reserves rose to a record $157.262 billion from the previous record of $155.196 billion in the previous week, enough to cover nearly 14 months of imports.  

India is the fifth largest holder of foreign exchange reserves in Asia after China, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea.

Government-run State Bank, which has more than 200,000 staff at some 9,000 branches across the country, is the biggest player in India's foreign exchange and bond markets. The nationwide strike began on Monday.
