title: India Bonds End Down On Auction, Rate Worries; Rupee Up
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Indian government bonds ended on the back foot Monday amid fears that that fresh bond supply will pinch money-market liquidity over the coming sessions.  

Worries that the central bank will likely tighten interest rates again when it meets to decide policy April 18 also weighed on sentiment, dealers said.  

The liquid 8.07% bond maturing in 2017 ended down at INR103.68 from INR103.85 at the last close. Its yield closed up at 7.56% from 7.54%.  

"Players are just biding their time, before the auction announcement," said a local dealer. "Till then, bonds will move sideways. Liquidity is better, but we don't really know whether it will last."  

The federal government is set to borrow INR890 billion from the market during the first half of the current fiscal year, which began April 1, with INR180 billion planned for April alone. The first auctions are due before April 12.  

Money-market liquidity, which has been tight ever since a large capital outflow drained the system of nearly $7.3 billion in December, has improved in recent sessions on higher government spending and the Reserve Bank of India's currency market intervention.  

The RBI infused only INR11 billion via Monday's repurchase auction compared with a daily average of INR48 billion last week, reflecting an improvement in system funds.  

"But we need to wait and see if the improvement will be sustained. There are rate rise worries," said a dealer at a private sector bank.  

Some analysts expect the central bank to raise its benchmark short-term reverse repurchase rate when it meets later in April - for the fourth time in a year - given the threat of high global oil prices and its impact on local inflation.  

Although latest domestic inflation slipped to 4.06% in the week to March 18 from 4.28% a week prior, it is still well above a three-and-a-half year low of 3.01% in late August.  

In the market for overnight funds, the call money rate ended down at 6.00-6.25%, from 6.00%-6.50%, previously on signs of improved system cash.  

"Mutual funds seem to have received some inflows that they've been deploying in the collateralized borrowing and lending obligation market," said a trader at a primary dealing firm. "Government spending also appears to have increased."  

CBLO's are secured money-market instruments, usually quoted below call loans.  

In the currency market, the rupee ended higher against the dollar as soaring stocks fueled hopes of robust portfolio inflows.  

Foreign funds have pumped close to $4.0 billion into local shares so far this year following a record $10.3 billion in 2005, drawn by an economy poised to grow a robust 8.0% in the current fiscal year.  

The dollar ended down at INR44.5950 from INR44.6200 at the last close.  

Dollar forward rates ended lower on signs of improving money-market liquidity. The forward contract maturing in March 2007 ended lower at a premium of INR0.7850 from INR0.8100 previously.  

Interest rate swaps benchmarked to the Mumbai interbank forward offered rate, or MIFOR, rose, tracking higher U.S. Treasury yields, with the five-year swap closing up at 6.67%-6.72% from 6.65%-6.70% previously.

title: RPT-UPDATE 1-India's  FX  reserves at record $148.66 billion
text:
(Repeats story issued late on Friday)  (Adds c/a deficit, external debt, byline)  

 By Anirban Nag  

 MUMBAI, March 31 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves rose to a record $148.662 billion in the week ended March 24 as the central bank intervened aggressively in the currency market to absorb foreign capital inflows.  

 Analysts said part of the reason for the intervention might be to keep the rupee competitive on trade-weighted terms but it also served to pump rupees into the banking system to ensure sufficient liquidity.  

 This in turn would help smooth the passage of the government's 1.53 trillion rupee ($34 billion) borrowing plan in the new financial year which starts on April 1.  

 Steady intervention by the central bank has seen India's foreign exchange reserves jump by more than $5 billion in the first three weeks of March and traders say the total could touch $150 billion when data for this week is released.  

 The reserves are about $30 billion more than India's external debt, which stood at $119.2 billion at the end of the October-December quarter, data showed on Friday.  

India's central bank intervenes through state-run banks in the currency market and it has absorbed much of the capital flowing into the booming stock market. The main share index has risen 20 percent in 2006, helped by an influx of about $3.8 billion in foreign funds.  

 The rupee <INR=IN> ended Friday at 44.6125/6225 against the dollar, 0.18 percent higher than the previous close. It hit a 2-½   month low of 44.7425 on Tuesday, according to Reuters data.  

 Despite Friday's rise, the local currency, which analysts say is overvalued by nearly 8 percent on a trade-weighted basis, has lost 1.95 percent in the financial year to March 2006.  

 HEADING TOWARDS WIDER CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT  

 Other data released by the central bank showed India's current account deficit widened to $13.47 billion in the April-December period, up from a deficit of $5.93 billion in the same period at year ago.  

 India registered a $5.4 billion deficit for the whole of 2004/05 (April-March), the first shortfall in four years.  

 The widening gap was mainly due to a bigger trade deficit, which was $41.53 billion in the first nine months of the financial year to March 2006, against a $26.5 billion shortfall in the same period a year ago as imports outpaced exports in a fast growing economy.  

 Analysts say firm prices of crude oil also increased the trade deficit, which is estimated to end the financial year at a record $50 billion.  

 Robust inflows from invisibles, which include earnings from services such as software exports and transfers from non-resident Indians, helped offset some of the trade gap on the current account. Rising foreign investments have also cushioned the rupee from the impact of the widening trade shortfall.  

 "The strong corporate earnings growth over the past several quarters and expectations of continuance of (a) higher growth phase maintained foreign institutional investment interest in Indian markets," the central bank said in a statement.  

 India's current account deficit in the October-December quarter stood at $3.85 billion, narrower than a revised $5.06 billion deficit in the July-September quarter, it said.  

 The balance of payments deficit in the end of Oct-Dec was $4.73 billion, compared with a surplus of $5.26 billion in the July-September quarter.

title: India Mohan: RBI Aims To Keep "Short-Term Rate Corridor"
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of India plans to intervene more in the secondary bond market in the coming fiscal year as part of its monetary management operations, a senior central bank official said Monday.  

"From April 1, we will not participate in the primary market (for government bonds) but it means that we will certainly need to step up our operations in the secondary bond market," RBI Deputy Governor Rakesh Mohan told a finance conference.  

Under the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, which comes into effect April 1, the RBI won't directly purchase bonds from the government. [ 27-03-06 0654GMT ]  

Earlier this month, RBI officials said the central bank had intervened in the bond market in recent weeks to infuse funds into the cash-strapped local banking system. System liquidity has remained tight in recent months due to unusually strong growth in bank loans.  

Bank credit rose 32% in the past 12 months, the fastest in 35 years.  

Mohan said credit growth continuing at the current rate could raise liquidity management problems for the banking system, but added that the central bank has enough policy instruments to manage the situation.  

Apart from intervening in the bond market, the central bank has also been buying foreign exchange, redeeming securities previously sold under the so-called Market Stabilization Scheme and lending via repurchase auctions to help ease the liquidity situation.  

Mohan said the inflow of foreign capital would remain an important factor in the central bank's liquidity management operations, and added that "unsterilized" inflows could fuel inflation and cause currency market volatility.  

The central bank has, in the past, sterilized excessive capital inflows by buying foreign exchange from the currency market and then absorbing the cash pumped into the system in the process by selling bonds.  

Turning to interest rates, Mohan said the central bank's recent monetary operations haven't yet had a significant impact on long-term interest rates in the country. The RBI steps, however, have had some impact on short-term rates such as treasury bill yields, he added.  

The RBI aims to maintain the "corridor" or spread between its two short-term interest rates, the 5.5% reverse repurchase rate and the 6.5% repurchase rate, at the current 100 basis points.  

Separately, Mohan said international oil prices are widely expected to remain high. The RBI has raised policy-setting reverse repurchase rate by 100 basis points since October 2004 to fight the threat of inflation raised by high global oil prices.

title: RPT-India cbank wants call money in rate corridor
text:
(Repeat of Saturday story for local subscribers)  

 MUMBAI, March 18 (Reuters) - India's central bank wants overnight interbank call money rates to stay in the corridor between the repo and the reverse repo rates and policy instruments need to be fine-tuned to ensure that, it said in a report on Saturday.  

 The reverse repo rate, or the rate at which the central bank absorbs funds from the market, is at 5.5 percent and the repo rate, at which it pumps funds into the banking system, is at 6.5 percent.  

 The Reserve Bank of India said in a Report on Currency and Finance on Saturday that opening up of the economy and management of liquidity due to strong capital flows were posing a challenge in the medium term.  

 "As there is a trade-off between the excessive volatility in financial markets, exchange rates and interest rates which are likely to result in erosion in the competitiveness of the economy on the one hand, and financial cost of sterilisation on the other, the Reserve Bank has to properly balance its sterilisation operations," the report said.  

 Sterilisation operations had implications for the stability of short-term money market rates which called for fine-tuning of policy instruments "so as to keep call money rates range bound (within the corridor of the repo and reverse repo rates)," it said.  

 Overnight interbank funding costs rose to a 3-½   year high of 8 percent in January due to a redemption of India Millennium Deposits in late December, a build-up of cash balances by the government with the central bank and sustained credit growth.  

 Overnight call money has since eased to around 6.5-6.75 percent on increased government spending and after central bankintervention in the foreign exchange market, in which it buys dollars and sells rupees, led to some cash surpluses with banks.  

 The RBI intervenes in the foreign exchange market through state-run banks. As it buys dollars to absorb the foreign capital inflows it releases rupees to the banking system.  

 These rupees, which could fuel inflation, are then absorbed or "sterilised" by the central bank by issuing market stabilisation securities, the interest on which is borne by the government.  

 Foreign funds have pumped more than $3.2 billion into the stock market since the start of the year, after putting in a record $10.7 billion in 2005.  

 The inflows so far this year have helped the rupee rise nearly 1.4 percent against the dollar but traders say the central bank has been intervening to keep it down.

title: India Fin Min: On Path For Sustained 8% Growth
text:
NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--India's Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said Friday that the country may soon be able to sustain an annual economic growth rate of 8% on the back of higher savings and investment rates.  

"We are on the road that will take us to sustained 8% growth and also give us the capability for 10% growth," Chidambaram said, addressing a Indo-U.S. seminar on economic cooperation.  

The Indian economy is expected to grow 8.l% in the current fiscal year. [ 03-03-06 0515GMT ]  

Chidambaram said his ministry hopes to see the investment rate increase to 36% of gross domestic product from the current 30%, while it is aiming for the savings rate to rise to 30% of GDP from the current 29%.  

The minister didn't specify a timeframe for these targets.  

"We need investments. The federal budget for the next financial year has given increased attention to infrastructure sectors like power, roads, and the oil sector," Chidambaram said.  

He said financial sectors like insurance, pension funds and banking are likely to see more reform by the year 2009.  

"We are committed to reforms, but it will be at our own pace," he said.  

Foreign companies are pushing the Indian government to allow greater foreign investment in the financial sector, although such moves face strong opposition from the current Congress Party-led government's communist allies.  

On insurance, Chidambaram said that 26% cap on foreign direct investment shouldn't pose an obstacle for new companies entering India, but added that the restriction hurts plans of foreign companies already in India and seeking to expand.  

"We have to be patient....We are discussing with our allies. I am confident of persuading them," he said, in reference to efforts to pass an amendment to the insurance law, increasing the FDI cap to 49%.  

Chidambaram also said India will require some more time before it can open up full capital-account convertibility.  

"There are certain parameters (for achieving full capital-account convertibility) like the fiscal deficit, foreign exchange reserves, inflation and non-performing assets of banks....We have come a long way, but there is still some way to go," he said.  

India currently follows partial capital-account convertibility, with the rupee kept under a managed float by the central bank.  

Though the government and the central bank say that the Indian currency's value is determined by the market, the Reserve Bank of India intervenes in case of excessive volatility.

title: FOCUS: Indian Bonds In Doldrums As Govt Soaks Up Liquidity
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Indian government bonds will likely remain stuck in the doldrums for the next few months, as official steps to drain excess liquidity from the financial system have left local banks with less cash to chase prices higher.   

Concerns that rising oil prices may lift wholesale price inflation from around five-year lows now could also take wind out of the sails of the bond market, analysts say.   

"There is little potential for a sizable rally," said Vikas Agarwal, fixed income and forex strategist at JPMorgan Chase Bank. "Tight liquidity will most likely restrain the market's performance. It is likely to remain lackluster."   

Bond prices have been trading in a narrow range in thin volumes for the past several weeks, as investors wait for clearer signals on the outlook for liquidity and inflation. The steady trading follows a mild rally last month, when prices got a boost from banks putting extra cash into the bond market.   

At 0915GMT Monday, the benchmark 10-year government bond yield was at 7.88%.   

Many analysts expect the benchmark yield to stay between 7.75%-7.95% until March 31, when the current fiscal year ends.   

Banks' surplus cash position is a crucial factor for the direction of the Indian government bond market as banks hold over 60% of the INR12.3 trillion in outstanding government bonds. Rules require lenders to keep 25% of their deposits in government bonds, gold or cash as reserves known as the statutory liquidity ratio.   

For months, liquidity had grown rapidly. Much of it was a byproduct of foreign exchange intervention by the Reserve Bank of India, which was fighting a rise in the rupee. The RBI's coffers swelled by $52 billion in the nine months through September, with the bulk of the rupee it sold ending up with local banks.   

But the tide has changed. The RBI has been increasing efforts to soak up some of that liquidity out of concern it could fuel inflationary pressures.   

Excess cash in the system fell drastically after the RBI drained INR160 billion by raising the cash reserve ratio - the share of deposits banks must keep with the central bank in cash - by 50 basis points to 7.50% from Nov. 10. Regular debt sales by the government and sterilization bond issues by the RBI have also absorbed sizable amounts of banks' surplus cash.   

Analysts say the RBI could ratchet up the reserve requirement even further in coming months, given its stated intention to keep liquidity in a check.   

"Right now, the RBI's attempt is to pre-empt excess liquidity and moderate inflationary expectations," said Mahendra Jajoo, Senior Vice President at  ABN Amro Asset Management (India) Ltd.   

Jajoo said the RBI may hike the reserve ratio again before the end of March.   

Foreign Fund Inflows Ease   

A reduction in foreign money flowing into India may also lead to less liquidity entering the banking system.   

India's stock market recently has wavered along with other markets on fears of a global rout driven by the U.S. subprime mortgage crisis, with some foreign investors starting to pull some money out.   

The latest data from Securities and Exchange Board of India show foreign investors have sold a net of $1.10 billion worth Indian stocks so far in November, compared with net purchases of $5.07 billion in October, when the benchmark Sensex crossed 20,000 points for the first time.   

The Sensex was at 19,282.07 points Monday afternoon.   

Recent curbs on foreign fund inflows into local stocks, such as a ban on the issue of participatory notes with derivatives as underlying assets, are also expected to slow the flow of overseas money into India.   

Such developments will likely ease upward pressure on the rupee, thereby minimizing the need for the central bank to intervene in the market. The result: less rupee hitting into the system.   

"The stock market is now consolidating and upward pressure on the rupee is not much there," said Ashish Nigam, head of fixed income at DBS Cholamandalam AMC Limited.   

What's more, advance tax payments by companies by mid-December will also strain banks' cash position again, Nigam said. Indian companies are expected to withdraw INR350 billion to INR400 billion from banks to pay their quarterly advance taxes, he said.   

Hawkish RBI Would Weigh On Bonds   

Some analysts say the bond market could still fare all right.   

They point to demand from insurance companies and employees' provident funds for long-tenure bonds as one factor that could breathe some life into the otherwise dull bond market.   

Indian rules require life insurers to invest 25% of their assets in government bonds while provident funds must keep 40% of their assets in such securities.   

Improvement in finances could mean the federal government may borrow lower than its projected INR590 billion from the market during the second half of the current fiscal year, which will likely reduce the supply of bonds.   

"I won't be surprised if the government doesn't borrow the full amount," said ABN Amro's Jajoo.   

Still, most analysts say the balance of forces points to a steady bond market for now.   

Indian banks don't need to boost their holdings of bonds in their reserves to meet statutory liquidity ratio requirements.  JPMorgan's Agarwal reckons banks already hold around 30% of their reserves in bonds compared with the mandated 25%.   

"The SLR position is still comfortable and there is little urgency on the part of banks to buy bonds to meet their requirements. So that factor is more or less relegated to the background now," says Agarwal.   

Also, while inflation has eased to its lowest level in five years at just 3.01% in the week ended Nov. 10, lingering concerns the central bank may take steps to keep inflationary pressures at bay could also keep bond prices in check.   

India's central bank is widely expected to hold rates steady at least until end of March after a string of rate hikes that began three years ago quelled price pressures.   

But if oil makes a run at $100 a barrel and the government decides to raise local fuel prices in order to pass some of the higher cost along to consumers, the RBI may stick to a tightening bias.   

"One thing is very clear: times aren't going to be easy" for bonds, said Ritesh Jain, head of fixed income at Kotak Mahindra Asset Management Company.

NEW DELHI, Nov 22 (Reuters) - India's central bank has been actively intervening in the currency market and will use all instruments to maintain price stability and manage liquidity, its deputy governor said on Thursday.   

"We have a managed float, but we do intervene in the market actively," Rakesh Mohan told a business gathering.   

The Reserve Bank of India bought almost $52 billion in the first nine months of 2007 to curb rupee gains against the dollar.   

The local unit has risen about 12 percent this year but eased on Thursday to close at 39.53/54 per dollar, slipping from the previous day's 39.390/395.   

Earlier this month, it hit 39.16, its strongest in nearly 10 years, but was pushed lower by central bank dollar purchases.   

Analysts said capital inflows into Asia's third-largest economy would continue to be robust in coming months, and this would keep the rupee <INR=IN> under pressure.   

"In view of large capital inflows, we had to use the instrument of cash reserve ratio (CRR)," Mohan later told reporters. "We are ready to use all instruments -- market stabilisation scheme, liquidity adjustment facility, and CRR -- depending on the situation."   

Officials are finding it difficult to manage large inflows with foreign funds pumping about $17 billion into local stocks.   

The central bank has repeatedly raised the cash reserve ratio and sold market intervention bonds (MSS) to soak up surplus cash with banks, and ease price pressures.   

"Inflows depend on sentiments and the fundamentals of the economy. I don't see flows moderating in the coming months," said D.K. Joshi, economist with domestic rating agency Crisil.   

"It may not be at this pace, but it will continue to pressurise the rupee."   

Mohan listed surging oil prices and food price inflation globally as risks to domestic inflation but said the central bank's stance remained unchanged from its October review.   

"Our objective are to ensure price stability, maintenance of growth and financial stability," he said.   

Mohan said the central bank had been successful in moderating prices and loan growth in sectors like real estate, housing and capital markets by raising the risk weightage on bank loans to these sectors. (Additional reporting Saikat Chatterjee in Mumbai, editing by Mike Peacock)

title: India has no plans to further curb inflows-minister
text:
NEW DELHI, Nov 20 (Reuters) - India has no plans for further checks on capital inflows that have been a major support for a strengthening rupee in recent months, a minister said on Tuesday.   

Foreign funds have pumped around $17 billion so far this year into the Indian stock market, sending the main index soaring to a series of life highs and pushing the rupee <INR=IN> up to near-decade peaks.   

"There is no proposal for more checks on inflow of capital at present," Junior Finance Minister Pawan Kumar Bansal said in a written reply to Parliament.   

Last month, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, tightened rules on foreign investors' use of an investment instrument known as a participatory note, in a step authorities said aimed both to improve flow transparency and moderate the amount of funds coming into the country.   

Earlier, the central bank ruled that money raised overseas by local firms in excess of $20 million must be spent abroad.   

India's economy has grown by an average of 8.6 percent over the last four years and the government wants to lift annual expansion to double digits.   

But officials are finding it difficult to manage large capital inflows while keeping inflation in check.   

"To the extent that Reserve Bank of India, with a view to reduce undue volatility, intervened in the foreign exchange market, such appreciation was moderated," Bansal said.   

"A depreciation of the U.S. dollar against major currencies and increased capital flows have led to appreciation of the rupee vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar," he said.

* Forecast: 38.88/dollar by end March, 37.63 by Dec-end 2008

By C.J. Kurrien   

MUMBAI, Nov 15 (Reuters) - Capital inflows should drive the Indian rupee to more gains against the dollar next year, but its climb will be less steep than in 2007 if foreign investment slows in tandem with the U.S. economy, a Reuters poll shows.   

The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> hit a near-decade high of 39.16 per dollar this month, driven by foreign funds which have pumped a record $17 billion into India's booming stock market this year, helping the rupee gain about 12 percent.   

The currency closed at 39.30 per dollar on Wednesday and a Reuters poll of 22 market participants this week forecasts it will stand at 38.88 by the end of March 2008. Analysts then see it gaining further 3.3 percent to 37.63 by the end of 2008.   

"Inflows will dictate that the rupee continues to appreciate at a fairly modest rate," said  HSBC's Asia economist Robert Prior-Wandesforde.   

Rapid economic growth averaging at 8.6 percent in the past four years has lured foreign capital into India's markets but the rupee's sharp rise has upset the country's efforts to boost exports this year.   

Indian firms, particularly in textiles and handicrafts, have complained it is hurting business and Finance Minister Palaniappan Chidambaram meets textiles sector representatives later on Thursday to discuss the impact of the rupee's strength.   

Analysts said a slowdown in the U.S. economy was likely to slow overseas investment flows into Asia's third-largest economy, though the rupee will be less affected by a U.S. downturn than many other emerging market currencies. They say India's economy is less dependent on exports to the United States than many of its peers.   

"(India is) clearly among the least exposed to the U.S. and one would expect it to survive pretty well any downturn in the U.S. spending," said Prior-Wandesforde. Still, any easing of capital inflows would give the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) room to intervene more aggressively against the rupee, as would any reduction in global crude oil prices.   

"If there is a U.S. slowdown ... commodity price concerns will moderate and the RBI will be a little more comfortable and perhaps a little more aggressive in aiding rupee depreciation," said Abheek Barua, chief economist with  HDFC Bank .   

India's central bank bought a record $11.87 billion in intervention in September to temper the rupee's rise after a U.S. rate cut drew huge inflows into the stock market. It bought $51.8 billion in the first nine months of 2007.

title: RPT-UPDATE 1- India  raises cbank firepower for rupee  intervention
text:
(Repeats story issued late on Wednesday)  (Adds details, analyst quotes)   

 By Anurag Joshi   

 MUMBAI, Nov 7 (Reuters) - India strengthened the central bank's hand to intervene in the currency market on Wednesday after the rupee touched a near-decade high, and analysts said the move would help ease the pressure of huge capital inflows.   

 A statement from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) after market hours said the ceiling on bonds it uses to suck cash from the banking system had been lifted by a quarter to 2.5 trillion rupees ($63.6 billion) for the fiscal year 2007/08.   

 Strong inflows into the world's fastest-growing major economy after China have pushed up the rupee, which is now close to a 9-½   year high at 39.3 rupees to a dollar.   

 The RBI has bought close to $40 billion over the first eight months this year.   

 The central bank has been selling market stabilisation scheme (MSS) bonds since March to soak up cash surpluses with banks, which enters the system when the central bank buys dollars to check the rupee's rise.   

 "There are two options before Reserve Bank of India -- either raise the cash reserve ratio or the MSS limit -- to manage excess liquidity. They are using both," said D.K. Joshi, principal economist, at Crisil in Mumbai.   

 "With the kind of capital inflows witnessed in last few months, they have to suck the excess liquidity. The situation warranted so, as government seems unlikely to put further curbs on capital inflows.   

 "Without this (increase in MSS limit), there is a danger of an upward pressure on inflation."   

 The central bank statement added the threshold at which the new limit would be reviewed would now be 2.35 trillion rupees.   

 "With the MSS auction of treasury bills held today, the MSS outstanding (face value) will be 1.8 trillion rupees as on Nov. 8," the statement added.   

 Analysts had expected the move.   

 "Assuming capital flows revert to normal patterns, we would still expect $3-4 billion monthly net surplus in the coming months, and by extension dollar-buying intervention of similar amounts," DBS said in a research note on Tuesday.   

 In a policy review last week, the central bank said it would raise banks' cash reserve ratio by 50 basis points to 7.50 percent. The move, which takes effect on Nov. 10, will drain 160 billion rupees from the banking system.   

 After the policy, RBI Governor Yaga Venugopal Reddy told reporters that a liquidity overhang in the system is the only area of concern for the central bank.   

 "All the indicators point to a greater normalcy than before and the only area of concern is the overhang of liquidity," he said.  (Additional reporting by Rajkumar Ray and Surojit Gupta)  (Editing by Mark Williams)

"There are two options before Reserve Bank of India -- either raise the cash reserve ratio or the MSS limit -- to manage excess liquidity. They are using both.

ARUN KAUL, GENERAL MANAGER (TREASURY), PUNJAB NATIONAL BANK, NEW DELHI:   

"We were expecting some action on this front. We are still seeing lot of inflows. This (increase in MSS limit) will certainly help suck out excess liquidity and stem inflationary expectations, especially at a time when oil prices are surging.   

"There will be some upward pressure on yields of bonds."

title: India  may have to raise  intervention  bond cap -DBS
text:
MUMBAI, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Indian policymakers may have to raise more bonds sold under the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) to drain surplus cash generated by its currency market operations, DBS said in a research note on Tuesday.

The MSS bond ceiling has been raised three times in 2007 -- latest in October. The outstanding issuance was around 1.74 trillion rupees below a self-imposed ceiling of 2 trillion rupees. It is reviewed if the outstanding hits 1.85 trillion.

"Bonds outstanding under MSS should reach $44 billion by early November and should hit $46-47 billion sometime in November or December, we reckon," it said.

"The sterilisation, however, should prove insufficient," it said.

Authorities may resort to capital controls if they are unable to stem the flood of money, but the measures are unlikely to be draconian in nature as India needs huge amounts of money to fund its infrastructure needs, the Singapore-based bank said. MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India government bond prices fell Monday on concerns banks' excess cash may soon fall, damping demand for securities, traders said.   

Bond prices will likely move in a narrow range in the coming sessions, they said.   

The benchmark 7.99% 2017 bond ended at INR100.80, down from INR100.87 at Friday's close.   

"The bond prices will stay rangebound in the coming days. And if at all there is a price action, it will be on the negative side, because I expect the liquidity to tighten," said Mohan Shenoi, treasurer at  Kotak Mahindra Bank.

Excess cash in the banking system will likely fall in the coming days as a 50 basis point increase in the cash reserve ratio of banks from Saturday will absorb about INR160 billion.   

The Reserve Bank of India raised the CRR at its monetary policy review last week to contain the surplus cash in the banking system which has the potential to fuel inflation.   

The CRR, which is the share of deposits banks must keep in cash with the central bank, will rise to 7.50% from Saturday after the RBI hiked the ratio for the fourth time since January.   

A sovereign debt auction worth INR80 billion scheduled for Thursday will also soak up banks' cash.   

Banks are the largest buyers in the Indian debt market, and any fall in their surplus cash affects demand for bonds.   

In the currency market, the Indian rupee ended unchanged against the dollar Monday after suspected central bank intervention pulled the U.S. currency back from nine-and-a-half-year lows.   

The dollar ended at INR39.31, unchanged from Friday's close.   

Although the dollar moved in a tight range for most of the session, heavy selling by some corporates pulled it down to INR39.22 in the last hour of trading.   

The Reserve Bank of India quickly intervened, and the dollar bounced back to its familiar territory of INR39.31/INR39.32, where it has found support in recent sessions from the central bank.   

"I don't think the RBI will let this level be broken convincingly in the coming sessions. The dollar/rupee will continue to stay in a range of INR39.30-INR39.40 band," a dealer at a private bank said.   

However, India's finance minister, P. Chidambaram, said the rupee is set to gain further, in line with the growth in the economy.   

"If the economy is growing at an average rate of 8.6%, the rupee is bound to strengthen and therefore we must learn to adjust to trade in the environment where rupee will strengthen," Chidambaram told a gathering of industrialists in Mumbai.

The benchmark 7.99% 2017-dated bond ended at INR100.98, up from INR100.85 at Tuesday's close.   

"The proposal to raise the foreign investment limit in bonds will increase market participation," said a state-owned bank's bond dealer.   

Under current regulations, foreign investors can invest up to $3.2 billion in government bonds and up to $1.5 billion in corporate bonds per year.   

"There is an appetite for bonds. There are limits on foreign participation in bond markets at this point in time, but you will see that moving away," Securities and Exchange Board of India Chairman M. Damodaran said at an event in New Delhi.   

Lower-than-expected yield cutoffs at a treasury bill auction by the central bank also helped bond prices to edge higher.

Currency dealers said the Reserve Bank of India intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the dollar at INR39.30.   

"The dollar-rupee's movement tomorrow (Thursday) completely depends on what the Fed will do," said a private bank's currency dealer.   

The U.S. Federal Reserve is widely expected to cut its benchmark rate by 25 basis points later in the global day.

MUMBAI, Oct 16 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee <INR=IN> could breach the 39 per dollar mark in the immediate term, despite sustained intervention mounted by the central bank to moderate its rise, Standard Chartered  said in a note on Tuesday.   

 "Clearly, the immediate bias is for further gains and USD-INR (dollar-rupee) could well break through 39.0," Stanchart said, adding that the latest bout of the rupee's strength has been fuelled by a strong risk appetite.   

 "Given our forecast that the Fed will cut rates again in October, risk appetite may stay high for a while longer," the British bank said. The Federal Reserve cut key U.S. rates by a half-percentage point on Sept. 18.   

 The rupee has risen more than 12.5 percent against the dollar in 2007, making it the best performing currency in Asia. The rupee's rise has been helped by foreign inflows into local shares of about $16.7 billion till date this year.   

 The currency has also been undeterred by a strong intervention by the Reserve Bank of India, which has bought $39.9 billion in the first eight months of 2007, including more than $11 billion in both February and July.   

 Stanchart estimates that the central bank has bought around $21 billion to $23 billion since Sept.18. "However, even this has not been enough to stop the INR (rupee)," the bank said.   

 "Longer term, we remain bullish on the INR. The Indian economy will be relatively insulated from the slowing U.S. economy due to strong domestic demand and a diversified export base," Stanchart said.   

 A balance of payments surplus is also supporting the rupee, Stanchart said. "We now expect the fiscal year 2007/08's balance of payments' surplus to be $42 billion, compared with our initial estimate of around $25.6 billion."

title: RPT-India cbank in  FX  swaps to tame cash, rupee-traders
text:
(Repeats story from Thursday)   

MUMBAI, Oct 11 (Reuters) - India's central bank has begun doing currency swaps with state banks to blunt some of the rupees it injects while buying dollars and to help exporters get a better exchange rate, dealers said on Thursday.   

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has been intervening heavily in the spot market this year to slow down the rupee's ascent against the dollar, but this has flooded the market with excess cash that could fuel inflation.   

The central bank has now started entering into swap deals with state banks -- by selling dollars in the spot market and buying them in the forward market, traders at five banks said.   

A central bank spokesman was not available for comment.   

The swap deals help the RBI to reduce some of the surplus rupees generated by its own intervention, while simultaneously raising the value of dollars in the forward market, enabling exporters to book their receivables at a higher margin.   

"It is a win-win situation for the RBI because it is not only preventing the rupee from rising sharply, but also keeps a check on system liquidity," a trader at a local bank said.   

The RBI has done an estimated $1-$1.5 billion worth of swap trades in two days with state-run banks and most of the forward deals were struck for December-March, traders said.   

"It's a third front in the battle against rising liquidity. First we had cash reserve ratio, then market stabilisation bonds and now this," said a senior currency trader at a European bank.   

Six-month annualised forward premiums moved up to 1.75 percent on Thursday from 1.49 percent on Wednesday, while three-month forwards climbed to 1.61 percent from 1.52 percent.   

"It's a small relief for exporters as it will give them a better value for their exports but at the same time it points to a liquidity build-up in the future," an analyst at a private bank said.   

On Thursday, the rupee <INR=IN> climbed to 39.27 per dollar -- its highest level since March 1998. It has risen 12.6 percent in 2007, making it the best performing currency versus the dollar in Asia.   

Last week, the central bank raised the ceiling for issuing intervention bonds by a third to 2 trillion rupees ($50.9 billion) to boost its firepower.   

The bonds are used to drain rupee funds caused by the currency intervention.   

The RBI bought $38.1 billion in the first seven months of 2007, according to latest data, and traders say the purchases have picked up in the last few weeks due to surging foreign portfolio flows in India's booming stock market. ($1=39.3 rupees)

title: Emerging  FX -Asia pauses as c.banks seek to cap peso, rupee
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were range-bound on Thursday after strong gains in recent sessions, with investors trying to guess the direction of the dollar ahead of a meeting of Group of Seven finance chiefs next week.   

Fears of heightened intervention by regional central banks kept some investors sidelined, as central banks in India and the Philippines were spotted trying to rein in their currencies.   

The high-yielding Philippine peso <PHP=> hit 44.05 per dollar, a seven-year high, but suspected dollar-buying by the central bank kept it away from the psychologically important 44 level.   

"The central bank is always there to smooth volatility or prevent the peso from strengthening too much," said a trader in Manila, adding that the 44 level would be tested soon.   

But a second trader felt that level would hold until next week due to the presence of the central bank and profit-taking.   

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=>, another high-yielder, steadied near 9,080 per dollar, down a fifth of a percent from late Asian trade on Wednesday.   

The rupiah has gained 3.3 percent since Sept. 18, when the U.S. Federal Reserve cut its benchmark interest rate by a hefty 50 basis points and sparked a rally in most Asian currencies.   

The peso has risen 4.3 percent versus the dollar since then.   

Meanwhile, the dollar fell versus the euro <EUR=> amid speculation that the Fed may cut rates again this month.   

Bank of America strategist Christy Tan said trading in Asian currencies was subdued ahead of public holidays in some Asian countries, and investors were looking to the G7 meeting for comments that could set the tone for the dollar.   

"The market focus will be likely to switch to the upcoming G7 meeting next week, where European officials are expected to step up calls for China and Asia to share the burden of global imbalance adjustments," she said.   

INTERVENTION

The Indian rupee <INR=IN>, Asia's best performer this year with gains of 12.6 percent, pulled back from its 9-1/2-year high of 39.275 per dollar as the central bank was seen intervening.   

Official data showed India's foreign exchange reserves swelled by $18.9 billion in September, highlighting the central bank's efforts to stem rupee gains fuelled by foreign funds.   

The South Korean won <KRW=> hit a two-week low at 921.30 per dollar on reports Dutch  Philips Electronics had sold a stake in  LG.Philips LCD. As expected, the central bank held interest rates steady on Thursday.   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> hovered near 1.4640 to the U.S. dollar, off its 10-year peak of 1.4625 hit on Wednesday after the central bank surprised the market by tightening monetary policy slightly.   

Many analysts believe Singapore's central bank will tolerate long-term appreciation, but they caution that it could step up intervention in the near term to prevent any sharp rise now.   

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> eased as far as 3.382 per dollar, a day after it rose past 3.38 to a 9-1/2-year high.

(Repeats story from Thursday)  (Adds more comments)   

 MUMBAI, Oct 4 (Reuters) - India raised the central bank's firepower to intervene in the currency market on Thursday by increasing the ceiling on the amount of special bonds it can issue to absorb the rupees generated by intervention.   

 The limit on the bonds, known as market stabilisation bonds, was lifted to 2 trillion rupees ($50.6 billion) from 1.5 trillion, a statement for the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said.   

 Following are some quick comments from analysts.   

 Latest...   

 SHUBHADA RAO, CHIEF ECONOMIST,  YES BANK, MUMBAI:   

 "It is absolutely in line with expectations. Probably even the CRR measure will be in the reckoning sometime soon, given the pace of inflows and the need for the RBI to intervene in the currency market."   

 - - - - -   

 ABHEEK BARUA, CHIEF  ECONOMIST AT  HDFC BANK, NEW DELHI:   

 "With this, the central bank is saying that they will continue to intervene fairly aggressively and the rupee may even slip in the near term if capital inflows slows a bit.   

 "With the government's borrowing programme frontloaded for the first three months of the second half of the year, it will have quite a draining effect on liquidity. I think the cash reserve ratio increase is put on the back burner at least for now.   

 "They have enough ammunition for the moment."   

 - - - - -   

 HARISH MENON, ECONOMIST,  ING VYSYA BANK, MUMBAI:   

 "Considering the scale at which the central bank has been intervening in the currency markets, I don't think this hike in the MSS ceiling is sufficient. They will have to hike the ceiling at least one more time and this hike has kept alive the chances of a cash reserve requirement increase in the near term."   

 - - - - -   

 D.K. JOSHI, PRINCIPAL ECONOMIST, CRISIL, MUMBAI:   

 "I think this measure will need to be complimented by CRR hike to deal with the deluge of capital flows.   

 - - - - -   

 Earlier...   

 INDRANIL PAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, KOTAK MAHINDRA BANK, MUMBAI:   

 "We have been expecting a hike in MSS limit as the outstanding issues have already breached the threshold. Given the more than 500 billion rupees of liquidity in the system, it becomes inevitable for more MSS issuances. With the enhanced limit on MSS, any apprehension of increase in CRR could be pushed to a later date, possibly till the announcement of the policy."   

 - - - - -   

 A. PRASANNA, ANALYST, ICICI SECURITIES, MUMBAI:   

 "It is more or less along expected lines. It looks like for sometime the RBI may not be using the CRR (cash reserve ratio) option, at least until the policy review."

 "This was broadly expected and markets should largely take it in their stride and bonds may start 0.05-0.07 rupees lower tomorrow. But with this, the cash reserve requirements increase is on the back burner until the policy meeting later this month as this has given them enough firepower until then."

By V. Ramakrishnan and Saikat Chatterjee   

MUMBAI, Oct 4 (Reuters) - India raised the central bank's firepower to intervene in the currency market on Thursday, a move analysts said might check the pace of rupee gains near term and lower chances of monetary tightening before a month-end review.   

Strong capital inflows into the world's fastest-growing major economy after China have pushed up the rupee <INR=IN>, making it Asia's best performing currency this year.   

The rupee has gained more than 12 percent against the dollar since the start of January and reached a 9-1/2-year high of 39.36 per dollar on Thursday.

text:
Oct 4 (Reuters) - India raised the central bank's capacity for currency intervention on Thursday by increasing the ceiling on the amount of market stabilisation scheme debt it can issue to 2 trillion rupees ($50.6 billion) from 1.5 trillion.   

For a related story, please see [ID:nMBI000634].   

Here are five facts about bonds and bills issued under the central bank's Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS): ---------------------------------------------------------------   

* Huge capital inflows have pushed the rupee to its strongest level against the dollar in 9-½ years, prompting the central bank to try to contain it by buying dollars. Latest data shows it bought $38.1 billion in the first seven months of 2007.   

* Such intervention releases rupees into the money market, which could be inflationary if left in circulation. MSS debt, which was introduced in April 2004, is sold to absorb the surplus funds in a process called sterilisation.

* The government has to pay interest on the MSS debt, so the government and the central bank meet to decide if the ceiling on issues need to be changed once sales hit a pre-determined level.   

* Since the central bank resumed selling MSS bonds in March, after a gap of 18 months, the ceiling had already been increased three times by a total of 700 billion rupees. It was raised by 150 billion rupees twice in April and by 400 billion rupees in August.

 The central bank has intervened heavily this year to limit the rupee's gains -- the most recent data shows it bought more than $38 billion in the first seven months of 2007.   

 Following are comments from economists and market analysts on what the rupee's rally means for policy makers and where it is headed in the near term.   

 ***********************************************************   

 GAURAV KAPUR, SENIOR ECONOMIST,  ABN AMRO BANK, MUMBAI:   

 "The rupee would continue to witness sharp appreciation pressures in the near term, given the exuberance in the equities market, wider interest rate differentials and the general weakness of the U.S. dollar."   

 "However, high crude oil prices and Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervention will counter these pressures and the rupee could see some weakness towards the end of this month."   

 "The oil price spiral above $80 per barrel has been ignored by the market till now, and that remains the key risk to a sustained appreciation of the Indian unit."   

 NIZAM IDRIS, FX STRATEGIST,  UBS, SINGAPORE:   

 "It hasn't broken the 40 level convincingly. The RBI could just push it back up over 40 and defend that for a bit longer.   

 "But that would require significant intervention, which would mean pressure on money supply to accelerate. Currently we do not have significant issues with inflation. Possible inflation would remain benign for the rest of year given the base effect. But food prices are higher, oil prices also increasing. Those are the two factors which could see RBI choosing a significantly lower line in the sand - possibly even near 38 for example."   

 "For now that inflation pressure is still not there and it hasn't actually broken 40 convincingly."   

 D.K. JOSHI, PRINCIPAL ECONOMIST, CRISIL, MUMBAI:   

 "It will be around 40 level even after three months. Right now, the sudden surge is euphoria driven. There are huge capital inflows and the expectation is for the rupee to appreciate, Fed has eased. All this has caused the sudden appreciation of the rupee, and I think it will stabilise once the euphoria stabilises."   

 "I think the RBI will try to protect it as much as they can because their ability to protect is also limited. I would say if the scenario continues, we will see another cash reserve ratio (CRR) hike so the RBI can intervene."  "The Market Stabilisation Scheme ceiling (MSS) has also been increased. It comes with a fiscal cost to the government. It is very difficult to say if they will increase the quota."   

 HAN-SIA YEO, ANALYST AT BANK OF AMERICA, SINGAPORE:   

 "There's still headroom for MSS. Inflation is still low now plus credit growth has moderated. So the central bank has room to intervene if it wants to. The RBI also hasn't been very eager to withdraw liquidity, though the liquidity cushion could be in part due to global financial market volatility."   

 "But I don't see this leading up to a likely cash reserve requirement increase in the near term, as broader economic conditions are very different from earlier and so the same aggressive policy response may not be that forthcoming."   

 "We expect the rupee to end 2007 at 39.50 per dollar."   

 SONAL VARMA, ECONOMIST, LEHMAN BROTHER, MUMBAI   

 "A resurgence in capital inflows will complicate the RBI's monetary policy. We expect the RBI to allow some rupee appreciation, encourage capital outflows and use the MSS and the CRR hikes to sterilise inflows. Strong capital inflows are also likely, at the margin, to make the RBI less willing to hike rates, lest it could provoke even stronger capital inflows.   

 Our research shows that of the Asian countries, India is among the least exposed to a global economic slowdown, and the interest rate differential is now strongly in favour to attract strong capital inflows. This will likely put pressure on the rupee to appreciate. We expect rupee/dollar at 40.0 by end 2007 and 37.5 by end 2008."   

 PETER REDWARD, HEAD OF RATES RESEARCH, EMERGING ASIA, BARCLAYS CAPITAL, SINGAPORE:   

 " Barclays Capital forecasts the Indian rupee to strengthen to 39.75 by year-end, but we see upside risk to our forecast. We project the current account deficit of $17.3 billion in FY08, to be largely financed by net FDI inflows and concessional loans."   

 "In addition, India is likely to experience further portfolio capital inflows and as U.S. interest rates decline, growth in non-resident Indian repatriation flows."   

 "In our opinion, liquidity is likely to rapidly return to the system as the RBI acts to stem rupee appreciation and injects liquidity into the money market. Consequently, we will be closely watching both the overnight rate and the volume of withdrawal via the LAF (liquidity adjustment facility) for signs of a build-up in liquidity."

title: Emerging  FX -Asian high-yielders surge after Fed rate cut
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 19 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso rose more than 1 percent against the dollar on Wednesday after a large Fed rate cut revived appetite for high-yielding assets and allayed concerns over global growth.   

The Federal Reserve slashed its benchmark rate to 4.75 percent from 5.25 percent, boosting stocks and high-yielding currencies on hopes that the monetary easing would shield the U.S. economy from the housing slump and financial market turmoil.   

The Aussie dollar <AUD=> posted its biggest daily gain in nine years after the Fed move. In emerging Asia, the rupiah <IDR=> and peso <PHP=> hit their highest levels in nearly six weeks.   

The rupiah touched 9,230 per dollar and the peso rose to 45.55 per dollar.   

The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> also gained nearly 1 percent, rising to about 3.4535 per dollar.   

"The Fed has paved the way for risk-taking by offshore investors," said Suresh Ramanathan, head of strategy at CIMB Bank in Kuala Lumpur.   

Ramanathan said there had been foreign currency inflows into Malaysian bonds as well as short-term bills, with 3-month bill yields <0#MYBILLS=> down by about 3 basis points.   

"Most of the interest seems to be within one to three months, an indication that investors are positioning for further rate cuts by the Fed in the next three months," he said.   

The spotlight in Wednesday's trading seemed to be on yields. The dollar was the clear loser and high-yielders such as the New Zealand dollar <NZD=> gained.   

The Japanese yen <JPY=> fell initially in an apparent sign that people were using it again as a cheap funding currency, but recovered later after Bank of Japan Governor Toshihiko Fukui said Japanese rates would still be raised if the economy performed in line with the central bank's view.   

The South Korean won <KRW=>, whose overnight call rate target is now above U.S. overnight rates after the Fed rate cut, gained half a percent to a high of 925 per dollar.   

"The mix of rising risk appetite, improved growth confidence, a markedly weaker dollar, clean speculative positions and emerging offshore interest to re-enter short dollar/Asia should help dollar/Asia push lower in response,"  JPMorgan Chase said to clients.   

JPMorgan said the rupiah, peso and ringgit were more sensitive to increased risk appetite, but the Singapore dollar <SGD=> would remain sensitive to sentiment about global growth prospects.   

While the won and Indian rupee <INR=IN> should also trade with a bias to appreciate, heavy intervention by the Reserve Bank of India and likely Bank of Korea resistance would offset their gains,  JPMorgan said.   

South Korea's second vice finance minister, Lim Young-rok, said on Wednesday that policy makers would take action if the won rose high enough to hurt the economy.   

SOME DOUBTS   

Some analysts felt the Fed's hefty rate cut might eventually bring to the fore concerns over growth in the United States and therefore in regions dependent on demand there, such as Asia.   

"That is the initial reaction, that the Fed reflation will work, but we think it won't," said  BNP Paribas strategist Thio Chin Loo.   

Thio said she was bullish on currencies such as the Singapore dollar in such an environment. The Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose half a percent to 1.5085 per U.S. dollar on Wednesday.   

"We are no longer in a carry environment strictly, as yields in U.S. dollar will lose attraction, the ECB is on hold and the Bank of Japan defers rate hikes.   

"Also, capital preservation is more important in a lower growth environment, and financing concerns dominate.   

"Countries with large current account deficits like the U.S., UK, and Australia have currencies that are most vulnerable compared to Asian economies," Thio said.   

With the Fed meeting out of the way, some analysts highlighted rising oil prices as a concern for Asia, which imports most of its crude requirements.   

Oil prices <CLc1> hit a new peak above $82 per barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange overnight, boosted by concern over supplies and the weather as well as expectations that the Fed rate cut would boost economic growth and therefore demand for oil. [nN18466256].

MUMBAI, Sept 19 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee hit a nine-year high on Wednesday as a sharp cut in interest rates by the U.S. Federal Reserve increased appetite for emerging market assets and a surging stock market attracted capital inflows.   

Dealers said the rupee's gains were capped by heavy dollar-buying intervention by the central bank.   

The rupee <INR=IN> ended at 40.20/21 per dollar, having risen to 40.18 during trade -- its highest since May 1998. The rupee gained more than half a percent from Tuesday's close of 40.48/49, and has risen more than 10 percent this year.   

The currency's previous high of 40.20 was hit in July.   

"Exporters got panicky and were selling their dollars throughout the day, and inflows are expected to be robust as evident by the soaring stock markets," said V. Soundarajan, a currency trader at  UCO Bank.

"I expect the rupee to break past the 40 per dollar mark before the end of this month," he said.   

The stock market <.BSESN> rose 4.2 percent, its biggest gain in 15 months, to a record-high close on hopes that the U.S. rate cut would help steady global credit markets and see foreigners return to emerging markets such as India.   

As well, Tuesday's cuts in U.S. interest rates raised India's interest rate premium over the United States to 300 basis points, which traders said would attract more capital inflows and add to the rupee's momentum.   

But those inflows complicate policy for the Reserve Bank of India, which has been intervening as the rupee rose this month and stepped in again as the currency neared its highs.   

"They bought at every level. I think they are going to protect it," a chief dealer with a foreign bank said.   

A Reserve Bank of India spokeswoman said the central bank did not comment on the day-to-day movements on the exchange rate.   

Data this month showed the central bank bought $11.4 billion in intervention in July, when the rupee was last near current levels, taking its dollar purchases in 2007 to 38.1 billion.   

The U.S. Federal Reserve lowered its benchmark federal funds target rate by 50 basis points to 4.75 percent to shore up the world's largest economy against a housing slowdown and credit market turmoil. title: ANALYSIS-In praise of capital controls in Asia
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 10 (Reuters) - It's not what the International Monetary Fund would espouse. But as Asia's biggest economies turn to capital controls to shield their markets from a torrent of foreign money, many feel policy makers are doing the right thing.   

One message rings out loud from India's and South Korea's efforts in the past week to restrict the flow of foreign funds: these central banks would gladly abandon free movement in their currencies for the liberty of setting interest rates at will. Economists sympathise with that stance. Until this week, when delinquencies in U.S. subprime mortgages drove a broad selling of risky assets in Asia and elsewhere in the world, most of the region was drowning in foreign money.   

Asian central banks were under fire from their export lobbies as currencies rallied and from their political masters as domestic asset prices soared. They were running out of tools to intervene in markets and were unenthusiastic about raising interest rates for fear that would bring in more cash.   

So when South Korea and India announced in the past week that they would restrict the amount of overseas borrowings locals could bring home -- effectively closing a small part of their capital accounts -- there was barely a murmur from proponents of free market principles.   

The implication was clear. When it comes to the crunch, Asia would rather have an independent monetary policy, even if that means a fettered currency.   

Bank of Korea's surprise rate rise on Thursday, its second in as many months, proved this.   

"The Bank of Korea has regained greater control of monetary policy," said  Morgan Stanley strategist Stewart Newnham.   

The capital controls should alleviate pressure on the won to appreciate by restricting the main domestic speculators, he said.   

"The Bank of Korea is thus faced with a more favourable trade-off in meeting its inflation and exchange rate objectives, which should reduce its policy dilemma," Newnham said.   

The speculative froth in won markets will subside. The won <KRW=> -- estimated to be the most overvalued in Asia in trade-weighted terms -- would be among the region's underperformers and Korean market rates could rise as more locals shift to borrowing onshore, he said.   

CONTROLS OVERDUE?   

Analysts reckon capital restrictions were overdue in India.   

Generous limits had allowed companies to raise huge amounts of external commercial borrowings (ECBs) at rates cheaper than domestic funds, which then undermined the central bank's monetary policy and put heavy pressure on the rupee to appreciate.   

ECBs doubled to $16.1 billion in the year to March 2007 from the previous year.   

The rupee <INR=IN> has risen 15 percent in a year and is close to hitting 40 per dollar, the stock market <.BSESN> has gained 60 percent since the end of 2005 and property prices all over the country have soared.   

Overnight rates crashed to near zero earlier this month, in spite of a 6 percent base policy rate and a hawkish central bank.   

The government has now said companies borrowing more than $20 million would have to spend the money overseas.   

Rajeev Malik,  JPMorgan's economist, said India's central bank was dealing with conflicting goals of a "gung-ho approach for attracting more capital inflows but resistance to further rupee appreciation".   

He reckoned the new rules would impact inflows and facilitate better handling of money market liquidity by the central bank. While the rupee could appreciate in the longer term, it was likely to fall to 42 per dollar by the year end, he said.   

GOOD CONTROLS, BAD CONTROLS   

One reason economists want to forgive governments in Asia that want to restrain their currencies is China's reluctance to let the yuan rise, despite a surging trade surplus.   

And because emerging Asia's biggest economy places greater priority on maintaining its pole position in export markets and on creating jobs, its neighbours would be ill-advised to let their currencies become uncompetitively overvalued.   

To their credit, India and Korea have turned to capital controls only as a last resort, after having let their currencies appreciate, raising interest rates and trying to encourage local investors to take their money abroad. Both have intervened extensively, with India's currency reserves up $36 billion in the first half of 2007 and Korea's up by nearly $12 billion.   

Neither has interfered much with foreign capital investment or other healthier funding flows coming into their countries.   

"It is very hard to regulate a capital account that has already been opened. Investors typically find loopholes and history shows that the measures tend to work only for a little while," said Rob Subbaraman, an economist with  Lehman Brothers.

"There are various degrees of imposing restrictions and I think this is a mild form. And I wouldn't see them in isolation," he said.   

Lessons had been learnt from Thailand's botched efforts to block capital flows in December, Subbaraman said, and policy makers in Asia were being extra cautious.

title: RPT-UPDATE 1- India  raises ceiling on  intervention  bonds - cbank
text:
(Repeats story issued late on Wednesday)  (Adds details, analyst comments and background)   

 By V. Ramakrishnan   

 MUMBAI, Aug 8 (Reuters) - India's government raised the central bank's currency intervention firepower on Wednesday, a day after it imposed limits on foreign borrowings by local firms in an effort to stem the strength of the rupee.   

 The Reserve Bank of India said the issue ceiling on bonds it can use to absorb funds generated by its currencyintervention had been raised to 1.5 trillion rupees ($37 billion) from 1.1 trillion rupees.   

 The new ceiling for the fiscal year ending in March 2008 would be reviewed if outstanding issues of market stabilisation scheme (MSS) bonds exceeded 1.35 trillion rupees, the central bank said in a statement.   

 The outstanding balance of MSS bonds, including an auction held on Wednesday, was 989.7 billion rupees, it said.   

 Analysts said the second increase in the ceiling this year -- it was previously raised in late April -- would give the central bank more control of the supply of cash in the money market, and that bond yields were likely to rise on Thursday. "The RBI itself has been surprised by the kind of liquidity," said Pradeep Madhav, chief operating officer at Securities Trading Corp of India.   

 The RBI has bought billions of dollars to rein in the rupee, which, powered by foreign investment inflows, has risen about 10 percent against the dollar this year to nine-year highs, causing policy headaches.   

 The intervention releases rupees into the local money market, which adds to inflationary pressures. To remove, or sterilise, the cash, the central bank in March resumed sales of MSS bonds.   

 "To absorb the liquidity already infused, the increase in the ceiling on MSS will help," said S.P. Prabhu, head of trading at IDBI Gilts, adding tighter cash conditions would push bond yields up.   

 "I expect the yield on the 10-year bond to rise 5 to 10 basis points tomorrow," he said.   

 On July 31, the RBI raised reserve requirements for banks, a step it expects to remove $4 billion from the money market, and on Tuesday the government announced restrictions on local firms bringing foreign borrowings into the country.   

 Earlier on Wednesday, Finance Minister Palaniappan Chidambaram had told Reuters that for now the government was not reviewing the ceiling on MSS bonds but would consider it if needed.   

 Asia's third-largest economy grew by 9.4 percent in 2006/07, its fastest pace in 18 years, but the growth was accompanied by a surge in prices.   

 Annual inflation hit a two-year high of 6.7 percent in late January, but has been below 5 percent since June.   

 The RBI raised interest rates five times in 2006/07, most recently in late March.   

 ($1=40.50 rupees)  (Additional reporting by Unni Krishnan in NEW DELHI and Anurag Joshi in MUMBAI)

title: UPDATE 1- India  not reviewing  intervention  bond cap now-finmin
text:
(Adds details, market comments)   

NEW DELHI, Aug 8 (Reuters) - India is not reviewing for now a 1.1 trillion rupee ($27 billion) limit on the sale of bonds used to absorb funds generated by currency intervention but will consider it if needed, the finance minister said on Wednesday.   

Outstanding intervention bonds will rise to more than 950 billion rupees after an auction on Wednesday -- which the Reserve Bank of India said in April was the threshold for a review -- and traders expect the cap to be raised as the rupee <INR=IN> trades near nine-year highs against the dollar.   

"You can't say a review is on," Finance Minister Palaniappan Chidambaram told Reuters when asked if the finance ministry was reviewing the limit for Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) bonds.   

"We will review it if it's necessary," he said.   

The RBI has bought billions of dollars to rein in the rupee, which, powered by foreign investment inflows, has risen about 10 percent against the dollar this year, causing policy headaches.   

The intervention releases rupees into the local money market, which adds to inflationary pressures. To remove, or sterilise, the cash, the central bank in March resumed sales of MSS bonds.   

At a July 31 policy review, the RBI increased reserve requirements for banks, a step which it expects to remove $4 billion from the money market, and on Tuesday the government announced restrictions on foreign borrowing by local firms.   

With the RBI wanting to contain inflation but also expected to avoid raising interest rates if it can -- higher rates would attract more foreign capital -- the market expects the MSS limit to be increased. It was last raised in April.   

"I think they will do it. The way things are going, it looks like (the RBI) is determined to suck out excess liquidity from the system," a senior dealer at a private sector bank said.   

Asia's third-largest economy grew by 9.4 percent in the 2006/07 fiscal year to March 31, its fastest pace in 18 years, but the growth was accompanied by a surge in prices.   

Annual inflation hit a two-year high of 6.7 percent in late January, but has been below 5 percent since June.   

The RBI raised interest rates five time in 2006/07, but has not raised them since late March. (Additional reporting by V. Ramakrishnan in MUMBAI) ($1=40.40 rupees)

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Indian government bond prices rose Thursday as banks bought securities to meet reserve requirements, but may come under pressure ahead of a federal government bond auction Friday, dealers said.   

The benchmark 7.49% 2017-dated bond ended at INR97.35, higher than its close of INR97.15 Wednesday. Its yield fell by 3 basis points to 7.88%.   

"We are seeing good buying from banks to meet their statutory liquidity ratio requirements before the reporting day tomorrow," said a trader at a private bank.   

Indian banks need to maintain 25% of their deposits in gold, cash or approved securities and have to report the position to the central bank every alternate Friday.   

Market participants also took comfort from a recovery in local stocks, which boosted hopes of more inflows in to the country.   

The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark 30-stock Sensex gained 49.93 points, or 0.3%, to end at 14985.70.   

The inflows could partly offset the squeeze expected in money markets next week, dealers said.   

Liquidity in the banking system is expected to tighten next week after the 50 basis point hike in the cash reserve ratio to 7% takes effect Saturday and the ceiling on the excess funds that RBI accepts via the reverse repo auctions is scrapped.   

"As long as capital flows are there in the market and the rupee is rising, the Reserve Bank of India will intervene and in turn release rupee funds back in to the system," said a dealer with a state-run bank.   

However, traders expect bond prices to retrace some of their gains Friday as investors may look for higher yields at a federal government bond auction.   

"With the auction coming up tomorrow, we could again see some selling as players are still unsure of how the liquidity situation pans out," the trader at the private bank said.   

The trader expects the 10-year yield to test 7.92% Friday.   

RBI will sell INR60 billion of the 7.99% 2017-dated bond and INR40 billion of 7.95% 2032-dated bond under the federal government's regular market borrowing plan.   

In the currency market, the Indian rupee rose against the U.S. dollar tracking the recovery in local stocks and gains by local currencies in other emerging market economies against the dollar.   

The dollar fell to INR40.42 from its finish of INR40.46 Wednesday.   

"Traders had been funding their dollar purchases at near zero overnight rates lately and with call rate likely to rise again next week, traders may start going short on the dollar," a trader at a private bank said.   

The trader expects the dollar to trade in a range of INR40.35-INR40.50 Friday.

title: Indian rupee heads back towards 9-yr high on flows
text:
(Updates to open)   

MUMBAI, July 26 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee headed back towards a nine-year high on Thursday, with the market shrugging off cues from other high-yielding Asian currencies that slipped against the dollar, in anticipation of strong capital inflows.   

At 9:45 a.m. (0415 GMT), the rupee <INR=IN> was at 40.31/32 per dollar, strengthening from the previous close of 40.3500/3575 and inching towards from a nine-year high of 40.20 hit earlier this week.   

"The market is looking for direction at the moment, and in the short run, its eyes are on the stock market," said a dealer with a foreign bank, who expects the rupee to trade in a 40.30-40.37 range on Thursday.   

Concerns over the fallout from the U.S. subprime market had abated slightly, and dealers built fresh positions in the rupee, expecting further appreciation.   

The rupee is the best performing Asian currency against the dollar this year, having gained nearly 10 percent in 2007, bolstered by robust investment flows into Asia's third largest economy.   

Foreigners have bought more than $10.4 billion of stocks so far in 2007, edging towards a record $10.7 billion inflow in 2005 and higher than $8 billion in 2006.   

Still, dealers expected the rupee to trade in a narrow range, with gains limited by possible central bank intervention and firm prices of oil, India's largest import.   

Oil prices <LCOc1> jumped on Wednesday after U.S. government data showed a draw in crude inventories as refiners stepped up runs to meet summer gasoline demand in the U.S., the world's top consumer.

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee rose to a new nine-year high against the U.S. dollar earlier Monday driven by strong foreign fund inflows to buy local stocks, before the Reserve Bank of India intervened to rein in the local currency.   

The dollar ended at INR40.29 against INR40.32 at its close Friday. It touched an intraday low of INR40.22, a level last seen in May 1998.   

Most dealers expect the central bank to allow a gradual appreciation of the Indian unit.   

"The supply of dollars in the market is phenomenal, and it is the only the central bank presence which is checking the slide for the dollar," said V. Rajagopal, head of foreign exchange trading at  Kotak Mahindra Bank.

He expects the dollar to test INR40 by the end of the week as strong capital inflows from overseas investors persist, pushing local shares to new highs.   

Indian shares ended at an all-time high with the Bombay Stock Exchange's key 30-stock Sensex closing 1.1% higher at 15,732.20.   

Foreign investors have bought over $9 billion worth of stocks so far in 2007, well over the $8 billion they bought in the previous year.   

In the bond market, Indian government bond prices rose as comfortable cash in the banking system and lower bond sales by the RBI spurred buying of securities, sending the benchmark 10-year yields to over five-and-a-half-month lows.   

The benchmark 7.49% 2017-dated bond ended at INR98.25, up from INR97.81 at the previous close.   

Its yield ended at 7.74%, down from 7.81% at Friday's close in India. It fell to 7.71% in intraday trade, the lowest yield for the 10-year paper since early February.   

Dealers said lower-than-expected sales of bonds slated for the week by the RBI under the market stabilization scheme helped bonds gain.   

The RBI will sell INR20 billion of 7.55% 2010 bonds Wednesday under its market stabilization scheme to suck up excess liquidity.   

"We did see some profit-booking come in towards the close of trade but the general sentiment remains positive for bonds, given the ample liquidity in the system," said Namrata Padhye, fixed income analyst at IDBI Capital Markets.   

Government spending and persistent intervention in the currency markets by the central bank have boosted rupee funds with banks, the biggest buyers of government debt. .

text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee climbed to a new nine-year high against the U.S. dollar Monday, helped by strong foreign fund inflows into local stocks, traders said.   

At 0740GMT, the rupee was trading at 40.25 to a dollar, its highest intraday level against the U.S. currency since May 1998.   

"There are strong foreign fund inflows into the market, and we are also seeing some selling by banks on behalf of their corporate clients," a local bank dealer said.   

The rupee has gained about 9.5% against the dollar since January.   

Foreign investors have bought over $9 billion worth of Indian stocks so far in 2007, well over the $8 billion they bought in the previous year.   

-By Vipin V. Nair; Dow Jones Newswires; 91 22 2288 4212; vipin.nair@dowjones.com
