   (Updates an item ran at 0750GMT with more quotes, background) 
    

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The dollar fell to a new nine-year low against the Indian rupee Monday, as the rupee was boosted by strong foreign fund inflows, and some traders expect the dollar to go below the key INR40 barrier soon.   

The dollar's previous nine-year low was recorded on May 28 when it hit INR40.28.   

At 1050GMT, the dollar was changing hands at INR40.29, up from INR40.22, its lowest level against the Indian currency since May 1998.   

Traders said the dollar recovered due to the suspected intervention of the Reserve Bank of India through state-owned banks.   

"State-run banks have again come back to support the pair at 40.24. The intervention, however, is not very heavy as the pair fell due to a one-off inflow," said a state-run bank dealer, who didn't wish to be named.   

The rupee has gained about 9.5% against the dollar since January, mainly due to continuing foreign fund inflows, analysts said.   

Foreign investors have bought over $9 billion worth of Indian stocks so far in 2007, well over the $8 billion they bought in the previous year.   

Traders said the dollar's global weakness also accentuated its fall in the local market.   

The dollar hit a record low versus the euro and a six-week low against the yen in Asia Monday on worries that problems in the U.S. subprime loan market could damage the broader economy.   

According to V. Rajagopal, head of foreign exchange trading at Mumbai-based  Kotak Mahindra Bank, the dollar may fall further to test INR40.00 by Friday as strong capital inflows from overseas investors persist.   

"The supply of dollars in the market is phenomenal, and it is only the central bank presence which is checking the slide for the dollar," he said.   

Traders said the central bank had been regularly intervening in the currency market in recent weeks to stem the rupee's sharp gains against the dollar.   

The Reserve Bank of India bought $4.43 billion in the foreign exchange market in May, up from $2.06 billion in April, according to lagged data available from the central bank.   

Exporters have been complaining that the rupee's gains have affected their profits.   

Software companies  Infosys Technologies (500209.BY) and  Satyam Computer Services (500376.BY) recently lowered their earnings per share guidance for the current fiscal year due to the sharp gains in the rupee.   

According to R. K. Gurumoorthy, head of foreign exchange trading at  ING Vysya Bank, though the rupee is poised to appreciate further in the near term, a widening trade deficit and rising crude oil prices could put pressure on it.   

"The biggest concern for the rupee is oil prices," he said.   

Global crude oil prices are hovering around a 11-month high of $75.92 a barrel. India imports over 70% of its crude oil requirements.   

India's trade deficit in the January-March period widened to $15.232 billion from $11.752 billion in the year-ago quarter.

title: India cbank buying more bonds with  FX  reserves
text:
MUMBAI, July 20 (Reuters) - India's central bank has increased the percentage of its rising foreign exchange reserves that are invested in foreign bonds, its half-yearly report on the reserves shows.   

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) invested $19 billion in overseas bonds, more than half of the $34 billion increase in its reserves for the six months to the end of March 2007.   

Deposits with other central banks, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) rose by $16 billion, while deposits with foreign commercial banks declined by $1 billion.   

The RBI said it held currency reserves worth $192 billion as at March 31, the end of the 2006/07 financial year. Of those, $53 billion were invested in sovereign bonds, $92 billion with other central banks, the BIS and IMF, and $47 billion were deposited with foreign commercial banks.   

The percentage of its reserves invested in sovereign bonds rose to 27.6 percent from 21.6 percent six months earlier.   

The RBI also held gold worth $6.7 billion.   

Reserves grew 20 percent in 2006/07, and have risen more than 12 percent since then to a record $215 billion in early July, which analysts say largely reflects the central bank's intervention to cap the strength of the rupee <INR=IN>.   

India's foreign exchange reserves are the fifth-largest holdings in Asia.   

India's booming economy -- it grew 9.4 percent in 2006/07 -- has attracted foreigner investors to its markets and industries, and their demand for rupees has pushed the currency to nine-year highs against the dollar.   

Foreign direct investment rose to $17.7 billion in 2006/07 from $7.7 billion a year earlier, the RBI said.

title: RPT-ANALYSIS-India's easy overnight rate not a policy signal
text:
(Repeats story issued late on Wednesday)   

MUMBAI, July 18 (Reuters) - Capital inflows and government spending have kept India's overnight rates below the central bank's lending rate for more than a month, but no one expects a cut when the Reserve Bank of India reviews policy on July 31.   

Overnight cash rates that are lower than a central bank's rates can often suggest pressure to lower the official rates.   

But Indian overnight money below 1 percent signals that policymakers are less worried that extra cash in circulation will stoke inflation, and means they could hold rates steady this time.   

After five rate increases between June 2006 and March this year, annual inflation has slowed from a two-year high of 6.7 percent in January to just above 4 percent at the end of June.   

As a result, the RBI has switched from containing inflation to containing rupee strength, by intervening heavily to keep the currency from breaching a nine-year high of 40.28 per dollar <INR=IN> set in late May.   

"Last year inflation had become a critical problem, now the rupee is more of an issue," said A. Prasanna, an analyst with ICICI Securities in Mumbai.   

"The RBI has achieved what it wanted -- now the focus is on the rupee."   

Overnight money rates <INROND=>, the rate at which commercial banks lend to each other, are a barometer of cash supplies in the banking system. At 0.10-1.0 percent, they are far below the 7.75 percent at which the central bank lends to the market.   

Much of the supply has come from intervention to absorb foreign funds flows into India's record-breaking stock market.   

Foreign investments into local stocks total a net $8.4 billion so far this year, more than the $7.9 billion for all 2006, and in May alone the RBI intervened to the tune of $4.4 billion, taking total intervention in 2007 to $23.4 billion.   

When it intervenes, the central bank buys dollars and sells rupees, which enter the banking system. It often sterilises these potentially inflationary sales by issuing special bonds, but these incur interest and analysts say issuance has not kept pace with intervention because policy-makers want to keep costs down.   

"Right now inflation is not high and you can allow some liquidity to come back into the market," said V. Anantha Nageswaran, head of investment research at  Bank Julius Baer in Singapore.   

WILD MOVEMENTS   

Prasanna at ICICI Securities said the central bank could be going slow on issuing intervention bonds because the cap is 1.1 trillion rupees ($27.23 billion), and it has already issued 802 billion rupees worth. It may also want to keep some firepower in case inflation or rupee pressures build later in the year.   

Others say rupee pressure is likely to ease later this year as capital inflows ease and oil refiners step up dollar buying to keep pace with rising global oil prices.   

But if pressure does continue, the RBI could raise banks' reserve requirements to reduce lendable resources -- a step it took three times between December and the end of March.   

Rajeev Malik, an economist at  JP Morgan in Singapore, said persistently easy cash has led some to expect the central bank to shift from a tightening stance to a neutral stance.   

"We think these expectations are optimistic," Malik said. "Although we expect no more repo (lending) rate hikes, it is too early to signal lower policy rates."   

Although wholesale price inflation, the most widely watched price indicator, is within the RBI's 5 percent comfort zone, money supply is still above target and the property and stock markets remain hot. Only loan growth has shown signs of cooling.   

Short-term borrowing by the government from the central bank topped 300 billion rupees in early July, reflecting higher spending, and analysts say this is also boosting cash supplies.   

But Malik said this could be transitory, with the government front-loading its spending for the fiscal year which began in April, and with less intervention as capital flows ease.   

Overnight rates have swung wildly, hitting a 10-year high of 70 percent in March and a decade low of 0.10 percent in June.   

ICICI Securities' Prasanna said rates would stabilise if the central bank removed a 30 billion rupee cap at its daily borrowing window, which limits how much it can drain from the market. Lifting the cap would incur higher costs for the central bank, but Prasanna said keeping it risked sending wrong signals.   

"If this continues for some more time, banks will likely take it as a signal that things have eased," he said.   

"Deposit rates will ease and so will lending rates and then there will be a dilution of the policy stance."

title: ANALYSIS-India's easy overnight rate not a policy signal
text:
MUMBAI, July 18 (Reuters) - Capital inflows and government spending have kept India's overnight rates below the central bank's lending rate for more than a month, but no one expects a cut when the Reserve Bank of India reviews policy on July 31.   

Overnight cash rates that are lower than a central bank's rates can often suggest pressure to lower the official rates.   

But Indian overnight money below 1 percent signals that policymakers are less worried that extra cash in circulation will stoke inflation, and means they could hold rates steady this time.   

After five rate increases between June 2006 and March this year, annual inflation has slowed from a two-year high of 6.7 percent in January to just above 4 percent at the end of June.   

As a result, the RBI has switched from containing inflation to containing rupee strength, by intervening heavily to keep the currency from breaching a nine-year high of 40.28 per dollar <INR=IN> set in late May.   

"Last year inflation had become a critical problem, now the rupee is more of an issue," said A. Prasanna, an analyst with ICICI Securities in Mumbai.   

"The RBI has achieved what it wanted -- now the focus is on the rupee."   

Overnight money rates <INROND=>, the rate at which commercial banks lend to each other, are a barometer of cash supplies in the banking system. At 0.10-1.0 percent, they are far below the 7.75 percent at which the central bank lends to the market.   

Much of the supply has come from intervention to absorb foreign funds flows into India's record-breaking stock market.   

Foreign investments into local stocks total a net $8.4 billion so far this year, more than the $7.9 billion for all 2006, and in May alone the RBI intervened to the tune of $4.4 billion, taking total intervention in 2007 to $23.4 billion.   

When it intervenes, the central bank buys dollars and sells rupees, which enter the banking system. It often sterilises these potentially inflationary sales by issuing special bonds, but these incur interest and analysts say issuance has not kept pace with intervention because policy-makers want to keep costs down.   

"Right now inflation is not high and you can allow some liquidity to come back into the market," said V. Anantha Nageswaran, head of investment research at  Bank Julius Baer in Singapore.   

WILD MOVEMENTS   

Prasanna at ICICI Securities said the central bank could be going slow on issuing intervention bonds because the cap is 1.1 trillion rupees ($27.23 billion), and it has already issued 802 billion rupees worth. It may also want to keep some firepower in case inflation or rupee pressures build later in the year.   

Others say rupee pressure is likely to ease later this year as capital inflows ease and oil refiners step up dollar buying to keep pace with rising global oil prices.   

But if pressure does continue, the RBI could raise banks' reserve requirements to reduce lendable resources -- a step it took three times between December and the end of March.   

Rajeev Malik, an economist at  JP Morgan in Singapore, said persistently easy cash has led some to expect the central bank to shift from a tightening stance to a neutral stance.   

"We think these expectations are optimistic," Malik said. "Although we expect no more repo (lending) rate hikes, it is too early to signal lower policy rates."   

Although wholesale price inflation, the most widely watched price indicator, is within the RBI's 5 percent comfort zone, money supply is still above target and the property and stock markets remain hot. Only loan growth has shown signs of cooling.   

Short-term borrowing by the government from the central bank topped 300 billion rupees in early July, reflecting higher spending, and analysts say this is also boosting cash supplies.   

But Malik said this could be transitory, with the government front-loading its spending for the fiscal year which began in April, and with less intervention as capital flows ease.   

Overnight rates have swung wildly, hitting a 10-year high of 70 percent in March and a decade low of 0.10 percent in June.   

ICICI Securities' Prasanna said rates would stabilise if the central bank removed a 30 billion rupee cap at its daily borrowing window, which limits how much it can drain from the market. Lifting the cap would incur higher costs for the central bank, but Prasanna said keeping it risked sending wrong signals.   

"If this continues for some more time, banks will likely take it as a signal that things have eased," he said.   

"Deposit rates will ease and so will lending rates and then there will be a dilution of the policy stance."

MUMBAI, July 16 (Reuters) - India's central bank bought $4.43 billion in intervention in May, the month the rupee rose to a nine-year high against the dollar, the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) monthly bulletin showed on Monday.   

May's intervention took the RBI's dollar purchases to $28.4 billion since the start of November 2006.

Record highs in the stock market have attracted foreign investors and pushed the rupee back to its May highs. On Monday, the rupee hit a high of 40.30, while India's main share index <.BSESN> ended at a record close.   

The rupee has appreciated more than 9.5 percent in 2007, making it Asia's best performing currency against the dollar.   

Foreigners bought $2.1 billion of equities in the first nine trading days of July, taking total purchases for 2007 to $7.8 billion -- just below the $7.9 billion they bought over all of 2006.   

India's foreign exchange reserves were $214.84 billion on July 6, up $37.6 billion so far in 2007. Traders said a large part of that increase was due to the RBI's dollar purchases.

title: India rupee strength to persist on flows-top dealer
text:
MUMBAI, June 21 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is likely to be rangebound through July and remain near a recent nine-year peak, buoyed by capital inflows into the surging economy, a top dealer at Standard Chartered said.   

The rupee would be underpinned by about $40 billion of capital inflows in the fiscal year ending March 2008, led by a spurt in equity-related investments, he said.   

"Capital flows are strong and are going to remain strong," Agam Gupta, head of foreign exchange and derivatives trading, told Reuters in an interview this week.   

"I also see a lot of money coming in the form of FDI (foreign direct investment) and private equity," said Gupta, who started his career in 1995 at  ANZ Grindlays. Standard Chartered bought it in 2000.   

The rupee has gained about 8.5 percent against the U.S. currency this year and hit 40.28 per dollar <INR=IN> late last May, its highest since 1998. It has since been trading in a broad 40.50-41.25 range and ended at 40.71/72 on Thursday.   

"40.50 is where the central bank has shown definite resolve to intervene, and when it spikes to 41.25, you see very, very good exporter interest and a lot of capital inflows."   

Gupta said he saw the rupee between 40.50-41.50 through to August.   

The Reserve Bank of India was unlikely to intervene aggressively against the rupee on a day-to-day basis but would move to stem strong appreciation in the currency, he said.   

"For the first part of the year its focus was primarily on controlling inflation. Now that the headline number is trending down, there is a definite shift in focus, partly to exchange rates."   

The central bank is widely suspected of selling rupees over to stem its rise. This has led to a surfeit of cash in the system, reflected in overnight interbank lending rates hovering near a recent 10-year low of 0.1 percent.   

"The market is getting slightly confused by what is happening in the call market and is starting to accept that call rates are going to remain volatile on both sides of the corridor," said Gupta, who expects call rates to rise to 6-8 percent next week.   

He said most Indian companies with sizeable foreign exchange exposures had hedged against currency fluctuations but many small exporters were still overexposed.   

"A lot of the smaller exporters have been dumbfounded by this extreme move and I hope they start hedging whenever they get a good level because I think this range is here to stay for some time."

title: India Markets-Share index at new high after scaling 6,500.
text:
BOMBAY, Dec 24 (Reuters) - India's key share index continued a dizzying climb on Friday, ending at a new high after scaling the 6,500 point mark amid a global holiday rally, while the rupee gave up gains to end weaker on central bank intervention.  

Federal bonds remained upbeat after data showed India's wholesale price inflation rate had eased more than expected and dropped below 7 percent for the first time since July.  

The 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange index ended up 0.87 percent at 6,498.06 points, just off a new intraday high of 6,507.94 points. Gainers beat losers 1,183 to 827 in heavy trade of 356 million shares.  

The index, which rose 2.4 percent on the week, has now gained more than 11 percent in 2004.  

Traders said hopes of an early end to a feud in the Ambani family that founded India's largest private company boosted shares of Reliance Industries Ltd. 3.5 percent. Reliance has a nearly 11 percent weightage in the Bombay index.  

News its chairman and the elder of two sparring brothers, Mukesh Ambani, was giving up a stake in a group telecoms company raised hopes a settlement was near. For a detailed story, please  

"Reliance was the major driver today, and foreign fund flows have been strong, supporting the index at these high levels," said Nimish Shah, chief executive of Parag Parikh Financial Advisory Services Ltd.  

"Besides, investors are beginning to look forward to a strong corporate earnings season in January," he said.  

Oil refiners gained as front-month NYMEX crude prices remained depressed, hovering just above $44 per barrel. State-run Hindustan Petroleum Corp. rose 2.7 percent and Bharat Petroleum Corp. rose 1.4 percent.  

Metal makers shone on expectations of robust demand and firm prices. Leading steel producers, state-run Steel Authority of India Ltd. and Tata Iron and Steel Co. rose 2.7 percent and 3.7 percent respectively.  

Software services firms shrugged off a weak U.S. dollar and rose on expectations of strong quarterly earnings growth, with Tata Consultancy Services Ltd., the No. 1 services exporter, rising 3.2 percent and third-ranked Wipro Ltd., adding 1.2 percent.  

Sentiment was also boosted by strong foreign fund inflows and a fall in local inflation. Offshore funds have bought a record nearly $8.3 billion of Indian shares this year.  

The rupee shed 0.06 percent in thin trade to close at 43.78/80 per dollar after the central bank's intervention to bring it off an early 43.65 peak dampened the mood.  

Still, the local currency ended the week 0.37 percent stronger, taking its gains in 2004 to 4.12 percent.  

Federal bonds ended the week on a strong note as investors cheered data that showed inflation was finally moderating.  

Energy and commodities prices had fuelled a spike in inflation from May, forcing the Indian central bank to tighten credit for the first time in four years in September.  

Lower food and energy prices helped India's wholesale price inflation in the year to Dec. 11 ease to 6.73 percent, from 7.02 percent in the previous week. The rate was also lower than the 6.95 percent median estimate in a Reuters poll.  

The yield on the actively traded 7.38 percent 2015 bond dipped to 6.5453 percent, 18 basis points lower in the week.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won weakens on  intervention  fears.
text:
By Rajat Bhattacharya
    SINGAPORE, Dec 17 (Reuters) - The South Korean won weakened
on Friday as indications of increased dollar-buying
intervention by the South Korean central bank and
better-than-expected U.S. current account data helped the
dollar.
    The won        lost a quarter of a percent to 1,059 per
dollar after the Bank of Korea said it had carried out
"smoothing operations" in the won market in the first half of
December, boosting the country's foreign exchange reserves by
$3.4 billion.
    Analysts said the central banks of South Korea, Singapore
and India had stepped up dollar-buying intervention since
November to slow an Asian currency rally triggered by concerns
that a record U.S. current account deficit would hurt the
dollar.
 
    Stronger currencies make Asian exports, a key source of
growth in the region, less competitive in the United States.
  


    "With domestic demand still fragile (in South Korea),
expect such smoothing' behaviour to persist if the won renews
its strong appreciation trend," ABN AMRO Bank said in a report.
    The won has led the rally in Asian currencies since the
  

start of October and is Asia's best performing currency this  

year, having gained almost 13 percent. It hit a seven-year high  

near 1,037 per dollar on December 6, but has since lost ground.  

It has fallen one percent since the end of November.  

The Taiwan dollar has gained 5 percent and the  

Singapore dollar strengthened 3.2 percent as the yen has  

appreciated 2.6 percent this year.  

Data showing the U.S. current account deficit was narrower  

than expected in the third quarter, even though at a record  

high, helped ease some concerns about the dollar.  

"Taken collectively, the data suggests that the financing  

of the current account deficit was not a major problem in the  

third quarter, in the context of solid but not spectacular  

official inflows," said Alan Ruskin, an analyst at 4CAST, in a  

report.  

"The bad quarters, in contrast, see the dollar under marked  

pressure, and the current account and financial account data  

for the fourth quarter is likely to provide a far less  

encouraging picture longer-term," he said.  

The third-quarter data came a day after U.S. Treasury  

figures showed net inflows into the United States in October  

were not enough to cover that month's record $55.5 billion  

trade deficit.  

TAIWAN DOLLAR, BAHT  

The Taiwan dollar and the Thai baht are expected to lead  

another Asian rally against a weakening dollar because of the  

strength of their economies and greater central bank tolerance  

for currency strength, JP Morgan said in a report.  

Improving labour markets in South Korea, Hong Kong and  

Singapore and increased foreign equity investment in South  

Korea, Taiwan and Thailand would support currencies, JP Morgan  

said.  

The baht weakened a quarter of a percent to 39.25 per  

dollar, paring gains made on Thursday after a surprise 25 basis  

point interest rate rise by the Bank of Thailand.  

The Indonesian rupiah lost half a percent on renewed  

concerns about a drop in foreign direct investment and higher  

fuel subsidies which have widened the budget deficit.  

On Thursday, Japan's trade minister, Shoichi Nakagawa, said  

Indonesia needed to tackle corruption and improve law  

enforcement if it wanted Japanese investment to return.

title: Indian Rupee Hits 7-Mo High Vs Dlr; Govt Bonds Higher
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee extended its rally against the dollar Tuesday, hitting a seven-month high as surging local share prices fueled hopes that strong capital inflows will persist.  

Broad dollar weakness and scaled-back central bank intervention underscored the rupee's strength. The Reserve Bank of India had been a dollar buyer in recent weeks, but has significantly slowed down its purchases since Monday, traders said.  

The dollar closed at INR44.63 Tuesday, a level last tested in early May. It ended at INR44.82 Monday.  

"The stock market rally has driven today's forex trend. With Indian equity still looking good to buy, foreigners are going to pump more money here," said a trader at a local bank.  

The key Indian share index, the Bombay Stock Exchange Sensitive Index closed at a record high of 6234.29 points on heavy inflows of foreign portfolio investment. Such inflows have reached a record high of $6.93 billion so far in 2004, beating the previous record of $6.59 billion for the whole of 2003.  

Analysts expect dollar weakness and increased capital inflows into the stock market to help the rupee rise further in coming months.  

Siddharth Mathur, head of research at J.P. Morgan in Mumbai, forecasts that the dollar will extend its slide to INR44.30 by the end of 2004, and to INR43.20 by mid-2005.  

Dollar forward rates edged up Tuesday, despite the U.S. currency's fall on the spot market, on buying by state-owned banks. The one-year forward contract ended at a 0.77% premium to the spot rate, up from 0.66% at the previous close.  

Mifor-based interest rate swaps ended slightly higher Tuesday, tracking forward-dollar premiums. The two-year Mifor swap hardened to 4.30%-4.35% from 4.18%-4.23% at the previous close, while the five-year swap rose to 5.10%-5.15% from 5.00%-5.05%.  

Government bond prices ended slightly higher Tuesday on scattered bargain hunting after Monday's decline. The actively traded 7.55% 2010 bond ended at INR103.20, up from INR103.05 at the previous close. Its yield edged lower to 6.83% from 6.87%.  

Bonds could drift lower in the coming sessions due to weak demand as traders await details of a federal government bond auction due in the first week of December.  

The overnight call money rate closed unchanged at 4.70%-4.80% in adequate money market liquidity. [ 30-11-04 1322GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1-Indian reserves composition a "dynamic situation".
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 24 (Reuters) - India's central bank chief said the composition of the country's foreign exchange reserves could change when asked on Wednesday if the bank was considering boosting its holdings of the strengthening euro.  

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) does not give a breakdown of its reserves - the world's fifth-largest - but analysts said it may already have reduced the proportion of dollar holdings and would likely continue to do so.  

India's reserves, which comprise dollars, euros, sterling and yen in undisclosed proportions, have risen by nearly $23 billion so far in 2004 to a record $123.5 billion.  

"The question of composition of reserves ... it's a very dynamic situation. You can't take a view on a daily basis," Governor Y.V. Reddy told reporters on the sidelines of a news conference.  

The dollar has long been held as a reserve currency, but the single European currency hit a record high against it on Tuesday, and again on Wednesday, after the Russian central bank said it could review the share of euros it holds among its $113 billion in reserves.  

Asian central banks have been among the largest buyers of dollars as the economic tide turned in their countries' favour leading to massive investment and trade inflows.  

These banks were partly looking to build up their ammunition following a crisis in 1997 and to protect their trade competitiveness.  

But the U.S. unit has declined sharply because of doubts about the fundamentals of the U.S. economy, which is running wide fiscal and trade deficits. It has fallen nearly 4.5 percent against the euro so far in 2004.  

"SHIFT PROBABLE"  

India's central bank has been actively intervening in the foreign exchange market, absorbing strong trade and investment inflows to temper a rising rupee , which is up 3 percent to 45.05 a dollar from a 2004 closing low of 46.45 in late July.  

Analysts said Reddy's statement suggested the RBI was following closely the fall in the dollar's value and would adjust the makeup of its reserves accordingly.  

"What Reddy tried to say today is that the RBI is dynamically reviewing the situation, which suggests the composition of the reserves will depend on the outlook for various currencies," said S.P. Prabhu, analyst with IDBI Capital Market Services.  

"So they would probably shift to more euros, pounds and yen."  

Analysts said they believed the bank may already have been reducing its dollar holdings.  

"I would say we have a mixed bag of currencies, and while the dollar may be the single largest, the holding will not be overwhelming," said Saumitra Choudhuri, economic adviser to rating agency ICRA Ltd.  

"Our studies suggest we have a significant holding of the euro and the sterling. Because we have diversified our basket over the years based on currency outlooks, the sharp fall in the dollar will not be much of a concern."  

Analysts say the RBI will likely continue with its policy of not disclosing the composition of its reserves.  

"Its not a good idea for the central bank to talk about this as it doesn't want to give the exact foreign exchange position," Choudhuri said. "Otherwise, people will start anticipating and speculating, which makes the central bank's life very difficult."  

Negative sentiment towards the dollar was reinforced last week after the Group of 20 rich and developing nations gave no indication they would take action to stem the dollar's fall at a high profile meeting in Berlin.  

The United States also appeared to accept the downtrend.  

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said last week that the market appetite for U.S. assets would dwindle, and forex inflows could become insufficient to offset the current account deficit.

title: India  central bank  bought $19 mln of  forex  in Sept.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 22 (Reuters) - India's central bank resumed its dollar-buying interventions after four months in September and bought a net $19 million in the local currency market, data from its monthly bulletin showed on Monday.   

The Reserve Bank of India had sold $875.5 million in August. Total sales over the four-month period between May and August, when the rupee was under pressure after foreign fund inflows were hit following a change of government, add up to $2.69 billion.   

In September, the central bank bought $143 million of foreign currency, while selling just $124 million.   

The central bank's outstanding net forward purchases at the end of September totalled $5 million, compared with $110 million a month earlier.

title: Indian rupee eases early as dollar's rise weighs.
text:

record lows against the euro after the U.S. Federal Reserve

    Traders were also wary about central bank intervention,

title: ANALYSIS-Wary of inflation, India cbank may let rupee rise.
text:
BOMBAY, Sept 14 (Reuters) - India's central bank is likely to allow the rupee to rise against the dollar in the near term to try to curb inflationary pressures that threaten growth and stability in Asia's fourth-largest economy, analysts said.   

Until a few weeks ago, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was selling dollars to check a sharp rupee slide. Now with the currency rising, it is unlikely to step in to buy dollars because rupee appreciation makes imports cheaper and the bank's task of combating inflation easier.   

"A stronger rupee will help checking inflation a bit," said M.R. Madhavan, strategist at Bank of America, Singapore.   

"A 1 percent appreciation in the currency will lower price levels by about 0.3 percent."   

The partially convertible rupee has gained 0.8 percent this week and broke past the key 46 per dollar level to end at a two-month high of 45.9050/9150 on Tuesday - with little indication the central bank would curb the relatively sharp rise.   

India's central bank has maintained it intervenes to curb volatility and does not use the currency to moderate inflation.   

The rupee has risen due to a broadly weaker dollar, hopes of improved foreign capital inflows into a rising stock market and on expectations that domestic inflation has peaked.   

India's inflation spiralled to a new 3-1/2-year high of 8.33 percent in the year to Aug. 28. from 4.32 percent in late April prompting the central bank to announce a 0.5 percent increase in banks' cash reserve ratio (CRR) which will absorb 85 billion rupees from the banking system.   

The CRR, or proportion of banks' deposits kept with the central bank, has been raised for the first time in four years.   

RBI MEASURE HELPS   

The measure announced on Saturday followed duty cuts by the government on fuel and commodities like steel a few weeks ago. Authorities have attributed the spike in inflation mainly to supply-side factors like firm prices of commodities such as crude oil as well as excess cash in the banking system.   

"With the decision to raise the reserve ratio, there is a growing perception that the central bank is unlikely intervene to buy dollars as it would add to more rupee liquidity in the system," said U. Venkatraman, head of trading at IDBI Bank said.   

"So I expect the rupee to gain to 45.80 in the near term, provided crude oil prices do not spike."   

Some analysts say the CRR increase may be the first signal that interest rates are set to rise from three-decade lows. That will likely help the rupee against the dollar as interest rate differentials between the United States and India widen.   

The rupee has lost ground since hitting a 51-month high of 43.5450/5500 per dollar on April 7, partly as a result of a slowdown in foreign capital inflows after a surprise change in the Indian government at elections in May.   

Rising U.S. interest rates and a spike in prices of crude oil, India's largest import item, have also weighed on the rupee.   

Foreign fund inflows are expected to increase on hopes of better earnings from Indian corporates after data showed industrial production rose 7.9 percent in July compared with a 6.6 percent rise last year.   

Foreign funds poured in about $4 billion in the first four months of the calendar year, but their investments have slowed since then. They invested $556 million in August and have pumped in nearly $181 million in the first 10 days of September.   

Analysts said the central bank's move to allow the rupee to appreciate was unlikely to harm exporters. Exports rose 20 percent in the year to March 2004, even as the rupee appreciated by 9 percent against the dollar.

title: India 's  forex  reserves fall on c.bank  intervention .
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 7 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves fell by more than 1 billion dollars for a second successive week on July 30, mainly due to the central bank's intervention to support a shaky rupee, data showed on Saturday.  

Analysts said a weaker euro, pound sterling and yen, all of which are part of foreign currency assets that are expressed in U.S. dollar terms, also contributed to the decline.  

The reserves dropped $1.26 billion to $118.32 billion on July 30 from $119.58 billion a week earlier, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said.  

The reserves in Asia's fourth-largest economy are now down about $2.8 billion from a record $121.11 billion on July 16, but are still up more than $15 billion so far in 2004.  

"There could have been some revaluation losses but the main reason for the decline appears to have been central bank intervention," said Indranil Pan, economist at Kotak Mahindra Bank.  

Foreign currency assets fell by $1.25 billion in the week, while the Reserve Tranche Position with the International Monetary Fund eased by $8 million. Reserves also include gold, special drawing rights in the IMF.  

At Friday's close of 46.36/37 a dollar, the rupee has lost about 1.7 percent this year after posting a record 5.2 percent gain in 2003.  

The rupee, which is only partially convertible, has been under pressure since hitting a 51-month high of 43.545/550 in early April as foreign capital inflows slowed on uncertainty over economic reforms after a shock win for a communist-backed coalition in national elections.  

After pumping in an average of more than $1 billion a month into Indian shares in the first 4 months of 2004, foreign funds were net sellers of nearly $740 million in May and made only relatively small purchases in the next two months.  

Analysts said the rupee was also under pressure due to a surge in oil prices, which hit record highs this week.  

India imports about 70 percent of its crude oil requirements and oil is the biggest single item on the import bill. It accounted for 30 percent of the country's imports of $22.4 billion in the April-June quarter.

title: UPDATE 1- India 's reserves fall on cbank  intervention .
text:
BOMBAY, July 31 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves fell by $1.53 billion in the week to July 23, as the central bank dipped into its war chest to supply scarce dollars and aggressively support a beleaguered rupee, analysts said.  

Data released on Saturday showed foreign exchange reserves in Asia's fourth-largest economy fell to $119.58 billion on July 23 from a record high $121.11 billion a week earlier.  

For details,  

"The fall in reserves definitely reflects the large-scale dollar-selling intervention by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) that week to calm a panicky market as the rupee depreciated to a year low," said Shubhada Rao, economist at Bank of Baroda.  

"While there could have been some revaluation losses in that period, the reserves used by the central bank to keep the market well supplied with dollars and prevent the rupee from falling too rapidly must account for the major portion of the fall."  

Despite the latest week's fall, India's reserves are still up nearly $18 billion in 2004, making it Asia's sixth-largest stockpile.  

The week's decline was almost entirely in the foreign currency assets portion of the reserves, which fell by $1.52 billion. Reserves also include gold, special drawing rights and India's Reserve Tranche Position in the International Monetary Fund.  

The RBI said the foreign currency assets expressed in U.S. dollar terms included the effect of appreciation or depreciation of other currencies held in its reserves such as the euro, pound sterling and yen.  

The euro depreciated by nearly 3 percent against the dollar in the week ended July 23, after the Federal Reserve chief's upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy bolstered expectations of an interest rate hike, spurring a greenback rally. The Indian rupee, which is only partially convertible, lost 0.77 percent against the U.S. currency that week to dip to a near 13-month closing low.  

The Indian currency has been under intense pressure in the past two months as foreign capital inflows have slowed on uncertainty over the pace of economic reforms after a Communist-backed government won national elections.  

The rupee has lost 6.2 percent since scaling a 51-month closing peak of 43.5450/5500 per dollar on April 7.  

Foreign funds' purchases of local assets, which had been a major factor in helping the rupee appreciate until the April peak, have fallen sharply since then.  

Although foreign funds' purchase have turned positive in July, at $198.4 million of net investments they are still less than a fifth of the $1 billion average in the first four months of 2004.  

That has affected the rupee, which at Friday's close of 46.4350/4550 per dollar was down 1.83 percent against the dollar in 2004, following a record 5.2 percent gain last year.

title: Asian central banks step in as  currencies  trip up.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, July 28 (Reuters) - Asian central banks appear
to be intervening in foreign exchange markets this week after a
three-month lull, but this time they have been buying their
currencies against a resurgent U.S. dollar, traders say.
    Central banks in India, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and
Indonesia are all suspected to have intervened as some of their
currencies hit lows for the year against the dollar this week.
    That represents a change in tack after the heavy
dollar-buying intervention they conducted through all of 2003
and the first few months of 2004, boosting their combined
foreign reserves to over $2 trillion.
 
    Traders cited dollar-selling intervention in India, where
the rupee hit a fresh one-year low of 46.35/40 on Wednesday.
    The Taiwan dollar has shed about 1.5 percent in less than
   

three weeks and on Wednesday hit 33.23, its lowest in eight   

months. Traders in Singapore said they had heard that the   

central bank offered U.S. dollars in onshore markets above   

34.20.   

Expectations of higher yields in a rebounding U.S. economy,   

weakness in technology stocks and diminishing interest in the   

once-popular Chinese yuan revaluation trade seemed to be   

driving foreign funds out of Asia, analysts said.   

But they felt that policy makers might be reacting too   

quickly, given they had been battling strength in their   

currencies for a couple of years, until April.    


 
    "Some of them are hypersensitive at this moment in time,"
said Claudio Piron, a strategist with Standard Chartered Bank.
    "And it seems to be a combination of where the currencies

are in historical terms, where they are in their trade-weighted   

baskets and also in terms of managing inflationary   

expectations."   

POLICY DILEMMA   

Piron said the Thai baht's two percent slide in two weeks   

had taken it to its lowest levels historically in   

trade-weighted terms. The baht hit 41.45, its weakest since   

August 2003, on Wednesday.   

Although Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula   

said the weak baht would not hurt the economy, traders   

suspected the authorities would sell dollars if there were   

further losses.   

Similarly, analysts said it was reasonable for the Monetary   

Authority of Singapore (MAS) to worry if the Sing dollar moved   

too far to the weaker side of the trade-weighted band it is   

managed in, particularly after the central bank announced in   

April it wanted to tighten policy by guiding the currency

higher.   

Local banks in Singapore were seen buying their currency

this week, spurring suspicion they were acting on behalf of the   

MAS.    


 
    South Korean markets have been baffled by conflicting
statements from policy makers.
    More than any country in the region, South Korea is faced
   

with the dilemma of whether to continue with a policy of   

boosting exports through a cheap currency, despite the risk of   

higher imported inflation from rising oil and commodity prices.   

"In Korea, they are getting a bit more sensitive in terms   

of price expectations and some of the inflationary pressure,"   

Piron said. "Some of the growth picture has started to fade,   

but they don't want price inflation to also deteriorate."   

Nonetheless, analysts said inflation was still benign in   

Asia and central banks might be acting to curb market   

volatility rather than signalling a shift in policy.

BOMBAY, July 5 (Reuters) - The Indian central bank's investments in foreign securities like U.S. Treasury notes rose 30 percent to $35.024 billion in the past year to March 2004, data from the central bank showed on Monday.   

But 40 percent of the $112.959 billion of foreign exchange reserves as on March 31, 2004, was deployed as deposits with other central banks and the Bank of International Settlements, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said.   

The RBI deployed $45.877 billion as deposits with other central banks, up 37 percent from the year earlier.   

India's foreign exchange reserves, currently at $119 billion, were built amid steady intervention by the central bank in the currency market as it sought to absorb the robust inflows from foreign funds, expatriate Indians and exports.   

India's central bank intervenes through state-run banks in the currency market to keep exports competitive and prevent sharp swings.   

The central bank last week said foreign portfolio investment shot up to $11.36 billion in the year to March 2004, compared with $944 million a year earlier helped up an upgrade of the country's soverign rating to investment status by Moody's Investors Service and lured by India's strong economic recovery.   

Deposits from expatriate Indians, seeking higher returns on local fixed income assets, rose to $3.6 billion in the year to March 2004, from $3.0 billion a year earlier.   

India's central bank in the statement on Monday said that the ratio of short-term debt to foreign exchange reserves declined to 4.2 percent as on March 31, 2004 from 146.5 percent at end March 1991 and 6.1 percent on March 31, 2003.

title: UPDATE 1- India 's reserves fall on cbank  intervention .
text:
BOMBAY, July 3 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves fell by half a billion dollars in the week to June 25, easing from a record high struck a week earlier, data showed on Saturday, and analysts said the fall was due to central bank intervention.   

Data released on Saturday showed foreign exchange reserves in Asia's third-largest economy fell to $119.41 billion on June 25 from $119.9 billion a week earlier.   

"It (the fall) is clearly not just the effect of revaluation and shows the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) sold dollars during that week," said Siddharth Mathur, strategist at JP Morgan Securities in Bombay.   

"Revaluation and foreign fund sales do not account for the whole amount. There seems to have been an outflow of around half a billion dollars in addition to these two factors," he said.   

The decline was almost entirely in the foreign currency assets portion of the reserves, which fell by $530 million. Reserves also include gold, special drawing rights and India's Reserve Tranche Position in the International Monetary Fund.   

The RBI said the foreign currency assets expressed in U.S. dollar terms included the effect of appreciation/depreciation of other currencies held in its reserves such as the euro, pound sterling and yen.   

Despite the latest week's fall, India's reserves were up some $17 billion since January, making it the sixth-largest pile in Asia.   

Traders said the central bank intervened during the week ended June 25 to stem volatility in the rupee.   

The rupee slid to an 11-month intra-day low of 46.34 a dollar during that week from the previous week's close of 45.6650/6800. The central bank's dollar sales helped the rupee trim its losses to end that week at 45.83/85.   

The RBI has said it does not target any exchange rate for the rupee, which is only partly convertible, and intervenes only to moderate volatility.   

The rupee has come under presure in the past two months as foreign investment inflows slowed down on uncertainty over the pace of economic reforms after national elections brought a Communist-backed government to power.   

Foreign funds have sold more than $900 million worth of Indian bonds and shares since May on those fears.   

The rupee has in turn suffered. It ended Friday at 45.88/89 a dollar, some 5 percent down from a 51-month peak of 43.545/550 struck in early April.   

It is down about 0.6 percent against the dollar in 2004, following a record 5.24 percent gain last year.

title: India Rupee Falls To 9-Mo Low; Breaks Key 46/Dlr Support
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee hit a nine-month low against the dollar in early trading Tuesday, breaking the key INR46 psychological barrier amid expectations that strong corporate dollar buying, which dragged the local unit down Monday, will continue.  

Thirty minutes into trading Tuesday, the dollar was at INR46.0700, a level last tested on September 18, 2003.  

The rupee closed at INR45.9250 Monday.  

Banks heavily bought the dollar as soon as the market opened, expecting the strong corporate demand for the greenback to continue.  

"Several companies appear to be securing their near-term import and debt payment needs on fears the dollar could strengthen from current levels," said a trader with a local bank.  

Indeed, after a lull that lasted many recent months when the rupee had been strengthening, corporate dollar demand has picked up in recent weeks on the view that the dollar's multiyear fall in international markets may be nearing its end. [ 22-06-04 0418GMT ]  

Apart from the rising dollar demand from companies, currency arbitrage between the local and the overseas Non-Deliverable Forward markets is also weighing the rupee down.  

"The fact that the rupee has fallen more in the NDF market has created an arbitrage opportunity - many banks are buying dollars against rupees in the local market and selling them in the NDF market at a higher rate," said a local treasury head.  

In the NDF market, the one-month forward dollar was quoted at INR46.40 Tuesday.  

Traders expect the rupee to extend losses Tuesday if corporate dollar buying continues as expected. However, a further sharp fall is likely to be prevented by central bank intervention - the Reserve Bank of India may sell dollars through state-owned banks to support the local currency.  

"The next support for the rupee could be INR46.25," says a currency strategist with a local bank.

title: WRAPUP 3-Indian stocks crash on fears left may stall reforms.
text:
BOMBAY, May 17 (Reuters) - Indian stocks plunged as much as 17 percent on Monday in their biggest ever intra-day drop in a frenzied sell-off on signs that a new government dependent on leftist support will struggle to push through economic reforms.  

The rupee and bonds fell sharply, having been boosted over the past year by record levels of foreign investment pouring into Asia's third-largest economy, though the rupee made a recovery on central bank intervention.  

The market turmoil forced the Reserve Bank of India to make an emergency statement, reassuring investors that it would intervene if necessary to make sure the banking system and foreign exchange market worked smoothly.  

The comments helped drag markets off session lows, but stocks still ended down 11.1 percent on the day, at their lowest since October, with $27 billion of investor wealth wiped out.  

"There is absolute chaos and my retail clients have lost heavily," said Hemang Raja, chief executive of Bombay brokerage IL&FS Investsmart. "People are talking about foreign funds looking to pull out $1 billion to $2 billion from India."  

Foreign funds sold around $615 million worth of Indian shares in the nine sessions to Friday, or around 15 percent of what they had invested this year prior to the sell-off.  

India's communist parties, after deciding not to sign up formally to Sonia Gandhi's Congress party and its allies, due to take office in two days, called on Monday for increased farm subsidies and a shutdown of the privatisation ministry.  

"The fact that the left parties have decided not to join the government is a further blow to sentiment," Raja said.  

TRADERS PROTEST, TRADE SUSPENDED  

The Bombay Stock Exchange and National Stock Exchange suspended trade twice on Monday after their benchmark indices fell 15.5 percent and 17.5 percent respectively.  

When markets resumed trade, buying by state-backed financial institutions helped pull benchmark indices off their lows.  

The market was closed for three hours and only open for two-and-a-half, yet volume totalled a healthy 121 million shares.  

The Bombay index closed 564.71 points lower at 4,505.16, its second-biggest daily points loss after a fall of 570.42 points on April 28, 1992, at the height of a stock market scandal. But at its low, it was down 842.37 points or 16.6 percent - a record.  

Hundreds of people, including stock brokers and dealers, piled onto the streets outside the Bombay Stock Exchange in an impromptu protest against the incoming government, screaming "Sonia Gandhi Hai Hai (Down with Sonia Gandhi)."  

Indian markets have been heading down for three weeks since exit polls first indicated the pro-reform Bharatiya Janata Party-led (BJP) government may not return. Including Monday's plunge, share markets have lost some $75 billion since then.  

"This is the worst day in our lives - we've lost everything, we're dead," said Bombay broker Sandeep Sirsalewalla.  

"We want the BJP back."  

The rupee dropped as much as 0.8 percent to an eight-month intra-day low of 46.01 rupees per dollar, before recovering in afternoon trade after the Reserve Bank statement. It ended at 45.515/525, up from Friday's close of 45.60/64.  

STATE-RUN FIRMS SUFFER  

Monday's falls were led by banks and state-run firms.  

Oil and Natural Gas Corporation, India's most valuable company, fell 13 percent to 629.75 rupees while Shipping Corporation of India slid 19 percent to 69.60 rupees.  

State Bank of India fell 13 percent and Oriental Bank of Commerce plunged 24 percent.  

Traders said the sharp slide was made worse by margin calls - in which brokers have to deposit money with the exchanges to back up transactions - following heavy losses last week.  

"Hedge funds are selling at any price. The fall today has more to do with technical positions (rather than) any political worries," said Ambareesh Baliga, vice president at Karvy Stock Broking. "Stop-losses got triggered, margin calls were made."  

Political leaders appealed for calm in the markets.  

"There is no need for panic," said Pranab Mukherjee, a senior Congress leader and a frontrunner for the finance minister's job.  

But the Communist Party of India repeated on Monday last week's statement that there was no need for a ministry charged with privatising firms.  

"The left parties should not have made such statements before the formation of the new government. It has totally demoralised the market," said Sudip Kothari, a Bombay-based businessman.  

Privatisation was one of the biggest reforms of the outgoing government, helping attract more than $10 billion in foreign equity investment into India since the start of 2003. This helped boost the Bombay share index by 73 percent last year, making it Asia's best performer after Thailand.  

The inflows also helped the rupee climb more than five percent against the dollar last year, as investors flocked to a country which is among the world's fastest-growing economies. (Additional reporting by Denny Thomas, Rina Chandran and Rosemary Arackaparambil).

title: UPDATE 1- India FX  reserves at new peak on cbank  intervention .
text:
BOMBAY, April 24 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves rose to a record $117.59 billion in the week ended April 16 as the central bank continued to mop up a bulk of the overseas capital flowing into the country, analysts said.  

Data from the central bank, showed India's foreign exchange reserves rose by $1.53 billion from $116.06 billion in the week ended April 9.  

The weekly rise was however less than half the previous week's $3.37 billion increase - which was one of the highest weekly gains.  

The pace of the reserve build-up in recent weeks has made Asia's sixth-largest pile of reserves one of the fastest growing as well, having risen 16.9 percent so far in 2004.  

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said the foreign currency assets expressed in U.S. dollar terms included the effect of appreciation/depreciation of other currencies held in its reserves such as the euro, pound sterling and yen.  

Analysts sadid reserve accumulation largely reflects the central bank's determination to stem sharp gains by the local currency against the dollar, which has rebounded overseas in recent sessions, to protect export competitiveness.  

"The reserves growth continues to reflect the currency management measures being undertaken by the central bank in the face of strong capital flows into the economy," said Siddharth Mathur, strategist at JP Morgan Chase, Bombay.  

"And given that this has happened in the backdrop of the dollar's appreciation versus the euro and other majors means that in real terms the accretion should have been slightly higher."  

BUOYANT PORTFOLIO FLOWS  

Analysts said overseas funds appeared unperturbed by the country's massive general election which began on April 20 and ends on May 10 and continued to pour money into local assets.  

Their net purchases of shares and debt so far in 2004 total $4.4 billion, already more than half the $7.7 billion they invested in 2003.  

"With the elections going on, one would have expected foreign capital flows to somewhat ease this month. But that does not appear to be happening," said Saumitra Chaudhuri, economic adviser at Indian credit rating agency, ICRA.  

Analysts said the fact that the Reserve Bank of India had armed itself with new stabilisation bonds to offset the effects of its currency market intervention in the new fiscal year from April 1, was likely a key factor in its stepped up interventions.  

The central bank can now tap into securities of up to 600 billion rupees ($13.6 billion) to drain the rupee funds it injects into the banking system every time it buys dollars.  

The Indian central bank which has been grappling with steady foreign capital inflows in the past two years, had almost run out of rupee assets towards the latter half of March, when it briefly loosened its grip on the local currency.  

That sparked a rupee rally that took the unit to a 51-month closing high of 43.5450/5500 per dollar on April 7, before the Reserve Bank of India reasserted its grip on the currency market.  

The rupee ended Friday at 44.0350/0450 per dollar, taking its losses over the past two weeks to nearly one percent.  

The local currency is, however, still 3.5 percent firmer against the dollar in 2004, as foreign capital surges into the Indian economy, which is estimated to have grown by 8.1 percent in the financial year to March 2004.  

Asia's third-largest economy is forecast to expand by more than six percent in the current fiscal on expectations of a second year of good monsoon rains in the farm-dependent economy.

title: ANALYSIS-India may have to loosen rupee grip as economy opens.
text:
BOMBAY, April 20 (Reuters) - India may have to give up its fixation with a stable exchange rate as the economy opens up, so the central bank can more effectively manage money, inflation and interest rates, analysts say.   

Asia's third-biggest economy continues to encourage foreign trade and investment, but the greater inflows expected will probably mean currency volatility because resisting further gains by the rupee will cost too much and could lead to excessive money supply and rising prices.   

"As an economy opens up and capital inflows swell, it becomes increasingly difficult to manage the exchange rate and intervention could lose its impact," said Ila Patnaik, senior economist at the National Council for Applied Economic Research, New Delhi.   

The rupee has been flexible and partly convertible for about a decade, but the Reserve Bank of India has policed the currency's moves as the emerging economy sought a footing in the global market.   

The central bank has sought to contain a rupee rally in the past two years caused by a weak dollar, strong exports and investment into an economy that expanded by 10.4 percent between the October-December quarters of 2002 and 2003, making it the fastest growing major economy in the world.   

Authorities have limited the appreciation to 12 percent, to around 44 per dollar from a historic low of 49.08 in mid-2002.   

The central bank's tireless dollar shopping has generated rupee surpluses in the banking system, estimated at $17 billion, while forex reserves have risen $40 billion over the past year to a record $116 billion.   

"But the cost of intervening is becoming too heavy," said Patnaik.   

EXCESS LIQUIDITY   

To tackle excess rupee liquidity, India has started selling up to 600 billion rupees in "stabilisation" securities over the next year.   

But these bonds pay around 4.5 percent, much more than what the central bank earns by investing reserves in low-risk securities such as U.S. treasury bills. Besides, the government cannot issue bonds indiscriminately.   

"The cost of forex (intervention) is made more contentious by India's worrying fiscal finances," said Rajeev Malik, economist with JP Morgan in Singapore.   

He estimated the central bank's net interest loss at around 0.4 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the last fiscal year to March.   

Some analysts also say the currency market has evolved and does not need the central bank to manage day-to-day volatility, while exporters will not be devastated by a stronger rupee.   

"There could be a sharp adjustment if intervention stops but after a while, capital flows could slow as some money is coming in on expectations of an appreciation," Patnaik said.   

There may also be less need for intervention.   

Exporters, who are affected by currency moves, are riding on their own competitiveness. Goods exports surged by more than 17 percent in the year to March. Services exports more than doubled in April-December, 2003 over the previous year.

title: Indian shares drop 1 pct on nerves before election.
text:
By Anirban Nag
    BOMBAY, April 19 (Reuters) - Indian shares shed one percent
on Monday, a day before the general election for the national
parliament starts, with investors worried about whether or not
the next government will speed up market-friendly reforms.
    The rupee ended flat as the Reserve Bank of Indiaintervened to keep it down, while federal bonds fell on
expectations the central bank may issue more to soak up rupees
in the money market flowing from its dollar-buying spree in the
currency market.
    The 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange benchmark index
fell 1.04 percent to 5,800.54 points, retreating from highs
last week not seen since the government flooded the market with
around $3 billion worth of shares in state-run companies in
early March.
   


    "There is a certain amount of buyer fatigue after the
recent listings, and there is also some uncertainty with regard
to the elections and the monsoon," said Shankar Char, a head of
institutional sales at Cholamandalam Securities.
 
    "So investors are holding on to their normal positions and
not over-extending them," he said.
    While quarterly earnings and guidance have been good to
   

better-than-expected so far, investors are looking to the   

election and what is forecast to be a "near normal" monsoon for   

cues, he added.   

India's parliamentary election, which runs from April 20 to   

May 10, is expected to return the Bharatiya Janata Party-led   

coalition to power. But doubts remain over its margin of   

victory, which will determine the pace of reforms and economic   

growth.   

The run-up to the election has also been marred by   

accidents and sporadic instances of violence. Tuesday's voting   

will take place in 13 of the 29 states.   

"The index will remain volatile and range-bound, with a   

sustained upward movement possible only beyond the   

5,950-level," Char said.   

Index heavyweight Reliance Industries Ltd (RELI.BO) slipped   

2.2 percent to 552.45 rupees, and other industrials fell   

despite expectations of strong demand in India's bustling   

economy.   

Grasim Industries Ltd (GRAS.BO), the No. 3 cement producer,   

fell 2.5 percent to 1,143.50 rupees. Tata Motors Ltd (TAMO.BO),   

the biggest vehicle maker, dropped 3.5 percent to 487.75   

rupees.   

Tata Iron and Steel Co (TISC.BO), the second-largest steel   

maker, shed one percent to 391.45 rupees, while power equipment   

maker Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd (BHEL.BO) slid 4.3 percent   

to 612.30 rupees.   

The rupee closed at 43.8900/9000 per dollar, off   

an early intra-day peak of 43.7900, and slightly below Friday's   

43.8850/8950 as the central bank drained the market of dollars.   

The yield on the 10-year benchmark bond ended   

at 5.0679 percent, up from its previous close of 5.0603

title: India FX  reserves at new high on c.bank  intervention .
text:
By Anirban Nag
    BOMBAY, April 17 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange
reserves soared to a record $116.06 billion in the week ended
April 9 as capital inflows gathered pace and the central bank
stepped up its presence in the currency market, analysts said.
    Data from the central bank, said India's foreign exchange
reserves rose by $3.37 billion -- one of its highest weekly
gains -- from $112.690 billion in the week ended April 2.
    The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said the foreign currency
assets expressed in U.S. dollar terms included the effect of
appreciation/depreciation of other currencies held in its
reserves such as the euro, pound sterling and yen.
    Analysts said the rapid reserve accumulation largely
reflects the central bank's determination to stem sharp gains by
the local currency against the U.S. dollar to protect export
competitiveness.
  


    The Reserve Bank of India has stepped up its dollar-buying,
after arming itself in the new fiscal year from April 1 with
stabilisation bonds to offset the effects of its currency market
intervention.
    The new securities will be sold in the market to drain the
rupees injected by the bank's dollar purchases. India plans to
sell up to 600 billion rupees ($13.67 billion) of the bonds in
the current financial year to March 2005.
    The Indian central bank which has been grappling with steady
foreign capital inflows in the past two years, had almost run
out of rupee assets to offset the inflows towards the latter
half of March.
    Analysts say this might have prompted the central bank to
stay away from the currency market during that period allowing
the tightly policed rupee to gain about 3.6 percent to hit
multi-year highs.
    "The intervention was expected after the market
stabilisation bonds came into the picture in the new financial
year," said Dhananjay Sinha, economist with ICICI Bank.
    The rupee          ended Friday at 43.8850/8950 per dollar,
down half a percent during the week as the central bank soaked
up foreign capital inflows.
 
 
    ROBUST CAPITAL INFLOWS
    But the partially convertible Indian rupee has gained about
four percent against the dollar since January on robust foreign
investments in one of the world's fastest growing economies.
    Data from the capital market showed net purchases by
  

overseas funds were at $490 million so far in April, taking  

their total net bond and stock purchases to $4.0 billion in  

2004.  

"The surge in reserves suggests that the pressure of capital  

inflows has stepped up in recent times," said Siddharth Mathur,  

strategist at JP Morgan Chase, Bombay. "This presents an  

interesting challenge for currency managment to the RBI."  

Foreign investments are surging into the Indian economy  

which is estimated to have grown by 8.1 percent in the financial  

year to March 2004, and is likely to grow at more than six  

percent in the current financial year on the back of growing  

demand for manufactured goods and services.  

The Institute of International Finance said international  

capital inflows to developing market jumped $194 billion in 2003  

from a 10-year low of $128 billion a year ago and could rise by  

15 percent in 2004.

BOMBAY, April 2 (Reuters) - The buoyant Indian rupee is
expected to extend gains into a tenth straight session on
Friday on strong foreign capital inflows but traders said they

intervention.
    "Everyone is keen to see the central bank's stance on the
first trading day of the new fiscal year," a dealer at a
state-run bank said.
    "While the pressure on the rupee to appreciate is quite
strong, how much and how fast it gains will all depend on
whether the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) resumes its aggressive

week."
    India's currency market was shut on the first day of the

to come in and if the RBI stays away we should see a range of

to 44 is quite possible," a dealer at a private bank said.
    The central bank, armed with fresh rupee assets under a new
stabilisation scheme, is seen resuming its dollar buying but
analysts are unsure of how aggressive it may be after India's
Finance Minister hinted that a stronger rupee could help in
inflation management.
    "The end of large scale forex intervention by the RBI is
permanent," said Barclays Capital's economist Dominique
Dwor-Freaut in a recent research report.
    "With a capital account open on the inflow side, the RBI
can no longer ignore the trade-off between competitiveness and
inflation," she said in the report, recommending clients to

coinciding with a surge in foreign funds' remittances towards

title: India Rupee Surges Vs Dlr, But Ends Off Highs; Bonds Up
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee rose sharply against the dollar Wednesday, breaking several key resistance levels on continued capital inflows and a growing conviction that the government favors a strong currency.  

However, the local currency ended off a 55-month intraday high after a government official called its gains "temporary," and also due to suspected central bank intervention.  

The rupee broke key psychological barriers against the dollar at INR44.000, INR43.750 and INR43.500, peaking at INR43.355, a level last tested Sept. 2, 1999.  

It fell back to end the day at INR43.670, still sharply stronger than Monday's INR44.070. The foreign exchange market was shut Tuesday.  

The rupee's rise was driven mainly by strong and persistent capital inflows following a string of recent privatization sales. The government sold part of its holdings in six state-run companies earlier this month, raising a total of $3.4 billion.  

But the local unit gained additional upward momentum Wednesday following comments by a top government official Tuesday, which suggested the government favors a strong local currency as this helps to bring down inflation.  

Finance Minister Jaswant Singh said Tuesday that his Bharatiya Janata Party, the leader of India's ruling coalition, "remains committed to a strong currency rate" as "a strong rupee has relationships with inflation management and currency flows."  

The rupee has also benefited from notably weak resistance to its rise from state-owned banks, which have bought dollars almost routinely in recent months on behalf of the central bank, to protect exports.  

"The Reserve Bank Of India has scaled down its intervention, possibly because the privatization-related capital inflows aren't speculative investments," a local analyst said. "Also, these inflows aren't debt-creating."  

Friday, RBI Governor Y.V. Reddy said the rupee's volatility against the dollar was less than the fluctuations in other international currencies. He also stressed the rise was entirely market-driven - a comment taken by many in the market to mean the central bank is comfortable with a stronger rupee.  

The rupee has gained 8.6% against the dollar in the past 12 months on capital inflows and general dollar weakness.  

Currency watchers expect the rupee to continue its uptrend in coming weeks, albeit at a slower pace, with some forecasting it to test INR42.50 in the next year.  

"Apart from higher inflows arising due to foreign subscriptions in recent privatizations, we believe a key reason for the recent rise is the (RBI's) limited ammunition to sterilize them," a Citigroup report said  

In the forward market, dollar premiums ended slightly lower Wednesday, tracking the dollar's sharp fall in the spot market.  

The annualized premium over the spot rate on the one-year forward contract ended at 0.69%, down from 0.72% at the previous close.  

Mifor-based interest rate swaps were slightly higher Wednesday, tracking U.S. Treasury yields, with the two-year swap ending 2.64%-2.69% from 2.60%-2.65% at the previous close. Mifor is the Mumbai interbank forward offered rate. It is derived from dollar forward rates.  

Government bond prices gained slightly Wednesday on mild liquidity-led buying. Expectations of stronger demand at the start of the new fiscal year also fueled buying, dealers said.  

The 10-year bond yield closed slightly lower at 5.15% compared with the previous close of 5.16%.  

Bond prices are expected to gain further in the coming days as banks make fresh investment allocations in the new financial year.  

The overnight interbank call money rate ended flat at 4.0%-4.25% amid ample money market liquidity. [ 31-03-04 1356GMT ]

title: Bond plan means India rupee surge may be its last.
text:
BOMBAY, March 26 (Reuters) - This week's near 1.5 percent rise of the rupee against the dollar is unlikely to be repeated because India's central bank is about to get new ammunition to help it smooth currency fluctuations, analysts said.   

The rupee's strengthening represented its highest weekly gain in six years, and took it to a 46-month closing high of 44.47/48 on Friday.   

It followed a firming of a mere 0.8 percent in the 11 weeks to March 18.   

The Indian central bank stayed away from currency intervention this week, but will probably be back in the fiscal year that begins on April 1, armed with sizeable funds for its new market stabilisation scheme.   

"They will be able to intervene more aggressively once they have the stabilisation (scheme) in their armoury," said Dhananjay Sinha, economist at ICICI Bank.   

On Thursday, India said it will issue stabilisation bonds or bills for 355 billion rupees ($7.9 billion) in the first quarter of the new fiscal year, giving the central bank more ammunition to offset the rupee's rise on foreign capital inflows.   

Capital inflows into India, one of the main drivers of the rupee's gains, were a record $7.7 billion in 2003 and lifted the rupee 5.2 percent last year. Foreign funds have already invested more than $2 billion in the rapidly expanding economy this year.   

India's central bank, like most of its regional counterparts, had been intervening in the forex market for the past two years to curb sharp gains by the rupee.   

In the process, it has built up record foreign exchange reserves of $110 billion. It has also flooded domestic money markets with excess rupees, which it must mop up by selling bonds, a process called sterilisation.   

"At a time when foreign exchange inflows into the country are set to rise in the near term, the central bank needed a huge chest as the current instruments available for sterilisation are not enough," said Shubhada Rao, an economist in the Bank of Baroda's risk management group.   

That shortage of rupee assets may have kept the central bank from buying dollars for rupees in recent days, analysts said.   

FLOODED WITH RUPEES   

The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) interventions have flooded the domestic money market, with excess cash estimated at around 550-600 billion rupees.   

The RBI has been draining that excessive liquidity by conducting daily repo auctions and by selling government bonds from its own investment portfolio in the market.   

But analysts estimate the central bank holds only about 800-900 billion rupees in securities, down from 1.5 trillion rupees on March, 2001 as it has been selling bonds to absorb excess funds from the money market.   

Nearly 500 billion rupees worth of bonds are used to drain funds on a daily basis through the repurchase auctions, leaving the RBI few securities to absorb rupees for longer durations.   

There should be no such shortage of assets in the coming fiscal year. Authorities have set aside up to 600 billion rupees for the stabilisation scheme in the financial year to March 2005.   

That should offer the RBI some relief, because the factors behind the rupee's gains have not changed. Traders said the recent gains were due to foreign funds chasing $3 billion of asset sales by state-run companies in February and March.   

With India expected to grow by over eight percent in the year to March, analysts expect foreign capital will continue to flow into Asia's third-largest economy.   

"We see continued strong inflows through portfolio investments, export earnings and renewed dollar weakness in global forex markets," JP Morgan said in a report on Friday.   

"The rupee will continue to face appreciation pressure in coming months."

title: India rupee ends firm for 6th day, but inflows ebb.
text:

sixth straight session on Thursday to hit a new 44-month
closing high but recent heavy foreign fund inflows were showing
signs of tapering, dealers said.
    Traders said dollar purchases by some companies checked the
rupee's gains on Thursday after it rose 1.1 percent against the
dollar in the past five sessions.
    The rupee          ended at 44.7400/7450 per dollar,
marginally higher than Wednesday's close of 44.7450/7550 which
was also its previous 44-month closing high.
    It last ended firmer on July 17, 2000 at 44.7125/7175.
    The rupee, which analysts say is fairly valued on a

trade and foreign fund inflows.
