title: MONEY VIEW-Indian rupee to rise to 44.75/dlr by end-March.
text:
BOMBAY, March 24 (Reuters) - Following is a comment on the outlook for treasury markets.   

The opinions expressed here are those of the author. They should not be seen as representing the views of Reuters. -   

V. RAJAGOPAL, HEAD OF FOREX TRADING, KOTAK MAHINDRA BANK, BOMBAY:   

"The rupee should rise to around 44.75 per dollar by the end of the month, though the stance of the central bank will be crucial.   

"In any case, sentiment on the dollar has weakened, with a question mark still hanging over the U.S. economic recovery as employment remains weak and inflation subdued.   

"The Reserve Bank of India has not intervened in recent sessions, which has accelerated the rupee's rise. If the view sets in that there is not going to be any controlling presence, the rupee could strengthen very rapidly.   

(The Indian rupee has gained by 1.6 percent so far this year after rising 5.2 percent in 2003). "Factors supporting the rupee are the expected continuation of the stock market rally - the recent bout of weakness is being regarded as a correction.   

"We expect more inflows from foreign investors on that account, and also on account of U.S. interest rates expected to stay at current historical lows.   

"Moreover, no concentrated demand for dollars is expected, given the comfort of a strengthening rupee. Hence, dollar supplies will continue to overwhelm the market.   

"We have revised upwards our target for the (calendar) year-end to 43.25-43.50 per dollar from 44.0 per dollar earlier, in view of the recent strong rally.   

"The dollar's weakness is expected to continue, and central banks in Asia - including the Bank of Japan - have not been intervening aggressively in recent days indicating these expectations.   

"If the Chinese yuan is re-valued, it will be a clear signal for further dollar weakness against Asian currencies." "We feel there is room for the dollar to weaken. The sluggish U.S. labour market remains a disturbing factor, which suggests that growth in corporate profits could be coming from cost-cutting, with jobs being freed up.   

"Moreover, the U.S. current account deficit remains chronically high." -.

title: India Rupee Closes Higher On Capital Inflows;Bonds Up
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee extended its rise against the dollar to a fresh 44-month high Wednesday, on continuing strong capital inflows following recent privatizations.  

The local unit ended at INR44.75 against the dollar Wednesday, a level last tested July 24, 2000. The rupee closed at INR44.87 Tuesday.  

"The foreign investments in the recent privatizations have literally flooded the banking system with dollars," a dealer at a local bank said. The government sold part of its holdings in six state-run companies earlier this month to raise a total $3.4 billion.  

The rupee's gains were underscored by unusually weak dollar demand from state-owned banks, which have been routinely buying dollars on behalf of the central bank in recent months to protect exports.  

Analysts now say the Reserve Bank of India has stepped down its market intervention, since the privatization-related capital inflows aren't speculative investments or debt-creating.  

The rupee is expected to continue rising in coming weeks with some analysts forecasting it will test INR43.80 by the end of September. The rupee has gained 5.7% against the dollar in the past 12 months on capital inflows and general dollar weakness.  

In the forward market, dollar premiums ended higher Wednesday as sellers of the U.S. currency in the spot market bought it back in the forward segment to square positions. The annualized premium over the spot rate on the one-year forward contract ended at 0.63%, up from 0.58% at the previous close.  

Mifor-based interest rate swaps also rose Wednesday, in line with forward-dollar premiums, with the two-year swap rising to 2.51%-2.56% from 2.46%-2.50% at the previous close. Mifor is the Mumbai interbank forward offered rate. It is derived from dollar forward rates.  

Government bond prices ended higher Wednesday on liquidity-driven buying. Record high bids at the RBI's daily repurchase agreement auction indicated a rise in money market liquidity, dealers said.  

The central bank accepted bids totaling INR555 billion at its repo Wednesday, up from INR531 billion Tuesday.  

Bond yields edged down across the board, with the 10-year bond yield ending at 5.17%, down from 5.18% at the previous close.  

Bond prices are expected to move in a narrow range around current levels in the coming days, as traders maintain near-square positions ahead of the March 31 financial year end.  

The overnight interbank call money rate ended steady at 4.00%-4.30% Wednesday, compared with 4.00%-4.25% at the previous close. [ 24-03-04 1325GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1-India rupee at 44-month high on foreign shr buying.
text:
By Anirban Nag
    BOMBAY, March 23 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee firmed past
   

45 per dollar on Tuesday for the first time since July 2000 on   

inflows from foreign funds chasing $3 billion worth of recent   

public offerings of shares in state-run companies.   

Dollar-buying by state banks acting on behalf of the   

central bank was muted, allowing the local unit to gain, they   

added.   

Central bank intervention over the past two years has   

curbed sharp gains by the rupee, but analysts said concerns   

about inflationary pressures in the rapidly expanding economy   

may have prompted authorities to ease their tight grip on the   

currency.   

Intervention has helped India build record foreign exchange

reserves of nearly $110 billion and has kept exports - nearly   

11 percent of gross domestic product - competitive.   

At 1:10 p.m. (0740 GMT), the partially convertible rupee   

was quoted at 44.9275/9375 per dollar, firmer than Monday's   

nearly 44-month closing high of 45.0875/0950.   

The rupee gained nearly 0.22 percent last week and has   

appreciated 1.5 percent against the dollar so far in 2004. It   

rose 5.2 percent last year on steady trade remittances and   

strong foreign investments in local assets.   

"The rupee is rising because of strong inflows into the   

local stock market," said Siddharth Mathur, strategist at JP   

Morgan Chase, adding that he expected further gains for the   

currency.   

"The dollar's overseas weakness, export and foreign   

investments and higher external commercial borrowings by local   

companies will bolster the rupee in the medium term."   

Traders said foreign investors had placed large bids in   

recent public offerings, especially from energy companies. That   

money is now coming into the country, they said.   

India raised over $3 billion by selling stakes in six   

state-run companies in February and March, including $2.3   

billion from a 10 percent share in the country's top crude   

producer, Oil and Natural Gas Corp. It also raised $365 million   

from the sale of its stake in gas firm GAIL Ltd.   

Data from the capital market regulator showed foreign   

funds' purchases of local shares and debt in March totalled   

$741 million, taking net investments for the year to over $2   

billion. In 2003, they bought a record $7.8 billion in local   

assets.   

Foreign funds have increased their exposure to India as   

Asia's third-largest economy is forecast to grow at more than   

eight percent in 2003/04 (April-March) aided by a rebound in   

the farm sector after the best monsoon rains in a decade. The   

economy expanded by four percent in the previous year.   

CENTRAL BANK'S CHOICE   

Analysts said the central bank is probably easing its tight   

grip over the currency to curb inflationary trends.   

"It is a choice between hiking interest rates or letting   

the rupee appreciate," said Dominique Dwor-Frecaut, director at   

Barclays Capital, Singapore.   

"Given that the economic recovery is still at a nascent   

stage, the central bank has to let the rupee gain so that the   

acceleration in inflationary trends is postponed."   

Inflation, as measured by the closely tracked wholesale   

price index, has recently eased after hovering around six   

percent for most of 2004. Weekly data released on Friday showed   

inflation fell to 4.91 percent in the year to March 6, well   

below the 6.21 percent peak in January.   

But analysts said inflation could rise from May, after   

general elections, as domestic fuel prices may be allowed to   

rise in line with global prices. State-run refiners have not   

hiked politically sensitive fuel prices since January.   

The economy is sensitive to global crude prices, currently   

at 13-year highs, as it imports 70 percent of its   

requirements.

title: Indian Rupee At 45.00/Dlr; Highest Since July 31, 2000
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee broke yet another psychological barrier against the dollar Tuesday, hitting a 44-month high on strong capital fund inflows following a string of privatization deals between the government and foreign investors, dealers said.  

The local unit broke through the much-watched level of INR45.000 to the dollar to touch an intraday high of INR44.9650, last tested on July 31, 2000. The rupee closed at INR45.100 Monday.  

India's relatively high interest rates and rallying stock markets have attracted foreign capital for over a year now, but such inflows have strengthened significantly since last week due to foreign buying of the government's stake sales.  

The Indian government sold part of its holdings in six state-run companies earlier this month to raise a total $3.4 billion. A significant part of the sale proceeds are believed to have come from foreign investors. [ 23-03-04 0558GMT ]  

The rupee is also benefiting from notably weak resistance to its rise from state-owned banks, which have bought dollars almost routinely in recent months on behalf of the central bank to protect exports.  

"The Reserve Bank Of India has scaled down its intervention, possibly because the privatization-related capital inflows aren't speculative investments; they are real inflows," says Siddharth Mathur, head of research at JP Morgan in Mumbai. "Also, these inflows aren't debt-creating."  

The rupee has gained 5.7% against the dollar in the past 12 months on capital inflows and general dollar weakness.  

Currency watchers expect the rupee to continue its uptrend in coming weeks, albeit at a slower pace, with some forecasting it to test INR43.80 by end-September.  

"As long as the state-run banks don't step in to support it, the dollar/rupee will continue to fall," said Rohan Lasrado, a foreign exchange dealer at HDFC Bank in Mumbai.  

However, Indian exporters are alarmed by the rupee's relentless rise, and have voiced worries in recent months that the currency movements could slow growth and erode the country's trade earnings.  

While exports may just about meet the government's target of a 12% growth in the current fiscal year ending March 31, a strengthening rupee erodes the chances of higher growth, said Subash Mittal, vice president of the Federation of Indian Export Organizations, an exporters' umbrella body.  

"The rupee's strength has already been hurting exports, now it will further damp growth in the sector," Mittal said. "We could have achieved 20% export growth this fiscal year if the rupee hadn't appreciated so much."  

Still, despite repeated calls by trade organizations to stem the rupee's rise, the RBI may not prune the local currency's gains as long as it is led by non-speculative capital flows.

title: WEEKAHEAD-Indian bonds seen rising on liquidity glut.
text:
BOMBAY, March 21 (Reuters) - Indian federal bonds are
expected to extend their rise into a third straight week,
supported by huge inflows from bonds that are maturing and on
expectations of a dip in inflation, analysts said.
    But chances that the central bank may intervene to absorb
some of the excess funds by selling bonds from its own
portfolio will keep gains muted, they added.
    Proceeds from two bonds maturing during the week total
nearly 162 billion rupees ($3.6 billion) and would add to the
surplus cash pile of about 400 billion to 450 billion rupees
that banks are already sitting on currently.
 "There should be some aggressive open-market sale of bonds by
the central bank," said Dhananjay Sinha, economist at ICICI
Bank. "But that will not impact sentiment much and we could see
the 10-year bond yield easing to 5.10 percent."
    The benchmark 10-year bond             eased to 5.1583
percent on Saturday, down from 5.1836 percent in the previous
week.
   


    India's central bank deputy governor, Rakesh Mohan, told
reporters in Dubai on Saturday that he had not ruled out the
use of open market sales to mop up surplus cash from the
system.
    Mohan also reiterated the central bank would continue to
intervene in the currency market to avoid volatility. Traders
said that was likely to lead to the infusion of more rupee
funds into the system, supporting support bond prices.
    The tightly policed rupee has appreciated nearly one
percent against the dollar this year, and could have gained
more but for the central bank's intervention.
    The intervention has seen India's foreign exchange reserves
rise to a record $109.6 billion as the central bank has
absorbed robust foreign investment inflows and export receipts.
    LOWER INFLATION
    Bond market sentiment will also be supported by a continued
fall in India's 12-month inflation rate, which analysts expect
it to ease to around 4.5 percent by the March 31 end of
financial year.
    Inflation, as measured by wholesale price index, has
recently begun showing a decline after hovering around six
percent for most of 2004. Data released on Friday showed
inflation in the year to March 6 had fallen to 4.91 percent,
way below the 6.21 percent peak seen in January.
    The rate has fallen to below five percent for the first
time in three months and is expected fall further due to lower
food prices and a higher base effect, analysts said.
    "We could see inflation finish the financial year at around
4.5 percent," said Indranil Pan, chief economist at Kotak
Mahindra Bank. "This along with the ample liquidity in the
system will help maintain the momentum in the bond market."
     Mohan said on Saturday the trend was in line with the
central bank's January forecast, in which it estimated
inflation to end the financial year at 4.0 to 4.5 percent.
    Traders said they would await the government's borrowing
calendar for the first half of 2004/05 (April-March), which is
likely to be announced on March 25, for cues.
    India relies heavily on its domestic debt market and public
savings of around 26 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) to
bridge the stubbornly high fiscal deficit.

title: Indian cenbank eyeing global interest rates - Mohan.
text:
DUBAI, March 20 (Reuters) - India's central bank Deputy Governor Rakesh Mohan said on Saturday that the country's monetary authorities were closely watching global interest rates, which he said were relevant in determing local rates.   

"The statements coming from the U.S. Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Japan don't at present indicate (hardening) as there is still good deal of excess capacities," Mohan told reporters on the sidelines of a money market and fixed income conference.   

"These central banks have not indicated any hardening of interest rates, but we watch all those things."   

Mohan said movements in global rates were relevant to India and these were considered along with local factors while formulating the monetary policy.   

Although India's central bank lays more emphasis on domestic factors such as inflation to set monetary policy, analysts say a soft global rate environment would support the steady pace of foreign inflows, a bulk of which were being mopped up by the Reserve Bank of India to keep exports cheap.   

The steady intervention has led to a glut of rupees in the banking system, supporting bond prices in spite of an economic rebound.   

Subdued domestic economic growth in the past three years along with benign interest rates globally had encouraged the Reserve bank of India (RBI) to lower official rates sharply.   

The key bank rate-which banks use to price loans-is at a three-decade low of six percent, while the central bank's overnight repo rate is at 4.5 percent, lowest since repo auctions were introduced in 2000.   

FOREX INTERVENTION

Mohan said the central bank will continue to intervene in the currency market to avoid volatility.   

"We do intervene to reduce volatility. We do not have a target nor a range as far as the exchange rate is concerned," he said.   

"Volatility in the international market has been very high in the last few months and we continue to have a policy of not having great volatility as we believe that is not good for our markets."   

His comments came a day after the Indian rupee rose to a near four-year closing high of 45.1575/1625 per dollar, as the central bank refrained from the heavy dollar purchases it had been making in recent months.

title: India Bonds Rise On RBI Mohan's Inflation Comment;Call Up

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a conference of Indian money market participants in Dubai, he said oil prices are unlikely to have any "significant impact" on local inflation in the near future.  

Although inflation has come off the eight-month highs tested in January, the bond has been worried in recent weeks that the rate may not fall as much as earlier expected amid rising oil and metal prices.

An apparent absence of intervention dollar buying by the Reserve Bank of India, which has bought dollars through the state-run banks almost routinely in recent months, helped the rupee strengthen.

title: Indian fund aims to tackle host of monetary issues.
text:
BOMBAY, Feb 26 (Reuters) - India is reloading its policy guns with a plan to sell special bonds to absorb excess rupees in the market from intervention, a move that may keep Indian markets in check and contain inflation.   

Over the next year, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will sell up to $13 billion worth of market stabilisation bonds issued to soak up excess rupees in the market, rupees that the RBI had sold in the first place. It's a process known as sterilisation.   

"The fund is definitely desirable. The RBI needs a tool to suck out liquidity from strong foreign inflows," said Indranil Pan, economist with Kotak Mahindra Bank.   

He said the system was awash with cash, raising the risk of higher inflation and an asset price bubble, while putting pressure on bond yields and other market interest rates.   

Surging foreign investment and other inflows have boosted the rupee, prompting the RBI to intervene and protect exports as high-potential sectors such as outsourcing take off.   

The cash overhang - the cost of limiting the rupee's rise to 5.2 percent in 2003 - threatened a bond market bubble last year, when yields plumbed new lows even as the economy recovered.   

"Containing liquidity will limit the risk of asset bubbles while allowing the central bank to continue its forex intervention," said Dhananjay Sinha, economist with ICICI Bank.   

India, among the world's fastest growing economies, has seen forex reserves surge $32 billion over the past year to a record $107.5 billion.   

Reducing the cash surplus will also ease price pressures, now a concern, with annual inflation around six percent.   

The market stabilisation bonds are separate from federal borrowings aimed at plugging the budget deficit.   

SMOOTHENING THE YIELD CURVE   

Better management of surplus cash will give the central bank the leeway to fashion its repo rate into a key monetary signal and smooth kinks at the short end of the yield curve.   

The RBI currently uses mostly repos to sterilise inflows. Average daily mop-ups have ballooned to 400 billion rupees this month from around 50 billion rupees a year earlier.   

But the impact is fleeting and excess cash continues to distort the short end of the yield curve, compromising the effectiveness of the repo rate.   

The central bank sees the repo as a tool for managing temporary cash mismatches and the repo rate has emerged as a signal for short-term market interest rates - a trend the RBI would like to see develop.   

Overnight unsecured inter-bank loans often cost less than the repo rate of 4.5 percent at which the central bank borrows against collateral. Even yields on longer-term instruments such as one-year treasury bills are lower.   

"Reduced liquidity will remove these distortions and make the repo rate more credible as a signalling device," said Sinha.   

Still, the scheme cannot guarantee the liquidity overhang will recede, as evidenced by China's experience.   

"There is definitely a possibility that inflows are much stronger than what we have seen," said Siddharth Mathur, strategist with JP Morgan Securities.   

"There is optimism about the Indian economy, and it could get difficult to deal with inflows with only one instrument."

title: India mulls $8.8 bln monetary stabilisation fund.
text:
BOMBAY, Feb 19 (Reuters) - The Indian central bank's planned market stabilisation fund, expected to be approved shortly by the government, will be backed by about 400 billion rupees ($8.8 billion) in bonds, a senior official said on Thursday.   

The move is meant to temper inflows that have swelled foreign exchange coffers to record levels, just 13 years after the country suffered a balance of payments crisis.   

Under the fund, the government would issue the bonds to the central bank, which would sell them when necessary to soak up excess money market liquidity, pumped up by the bank's rupee-selling intervention, officials say.   

"Central bank officials and we are meeting on February 23 to discuss several issues, including the tenor of these bonds," said a senior finance ministry official on Thursday.   

A central bank panel in December proposed the fund in response to the bank's dwindling supply of government bonds - currently the main weapon for sterilisation - which fell to 369 billion rupees last month, from 1.5 trillion rupees in March 2001.   

The central bank would keep the money raised in a separate account that the government would not be able to access, but interest on the bonds would be paid by the government, and analysts say that could weigh on the already huge fiscal deficit.   

Analysts say setting up the fund reflects the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) resolve to intervene more aggressively to cap the rupee's rise against the dollar.   

The policy is in line with other Asian central banks that have also been grappling with hefty capital inflows. Central bank intervention boosted Asia's combined foreign exchange reserves to more than $2 trillion at end-January.   

REINING IN THE RUPEE   

The RBI says it does not target a level for the rupee but analysts say it has managed the currency in a plus-to minus-five percent band around its real effective exchange rate.   

"Given that India still has a trade deficit of 3-4 percent of GDP, the RBI would prefer to keep the rupee in the centre to the weaker half of the band by absorbing dollars," said M.R. Madhavan, strategist at Bank of America in Singapore.   

"The fund would enable the central bank to do this more effectively, without any adverse monetary effect."   

Sustained intervention has swelled India's reserves, which hit a record $106.6 billion on February 6. In 1998, India was forced to tap expatriates for $4 billion to shore up reserves.   

India, home to one-sixth of the world's population, is forecast to see economic growth of over eight percent in the fiscal year to March, after expanding by only four percent a year earlier.   

Foreign funds pumped $6.7 billion into Indian shares in 2003, helping fuel a 73 percent surge in stock prices.   

The inflows pushed the rupee , which is only partly convertible, 5.2 percent higher against the dollar last year, its steepest gain in a decade. It has strengthened 0.8 percent in 2004.   

Intervention helped limit the rupee's rise, but the resultant flood of rupees into domestic markets and three years of soft monetary policy have powered a steep fall in government bond yields.   

But with the economy expected to boom, and inflation stubbornly high around six percent, traders expect the central bank to keep rates steady and yields to rise. (Additional reporting by Surojit Gupta in NEW DELHI).

volatility.

title: UPDATE 1-India's  forex  reserves cross $100 billion.
text:
NEW DELHI, Dec 20 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves crossed the $100 billion mark for the first time, boosted by foreign investment inflows, trade flows and revaluation gains on the dollar's weakness against global currencies.   

"The governor RBI informed me today that India's foreign exchange reserves comprising foreign currency assets, gold and Special Drawing Rights have reached $100.248 billion on December 19," Finance Minister Jaswant Singh said in a statement. "The RBI has assured me that these forex reserves will, as in the past, continue to be used to contain volatility in the forex market and to withstand any possible supply shocks."   

The reserves will also enable Indian firms to borrow overseas at "finer and more favourable rates", Singh added.   

Earlier on Saturday, central bank data showed India's reserves climbed $1.44 billion in the week to December 12, notching their seventh straight week of gains and extending rises over the past year to $30.5 billion, or nearly 45 percent.   

"The entire rise may not be attributable to money flows, part of it is due to revaluation as the dollar has been depreciating against other currencies," said Siddharth Mathur of JP Morgan.   

The central bank said the numbers included the effect of appreciation or depreciation of non-dollar currencies held in the reserves such as the euro, sterling and yen.   

The euro has appreciated roughly 19 percent against the dollar this year and hit record highs against the greenback this week. The sterling and the yen are up around 10 percent each against the dollar this year.   

Finance Secretary D.C. Gupta told reporters there was "no reason that the government should not continue with its policy of paying foreign debt ahead of schedule but needed to examine whether it would save on interest".   

On Friday, an official said the country would pre-pay $1.3 billion to the Asian Development Bank before end-March.   

A senior government official said earlier this year that India would pre-pay external debt worth nearly $3.0 billion to more than a dozen countries.   

PROBLEM OF PLENTY   

Grappling with a problem of plenty, the government earlier this year also tightened its policy on foreign borrowing by Indian firms in what analysts saw as a move to stem inflows.   

Earlier this week, global rating agency Standard and Poor's raised its outlook on the country's foreign currency rating to stable from negative, acknowledging the improvement in reserves, although it kept the rating at a speculative 'BB'.   

India is placed sixth in Asia in terms of reserves and its reserves are equivalent to around 20 percent of its GDP.   

The rise in reserves, besides the revaluation gains, reflects heavy intervention by the central Reserve Bank of India to mop up inflows from foreign investors, remittances from Indians working overseas and trade flows.   

The central bank's intervention is aimed at preventing excessive rises in the rupee, which would affect India's export competitiveness. Despite the intervention, the rupee has risen by around 5.4 percent against the dollar in 2003.   

Foreign funds have made net investments of some $7.1 billion in Indian assets in 2003, their highest annual investment since local markets were opened to foreign funds a decade ago, on expectations Asia's third-largest economy will expand by over seven percent in the current fiscal year to March.   

Deposits by non-resident Indians rose by $2.6 billion in the first half of the fiscal year which started in April but are expected to have grown more slowly since as the central bank cut rates on such deposits in September.

"The entire rise may not be attributable to money flows, part of it is due to revaluation as the dollar has been depreciating against other currencies," said Siddharth Mathur, strategist at JP Morgan.   

The central bank said the numbers included the effect of appreciation or depreciation of non-dollar currencies held in the reserves such as the euro, sterling and yen.   

The euro has appreciated roughly 19 percent against the dollar this year and hit record highs against the greenback this week. The sterling and the yen are up around 10 percent each against the dollar this year. Analysts expect reserves, currently equivalent to around 20 percent of India's gross domestic product, to touch the psychological $100 billion mark before the end of the year and said the healthy numbers could encourage the country to pay more of its external debt ahead of schedule.   

"It makes sense to pre-pay more and to contract our external debt, given the level of reserves," said Mathur.   

On Friday, an official said the country would pre-pay $1.3 billion to the Asian Development Bank before end-March. A senior government official said earlier this year that India would pre-pay external debt worth nearly $3.0 billion to more than a dozen countries.   

Grappling with a problem of plenty, the government earlier this year also tightened its policy on foreign borrowing by Indian companies in what analysts saw as a move to try and stem inflows.   

Earlier this week, global rating agency Standard and Poor's raised its outlook on the country's foreign currency rating to stable from negative, acknowledging the improvement in reserves, although it kept the rating at a speculative 'BB'.   

India is places sixth in Asia in terms of reserves.   

The rise in reserves, besides the revaluation gains, reflects heavy intervention by the central Reserve Bank of India to mop up inflows from foreign investors, remittances from Indians working overseas and trade flows.   

The central bank's intervention is aimed at preventing excessive rises in the rupee, which would affect the competitiveness of Indian exports. But despite the intervention, the rupee has risen by around 5.4 percent against the dollar so far in 2003.   

Foreign funds have made net investments of some $7.1 billion in Indian assets in 2003, their highest annual investment since local markets were opened to foreign funds a decade ago, on expectations Asia's third-largest economy will expand by over seven percent in the current fiscal year to March.   

Deposits by non-resident Indians rose by $2.6 billion in the first half of the fiscal year which started in April but are expected to have grown more slowly since as the central bank cut rates on such deposits in September.

title: UPDATE 1-Indian cbank says recent rupee weakness not volatility.
text:
COLOMBO, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Recent weakness in the Indian rupee cannot be termed volatility, a top Indian central banker said on Friday, causing the rupee to ease to a two-month low.   

"We cannot characterise the exchange rate market as having been volatile in the last couple of weeks," Reserve Bank of India Deputy Governor Rakesh Mohan, in Colombo to deliver a lecture, told Reuters.   

"The exchange rate is market determined. We would like to see an orderly market," Mohan said.   

The rupee fell to 45.92/96 per U.S. dollar after the comments, a level not seen since mid-September. The currency was trading at 45.88/90 per U.S. dollar before the comments and 45.7650/7750 on Thursday.   

Traders said the latest fall was due to Mohan's comments.   

"These comments mean the central bank is comfortable with the weakening rupee," said a dealer at a foreign bank.   

"We could see the rupee dipping to test the 46 level soon as foreign fund inflows are also slowing."   

The rupee has lost 1.5 percent since November 7. Factors include foreign funds booking profits as the year draws to a close, importer demand and aggressive intervention by the Reserve Bank of India.   

But the rupee is still up 4.5 percent since the start of 2003 on the back of robust foreign investment, export inflows and expatriate remittances.   

SOFT AND FLEXIBLE   

Mohan also told Reuters that the bank had not changed its stance on the cash reserve ratio and interest rates from that outlined in its mid-year policy review.   

The central bank had said in its review on November 3 that its soft and flexible monetary stance continued.   

The bank rate, a benchmark that banks use to price loans, is at a three-decade low of six percent after being chopped two percentage points by the central bank over the past three years.   

The repo rate, at which the central bank borrows overnight funds, is at 4.5 percent after the central bank lowered it in August by half a percentage point.   

"There has been no material change in conditions since the policy," Mohan said. "We don't make policy changes on a daily basis."   

Bond traders say the central bank will not cut official rates further amid signs of a local and global economic pick-up. The yield on 10-year federal bonds has risen to 5.1 percent from a historical low of 4.94 percent hit in mid-October.   

"The market has been working efficiently in India and the market is responding to objective circumstances," Mohan said.

title: INTERVIEW: Indian Rupee Fall Vs Dlr Likely Temporary
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee is likely to resume its advance despite a correction this week, when it fell 1% against the dollar caused by central bank intervention, says HSBC India's head of treasury Tarun Mehrotri.  

Mehrotri believes the rupee will soon overcome its current bout of weakness and resume rising on inflows into the local stock market and the dollar's global weakness. He expects the rupee to test INR44.50 by March-end, a level last reached in May 2000.  

The local currency, which has gained 4.5% against the dollar so far in 2003, fell sharply this week on heavy dollar buying by big state-owned banks. It closed at INR45.77 Thursday, sharply weaker than INR45.61 Wednesday and INR45.35 a week ago. This fall raised concerns that the rupee's long spell of strength may be over.  

Mehrotri disagrees.  

"I don't believe that dollar has bottomed out yet against the rupee," he says. "What we saw this week was probably a clear and concerted effort by the central bank to stall the rupee's rise."  

The RBI is believed to have been indirectly buying dollars on the spot market in recent months to temper the rupee's gains and protect the country's exports. But an apparent intensifying in the buying since last week has puzzled many in the market.  

"The strengthening of central bank action since may be linked to the government's upcoming $2.9 loan repayment to the Asian Development Bank," suggests Mehrotri. "They can now buy dollars in a big way, knowing that the ADB outflow will neutralize any increase in money supply or forex reserves the dollar purchases may cause."  

Indeed, the RBI probably refrained from making big interventions on the spot market in recent months due to concerns over the possible side-effects - such as higher money supply and inflation - that could jeopardize its soft monetary stance.  

Mehrotri believes a recent slowdown in foreign capital inflows into the local stock market, which has added to the rupee's current weakness, is temporary.  

Foreign portfolio investments in India, a key booster for the local currency in recent months, totaled $664 million so far this month, compared with $1.43 billion during the whole of October.  

But, says Mehrotri, "there are bound to be swings in capital flows, it's natural. The outlook is still quite bullish for Indian stocks, so foreign investors should stay."  

Furthermore, the weak global outlook for the dollar should continue to favor the rupee, he says.  

"The U.S. trade gap continues to be a concern for the dollar," says Mehrotri, who expects the dollar to weaken further against other major currencies in the coming months.

title: Indian Rupee Ends Up Despite RBI  Intervention ; Bonds Dn
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee ended higher against the dollar Tuesday as investors sold the U.S. currency amid continued inflows into the local stock market, although central bank led intervention limited the gains.  

The dollar ended at INR44.2050, down from INR44.2350 at the previous close and off its intraday high of INR44.3050.  

Foreigners have bought stocks worth $550 million so far this month, following purchases worth $805 million in January, helping the Bombay Stock Exchange to scale the psychological 10000 mark Monday.  

However, large dollar purchases by state-run banks acting on behalf of the Reserve Bank of India limited the rupee's gains. The RBI has been intervening in the foreign exchange market over the last few sessions, buying the dollar to keep the local currency from appreciating too much.  

But they scaled back their purchases later in the session Tuesday, traders said. Dealers estimate that the central bank has mopped up around $1 billion-$1.5 billion in the past few days.  

"The rupee has been strengthening in line with the dollar's recent weakness overseas," a trader at a European bank said. "But the central bank has been keeping the rupee on a tight leash."  

The dollar fell to a new four-month low of INR44.07 against the rupee last week as foreign funds bought into Asia's fastest growing economy after China.  

"They have been intervening to curtail the rupee's overvaluation against other currencies on a trade-weighted basis," said Sundeep Bhandari, regional head, global markets-South Asia in Standard Chartered Bank, India.  

The rupee has gained 1.87% against the U.S. currency since the start of 2006. Analysts say it is already 8%-9% overvalued in trade-weighted terms.  

Indian government bonds ended lower Tuesday after the central bank set lower-than-expected cutoffs at twin federal bond auctions, suggesting that bond yields may rise in coming weeks.  

The actively traded 8.07% bond maturing in 2017 closed down at INR105.28 from INR105.53 previously. Its yield rose three basis points to 7.36%.  

Earlier Tuesday, the Reserve Bank of India set a cutoff of INR100.60 on the 7.46% bond maturing in 2017, below the widely expected INR100.70, while the cutoff on the 7.40% paper maturing in 2035 was set at INR97.27, well below market expectations of INR98.50-INR98.80.  

"With robust economic growth expectations and liquidity remaining tight, the mood is very bond bearish at the moment," a fund manager said.  

The government estimated economic growth in the current fiscal year at 8.1%, fueled by robust consumer demand and rising credit boosting manufacturing and demand for services.  

Shrinking banking system liquidity is evident from the bids received by the RBI at its daily repo auctions. It injected funds worth INR149 billion Tuesday, compared with last week's INR115 billion daily average.  

In the market for overnight funds, the call money rate ended slightly lower as tepid demand from banks to meet reserve targets was offset by shrinking banking system liquidity. The call money rate closed at 6.90%-7.10% from 7.00%-7.25% at the previous close.  

Dollar forward rates fell, tracking lower money market rates. The dollar forward contract maturing in January 2007 ended down at premium of INR0.630 from INR0.640 previously.  

Interest rate swaps benchmarked to the Mumbai interbank forward offered rate, or MIFOR, also fell, tracking lower dollar forward rates. The five-year swap slipped to 6.31%-6.36%, compared with 6.39%-6.44% at the previous close.  

Overnight indexed swap rates ended higher, tracking higher government bond yields. The five-year swap ended up at 6.72%-6.73% from 6.69%-6.70% at the previous close. [ 07-02-06 1257GMT ]

Analysts said the intervention might have been done with an eye on easing tight liquidity in the banking system ahead of the borrowing of 60 billion rupees by the government early next week.  

Traders said the rupee might give up some strength on Monday if the dollar kept gains against the yen and the euro after the release of key U.S. jobs data later on Friday.  

Despite the central bank's intervention, the partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> made modest gains to end at 44.1950/2050 per dollar, up 0.13 percent from Thursday's close of 44.2550/2650.  

The rupee hit a four-month intra-day high around 44.0425 on Tuesday but quickly retreated as the dollar's rise and defence-related import payments weighed it down.  

Dollar purchases by state-run banks also pushed down the rupee on Thursday. State banks often buy dollars on behalf of the central bank, which intervenes through them when it wants to calm currency volatility.  

"The dollar purchases by the state-run banks which we saw yesterday continued," said a trader at a government-run bank. "The rupee would have gained much more but for their purchases. But the rupee could ease a bit on Monday if the dollar gains overseas."  

The dollar hit a seven-week peak against the yen <JPY=> as the market held fire before the jobs report, which could provide clues on whether the U.S. Federal Reserve will continue to push up interest rates.  

Since the U.S. Federal Reserve began a campaign of rate rises in 2004, the interest rate gap between the United States and India has shrunk to 100 basis points from 350, with U.S. rates at 4.5 percent and India's at 5.5 percent.  

Many in the market say that if the gap narrows further it could hurt the rupee since the Indian currency is supported by foreign capital in search of extra yield.  

India's share index has risen nearly 3.8 percent in 2006 on the back of foreign portfolio inflows of $816 million.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Weakness on US rate view seen brief
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 2 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were broadly weaker on Thursday, retreating from the previous day's multi-year peaks as markets pushed the dollar higher to price in more U.S. rate rises.  

But most analysts said weakness in Asian currencies would be short-lived because flows into regional equity markets were strong and positioning in favour of the regionals was still light.  

The dollar rose to a seven-week high above 118 yen <JPY=> and also rallied against the euro <EUR=> and other European currencies as interest rate markets priced in further monetary tightening in the United States this year.  

The Federal Reserve raised the fed funds rate on Tuesday for the 14th time in 19 months and hinted further rises could follow.  

The South Korean won <KRW=> dropped a percent on the day to around 974 a dollar, pulling further back from Wednesday's eight-year peak around 957.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> and the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> were also big losers. The Singapore dollar slipped to the weaker side of 1.63 per U.S. dollar, ceding more than a cent from the previous day's high.  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> rose early to 52.03 per dollar, its strongest level since May 2003, and then slipped. It has risen about 1.8 percent since Jan. 23, buoyed by expectations of foreign portfolio inflows and a possible upgrade in the country's credit ratings.  

Markets in China and Taiwan were closed for Lunar New Year holidays.  

Sean Callow, Westpac Bank's currency strategist, said the dollar's rebound was no surprise.  

"The market did get a little bit carried away with the notion that the dollar should decline as soon as the Fed even hints at finishing tightening.  

"There is no guarantee that they have finished hiking yet and that the yield story will be broadly supportive of the dollar overall," he said.  

Still, the strength of economic fundamentals would support currencies such as the won, ensuring their losses were limited, Callow said.  

"Dollar/won could track higher in the short-term but it is hard to argue for a major pullback on any of the won crosses. The fundamental story for the won is very strong," he said.  

INTERVENTION

Analysts suspected central banks in Korea, India, the Philippines and Singapore had intervened this week to rein in the strength of their currencies.  

"They are never going to sit passively while markets take their currencies stronger against the dollar," Tim Condon, ING's currency strategist said.  

"They are always going to be dollar defenders but I suspect that means they slow but not reverse the pressure," he said, while citing the strength of flows underpinning Asian currencies.  

South Korean foreign exchange reserves jumped $6.5 billion in January, the biggest monthly gain in 14 months, which dealers said indicated heavy dollar-buying intervention by the Bank of Korea.  

Yet, the commerce ministry said on Wednesday the central bank had been complacent and had allowed the won to strengthen rapidly.  

This week, the won hit an 8-year high near 8.14 per yen <JPYKRW=R>, as Asian currencies outperformed the yen.  

ABN AMRO Bank's Shahab Jalinoos said the outperformance against the Japanese currency would persist.  

"This reflects the fact that low-yielding yen is currently a global funding currency in a risk-loving environment, while Asian currencies are beneficiaries of risk-seeking global capital seeking returns in their asset markets," he said in a note. title: Emerging Asia  FX -Higher,  intervention  fears surface
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 1 (Reuters) - Asian currencies bucked the dollar's strength against the yen on Wednesday and hit multi-year highs against the U.S. currency, raising concerns that regional central banks will step up intervention.  

In late Asian trading, the Korean won <KRW=>, Singapore dollar <SGD=>, Thai baht <THB=> and Philippine peso <PHP=> were off their intra-day peaks against the dollar. Traders suspected central banks in India and Korea had intervened to buy dollars.  

The moves took place even as the U.S. dollar remained near a four-week high against the yen <JPY=> after the Federal Reserve raised interest rates as expected on Tuesday for the 14th time in a 19-month tightening cycle. The Fed also indicated further tightening could follow.  

The peso ended at 52.09 per dollar, just off a high of 52.05, its strongest level since May 2003 as markets positioned for foreign investment in Philippine equities.  

The won briefly hit 957 per dollar, last seen when Asia was in the midst of a financial crisis in November 1997, before retreating modestly.  

The Thai baht crept to the firmer side of 39 per dollar and then fell back, while the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> stayed close to 9,300 per dollar and at its highest since March.  

The Singapore dollar met resistance near 1.6207 per U.S. dollar, some distance away from last week's highs around 1.6170.  

Markets in China, Malaysia and Taiwan remained closed for the Lunar New Year holidays.  

Mirza Baig, a Deutsche Bank currency strategist, said operators who had been bearish were now buying Asian currencies.  

However, he said he would hesitate to buy Asian currencies at these levels.  

"The speculative position overhang has become extended and there is a higher probability of a squeeze like the one we saw in dollar/yen overnight.  

"People have realised that Asia is appreciating and have jumped on the bandwagon and we are likely to see a correction in the next few days."  

Manila-based traders said the peso was approaching resistance between 52 and 51.80, the latter level being the May 2003 peak.  

Expectations of foreign portfolio inflows underpinned sentiment. Foreigners have bought a net $2.35 billion of South Korean shares in the past 10 sessions.  

In the Philippines, news that 80 percent of power producer First Generation Corp.'s 8.5 billion peso IPO had been sold to overseas investors buoyed the peso.  

SING DOLLAR SEEN CAPPED  

Analysts said the Sing dollar's 2.5 percent rise last month had pushed it to the top of what they estimated was the central bank's policy band for the currency, and that markets should be on guard for possible intervention.  

The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) conducts monetary policy by managing the Singapore dollar within an undisclosed band against a trade-weighted basket of currencies.  

Rising asset prices, robust export growth and the strength in economic growth numbers have prompted thinking among economists that the MAS is on the verge of announcing a policy suggesting a faster pace of appreciation for the currency.  

UBS's currency strategist Ashley Davies said the currency was about 1.8 percent stronger than his estimate of the mid-point of the band. UBS assumes the band is 4 percent wide and the central bank allows a modest pace of appreciation for this mid-point, he said.  

Davies said the Singapore dollar would now be stable, but could gain further in the medium term.  

"We still think that SGD will perform well on a medium-term view given the potential for the MAS to adopt a more aggressive tightening bias, should the strong data continue," he said in a note.

title: India Rupee Ends At 3-Mo High On Global Cues; Bonds Dn
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee ended at a fresh three-month high against the dollar Thursday, tracking the rise of other Asian currencies against the U.S. unit.  

Expectations that capital inflows will continue to remain robust also supported trade, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at INR44.1350, last tested Oct. 3 and nearly 0.4% below Tuesday's INR44.3100 close. Indian financial markets were closed Wednesday for a religious festival holiday.  

"Dollar/rupee was only following a global trend today, but with every sharp downward move, expectations the Reserve Bank of India would intervene were rising," said a senior dealer at a foreign bank.  

Contrary to expectations, the central bank stayed away from the foreign-exchange market Thursday. The RBI was expected to intervene to protect the country's export competitiveness and check volatility.  

"It took the rupee two months to fall from INR44.43 in October to INR46.33 in December but in just under a month, the rupee has risen by more than that," said an analyst at a private-sector bank. He noted the rupee was almost 8% overvalued in trade-weighted terms and a correction was due.  

"But as long as the rupee is tracking global trends, the central bank appears to be comfortable. RBI is unlikely to intervene unless dollar-rupee falls sharply below 44," he added.  

Central bank intervention was expected to boost money market liquidity, which has shrunk in recent weeks.  

Surplus banking system liquidity has dwindled in recent weeks, triggered by the redemption of the State Bank of India's (500112.BY) $7.3 billion India Millennium Deposits - the country's largest-ever capital outflow - in December after companies paid nearly INR200 billion in quarterly taxes.  

Strong demand for bank loans has also put pressure on system liquidity. Latest data show bank loans grew 30% in the year to Dec. 23, well above 19% growth in deposits during the same period.  

Crunched system cash hit the market for interbank funds, pushing up the call money rate to over 7.0% from a notional 5.25% floor in recent sessions, making bond investments more expensive. The rate ended steady at 7.00%-7.25% Thursday.  

"Strong credit growth, a large capital outflow in December and recent bond auctions (INR100 billion Monday) have squeezed money market liquidity," said a local dealer. "Cash will remain tight until government spending picks up."  

The RBI infused about INR282 billion at the day's repurchase auction, up from INR245 previously, reflecting shrinking system funds.  

Although liquidity is expected to improve once the government resumes spending on infrastructure and salaries this month, the federal government's next bond auction, worth INR140 billion, in February, is expected to again dent system cash.  

Indian government bonds ended down as investors sold bonds amid thin volumes in directionless trade. Most participants stayed on the sidelines, hoping for cues on yield direction when the RBI meets to review policy Jan. 24.  

"Cash should improve next week, there are some inflows from treasury bill redemptions (around INR38 billion) due tomorrow," said a local dealer. "Also, banks ease off product covering in the second week of the reporting fortnight, so call rates are likely to come off."  

Banks typically borrow funds in the call money market to cover reserve needs and report average cash reserve positions to the RBI every two weeks. The current reporting cycle ends next Friday.  

The popular 7.27% 2013 bond ended lower at INR102.08 from INR102.09 previously. Its yield closed unchanged at 6.91%.  

In the forward segment, dollar rates ended higher as tightening system liquidity pressured money market interest rates up. The dollar forward contract maturing in December 2006 closed at a premium of INR0.6200, from INR0.5800 previously.  

Interest rate swaps benchmarked to the Mumbai interbank forward offered rate, or MIFOR, rose on large overseas corporate hedging to the tune of nearly $500 million-$1 billion. The five-year swap ended higher at 6.36%-6.41% from 6.35%-6.39.  

Overnight indexed swap rates ended up on worries about tight liquidity. The five-year swap ended up at 6.41%-6.43% from 6.38%-6.39%. [ 12-01-06 1318GMT ]

MUMBAI, Dec 2 (Reuters) - The rupee fell to a near-15-month closing low on Friday, weakening 0.4 percent, after foreign banks and investors bought dollars to capitalise on an arbitrage against costlier offshore forwards.  

Traders said the dollar's steady climb against the yen to a 32-month high, an afternoon slide off highs by Indian stocks and the absence of sustained intervention by the central bank had also contributed to the weak sentiment on the rupee.  

The partly convertible rupee <INR=IN> suffered its biggest percentage fall in nearly a month to end at 46.18/19 per dollar. It previously closed lower at 46.265/270 on Sept. 10, 2004.  

But the currency, which closed at 45.995/46.005 on Thursday, was off a session low of 46.24, helped by long dollar unwinding near close as some banks opted for caution ahead of the weekend.  

"The NDF(non-deliverable forward)-related (dollar) buying started the rupee's fall initially," a chief dealer at a foreign bank said.  

"With the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) only trying to smoothen the move rather than intervening in a sustained manner, the yen losing more ground against the dollar and stocks retreating in the afternoon, there were really no positives for the rupee."  

The opportunity to gain more than 0.10-0.15 rupees by selling dollar-rupee in the one- to three-month segment in the NDF market <PNDF> had fuelled demand for the strengthening U.S. currency in the morning.  

Traders said the Indian central bank, which had briefly supported the rupee early with a verbal intervention leading to dollar selling by state-run banks, had probably refrained from stronger action on concerns about draining rupees.  

Liquidity in the banking system fell sharply last month, pushing up overnight borrowing costs and traders said the central bank may have been keen to ensure that cash surpluses remain ample ahead of an 80-billion-rupee federal bond sale on Dec. 6.  

The rupee has lost nearly 6 percent in 2005 on growing worries about a widening trade deficit -- forecast to hit a record $48 billion in March -- and the dollar's gains overseas.  

Only robust foreign fund inflows of more than $8.6 billion into Indian stocks this year have given some relief to the rupee.  

But with the main Mumbai stock index <.BSESN> sliding off a new high on Friday to end just 0.19 percent up, in a market where losing issues outnumbered gainers, the rupee's outlook remained weak, traders said.  

"Unless the dollar's trend reverses overseas, we should still see the rupee under pressure," a dealer at a state-run bank said.

text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee extended losses against the U.S. dollar for the second straight session Monday but ended off the day's lows as state-run banks sold dollars, possibly on the central bank's behalf.  

Earlier in the session, the rupee slid, unnerved by the dollar's rise against other global majors and month-end demand for the U.S. currency from oil importing companies, dealers said.  

The dollar ended at INR45.96, just shy of the psychologically crucial INR46.00 mark, although above Friday's INR45.82.  

"A large state-owned bank sold dollars at 45.9850, then bought around 46.0000 and again sold around 45.9700," said a foreign bank dealer. "It's difficult to say whether the move was a trading punt or central bank intervention, but it appears the second possibility is stronger, as several state-run banks sold all at once."  

India's central bank usually intervenes through state-run banks to curb excessive volatility in the currency market.  

Some market watchers believe the rupee's weakness is "an automatic response" to India's widening current account deficit.  

"The fall was imminent, considering strong import growth in recent months coupled with high global oil prices," said Raja Bandhyopadhyay, analyst at Debtonnet.com.  

India's current account deficit ballooned to $6.20 billion during April-June from a $3.39 billion surplus in the same year-ago period. Economists said rising investment demand in a growing economy is expected to push the trade gap further into the red.  

Tarini Vaidya, country treasurer at private-sector Centurion Bank, believes the rupee's weakening could be sustained on account of strong demand for oil. "If this trend continues, dollar-rupee could soon test 46.25," she said.  

Indian government bonds rose Monday as investors cheered the introduction of an additional daily liquidity adjustment facility on hopes it will improve system cash.  

"The new system will help ensure the call money rate doesn't go through the roof whenever liquidity is a bit tight," said a private sector bank dealer. "It will aid better liquidity management."  

After close of trade Friday, the central bank said it would conduct the repurchase and reverse repurchase auctions twice daily from Monday.  

Traders said the move would help stabilize the overnight call money rate, which had risen to nearly 7.0% earlier this month from the usual 5.25%-5.50% when outflows toward bond sales and stronger demand for loans caused a cash crunch.  

The actively traded 7.49% bond maturing in 2017 closed at INR102.10, up from its previous close of INR101.91. Its yield fell three basis points to 7.21%. The benchmark 10-year bond's yield slipped two basis points to 7.06%.  

Underlying sentiment was slightly cautious as market participants await fresh bond issues due early next month. As part of its regular market borrowing, the government is set to raise INR80 billion between Dec. 1-8.  

"Some profit booking came in toward the close of trade. Although the broad trend will be for a rise, the upside will be limited, at least until the auction announcement," said a trader at a primary dealing firm.  

The overnight interbank call money rate ended up at 5.30%-5.40% from 4.00%-5.00% as banks upped demand for funds at the start of a new reporting fortnight.  

Local banks typically report their cash reserve positions over two weeks to the RBI - banks are required to maintain reserves equivalent to 5% of net liabilities and report such positions to the central bank on alternate Fridays.  

Dollar forward rates ended lower in lackluster trade. The dollar forward contract maturing in October 2006 closed down at a premium of INR0.2150 from INR0.2200 previously to the spot rate.  

Interest rate swaps benchmarked to the Mumbai interbank forward offered rate, or Mifor, closed little changed. The two-year swap rate ended marginally up at 5.47%-5.52% from 5.46%-5.51%, while the five-year rate ended at 5.85%-5.90% from 5.83%-5.88% at the previous close.

title: UPDATE: India's Sensex At New Milestone; Rupee Stumbles
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Bullish foreign investors pushed Indian shares to a fresh record high Monday but the rupee fell as the currency market ignored the capital inflows to fret over the country's current account deficit.  

The key Indian share index, the Bombay Stock Exchange's 30-share Sensex, broke the 9000-point barrier for the first time in its 130-year history in Monday's intraday trading but slipped back later on profit-taking.  

It still ended the day at a record-high 8,994.94 points, up 1.2%, or 105.91 points, from Friday. The index has gained 49% in the past 12 months and 41% since the current fiscal year began April 1.  

The 9000-point mark is the third major milestone the index has crossed in 2005, after passing the 8000 level in September and the 7000 level in June.  

Market-watchers say many more are to come in the years ahead.  

The 9000 mark "is one of many more milestones we are likely to see in the likely bull run over the next few years," said Jawahir Mulraj, India representative at U.S.-based publication Institutional Investor.  

"Sensex should be heading toward 15,000 over the next two to three years," as the country's strong economy continues to attract capital, he said.  

Being Asia's fastest-growing economy after China, has kept India an attractive destination for investors, even though some investment houses have started saying local assets are too expensive.  

Official forecasts peg the country's economic expansion in the current fiscal year at 7.0%-7.5%, up from 6.9% in fiscal 2004-2005.  

The strong economy and the stock-market rally have attracted foreign investment worth $8.49 billion in Indian shares so far in 2005. This is just shy of the record $8.51 billion foreigners invested in 2004.  

However, some are worried the party has lasted too long.  

Earlier in November Merrill Lynch downgraded India's equities rating to underweight, citing rising inflation and interest rates, falling currency and expensive valuations.  

Merrill also noted Sensex valuations are the most expensive among all emerging countries at 14.4 times earnings for the current financial year, compared with 13.6 times for Malaysia, 11.5 times for Taiwan, 9.5 times for Thailand, 9 times for Indonesia and 8.9 times for South Korea.  

Indeed, even as the long-term prospects for Indian equities remain positive, the near-term outlook is one of caution.  

Ajit Sangvi, director at Mumbai-based MSS Securities, noted the latest rise in local stocks hasn't been as broad-based as past rallies, and was characterized by the sizable gains of a handful of heavyweights.  

Monday's rally was led by blue chips such as Oil & Natural Gas Corp., consumer goods major Hindustan Lever and technology firm Wipro.  

Sangvi said the trend in local shares may depend increasingly on liquidity in the financial system in the coming weeks.  

He expects the Sensex to remain in a 8850-9250 range in the near term.  


 
   Rupee Falls 
   

The rupee fell sharply against the dollar Monday, briefly slipping below key psychological support at INR46 a dollar as banks and companies bought a globally strong U.S. currency. It later recovered partly on suspected central-bank intervention.  

The dollar ended at INR45.96, sharply up from INR45.82 at the previous close but below an intraday high of INR46.02.  

Raja Bandhyopadhyay, analyst at Debtonnet.com, said the rupee's fall is "an automatic response" to the country's widening current account deficit. India's current account showed a $6.20 billion deficit in the April-June quarter, compared with a $3.39 billion surplus in the year-ago period.  

With the current account deficit set to widen more, the downward pressure on the rupee may only increase.  

"Despite the recent evidence of a recovery in equity flows, we maintain a bearish rupee view. Even if the capital account posts a surplus ... the overall balance of payments will be down substantially owing to a wider current account deficit," Siddharth Mathur, strategist at JPMorgan India, said in a recent research report.  

JPMorgan recently revised upward its forecast of the Indian current account deficit for the current fiscal year to 2.2% of the country's gross domestic product from 1.3% earlier.  

It forecast the dollar at INR46.50 by the end of March 2006 and INR47.50 by the end of December 2006.  

The rupee's trade-weighted overvaluation also may work against it. The rupee is overvalued by more than 8%, according to analysts.  

Market-watchers believe although the Reserve Bank of India may intervene in the market to smooth out undue volatility, it will tolerate a gradual rupee decline in the coming months, as that could help correct the local currency's trade-weighted overvaluation and help make Indian exports more competitive in the global markets.  

The Indian central bank doesn't fix any target level or range for the rupee, but often intervenes in the market to smooth market volatility or to prevent the currency from straying too far from fair valuation.

title: RBI WATCH: India Unlikely To Stem Rupee Slide For Now
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of India has finally signaled what many foreign exchange market participants had suspected - that the rupee's recent weakness isn't yet a concern for the central bank so it won't intervene in the market to stem the currency's slide.  

India's deteriorating current account deficit and relatively expensive currency in trade-weighted terms mean that the RBI appears happy to let rupee weaken against the dollar, which has strengthened against most currencies in recent weeks.  

Analysts say that the rupee's weakness won't start to worry the central bank unless the currency's trade-weighted overvaluation is significantly reduced.  

Some in the market expect the RBI to step in if the dollar breaks strong resistance at INR46.50, which is a level that the U.S. currency tested but failed to break more than 15 months ago. Market watchers say this level could break in coming weeks.  

RBI Deputy Governor Rakesh Mohan said late Wednesday that the rupee market has been "very orderly" of late, and that "genuine" dollar demand caused a sharp recent rupee fall.  

"Yes, of course, the rupee has been moving but...it has been moving in two directions - it is what a healthy market ought to have," Mohan told reporters when asked about the rupee's sharpest six-week fall in over a year.  

The dollar has risen 4.5% against the rupee so far this fiscal year, which started on April 1. It gained 3.9% in the past six weeks alone. The last time the dollar rose as much against the rupee over as short a period was in April and May 2004. The dollar closed at INR45.81 Wednesday.  

The Indian central bank doesn't have a target level or range for the rupee, but often intervenes in the market to smooth market volatility. But the RBI so far has done little to slow the rupee's accelerated fall in recent weeks.  

The government too has indicated it isn't concerned about the currency's fall.  

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said Wednesday that "orderly movement" of the rupee is acceptable as long as such moves are in line with the currency's trade-weighted value.  

Most analysts expect the rupee to extend losses in the coming weeks although some anticipate a partial recovery later, helped by a recovery in inflows of foreign investment into the local stock market.  

"The dollar can still head higher against the rupee in the short term, possibly testing the INR47 level. But I expect it to stabilize around the INR46 level by year-end helped by an improvement in foreign equity flows," said JPMorgan Chase Bank's Asian head of currency strategy, Claudio Piron. Foreigners bought local shares worth $353.4 million so far this month, after making sales worth $866 million last month.  


 
     Current Account Has Deteriorated 
   

Despite its recent fall, the rupee remains significantly overvalued in trade-weighted terms, indicating there is room for further weakness.  

Analysts estimate that an index of the rupee's real effective exchange rate, or its value in trade-weighted terms, is currently above 107, indicating overvaluation of more than 7%. The rupee is considered at fair value when its REER is 100.  

"The market will take dollar-rupee to a level that is justified by fundamentals such as the trade-weighted valuation of the rupee...that shouldn't be a cause for concern for the RBI," said Agam Gupta, head of currency trading at Standard Chartered Bank India.  

Currency watchers say the central bank is tolerating rupee weakness because it reflects the dollar's global strengthening and India's current account deficit.  

"The RBI's comments confirm that the central bank isn't uneasy about the rupee's weakness...(and) that the RBI believes the rupee fall reflects fundamentals such as the current account deficit and the dollar's global strengthening," said P.H. Ramaswamy, managing director at Calyon India.  

India's current account swung to a $6.20 billion deficit in the April-June quarter from a $3.39 billion surplus in the same quarter a year earlier.  

Economists expect the deficit for the whole of fiscal 2005-2006 in the $16 billion-$18 billion range, as high global oil prices inflate the country's oil import bill.  

Some say that the RBI also isn't likely concerned that a sharp rupee fall could damp import demand, which is a key driver of investment activity, because imports may be like exports and be unresponsive to currency changes.  

"India's exports grew strongly when the rupee was strengthening so there isn't much reason to believe imports could contract due to a currency fall," said Calyon's Ramaswamy.  

India's exports rose 20.5% in the six months between April and September, compared with a year earlier, well above the government's 16% growth target for fiscal 2005-2006. Imports grew even faster at 33.1% during the same period.  

In the past, the RBI has mostly intervened in the currency market when it sensed speculation was making the market volatile.  

But "at current levels of dollar-rupee, there is hardly any speculative activity," notes Pankaj Sharma, chief foreign-exchange dealer at state-owned Union Bank of India.  

Sharma said the rupee's weakness reflected a dollar demand-supply gap of around $3 billion per month in the local currency market, caused by the current account shortfall and a slowdown in capital inflows due to rising U.S. interest rates.  

A series of interest-rate hikes by the U.S. Federal Reserve since mid-2004 has sharply cut the U.S.-India interest-rate differential. The Fed has raised the Federal Funds rate by three percentage points to 4.00% since June 2004 while the RBI increased its benchmark rate by just 0.75 percentage point to 5.25%, narrowing the interest-rate gap by 2.25 percentage points to 1.25 percentage points.

title: RPT-Indian rupee seen testing 46/dollar, cbank absent
text:
(Repeats to local subscribers)  

MUMBAI, Nov 7 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is likely to test 46.00-46.50 per dollar <INR=IN> shortly in the absence of central bank support after falling 0.8 percent on Monday to a 13-month low of 45.9200, traders say.  

The central bank intervenes to calm volatility on the exchange rate but dealers say it has not stepped in to buy rupees since Oct. 18, when it did so briefly through state-run banks to stop the currency falling too acutely.  

Since then the rupee has shed 1.6 percent. Dealers expect a test of 46.00 or even 46.50 over the next day or two, levels untouched since September last year, before the central bank steps in to support it.  

"They vehemently defended that level last year and so we expect 46.50 to be a strong support level for the rupee," a chief dealer at a state-run bank said.  

The rupee closed at 45.91/92 per dollar and other traders also said they did not expect the central bank to act before 46.00.  

The government auctions 80 billion rupees ($1.74 billion) worth of debt on Tuesday and traders said the Reserve Bank of India would not want to intervene and drain rupees from the system beforehand as this would diminish cash surpluses which would normally be used to buy bonds.  

"We shouldn't see the RBI for sometime now as we have very thin liquidity in the system and the auction could totally suck out liquidity," said R.K. Gurumurthy, acting Treasury head at ING Vysysa Bank in Bangalore.  

"I have only a resistance at 46.05 and the next 46.50. We could test these most likely this week," he said.  

The 46.05 level is a 50 percent retracement of the move to a 6-year high of 43.01 set in July this year from its all-time low in May 2002 which he charted at 49.09. The 46.50 level is a previous big dollar/rupee top of August 2004.  

The rupee has fallen as a wealth of foreign fund inflows in the first nine months of this year dried up and began to reverse in October on the back of a sharp stock market correction.  

India's current account has turned into deficit this year and, without the fund inflows, that gap has exerted downward pressure on the currency. In addition, Indian importers, nervous that the dollar is on the rise as a result of higher U.S. interest rates, have been buying up the U.S. currency.  

Traders said there was another reason why the central bank had not stepped in to curb weakness up to this point.  

"Despite the fact that the rupee is depreciating against the dollar, it has gained against the euro and sterling, which means that it is still overvalued," said a chief dealer at a state-run bank.  

JP Morgan's real effective exchange rate <JPMREER>, which is similar to that of the RBI, shows the rupee is 7.5 percent overvalued compared with just 1.7 percent a year ago.

title: Indian Rupee At Fresh 11-Mo Low On Outflows, Trade Gap
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee broke key psychological supports to end at a fresh 11-month low Tuesday as a widening trade gap and a negative stock market trend fueled concerns about portfolio outflows.  

Widening differentials between the rupee market and the overseas non-deliverable forward rate combined with the dollar's broad rally overseas also weighed on the domestic unit, traders said.  

The dollar broke through the key INR45.00 resistance level to end up at INR45.1650 from INR44.8800 at the last close. The U.S. currency has appreciated 3.3% from April 1, when India's current fiscal year started, gaining almost 2.7% so far this month alone amid signs of a slowdown in stock-related flows into local shares.  

Foreigners have sold local stocks worth $228.9 million so far this month, compared with purchases of $971.7 million in September and $1.014 billion in August.  

Although some expect the rupee to weaken more during the coming weeks due to a widening trade deficit, they believe the trend may not attract Reserve Bank of India intervention as the weakness "is a part of a global trend," said Sreebhashyam Srinivas, a senior currency dealer at Nova Scotia Bank in Mumbai. He expects the rupee to test INR45.50 by December.  

The Indian central bank typically intervenes to smooth market volatility or prevent the currency from straying from its fair valuation. In trade-weighted terms, the rupee is currently more than 8% overvalued.  

Latest data show India's current account deficit in the April-June quarter was $6.20 billion compared with a $3.39 billion surplus in the same period of 2004.  

Widening differentials between the non-deliverable forward and the onshore market have also pressured the rupee down in recent sessions.  

"The differential between the onshore dollar/rupee and the one-year forward in the non-deliverable forwards market is huge, nearly INR0.21, and it has had a domino effect," said a dealer at a private bank.  

NDFs are offshore financial instruments used by foreign investors to bet on the value of the rupee. A cheaper offshore rupee prompts foreign investors to buy dollars in the local market and sell them overseas, thus opening an opportunity to arbitrage between the two markets.  

In the debt market, government bonds ended lower as a sharp fall in the rupee reinforced worries the RBI would likely hike the reverse repurchase rate by 25 basis points at its Oct. 25 policy review.  

Volumes were modest, with few investors willing to build fresh positions ahead of next week's policy statement.  

The popular 10.25% 2021 bond ended down at INR125.07 from INR125.32 at the last close. Its yield rose to 7.50% from 7.47%. The yield on the 10-year benchmark, 7.38% bond was higher at 7.16% from 7.15%.  

"A sharp drop in the rupee below critical resistance levels (likely 45.20) could set in motion monetary forces. A rate hike seems likely," said an ABN AMRO report.  

Most market participants expect the central bank to raise key short-term interest rates to contain price pressures caused by strong domestic demand and high oil prices.  

Data show wholesale-price-based inflation rose 4.24% during the week ended Oct. 1. Although inflation had eased to three-year low of 3.01% in August, economists say a local oil price hike and a waning statistical base effect could push it up to around 5.0%-5.5% by March.  

"There are also concerns liquidity may not be very comfortable for long," said a state-run bank dealer.  

"A lot depends on how the redemption of the India Millennium Deposits is handled," said K. Harihar, treasurer at Development Credit Bank. The State Bank of India's $5.5 billion, five-year IMD is due to mature in December, possibly the country's single-biggest capital outflow this year.  

Money market liquidity - as indicated by bids at the RBI's daily reverse repo auction - has ebbed in recent sessions on the back of a pullout by foreign funds from domestic stock markets and the RBI's recent intervention when it sold dollars to cushion the domestic unit's slide.  

The RBI accepted average daily bids worth INR202 billion so far in October compared with INR305 billion and INR356 billion in September and August respectively.  

The overnight call money rate closed unchanged at 5.0%-5.1% with banks' demand for funds modest amid dull trade.  

"Markets were mostly quiet today, the rate hovered around 5.0% for most of the session," said a trader at a primary dealing firm.  

In the derivatives segment, dollar forward rates fell Tuesday, as banks and exporters sold dollars in a mild bout of profit taking. The dollar forward contract maturing in September 2006 closed down at a premium of INR0.1800 to the spot rate from INR0.2050 previously.  

Near-term interest rate swaps benchmarked to the Mumbai interbank offered rate, or Mifor, closed marginally down, in line with the slip in dollar forward rates. The two-year swap rate ended lower at 5.32%-5.36% from 5.34%-5.38% while the five-year rate closed marginally up at 5.80%-5.84% from 5.79%-5.83%.  

Overnight indexed swap rates inched up, in line with a rise in government bonds yields. The 5-year swap ended higher up at 6.39%-6.41% from 6.37%-6.39% at the previous close. [ 18-10-05 1408GMT ]
