title: India Rupee At Fresh 10-Mo Low; Weak Bias To Persist
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee ended at a new 10-month low against the U.S. dollar Monday as a widening trade deficit and the dollar's firm trend overseas triggered heavy dollar purchases by oil companies.  

Slowing portfolio investments and increasing differentials between non-deliverable rupee forwards and the onshore market also weighed on the domestic currency, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at INR44.7550, up from INR44.3800 at the previous close. It last reached a similar level of INR44.7900 Dec. 10.  

The rupee has weakened some 1.5% over the past two weeks but traders say the Reserve Bank of India is unlikely to intervene to support the rupee as the domestic unit is still overvalued in trade-weighted terms.  

"Other Asian currencies have also been weakening, and moreover, the rupee is 10% overvalued in trade-weighted terms," said a private sector bank trader. "I personally don't think the RBI will step in."  

He expects the dollar to trade between INR44.75 and INR44.80 this week, buoyed by continued dollar demand from oil companies.  

Sentiment towards the rupee has been hit in recent sessions by signs of falling portfolio investment in Indian shares, pressuring a currency already weighed down by a widening trade gap and high global oil prices.  

"The general theme has been that of rupee weakness; there is a case for the dollar to rise to 45 by December," said Monish Tahilramani, head of treasury at HSBC, India.  

The latest data from the Securities and Exchange Board of India show that foreigners sold shares worth $56 million over the past five sessions compared with purchases worth $17.4 million.  

"Until now, the rising trade deficit was cushioned by portfolio inflows, but now with some slowdown on that front, the rupee looks set to weaken," said S.P. Prabhu, fixed-income analyst at IDBI Capital Markets.  

Prabhu expects India's trade deficit to widen to $50 billion by the end of the current fiscal year in March 2006 from $38 billion last year. This could contribute to the rupee's weakening bias, taking the dollar to INR45 by March, he said.  

Some currency market participants say the widening differential between non-deliverable rupee forwards and onshore markets is also weighing on the local unit.  

"One-month differentials between NDF and onshore markets were around INR0.15 last, which is quite attractive," said a local dealer.  

NDFs are offshore financial instruments used by foreign investors to bet on the value of the rupee. The rupee is typically cheaper against the dollar in the offshore market, prompting foreign investors to buy dollars in the local market and sell them overseas for a better price.  

Indian government bonds ended lower Friday, as a fall in the rupee "spooked sentiment" and most investors remained sidelined ahead of the central bank's Oct. 25 monetary policy review, dealers said.  

"It's still a 50-50 call on what the central bank is going to do this policy review and the market is trading in a narrow INR0.10-0.15 range," said a local dealer.  

Although some segments of the market expect a 25-basis-point hike in the reverse repurchase rate to contain inflationary pressures, others believe there is little reason for the central bank to raise rates given that the domestic economy is strong but not overheating.  

The latest data show the Indian economy grew by 8.1% during April-June, the first quarter of the current fiscal year, after expanding by 7.6% in the year-ago period.  

But inflation still poses a threat. Although the rate eased to three-year low of 3.01% in August, analysts say a local oil price hike and a waning statistical base-effect could push it up to around 5.0%-5.5% by March. The latest year-on-year inflation was 3.97% in the week to Sept. 24.  

The liquid 10.25% 2021 bond ended down at INR125.10 from INR125.23 at the previous close. Its yield edged up to 7.50% from 7.48% previously. The yield on the benchmark 10-year, 7.38% bond ended up at 7.18% from 7.16%.  

In the market for overnight funds, the call money rate closed flat at 4.95%-5.05%, with banks' demand for funds to meet mandatory cash reserve targets offset by adequate system liquidity.  

Money market liquidity has been ample in recent sessions, as indicated by bids at a recent RBI reverse repurchase auction - the lowest yielding money market instrument. The RBI accepted daily average bids worth INR244 billion last week, above INR224 billion accepted in the week prior.  

But "if the rupee continues to fall sharply, then the RBI might step in to stem excessive volatility and that may pressure liquidity," said a trader at a primary dealing firm.  

Dealers are concerned the RBI could buy rupees and sell dollars to support the local unit, thus sucking out liquidity from the money market.

title: RBI WATCH: Rupee Support Favored To Beat Inflation
text:
By Anil Varma 
 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
   

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of India's intervention in foreign-exchange markets last week to stem the rupee's fall against the dollar indicates the central bank is worried that the currency's fall will exacerbate growing inflation pressures.  

Despite helping engineer six weeks ago the rupee's fall from its recent peak through heavy dollar purchases, the RBI appears to have decided that enough is enough.  

Central bank rupee purchases last week have helped the currency recover from a near nine-month low against the dollar.  

Analysts say that the RBI, keen to keep a lid on inflation, will use its currency reserves to offset mounting downward pressure on the rupee due to a widening current account gap and a falling capital account surplus until the outlook for domestic prices is more stable.  

They say that the central bank is more likely to focus on supporting the rupee, rather than raise interest rates, in its fight against inflation.  

"With global oil prices continuing their relentless upward march, the desire to limit the local impact of higher international oil prices and to keep inflationary pressures in check will keep the pressure on RBI to restrain any (downward) correction in the rupee," said Siddharth Mathur, strategist at JPMorgan India, in a recent research report.  

The RBI sold dollars in the spot market last week after the dollar hit INR44.15, the greenback's highest level since Dec. 15, 2004.  

Not many weeks prior, the RBI was buying dollars to pare the rupee's trade-weighted overvaluation after the dollar fell to a six-year low of INR43.12 following the Chinese currency revaluation.  

At 0820 GMT, the dollar was quoted at INR43.95.  

Despite the RBI dollar sales, analysts estimate that the rupee remains overvalued by more than 7% in trade-weighted terms. But the central bank will probably tolerate this for some time in order to fight a more serious threat - inflation.  

Inflation has remained the main policy challenge for the RBI since mid-2004. The bank has raised its key policy rate twice since then to stabilize prices and the latest spurt in global crude prices has aggravated this inflation threat.  


 
   Inflation To Rise Again 
   

To be sure, year-on-year inflation in India has eased in recent months but this is only because of a high-statistical-base effect, which is set to wear off by the end of this month.  

After that, inflation should start rising, gaining additional upward momentum from the government's move Tuesday to raise local fuel prices to align them with high global crude prices.  

The proposed INR3-a-liter increase in gasoline prices and INR2-a-liter hike in diesel prices could add 30 basis points to domestic inflation by late September, says Abheek Barua, economist at ABN Amro Bank India.  

Inflation measured 3.08% in the week ended Aug. 20 from a year ago, down from 5.70% in early April.  

Central bank watchers believe the RBI will likely rely more on currency management than raising interest rates to counter the price increases.  

"The RBI may not prefer to raise interest rates much to fight inflation because such a move would expose Indian banks, which hold large amounts of government bonds, to high interest-rate risk," said an economist at a U.K.-based bank.  

The central bank isn't expected to raise its reverse repurchase rate, currently at 5%, more than a modest 25 basis points during the rest of 2005. The bank last raised the rate by 25 basis points in April.  

Higher-than-expected export growth also will encourage the RBI to allow the rupee to remain overvalued in the near term. Exports rose 21% during the April-to-July period from a year earlier, well above 16% growth forecast by the government for the current fiscal year, which began April 1.  

The RBI is also unlikely to worry that a strong rupee, which makes imports cheaper, could help inflate the trade and current account deficits to unmanageable proportions.  

In its annual report released last week, the RBI said India's trade deficit would "remain within acceptable limits that can be financed by normal capital flows."  

"The current level of the trade deficit appears to be manageable and...consistent with India's growth aspirations," it added.  

India recorded a current account deficit of $6.43 billion in fiscal 2004-2005, compared with a $10.56 billion surplus the previous year, as the trade deficit more than doubled to $38.13 billion from $15.45 billion.  

Some in the market expect India's central bank to intervene in foreign-exchange markets to limit the rupee's movements to a small range for some time, since both a rise or fall of the rupee could harm the economy.  

"Barring temporary sharp fluctuations, I expect the RBI to keep the rupee broadly in a INR43.40-INR43.80 range for some time," said Mohan Shenoi, head of treasury at Mumbai-based Kotak Mahindra Bank.  

"A rupee fall beyond this can be inflationary, while a sharp rise could fuel a consumption-led widening of the current account deficit," he said. "The RBI wouldn't want to encourage either."

title: Indian rupee ends at 8-½ mo low, cbank supports
text:
(Updates to close)  

MUMBAI, Aug 30 (Reuters) - The rupee fell to its weakest close since mid-December on Tuesday, easing beyond 44 to the dollar on mounting concerns that costly crude oil would widen India's trade deficit.  

The market was also weighed down by cash dollar shortage to fund immediate import needs, the dollar's strength overseas, arbitrage between offshore and onshore forward markets and worries about slowing foreign investment, dealers said.  

"Oil companies have been on a dollar buying spree in the past few sessions," said N.S. Paramsivam, head of treasury at Essar group, Mumbai. "The rupee is catching up with fundamentals like a widening trade deficit, the dollar's overseas strength and weaker Asian currencies."  

The rupee, which analysts say is overvalued on a trade-weighted basis, ended at 44.0325/0375 per dollar, its lowest since Dec. 14 and down from the previous day's 43.885/890.  

It fell as low as 44.15, stretching losses to 1 percent in two sessions, before suspected central bank intervention helped pull it back, dealers said. India's central bank usually steps in to curb excessive volatility in the currency market.  

JPMorgan said in a report on Monday, it expected the rupee to weaken to 45 by end-December.  

Traders said the central bank intervention was not very strong as it would drive up the spot rupee and increase the price differential between the onshore and offshore forward markets.  

"The intervention was sporadic," said the chief dealer at a private bank. "If they sell dollars aggressively, the arbitrage between the offshore and the onshore market will widen."  

One-month non-deliverable rupee forwards (NDFs) <PNDF> were quoted at 44.23/33 while on the onshore market, the one-month forward rupee was at 44.05/06, prompting foreign investors to buy dollars in the local market and sell them overseas.  

NDFs are offshore financial instruments used by foreign investors and companies to bet on the value of the partially convertible rupee.  

OIL A BIG WORRY  

Crude oil futures, which hit a record $70.80 a barrel on Monday ahead of Hurricane Katrina's impact, were trading around $68 a barrel. Oil is India's top import and its price has risen more than 60 percent this year.  

India's central bank said in its annual report released on Monday that the merchandise trade deficit was expected to widen in 2005/06 due to substantially higher oil and non-oil imports and would push up the current account deficit.  

A Reuters poll conducted last month showed India's trade deficit was forecast to widen to a record $47 billion for 2005/06, from $38.13 billion a year earlier. A widening deficit means imports are outpacing exports and demand for the dollar is expected to increase to pay for them.  

The rupee has so far been supported by strong capital flows into India's stock market. Net investment of $7.4 billion this year has cushioned some of the adverse impact of high oil prices. The rupee hit a six-year high after China revalued in July.  

But the BSE share index <.BSESN> has slid 2.2 percent since hitting an all-time high on Aug. 18, partly on fears that India would have to raise retail fuel prices. That move could raise costs for manufacturers and crimp consumer spending in Asia's third-largest economy.

title: INTERVIEW:  India  May Cut  FX Intervention  - Barclays
text:
COCHIN, India (Dow Jones)--A looming inflation threat could spur the Reserve Bank of India to suspend or scale back currency intervention in coming months and let the rupee rise in a bid to temper price pressures, said Barclays Capital's Singapore-based economist, Dominique Dwor-Frecaut.  

Dwor-Frecaut expects high global oil prices will push up India's inflation rate in coming quarters, but said the RBI will likely rely more on currency management than interest rate policy to counter the price increases.  

"The central bank may not prefer to raise interest rates much to fight inflation because such a move would expose Indian banks, which hold large amounts of government bonds, to high interest rate risk," Dwor-Frecaut told Dow Jones Newswires in a recent interview in the southern Indian city of Cochin.  

"That leaves the exchange rate as the main option for checking inflation - the RBI may allow some rupee appreciation if India's inflation accelerates as expected," she added.  

The economist forecasts the dollar will fall to INR43.00 by end-December from INR43.53 Wednesday afternoon. A stronger rupee would lower import costs and help moderate inflation.  

The RBI has intervened heavily in the foreign exchange market in recent weeks to prevent the rupee, which analysts say? is currently overvalued in trade terms by nearly 9%, from appreciating further.  

The central bank's dollar buying has pulled the rupee down from a six-year high of INR43.12, which was hit on July 22 after China revalued its currency.  

RBI foreign-exchange reserve data show that the central bank bought at least $5 billion in the local foreign exchange market in the two weeks ended Aug. 5. The bank's foreign exchange reserves measured $142.64 billion on Aug. 5, up $23.30 billion from a year earlier.  

However, the bank probably won't sustain such intervention in the coming months since the latest spurt in global crude prices has aggravated the threat of inflation in India, said Dwor-Frecaut.  

India's year-on-year inflation rate has eased in recent weeks due to a high-statistical-base effect. The rate fell to 3.84% toward end-July from 5.70% in early April. But this is likely a temporary trend.  

Dwor-Frecaut expects the government to raise local oil prices in the near term, which would fuel inflation, to realign them with global crude oil prices, which recently crossed the $65-per-barrel mark.  

Apart from scaled-back central bank intervention, continued capital inflows also could support the rupee during the rest of the year, she said.  

"Equity-related inflows to India should continue because of the economy's strong prospects, unless there is a broad sell-off across emerging markets," said Dwor-Frecaut. "Indian equity isn't yet considered expensive."  

Foreigners have bought Indian stocks worth $7.3 billion so far in 2005, compared with a record-high $9 billion in the whole of 2004.  

Dwor-Frecaut's expectation of possible rupee gains in the coming months differs from the view of some other analysts, who expect the local currency to be pressured lower by a deepening current account deficit. India recorded a current account deficit of 6.43 billion deficit in the fiscal year ended March 31, compared with a $10.56 billion surplus in the previous year.  

But Dwor-Frecaut believes India's current account shortfall will be more than offset by its capital account surplus in the current fiscal year.  

"India will have a balance of payments surplus this year," she said.  

In 2004-2005, the country's overall balance of payments registered a $26.16 billion surplus despite the current account gap, mainly due to a surge in capital inflows.

title: RPT-INTERVIEW-India may allow rupee rise-Barclays Cap official
text:
(Repeats story issued on Sunday)  

COCHIN, India, Aug 14 (Reuters) - India's central bank is likely to loosen its tight grip over the rupee and allow it to appreciate from current levels to curb inflationary pressures, a senior official at Barclays Capital said on Sunday.  

"Oil prices are at $65 a barrel and the government will have to increase retail prices," Dominique Dwor-Frecaut, a director at Barclays Capital, Singapore told Reuters in an interview on the sidelines of the Forex Assembly of India.  

"Also, demand pressures are not yet showing up in the inflation index now, but they are building up."  

The Indian government is not willing to take fiscal measures such as cutting taxes on fuel products, while there is also some political pressure on the central bank to go slow on interest rate increases, Dwor-Frecaut said.  

"So, by default, the exchange rate is the best tool to control inflation. I think the rupee will rise to 43 against the dollar by December's end," she said.  

India's central bank says it intervenes to curb excessive volatility in the currency market.  

It has bought an estimated $5 billion in the two weeks to Aug. 5, intervening after the partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> rose to a six-year high of 43.12 per dollar on July 22, a day after China revalued the yuan <CNY=CFXS> by 2.1 percent.  

That intervention swelled reserves to $142.6 billion and the rupee has since fallen by nearly a percent to 43.54 per dollar.  

The rupee has held its ground since January despite the dollar's rise overseas, supported by foreign fund investments of $7.2 billion this year into India's booming stock market.  

Analysts say the rupee is overvalued by nearly 9 percent on a trade-weighted basis and expect the central bank to continue its dollar buying to keep exports competitive.  

"A higher rupee will translate into cheaper imports, bringing down inflation," Dwor-Frecaut said.  

STRONG DEMAND  

Dwor-Frecaut said there was strong demand for goods and services in Asia's third largest economy, which is on course for 7 percent growth for the year to March. India's economy has expanded at an average of 7.7 percent in the past two years.  

Bank credit has grown at more than 30 percent and industrial production expanded by 11.7 percent in the year to June -- the fastest in nearly a decade -- as companies produced more to feed growing demand from Indian consumers.  

"Under such circumstances, the central bank should raise interest rates. But they haven't done it in July and this has left me very confused," she said.  

"It will be more difficult to tighten monetary policy later on when there is a surge in inflation."  

Last month, the central bank held the key short term interest rate steady at 5 percent at its quarterly review, saying it wanted to ensure India's growth momentum despite inflation worries caused by record prices of oil, India's biggest import.  

It will review policy again in October, when most analysts expect it will raise the interest rate by 25 basis points.  

Inflation has dipped to 3.84 percent, but economists expect it to rise to 5 percent by end-December as demand pressures show up and high oil prices kick in.

BOMBAY, Aug 12 (Reuters) - The rupee recovered from the previous day's one-month low to end firm on Friday as the dollar fell against major overseas currencies.  

But the gains were limited by a cash dollar shortage caused by the central bank's dollar-buying intervention, record high oil prices fuelling concerns about India's ballooning trade deficit and commercial demand for the U.S. currency.  

Rupee trading had finished before the release of U.S. data on the June trade deficit, which widened 6.1 percent to $58.82 billion from a revised $55.43 billion in May. The U.S. currency slipped further after the data.  

The partially convertible Indian rupee <INR=IN> ended at 43.5350/54 per dollar, 0.13 percent stronger than the previous close of 43.5925/5975, the lowest finish since July 8.  

"There was commercial and oil-related dollar demand, due to which some traders went long on the dollar. But with the extended weekend and the fall in dollar against majors, there was (dollar) selling later," said a chief dealer at an Indian bank.  

Banks in India's financial capital, Bombay, are shut on Monday due to a national holiday.  

U.S. light crude <CLc1> was up 25 cents at $66.05 a barrel on Friday, after charging to a record high of $66.15 as investors fret over the world's strained capacity to refine and pump crude.  

But traders said the rupee, which analysts say is overvalued by 9 percent on a trade-weighted basis, was supported by robust foreign fund flows into the booming stock market.  

The local unit has held its ground this year, helped by the $7.2 billion that foreign funds have moved into the Indian stock market since Jan. 1, which has helped lift the benchmark BSE index <.BSESN> by more than 18 percent.  

Indian foreign exchange dealers are holding their annual meeting this weekend, and dealers will be looking for signals on the central bank's stance on the rupee after China's revaluation last month and as foreign investors keep pumping in money.  

Almost 400 currency dealers will meet in the southern city of Cochin from Aug. 13 to Aug. 15, where Shyamla Gopinath, the central bank's deputy governor in charge of currency market operations, will be the star speaker.

The only stocks among the BSE index shares to have ended higher were state-run power producer National Thermal Power Corp. and oil explorer Oil and Natural Gas Corp. .  

The rupee slid, dragged down by a cash dollar shortage that traders said had been triggered by the Indian central bank's sustained mop-up of the U.S. currency in recent sessions.  

The Reserve Bank of India resumed its rupee-selling interventions last month, after a three-month gap, to pull the rupee back from a six-year peak of 43.115/135 struck in the wake of China's yuan revaluation.

title: Indian rupee virtually pegged to US dollar -study
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 5 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee, contrary to market perceptions, is virtually pegged to the U.S. dollar, according to a study presented by two economists on Friday.  

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) says it follows a "managed float" for the rupee <INR=IN>, implying that it guides the currency against a basket of currencies of India's major trade partners.  

But an analysis from Tony Cavoli of the University of Adelaide and Ramkishen S. Rajan from Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy suggests that the central bank guides the rupee's exchange rate against the U.S. dollar.  

In contrast, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) manages the Singapore dollar <SGD=> against a basket of currencies of its top trade partners, the study found, confirming Singapore's official stance.  

"The Indian rupee appears to be a de facto U.S. dollar peg while the Singapore dollar is a genuine basket pegger," Cavoli said, presenting the paper at the Singapore Economic Review Conference.  

"The degree of influence of the U.S. dollar on the rupee is quite high."  

Central bank officials often cite the rupee's real effective exchange rate (REER) to indicate that the rupee is overvalued or undervalued against a basket of currencies of its main trade partners.  

"The perception that RBI is targetting the REER is not right," said Rajan. "Since 1996, that's not true. That's not what we find."  

Other currencies have a negligible influence on the rupee, he said, although the the euro <EUR=> is gradually gaining in importance.  

"The euro is becoming more important at the expense of the pound sterling <GBP=> and the yen," Cavoli said.  

For the Singapore dollar, the Japanese yen <JPY=> has been growing in influence since 1998, he said.  

The study also found that the degree of flexibility in currency movements allowed by the Monetary Authority of Singapore was lower than that allowed by the Reserve Bank of India.  

That means the degree of intervention by the Singapore authority to keep the currency within its preferred trading band is higher than that of the Indian central bank, Cavoli said. title: Emerging Asia  FX -Firmer on China remark but caution prevails
text:
SINGAPORE, July 28 (Reuters) - Asian currencies crept higher against the dollar on Thursday, recovering some of this week's losses after a Chinese newspaper report that China would allow markets to decide yuan rates.  

But gains were limited and traders said uncertainty remained over just how much China would allow its currency to appreciate following the yuan's 2.1 percent revaluation one week ago.  

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> firmed 0.4 percent to 1.6633 and the Thai baht <THB=> added almost a quarter of a percent to 41.67 per dollar -- above Wednesday's one-week low at about 41.80.  

The South Korean won <KRW=KFTC><KRW=> gained almost half a percent to 1,026.3 per dollar, with hefty foreign buying of local equities also boosting the won.  

The official Shanghai Securities News quoted a senior central banker as saying China's central bank would allow market forces to decide its yuan exchange rates following the yuan revaluation.  

"China is stating the logical path for a currency but we need to be very mindful that this is not going to happen today or tomorrow," said Philip Wee, senior market strategist at DBS Bank.  

"It is still a process, one that is likely to be slow. Markets generally have been divided over what China will do and trading has been listless."  

Comments from Chinese authorities in recent days have dampened talk that further rises in the yuan would follow the revaluation, undermining Asian currencies. Markets remained sceptical about a rapid appreciation of the yuan.  

Yuan non-deliverable forward markets showed the derivatives priced in a mere 0.2 percent gain in the currency in a month <CNYNDF=>, a sharp cut back from a 0.9 percent appreciation they had factored in on Friday.  

"On the one hand there is room for further disappointment with how little China has actually done, but on the other hand economic data is improving and growth expectations have improved," said UBS currency strategist Ashley Davies.  

The yuan <CNY=CFXS> strengthened to a post-revaluation high of 8.1080 per dollar and closed at this level.  

TAX FOCUS FOR PESO  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> briefly tested Wednesday's two-week trough at about 56.20 per dollar before firming alongside other Asian currencies.  

News late on Wednesday that the country's Supreme Court may not decide until mid-August whether to lift its freeze on an expanded sales tax initially pressured the peso. A ruling on the key tax change had been expected in the first week of August.  

Worries about the delay in implementing the tax, together with a political crisis, have dealt the peso a blow. The currency has shed about four percent against the dollar since early May.  

"We've got a delay on the tax ruling, but the yen is also stronger so this is helping the peso a bit," said a Manila trader.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> was the day's laggard, trading steady from late Asian trading levels on Wednesday at about 9,835 per dollar.  

"Demand for the dollar is strong and coming from government-owned companies importing oil. Also, there is some month-end demand from corporates," said a Jakarta trader.  

Indonesian demand for oil means extra demand for dollars, and that has resulted in rupiah sales. Dealers said that while the Indonesian central bank had been checking rates in the currency market there had been no intervention to bolster the rupiah.

title: = Indian Exporters Give Yuan Revaluation A Cautious Cheer
text:
NEW DELHI, Jul 24, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

(This article was originally published Friday.)  

By P.R. Venkat
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES
  

India's exporters, who have long complained of China's unfair currency advantage, say the yuan's revaluation will help level the playing field. But analysts say the real benefits to India will depend on the rupee's behavior in coming weeks.  

China has had an artificial peg for a long time, Commerce and Industry Minister Kamal Nath told reporters Friday, when asked to comment on the revaluation. "This should be corrected to some extent now," he said.  

Thursday, the People's Bank of China said the yuan's de facto peg to the dollar would be dropped in favor of a managed float against a basket of currencies. In the process, the yuan was revalued about 2%, to CNY8.1100 to the dollar from CNY8.2765.  

Nath said India's textile exports in particular would benefit from China's move.  

Others said global demand for India's textile products and gems and jewelry would rise as China's exports become costlier.  

India's textile industry, which contributes about 23% to total exports of $80 billion, is struggling to compete with China after the elimination of quotas that regulated world trade until Jan. 1 this year.  

Gems and jewelry account for nearly 17% of India's exports.  

India's textile companies have said China's undervalued currency gives its products a price advantage in key markets such as the U.S. and E.U.  

The yuan revaluation "will benefit us slightly," said Siddhartha Rajagopal, executive director of the Cotton Textiles Export Promotion Council.  

Rajagopal said that while China had a 40% cost advantage in textiles in the past due to its currency levels, the advantage will now narrow by 5%.  

"Even a small gain like this will help," said Rafeeque Ahmed, a leather exporter and former president of the Federation of Indian Exporters Organization, or FIEO.  

Ahmed said there are prospects for a further appreciation of the yuan and this will increase business for India from the U.S. and the E.U., key markets for both India and China.  

The key question for exporters now is how the rupee responds to global currency changes due to the revaluation.  

Ajay Sahai, director general of FIEO, said Indian exporters will be happy with a rupee level of INR43.50 to the dollar.  

"Any level below INR43.50 will be cause for worry," he said.  

Soon after China's move, the rupee strengthened, hitting a six-year high of INR43.14 against the dollar Friday.  

It ended at INR43.47 to the dollar after suspected intervention by the Reserve Bank of India earlier in the day to pull the rupee down.  

"The central bank probably also wants to keep the rupee's overvaluation in check," said a dealer at a local bank.  

Analysts say the rupee is currently overvalued by more than 10% against a basket of major currencies in trade-weighted terms.  

Stock-related capital inflows and broad dollar weakness have pushed the rupee up 6.2% against the dollar over the past 12 months, hurting exporters.  

Currency watchers say the rupee is likely to hold its ground or even strengthen modestly in the near term as it adjusts fully to the yuan revaluation.  

The commerce minister Friday said India will retain its export target of $92 billion for the current financial year that ends on March 31, 2006, a 15% rise on the year.  

"We will stick to it despite the yuan's revaluation," said Nath.  

-By P.R. Venkat, Dow Jones Newswires; +91-11-2307 4020; venkat.pr@dowjones.com  

(Anil Varma also contributed to this article)

title: India Fin Min: Stk Mkt Reflects Current Econ Potential
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--India's Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said Friday the stock market trend showed the current economic potential of the country, but cautioned investors against excessive exuberance.  

Indian shares ended at a record high Friday on fund buying in blue chip shares amid hopes that the Chinese yuan revaluation would boost foreign fund inflows and lead to strong export growth for domestic companies.  

The Bombay Stock Exchange's 30-share Sensitive Index, or Sensex, rose sharply by 118.93 points, or 1.6%, to close at an all-time high of 7423.25.  

"Markets will rise and markets will fall...We urge investors that their response be measured," Chidambaram said at a tax conference.  

Chidambaram also said the Indian economy has the capacity to perform better than at present.  

India's economy is expected to grow 7% during the current fiscal year that started April, from 6.9% in the previous year. [ 22-07-05 1135GMT ]  

Turning to China's revaluation of its currency, Chidambaram said the development is unlikely to have a "major impact" on India.  

"As far as the government is concerned, and as far as the RBI is concerned, this won't change our exchange rate policy," he said.  

On Thursday, China scrapped the yuan's peg to the dollar and said it would now use a basket of currencies to manage the yuan.  

As part of the move, the People's Bank of China revalued the yuan to CNY8.11 to the U.S. dollar, effectively a 2% increase in the local currency's value.  

Soon after China's move, the rupee strengthened, hitting a six-year high Friday against the U.S. dollar, which touched INR43.14.  

Suspected intervention by the Reserve Bank of India later in the day pulled the dollar up. At 1140 GMT the dollar was at INR43.47, up from its close of INR43.22 Thursday.  

Asked about prospects for local interest rates, Chidambaram didn't reply directly, but said: "There is enough liquidity in the market today."  

The market has been expecting the central bank to raise the reverse repurchase rate by 25 basis points from the current 5% since RBI Governor Y.V. Reddy last week said global uncertainties had gone beyond the central bank's estimate.  

The RBI is scheduled to detail its quarterly review of monetary policy Tuesday.

title: INTERVIEW-Indian construction firm L&T bullish on rupee
text:
BOMBAY, July 7 (Reuters) - Larsen & Toubro Ltd. , a major Indian engineering and construction services exporter, sees the rupee gaining 2.6 percent in the next nine months as foreign investment into the country swells, a senior official said.  

L&T generated a third of its $3.3 billion revenue in the last financial year from exports and is a key player in India's currency market.  

R. Govindan, its treasurer, told Reuters on Thursday he sees the rupee strengthening to 42.50 per dollar <INR=IN> by March 2006, which would be an increase of 2.6 percent compared with 43.61 on Thursday.  

He said he expects foreign investment in infrastructure projects in Asia's fourth-biggest economy to boost the rupee, while oil-and-gas finds in India would offer some cushion for the currency against soaring international crude costs.  

"It used to be a small market, international flows used to be small... you used to have capital shortage. Now, the service sector has become a very serious component of trade or the flow of foreign exchange," he said.  

India's economy is forecast to grow 7 percent in the financial year ending March 2006 after expanding 6.9 percent last year.  

A 9.3 percent rise in services output, which now accounts for half of gross domestic product, powered growth in the year to March 2005.  

External trade represents about a third of India's GDP with invisible receipts and payments -- mainly comprising services sector flows -- up 46 percent and 70 percent on the year respectively in 2004/05, to $31.7 billion and $45.8 billion.  

L&T has interests in the Middle East, Africa and Central Asia.  

SEES CENTRAL BANK INTERVENING

Govindan said he expected the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to continue intervening by buying dollars in the currency market to curb rupee strength.  

"It makes sense for the RBI over the next two to three years to intervene at lower (dollar) levels to provide a cushioning impact for the external capital that is coming in, as stable currency conditions are preferred by long-term investors."  

Limiting the rupee's gains also helps Indian exporters stay competitive on price.  

"They should keep accumulating dollars at lower levels so that it encourages foreigners to pour in money and we can use the money to create infrastructure," he said.  

Overhauling and modernising India's rickety infrastructure would also be a big draw for foreign investors, which would boost the rupee.  

"Probably we are one of the few countries where the infrastructure is really creaking," he said.  

"Our assessment is over three to four years the civil infrastructure, roads, ports, dams, buildings, water and process industries will see at least $275 billion of investments."  

Foreign funds -- including first-time investors from Japan and South Korea -- have pumped more than $1.5 billion into Indian shares since June 1, attracted by India's growth prospects.  

Govindan said domestic oil-and-gas finds plus overseas acquisitions by the country's top explorer, Oil and Natural Gas Corp. Ltd. , would help offset the impact on the rupee of a record-breaking rally in international crude prices.  

India imports about 70 percent of its crude, making the country's widening trade gap, and therefore the rupee, vulnerable to sharp spikes in international crude prices. ($1=43.58 Indian rupees)

title: Indian cbank panel wants  forex  controls relaxed
text:
BOMBAY, June 24 (Reuters) - An Indian central bank panel on Friday recommended the country, which is sitting on a huge pile of foreign exchange reserves, should further relax capital controls and push forward more reforms in the currency market.  

To allow more hedging flexibility, the panel said residents should be allowed to cancel and rebook foreign currency swaps, while companies should deal in covered call and put options.  

And Indian banks should be allowed to accept deposits from non-resident Indians in more foreign currencies, including the Canadian dollar, Australian dollar and New Zealand dollar.  

The panel's report has been posted on the central bank's website:  www.rbi.org.in ("http://www.rbi.org.in").  

India's rupee is only partially convertible and last month, in a bid to curb speculation and develop a local long-term forward rupee-dollar curve, the central bank barred a foreign benchmark to price a key interest rate derivative used by companies to hedge foreign currency exposures.  

The Reserve Bank of India often intervenes to curb sharp currency swings, which has boosted foreign exchange reserves to $138 billion from about $25 billion five years back.  

Since the reserves could pay for 15 months of imports, analysts say the central bank should relax its strict capital controls, imposed decades ago when foreign currency was scarce.  

The committee has also recommended that certain banks, trading in India's $9 billion-a-day foreign exchange market, should be allowed to hedge commodity risks for corporate clients and provide capital against their actual open exchange position.  

"Banks may be given the freedom to decide on the period of crystallisation of unpaid export bills," the central bank said.  

The committee also said forex data including traded volumes for derivatives, such as foreign currency-rupee options, should be made available to the market on a regular basis.

title: RBI WATCH: India Lets Rupee Rise, Helps Fight Inflation
text:
By Anil Varma 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
   

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee is more expensive now than at anytime in more than eight years against a basket of currencies from India's biggest trading partners, but unusually the central bank seems little worried.  

Rather than intervene in foreign exchange markets to stem the rupee's rise and keep India's exports competitive as it might have done in the past, the Reserve Bank of India has scaled back its intervention.  

Analysts say the RBI is letting the currency appreciate to help it fight rising inflation and is unlikely to intervene strongly in the near future.  

The rupee is regarded at fair value when an index of its real effective exchange rate, which both the RBI and private-sector economists calculate, is around 100.  

But analysts say the index, which measures the rupee against five currencies, is now 107.10, indicating that the currency is overvalued by around 7%. That is the largest overvaluation since the Asian financial crisis in 1997.  

The RBI last issued an official estimate of the exchange rate index as on April 15, when the index was 107.41.  

This change in tactic by the RBI in allowing an overvalued exchange rate indicates that, to the extent possible, the central bank prefers such indirect methods to counter inflation than a more aggressive approach of increasing interest rates.  

The currency has been pushed higher in the past 10 months by heavy portfolio investment inflows attracted to India's strong economy. The RBI intervened heavily in the currency market to clip the rupee's gains during February and March, but market participants say there has been a significant decline in the central bank's dollar buying since the second half of April.  

The decrease in intervention has helped push down India's previously fast-growing foreign-exchange reserves to $139.65 billion on May 20, from a record-high $142.55 billion a month earlier.  


 
     Strong Rupee Keeps Lid On Inflation 
   

The rupee's sustained strength in recent months has dented a favorite theory of many market watchers that the RBI doesn't want the rupee to stray more than 5% from its fair value level.  

At 0400 GMT Friday, the dollar was at INR.43.64, above a near-six-year low of INR43.26 set on May 12. The rupee has gained 6.5% against the dollar in the past 10 months and has also rallied against the euro in recent months, benefiting from the single currency's general weakness. The euro was last quoted INR53.61, down 10.5% from an all-time high of INR59.88 in November 2004.  

"The RBI hasn't strongly resisted the rupee's overvaluation in recent months, probably because currency strength helps moderate inflation," said Amit Bansal, head of treasury at Barclays Bank India. "If you look back, the key policy moves made by the RBI in the past one year or so were aimed at containing inflation."  

High inflation fueled by surging global oil prices has been the biggest challenge to the RBI's monetary policy in the past year, forcing the bank to tighten policy twice since October 2004 and reverse a four-year easing trend.  

The RBI forecasts inflation of 5.0%-5.5% for the fiscal year that started April 1 and has said that price stability is one of its prime policy objectives. In its annual policy paper issued late April, the bank warned that the impact of high global oil prices is yet to be fully transmitted to the domestic economy and as a result "upside risks" to inflation persist.  

India's inflation hit a three-and-a-half-year high of 8.74% in August 2004, but has moderated since then and was 5.55% in the week ended May 14.  

Aside from statistical reasons and a government decision not to pass on to domestic oil product prices increases in global prices, the rupee's rise has helped reduce inflation.  


 
     Rising Rupee OK While Exports Rise 
   

Market watchers believe economics will eventually prevail over politics and the government will raise local oil prices sooner or later so the RBI will likely continue to tolerate an overvalued rupee, particularly as the country's exports are showing no sign of weakness.  

Exports grew 24.4% in the fiscal year ended March 31, well above the official target of 16.0%. The government has maintained a similar target for the current fiscal year. Exports grew 17.2% in April.  

Aside from helping keep a lid on inflation, an appreciating currency will encourage capital inflows,  

"The RBI is probably not in a hurry to see the rupee depreciate because that would discourage foreign portfolio investors who are looking at India," said a treasury official at a local bank.  

India received record-high portfolio inflows - over $9 billion - in 2004 and through the first quarter of 2005, as the country's rallying stock market and a strong rupee attracted global investors. Such inflows helped offset the country's current account deficit.  

However, portfolio investments have turned negative more recently. Foreigners pulled out $656 million from India's equity and debt markets during April and May, after investing $3.84 billion during the January-to-March quarter.  

"Given the recent weakness in portfolio inflows, the RBI may allow rupee overvaluation for some more time," added the bank official.

title: RPT-TECHNICALS-Indian rupee seen weakening in medium term
text:
(Repeats story from late on Tuesday)  

BOMBAY, May 31 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is set to weaken further in coming weeks, after slipping off a 5-1/2-year peak in mid-May, with most technical indicators signalling more losses against the buoyant dollar, technical analysts said on Tuesday.  

The rupee has fallen 1.1 percent to a one-month low since hitting the 5-1/2-year intra-day high of 43.26 per dollar on May 11.  

The slide has accelerated in the past two sessions with the market nervous that foreign funds are cutting their exposure to Indian assets. It was at 43.735 per dollar <INR=IN> at 1100 GMT.  

"Most indicators point clearly to a positive divergence since the rupee hit 43.26, which signals that the dollar should gain against the rupee in the medium term," said T. Gnanasekar, a chartist and director at Commtrendz Research.  

"Charts point to a near-term support for rupee at 43.85, with a break pointing to 44.50 which is the 38.2 (percent) retracement of the rupee's move from 46.49 in July 2004 to 43.26."  

The rupee, which is only partially convertible on the capital account, has lost 0.5 percent so far in 2005, after gaining 10.6 percent in the three years from December 31, 2001.  

Worries about a widening trade deficit, a slowdown in foreign investment in the local stock market and the dollar's rebound overseas have all weighed on the rupee, which had been supported in the past couple of years by robust portfolio fund inflows.  

NEAR-TERM LESS BEARISH  

Technical analysts warn that rupee charting can be distorted by central bank action as the Reserve Bank of India frequently intervenes to smooth volatility.  

The outlook for the rupee is, however, less bearish from a near-term perspective, with charts showing it well supported at 43.85, a level not breached on a closing basis since January 10.  

"In the immediate term, 43.85 is still a very strong resistance level for the dollar, as it is a multiple top," said R.K. Gurumurthy, vice president on the proprietary trading desk at ING Financial Markets in Singapore.  

"On as many as six occasions, it has failed to break past that level."

title: India may allow rupee to rise on inflation, yuan
text:
BOMBAY, May 12 (Reuters) - India's central bank may allow the rupee to gain gradually in the next few weeks in a bid to stave off rising inflation and as it prepares the ground for a possible revaluation of the Chinese yuan, analysts said.  

The partially convertible rupee <INR=IN> surged to a 5-½ year peak of 43.26 per dollar on Wednesday after a Chinese newspaper report -- that was denied by China's central bank -- suggested Beijing would revalue the tightly controlled yuan as early as next week.  

The rupee has since retreated to 43.29 but analysts say a stronger yuan would boost other Asian currencies and speculation a move is close has been one factor behind recent rupee gains.  

India's central bank intervened heavily to curb the currency's rise after it hit a five-year high in February but, with interest rates rising and wholesale price inflation pushing up to 6 percent from around 5 percent in March, keeping it down could prove tough.  

"The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will have no choice but to let the currency appreciate in the medium term," said Bhanu Baweja, strategist at UBS in Singapore.  

"It's the unholy trinity -- interest rates, inflation and forex -- and one cannot control all of them together. I expect the rupee to touch 42.50 by December-end as the central bank seeks to manage inflation."  

The RBI says it intervenes in the currency market to smooth volatility rather than target an exchange rate level but it successfully drove the rupee back from February's high with large-scale selling.  

The central bank lifted its short-term interest rate by 25 basis points to 5.0 percent on April 28, citing inflation concerns in Asia's fourth-largest economy.  

In its statement it saw firm crude oil prices as a permanent feature, igniting talk the rupee may be allowed to rise to help offset imported inflation.  

India imports 70 percent of its crude oil and while the government has frozen local fuel prices since November it is debating whether to raise them so they align more with higher global prices. The central bank estimates every $1 rise in crude oil adds 30 basis points to the wholesale price index.  

CHINESE REVALUATION  

The rupee's rise and the central bank's absence from the market in recent weeks have coincided with market expectations China's yuan could be revalued soon.  

"The talk of a yuan revaluation is coming at a time when I think the RBI may allow a gradual appreciation in the rupee to check inflation," said M.G. Srinivas, a senior foreign exchange dealer at ING Vysya Bank, Bangalore. He expected the rupee to touch 43.10 by mid-June.  

Central bank governor Yaga Venugopal Reddy said two weeks ago he did not expect an adverse impact on the rupee from a potential revaluation of the yuan. But he said the authority was watching the currency market carefully.  

Rajeev Malik, senior economist at JP Morgan in Singapore, said the rupee could gain to 43.0, although it may correct a little now the immediate revaluation speculation had faded.  

He said the rupee was overvalued on a real effective exchange rate but the RBI would consider how far other Asian currencies would rise against the dollar if the yuan was revalued.  

"That gives them some flexibility not to do anything. Technically, it would be a structural change."  

Trade between India and China quadrupled between 2000 and 2004 to $13 billion and Reddy said recently India was likely to benefit in trade terms if the yuan was revalued, a comment which boosted the rupee.  

Trade with Japan was worth just $4.4 billion in 2004 but Japan is one of five economies -- including the United States, Britain, France and Germany -- in a trade-weighted basket which analysts say the central bank watches to monitor the rupee.  

"As China's importance as a trading partner grows with India, the renminbi will eventually be included in the five-country basket," said Prasenjit Basu, managing director Robust Economic Analysis in Singapore.  

"So the renminbi will have a modest influence on the rupee's movement."

title: India Rupee Rally On Bogus Yuan Reform Report; Bonds Up
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee rallied to its highest level since July 1999 against the dollar Wednesday after a bogus report on the Web site of one of China's top official newspapers said Beijing was about to announce a revaluation of the yuan.  

But the local currency ended slightly below its intraday high after China's central bank subsequently said it had no new information on the yuan exchange rate.  

The dollar ended at a 70-month low of INR43.2850 Wednesday, down from INR43.4350 at the previous close, but above the day's low of INR43.2600.  

A report on the English-language Web site of the People's Daily, the official mouthpiece of the Chinese Communist Party, said an expansion of the yuan's narrow trading band against the dollar "will be announced" at an unspecified time. It said the resulting rise of the yuan was estimated at 1.26% within a month and 6.03% within a year after a meeting between Chinese and U.S. financial officials.  

The story, which sent the dollar down against most Asian units, was later removed from the Web site.  

"China is one of India's competitors in the global exports market. If the Chinese currency is allowed to strengthen, that would definitely give the rupee more room to rise," said a trader at a local bank.  

The rupee has gained 4.3% against the dollar in the past six months, mainly due to capital inflows into the local stock market and the U.S. currency's global weakness.  

The rupee is currently overvalued by nearly 6% in trade-weighted terms and the Reserve Bank of India has frequently intervened in the market in recent months to check its gains and protect export competitiveness.  

However, many currency-watchers now believe the Indian central bank would loosen its grip on the currency if China allowed the yuan to strengthen. The prospects of higher inflation may also spur the RBI to tolerate a more gradual appreciation of the rupee.  

Dollar forward rates ended lower Wednesday, tracking the trend in the spot market. The forward contract maturing in April 2006 closed at a premium of INR0.545 to the spot rate, down from INR0.585 at Tuesday's close.  

MIFOR-based interest rate swaps closed lower. The five-year swap ended at 5.93%-5.98%, while the two-year swap was at 5.41%-5.45%.  

Overnight index swaps ended steady, with the five-year swap closing at 6.59%-6.61%.  

Indian government bond prices ended marginally higher Wednesday on mild bargain hunting by traders after prices fell in early trade following an RBI announcement of a state government bond auction.  

The widely traded 7.55% paper, due 2010, ended at INR102.92, up from INR102.85 at Tuesday's close. Its yield slipped to 6.85% from 6.87%.  

Earlier, bond prices slipped after the RBI announced a state government bond sale late Tuesday evening after the market closed for trading.  

Twenty-six of India's 29 state governments plan to sell 7.77% 10-year bonds worth INR73 billion Tuesday. The Reserve Bank of India said in a press release the bond sale will be on-tap. Under the on-tap method, bonds are sold at a fixed price until stocks last.  

"Bonds may remain in tight range Thursday as there are no triggers available till the bond auction next week," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "Most market participants are also waiting for the U.S. trade data release later today," he said.  

The overnight call money rate ended mostly steady Wednesday at 4.95%-5.05%, compared with 4.90%-5.05% at the previous close in plentiful money market liquidity. [ 11-05-05 1259GMT ]

title: Indian rupee at new 3-month high, near 5-year peak
text:
BOMBAY, May 5 (Reuters) - The rupee rose to end at a new three-month high on Thursday, on continued speculation of a yuan revaluation and a rally in local stocks after India proposed scrapping a voting rights cap in private-sector banks.  

The rupee <INR=IN> ended at 43.4200/4250 per dollar, its strongest close since Feb. 3 and 0.2 percent firmer on the day. It inched up to 43.3850 per dollar in intra-day trade, within sight of a five-year peak of 43.30 hit in early February.  

"Everything in India is against the dollar. Stocks are rising, there are fresh reforms for the banking sector and the yuan revaluation talks still remain," said a dealer at a state-run bank.  

Traders said talk that China would eventually revalue the yuan refused to go away, even though China's finance minister said speculation made it hard for currency reform right now.  

Speculation over a possible yuan revaluation has helped lift the rupee and other Asian currencies over the past two weeks.  

In overseas trade, the dollar remained weak against the euro and the yen as investors focussed on news about China and an uncertain outlook in the United States ahead of Friday's jobs data.  

The market was, however, wary of India's central bank, which intervened aggressively earlier this year to check the rupee's gains.  

But some analysts said the central bank may not be as worried about rupee strength as it was in February, as it was now focused on containing inflation pressures after raising the key short-term interest rate last week.  

A JP Morgan real effective exchange rate index <JPMREER> shows the rupee is overvalued by nearly 5 percent.  

India's government approved a proposal late on Wednesday to scrap a 10 percent voting rights cap in private sector banks, a move which analysts said would attract more foreign investment into local banks.

The Indian currency ended at 43.6550/6650 per dollar, retreating further from a five-week closing high of 43.55/56 set on Monday.  

The benchmark 30-share Bombay index closed 1.15 percent lower at 6,669.52 points, its lowest close since March 1, weighed down by record high oil prices that fuelled fears of rising inflation in the energy-hungry country.  

In spite of the losses, shares of UTV Software Communications Ltd. jumped on the debut of the television show producer. UTV rose as much as 35 percent to 175.40 rupees before closing at 168.50 rupees.  

Signs that foreign buying, a key support to shares and the rupee, has slowed also weighed on the share index, dealers said. Data on Wednesday showed that foreign funds were net sellers of local shares on Tuesday for the first time since Jan. 25.  

The Bombay index climbed to record highs above 6,900 last week, rallying on strong foreign investment inflows. Foreign funds have bought some $4 billion worth of Indian shares so far in 2005 - nearly half of last year's record level.  

"The figures for foreign fund inflows were negative yesterday. That was a little unnerving. High oil prices are acting as a bit of a dampener as well," said Raju Mewawalla, a relationship manager at Emkay Share and Stock Brokers.  

India imports 70 percent of its crude oil needs and an oil spike drove the domestic inflation rate to a 3-1/2-year high of 8.74 percent last August, prompting the central bank to raise interest rates for the first time in four years in October.  

The yield on the 10-year benchmark bond ended at 6.6740 percent on Thursday, its highest since Feb. 5, as dealers eyed surging world oil prices and awaited a slew of federal debt issuances in the new year starting in April.  

The Indian economy is poised to grow nearly 7 percent in the current fiscal year but a continued rise in oil prices could pose a problem next year. Analysts said a $5 per barrel rise in oil prices would cost 0.5 percentage points of economic growth. title: ANALYSIS-Asia raises its game to curb  currency  strength.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 16 (Reuters) - Asian authorities, facing a fourth straight year of strengthening currencies, are stepping up verbal warnings and appear to be intervening more to shoo off speculators and keep their exporters competitive.    

 The latest broadside has come from Taiwan.    

 On Monday its central bank said it was worried about a buildup of almost T$150 billion (US$4.8 billion) in uninvested Taiwan dollar holdings by foreigners. It wants foreign investors to buy stocks or take the money home, aiming to discourage speculators from causing sharp fluctuations in the exchange rate.    

 Central banks in South Korea, India and Thailand have also voiced concern about a surge in portfolio investments that has helped drive stock indices in some of those countries to record highs and currencies in some of them to their strongest levels since the 1997/98 financial crisis.    

 A month ago Asian central banks seemed to be willing to let their currencies rise against the dollar after a bout of heavy dollar-buying in 2004.    

 But analysts said signs that China was still reluctant to allow its tightly pegged currency to strengthen had hardened the resolve of other countries to keep their currencies in check.    

 "Nobody wants their currencies to gain too far compared with China's currency," said Mark Cranfield, head of treasury in Asia at Landesbank Baden-Wuerttemberg in Singapore.    

 "When China does relax, they'll relax. Nobody wants to lose too much ground to China."    

 Asian central bank reserve figures showed signs of stepped up dollar-buying in February. Taiwan, South Korea, India, Singapore and Thailand together added $18 billion to their foreign currency reserves in February.    

 That followed a $2.9 billion decline in those countries' total reserves in January. It compares with average monthly reverve gains of $11.1 billion during 2004 for the five.    

 SALVO FROM SEOUL    

 Last Thursday alone, traders said the Bank of Korea spent almost $2 billion to halt a surge in the won.    

 "The idea that there may be more to come is credible," said David Simmonds, currency strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland, referring to the South Korean dollar-buying. "Intervention efforts may be quite persistent for a while."    

 Japan, which has not intervened in the currency markets since March 2004, has continued with its verbal threats to step in. The Bank of Japan is under relatively less pressure because the yen has underperformed other Asian currencies so far this year.    

 But elsewhere, signs all point to interventionist policies.    

 The Reserve Bank of India's foreign currency reserves surged about $8.7 billion in February alone, the largest increase among Asian central banks last month.    

 Part of the rise came from more than $3 billion in foreign investments into the country's stocks this year, which drove the local benchmark stock index to a record high on March 9.    

 RBI Governor Yaga Venugopal Reddy said last month that large foreign inflows posed a challenge to exchange rate management and monetary policy. The rupee has lost 0.2 percent this year.    

 Thailand's central bank has been less verbal and more active in the currency markets lately. The Bank of Thailand's net forward foreign exchange contracts to sell the baht jumped to $7.7 billion as of March 4 from $4.6 billion at the end of 2004.    

 Foreign currency reserves rose by $1 billion in February.    

 "The increase in forex reserve holdings, combined with the rise of forward commitments, underscores the policy desire to prevent a sharp appreciation in the baht and yet also tighten domestic liquidity," said Sin Beng Ong, an economist at JPMorgan Chase, in a report.    

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) may also have less appetite for a gradually appreciating currency. The MAS uses the level of its currency as its main monetary policy tool.    

 Emmanuel Ng, currency strategist at ABN AMRO Bank in Singapore, expects the MAS to switch to a neutral bias for the Singapore dollar at its half-yearly monetary policy meeting next month after keeping an appreciating bias over the past year.    

 Singapore reserves rose $1.9 billion in February. The currency has gained 0.5 percent this year, compared with 3 percent gains in the won and Taiwan dollar.    

 Ng said Singapore had kept the currency on a "tight leash" this year because it was worried about a slowdown in electronics and biomedical industries.    

 "Inflation is not perceived to be a major cause for concern and the pass-through effects of higher oil prices should be limited, weakening the argument that a stronger exchange rate would stem inflation," Ng said.

title: Indian Govt Bonds End Dn,Mkt Quiet Before New FY;Rupee Up
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Indian government bond prices ended slightly lower Monday in quiet trade as most market participants were wary of making fresh purchases ahead of the end of the current fiscal year March 31.  

India's fiscal year runs through April to March.  

Quarterly corporate tax payments beginning Tuesday also raised near-term liquidity concerns, dealers said.  

Friday's rally in global oil prices and U.S Treasury yields also weighed on bonds.  

The actively traded 7.38% paper, due 2015, ended at INR106.05, down from INR106.11 at the previous close and Monday's high of INR106.14.  

The yield on the paper rose to 6.57% from 6.56% Saturday.  

"Most people believe that there will not be any buying support as everyone is buying very selectively before the financial year end," said a dealer at a state-run bank.  

Market participants are wary of building large positions ahead of the fiscal year-end due to liquidity concerns.  

Earlier, bond prices rose marginally as some state-run banks and an insurance company bought bonds selectively.  

However, prices soon started sliding as demand ebbed, said dealers.  

"There are absolutely no fresh factors to guide the market," said a dealer at a private sector bank.  

"Any significant price changes will take place only after the federal government announces the schedule for its borrowing program next year," he added.  

Dealers said any sharp changes in global oil prices also could act as a trigger.  

Bonds may remain in a tight range for next two weeks due to lower demand, as major buyers of government bonds are unlikely to buy large volumes ahead of the fiscal year end, dealers said.  

The overnight call money rate ended steady Monday at 4.25%-4.50% in ample system liquidity.  

The rupee ended marginally higher against the dollar, but off the day's highs as state-run banks bought dollars in the late trade.  

The dollar ended at INR43.5550 Monday, down from INR43.5650 Friday, but off the day's low of INR43.5000.  

"The rupee started on a strong note, but began falling after state-run banks started buying (dollars)," said a dealer at foreign bank.  

State-run banks have been major buyers of dollars in the spot market in recent sessions, possibly on behalf of the Reserve Bank of India, dealers said.  

The central bank often intervenes in the foreign exchange market to curb the overvaluation of the rupee in trade terms, dealers said.  

Earlier, the rupee had risen on strong dollar sales by foreign banks, possibly for foreign portfolio investors, dealers said.  

Foreign funds invested more than $1.27 billion in the local stock market in March, compared with around $1.9 billion in February.  

"The rupee could have breached 43.50 level if the state-run banks had not started buying dollars," said dealer at a private sector bank.  

Dollar forward rates ended mostly steady Monday, with the forward dollar contract maturing in February 2006 ending at a premium of INR0.535 to the spot rate.  

MIFOR-based interest rate swaps ended up on corporate buying. The five-year swap rose to 5.90%-5.95% from 5.82%-5.84% at the previous close, while two-year swap hardened to 5.25%-5.30% from 5.20%-5.24%.  

Overnight indexed swaps ended slightly higher in line with government bond yields. The five-year swap closed at 6.36%-6.39%, compared with 6.35%-6.38% Friday. [ 14-03-05 1321GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1- India 's  fx  reserves at record high on  intervention .
text:
BOMBAY, March 12 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves rose by nearly $2 billion to a record high in the week to March 4 as the central bank worked to keep exports competitive by absorbing equity investments from foreigners, analysts said.  

Data from the Reserve Bank of India on Saturday showed the country's foreign exchange reserves rose to $137.56 billion on March 4 from $135.66 billion a week earlier, the fourth consecutive weekly increase.  

India's reserves holdings are the sixth largest in the world.  

"Clearly we are seeing increased presence of the central bank in the currency market and this is driving up reserves," said Shubhada Rao, director at Economic Consulting Group, Bombay.  

"The dollar's weakness in past week against the major currencies should also boost reserves in the near term."  

India's central bank governor, Yaga Venugopal Reddy, said last month that large foreign inflows posed a challenge to exchange rate management and monetary policy.  

Overseas portfolio investors have pumped nearly $3.3 billion into stocks this year, more than a third of 2004's record $8.5 billion, on expectations of increased corporate profits.  

The inflows have driven India's key stock index to a record high, hit on March 9, putting pressure on the rupee to strengthen and prompting the central bank to intervene regularly in the currency market.  

The rupee hit a five-year high of 43.30 per dollar in early February, but the central bank's dollar buying since then has driven it down 0.6 percent to 43.57 on Friday.  

The central bank seeks to keep the Indian rupee in a 3 to 5 percent trading band, and has been intervening heavily in a bid to ensure that the currency is not highly overvalued on a trade-weighted basis.  

DIVERSIFICATION  

On Friday, Reddy told reporters that diversification of foreign exchange reserves was being discussed at the central bank, similar to recent comments from Japan and South Korea, the world's first and fourth largest holders of reserves.  

"Yes it is being discussed. We are always discussing. It's a continuous process," Reddy said. "It is an ongoing debate with all central banks and you cannot expect a central bank governor to say anything further on this."  

His comments sparked speculation on whether the talk of diversification was part of a coordinated plan by Asian central banks.  

Asian economies hold almost $2.5 trillion of reserves, and the majority are thought to be invested in U.S. dollar assets. Talk of a shift away from dollars, either in existing holdings or in allocations of new reserves, creates a great deal of nervousness in global markets over the dollar's prospects.  

Asia's sharp build-up in reserves in recent years - India's have almost doubled since the end of 2002 - has limited falls in their currencies against the dollar and helped keep the region's exports competitive.  

The dollar has been under pressure because of the huge U.S. budget and current account deficits. It hit a record low against the euro at the end of 2004, and has hit multi-year lows against a number of Asian currencies this year.

title: India Markets-Shares off peak as oil cos slide, bonds tumble.
text:
BOMBAY, March 1 (Reuters) - India's key share index slid back nearly 1 percent on Tuesday, after touching a record high, as investors cashed in on budget-led gains, while federal bonds slid to their lowest in more than three weeks on supply worries.   

The rupee ended slightly weaker as active central bank intervention to keep the local currency's gains in check blunted the pro-growth federal budget's upward pressure on the unit.   

The benchmark 30-share Bombay index closed 0.94 percent lower at 6,651.08 points, after rallying to an all-time high of 6,725.92 points at the start. The previous high was 6,721.08 on Monday, when the index gained more than 2 percent.   

India's Congress-led coalition said in its 2005/06 (April-March) budget unveiled on Monday it would step up spending on infrastructure and the rural economy to spur growth and fight poverty. It also cut the corporate tax rate to 33 percent from 35.   

"Post-budget, we had a bit of euphoria in the market, and this has been a correction," said Sashi Krishnan, chief executive officer at Cholamandalam AMC Ltd.   

"It is nothing to get worried about at all. For a long-term investor, most budget proposals have little impact. A change of 2-3 percent in a company's profits will not impact your decision to invest in a fundamentally sound stock," Krishnan said.   

But a tax rejig for the energy sector is expected to increase losses for oil companies, already hurting from subsidies they provide on fuels like kerosene and cooking gas.   

State-run market leader Indian Oil Corp. Ltd. (IOC.BO) estimated oil companies would suffer additional losses of 4.5 billion rupees a month on higher excise duties on petrol and diesel, unless they were able to pass these on to the consumers.   

IOC's shares fell 4.76 percent, while shares of Bharat Petroleum Corp. Ltd. (BPCL.BO) fell 4.51 percent.   

Shares of UTI Bank (UTBK.BO) fell 6.2 percent after the central bank's new banking guidelines on Monday failed to raise the limit on foreign direct investment in private banks.   

Federal bonds tumbled as investors dumped debt over the government's plan to borrow a net 1.03 trillion rupees in the fiscal year starting in April, much higher than the 940 billion rupees forecast in a Reuters poll last month.   

The yield on the 10-year benchmark bond closed nearly 10 basis points higher at 6.6442 percent, taking the rise over the past two sessions to 18 basis points. It last closed higher at 6.7140 percent on Feb. 5.   

"The intended supply is ridiculously large and we could see monthly issuances jump by an additional about 60 billion rupees on average, which will see the curve surely steepening," a foreign bank trader said. The rupee surrendered most of the previous session's gains, losing 0.11 percent to close at 43.7250/7350 per dollar.   

The rupee, which has been supported by capital inflows into the soaring stock market, firmed 0.13 percent on Monday after the budget, but dealers expect the local currency to remain in a broad 43.50-44.00 per dollar range in the next few sessions.   

The Indian currency, which set a five-year high of 43.30 per dollar in early February, has since drifted lower on sustained intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which analysts say is keen to ensure local exports remain competitive.

title: Indian Govt Bonds Up On Bargain Hunting; Rupee Up
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Indian government bond prices ended higher Monday on bargain hunting after losses in the recent sessions.  

However, the prices ended below the days high as some banks sold bonds to raise cash for investing in the state government bond sale Tuesday.  

Sixteen of India's 29 state governments plan to sell bonds worth a total INR63 billion Tuesday.  

The actively traded 7.38% paper, due 2015, ended at INR106.59, up from INR106.50 Saturday, but below the day's high of INR106.62. Its yield fell to 6.51% from 6.52%.  

"Banks were buying steadily, but they were a bit cautious because of tomorrow's state government bond sale," said a dealer at a state-run bank.  

The federal budget, due Feb. 28, also weighed on market sentiment.  

"You won't see any sharp movement in government bonds in the near term. Most players would wait for the budget before making big purchases," said a dealer at a private sector bank.  

Bonds are expected to remain mostly in a narrow range Tuesday morning as market participants are likely to wait for the outcome of the state bond sale.  

The overnight call money rate Monday closed slightly higher at 4.70%-4.80%, compared with 4.60-4.80% Saturday, amid ample money market liquidity.  

The rupee ended higher against the dollar Monday as state-run banks, the main buyers of the U.S. unit in past two weeks, stayed away from the market.  

However, the rupee fell back from the day's highs on scattered bargain hunting for the U.S currency, especially in late trade, dealers said.  

The dollar ended at INR43.8150, down from INR43.8450 previous close, but above the day's low of INR43.7900.  

"Players are treading very cautiously. Nobody wants to build a large position because everyone is convinced that state-run banks may start buying the dollar again," said a dealer at a foreign bank.  

State-run banks have been buying dollars consistently in the past two weeks, possibly on behalf of the Reserve Bank of India.  

The RBI often intervenes in the foreign exchange market through state-run banks to curb the appreciation of the rupee to maintain the export competitiveness of Indian companies.  

The central bank may continue to intervene in the market as the rupee is still considered overvalued by more than 3% in trade-related terms, said analysts.  

"If you look at the pattern of state-run banking, you may find that they always start buying around 43.75-43.77 levels. It means they will not let rupee appreciate beyond this level," said a dealer at a foreign bank.  

However, without the intervention of the central bank, the rupee may appreciate against the dollar as fundamentals support a stronger rupee, said dealers.
