title: RBI WATCH: India Moves To Correct Rupee Overvaluation
text:
By Anil Varma 
 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
   

MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Intensified currency intervention by the Reserve Bank of India caught the rupee market off guard this week, but the bank's move is hardly surprising as falling inflation now allows it to sterilize capital inflows without compromising on other policy aims.  

The Indian central bank, which resumed heavy dollar buying this week after a gap of at least three months, is possibly seeking some downward correction in the overvalued rupee now to keep the country's burgeoning current account deficit within sustainable limits.  

The RBI's dollar buying has already pulled the rupee well below the 10-month peak scaled last week. Before the intervention, the local currency had risen steadily for weeks on strong stock-related capital inflows and broad dollar bearishness.  

At 0530 GMT, the dollar was at INR43.80, up from INR43.47 a week ago.  

Capital flows into the rallying Indian stock market topped $9 billion in 2004 - a record high. With inflows expected to stay strong this year, the RBI will likely continue siphoning out excess foreign exchange supply to stress its well-known policy preferences - keeping the rupee fairly valued in trade-weighted terms and protecting export competitiveness.  

"With the fall in inflation...and given the large current account deficit registered during July-September 2004, the RBI is more likely to use forex policy to target competitiveness than inflation," said Barclays Capital in a recent research report.  

"The RBI is likely to believe that the most effective way, in the short run, of maintaining the current account deficit within sustainable limits, is by adjusting the rupee's real effective exchange rate," the report added. The real effective exchange rate, or REER, represents the rupee's value in trade-weighted terms.  

India's current account plunged into a $6.42 billion deficit in July-to-September 2004 from a $3.16 billion surplus in the previous quarter, mainly due to a sharp widening of the country's trade deficit. Its trade shortfall rose to $12.30 billion in July-September from $5.14 billion in the previous three months.  

Barclays suggested that the RBI probably made a "tactical retreat" by scaling back currency intervention in recent months, for fear of swelling money supply that could aggravate inflationary pressures.  


 
   Lower Inflation To Help RBI 
   

Indeed, persistently high inflation curbed the central bank's ability to resist the rupee's rise through most of 2004. India's inflation hovered mostly close to multiyear highs in the second half of 2004 - it hit a 3 1/2-year high of 8.74% in August - mainly because of record high international oil prices.  

However, year-on-year inflation has moderated significantly since mid-December, falling to 5.25% by late January. Furthermore, inflation is expected to remain relatively moderate through 2005 due to a high statistical base.  

This should give the RBI more elbowroom to sustain the stepped-up currency market intervention.  

Siddharth Mathur, head of research at JP Morgan India, believes that the rupee's current overvaluation in trade terms is a dominant factor driving the RBI's intervention plan. The rupee's REER is currently around 104, indicating overvaluation - the rupee is considered fairly valued when its REER is 100.  

The RBI may go slower on its dollar buying as the rupee's REER moves closer toward 100, he said.  

"The rupee's about close to 4% overvalued as of today. It's interesting to note that the rupee was even more overvalued - by almost 5% - on Tuesday, the day the RBI started buying dollars," said the treasury head at a local bank.  

Indeed, the rupee hasn't been allowed to become overvalued or undervalued in trade terms by more than 5% since the Asian currency crisis of 1997, noted Barclays Capital.  

The dollar's recent recovery against other major currencies this week is one factor that has fed the rupee's current overvaluation. Several Asian currencies slipped this week as the dollar gained - the South Korean won by 1.2% and the Indonesian rupiah by 0.9% - but the rupee has lost only 0.6% so far, that too only because of the RBI's dollar buying.  

Apart from the prospect of lower inflation, a recent slowing of India's export growth also may spur the RBI to sustain its dollar purchases. India's year-on-year export growth slowed to 14.6% in December 2004 from 26% in November and 43% in the year-ago period.  

-By Anil Varma, Dow Jones Newswires, 91 22 22884212; anil.varma@dowjones.com  

(Anil Varma covers India's money and fixed income markets for Dow Jones Newswires)

title: UPDATE 1-Indian  fx  reserves top $90 bln on  intervention .
text:
BOMBAY, Oct 18 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves surged to a record $90.35 billion in the week to October 10 on the back of heavy central bank intervention in the currency market, traders and economists said.  

Data released by the central bank on Saturday showed that the reserves were up $2.61 billion during the week. So far in 2003, the reserves are up by more than $20 billion, with average weekly accretions at more than half a billion dollars.  

"The RBI (Reserve Bank of India) was very aggressive in the market last week, which could account for the huge reserves build-up," said a trader at a state-run bank.  

"The central bank could have absorbed dollar inflows, which had come into the market in earlier weeks as well. Portfolio inflows were strong, and there could have been some deposit inflows. Trade inflows were minimal."  

There could have been re-investments in the local market, following the $5.2 billion redemption of the Resurgent India Bonds issued to overseas Indians earlier this month.  

"Part of that money could have been re-invested in local bank deposits, or mutual funds, as overall returns are good with Indian yields attractive and the rupee strong," said Saumitra Choudhuri, economic advisor to rating agency ICRA Ltd, local affiliate of Moody's Investors Service.  

Strong inflows had helped the rupee climb to a three-year closing high of 45.26/27 against the dollar on October 9, taking gains for calendar 2003 to six percent. But intervention pulled it back. The rupee closed Friday at 45.34/34.  

Still, the country's growing economy may continue to draw portfolio investments, which could lift the rupee and further add to the reserves.  

Foreign funds have already pumped in more than $4 billion so far in 2003, which is about five-and-half times the investments they made in the whole of 2002.  

"The growth story is very good, which will keep portfolio investments strong for some more time," Choudhuri said. "Exports of services are also quite strong, and should offset outflows towards imports, which will support the rupee."  

Investors expect Asia's third largest economy to grow by more than six percent this year and sustain its momentum next year as it benefits from good rains, low interest rates, strong consumption and rising investment spending.  

Growth had shrunk to 4.3 percent last year from 5.6 percent the previous year, because of a severe drought.

title: WRAP: India Rupee Breaches Key 45.50/Dlr Resistance Fri
text:
MUMBAI (Dow Jones)--Spurred by continuing strong capital flows, the Indian rupee broke key resistance of INR45.50 against the dollar in morning trading Friday, a level many in the market recently believed would only be reached by the end of the year.  

Currency watchers now say the rupee is heading for INR44.80 against the dollar by year-end, a level that would be a 6.5% rise since the start of 2003. So far this year, it has risen 5.2%.  

In morning trading Friday, the rupee touched an intraday high of INR45.45, its highest since Aug. 8, 2000.  

It closed Wednesday at INR45.57.  

Traders attributed Friday's particularly strong gains to trade and portfolio inflows that accumulated during Thursday's national holiday. Furthermore, the rupee's gains have been stronger in recent weeks after a Sept. 20 statement from the Group of Seven leading industrial nations called for more flexible exchange rates - interpreted by many as a call to drop support for the dollar.  

"By and large the dollar will remain weak in the coming months, and capital inflows to India will continue," says Surendra Rosha, head of treasury sales at HSBC India, forecasting the rupee at around INR44.80 by the end of the year.  


 
   Dlr At INR45.25 Next Target 
   

On a nearer horizon, INR45.25 appears to be the market's next target, says IndusInd Bank's treasurer Sharukh Wadia, who expects that level to be tested by the end of this month.  

India's exporters reiterated Friday their concerns over the country's competitiveness in global markets from the sharply rising rupee. "We want the government to do something now otherwise it will hurt our competitiveness very badly," says M. Rafeeque Ahmed, President of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations.  

The strong rupee has slowed export growth over the past several months, with shipments rising only 4.2% on the year in August. By comparison, exports rose 20% in the same month of 2002.  

In recent months, trade and business organizations have repeatedly called on the Reserve Bank of India to intervene in the spot currency market to slow the rupee's rise.  

RBI Deputy Governor Rakesh Mohan said in a television interview Thursday that the central bank would only intervene to stem excessive exchange-rate volatility - a statement that monetary officials have repeated several times in recent months.  

However, many in the market believe the RBI may not resist the rupee's rise as long as it is driven by fundamentals, such as capital inflows and the dollar's global weakness.

bombs rocked the country's financial capital, killing 52 people
and injuring about 150 others.
    "Dollar inflows from exporters and foreign funds were good.


 But central bank intervention ensured that the rupee gave up 

 its gains," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "It's unlikely 

 that the rupee will break the 45.82 level in the next few 

 days." 

India's central bank usually intervenes in the currency

 market to contain sharp swings and maintain the country's 

 export competitiveness. 


 
    The rupee had weakened slightly in the morning on technical

    Banks routinely sell dollars on Wednesdays and buy them



back before the weekend to benefit from a swap differential of



nearly 1.50 paise. The settlement for Thursday's spot deals has



been shifted to Tuesday because of a holiday in New York on



Monday.



Traders said there were sporadic dollar purchases by a



state-run oil company. Oil companies routinely buy dollars at



the month-end to pay for imports.



But the rupee has been drawing support from continued



dollar inflows from foreign investors, who have stepped up



their exposures to Indian stocks on expectations of stronger



growth.



India's economy, Asia's third largest, is likely grow more



than six percent this year due to increased farm output and



demand for manufactured goods, the central bank forecast on



Wednesday.

to March.

Equity purchases by overseas investors between January 1



and August 26 totalled nearly $2.15 billion, almost thrice the

FORWARDS SLIDE

title: Indian rupee ends at near 3-year high, seen firm.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 18 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee resumed its
appreciation after a two-day pause to end at a near three-year
high on Monday, helped by dollar inflows piled up over a long
weekend.
 
    Traders said the gains were however capped by dollar buying
by state-run banks acting on behalf of the central bank.
    The rupee          finished at 45.8500/8550 per dollar, off


 the day's high of 45.83 but stronger than Thursday's close of 

 45.9025/9125. The market was closed on Friday for India's 

 Independence Day holiday. 

 "Supplies had bunched up at the nostro accounts of banks' 

 overseas branches over the three-day weekend," a chief dealer 

 at a foreign bank said. "And the outlook remains firm, with 

 only the central bank holding the rupee back from a test of 

 45.75." 

 The rupee, which has now risen 4.64 percent against the 

 dollar since the start of January, last ended higher on 

 September 15, 2000 at 45.7750/7800. 

 Traders said comments from senior central bankers last week 

 signalling that the monetary authority was not uncomfortable 

 with the rupee's appreciation had also backed sentiment. 

 The central bank chief Bimal Jalan on Thursday ruled out 

 the possibility that the Reserve Bank of India would intervene

 to keep the rupee from rising further in the face of strong 

 inflows, terming such a move "unsustainable over any length of 

 time". 

 "All these comments indicate that they are more keen to 

 keep the investment inflows into the economy robust," a private 

 bank dealer said. 

 A senior central bank official also told members of the 

Forex Association of India on Saturday the monetary authority

 had no target for foreign exchange reserves, although it was a 

 conscious policy to accumulate them. 

 Buoyant foreign investments, including portfolio flows into 

 Indian shares, and trade and expatriate remittances have all 

 bolstered the rupee. 

 Foreign funds have pumped in $1.57 billion into Indian 

 shares since May, more than twice the amount they invested in 

 the whole of last year, as they bet that corporate earnings are 

 set to jump on the back of a monsoon-led economic rebound.

title: Indian Bonds End Higher On Low Inflation; Rupee Up Vs Dlr
text:
MUMBAI -(Dow Jones)- Indian government bond prices ended higher Monday following the release of low inflation data and as the market shrugged off fears of further central bank intervention. 

 However, a temporary mismatch in liquidity limited gains. 

 Dealers said sentiment in the government bond market may be turning bullish again, with recent Reserve Bank of India intervention having only marginally subdued buying interest. 

 Further, hopes of lower interest rates have buoyed sentiment after the inflation rate slipped to 3.96% in the week ended Aug.2, its lowest level since the start of the fiscal year in April, dealers said. 

 The yield on the benchmark 10-year bond ended at 5.53%, from 5.54% at the previous close. 

 Dealers said that the RBI was unlikely to conduct another open market sale of bonds ahead of the sale of state government bonds scheduled for Aug. 25. The state governments of India are aiming to raise a total of INR80 billion through the sale of 12-year bonds. 

 Further, with liquidity expected to remain good on strong foreign currency inflows, the government bond yield curve is only headed downwards, dealers said. 

 But liquidity was a little tight Monday after recent outflows because of last week's bond auctions. The call rate ended at flat at 5.00%-5.05%. 

 In the foreign exchange market, foreign currency inflows held over a long weekend - the foreign exchange market was closed Friday for the independence day holiday - and bearish dollar sentiment put the U.S. currency under downward pressure. The dollar ended at INR45.855, above an intraday low of INR45.825 as state-run banks supported the U.S. currency. 

 This didn't however prevent the rupee from strengthening  to a 35-month high. 

 Dealers said they expect the rupee to appreciate steadily to INR45.75 over the next two weeks. 

 As the dollar weakened in the spot market, forward dollar premiums eased. But the fall was limited as state-run banks bought short-term forward dollars. 

 The annualized one-year premium ended steady at 1.86% Monday. Dealers said they expect premiums to drift lower during the current week. 

 Indian interest swap rates ended marginally lower in line with the fall in the forward dollar premiums. 

 The five-year Mifor swap rate fell to 4.51%-4.56% from its previous close of 4.54%-4.59%. Mifor is the Mumbai interbank forward offered rate, which is derived from dollar forward premiums.

title: India's  fx  reserves pile to aid reforms-analysts.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 9 (Reuters) - India's surging foreign exchange reserves, now approaching $85 billion, gives Asia's third largest economy a safety net against external shocks and provides it with muscle to push ahead with reforms, economists say. 

 But the world's second most populous nation must utilise these resources for growth-oriented investments because maintaining high levels of reserves is costly, they said. 

 India's foreign exchange reserves stood at $84.7 billion on August 1, equivalent to more than a year's imports, having risen by an average $480 million each week this year. It is just off the all time high of $84.904 billion struck a week before. 

 "It gives substantial room for independent policy manoeuvre and ensures that India will not really have a problem with external liquidity in the foreseeable future," said P.K. Basu, managing director at Robust Economic Analysis, Singapore. 

 Analysts say that high reserves mean India can continue to liberalise capital controls and should allow it to cut tariffs without risking a run on its currency. But there are stiff costs linked with maintaining this mountain of reserves. 

 For one, there is the erosive impact of the dollar's fall. Besides, bulk of the funds are invested in low-yielding U.S. assets and the central bank has the additional task of managing the surge in domestic money market liquidity - a result of its interventionist dollar purchases. 

 A decade of reforms has transformed India from a foreign exchange starved economy to one with a robust external sector position. The sluggishness in advanced economies and better local interest rates have also drawn in foreign investment flows. 

 "One of the big benefits of the strong external sector is that it has made foreign investors more confident," said Ajit Ranade, ABN Amro Bank's India economist. 

 He said while the expected buoyancy in economic growth was drawing foreign portfolio investments, an appreciating rupee backed by huge reserves was a significant confidence-booster. 

 Foreign funds' net investments in India stood at $2.7 billion in the first seven months of 2003 as against $744 million in the whole of the previous year, lured by attractive equity valuations and the prospects of a period of robust growth. 

 Portfolio investments, or 'hot money', comprise just a fifth of total reserves and analysts say that a bulk of the reserves were a result of inflows which would not reverse at short notice. 

 BETTER USES 

 But rising reserves in a capital-deficient country suggest that not enough has been done to enable resources coming from abroad to be used by sectors that need them, economists say. 

 The government has made little use of the reserves, pre-paying external debt worth nearly $3 billion in February. 

 "Sectors such as infrastructure need huge amounts of investments," said D. K. Pant, economists at the New Delhi-based National Council of Applied Economic Research. 

 "But our policies are still not conducive to a high level of investments because of which the foreign exchange flows entering the country are not being absorbed by productive avenues." 

 He said political dithering on crucial reforms such as privatisation were holding back private and foreign investments. 

 A high deficit was also slowing growth by diverting resources away from investments, and limiting a fall in interest rates. 

 But the strong external balance could help India sustain low interest rates and thus provide an incentive for investments, Basu said. 

 Analysts say that a reduction in domestic interest rates could induce local companies to borrow more and would also discourage arbitrage-seeking foreign inflows.

title: Indian rupee at fresh 33-month high despite c.bank.

title: WEEK AHEAD-Indian bonds seen stable, eye state loans and c.bank.
text:
BOMBAY, June 8 (Reuters) - Indian government bond yields are expected to hover near record lows this week in a market flush with funds and bolstered by a favourable outlook for domestic inflation, analysts said. 

 But yields are unlikely to drop much after hitting record lows last week, since most investors will be on the sidelines ahead of loan sales by state governments, they said. 

 Also, the market would be apprehensive of central bank intervention if yields dropped too much. 

 "Bonds are likely to trade in a range this week," said Siddharth Mathur, strategist at JP Morgan Chase. "The state loan sale and the central bank's statements towards the end of last week will keep investors cautious." 

 Twenty eight state governments will raise a total of 70 billion rupees ($1.46 billion) by selling 10-year loans on June 12 under a debt swap plan. 

 This is the first tranche of borrowings by states under the plan, which seeks to lower their interest burden, for the current fiscal year, to March 2004. 

 The benchmark 10-year bond , which struck a record low of 5.7541 percent on Friday, ended the week at 5.7563 percent, down from the preceding week's 5.7963 percent. 

 It has lost has nearly 40 basis points since start of the financial year in April in a rally driven by liquidity that had been boosted partly by robust foreign exchange inflows. 

 India's inflation rate measured by wholesale prices fell to 5.65 percent in the 12 months to May 24, compared with 5.90 percent a week earlier. 

 The trend in the inflation rate has been downwards since it hit a two-year high of 6.47 percent in the year to April 12. 

 Analysts say more dips are likely in the next few weeks due to a fall in energy prices. 

 EYES ON CENTRAL BANK

 Traders said they would keenly watch the central bank for cues after it said towards the end of last week that it was unlikely to cut the repo rate in the near term until the monsoon and inflation situation become clearer. 

 Analysts said this verbal intervention indicated the Reserve Bank of India was uncomfortable with falling yields and wanted bond prices to stabilise. 

 Traders have been speculating that a global easing bias could prompt the central bank to lower its repo rate, a benchmark for short-term interest rates, from the current five percent. 

 That speculation was stoked further last Thursday after the European Central Bank cut its key interest rate by half a point to two percent. 

 Although the Reserve Bank gives more weight to local factors, such as the monsoon and inflation, and does not necessarily follow rate decisions by other central banks, reductions overseas give it more leeway to pursue a soft rate bias, analysts say. 

 "There is considerable uncertainty about the monsoon," said M.R. Madhavan, analyst at Bank of America. 

 "The central bank through its statements last week is telling the market not to price in a repo rate cut until the picture about the monsoon becomes clearer." 

 The Indian economy, Asia's third-largest, depends heavily on monsoon rains for demand as around 70 percent of the population lives off the land and agriculture makes up a quarter of the economy.

title: RBI WATCH: Ctrl Bk's Hands Tied On Indian Rupee Rise
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column 

 MUMBAI -(Dow Jones)- The Reserve Bank of India is unlikely to make intrusive interventions into the foreign exchange market to temper the rupee's sharp rise against the dollar for fear of swelling money supply that could threaten inflation. 

 In fact, the central bank's resistance to the rupee's appreciation - a potential handicap to exports - appears to be caving in due to constraints on making currency intervention money supply-neutral in its open market securities sales. 

 But with the rupee at a two-year high against the dollar, Indian exporters have grounds to be worried over the impact on their revenues from a rising local currency and subdued global demand. 

 Indeed, one foreign investment house forecasts India's export growth slowing to 6% in the current financial year, which ends March 2004, after an 18% expansion in the previous fiscal year. 

 Over the past 12 months, the rupee has risen 4.4% against the dollar after nearly a decade of depreciation, with India's relatively high interest rates and a globally weak dollar attracting strong foreign-exchange inflows to the country. 

Currency watchers expect the rupee to continue rising, with some forecasting INR46 to the dollar by the end of the year. 

 In morning trading Wednesday, the pair was at INR46.78. 

 Although traditionally a staunch sentinel of exports, the RBI has offered surpassingly little resistance to the rupee's particularly sharp gains over the past two weeks. 

 The central bank may be reluctant to resist the rupee's rise by aggressively buying dollars due to potential inflation dangers as the process would pump rupees into a financial system that is already short of assets to buy. In other words, too much money could end up chasing too few assets, causing price to rise. 

 The RBI has in the past expressed concerns over the potential fallout on inflation from extensive non-sterilized intervention to contain potentially volatile gains in the local unit. 


   Strong Money Supply Growth



As matters stand, money supply growth as measured by the broad M3
aggregate is 15% on year, well above the 6% gross domestic product
growth forecast for the current fiscal year.



Some economists regard money supply growing faster than GDP as a
warning sign for higher inflation.



With a number of uncertainties already clouding the inflation horizon,
the RBI appears to be staying its hand on the rising rupee to sustain
its soft monetary policy stance.



At its monetary and credit policy announcement in April, the RBI cut
its bank rate - a key signaling tool for market-determined interest
rates - by 25 basis points to a three-decade low of 6%.



While policy rates are probably close to bottom in the current cycle,
the challenge for the RBI is to keep interest rates as low as possible
for as long as possible.



But an uncertain inflation outlook may be jeopardizing that stance. In
April, the wholesale price index, which is used as a proxy for wider
inflation, hit a two-year high of 6.47%.



When caught between the policy challenges of curbing inflation and
slowing a rapidly rising home currency, many central banks resort to
sterilized foreign-exchange intervention.



Here, the impact of intervention on money supply is neutralized by
draining local currency liquidity through open market securities sales.
However, the RBI doesn't seem to be in a position to do this due to a
sharp drop in its stock of domestic securities.



The RBI's domestic assets fell to just 9% of its average outstanding
reserve money in the last fiscal year due to the impact of open market
sales and changes in the composition of reserve money from rising
currency reserves. A decade ago, the level was 90%.



Concerns about an adverse reaction in the government bond market to
another open market securities sale, which would likely result in an
unwelcome rise in yields, also appears to be hampering the RBI's ability
to intervene in the foreign exchange market.



The RBI's role as the government's debt manager puts demands on it to
reduce federal borrowing costs by keeping market interest rates as low
as possible.

title: POLL-Indian rupee to rise versus dollar to September.
text:
BOMBAY, May 9 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is expected to rise against the dollar until September and then hold steady for the rest of 2003, supported by robust trade and a strong interest rate premium over U.S. rates, a Reuters poll showed. 

 A poll of 20 banks, companies and research firms forecast a dollar/rupee exchange rate of 47.135 rupees at the end of June and 46.98 rupees at the end of September, compared with 47.18 rupees on Friday. 

 However, the poll suggested the rupee, which has weakened against the dollar for most of the past decade, would be little changed at the end of the year compared with the end of September as the dollar finds support from a pick-up in the U.S. economy. 

 "I expect the dollar to remain weak against the euro till autumn," said Saumitra Chaudhuri, economic adviser at ratings agency ICRA Ltd. "Also, exports should grow by around seven to eight percent this fiscal and capital inflows should continue." 

 Robust trade, capital and expatriate remittances and the dollar's global weakness pulled the rupee up from a life-low of 49.08 hit in mid-May 2002, helping it post its first annual gain in a decade. 

 It ended 2002 up 0.55 percent at 47.9825 and has already gained 1.7 percent so far in 2003, despite central bank intervention. 

 The Reserve Bank of India has said it will let the market determine the exchange rate but will smoothen movements in the rupee, which is only partly convertible on the capital account. 

 Its persistent dollar purchases in recent months have boosted the country's foreign exchange reserves, which stood at a record high of $77.01 billion on April 25. 

 RATES TO BOOST INFLOWS 

 India's high interest rates will also continue to spur dollar inflows, analysts said. 

 Rates have eased in recent years to multi-decade lows - the repo rate is now at five percent - but they are still way above the U.S. federal funds rate of 1.25 percent. 

 "There is a clear interest rate advantage and this should continue to attract flows from overseas funds and expatriates," said V Rajagopal, head of forex treasury at Kotak Mahindra Bank. 

 Indian expatriates' rupee deposits, for example, quadrupled in the ten months to January 31, 2003 to $5.04 billion. 

 The average of the poll's 20 responses forecast the rupee would end the year at 46.978, unchanged after September, while one-third saw it actually depreciating to an average 47.625 due to a pick-up in the U.S. economy. 

 The rupee could also face some pressure from a large outflow of about five billion dollars in repayments on Resurgent India Bonds due at the end of September, analysts said. 

 "We expect growth signals from the U.S. economy to be far better by the fourth quarter, helping slow the dollar's depreciation," said Sanjeet Singh, analyst at ICICI Securities and Finance Company Ltd. 

 "So you can see the rupee's appreciation dying down towards the end of 2003."

title: Indian Forward Dollar Premiums Up; Rupee At 20-Mo High
text:
MUMBAI -(Dow Jones)- Dollar premiums in the forward market rose Friday, after Thursday's fall to record lows, on concerns the central bank could be considering intervening to support premiums. 

 Market participants interpreted Reserve Bank of India Deputy Governor Rakesh Mohan's comment that undue foreign-exchange volatility isn't favorable, referring to Thursday's premium fall, to mean the central bank may soon step in to support premiums. 

 Mohan also said the RBI was watching forward market developments closely, which prompted caution among traders and nudged premiums higher. 

 Premiums hit all-time lows Thursday as a bullish outlook for the rupee triggered heavy selling of exporters' future dollar receivables. 

 The annualized one-year forward dollar premium ended at 1.32% Friday, up from 1.17% Thursday. The one-year premium hit a record low of 1% Thursday. 

 Dealers said forward premiums are unlikely to fall much more as importers may find current low levels attractive to pay. Further, exporters' selling may decline as current levels are no longer attractive to sell. 

 In the spot market, the rupee extended its gains against the dollar, ending at a 20-month high of INR47.1900, compared with INR47.2400 at the previous close. 

 Traders said the rupee's advance against the dollar mainly reflects the bearish outlook for the U.S. currency and expectations that India's high interest rates will continue to attract healthy foreign-exchange inflows. 

 Many dealers expect the rupee to touch INR47.00 in three months' time. 

 Meanwhile, most government bonds continued to rise slowly Friday, with demand driven by plentiful money market liquidity. The ample liquidity in the system was evident from the large INR200.20 billion subscription the Reserve Bank of India received at its securities repurchase auction, dealers said. 

 The yield on the benchmark 9.81% bond due 2013 ended at 5.91%, down from 5.92% at the previous close. 

 Bonds may remain in a narrow range over the next two weeks, limited on the upside by an uncertain inflation outlook but supported by the surplus liquidity. 

 The overnight interbank call money rate ended nearly flat at 4.75%-4.90%, compared with 4.75%-5.00% at the previous close, amid the comfortable liquidity. 

 In the rupee interest rate swap market, the five-year Mifor-based swap ended at 3.95%-4.05%, up slightly from the previous close of 3.90%-4.00%, in line with the higher forward premiums. Mifor is the Mumbai interbank forward offered rate, which is derived from forward-dollar premiums.

title: Indian rupee snaps 3-day rise as cbank buys dollars.
text:
BOMBAY, March 28 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee ended weaker on Friday, snapping a three-day rally as the central bank intervened to check its rise and its subsidiary bought dollars to make overseas payments, traders said. 

 The rupee  finished at 47.5500/5525 per dollar, down from the day's high of 47.5325 and Thursday's 18-1/2-month closing peak of 47.5400/5425. 

 "There was support at around the 47.56 level from state-run banks," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "That, combined with demand from a public sector finance company repaying some external borrowing, helped push the rupee down slightly." 

 The Reserve Bank of India, though committed to a market-determined exchange rate, often intervenes through state-run banks to check volatility in the rupee, traders said. 

 The rupee, which rose 0.24 percent in three sessions to Thursday, has gained nearly one percent since the start of the year. Analysts said it was, however, still undervalued against the dollar on a trade-weighted basis by about 1.25 percent. 

 Traders said the robust remittances from software exporters and expatriate Indians seeking to convert their weakening dollar assets into the local currency ones were likely to continue next week, helping the rupee gain further. 

 Technical analysts said the rupee's weakening on Friday was only a technical correction, with charts signalling a climb up to the next support level for the dollar at 47.36. 

 Rupee premiums on the forward dollar ended lower, helped by the strong outlook for the rupee. 

 The benchmark six-month forward ended four basis points lower at an annualised 3.21 percent. It had eased even lower during the day to 3.15 percent.

title: Indian rupee seen gaining, cbank and oil prices eyed.

BOMBAY, March 28 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee , is expected to extend gains on Friday on strong trade inflows, with the range likely to be set by central bank intervention, traders said.

 "There is absolutely no demand for dollars right now because of its (dollar's) weakness. Importers are in a wait-and-watch mode while exporters and companies are bringing in their dollars," a trading head at a private bank said.

title: Indian IRS end down, track forward dollar premiums.
text:
BOMBAY, Feb 20 (Reuters) - Indian interest rates swaps (IRS) ended lower on Thursday, tailing forward dollar premiums, which edged down due to a firm outlook for the rupee and talk of central bank receiving, dealers said. 

 The five-year swap linked to the implied rupee rate benchmark, the Reuters MIFOR , ended at 6.18/25 percent, down from Wednesday's 6.28/38 percent. The MIFOR is derived from rupee-dollar forwards and U.S. overnight rates. 

 But the five-year swap indexed to the overnight fund benchmark (OIS) ended steady at 6.33/38 percent with the outlook for liquidity remained uncertain as huge bond supplies from several Indian states are expected in the next few weeks. 

 India's central bank said earlier in the day it will conduct an on-tap sale for 10-year loans issued by 27 states for a targeted 73.25 billion rupees on February 25. 

 This will be followed by more sales for 68.26 billion before March-end. 

 But some traders are of the view that the sales could go through without impacting liquidity much as the central bank continues to mop up some of the strong forex inflows. 

India's central bank often intervenes in the currency market to absorb forex inflows to curb a sharp upswing in the rupee and in the process boosts money market liquidity. 

 The rupee , which analysts say is undervalued by nearly three percent on a trade-weighted basis, ended steady at 47.6975/7075 per dollar, off a low of 47.7175 in early deals. 

 Rupee premiums on the forward dollar eased in late trade as talk of central bank receiving prompted some exporters to sell forward dollars in anticipation of further drops. 

 The annualised premium on the six-month dollar closed at 3.62 percent against the previous 3.7 percent.

title: Indian bond yields off lows, call ends steady.
text:
BOMBAY, Feb 20 (Reuters) - Yields on Indian government bonds came off lows by Thursday afternoon as traders booked profits, unclear about the rates outlook and the impact on liquidity due to huge supplies from states, dealers said. 

 The benchmark 10-year bond, the 9.81 percent 2013 , was at 6.5019 percent, up from the morning's 6.4553 percent and unchanged from the previous close. 

 "The market lacks conviction about interest rates and liquidity," the chief dealer in a private bank said. "At every uptick in prices, there is profit taking by traders and with volumes low, the movement is sharp." 

 The central bank said on Wednesday the federal government had approved borrowings of 141.51 billion rupees by several states before the financial year ends on March 31, a move which could sap liquidity and lead to a sell-off in bonds. 

 But a few traders are of the view that with forex inflows strong, the sales could go through without impacting liquidity much. 

India's central bank often intervenes in the currency market to absorb forex inflows to curb a sharp upswing in the rupee and in the process boosts money market liquidity. 

 In the money market, call money  ended steady at 5.40-5.50 percent, with most banks having finished covering their reserve positions ahead of the two-weekly reporting cycle.

title: Indian IRS steady, firm outlook for rupee helps.

India's central bank often intervenes in the currency market to absorb forex inflows to curb a sharp upswing in the rupee and in the process boosts money market liquidity.

title: Iraq War Poses Risk For India's Bond Markets
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 MUMBAI -(Dow Jones)-  War in Iraq will send shock waves through some of India's banks and companies which stand exposed from having invested heavily in government bonds or leaving their foreign exchange loans unhedged. 

 After testing new highs over several weeks, bond prices have been thrown into reverse on fears of a war in the Gulf. The momentum increased Monday after U.N. inspectors said Iraq didn't do enough to help in the search for weapons of mass destruction. 

 Market players said a conflict would lead to a spike oil prices, temporary inflation and probably financial turbulence. 

 "Its not yet a panic situation. We are only at the first stage. The bottom may fall out later depending on how the war develops," said Amitabh Mohanty, fund manager, Alliance Capital Mutual Fund. 

 To ride out any shocks, the central bank is likely to take the necessary interest rate measures to minimize the impact on the economy of higher inflation, which will reverse a two-year downtrend in rates. 

 In the last two or three trading days, the government bond markets have given a sneak preview of the volatility scenarios analysts have been conjuring up against the backdrop of a potential U.S-Iraq conflict. 

 Since Friday, war fears have pushed bond prices off recent highs. The benchmark 10-year yield has come off from record low of 5.83% and edged back up over 6.10% 

 "In the next few days there will be volatility amid lower volumes," said Binai Chandgothia, head of fixed income at IDBI Principal. 

 Indian money markets have been bullish for nearly two years due to a low interest rate environment and low inflation expectations. 

 Despite United Nations inspectors' departure for Iraq two months ago, Indian markets stayed on a headlong bull run with no signs of letting up despite occasional intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). 

 Analysts said the rally probably sprung from a belief that the downtrend in interest rates was irreversible - because of the massive liquidity in the system - and the RBI's often repeated stance of a softer interest rate policy and low inflation. 

 The rate of inflation has stayed within the RBI's forecast of 4% so far in the current financial year which ends March 31. 

 Over the year, bond yields have fallen over 200 basis points, most of it coming after RBI cut key interest rates late October. The bullish mood ran through the foreign exchange market too, where the rupee gained nearly 2% against the U.S. dollar. 


   War Risks On Interest Rate Reversal



The risk of war, however, has highlighted the vulnerability of the
financial system as banks kept buying more and more bonds as prices kept
rising. But such a build up of positions is vulnerable if interest rates
were to make an about turn and rise again.



"Liquidity could go the other way," said Mark Parsley, treasurer at
Credit Agricole Indosuez, citing not only the war risk but also the
recent easing of foreign exchange controls facilitating Indian residents
and corporates to invest abroad, which could result in an outflow of
dollars.



Investments by banks in bonds is over INR5 trillion compared with
aggregate deposits of INR12.5 trillion, according to the RBI's latest
data.



A recent study by the Indian Council of Research on International
Economic Relations and the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development
Research said nearly two-thirds of the top banks they sampled would
stand to lose over 25% of their equity capital in the event of a
320-basis point rise in interest rates.



Companies earlier felt safe in the belief that the rupee would
continue to appreciate, and so did not hedge large foreign exchange
positions.



Banking circles estimate that Indian companies have a total unhedged
foreign exchange position of around $7 billion to $8 billion.



Keeping unhedged positions is fine as long as the rupee appreciates
against the dollar.



But the day that changes, a scramble for dollars will trigger
volatility which in turn could cost the RBI a few billion dollars to
return stability to the markets.



But that, like the possibility of war and the global fallout remains a
scenario and a matter of conjecture.



-By Nivedita Prabhu and Manish Jaradi, Dow Jones Newswires; 91 22
22884212; nivedita.prabhu@dowjones.com

title: Indian call rate rises, checks dip in bond yields.
text:
BOMBAY, Jan 17 (Reuters) - India's overnight funds rate jumped on Friday due to huge outflows towards the previous day's open market bond auctions, slowing a fall in bond yields, dealers said. 

 But they said investors drew some comfort from a senior central banker's comments that the market would determine the realistic levels of bond yields. 

 Call money  was quoted at 6.00-6.25 percent at 10:00 a.m. (0430 GMT), up from the previous close of 5.25-5.50 percent, with auction outflows of nearly 109 billion denting fund supply. 

 "But this is not detering investors to buy bonds in small quantums at the long end," said a trader at a primary dealer. "They are convinced that the spike (in call money) is temporary and the liquidity situation will improve in a few days." 

 The benchmark 10-year 9.81 percent bond was at 5.9125 percent, down from the previous close 5.9275 percent. 

 The central bank's persistent purchase of dollars in the foreign exchange market has boosted supplies in India's domestic money market, fuelling a bond market rally and spurring hopes a repo rate cut. 

India's central bank has intervened in the past to mop up excess funds through open market bond sales, a possibility the central bank deputy governor reiterated on Friday. 

 "Liquidity continues to be under constant watch and that is why we did the open market sales (on Thursday)," RBI Deputy Governor Rakesh Mohan told reporters on the sidelines of a management seminar. 

 "We will continue to monitor the situation," he replied, when asked whether the central bank would consider more open market sales. 

 He said monetary authorities were neither comfortable nor uncomfortable with the current bond yield levels. 

 "The market will decide the realistic level of bond yields," he answered, when asked to comment on why yields had fallen despite the open market auctions on Thursday.

title: WEEK AHEAD-C.bank sale fears to support Indian bond yields.
text:
BOMBAY, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Indian bond yields could ease to fresh life lows this week, but fears the central bank will sell stock should temper any decline, traders said. 

 "The RBI (Reserve Bank of India) is well armoured to intervene should yields fall too fast," said S. Ananthanarayan, vice president at Kotak Mahindra Capital Co. 

 "I expect a very mild easing, with the 10-year yield falling to 5.97 percent over a week to 10 days. The market will correct itself at every stage in the anxiety of a central bank sale." 

 The 10-year yield was 6.0080 percent on Saturday, after hitting a life low of 5.9984 percent on Tuesday. 

 Surplus cash from strong foreign exchange inflows have pushed bond yields to historic lows, leaving 10-year bonds yielding just half a percentgae point over interbank overnight interest rates. 

 But with banks still holding surplus cash, traders said pressure on bond yields would continue. 

 The central bank, wary with yields at such low levels, is well positioned to intervene having added four new bonds to its portfolio after special federal securities worth 200 billion rupees were converted in early January. 

 The key 10-year yield fell a percentage point between the end of October and December and has fallen a further six-basis points in January because of the easy money conditions, benign inflation and fears for the economy after a severe drought. 

 Central bankers have said there were no plans to cut interest rates in the near term, but traders are factoring in a 50-basis-point cut in the key short-term benchmark - the repo rate, which stands at 5.5 percent. 

 This rate, at which RBI borrows overnight funds from the market, influences the cost of interbank funds and consequently, bond yields. 

 The next monetary policy is to be announced in April. 

 MORE FLATTENING 

 The yield curve has already flattened considerably since the end of October and medium and long end could fall further on the loose liquidity conditions. 

 Traders said the curve would continue to flatten till the repo rate was cut as only then would yields fall at the short end of the curve. 

 The spread between the one-and 10-year bond yields have narrowed to 62 basis points from 124 basis points, while the spreads between the 10-and 15-year bond yields have tightened to 14 basis points from 31.

title: Investment inflows boost Indian rupee for 3rd day.
text:
BOMBAY, Jan 8 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee appreciated against the dollar for the third straight day on Wednesday as robust direct investment inflows were met by indifferent demand for the U.S. unit. 

 The rupee  closed at 47.9750/47.9800 per dollar, off an intra-day high of 47.965 but up from Tuesday's 47.9775/47.9825. It has appreciated 0.05 percent since last week. 

 "The rupee initially strengthened on some foreign direct investment remittance and selling by some exporters, but some buying towards the end by corporates covering unhedged positions brought it off," said a trader at a state-run bank. 

 Traders said the lack of concerted dollar buying by state-run banks on behalf of the central bank also helped the rupee. 

 "There was no visible support in the market today," a bank dealer said. 

India's central bank has been intervening through state-run banks to support the dollar in recent weeks to protect the country's export competitiveness, traders said. 

 It has tried to cap the local unit's rise at around the 48 level. 

 The rupee rose 0.55 percent in 2002, its first annual gain in more than 10 years, helped by heavy remittances by overseas Indians, exporters and foreign investments. 

 In Europe, the dollar paused a cent above last week's three-year low against the euro as dealers awaited U.S. jobs data and news regarding Iraq before deciding whether to extend the greenback's recent slide. 

 The dollar's woes overseas have boosted remittances from non-resident Indians seeing a safe haven in the undervalued rupee and looking for better returns in view of the higher interest rates in India. 

Foreign exchange reserves leapt $22.25 billion last year to more than $70 billion as the central bank persistently absorbed inflows to rein in the rupee. 

 But forward dollar premium firmed after exporters holding received positions opted to pay to book profits from a narrowing spread. 

 The benchmark six-month premium closed at an annualised 3.48 percent against its previous close of 3.46 percent.

 unveil an economic stimulus plan expected to be worth up to as 

 much as $670 billion.

 producers were preparing to raise output as soon as possible to 

 cool crude markets, overheated by the threat of war in Iraq and 

 a continuing strike in Venezuela, the world's fifth biggest oil 

 exporter.

 dollar in recent weeks in its keenness to protect the country's 

 export competitiveness. The interventions have been aimed at 

 capping the local unit's appreciation at around the 48 level.

 in more than 10 years, helped by heavy remittances by overseas 

 Indians, exporters and foreign portfolio and direct investors. 

Foreign exchange reserves leapt $22.25 billion last year to 

 more than $70 billion as the central bank absorbed most of the 

 inflows to rein in the rupee.

title: UPDATE 1-Indian  forex  reserves vault over $67 bln.
text:
BOMBAY, Dec 14 (Reuters) - Indian forex reserves rose by a sharp $828 million in the week to December 6, to a new high of $67.753 billion, data from the Reserve Bank of India's Weekly Statistical Supplement showed on Saturday. Analysts said the foreign currency reserves were boosted by continuing exporter remittances, coupled with steady dollar purchases by state-run banks on behalf of the central bank, to temper the rupee's gains. 

 "Since the Reserve Bank of India had been intervening in the currency market, we had expected reserves to rise," said Sanjeet Singh, analyst with ICICI Securities and Finance Company. 

 "But the quantum of the rise is a bit higher than expected and that is probably on account of revaluation of the dollar against other currencies," he said. 

 India's foreign curreny assets, expressed in dollars, include the effect of appreciation or depreciation of other currencies like the Euro, Sterling and Yen. 

 The Euro gained 1.52 percent against the dollar in the week ended December 6. 

 The central bank has been checking the rupee's gains since June to maintain the export competitiveness of Indian goods and servces and beef up reserves. 

 The Indian rupee closed at 48.1675/1775 per dollar on Friday against the previous close of 48.1875/1975. It is up 1.87 percent since hitting a lifetime low of 49.08 per dollar in mid-May, but is still undervalued by two percent on a trade-weighted basis. 

 Given the country's healthy external finances, as reflected in a small current account surplus in the first quarter of the current year, and favourable interest rate differentials, dollar inflows are likely to gather pace in the next few months, analysts say.

title: Indian rupee ends at 2002 high, fwds up on cbank.
text:
BOMBAY, Dec 11 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee ended at a 2002 closing high against the dollar on Wednesday, boosted by robust remittances by exporters and banks going short on the greenback on hopes that more gains were in store for the local currency. 

 They added that the rupee was also encouraged by indications that the central bank was not making wholehearted attempts to intervene and temper gains. 

 The local currency  ended at 48.1475/1575 per dollar, up from the previous close of 48.1950/2050, itself a two-week closing high. The last time the rupee finished around this level was on December 26 last year. 

 It has so far gained 1.9 percent from its mid-May life low of 49.08, but is still undervalued by about two percent on a trade-weighted basis due to the latest bout of weakness afflicting the dollar overseas. 

 The unit was undervalued by about one percent last week, analysts said. 

 "There were attempts by the central bank to support the dollar at every level," a dealer at a foreign bank said. "But the inflows were quite robust." 

 Traders had expected state-run banks, which often act on behalf of the central bank, to prevent the rupee from rising beyond 48.18 on Wednesday. 

 The Reserve Bank of India has been absorbing a bulk of the dollar supplies in recent months to maintain the export competitiveness of Indian goods and beef up foreign exchange reserves. 

 FORWARDS TREND UP 

 Despite the firm local unit, rupee premiums on the forward dollar ended firmer on sustained paying (sell-buy swaps) by banks, possibly acting for the central bank. 

 Traders said the intervention showed that the Reserve Bank of India was keen to correct a distortion in short-term rates by sucking out rupee funds. 

 As a result of their persistent paying, the six-month dollar-rupee implied rate  inched up to around the repo rate of 5.50 percent after staying below the overnight funds rate for the past three weeks. 

 The implied rates indicate how much rupee loans can earn in the local money market and are derived from the forward dollar premiums and U.S. interbank rates. 

 Forwards reflect the hedging requirements by importers and the interest rate differentials between the United States and India. 

 The one-month forward closed at 3.87 percent, up from previous close of 3.82 percent while the six-months ended at 3.97 percent, higher than the previous close of 3.96 percent.

title: Indian rupee ends 3-day rising streak, forwards up.
text:
BOMBAY, Dec 5 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee snapped a three-day rising streak to end weaker on Thursday after dollar bids from state-run banks, possibly on behalf of the central bank, pushed it down and prompted some banks to cover short positions. 

 The local currency ended at 48.2425/2575 per dollar, down from the previous close of 48.2025/2100. At Wednesday's close, the rupee had gained 0.2 percent during the week. 

 It has risen about 1.8 percent since it hit a lifetime low of 49.08 in mid-May but is still undervalued about a percent on a trade-weighted basis, which analysts say is probably prompting the central bank to support the dollar. 

India's central bank often intervenes in the currency market to maintain the rupee's real effective exchange rate and beef up foreign exchange reserves. 

 Traders said banks were also paying (sell-buy swaps) at the short-end of the forward segment which led to a spike in rupee premiums across the curve. 

 "The banks paid on behalf of some importers and the market is correcting itself," said a trader at a state-run bank. 

 The one-month forward ended at at an annualised 3.08 percent up from the previous close of 2.51 percent. The six-month forward closed at 3.66 percent, firmer than the previous 3.57 percent. 

 Low premiums in the past two weeks have kept the one-year implied dollar-rupee rate  below the overnight funds rate, a short-term benchmark in the domestic money market. 

 Traders said the paying by the banks was correcting this discrepancy. 

 A lower one-year implied rate means that borrowers can raise short-term dollar funds at a cheaper rate than the overnight domestic money market level. 

 Forwards also reflect the hedging needs of importers and interest rate differences between the United States and India.

title: India  Jalan: RBI To  Intervene  In  Forex  Mkt When Necessary
text:
NEW DELHI -(Dow Jones)- The Reserve Bank of India Governor, Bimal Jalan, said Saturday that flexibility in the exchange rate was necessary so that the central bank had the ability to intervene in the market as and when necessary. 

 Jalan was speaking at a panel discussion at the meeting of the central bank governors and finance ministers of the Group of 20 nations. The Group of 20, created in 1999 to address international financial concerns, consists of the European Union and 19 separate nations: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, South Korea, Turkey, the U.K. and the U.S. 

 The Reserve Bank of India has been mopping up dollar inflows, building up foreign-exchange reserves and preventing the rupee from sharply gaining against the dollar. 

 The Indian rupee has so far gained over 1.2% since the start of the fiscal year in April. 

 Jalan also said that the policy of building high level of foreign-exchange reserves should take into the anticipated current account deficits and liquidity at risk from unanticipated capital movements. 

 India's foreign-exchange reserves are at a record high of $66.024 billion with the Reserve Bank mopping up dollars sold by exporters bullish on the rupee. Dollar inflows have been rising steadily as Indians living abroad send money home to take advantage of higher local interest rates. 

 The Governor said a stable macro-economic environment with low inflation, low current account deficit and reasonable growth was essential to prevent crises. He said India had all three: inflation around 3%, current account deficit below 1% and growth above 5%.

title: Indian rupee may gain on rating upgrade prospects.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 15 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee could extend gains on Friday on prospects that Moody's Investors Services may upgrade the country's foreign currency debt rating, traders said. 

 News of the possible review has lifted sentiment, which was earlier boosted by Iraq's decision to accept a tough U.N. resolution to disarm on Wednesday. 

 "I expect the rupee to be stronger, as an upgrade could mean increased foreign investments into the country," said a trader with a private bank. 

 Moody's said on Thursday it had placed India's Ba2 foreign currency country ceiling for debt and Ba3 foreign currency country ceiling for bank deposits on review for a possible upgrade. 

 "The review is primarily based on the substantial strengthening of the country's external financial situation," Moody's said in a statement. 

 The improvement in the country's external sector, showing growth in exports of goods and services, has helped the rupee to appreciate by 1.7 percent to 48.2625/2700 at Thursday's close from a life low of 49.08 hit in mid-May.

title: Indian rupee extends rise, state banks curb gains.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 21 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee extended gains on Wednesday afternoon, helped by exporter remittances, although state-run banks, which sometimes act on behalf of the central bank, curbed its rise, dealers said. 

 At 1:15 p.m., the Indian unit was quoted at 48.5350/5450 against the morning's 48.5525/5625 and Tuesday's six-and-a-half month closing high of 48.56/57. 

 "The central bank seems to be allowing a gradual appreciation in the rupee, while slowing a rise," said a dealer at a state-owned bank. 

 The Reserve Bank of India's stated objective for intervening in the currency market is to maintain stability, which analysts say it does by tempering sharp movements in the rupee and steering it towards its trade-weighted value.

title: Fwd payments under 1% of Indian  forex  reserves-RBI.
text:
BOMBAY, July 5 (Reuters) - India's forward dollar liabilities are under one precent of its foreign exchange reserves and its overseas short-term debt was also very low, Central Bank Governor Bimal Jalan said in London on Friday. 

 "This has gained us the confidence of the markets, which has been more evident even during the recent period of uncertainties," Jalan was quoted in a statement as saying at a symposium for central bankers organised by the Bank of England. 

 The country's reserves stood at an all-time high of $57.07 billion on June 21, enough to cover all capital outflows and current account deficits. 

 The reserves are up $9 billion in calendar 2002, boosted by capital inflows, including from foreign direct investors and exporters' earnings. 

 Jalan said holding adequate reserves was one of three requirements for countries if they wanted to avert financial crises and cope with instability and volatility. 

 Drawing from the Indian experience he said reserves should be enough to cover not only anticipated current account deficits but also unanticipated capital movements. 

 The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) intervention is believed to have cushioned the rupee in mid-May when the spectre of war between India and Pakistan sent ripples through the financial markets. 

 Other requirements included careful monitoring and management of exchange rates without a fixed target or a pre-announced target or band and a judicious policy for management of the capital account, he said.

title: UPDATE 1-India's reserves drop from high on c.bank sales.
text:
BOMBAY, May 25 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves fell in the week to May 17, after rising for 32 straight weeks, strengthening the market's belief that the central bank intervened when war fears were strong, to steady a shaky rupee. 

 By May 17 - three days after an attack on an Indian army camp in Kashmir by suspected Pakistan militants jolted financial markets - the reserves fell $139 million to $55.573 billion, from the previous week's lifetime high of $55.712 billion. 

 The dip was mostly in the currency assets which fell $136 million to $52.433 billion, data from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) showed. 

 "The drop can be attributed to intervention by the central bank. It looked like it was selling dollars last week," said M.R. Madhavan, head of research at Bank of America. 

 The RBI, which has been buying dollars for most of the past year-and-half, absorbing strong capital inflows, reportedly turned a seller last week when war fears hit. 

 In the aftermath of the attack, bond prices fell around 2.5 percent and the benchmark share index slid nearly 10 percent. 

 But the rupee shaved off just 0.2 percent, which traders said was because of central bank support. 

 War concerns have eased since Thursday on softer rhetoric from Indian Prime Minister Atal Behari Vajpayee and international efforts to diffuse tensions between India and Pakistan. 

 Vajpayee allayed fears of a full-scale war, telling a press conference in Kashmir he hoped for "clear skies" when reporters asked if he saw war clouds. 

 The markets are bouncing back. 

 The rupee has fully recovered, closing Friday at 48.9850/9925 per dollar - of its May 16 lifetime low of 49.08 - returning to levels it was at before the attack. 

 Tensions, however, still run high after a week of fighting across the ceasefire line in Kashmir. 

 RESERVES STRONG 

 The $139 million dip in the reserves is hardly a ripple. 

 But, should India face a more severe shock needing stronger intervention, analysts feel the reserves will withstand it. 

 "If tensions worsen, the reserves may be hit," said Siddharth Mathur, strategist with JP Morgan. "The strong growth trend may not be sustained. We could even see some depletion. But, I don't think the reserves are so volatile to see a substantial outflow. 

 The RBI does not reveal the composition of the reserves but analysts think "hot money" may not comprise much more than a fifth of the reserves. 

 In financial year 2001/02 (April-March), the reserves rose by around $12 billion to touch $54.154 billion on March 29, helped by strong capital inflows. 

 Analysts see more growth in 2002/03 though the strength may be less. 

 "I expect the reserves to touch $60 billion by end March 2003 helped by a current account surplus and some direct and portfolio investments," Madhavan said. 

 Foreign investments in India so far in 2002 have been subdued at $622.8 million compared with the previous year's $2.8 billion. 

 But, analysts are hoping for a pickup as the government pushes with reforms, particularly a privatisation process.

title: WRAP: India,Pakistan Mkts Hit As Investors Run For Cover
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 BOMBAY -(Dow Jones)- Markets in India and Pakistan took a direct hit Tuesday as investors ran for cover, fearing war in the troubled region. 

 In India's commercial capital Bombay, shares sank to a low soon after the army redeployed troops, stationed in western Gujarat state to prevent communal violence, to "areas of operational responsibility." 

 The troop movement came as Indian Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee began a three-day tour of Jammu and Kashmir state to meet troops and visit an army base where alleged Pakistan-sponsored militants last week killed 34 people. 

 Shelling continued on both sides of the so-called Line of Control that separates Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir. 

 Equity markets in both countries were hit on heightened tensions. The Bombay Stock Exchange Sensitive Index, or Sensex, closed down 2.9% at 3186.53 - its lowest level this calendar year - but off an intraday low of 3127.87. The index finished at a low of 3184.44 Dec. 28. 

 Across the border, the Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index ended down 3% at 1598.16 points - its lowest level since January - in spite of regulatory measures imposed to stem a sharp fall. 

 The mood on the Bombay bourses was glum, as traders crowded around to watch live television coverage of the shelling along the border. 

 "There's panic all round, but there are technical reasons too, for today's (Tuesday's) sharp fall," said Kisan Ratilal Choksey, chairman of KRC Shares & Securities. 

 "Most stocks are fundamentally strong and there's no specific reason to exit them. But most mutual funds or institutional investors don't like these certainties and are selling," Choksey said. 

 Shares across the board suffered, including those of petrochemicals concern Reliance Industries Ltd. (P.REL) and Hindustan Lever Ltd. (P.HLV), India's largest conglomerate. Reliance Industries fell 4.7% to 262.40 rupees ($1=INR48.9850), while Hindustan Lever lost 1.2% to INR197.25. 


   Regulator Fails To Curb Karachi Losses



In Pakistan, emergency measures failed to prop up stocks on the
Karachi Stock Exchange as retail investors heavily sold their
shareholdings.



KSE authorities tightened the bourse's circuit-breakers after the
KSE-100 share index plunged 7.4% Monday, in its biggest one-day loss
since October 1997.



Shares will now be allowed a maximum daily fall of 5%, instead of
7.5%. They will continue to be allowed to rise a maximum of 7.5% daily.



Selling, triggered by the border tensions, intensified on settlement
fears, said Mohammad Sohail, research head at Investcap Securities.



"I expect some recovery Wednesday as institutions will be supportive
and retail investors will cover short-positions," Sohail said.



Others, however, were less certain.



In Pakistan's bond markets, no bids were reported for three- and
five-year government bonds ahead of their auction Thursday.



"The bond market is as dull as you can get. Yesterday (Monday), we had
some bids, but today (Tuesday) players have disappeared," a dealer in
Karachi said.



The foreign exchange market had a brief respite on the absence of
demand from importers. Also, inflows from exporters allowed the rupee to
rise to PKR59.95 to the dollar, breaching the critical PKR60.00 barrier
for the first time since March.



The rupee's gains came in spite of dollar buying by Pakistan's central
bank.



"We will not allow any speculator to play with the (Pakistan) rupee
due to tensions with India. We won't allow what happened to the stock
market yesterday (Monday)," Zafar Sheikh, foreign exchange adviser of
the State Bank of Pakistan, told Dow Jones Newswires.



   Indian Bonds Fall As Rupee Gains



In Bombay, government bonds fell in thin trade due to uncertainties
caused by rising tensions with Pakistan.



The 10-year bond touched 8.22%, up from the previous close of 8.14%.



However, selling was limited as traders avoided the markets, dealers
said.



In contrast, the Indian rupee ended higher at INR48.985 to the dollar,
against Monday's close of INR49.030, due to Central Bank intervention
through state-owned banks.



The Reserve Bank of India probably didn't want the rupee and the
Sensex to fall sharply on the same day, dealers said.



"(The RBI) feels there isn't enough customer demand. The rupee
shouldn't weaken on speculation - that is the RBI's message," said K.
Jayaram, chief dealer at Credit Lyonnais Bank in Bombay.



The threat of conflict was evident in the forward market. Rupee
premiums on forward dollar and Overnight Indexed Swap rates climbed.



April premiums closed at 2.80 against the previous close of 2.75,
while one-year Overnight Indexed Swap rates ended sharply higher at
7.46%-7.50%, against the previous close of 7.30-7.34%.



- By Saeed Azhar and Steve Percy, Dow Jones Newswires; 91-22-288-4212;
djn.in@dowjones.com



(Nivedita Prabhu, Sophia Rodrigues and Ashok Bhattacharjee in Bombay
contributed to this story)

title: India rupee set for cool stint,some cbank-steering.
text:
BOMBAY, April 10 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee, driven to new lows this week, will keep its softening bias over the next 12 months though its decline should be cushioned by improving global growth and strong foreign capital inflows. 

 Economists polled by Reuters expected the rupee to continue weakening in keeping with the central bank's perceived preference for an export-supportive exchange rate, but its fall should be in line with inflation differences with the dollar. 

 The risks to that firm view could come from a sharper-than-expected spike in international oil prices, a sudden devaluation of the Chinese yuan or domestic political turmoil. 

 "Barring the unforeseen event that oil prices go up significantly, the rupee will remain very strong," said Sanjay Mathur, economist with UBS Warburg, Singapore. 

 "Exports would start to perform this year, inflation is low and the external account is strong," he added. The poll forecast the rupee at 49.66 per dollar by the end of September and 50.54 at the close of 2002/03 (April-March), a drop of 3.2 percent during the year from current levels of 48.90/91. 

 That compares with a four percent average annual fall in the past decade since partial trade account convertibility was introduced, and a five-year average depreciation of 5.3 percent. 

 Economists said their forecasts factored in the likely risks of further tensions in the Middle East or a threat to India's multi-party government from ongoing Hindu-Muslim clashes, re-ignited last month by the dispute over a religious site. 

 "The premium on these event risks has been added to the trend rate of depreciation," said Ajit Ranade, ABN AMRO Bank economist. 

 "If the Hindu-Muslim conflict flares up, all the government's resources and management process will be diverted from reforms." The partly convertible rupee lost 4.5 percent in the previous year and struck an all-time low of 48.96 on Tuesday. 

INTERVENTION

 Last week the rupee was tripped up by fears the government would use its huge $54 billion foreign exchange reserves to retire external debt in advance, and rocked by rising oil prices. 

 Government borrowings account for a large chunk of the $100 billion external debt, of which funds raised through placement of bonds with expatriates in 1998 and 2000 account for a tenth. 

 Bankers say the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) aggressive intervention in recent months was to accumulate funds for repaying the first set of those bonds in 2003 while also keeping the rupee fairly valued in trade-weighted terms. 

 The RBI added about $3.4 billion to reserves in March alone. 

 And, its constant presence in the regulated market was an important factor in all calculations, analysts said. 

 "As an economist, I expect that the rupee should depreciate about 2.5 percent to restore real parity, based on the difference in consumer prices inflation," said Sanjeet Singh, analyst with ICICI Securities and Finance Corp (I-Sec). 

 "To that one has to add the inelastic dollar demand from the RBI, because of its conscious strategy of building up reserves." 

 IMPORT BARRIER 

 A key reason the RBI would want to keep the rupee on a downward gradient was the need to boost exports and counter the likely onslaught of imports as tariffs drop, traders said. 

 "There would be some tendency to use the rupee to protect domestic industry from imports and push exports, a transition from old methods like tariffs and export subsidies," said Ranade. 

 Still, despite the cyclical upturn in the economy, dealers said there was no threat of an increase in imports. 

 "There could be a consumption boom, but an investment boom is unlikely. There is no capacity constraint yet," said Sanjeev Sanyal, regional economist with Deutsche Bank in Singapore. 

 The RBI estimates the current account will be in surplus for the past year ended in March, for the first time in 25 years, helped by shrinking imports and nearly flat export growth. 

 Economists say current account balances are in any case small and any deficit next year will easily be soaked up by sustained capital inflows from portfolio and direct foreign investments. 

 They expect fresh investments will flow into labour-intensive exports, drawn by incentives in the special export-focused economic zones announced in the government's new trade policy.

title: Indian rupee steady at open, bias firm.
text:
BOMBAY, March 18 (Reuters) - The rupee traded steady in thin Monday morning deals with traders saying the incentive to sell dollars remained strong despite likely central bank intervention. 

 Traders also said they expected the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will continue its vigorous intervention by buying dollars through state-run banks to check the rupee's gains. Despite a one percent fall so far in 2002, the rupee is nearly a percent overvalued in real terms. 

 "It's judicious to keep a short or square dollar position," said a dealer with a foreign bank. 

 "There is no reason to expect pressure on the rupee, and the carry may keep rising as the year end approaches." 

 The rupee was quoted at 48.71/72 per dollar in early trade, little changed from Friday's close at 48.7050/7150. 

 Call rates continued to be in a higher range around seven percent. They rose last week from steady levels around the 6.5 percent refinance rate on outflows towards tax payments and the pressure of the approaching fiscal year end. 

 Last week's tensions, because of plans by Hindu hardliners to hold a prayer ceremony in Ayodhya, had receded and traders were indifferent to reports of firing across the border between India and Pakistan in Kashmir, saying it was routine. 

 Traders expect foreign currency inflows to continue, especially regular flows from multinationals hiking their stake in Indian subsidiaries. 

 The latest was UK household products firm Reckitt Benckiser Plc , which last week made an open offer to buy out the remaining 49 percent holding in Reckitt Benckiser (India) . 

 They also expect a spillover of last week's quarterly payments for a television broadcasting firm.

text:
BOMBAY, March 4 (Reuters) - The government has allowed the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to start using the euro to intervene in the foreign exchange market, the central bank said in a statement on Monday. 

 This is in addition to the U.S. dollar, which the central bank routinely buys or sells in the currency market to stem volatility and build foreign exchange reserves.

title: UPDATE 1- India forex  reserves at new high, intervention  seen.
text:
BOMBAY, Feb 16 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves have touched a new high for the 20th straight week, which analysts said showed the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was intervening to keep the rupee down. 

 On February 8 the reserves stood at $49.766 billion, up $201 million from the previous week, the RBI said in a weekly statistical supplement. 

 Traders and analysts said the reserves were bolstered by trade and investment related inflows which the central bank had absorbed in the face of weak importer dollar demand, and the $50 billion mark now beckoned. 

 "I think there was an overt intervention to drive the rupee slightly lower during the week," said Uday Mulgaonkar, associate vice president at Kotak Mahindra Capital Company. 

 "A correction was justified as an overvalued rupee would hurt India's export competitiveness in the sluggish global economic conditions," he added. 

 The rupee closed Friday at 48.6650/6750, still overvalued by over a percent, according to analysts. On February 8 it had closed at 48.7000/7100. 

 After a period of relative stability in the last quarter of 2001, the rupee has depreciated by around two percent since late December while the reserves have risen by around $1.67 billion. 

 Traders and analysts said this indicated the central bank's hand to keep the rupee fairly valued on a traded-weighted basis as the currencies of some of India's largest trading partners, including Europe and Japan, have weakened. 

 Left to market forces, traders said the rupee would have traded much above its fair value because of robust investment inflows and falling import payments due to sluggish domestic industrial activity and softer oil prices. 

 MORE RISES IN STORE 

 Over the past year, India has amassed a substantial $8 billion in reserves, but traders foresaw more rises. 

 They expect the reserves to top the $50 billion mark by the end of the month as investment related inflows remained strong. 

 Portfolio inflows have picked up in February since the government successfully sold its stake in some leading firms. 

 Between February 1-14, their net foreign fund investments in the secondary market totalled $201.2 million compared with $137.4 million through January. 

 And they are expected to pump in more funds with the stock market looking forward to an expected rally ahead of the 2002/03 (April-March) federal budget announcement on February 28. 

 Foreign direct investments have also come in, as have inflows from foreign currency loans in recent sessions, traders said.
