title: UPDATE 1-Indian rupee hits new low, market sees cbank hand.
text:
BOMBAY, Feb 5 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee tumbled to a historic low on Tuesday, but caused few flutters among traders who viewed it as another routine central bank-inspired depreciation to adjust an overvaluation. 

 The rupee hit a low of 48.7450 per dollar, erasing last week's intraday trough of 48.6250. The fall took the losses to one percent in 2002 and 4.38 percent since the start of the financial year on April 1. 

 It ended at a new closing low for a second day at 48.6450/6600 against 48.61/62 on Monday. 

 "No doubt it is a central bank-planned move to depreciate the rupee. But they also want a slower pace and maybe felt today's fall was overdone," a dealer with an American bank said. 

 Dollar sales by state-run banks that normally intervene for the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) helped the rupee recover partially, but traders said the bout of weakness may continue. 

 Even after Tuesday's drop, the rupee is estimated to be overvalued by more than 2.5 percent on a trade-weighted basis, and analysts say the central bank is constrained to ensure export competitiveness of the rupee to support economic growth. 

 Year-on-year export growth in the first nine months has been almost flat and GDP growth last year was a low four percent. 

 "Every new level being defined has the RBI's tacit approval," said a foreign bank's head of treasury. 

 The current bout of weakness in the rupee was triggered last week by talk of some currency swap deals and heavy payment of overseas dividends by a telecommunications firm. 

 Although state-run banks sold dollars when the rupee hit lows last week, traders felt the central bank would not be averse to a downward move in the overvalued rupee. 

 "There must be some pressure on the RBI...for export performance to improve they must be having some notional target," said Sanjeet Singh, analyst with ICICI Securities and Finance Corp (I-Sec). 

 "And our comfort is drawn from RBI's comfort," Singh said. 

 SLOWING FUND INFLOWS 

 Foreign direct investment and expatriate flows have been heavy in the past two months, pushing reserves to record highs of more than $49 billion, but portfolio flows have been fickle. 

 Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) invested just over $137 million in Indian stocks and bonds in January, sharply lower than the $908 million in the same month last year. 

 "...the lack of supply from the FII front is showing up now as the nationalised demand remains at consistent levels," Standard Chartered Bank said in a market commentary. 

 BONDS UNPERTURBED 

 The rupee's fall halted a sharp rally in government bonds, but traders said the currency's weakness was not a big concern. 

 The possibility of the central bank reversing a softening interest rate policy to defend the rupee was virtually ruled out given the sluggish demand and languishing industrial sector. 

 The benchmark 10-year yield, at 7.5623 percent, was off an early low of 7.5490 percent but is down some 35 basis points since January.

title: WRAP: Indian Rupee Sells Off As Border Tension Increases
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 BOMBAY -(Dow Jones)- The Indian rupee closed at an all time low against the dollar for the fourth successive day Friday after the army chief spoke of a worsening crisis on the border with Pakistan. 

 The rupee, which was already weakening early Friday, driven down by demand for dollars from state-run banks, fell further when Army Chief S. Padmanabhan described the situation on the border as "serious" after the recent troop build-up by both India and Pakistan. 

 The rupee closed at INR48.4150 to the dollar, down from its previous close of INR48.36. The record intraday low is INR48.44 Sept. 17, a week after the terrorists attacks in the U.S. 

 With the central bank not taking any measures to stop the fall, dealers expect the rupee to remain under pressure. 

 On Monday it is expected to trade in a INR48.35-45 range and touch INR48.50 by the end of January. 

 The deployment of troops along the border follows an attack on the Indian Parliament on Dec. 13 by militants whom India says were based in Pakistan. 

 The rupee has been steadily weakening nearly every day of the current week, largely driven down by state-run banks buying dollars at a steady pace, possibly to pay for oil and defense imports. 

 "After the army chief's remarks, no one wanted to remain short on the dollar," said K. Jayaram, Vice President, Forex, Credit Lyonnais, who noted that some importers may have wanted to cover their positions ahead of any developments over the weekend. 


                Correction Overdue



The rupee's fall in reaction to the Army Chief's press conference
wasn't sharp, however, dealers noted.



The market had been expecting the rupee to continue to weaken Friday
after closing at a record low Thursday following dollar purchases by
state-run banks.



The expectation was based on the assumption that the Reserve Bank
would like the rupee to weaken as it was overvalued on a trade-related
basis, specially after the recent fall of the yen against the dollar.



The Reserve Bank of India doesn't directly intervene in the foreign
exchange market. However it operates in the market through state-owned
banks.



"Some correction has ensued from state-run banks buying dollars but
there is still room for more," Jayaram added.



Dealers said that the Reserve Bank is allowing the rupee to weaken
steadily. "Ever since the beginning of January, a lot of the downward
move of the rupee seems to have been driven by the Reserve Bank of
India," said Rajesh Gosain, Senior Dealer, Centurion Bank.



But Gosain felt that it wasn't necessary to link the RBI's role in
engineering a weaker rupee to the fall in the yen. "There is no pressure
in the rupee from a weaker yen, " he said. "There are other currencies
such as the euro and the dollar which are more important," he added.



However market analysts have been expecting the RBI to prefer a weaker
rupee to help India's export competitiveness. The government recently
revised the export growth target to 3% from 12% as the global economy
slowed down.

title: UPDATE 1-India's  forex  reserves fall for second week.
text:
BOMBAY, Sept 29 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves fell for a second straight week which analysts attributed to central bankintervention to support the wobbly rupee. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Saturday said the reserves were down $584 million at $44.704 billion on September 21, from $45.288 billion the previous week. The fall was entirely due to a decline in currency assets. 

 The rupee plunged to record lows that week with the market, gripped in the storm that engulfed global and domestic financial markets in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks on the United States. 

 On September 17, the rupee fell to its lifetime low of 48.43 per dollar, down 2.7 percent from September 1 and 3.7 percent from the beginning of the year. 

 "It was heavy RBI dollar sales that week and the week before that was key in stemming the slide and prompting a partial recovery (in the rupee)," an analyst said. 

 The rupee ended September 21 at a lifetime closing low of 48.01/03 per dollar before clawing its way back to close on Friday at 47.865/8700 per dolllar. During the week ended September 21, major currencies also fell against the dollar with the euro and yen depreciating by around 0.6 percent and the British pound by around one percent. 

 Part of India's reserves are denominated in these currencies. 

 The reserves are down from an all-time high of $45.365 billion recorded on September 7. 

 RESERVES COMFORTABLE TO SUPPORT RUPEE 

 Traders said India's reserves were more than adequate to hold off any undue attack on the rupee which, in any case, is unlikely to come under pressure unless war tensions escalated. 

 "So, I don't see any more pressures on the reserves at least not for a while," an analyst said. "The rupee's trend is weaker. But there is not cause for any sharp tumble."

title: Indian rupee falls prey to too much stability.
text:
BOMBAY, Sept 19 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee has once again bucked the regional trend to hit new troughs against the dollar, and analysts said the currency's long period of stability, besides new uncertainties, is a factor driving it lower. 

 In Wednesday morning deals, the rupee traded a 47.92-47.96 range, steadier than it has been in nearly a week and down about 1.7 percent this month. 

 A major part of those losses came after September 11, the day aerial attacks destroyed the World Trade Center in New York, paralysing the U.S. and world financial markets. 

 During the week, major currencies like the euro and Japanese yen have gained sharply against the dollar, prompting Japanese authorities to intervene to support the currency, while regionals have firmed or been stable. 

 Traders said the rupee had diverged from this trend as it had started sliding a week before the U.S. attacks, after two months of stability and a decline of just a percent until end-August. 

 That was bound to accelerate as the currency hit stop-losses and unnerved importers as it fell, they said. 

 Many believed the central bank had encouraged the initial move to correct an over-valuation in trade-weighted terms, although it probably intervened later to check a runaway drop. 

 The rupee has traditionally been prone to sudden, rapid bouts of depreciation after months of stability. At its lifetime low of 48.43 hit on Monday, it was down just 3.65 percent this year. 

 "Technical factors are driving the rupee lower. It had been overvalued and it had to drop substantially after a long period of stability," a currency analyst with an American bank, said. 

 Others blamed market controls for the rupee's runaway slide. 

 Speculative trade in the rupee, which is only partially convertible on the capital account, is banned and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) often intervenes to check volatility. 

 "The rupee is very susceptible to event risk. The fear psychosis in Indian markets is such that any bad news causes all the nervous shorts to cover," said V. Ravikumar, treasury head at private sector Vysya Bank. 

 "Other markets are far more rational." 

 UNCERTAINTIES MOUNT 

 Despite the Indian currency market being relatively sheltered, analysts said the U.S. attacks had raised risks for the currency. 

 "This is a natural reaction to uncertainty. There are a larger number of unknowns now," said Siddharth Mathur, economist with JP Morgan in Bombay. 

 Strong foreign portfolio investments totalling $2.7 billion supported the rupee through the first eight months of 2001, helping it weather political scandals, a stock market crisis and downgrades by international rating firms. 

 The RBI added $10 billion to its currency reserves, which are in excess of $45 billion, in the 12 months to August. 

 But analysts say even those flows are now at risk. 

 And, they said, it was immaterial whether India supports the United States in the retaliation being planned against Afghanistan, which is sheltering Saudi-born dissident Osama bin Laden, the prime suspect in last week's attacks on Washington and New York. 

 It is willy-nilly going to bear the brunt of mounting tension in the immediate neighbourhood. 

 "Unfortunately we are grouped with other South Asian nations, and hence more vulnerable to any fallouts of these U.S. attacks," said a spot rupee trader with a European bank. 

 Economists said investors scaling back exposures to the United States may choose eastern countries like Singapore and Indonesia over India, both for their open markets and location. 

 RISK FACTOR 

 Merrill Lynch said it favoured countries with large domestic economies, but ranked India after China and Australia because its "geographical proximity to Afghanistan could be a risk factor". 

 The trade account could be hit on both sides. Any rise in oil prices will be a big blow for the country, which imports a large part of its crude oil needs. 

 JP Morgan's Mathur said another risk comes from further deceleration in consumer spending in the United States, which besides being the market for a fifth of India's exports is also the biggest buyer of the country's consumer goods. 

 The key Bombay share index plunged close to an eight-year low on Monday, making the domestic market among the worst performing in Asia this year, although news on Tuesday of government moves to boost trading helped shares partly rebound.

title: UPDATE 1-India rupee breathes easy, shares in relief rally.
text:
BOMBAY, Sept 18 (Reuters) - India's battered currency got some respite on Tuesday after the central bank soothed sentiment, while shares saw a relief recovery after Wall Street performed within expectations on reopening for trade. 

 But traders said sentiment remained cautious, given that the domestic economy was grappling with a two-year slowdown and there were growing concerns of a global recession. 

 Fears over the possible fallout from expected U.S. reprisals against Afghanistan, which is sheltering Osama bin Laden, the prime suspect in last week's attacks on the United States, also weighed on the market. 

 The rupee hit a new closing low of 47.97/99 per dollar, dropping below its previous closing low of 47.83/88 hit on Monday, but well off its lifetime trough of 48.43, struck on the same day. It has now hit new closing lows for eight days in a row. 

 The benchmark Bombay exchange index snapped a nine-day losing streak to end up 3.79 percent at 2,782.47 points, off 2,814.07. 

 At its close on Monday, the index had lost 15 percent since the attacks on the U.S.. In comparison, the Dow Jones index fell only 7.13 percent on Monday, when it resumed after a four-day shut down. 

CENTRAL BANK SUPPORT 

Currency and debt markets were heartened by central bank intervention - the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has offered to purchase four bonds on Tuesday to provide market liquidity. 

 On Monday it was believed to have sold dollars through state-run banks after the rupee hit record lows for the seventh straight session. 

 Dealers said state-run banks sold dollars on Tuesday also, boosting the rupee to an intra-day high of 47.85 before it eased on demand for the U.S. currency from private and foreign banks. 

 "The event risk (of a war in the region) is there, forcing banks to buy dollars," a dealer in a private bank said. 

 Dealers said trade was much less volatile than on Monday when the Indian currency fell 0.61 rupees or 1.28 percent. 

 At Tuesday's close, the rupee had lost 2.77 percent against the dollar, compared with an average annual depreciation of five to six percent in recent years. 

 Dealers suspect its latest spell of weakness, which started before the attacks in the U.S., was initially with the RBI's blessings and meant to correct an overvaluation in trade-weighted terms against major trading partners. 

 It is now estimated to be undervalued by over one percent. 

 While the immediate impact of current global developments on India's relatively closed economy are still unclear, analysts fear they will delay hopes of a recovery from a two-year slowdown. 

 They are worried over a possible slowdown in foreign investments and a hike in global crude oil prices if tensions flare up. India imports more than two-thirds of its crude oil requirements. 

 SHARES FIRM ON REGIONALS 

 Share prices took comfort from firm regional markets. 

 "The overnight Fed rate cut and firm strong regionals have held the market," said Chetan Kapoor at KJMC Capital Markets. 

 Advances outnumbered losers 670 to 308 on the Bombay exchange but traders said underlying sentiment was shaky and investors were unwilling to take on bigger positions. 

 "A rebound was expected after the sharp decline but investors are yet to be convinced about a sustained rally," said Prabhakar Rao, a fund manager with UTI Bank.

title: Indian Rupee Rescued By  Intervention  As US Fears Mount
text:
BOMBAY -(Dow Jones)- Three major state-owned banks intervened in the foreign exchange market Monday to support the rupee, which is suffering from fears India could get caught up in any conflict involving Afghanistan and the U.S. 

 Bankers told Dow Jones Newswires the moves could bring respite to the rupee, though this may only prove temporary. 

 The banks concerned, acting on behalf of the Reserve Bank of India - which doesn't directly intervene in the market - aggressively sold dollars, helping the rupee to end at INR47.76, sharply up from its all-time traded low of INR48.40. The rupee closed Friday at INR47.83, its seventh consecutive closing low. 

 "It was good the RBI intervened as the market was turning very volatile," said Jayesh Doshi, general manager (treasury) at Gujarat Ambuja Cements Ltd. 

 The American government's prime suspect in last week's airborne attacks on New York and Washington D.C., Osama bin Laden, lives in Afghanistan. 

 A fall in the local stock market also damped rupee sentiment as there are fears that foreign funds selling Indian shares would step up dollar purchases as they send the proceeds back home. 

 The benchmark Bombay Stock Exchange Sensitive Index or Sensex ended down 149.14 points, or 5.3%, at 2680.98 Monday, an eight-year low. 

 The Reserve Bank's moves came after its statement on Saturday that it would sell dollars directly or indirectly to ease any demand-supply gaps in the foreign exchange market. The central bank also said with foreign exchange reserves of over $45.00 billion it could easily provide liquidity in the forex market. 

 Bankers said that by choosing to intervene when the dollar touched a high of INR48.40, the central bank was able to drive home its message. 

 "The market was already at thin volume at INR47.40 and the dollar sales forced banks to liquidate their long dollars in a hurry," said a dealer at a large European bank. 

 Monday's intervention was estimated at between $100-$200 million. 

 Nerves Will Persist 

 Piyush Kaul, head of forex trading at Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp. said he expects the rupee to trade in a narrower intraday band Tuesday. "I am looking at a INR47.75-48.10 range tomorrow (Tuesday)," he added. 

 However, the current political flux resulting from the U.S outrage may yet prevent the rupee from regaining a stable footing, though some bankers added that INR48.50 may be the low for the currency in the short term. 

 Kaul said developments in the South Asian region and the recent grim statements on the economy from the Prime Minister will continue to keep the market long on the dollar rather than short. 

 Prime Minister A.B Vajpayee, in a speech to the nation Friday, said exports from India and foreign direct investment into the country may slow down in the aftermath of the tragedy, while even a small increase in global oil prices could push up the country's oil import bill sharply. 

 Bankers also said the Reserve Bank may not be eager to sell dollars in the market every day if it fears that foreign capital inflows may be lower in the months to come. 

 Foreign funds have already net sold shares and bonds worth $39.7 million so far in September - the first month when they turned net sellers - and there are fears that they may sell more if they face redemption pressures back home in the U.S. The recent sell-off in the Indian stock markets has been attributed to share sales by U.S-based foreign funds. 

 -By S. Anuradha, Dow Jones Newswires; 91 22 2884211; su.anuradha@dowjones.com

title: India RBI View May Soothe Mkts, But Event Risks Remain
text:
OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 BOMBAY -(Dow Jones)- The Reserve Bank of India's Saturday statement that it won't change current rate policy and will intervene to protect the rupee will soothe Indian bond and rupee markets. However, statement unlikely to have lasting impact given the uncertainty over global events after the terrorist attacks in the U.S. 

 "RBI statement will do more good than bad," an analyst at foreign broking house said. 

 On the other hand, the head of dealing at a U.S bank said, "RBI's statement may bring stability in the market, but there is still too much event risk. No one has seen a scenario like this before." 

 The Reserve Bank of India said Saturday there wouldn't be any change in its interest-rate policy and that it will sell dollars to protect the rupee. Reserve Bank also said that with record high foreign exchange reserves of $45.00 billion it could ensure liquidity in the foreign exchange market. 

 Indian bond and financial markets have weakened sharply on fears that the country may also be drawn into a conflict possibly involving the U.S. and Afghanistan, home of prime suspect Osama bin Laden. The Indian government has already offered the use of its facilities for any U.S. military operations against terrorists targets, including air strikes on Afghanistan. 

 On Friday, the rupee closed to a record of INR47.83 against previous close INR47.57. This was the sixth consecutive day the currency fell to a new low. Bonds prices have also crashed with benchmark ten-year 11.50% 2011 bond falling to a low of 110 on Saturday from 115.49 on Tuesday when the terrorist attacks took place. 11.50% 2011 closed at 111.50 Saturday. 

 The Reserve Bank's comments Saturday come after spending, according to market sources, anywhere between $200 million-$400 million since Wednesday to curb the rupee's fall in the foreign exchange market. In the money market, it also has reportedly persuaded the State Bank of India (P.SBI), the country's largest bank to lend interbank call money at 7.00% Friday much lower than the then prevailing 8.00%. RBI's desired to keep call rates stable because a rising rate would cause banks to sell bonds more aggressively. 

 Market Awaits RBI Dlr Sales 

 But the market waking up to bad news everyday wants more. 

 Siddharth Mathur, analyst at JP Morgan Securities Ltd. said Reserve Bank's statement are a little less that what market expected. "Market wants to see at what level RBI will start aggressively supporting the rupee." 

 Not surprising then that market is waiting for Monday to see whether state-owned banks will start selling dollars on behalf of the Reserve Bank. India's central bank indirectly intervenes in the market through a couple of state-owned banks. 

 "If RBI doesn't ensure a stable or a slightly lower opening for the rupee it could easily slip to INR48-48.20," the U.S bank dealer said. 

 Dealers, though, remain divided over whether aggressive intervention is required from Reserve Bank to help the rupee. Some dealers said that disruption of banking activities in New York has held up dollar supplies and could ease pressure on the rupee when they find their way into the market. 

 On the other hand, the treasurer at a U.K. Bank said rupee is unlikely to recover lost ground on its own. "In a volatile market rupee never settles down on its own. It needs RBI's help." 

 The bond market also thinks it could do with some active intervention from the Reserve Bank although some its problems will be solved if some sanity is restored to the rupee market. 

 The treasurer at the U.K. bank said the market is waiting for the central bank to provide a rate signal by purchasing bonds from the market through its open market operations. Some dealers though think Reserve Bank won't buy bonds aggressively because the increased liquidity in the system will add to speculation in the foreign exchange market. 

 A market source also said it was unlikely Reserve Bank will buy bonds from the market. "RBI has two options either sell dollars or tinker with the repurchase agreement rate," he added. 

 -By S. Anuradha, Dow Jones Newswires; 9122-2884211;su.anuradha@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-Indian markets discount downgrades, but analysts wary.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 9 (Reuters) - Indian financial markets were steady on Thursday despite the move by Moody's Investors Service to follow its ratings agency peer Standard & Poor's (S&P) in downgrading the country's rating outlook. 

 Traders said the downgrades held little new downside risk for markets which have already been rattled this year by a series of political and financial sector scandals and an economic slowdown. 

 They noted that the Indian economy did not rely heavily on foreign borrowings, the one source of capital most likely to react immediately to revisions in ratings. 

 The rupee ended at 47.1225/1300 per dollar, off 47.14 hit in some morning deals and compared with Wednesday's close of 47.11/12. 

 The benchmark Bombay exchange share index ended up 0.52 percent at 3,319.61 points. 

 The 10-year bond was traded at 114.30 rupees in evening trade, compared with 114.14 the previous day. This bond was traded at 113.70 rupees on Tuesday evening before the two downgrades were announced. 

 Late on Wednesday, Moody's said it was lowering the outlook for India's foreign currency rating to stable from positive and that on domestic currency to negative from positive, citing the government's failure to implement macroeconomic reforms. 

 The move came a day after S&P downgraded India's local currency rating and outlook, citing high budget deficits and rising domestic debt. 

 Both agencies have a junk bond rating on India. 

 Traders said the reasons cited by the two agencies were not new and had been discounted by local markets, which have been shaken over the past six months by a series of political and financial sector scandals. 

 RBI MAY HAVE BEEN IN MARKET 

 Some currency and bond traders suspected that central bank intervention had also helped ensure market stability. 

 Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Bimal Jalan told reporters in New Delhi that there was no need for an immediate interest rate cut but added that the central bank would make one if the economy required such a move. 

 Most bond traders took heart from Jalan's comments, interpreting them as an indication that the central bank would continue with an easy money policy. 

 Some saw the comments as an attempt to talk up a market which while stable, appeared to be nervous about future direction. 

 "Bonds are moving up, but Jalan's comments seem to be some attempt to undo negative (sentiment)," said a dealer at a private bank. Jalan made similar comments on Wednesday. 

 Besides the verbal intervention, some currency traders suspect that the central bank also sold dollars through state-run banks on Wednesday to shore up the rupee when it slipped to 47.185 per dollar in thin early deals - within striking distance of its lifetime low of 47.21 on July 3. 

 Share prices were stable as traders saw little impact on foreign fund inflows from the rating revisions. 

 "It will make no difference to equity flows," said the chief investment officer at a domestic mutual fund. 

 "For the foreign investor India is not a macro story. They have always adopted a bottom up investment strategy, the stock picking approach," he said. 

 Foreign funds have poured money into Indian stocks despite a steep fall in share prices this year, with the market rocked by broker payment defaults, liquidity problems on stock exchanges and a crisis at the country's largest mutual fund. 

 The benchmark Bombay exchange index has lost nearly 17 percent since January. Yet net investments by foreign funds in shares total some $2.5 billion so far this year against $1.53 billion in the whole of last year. 

 ANALYSTS WARY 

 But analysts were cautious, saying that while the downgrades would not result in a pullout by foreign funds from India, it would scare off potential investors in the short term and add to the negative sentiment afflicting investors. 

 The economy has slowed for two years in a row, with no signs of an immediate turnaround. 

 The government has spent most of its time fighting off opposition allegations of involvements in scandals - weakening its ability to push through key reforms.

title: Will flows help Indian rupee escape August blues?
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 9 (Reuters) - Strong foreign investment inflows seem to be helping the Indian rupee ride out what has traditionally been the most tumultuous month of the year, but traders are still keeping their fingers crossed. 

 The rupee has fallen an average five to six percent annually in the past six years, with some of the sharpest drops taking place in August. 

 It has not reacted much so far to bad news this month. 

 International rating agencies have downgraded their outlook on the country, foreign portfolio inflows have slowed to a trickle and the federal coalition government is fending off accusations over a crisis at the largest mutual fund manager. 

 Standard & Poor's downgraded India's local currency rating and outlook on Tuesday and was followed by rival rating agency Moody's Investors Services revising its outlook the next day. 

 That's against the backdrop of sharply slower economic growth, a near recession in industry and no signs that India can trim its burgeoning government fiscal deficit. 

 The rupee however seems loath to react. 

 In Thursday afternoon deals, it was quoted at 47.14/15 to a dollar, down less than a percent since the start of 2001. It has stayed in a steady 47.10-47.16 range since early July. 

 Traders said the slowdown in industrial and capital imports coupled with inflows from overseas equity raised by some sectors was supporting the rupee. 

 "There's definitely a recession, demand for dollars has been muted. At the same time, inflows have been positive," said V. Ravikumar, head of private sector Vysya Bank's treasury. 

 Others felt it was central bank intervention, through state-owned banks, and Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Bimal Jalan's assurances on an easier monetary policy that were helping the rupee check losses this week. 

 Some traders said the current stability was only a postponement of an inevitable downmove. 

 "The immediate short-term fortunes of the rupee are driven by actual flows, so it is a very difficult call to take," said S.Varadarajan, dealer at Chase Manhattan. 

 "But foreign flows are turning negative, that's worrying." 

 FICKLE FOREIGN FLOWS 

 So far, foreign direct and equity investment has been robust, and has boosted foreign currency reserves to record highs over $43 billion. 

 Several firms including telecommunications giant Bharti Enterprises and private sector HDFC Bank have raised money from foreign investors. 

 The country has just obtained half a billion dollars worth of preferential trade access with the United States, which could boost flagging exports. 

 But export growth in the April-June quarter was just 1.76 percent compared with the 20 percent jump in 2000/01. 

 Analysts say the downgrades will not affect sector-specific equity investments, yet India's credibility with foreign investors is under a cloud after a bitter dispute between energy giant Enron Corp and local utility Maharashtra State Electricity Board over high tariffs and payment defaults. 

 Enron is keen to exit the $2.9 billion project, the largest single direct investment in the country. 

 Foreign investments in stocks and bonds have been heavy, despite the host of scandals the stock market has suffered since March and the 17 percent drop in the benchmark Bombay index so far in 2001, but have ebbed of late. 

 Foreign portfolio inflows so far in 2001 exceed $2.6 billion compared with $1.56 billion through the whole of 2000, but in July they were just $91 billion 

 THE "AUGUST" FACTOR 

 AUGUST 1995 - Heavy oil imports and media reports that the government will start routing foreign debt repayment through the market pressured the rupee which had been stable in a 31.30-31.40 band for nearly 18 months. It hit 33.90 in September 1995. 

 AUGUST 1997 - The rupee slipped to 36.50 after a year of trading 35.70-35.85. Several factors played a role, including reports that the government was contemplating a five percent trading band and Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Deputy Governor Y.V. Reddy's remarks that the rupee was overvalued in real terms. 

 AUGUST 1998 - It fell from around 42.50 to a low of 46.27, recovered and resumed the decline in later months. The reasons were weak regional currencies and heavy import demand. 

 AUGUST 2000 - Decade-high global oil prices raised concerns about India's trade account. The rupee fluctuated between a high of 45.02 and a low of 46.08 in August 2000.

text:

title: Indian rupee ends firmer, forwards close off highs.
text:

title: India's  forex  reserves rise to record $42.7 bln.
text:
BOMBAY, April 21 (Reuters) - India's forex reserves rose to a record $42.722 billion in the week to April 12, up $33 million over the previous week, data from the central bank showed on Saturday. 

 Dealers said the rise in reserves was despite the central Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) suspected intervention through state-run banks to defend the falling rupee during that week. 

 The rupee began sliding on April 10 after weeks of steady trade, dragged by a plunging stock market and fears foreign investment flows would fall. 

 The rupee's fall was exacerbated by the market view that the rupee was overvalued against its trade-weighted index following recent falls in regional currencies. 

 "The increase in reserves is hardly anything. It could be on account of revaluation of other currencies in the basket, or interest on investments, or the foreign fund inflows that we have seen," M.R. Madhavan, head of research at Bank of America, said. 

 India's foreign currency assets expressed in dollar terms include the effect of appreciation or depreciation of non-U.S. currencies like the euro, sterling and yen, held in reserves. 

 Foreign funds have been net buyers of $318.3 million in Indian markets in April so far. 

 The rupee fell more than one percent to an all-time low of 47.10 on April 17 before recovering on a central bank official's remarks the market might have been overestimating the rupee's overvaluation. 

 It ended Friday at 46.8000/8150 per dollar. 

 There has been an almost continual rise in reserves since the end of 2000, helped by foreign capital inflows. 

 Besides the $5.5 billion raised from expatriate Indians through the Millennium Deposit Scheme last November, portfolio inflows in 2001 have been heavy, totalling a net of over $2 billion so far. 

 Analysts said the rupee still has room to depreciate. 

 "On a trade-weighted basis, the rupee is still overvalued by close to three percent," JP Morgan Securities said in a recent report. 

 "A further one percent correction in the rupee value appears likely in the near term and the RBI would be willing to tolerate this," it said. 

 In its monetary policy for 2001/02 released on Thursday, the RBI estimated GDP growth this financial year at 6.0-6.5 percent despite the uncertain industrial outlook. 

 The central bank left unchanged the bank rate, which it has cut by 100 basis points since February, but indicated a bias for softer rates and assured markets it would provide the needed liquidity. 

 It cut the ceiling on the rates banks can offer on foreign currency expatriate deposits to LIBOR from the earlier cap of LIBOR plus 50 basis points.

title: Indian rupee rallies off new low on cbank jawboning.
text:
BOMBAY, April 17 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee hit a new low against the dollar on Tuesday before rebounding after a central bank official suggested the currency was not as overvalued as estimated by the market. 

 By midday the rupee was quoted at 46.94/97 per dollar after it slid to a record intra-day low of 47.10 in early trade - taking losses to over one percent in the past week. It closed at 47.00/02 on Monday. 

 The dollar was unable to hold ground above 47 rupees as exporters hedged future receipts, state-run banks maintained a steady supply of dollars and banks which are known custodians to offshore funds joined in selling the greenback. 

 A central bank official said current market estimates of the rupee's overvaluation against its trade-weighted index, the real effective exchange rate (REER), may not have factored recent falls in the country's inflation rate. 

 Dealers said the comments helped firm the rupee's direction in a market waiting for a signal from authorities. 

 Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha's commment on Monday that the rupee's fall should be viewed in the context of global dollar strength did little to remove the uncertainty. 

 "I think the 46.90-47.10 range is the right level for the rupee now...it has depreciated one percent in a week," said V. Ravikumar, head of treasury at Vysya Bank. 

 "The market had been waiting for a comment from the central bank...and the price action from state-run banks this morning also indicates the slide will be checked here," he said. 

 State-run banks have often intervened on behalf of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in the past. 

 OVERVALUED 

 The depreciation started when a foreign fund bought dollars last Tuesday, sparking concerns foreign investors may withdraw from the plunging, scandal-ridden stock market. 

 The benchmark Bombay share index has fallen about 27 percent from its high on March 1. 

 Analysts said last week the central bank may not be averse to a fall in its currency since the rupee was nearly three percent overvalued following recent falls in regional currencies. 

 But on Tuesday, the RBI official told Reuters the market may be overestimating the rupee's appreciation against the REER and reiterated the central bank's stance that the trade-weighted index is more a medium-term reference for the rupee. 

 "...the level of REER perceived by the market right now does not seem to be reflecting the fall in India's inflation level by about two percent in the last fortnight of March 2001," the official said. 

 India's year-on-year inflation rate, measured by the wholesale price index, fell to 4.87 percent in the week ended March 31 from 6.5 percent in the week ended March 17. 

 But currency analysts were quick to point out the actual wholesale price index used in computing the REER has remained steady between 158.4 and 159.2 over the past four months, and only the year-on-year growth levels have dropped. 

 M.R. Madhavan, head of research at Bank of America, said the rupee was still one to two percent overvalued. 

 "The reason the extent of overvaluation is now lower is that the rupee has depreciated one percent in the past week and the Japanese yen has recovered a bit," Madhavan said. 

 "But the euro remains weak, and from the inflation point of view there has been little change," he said. 

 MORE WEAKNESS LATER 

 The depreciation may be contained for now, but traders said the rupee may weaken later in the year and risks for the currency could come from rising crude oil prices, lower demand for exports and a possible decline in foreign investment. 

 There is also political risk over an arms bribery scandal that paralysed parliament on Tuesday. Parliament, which reopened on Monday after a three-week recess, was crippled by an opposition uproar over the scandal for eight days last month before the break. 

 Vasan Shridharan, regional economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore, said the central bank's priority will be managing the massive 1.19 trillion rupees government borrowing for 2001/02 (April-March) which has just begun. 

 "The RBI has to ensure the spot rupee weakness does not propagate across the forward curve and push up rates," he said.

title: Indian rupee slightly weaker, seen under pressure.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 28 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee was marginally weaker little changed in early Tuesday deals but the undertone on the currency was weak on steady dollar bids, dealers said. 

 At 9:20 a.m. (0350 GMT), the rupee was quoted at 46.88/89 per dollar, compared to its previous close of 46.875/88. 

 Dealers said early trade was thin, with state-run banks quoting in line with the market. State-run banks are often seen as central bank surrogates and are closely watched for clues to the rupee's direction. 

 Dealers said the longer term outlook for the rupee remained bearish, given the dollar's strength against other major currencies. 

 "The rupee now appears to be be over-valued on its real effective exchange rate by around two percent," said a dealer at a foreign bank. 

 "So we should see some more weakness in the rupee," he said. 

 Dealers said other factors exerting pressure on the rupee were firm global oil prices and sluggish foreign fund inflows. 

 "Overall, there are no positives for the rupee at the moment," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "There should be a gradual slide in the coming days." 

 Dealers said they expected the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to intervene, mainly through state-run banks, only if there was sharp volatility in the market. 

 They said the RBI was in a position to tackle any unexpected pressure on the rupee, thanks to a recent sharp jump in foreign exchange reserves. 

 In the two weeks to November 17, foreign exchange reserves rose by $2.34 billion to $37.077 billion, crossing $37 billion for the first time since June. 

 Dealers attributed the rises to inflows from an overseas deposit offering by the State Bank of India, which closed on November 6 after raising $5.5 billion.

title: Indian rupee hits new low as dollar supplies dry up.
text:
BOMBAY, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee hit new lows against the dollar on Friday as corporates stepped up dollar purchases amid concerns over firm world oil prices and weak regional currencies, dealers said. 

 They said demand was sparked by the absence of central bank intervention despite the rupee breaching psychological barriers but stressed that volumes were low. 

 In afternoon deals, the rupee was quoted at 46.74/75 per dollar, slightly off its lifetime intra-day low of 46.765. 

 At its new low the rupee, convertible only on the current account, was nearly seven percent weaker than at the start of the calendar year. 

 Traders, however, expect some respite for the rupee next week. 

 "Corporates are covering their requirements in a thin market, but I think the rupee should stabilise in a broad 46.75/90 level," Surendra Rosha, head of treasury sales at HSBC, said. 

 "I expect better dollar supplies next week as these are extremely attractive rates for exporters to sell," he said. 

 However longer term concerns have not yet been cleared and the undertone on the currency would remain bearish, dealers said. 

 The rupee has been under pressure since May this year as foreign capital inflows slowed while global crude oil prices remained firm. 

 Foreign funds has so far invested a net of $282.5 million in the current financial year, compared with $2.34 billion in 1999/00 (April-March). 

 While inflows from foreign funds have slowed to a trickle, outflows on account of oil have risen. 

 India imports a large part of its crude oil requirements and its import bill for 2000/01 (April-March) is expected to jump to $17.5 billion from $12.3 billion a year earlier if global prices remain at current levels. 

 Analysts expect India's balance of payments position to be square in 2000/01 after four years of surpluses. India had a $1.021 billion deficit in its balance of payments in the first quarter of 2000/01. 

 "Periodical upheavals in the capital market might drive the rupee lower in the near term and I do not expect it to recoup any of its earlier losses as longer term concerns are still there," K.S Harshan, head of international banking at ICICI Bank said. 

 EURO, STERLING FALLS NOT HELPING THE RUPEE 

 A weak euro and sterling were also adding to pressure on the rupee, traders said. 

 The rupee has fallen nearly one percent this week, with no signs of intervention from the central Reserve Bank of India (RBI). 

 The RBI has said that the rupee's value is market-determined and that the central bank has no target for its value. 

 Traders said the central bank's past actions indicated that it would intervene only if there was excessive volatility or indications that trade was speculative. 

 "With the central bank allowing the rupee to find its own levels, my guess is the rupee should weaken further gradually," a dealer in a foreign bank said. 

 He said the rupee was still overvalued by nearly two percentage points on trade-weighted terms due to a recent jump in the domestic inflation rate and the weakness of the euro and sterling. 

 MILD BOOST SEEN FROM OVERSEAS DEPOSIT SCHEME 

 Sentiment for the rupee might get a mild boost in the short term on inflows from an ongoing overseas deposit scheme launched by the State Bank of India (SBI), dealers said. 

 The SBI's India Millennium Deposit scheme, which was launched on Saturday, has so far collected $1 billion, a senior SBI official said. 

 Inflows through the scheme will boost India's foreign exchange reserves which are down nearly eight percent from their mid-April peak of $38.34 billion.

title: Indian rupee hits fresh low of 46.27 vs dlr.
text:
BOMBAY, Sept 19 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee eased to a new record low against the dollar in volatile trade on Tuesday as the the initial demand for dollars continued from corporates and banks, dealers said. 

 They said the impact of high global prices on India's financial resources remained a chief source of worry for corporates looking to hedge their future requirements. 

 The rupee was quoted at 46.18/23 at 9:40 a.m (0410 GMT) off fresh intra-day lows of 46.27 and after it opened wide at a 46.05/15 per dollar. 

 The earlier intra-day low of 46.08 was hit on August 11. 

 On Monday the Indian currency closed at a record low of 45.99/46.01. 

 Oil scaled new ten-year peaks on Monday as tension in the Middle East and low Western stocks continued to buoy prices. 

 Dealers said the intial burst of demand for dollars from corporates and banks was likely to taper off later in the day. 

 Indian officials were preparing the ground for an overseas bond issue to augument falling reserves and meet the spiralling oil import bill estimated at $22 billion for 2000/01. 

 The issue would be targeted at non-resident Indians and would be similar to the Resurgent India Bond (RIB) issued by State Bank of India in 1998. 

 That issue raised over $4 billion and helped India weather U.S. economic sanctions following India's nuclear tests that year. 

 A senior monetary official told Reuters on Monday that the central bank was working on a three-month schedule to ease the debt burden of oil companies and build the country's forex reserves - which are nearly $3 billion down from their mid-April peak of $38.341 billion. 

 Reserves fell sharply in the week to September 8 dragged down by a weak euro, which has fallen nearly 27 percent since its birth in January 1999 and by the weakness of other european currencies against the dollar. 

 The official said the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was unlikely to intervene by selling dollars or tighten monetary policy at this stage to ward off pressure on the rupee, which is now around six percent below early January levels. 

 The RBI was also not in favour of scrapping the Exchange Earners Foreign Currency (EEFC), a special foreign currency account for exporters, which was halved last month to increase dollar supplies, he said.

title: UPDATE 1-Pakistan defends rupee, watching  India .
text:
KARACHI, Aug 22 (Reuters) - Pakistan's central bank intervened twice in the market on Tuesday, selling dollars to prop up the local rupee against the dollar in what analysts saw as an effort to match moves by India's currency. 

 Bankers said the State (central) Bank of Pakistan sought to keep the currency from breaching the 55 mark against the dollar in the interbank market for the second consecutive day. 

 The Pakistani rupee , convertible on the current account, clawed back to 54.57/54.67 in afternoon trade from 55 earlier in the day. The latest level was a 5.3 percent depreciation against the dollar since January. 

 "Basically they are following the Indian rupee. After today's intervention you've almost matched the Indian currency," said Mansoor Ali, research head at brokerage firm Jahangir Siddiqui & Co Ltd. 

 The Indian rupee was at 45.68/45.69 in afternoon trade, down almost five percent against the dollar since January, but off early August lows that saw it 5.6 percent below the January levels. 

 In the kerb market, the Pakistan rupee was 57.05/57.20 to the dollar in afternoon trade against Monday's close of 57.15/57.25. 

 FIRST TIME 

 Bankers said the central bank for the first time ever also sold some dollars for forward transactions in the three-month period to speed up repatriation of delayed export proceeds. 

 "The three-month rate has come down from a high of 56.10 rupees (to a dollar) to 55.35. This will hit exporters hard," said a treasury dealer at a foreign bank. 

 He said the central bank injected dollars in a much larger quantity than on Monday, although no exact figures were available. 

 Exporters have withheld around $300 million in the hope of cashing in on a weaker local currency. 

 Analysts said the central bank was trying to match Pakistan's currency moves with India's because the two countries were competing in exports of mainly cotton-based textile products. 

 The central bank first intervened in the interbank market this year on July 27, 10 days after lifting an unofficial trading band for more than a year that had kept the rupee stable against the dollar. 

 The band was eased in May and finally lifted in July. 

 Bankers said Pakistan's foreign exchange woes, compounded by the absence of multilateral funding due to the suspension of an International Monetary Fund (IMF) programme in mid-1999, were also playing a key role in the currency weakening. 

 Pakistan recorded a trade deficit of $1.77 billion in the fiscal year that ended in June and has annual debt payments of $2.6 billion, which is 40 percent lower than before 1998 when the country rescheduled payments on its bilateral debt. But that rescheduling period ends in December.

 There was no sign of central bank intervention and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is depending on a progressive tightening of money market liquidity to drive short-term interest rates higher to curb any excessive rupee selling. 

 The yield on the one-day government securities repurchase agreements (repos) was set at 14.0 percent on Tuesday from 8.25 percent last Thursday. 

 The rupee ended at a new low of 45.73/74 per dollar after being dealt at an intra-day low of 45.745. It closed at 45.55/56 on Monday. 

 The rupee has now lost 0.7 percent in the last two trading sessions and is 4.9 percent lower against the dollar than at the start of the year, although it has held its ground or appreciated against most other major currencies. 

 Analysts said there had been little reaction to Monday's announcement by Singapore Telecommunications that it planned to invest $400 million in two Indian telecoms firms, but news of more foreign direct investment could bolster the rupee. 

 Technical analysts said, however, that the charts pointed to further weakness for the rupee. 

 Tom Schroeder, head of global technical analysis at SG Securities said he saw the rupee dropping to 46 per dollar in the next two or three trading sessions. 

 Analysts said the weaker rupee reflected India's widening trade deficit, a slowdown in foreign capital inflows and the dollar's recent strength against other currencies. 

 Dealers and analysts did not expect any fast turnaround in those fundamentals and expected the rupee to ease further. 

 "If the current trend against the rupee has to reverse, it could only be with aggressive central bank intervention," said a dealer at an European bank. 

 But that seems a limited option. The RBI has run down its foreign exchange reserves by more than $2.0 billion from their mid-April peak of $38.341 billion. 

 Analysts are doubtful about the effectiveness of the RBI's liquidity tightening measures as demand for dollars appears to be genuine importer demand, which is outweighing dollar receipts from exporters and foreign investors. 

 The next phase of the RBI's rupee support package, announced on July 21, kicks in on Saturday when banks' cash reserve ratios (CRR) will be raised from 8.25 percent to 8.5 percent and their refinancing limits will be cut further. 

 FOREIGN FUND SELLING ABATES 

 India's trade deficit - most of India's trade is denominated in dollars - rose around 26 percent in the April-June quarter compared to last year, driven up principally by a 94 percent increase in the oil bill. 

 While there are hopes the rate of increase in the oil bill will taper off in coming months due to lower global crude prices, analysts still expect the current account deficit to rise to around 2.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2000/01 (April-March) from around 1.5 percent a year earlier. 

 And foreign funds have been heavy sellers recently, dumping equity worth nearly $550 million in June and July. 

 While funds have bought a net $51.6 million so far in August, analysts say it is too early to report whether the selling trend has been reversed. 

 The benchmark top-30 share index of the Bombay exchange is some 30 percent off its record high of 6,150.69 hit on February 14 although it is up some 13 percent from the year's low hit in May. ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

text:

 BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee fell for the seventh consecutive session and ended at its lowest ever close against the dollar Tuesday, dealers said. 

 The dollar ended at INR45.74, up from INR45.55 Monday. 

 The rupee hit a new traded low of INR45.7450 to the dollar on sustained dollar-buying by companies in thin trade. 

 The Indian rupee has lost 5.2% of its value against the dollar in the past year. 

 Adding to the bearish sentiment was the absence of central bankintervention. Despite Reserve Bank of India Governor Bimal Jalan's reassurance Thursday, the rupee has continued to fall as demand for dollars continues to outstrip supply. 

 The Reserve Bank of India Thursday issued a statement urging the markets to view the rupee's fall in the perspective of the dollar's rise vis-a-vis other currencies. 

 The Indian rupee opened on a bearish note Tuesday and weakened in early trade on sustained dollar-buying in an illiquid market. 

 The central bank has been conducting repurchase auctions daily to mop up liquidity and deter banks from holding long-dollar positions. 

 Tuesday the Reserve Bank accepted INR36.45 billion of overnight funds at 14% and INR23.25 billion of three-day money at 15%. 

 However the tighter liquidity hasn't arrested the rupee's fall as most of the demand for the dollar is genuine demand from companies and not speculative. 

 Two years ago, the central bank imposed restrictions on corporate foreign exchange transactions making it difficult for them to take speculative positions. 

 However dealers said importer dollar demand is waning and exporters are beginning to show an interest in selling dollars. 

 In the forward market, rupee premiums on the forward dollar ended lower as most banks reversed their positions and few large banks sold forward dollars in the market. 

 January premiums ended at INR1.09, down from INR1.11 Monday, while July premiums ended at INR2.09, unchanged from Monday. 

 Looking ahead, dealers said demand for the dollar has begun to wane, adding that the rupee's current fall appears to be at an end. 

 "I think we are almost at the end of the fall," a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 Rupee premiums are expected to move up if the Reserve Bank tightens liquidity further.

title: WRAP:India RBI Comment Cheers Mkt,But Rupee To Fall More
text:
BOMBAY -(Dow Jones)- The market greeted with a mixture of relief and unease the Reserve Bank of India's verbal intervention in the foreign-exchange market Thursday to boost the flagging rupee, bankers said. 

 While market participants expressed relief that the Reserve Bank didn't raise interest rates or impose restrictions on trading to stem the rupee's decline, it also means that the currency is left to its own devices and is therefore susceptible to further weakening, bankers said. 

 The Reserve Bank of India Thursday issued a statement urging the market to view the rupee's fall in the perspective of the dollar's rise against other major currencies, adding that the rupee strengthened against the euro and yen and was stable against sterling. 

 The Indian currency has hit record lows for three consecutive sessions this week on sustained dollar-buying by state-owned companies, importers and foreign funds. The rupee fell to a new low of 45.44 Thursday, but recovered to end at 45.34, it lowest close. The Indian rupee has lost 1% of its value against the dollar this week. 

 In the past, the central bank has raised short-term interest rates and imposed restrictions on bank trading to stem the rupee's fall. 

 "The statement (Thursday) reflects a paradigm shift in the central bank's approach," said V. Ravi Kumar, chief foreign-exchange dealer at ABN-Amro Bank in India. "It is an effort to calm the market and give a rationale to the developments." 

 Dealers believe the central bank is comfortable with the falling rupee and is only attempting to ease the panic-buying of dollars. 

 But the sustained dollar demand will continue to exert pressure on the Indian currency and the rupee is expected to test INR45.50 against the dollar. 

 "We expect the rupee to settle between INR45.30-INR45.50 for the time being," a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 "But our recommendation to our clients will continue to be buy on dips and cover a part of your exposures," said a treasurer at a private sector bank.

 The dollar opened higher, but was expected to cap at INR44.90, when State Bank of India bought dollars at INR44.9050, sending jitters through the market. 

 State Bank of India is the country's largest commercial bank and buys dollars on behalf of state-owned companies, including the oil majors. It is also seen as the central bank's proxy in India's currency market. 

 Dealers said some banks had gone short on the dollar at INR44.90 Friday and buying by State Bank of India Monday led them to cover their positions. A few importers had been buying since early trade and this added to the pressure on the Indian unit. 

 The Indian unit breached INR45.00 and slipped to the day's low of INR45.03, before a state-owned bank sold dollars, leading other banks to book profits. 

 Dealers said these banks were selling at the behest of the Reserve Bank of India. 

 The Indian unit hovered between INR44.97 and INR45.03 for the rest of the session. 

 In the forward market, rupee premiums on the forward dollar moved up sharply in tandem with the spot dollar.

title: UPDATE 1-Indian  central bank  hikes rates to prop up rupee.
text:
BOMBAY, July 21 (Reuters) - The Indian central bank raised its key interest rate by one percentage point to eight percent and tightened liquidity on Friday to support the rupee after it hit record lows. 

 The rupee hit a new low on Friday, extending a two-week downtrend as foreign investors exiting the stock market converted their rupees into dollars. 

 It hit its weakest intra-day level of 45.075 per dollar before recovering on suspicion of covert intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) through state-run banks. 

 The rupee, convertible only on the current account, has slipped just under one percent in the past two weeks. 

 But it has depreciated by 3.5 percent since the start of the year against a U.S. dollar which has been flying high against other major international currencies. 

 The RBI said it was hiking interest rates after reviewing recent developments in the international and domestic financial markets, including the foreign exchange market. 

 It raised the key bank rate, at which it refinances banks, by one percentage point to eight percent, but simultaneously halved banks' refinance limits. 

 It also raised banks' cash reserve ratio (CRR) by 50 basis points to 8.5 percent - to be carried out in two stages, on July 29 and August 12. The measure will mop up 38 billion rupees from the banking system. 

 Bankers, industrialists and analysts were surprised by the sudden monetary tightening and hoped they were temporary. 

 "This is an unexpected move. It is a cause for concern since the RBI had reduced interest rates a few months ago. This does not spell good news for the stock market," said Sangeeta Purushottam, head of research at SG Asia Securities (India). 

Currency traders said the rupee will recover sharply to 44.50 levels when the market opens on Monday. 

 R. Govindan, assistant general manager, treasury, Larsen & Toubro, said the rupee's weakness was more due to genuine dollar demand and the RBI could have responded by selling dollars. 

 "These money market measures may end up affecting the economy and industry. Of course, if they are short term it is okay," he said. 

 TAKES THE PRESSURE OFF FOREIGN EXCHANGE RESERVES 

 When the RBI lowered key interest rates at the start of the year, analysts said it would help push through an aggressive 1.17 trillion rupees government borrowing programme and encourage faster economic growth. 

 The first quarter saw a strong growth in bank credit, and a near 100 basis points rise in long-term government bond yields. 

 The RBI said it would not tighten liquidity to curb rising inflation and even during volatile swings in the rupee in May and June, it intervened through warnings against speculation and by selling dollars. 

Foreign exchange reserves are down $1.67 billion from all time highs of $38.34 in mid-April. 

 Analysts feel it is the concern over dwindling capital inflows and a likely drop in the balance of payments surplus that has prompted the RBI to tighten. 

 "The bank rate hike was expected. The economy is moving at a fast clip and the balance of payments pressure has resulted in a weaker currency...after spending around $2 billion of reserve money this was the only resort left to the central bank," said Aashish Pitale, head of research at J P Morgan. 

 Foreign investors have so far sold $448 million worth of Indian stocks in June and July, and are believed to be the main drivers of the 10 percent fall in the benchmark Bombay stock index in the past two weeks. 

 The BSE index .BSESN) closed down 2.45 percent at 4,463.66 points on Friday. 

 Political concerns also weighed on the stock market. There were fears the possible arrest of Bal Thackeray, leader of the Hindu Shiv Sena party, would spark unrest in Bombay and unsettle the ruling coalition in which the party has three cabinet ministers.

title: India says balance of payments level comfortable.
text:
NEW DELHI, July 13 (Reuters) - India's balance of payments position is comfortable despite a recent fall in its foreign exchange reserves, a finance ministry official said on Thursday. 

 "The outlook on the balance of payments remains reasonably good, exports are doing well," Shankar Acharya, the ministry's chief economic adviser told reporters. 

 He was responding to a question on whether recent depletions in the foreign exchange reserves were a cause for concern. 

 India's foreign exchange reserves were $36.73 billion on June 30, some $1.6 billion down from a peak of $38.34 billion in mid-April. Reserves fell for 10 weeks in a row until June 23 before gaining again the following week. 

Currency traders attributed the fall to a surge in India's oil import bill and to central bank intervention to defend the rupee when it was under pressure earlier this year. 

 The rupee fell to a record low of 44.95 per dollar on June 8 before recovering on central bank intervention. Since then it has been trading in a 44.64-44.70 per dollar range. 

 "There is no concern that the forex reserves will be hit by rising oil prices. Reserves are meant to be used," Acharya said. 

 India's oil import bill more than doubled to $2.63 billion in April-May from the same period a year earlier due to spiralling global oil prices. 

 "Probably by the end of the year, we won't see any significant change in reserves. A drop of $1-2 billion in my opinion is not something to worry about," he said.

title: Indian rupee unlikely to weaken further - CRISIL.
text:
BOMBAY, July 5 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee which has lost over 2.5 percent against the dollar since the beginning of May is unlikely to weaken further, rating agency Credit Rating Information Services of India Ltd (CRISIL) said on Wednesday. 

 "With the dollar's appreciating trend against major currencies showing signs of receding, and with domestic inflation stabilising, CRISIL believes that there do not appear to be any immediate reasons for the rupee to depreciate sharply from the current levels," the rating agency said. 

 It said the depreciation may only be gradual. 

 The Indian currency which is convertible on the current account touched an all time low of 44.95 per dollar on June 8 before verbal intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and persistent dollar sales by state-run banks helped the rupee to stabilise around the current levels of 44.63/69 per dollar. 

 The central bank also restricted rupee supplies in the domestic money market to curb banks from going long on dollars. 

 The agency said the sharp depreciation in the rupee vis-a-vis the dollar was partly due to higher domestic inflation and the hardening of the U.S. dollar against other major currencies. 

 Inflation, based on the wholesale price index, in the current financial year (April-March) 2000/01 rose from 2.74 percent in the week ended March 4, 2000 to a high of 6.59 percent in the week ended May 27. 

 It has since stabilised around six percent and was at 6.28 percent for the week ended June 17, 2000. 

 Crisil said the Indian currency had to depreciate in a bid to maintain the country's export competitiveness. 

 "With rising domestic prices, measured by wholesale price index (WPI) inflation and foreign price levels remaining constant, this led to a relative price movement against India or a worsening trend in India's export competitiveness," CRISIL said. 

 The rating agency said while the rupee has been stable since October 1999, depreciating by only 0.5 percent between October 1999 to April 2000 it appreciated by 11.3 percent against the euro and the Deutche mark and by 4.1 percent against the pound during the same period. 

 India's major trading partners, apart from the U.S, are the European Union, United Kingdom and Japan.

title: Indian rupee seen at $46.50-47.0 to dollar - study.
text:
NEW DELHI, June 10 (Reuters) - A leading Indian industry body on Saturday said that the rupee would fall further and stabilise between 46.50 rupees and 47 rupees to a U.S. dollar towards the end of 2000/2001 (April-March). 

 An Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India (ASSOCHAM) study said the widening trade deficit and shrinking foreign direct investment inflows would put pressue on the domestic currency. 

 "....the sudden depreciation of the rupee in the recent weeks indicates that the bright spots built up in the external sector are suddenly losing lustre," the association said in a statement. 

 On Friday, the rupee closed at a record low of 44.76/78 to the dollar against 44.72/735 on Thursday, having lost 2.5 percent since early May. During May the Reserve Bank of India twice intervened with strong verbal warnings when the markets turned volatile. 

 Government data released earlier this month showed India's trade deficit leapt to $1.11 billion in April 2000, some 112 percent above the defifit in the same month a year ago. 

 The ASSOCHAM said that with enough foreign exchange reserves at the central banks disposal, the "RBI will certainly be able to reduce the volatility in the exchange rates and ward off speculators. But it is unlikely that the central bank would be able to stand on the way of the broad market trends." 

 India's foreign exchange reserves stood at $37.069 billion on June 2, according to latest RBI data. Reserves stood at $33.433 billion on June 4, 1999.

title: Indian rupee ends steady,RBI statement clips trade.
text:
BOMBAY, June 8 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee ended little changed from its previous close after the central bank verbally intervened to check the currency's slide to a record low, dealers said. 

 Volumes dropped after the central bank's action and the rupee ended at 44.72/735 per dollar, almost unchanged from Wednesday's close at 44.725/735. 

 The currency had swung sharply during the day from initial record intra-day lows of 44.95 to firmer levels around 44.58. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened when the rupee fell sharply in morning trade, warning against speculative positions and asking banks to unwind long positions. 

 Dealers said trade came to a near standstill after the RBI statement, with most banks opting to just cover corporate transactions. 

 State-run banks were active in the market, absorbing dollars offloaded by other players and buying dollars at times, they said. 

 Most were also confused about the direction for the rupee. 

 "If they indicate comfort levels, then that will bring in exporters and importers and automatically reinforce a range for the rupee. This way, one cannot even form a view," the chief dealer of a foreign bank said. 

 There was a lot of wariness about buying dollars above 44.75, the level at which the RBI has intervened twice. The earlier occasion was on May 25. 

 But dealers said a range of 44.72-44.77 was likely on Friday. 

 Most were also uncertain about whether the central bank will extend its restrictions on banks' dollar positions to the next few days. 

 "Traders are going home with square positions today, so tomorrow morning will be steady," a dealer with a state-run bank said. 

 Forward dollar premia ended higher, amid light paying towards close after being steady through the day. 

 The six-month premium ended at an annualised 3.06 percent compared with Wednesday's 2.90.

title: UPDATE 2-Indian rupee rebounds, c.bank talks tough.
text:
BOMBAY, June 8 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee rebounded sharply from a record intra-day low on Thursday after the central bank issued a strong warning to banks against speculation and asked them to unwind long dollar positions. 

 The market, which had been expecting some form of action by the central bank, reacted by yanking the rupee from its record low of 44.95 to the dollar to 44.54/61. It closed at 44.72/735. 

 The volatility subsided, but the comments left markets wondering about the central bank's comfort with the rupee. 

 "If they (the central bank) indicate comfort levels, then that will bring in exporters and importers and automatically reinforce a range for the rupee. This way, one cannot even form a view," the chief dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has always maintained it is not against orderly depreciation but will curb volatility. It normally intervenes through select state-run banks. 

 "The Reserve Bank of India wants a gradual slide in the rupee, so it is not surprising they intervened. I still expect the rupee will weaken to 45 over the next three days," a chief dealer at a European bank said. 

 The central bank's warning was terse: 

 "The inter-bank activity this morning, despite RBI's repeated reminders, seem to be speculative in nature. RBI has instructed banks to maintain square position for the day," the statement read. 

 It is the second time in two weeks the RBI has moved to support the rupee. The bank last stepped in on May 25 when the rupee fell to a low of 44.75. Bbut it has maintained silence over the past two weeks as the currency gradually lost ground. 

 On Wednesday, Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha said he saw the pressure on the rupee as a temporary phenomenon. 

 India has enough foreign exchange reserves to weather the pressure on the currency, he said. 

 CORRECTION OVER, BUT SOME BEARS REMAIN 

 Analysts said the rupee's correction, engineered by the central bank, was over and the currency was no longer overvalued against its inflation-adjusted trade-weighted rate. 

 "What we are seeing right now is a healthy correction which will check out some of the short, volatile and speculative positions remaining in the dollar market," N. Balasubramanian, head of trading at ICICI Ltd told Reuters Television. 

 The rupee's sudden sharp fall on Thursday notwithstanding, the market predicted a gradual and marginal slide during the rest of the year. 

 A Reuters poll of 14 corporate treasurers and economists released on Thursday predicted the currency would fall only 1.8 percent to 45.30 by December and to 45.57 by March 2001. 

 These levels are a big change from expectations at the start of the year when a Reuters poll had predicted the rupee at 44.02 by September 2000 and 44.54 by March 2001.

title: Indian short tenor bonds dip, weak rupee weighs.
text:

 Short and medium tenor bonds fell 5-7 paise (0.05-0.07 rupees), while long dated bonds were flat in a dull trade.

title: Indian rupee seen weakening gradually vs dollar.
text:
BOMBAY, April 16 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is expected to weaken gradually to around 40.25 per dollar by the end of June and further to 41.50-42.0 by March 1999, dealers said on Thursday. 

 "We are beginning to see a bit of corporate (dollar) demand hit the market," said the chief foreign exchange dealer at a state-run bank. "Earlier, corporates were under the impression the new government would be in favour of a strong rupee." 

 The coalition led by the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) took power last month amid widespread expectations it would usher in policies leading to a strong rupee to boost exports and protect Indian industry. 

 But on Monday, Commerce Minister Ramakrishna Hedge said he did not think a fall in the value of the rupee affected exports. 

 "Exchange rate management will have to balance the needs of the exporters as well as the other macroeconomic requirements for maintaining price stability," Hedge said. 

 "I think the message is quite clear," the state-run bank dealer said. "The government does not mind a slow depreciation in the rupee." 

 Five bankers polled by Reuters said they saw the rupee touching 40.25 per dollar by the end of June. The currency could weaken further to 41.50-42.0 by March 1999, they said. 

 A former central bank official - who also headed a committee to guide the country towards capital account convertibility - on Wednesday said the rupee was overvalued by around 6-7 percent in real effective exchange rate terms. 

 Dealers said the immediate trigger behind a near 25 paise (0.25 rupee) fall in the rupee's value this week could have been technical - triggered by pent-up dollar demand after banks were shut for holidays last week. 

 "The holidays did lead to a bunching of corporate demand," said a dealer at an American bank. "But the point is that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is not intervening actively in the market and it appears they are happy with a slow slide." 

 Dealers said the central bank mopped up dollars from banks. 

 "When these banks bought in the market to cover their positions after selling to the RBI, it started the rupee's fall on Monday," the American bank dealer said. "But then corporate demand started to trickle in, weakening the rupee further." 

 The rupee was quoted around 39.71/72 per dollar in afternoon trade on Thursday. It opened on Monday at 39.51/54. 

 The dealer said there had not yet been a rush of corporate demand that could push the rupee into a free fall. 

 "At the moment much of the demand is from banks or corporates who have taken loans against foreign currency deposits," he said. 

 "Exporters are holding back a bit, waiting to see if the rupee will dip further and give them better realisations. Further premiums are low and exporters do not see much profit in selling at these levels," he added. ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: India Rupee Open -2: No Big Dollar Demand Seen - Dealers

BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee (INR) opened little changed against the dollar Wednesday in a quiet interbank market because dealers said that there isn't expected to be any major merchant demand for dollars 'unusually' at the end of the financial year, March 31, 1998, dealers said. 

 The dollar opened little changed Tuesday at INR39.52-.53, from its Tuesday's close of INR39.520-.525. 

 At 0420 GMT (11:20 p.m. EST), the dollar is trading slightly higher at 39.530-.535 on some small interbank buying. 

 'It is a small movement and no reason can be given to it,' said a dealer at a U.S. bank. 

 They also said that the dollar will be in a tight range because of dealers positive sentiment on the coalition government led by Bharatiya Janata Party. 

 'It is very unusual that there isn't much of a merchant demand for dollars at the end of the financial year,' said a senior dealer at a European bank. 

 He explained that usually at the end of the year there is dollar buying for payment of their imports. 

 Dealers said that in the last couple of months when the rupee was sliding against the dollar importers had panicked and bought a lot of forward dollars. 

 'Probably most of these importers had bought excess dollars and would be selling it back' keeping the market with more than enough dollar supplies, said the dealer at a European bank. 

 A dealer at a foreign bank said that the dollar is expected to be in a tight range of INR39.50-.55 because of State Bank of India, the country's largest commercial bank, and the Reserve Bank of Indiaintervening in the foreign exchange market. 

 He said if banks go and offer dollars to the RBI both in the spot and the forward market 'than the central bank accepts these trades and buys dollars.' 

 He said that the RBI is also swapping its March-end forward contracts for April-end delivery. 

 Dealers said that the rupee premiums for the six-month forward dollar will range between 7.00% and 7.50%, below the 8.00% rate fixed by the RBI on its daily repurchase agreements of government securities.
