 The rupee ended at 39.515/525 per dollar against its Monday close of 39.535/545. 

 "Corporates are expecting the currency to be stable for some time and there is little demand," a private bank dealer said. 

 "Even the State Bank of India (SBI), India's largest commercial bank, was not very active today," he said. 

 The rupee ended stronger against the forward dollar as sentiment on the Indian currency was strong after the RBI moved to improve liquidity and signal lower interest rates, dealers said. 

 The RBI on Monday said it will cut banks' CRR to 10 percent from 10.5 in two slabs of 25 basis points each, effective March 28 and April 11. Last week it cut its repo rate to eight percent from nine and the key bank rate to 10.5 percent from 11. 

 "Corporate volumes were very poor, since they are waiting for lower rates," a foreign bank dealer said. 

 "The RBI has been signalling an easy money policy which is causing expectations of softer forward dollar premiums also," he said. 

 Forward dollar premiums fell by around 20 paise (0.2 rupee) on Monday in trade after the official close after the RBI's announcement of cuts in banks' CRR. 

 Premiums opened down on Tuesday and were weak through the day, dealers said. 

 The RBI did sell-buy swaps for April-dollars in what dealers described as "passive" intervention. 

 Some dealers said the central bank's intervention was through outright forward dollar purchases. 

 "RBI was not very active, they did deals with banks who went to them," a dealer said. "Their actions were aimed more at checking volatility in the market than setting levels." 

 Some dealers said the RBI also intervened in March-dollars. 

 "The RBI intervention, along with some profit-taking by banks, caused premiums to firm up slightly from opening levels," a dealer said. 

 The annualised premium on six-month dollars ended at 7.27 percent against the previous close of 7.69, after hitting an inntra-day low of 6.95 percent.

title: Indian rupee slides, market awaits RBI support.
text:
BOMBAY, Feb 23 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee hit a month-low on Monday as lack of central bank intervention coupled with an uncertain political situation and a regional downtrend in foreign exchange markets triggered a rush for dollars. 

 Shortly after 1300 local time (0730 GMT), the rupee was quoted at around 39.16/20, down from Friday's 38.92/95. 

 Traders said the slide in regional currencies added to the pressure, but the main factor driving trade on Monday was the central bank's absence from the market since Friday when the rupee was at the psychological barrier of 38.90 per dollar. 

 "Once the rupee went past 38.90 on Friday and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) did not intervene, I think corporates got jittery," the chief dealer at an American bank said. 

 Traders said the market perceived the rupee overvalued at its present level but said it had been held there by the central bank's tough defence. 

 Last month, when the rupee touched a historic low of 40.45 to the dollar, the central bank reacted by raising its bank rate by 200 basis points to 11 percent. 

 It also tightened liquidity by raising reserve requirements. 

 The firm defence had propped up the rupee but the RBI's absence from the market on Friday and market talk that the bank was under pressure from industry to lower interest rates had sent the market scurrying for dollars again, traders said. 

 "The RBI's measures only bottled up demand. It was lying there waiting to be triggered off," said J Moses Harding, head of foreign exchange trade at Indusind Bank. 

 One dealer said uncertainty over the electoral verdict in ongoing polls had also contributed to the rupee's weakness. 

 "I think it is becoming clear that we will have a hung parliament," he said. "And this is worrying some corporates." 

 Monday was the third day of voting in India's second election in as many years in a staggered schedule which runs until March 7. Two snowbound constituencies vote in June. 

 Opinion polls have said no single party will get a majority, forcing another coalition government. 

 "This throws up a whole host of problems for India," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "We have to look at a slowdown in policy-making which in turn will affect the economy." 

 Traders said if the rupee breached the 39.20 level, it could slide to 40. But they hoped the RBI would intervene before that. 

 Another factor putting pressure on the rupee was the fall of regional currencies, dealers said. 

 Asian currencies weakened on Monday after a meeting of G7 finance ministers failed to announce new moves to bolster the currencies. 

 "At the moment it is not very clear whether the south and east Asian economies are out of the woods," one dealer said. 

 "The rupee will have to weaken to maintain our export competitiveness if other regional currencies drop," he said. 

 The Indian rupee has weakened around nine percent since the Asian turmoil began while some regional currencies such as the Indonesian rupiah have dropped by more than 70 percent. 

 Even regional heavyweight Singapore has seen its currency shed more than 12 percent of its value in the same period.

title: Indian rupee ends weaker on strong dlr demand.
text:
BOMBAY, Feb 23 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee hit a month low against the dollar on strong demand for the U.S. currency from banks and corporates, dealers said. 

 The rupee closed at 39.25/28 per dollar against its previous close of 38.92/95, they said. 

 Dealers said a sudden surge in dollar demand weakened the rupee past the 39 per dollar level. 

 Sustained buying interest during the day and a lack of intervention from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) pushed the rupee down to 39.20/23 by 4:00 p.m. (1030 GMT), they said. 

 "The rupee fell through 39 within about 45 minutes of start of trade," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "It was under pressure right through the day." 

 Late evening covering of short positions by a few foreign banks weakened it further to a close of 39.25/28. 

 "There is strong underlying demand and we expect the market to open around this level tomorrow," said a dealer at a private bank. 

 Dealers said there was dollar demand on Monday from both banks and corporates. 

 "Initially there was demand only from a few foreign banks who were probably covering shorts after they were hit on Friday," said a dealer. 

 "But later in the morning other banks joined in the dollar-buying spree," he said. "And as the rupee kept weakening with no sign of central bank intervention, corporates also came in." 

 Dealers were mixed on the factors driving the surge in demand on Monday. 

 "It could have been banks' covering of short positions or their buying in anticipation of corporate month-end demand," said a private bank dealer. 

 "Further, the year end is also not very far off and there is bound to be increased demand on this account as well," he added. 

 The Indian fiscal year ends in March. 

 Other dealers said uncertainty over the results of ongoing elections could also have induced some corporates to buy dollars. 

 Monday was the third day of voting in elections to elect India's parliament -- the second election in as many years. 

 Opinion polls point to a hung parliament. 

 Dealers said the rupee rebounded from morning lows against the forward dollar to end Monday slightly firmer than the weekend close. 

 Premiums on six month dollars closed at 15.79 percent after hitting 16.52 percent in afternoon trade. They closed the weekend at 15.99 percent. 

 "Premiums were up initially on demand as importers came to the market, reacting to the rupee's fall in spot," said a dealer. title: FOCUS-India rupee stability hinges on majority govt.
text:
BOMBAY, Feb 22 (Reuters) - A majority government would offer a stable plank for India's economic policy-making and ensure steady growth, shielding the rupee from sharp fluctuations, bankers and analysts said. 

 "The economic reforms process is irreversible and whichever party comes into power, economic policy won't change much," said Ravi Pai, vice president, treasury and foreign exchange at the private sector HDFC Bank. 

 He said a majority government would encourage foreign institutional investors who prefer India's steady reform process to the confusion now reigning in Southeast Asian countries. 

 But the rupee was likely to depreciate irrespective of which party came to power, Pai said. 

 "Immaterial of which government comes into power, the authorities want the rupee to depreciate by a certain percentage on a crawling basis," he said. "They will intervene to support this objective." 

 The second leg of India's general elections began on Sunday. The first phase last Monday was marred by violence and charges of vote rigging. Opinion polls have suggested no single party will get the majority needed to form a government. 

 The elections, the second in two years, were forced on the country when the Congress party last year withdrew its support to the minority 15-party United Front coalition government. 

 The fragility of India's coalition politics was again exposed on Saturday when the government of Uttar Pradesh, the country's most populous state, was dismissed by the state governor after it was deserted by a coalition ally. 

 Analysts said a stable government would boost the economic reforms process started in the early 1990s and ensure steady growth. India's gross domestic product (GDP) has grown by an annual average of around 7.0 percent over the last three years. 

 A strong elected government combined with existing fundamentals could help currency stability and keep prices down, Citicorp International Securities Limited said in a research report this month. 

 "A stable rupee, reduced oil prices, large food reserves and a manageable deficit will keep inflation within four to five percent," Citicorp's report said. 

 Despite falling by some 8.3 percent in the last six months the rupee has been stable since the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) hiked interest rates in a currency defence package after it hit a historic low of 40.45 per dollar on January 15. 

 It closed on Friday at 38.92/95. 

 The rupee's fall came amid a slowdown in capital inflows and increased competition from plummeting Asian currencies. 

 If the elections resulted in a majority government or a majority-led coalition the rupee was unlikely to depreciate more than the rate warranted by inflation, Citicorp said. 

 A coalition without ideological agreement would slow the pace of reforms and cause stagnant development, the report said. 

 This would hurt industry and pile pressure on the rupee, it said. 

 The rupee might depreciate 8-10 percent a year in such a case, the report warned. 

 India's year-on-year wholesale price indexed inflation rose to 5.42 percent in the week ended February 7 from 5.29 percent the previous week and compared to 7.83 percent a year ago. 

 "The key question is whether the portfolio inflows, which showed signs of picking up in February after declining during November to January, will be sustained," said foreign exchange consultant A V Rajwade. 

 Net investments by foreign institutional investors rose $36.1 million during February 1-13, reversing a three-month trend, India's capital market regulator said. 

 Net FII outflows in November-January were $385.8 million. 

 Rajwade said India could face competition in attracting foreign investments as other Asian economies recovered. 

 "If portfolio investments (into India) are positive then the rupee will be fairly stable over the next seven months," he said. 

 "Since industrial activity has picked up only moderately, import demand is not much," he added. 

 Industrial production grew by 4.7 percent in April-December 1997 compared to the same period last year. 

 Bankers said the level  of interest rates was a key factor determining the stability of the rupee. 

 "The rupee stabilised after mid-January, thanks largely to sledgehammer tactics used by the RBI," said the country treasurer of a foreign bank, who did not want to be named. 

 The RBI hiked banks' cash reserve ratio requirements by 50 basis points to 10.5 percent. It also raised the rate at which it lends to commercial banks to 11 percent from nine. 

 "After elections, there will definitely be pressure on the central bank to cut rates to help industrial recovery," he said. 

 "Lower interest rates could fuel speculation on the rupee, given that other factors such as political instability will undermine sentiment on the currency," the banker said. 

 The treasurer said the RBI resorted to hiking interest rates after foreign currency reserves had been drawn down, in part due to central bank intervention to stabilise the rupee in the foreign exchange market in the last quarter of 1997 and January 1998. 

 India's foreign currency reserves stood at $24.11 billion on February 13, the RBI said on Saturday. This represents a $1.74 billion increase in the current financial year (April-March) but is considerably lower than the $26.43 billion it reported at the end of August 1997.

title: India  RBI/ Intervention  -2: Responding To Fin Sec Comments
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--There is no cap on the amount of reserves the Reserve Bank of India can use for its forward market operations in the foreign exchange market, but it does ensure reserves are used wisely, a senior official at the central bank told Dow Jones Friday. 

 'There is no cap on the RBI's forward operations' either set by the central bank or the government, the official who did not wish to be named said. 

 But 'as a prudential norm the RBI keeps a close watch' on its forward operations, he said and added that 'sometimes they are less than 10% (of the total reserves) and sometimes more than 10%'. 

 India's Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia Thursday said that the RBI's forward operations in the foreign exchange market is limited to 10% of its total reserves, which currently stand at around $27 billion. 

 'At times of currency crisis this 10% could go up to 13%,' he told journalists Thursday. 

Foreign exchange reserves stood at $27.74 billion in the week ended Feb. 6. The latest data for the month ended December shows the RBI has an outstanding net forward sales position of $1.96 billion. 

 But the RBI also regularly buys and sells its forward positions via swap operations. 

 Ahluwalia said this is in reference to the Asia currency crisis and in contrast to the situation in Thailand where virtually 90% of the foreign exchange reserves was used up in forward market operations. 


Ahluwalia's statement triggered speculation that the government has
set a cap on the RBI's intervention.

 "Forward transactions of the Reserve Bank are currently within 10 percent of the total foreign exchange reserves," the finance secretary was quoted as saying at an industry seminar by the Financial Express daily on Friday.

 The newspaper said Ahluwalia made the remarks in a seminar hosted by the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI) in the city on Thursday. 

 The rupee closed on Thursday at 38.88/89 to the dollar, and has remained steady below 39.0 since mid-January after the central bank raised interest rates and squeezed money market liquidity to halt speculation against the currency.

Ahluwalia said that though the current consensus is that an excessive flow of funds led to the southeast Asian crisis, the fault seems to lie with the international finance companies who invested too much in certain sectors.

title: India /RBI  Intervenes  -2: Bought Dlrs For Feb Delivery

title: India Call Rate Ends Up On Lenders Pushing For Higher Rates
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian interbank overnight call rate closed higher Tuesday because lenders pushed for higher call rates, dealers said. 

 The call rate closed between 9.25% and 10.00%, higher than its Monday close of between 8.75% and 9.50%. 

 The call rate was briefly traded at 10.00% and 10.50% in afternoon trades, 'but after the afternoon check clearances of banks the call was traded lower at around 9.25% and 10.00%,' said a primary dealer. 

 He said the call rate isn't expected to rise substantially this week despite the Reserve Bank of India intervening in the foreign exchange swap market by paying rupee premiums for forward dollars. 

 The RBI intervened in the forward market via swap deals to absorb rupees and stop the dollar from rising to the INR39.00 mark, dealers said. 

 But the primary dealer said the currency outflow from the sale of fixed-rate three-day repurchase agreements of government securities held by the RBI earlier Tuesday was only INR620 million, lower than the INR9.87 billion that the central bank received Monday. 

 Moreover, the INR9.87 billion will be flowing back to the banking system Thursday. 

 A dealer at a large mutual fund who confirmed lending money at around 10.25% said the call rate could be firmer next week if the RBI continues to intervene in the foreign exchange market and absorb rupees. 

 The call rate had risen to between 40% and 100% after Jan. 16 because of the RBI's measures to reduce liquidity in the banking system and stop speculation in the foreign exchange market. 

 'If the RBI feels that there is once again excess rupees in the system then they may decide to reduce liquidity,' said the primary dealer.

text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian interbank overnight call rate closed lower Monday on more than enough money available in the banking system, dealers said. 

 They said that the Reserve Bank of India's dollar-buying intervention in the foreign exchange market over the last two weeks has released significant rupee funds into the banking system. 

 The call rate closed Monday between 8.75% and 9.50%, lower than its Saturday close of between 8.00% and 10.00%. 

 The call rate was higher, however, in morning trades since large financial institutions weren't lending money as they waited for rates to rise, dealers said. 

 But, 'with no major pressure for rupee funds from banks, financial institutions started lending money at around 9.50% in afternoon trades,' said a primary dealer. 

 The liquidity in the market was indicated by the RBI receiving 9.86 billion rupees (INR) of applications to its fixed-rate three-day repurchase agreements (RPs) of government securities earlier Monday. 

 On Saturday, the RBI had received only INR300 million of applications at its RP auction. 

 However, 'the call rate could slightly open higher at around 10.00% on Tuesday,' said the primary dealer. 

 He explained that lenders will try for higher call rates at the opening because of the outflows to RPs. 

 The call rate had risen to trade over 40.00% for the last two weeks following the RBI's decision to raise its bank rate, cut refinance facilities to banks, and raise banks' cash reserve ratio to reduce liquidity in the banking system and stop speculation in the foreign exchange market. 

 But a dealer at a large lending institution said that the RBI's intervention has released significant rupees into the banking system over the last two weeks. 

 According to the RBI's weekly data, the foreign currency holdings rose by $369 million to $27.118 billion in the week ended Jan. 23. 

 The increase was mainly due to the central bank's dollar purchases, thereby releasing rupees, from the foreign exchange market, said a dealer at a European bank.

title: India /RBI/Cool Rates -2:  Intervention  Expected In Feb
text:
Dealers said call rates could rise once again over 100% Saturday and next week as banks will have only four trading days to meet their cash reserve requirements. Monday and Friday are trading holidays. 

 Currently the sentiment in the money market is bad and the call rate is high because of panic among banks and lenders refusing to lend money at lower levels, said a dealer at a U.S. bank. He said the high call has led to speculation in the money market by companies. 

 He explained that companies are buying commercial paper at high yields from banks who in turn are lending the rupees received by companies in the call money market at high levels. 

 The yields on the commercial papers have doubled to between 20% and 25%, he said. 

 There is lot of panic and speculation in the money market and the call rate will come down with a little intervention by the RBI because 'there aren't any major outflows from the banking system until the advance-tax outflows at end-March,' said Ashish Parthasarthi, chief of money market at HDFC Bank Ltd. 

 The RBI cannot shift the problem in the foreign exchange market to the domestic money market, said a senior dealer at state-owned Dena Bank. 

 If they don't reverse some of the measures or don't intervene then 'the sky is the limit for the call rate,' said the dealer at the U.S. bank. 

 The primary dealer said that the RBI isn't likely to cut banks' cash reserve ratio or reverse its other measures because it would lead the market to believe that the RBI is comfortable with the situation and again lead to speculation in the foreign exchange market. 

 The RBI won't intervene immediately because they don't want the problem to resurface in the foreign exchange market, said the primary dealer. 

 'The correction in the foreign exchange market has to look enduring and the best way to deal with the situation is via repurchase transaction wherein the banks requiring rupees get financed by the central bank,' he said.

title: Exotic  Currency  Focus: India Rupee Falls To Record Low
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee fell to an all-time low against the dollar Wednesday despite central bank intervention, and traders said only a spurt in dollar inflows can keep the rupee from falling further over the next few weeks. 

 Traders said the rupee opened lower on early demand for dollars from banks, and quickly broke through its record low of INR 39.95 to the dollar with no sign of any large dollar sellers in the market. 

 After the Reserve Bank of India didn't intervene when that low was broken, the market quickly took the rupee below the key level of INR 40.00 to the dollar. 

 Market players had expected at least the State Bank of India, the country's largest commercial bank, to sell the U.S. currency to stem the rupee's fall. But it too stayed away. It has sold dollars over the last week and the market's perception is that those sales were at the behest of the RBI. 

 Eventually, the RBI intervened and sold dollars in two rounds. Those sales effectively prevented the rupee from falling below 40.20 to the dollar, helping it close between INR 40.10 and INR 40.15, versus INR 39.86-.89 Tuesday. 

 Although analysts said they expect the rupee to continue to fall, senior government officials tried to downplay Wednesday's drop. 

 'This is a minor adjustment and the RBI is watching the situation for any excess volatility,' Indian Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia told Dow Jones Wednesday. 'There is no reason to be alarmed,' 

 Ahluwalia also said the rupee's fall has to be viewed in the backdrop of the fall in currency values across Southeast Asia.

title: India rupee sinks below key 40 per dollar barrier.
text:
BOMBAY, Jan 14 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee broke through the key psychological barrier of 40 to the dollar early Wednesday as the central bank watched and the government played it down. 

 India's finance secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia said the government was "not alarmed". 

 "The RBI (Reserve Bank of India) is of course watching the market carefully and we are not alarmed at the developments," Ahluwalia told Reuters. 

 The rupee closed at 40.13/15 to the dollar after hitting a historic low of 40.22. 

 It started at 39.89/94 against the previous close of 39.88/90 and slipped past 40 within minutes of opening. 

 The rupee has weakened over 12 percent since August 1997, in contrast to most Asian currencies which have fallen much further. 

 "The dollar has hardened against all currencies in the past few days and focusing on the rupee-dollar rate gives an exaggerated picture of the situation," Ahluwalia said. 

 He said the government had made it clear it does not propose to defend the rupee at any particular level. 

 "The rupee has become an orphan," said the chief dealer at a public sector bank, referring to absence of Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervention when the rupee pierced the 40 per dollar level. 

 The rupee's decline has been slowed to a crawl by a series of central bank measures to kill corporate and interbank speculation since December. 

 This meant that all dollars have to be backed by genuine trade transactions, dealers said. 

 But a worsening dollar demand-supply mismatch ensured that the rupee weakened and the RBI has been shy in intervening in the spot market for fear of depletion of reserves, they said. 

 RBI intervention has been mostly in the swap market which is reserve-neutral, the dealers said. 

 RBI intervened in the spot market only after the rupee sank to 40.20 level on Wednesday. 

 Dealers said the rupee's further fall would be easier now that the 40-per dollar hump has been crossed. 

 "Forty has now become the base," Ravi Kumar, chief dealer at ABN-AMRO Bank said. "We are looking at a 40-42 (rupees to the dollar) band for the first quarter of 1998." 

 He said Indian importers were keenly watching the developments in South-east Asia. If the major Asian currencies stabilise, it would have a positive impact on the Indian rupee, he said. 

 The rupee could stabilise at 40-41 to the dollar if a stable government is installed after the general elections in February-March, Kumar said. 

 Leading Indian firms said the rupee's weakening proved that India was no longer insulated from Asian developments. 

 S.D. Kulkarni, managing director of engineering firm Larsen & Toubro Ltd said India was no longer insulated from developments in rest of Asia. 

 "The depreciation of South-east Asian currencies is going to have some impact on us," he said. Other industrialists agreed. 

 "It (the rupee) will stabilise (at current levels)," Keshub Mahindra, chairman of automobile firm Mahindra & Mahindra said. 

 "But we have to see how the East-Asian currencies will go." 

 The rupee was buoyant through most of 1996 and 1997 on strong capital flows, forcing the RBI to buy dollars as recently as October 1997, to prevent the rupee from rising. 

 But foreign portfolio investments into India suffered as investors pulled out funds in the wake of the Asian stocks and currency turmoil.

title: Indian firms see rupee stabilise at new level.
text:
BOMBAY, Jan 14 (Reuters) - Leading Indian industrialists said on Wednesday the rupee should stabilise at the new, weaker level after it breached the crucial 40 per dollar barrier in early morning trade. 

 The rupee opened Wednesday at 39.89/94 to the dollar compared with the previous close of 39.88/90 and slipped past the psychological barrier of 40 in early morning trade. 

 It has fallen over 12 percent since August 1997. 

 Bank dealers had forecast on Tuesday the rupee would test the 40 barrier on Wednesday unless the central bank intervened. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) stepped in only after the 40 level was breached. 

 Keshub Mahindra, chairman of automobile firm Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd said he expected the rupee to stabilise at the new level. 

 "It (rupee level) should stabilise. But we have to see how the East Asian currencies will go," Mahindra told Reuters. 

 S.D. Kulkarni, managing director and chief executive officer of engineering conglomerate Larsen & Toubro Ltd said India was no longer insulated from developments in the neighbouring countries. 

 "Current levels (of rupee) should be okay," Kulkarni said. 

 "We are not insulated today. The depreciation of the South-east Asian currencies is going to have some impact on us." 

 "There has to be some sort of competitive devaluation." 

 Hari L. Mundra, chief financial officer at diversified business group RPG Enterprises, said Wednesday's move was the result of recent central bank measures and a thin interbank foreign exchange market. 

 "This is a result of panic in a very thin market because of RBI's measures," he said, referring to RBI's order earlier this month asking banks to square up their end of day dollar positions. 

 "At this juncture, the fall is not because of fundamental issues. The RBI needs to take a relook at its measures," he said. 

 The rupee was trading at 40.12/17 at 12.35 p.m. 

 India's finance secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia told Reuters in New Delhi there was no cause for alarm. ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com))

text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee opened unchanged against the dollar Tuesday but slipped immediately and is trading very close to its all-time low, dealers said. 

 The dollar opened Tuesday at 39.80-.85 rupees (INR). It had closed Monday at INR39.82-.84. 

 The dollar is trading at INR39.85-.87 at 0345 GMT (10:45 p.m. EST). Traders said it has been traded at INR39.87 Tuesday. The dollar traded at a record high of INR39.95 on Dec. 2. 

 Dealers said while there is small early demand for the U.S. currency, there isn't much supply in the market. 

 'State (Bank) hasn't sold anything in the market but his price indicates that he is a seller,' a dealer at a private sector bank said. 

 As reported, continuous dollar sales by the State Bank prevented the rupee from falling Friday and Monday. 

 State Bank is the country's largest commercial bank and its actions often set the trend for the market because it deals on behalf of several large corporations, including state-owned oil companies. 

 Dealers said the dollar is likely to rise above INR39.90 Tuesday unless the Reserve Bank of India intervenes to sell spot dollars. 

 But others said the central bank may stay out of the market and let the State Bank do its bidding instead. The State Bank's dollar sales in recent days are perceived to be prompted by the RBI. 

 Trading volumes are low because the RBI Wednesday directed banks to hold square or near-square positions at the end of each trading day until further notice. The measure was aimed at easing the downward pressure on the rupee, which the RBI believes was mainly caused by interbank speculation. 

 Dealers said the forward premiums are likely to fall slightly after the Reserve Bank of India intervenes and sells forward-dollars after buying spot dollars. The RBI had been swapping forward dollars almost every session over the last three weeks to prevent the forward premiums from rising.

title: India rupee revisits record low, aims 40/dlr level.
text:
BOMBAY, Jan 12 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee on Tuesday touched a new record closing rate against the dollar for the second successive day, dealers said. 

 The spot rupee revisted its record traded low of 39.93 to the dollar before dollar sales by the State Bank of India (SBI) helped it recover to close at 39.88/90, they said. 

 The rupee had closed Monday at 39.81/83, its previous lowest closing rate, dealers said. 

 The rupee's weakening continued on the back of rising corporate dollar demand and dwindling supplies, they said. 

 Many dealers said they expected the rupee to hit the 40 per dollar level soon. 

 "There was steady demand for dollars throughout the day," said a foriegn bank dealer. "We might see the rupee trading at a new horizon in couple of days -- might be tomorrow," he said. 

 "The long awaited 40 per dollar level might face the acid test tomorrow," a dealer at a brokerage said. 

 "SBI is the only one to supply sedative in a sliding market," a foreign bank dealer said, referring to SBI's dollar sales. The state-run SBI is India's leading commercial bank. 

 "We might not see a dramatic down fall of the rupee in the next few days but it will steadily slip," a dealer said 

 Dealers said the rupee's weakening on Tuesday was a matter of concern as most Asian currencies staged a recovery which was not reflected in the local market. 

 The rupee saw a traded high of 39.83 and a low of 39.93 on Tuesday, with majority of the deals struck within the 39.85-39.90 range, dealers said. 

 The rupee had hit a lifetime low of 39.93 on December 16, but strong central bank intervention had helped it recover. 

 The rupee weakened in the forward dollar market on Tuesday but a steep fall was averted by central bank intervention in the swap market, dealers said. 

 Dealers said the market had started discounting the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) interventions in the swap market which have become regular in recent weeks. 

 The intervention is yielding diminishing returns as the market had discounted it and a hungry market absorbed all the supplies, dealers said. Only massive intervention could make a difference, dealers said. 

 Compared to the steady one way slide in the spot market, the the forward dollar market saw two way movement. 

 The six month dollar premiums closed at 10.50 percent compared to its previous close of 10.24 percent.

title: FOCUS-Indian rupee at lowest closing rate vs dlr.
text:
BOMBAY, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Rising dollar demand from Indian firms in the wake of the Asian currency and stocks meltdown and dwindling supplies dragged the rupee to its lowest ever closing rate on Monday, dealers said. 

 "That the rupee is  weakening almost by 10 paise (0.10 rupees) a day is a matter of concern," said Moses Harding, chief dealer at IndusInd Bank, leading private bank. 

 On Monday, the rupee closed at 39.81/83 per dollar, its lowest ever closing rate, slipping past the previous record close of 39.74/76 hit on Friday. 

 The rupee has been among the least affected currencies in the region, falling by only around 10 percent against the dollar since August 1997. 

 The rupee had hit a record traded low of 39.93 on December 16, but aggressive intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had propped it up. 

 "It is purely corporate dollar demand," said a dealer at a French bank in Bombay. 

 He said the rupee's current weakness faithfully mirrored the dollar supply demand mismatch as the central bank last week disallowed banks from taking speculative positions, thereby snuffing out interbank speculation. 

 A dealer at a leading foreign bank said the rupee would hit the 40 per dollar level in the next few trading days if the current trend continued unchecked. 

 "The rupee is continuously under pressure as corporate dollar demand is rising and supply dwindling," said one dealer. 

 Many dealers attributed the rising corporate dollar demand to worries that the Asian currency meltdown would eventually lead to a further weakening of the Indian rupee. 

 Share prices in Bombay exchanges closed sharply lower on the back of worsening Asian economic woes, traders said. 

 The Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) top 30-share index slumped 3.83 percent or 135.16 points to 3,395.04 points. 

 Portfolio investment by foreign institutional investors (FIIs) fell by $4.7 million in January 1-8, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) said on Friday. 

 The market regulator said net FII investments dropped by $155.4 million in December, the second straight month of net outflows as foreign investors pulled out of the troubled region. 

 The only dollar suppliers in recent months have been either the central bank or the state-run State Bank of India (SBI). 

 "At present, SBI is the only major dollar supplier in the market," said one dealer. "The rupee's sharp fall has been averted by SBI's supplies." 

 The RBI did not intervene in the spot market on Monday, but was a large player in the forward dollar market, dealers said. 

 The RBI intervened in June, July and August maturities in the swap market on Monday. 

 Premiums fell across the board on the impact of dollar sales by the RBI and SBI. Six-month dollar premiums closed at 10.24 percent compared with a weekend close of 10.84 percent. ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com))

title: India Rupee Slightly Lower In Early Trading
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee (INR) opened higher against the dollar Friday but fell immediately and is trading slightly below its previous closing levels, dealers said. 

 The dollar opened Friday at INR39.61-39.66. It rose immediately and was traded at INR39.71. 

 The dollar is trading at INR39.68-39.71 at 0350 GMT (10:50 p.m. EST). 

 Dealers said a few banks sold dollars at higher levels, causing the U.S. currency to fall back slightly. 

 Dealers are divided on whether the Reserve Bank of India will intervene in the spot market to sell the U.S. currency Friday. 

 While a few dealers say the central bank will have to intervene to keep the rupee from falling further sharply, others said the central bank could use other methods to cool the market. 

 One favorite theory in the market is that the State Bank of India trades on behalf of the RBI several times. 'You may see State Banks selling today, not RBI selling,' a dealer at a large European bank said. 

 State Bank is the country's largest commercial bank and its actions often set the trend for the market because it deals on behalf of several large corporates including state-owned oil companies. 

 Trading volumes have fallen substantially since Wednesday after the RBI directed banks to hold square or near square positions at the end of trading everyday until further notice. The measure was aimed at easing the downward pressure on the rupee a major part of which the RBI believes was caused by interbank speculation. 

 The rupee traded at a record low of INR39.95 to the dollar on Dec. 2. 

 'We have to wait and see what happens, we are going with the market,' a dealer at a state-owned bank said. 

 There was substantial corporate demand for the U.S. currency Thursday, he noted. 'I think that demand will continue.'

title: Indian rupee bows under rising dollar demand.
text:
BOMBAY, Jan 6 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee came under renewed pressure on Tuesday, unsettled by rising dollar demand from industry and the impact of wilting Southeast Asian currencies, dealers said. 

 Sporadic dollar sales by the State Bank of India (SBI) and a token intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) with one Bombay bank could only temporarily halt the rupee's slide, they said. 

 The rupee saw a traded low of 39.62 to the dollar compared with 39.42/45 at the opening and a previous close of 39.41/43. 

 Dealers said a major reason behind the rise in dollar demand appeared to be a revival in industrial activity. 

 "What we saw in December was a lull in industrial activity," said a foreign bank dealer. "The dollar demand reflects the revival of activity in several industries," he said. 

 Another reason for the spurt in dollar demand was the travel requirement of Haj pilgrims who go to Moslem's holiest city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia, a dealer at a public sector bank said. 

 "This is the Haj season and they need to carry dollars," he said. 

 The rupee has weakened around nine percent since August, 1997. 

 The rupee hit an historic low of 39.90 to the dollar on December 2, 1997, prompting the central bank to launch a rescue package. 

 The RBI tightened domestic liquidity and hiked export credit in late 1997 with a view to prevent diversion of cheap rupees to fund speculation and encourage faster repatriation of export proceeds by Indian exporters. 

 The central bank's steps brought calm to the market and in late December it began rolling back some of its measures. 

 "It seems the withdrawal was a little too early as free falling South-east Asian currencies have created apprehensions of a domino effect on the rupee," Societe Generale bank said in an India report. 

 "With dollar on the rampage against major (Asian) currencies, corporates are likely to be nervous to hold short dollar positions," the report said. 

 Forward dollar premiums also flared up on Tuesday, reflecting the rupee's weakness in the spot market. 

 One year dollar premiums were quoted at 8.50 percent on Tuesday afternoon compared to the previous close of 7.88 percent. 

 "The overseas NDF (non-deliverable forward) market is retesting an all-time high of 44.70 (rupees to the dollar) for one year forward with premium quoted at 5.35 rupees," a dealer said. 

 The NDF market is mainly patronised by foreign institutional investors who are not allowed to hedge their Indian equities exposures within India. 

 The chief dealer at a foreign bank said the rupee would hit the 40 per dollar mark by March. 

 "It could happen much earlier," he said.

title: India rupee exchange rate band inappropriate-RBI.
text:
BOMBAY, Dec 25 (Reuters) - An exchange rate band for the Indian rupee is inappropriate in the current circumstances, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said on Thursday in its "Report on Currency and Finance 1996-97". 

 The RBI said stabilising the rupee-dollar exchange rate continues to be an important factor guiding exchange rate policy. But it rejected suggestions that a currency band could be set as a stabiliser. 

 "In view of the complexities involved in exactly identifying the course of the equilibrium rate, there is a suggestion for use of bands to represent fundamentals, but this would be inappropriate on credibility grounds," the RBI's report said. 

 The rupee has fallen around nine percent against the U.S. dollar since mid-August, ending Wednesday at 39.16/18 to the dollar. 

 The RBI stopped the rupee breaking through the 40-mark earlier this month by erecting a defence package. This includes forcing up short-term interest rates, speeding up exporters remittances and making imports of non-essential goods more costly. 

 The RBI also spent nearly $2.5 billion intervening to try to stop the currency's fall since the end of October. 

 The rupee's decline started in August when a senior central bank official said the currency was overvalued on a trade-weighted basis after the rupee had held firm for a year against a dollar. 

 There were also media reports in August that Indian authorities were considering introducing an exchange rate band. Despite subsequent denials by authorities, the idea occasionally bobbed up during the rupee's recent volatility. 

 An expert group set up earlier this year to chart a phased move to capital account convertibility had recommended a band of five percent above or below the neutral real effective exchange rate (REER). The group proposed that this would happen once the rupee was made convertible on the capital account, which is planned in the next few years. 

 REER measures a currency's performance against those of major trading partners taking into account differentials in inflation rates, interest rates, productivity, financial asset values and several other components. 

 The rupee's fortunes have largely depended on the ebb and flow of foreign capital coming into India. 

 Until last August, the central bank intervened regularly to buy dollars to stop the rupee firming beyond 35.70. 

 The RBI bought $7.8 billion in 1996/97, and up until the end of October was still a dollar buyer. But when capital inflows dried up in the wake of the market crisis in Asia, the RBI turned into a heavy dollar seller as the rupee's fall accelerated. 

 It said a band can be based on REER, but constructing REER indicators is fraught with difficulties. As it only takes the trade account into its reckoning it would not represent all the fundamentals. 

 Developments in capital flows also had to be factored into policy making, although they should not be the sole determining factor, the RBI said. 

 "In the face of large destabilising capital flows and/or periodic deviation from norms suggested as pre-conditions, rigid pursuance of such a band could however be costly and disruptive," the RBI cautioned.

title: Indian rupee ends at 39.27/30 per dlr, off 39.90.
text:
BOMBAY, Dec 2 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee ended Tuesday at a new record low of 39.27/30 per dollar, slightly weaker than its previous close of 39.25/30 but off an intraday low of 39.90 hit in morning trade, dealers said. 

 They said the rupee weakened on strong dollar demand from banks which bought ahead of anticipated demand from corporates and rapidly fell to a lifetime low of 39.90 in the absence of intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). 

 Dealers said the rupee appreciated later on news of RBI's package of measures to support the Indian currency. 

 "When this news was known to the market, speculators began to back off," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "There was also profit-taking from players holding dollars." 

 Dealers said the rupee rallied to around 39.50 levels when a large state-run bank sold dollars. 

 "Then the RBI announced its package and the rupee bounced to to 39.10/17 levels," said a dealer. 

 Dealers said the central bank's package along with expectations of dollar inflows from a global depositary (GDR) issue by a leading state-run firm could help the rupee stabilise after a fall of around 10.0 percent in just over three months. 

 The GDR issue by the Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Limited (MTNL) is expected to raise around $370 million. 

 "We expect the rupee to stabilise on the MTNL factor and the package," said a dealer at a private bank. "But how long this will last remains to be seen." 

 "The rupee is likely to come back under pressure unless RBI intervenes," he said. 

 Other dealers said the RBI was placing excessive emphasis on the speculation factor. 

 "There is some pretty strong demand from corporates and this will have to be met from somewhere," said a dealer. 

 The package of measures announced by the RBI included steps to tighten liquidity and raise short term interest rates. 

 But the move to tighten liquidity pushed up forward premiums, weakening the rupee against the forward dollar. 

 Premiums rose 10-15 paise across all maturities but ended little changed from Monday's close. 

 Among the measures announced by RBI on Tuesday were a hike in banks' cash reserve ratio (CRR) to 10.0 percent from 9.5 percent and in interest on repos to 5.0 percent from 4.0 percent. 

 The central bank also said it was holding in abeyance a planned reduction in the CRR announced in a credit policy statement in October. The RBI had scheduled a series of cuts announced to bring the CRR down from 10 percent to eight percent by March. 

 These moves superseded a milder support package announced last Friday by the central bank. 

 The RBI also said it was removing a 10 percent incremental CRR on non-resident rupee deposits. 

 "This move is an attempt to get banks to canvass more foreign currency accounts," said a dealer. "It should help in improving inflows to some extent." 

 The RBI also said authorised currency dealers needed to see customers' evidence of currency exposure before offering forward currency contracts. 

 The rupee had come under mounting pressure as foreign currency inflows dried up in the aftermath of the Asian markets crisis and Indian firms exhausting their external commercial borrowing limits. 

 A perception that the rupee needed to depreciate to take into account the dramatic falls in other Asian currencies against the dollar also gripped the market. 

 And a political crisis culminating in the fall of the United Front coalition government on Friday piled on the speculative pressure. 

 Indian political parties on Tuesday were still trying to cobble together a new coalition, otherwise the country faces fresh elections.

title: India  rupee weaker,  intervention  fears limits scope.
text:
BOMBAY, Dec 1 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee was weaker against both the spot and forward dollar in late morning trade Monday and dealers said fears of central bank intervention had checked a sharper fall. 

 Dealers say political uncertainty, after prime minister Inder Kumar Gujral resigned on Friday, gives fodder to speculators, but fear of heavy RBI intervention has stopped a sharp move so far. 

 No single party or political bloc commands absolute majority in India's parliament and a snap poll is likely, analysts say. 

 "Nobody is quite sure when Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will come in," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "Corporates are keeping off the market at the moment to see what RBI will do. There are no bids above 38.80." 

 "The rupee has broadly traded in 38.70-38.80 per dollar range so far," he said. "There have been stray deals at 38.68 and 38.81." 

 The rupee hit a record low of 38.85 per dollar on Friday before rallying to close at 38.55/58 on Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervention. 

 Later on Friday, RBI announced a package of measures to speed up inward remittances of foreign currency by exporters and to mop up excess domestic liquidity to prevent banks using the extra funds to speculate in forex market. 

 Dealers said RBI had checked for prices in the morning. 

 "They have been prowling around, checking out prices," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "But so far there has been no intervention." 

 "But RBI will have to come in soon," he said. 

 "If they stay off the market for another hour or so, then I think corporates may start buying," the dealer said. "And pressure will then start building for a test of 39." 

 Dealers said forward premiums had risen on corporate demand. 

 "There has been some booking of forward cover in near months in particular," said a dealer. "Premiums are up across the board largely in reaction to the weakening in spot. The prospect of a tightening in domestic liquidity has also hit sentiment."

title: FOCUS-Safety net arrives for rupee as government falls.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 28 (Reuters) - India's central bank announced a package on Friday to prop up an ailing rupee, but even as it acted the government fell, raising the prospect of more pressure on the currency, bankers said. 

 Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral resigned late on Friday night after the opposition Congress party withdrew support for his minority government, junior minister Jayanti Natarajan said. 

 The climax of the political drama came at the end of a day when the rupee had already plunged to all-time lows. 

 It hit a record 38.85 per dollar, eight percent below mid-August levels, before a Reserve bank of India (RBI) intervention made for a half-hearted recovery. 

 The rupee closed at 38.55/59, a shade stronger than its previous close of 38.60/63, but dealers said strong dollar demand was still bubbling. 

 And the central bank decided to take steps to curb speculation against the rupee and force Indian firms holding foreign currency abroad to bring it home quickly. 

 And measures taken to reduce liquidity, forcing up demand for rupees, are likely to drive money market interest rates higher in the short term, bankers said. 

 However, dealers were sceptical whether the RBI package would have the desired effect, given the political denouement, and said it would have to come out with more measures. 

 The knock-on effect of the east Asian currency crisis pushed the rupee into a slide that gathered momentum in the past two weeks. 

 The Congress party said it had withdrawn its make-or-break support to the United Front alliance of 15 parties and was staking a claim to form the next government. 

 However, no single political bloc now commands an absolute majority in parliament, raising the prospect of snap elections unless one group musters enough support to form a government. 

 Political uncertainty has been one of the factors driving speculation on the rupee, which the RBI says is a major cause for its recent fall. 

 Besides speeding up foreign currency remittances by exporters, the RBI's package of measures is also aimed at tightening liquidity in the domestic money market to prevent banks using extra funds to speculate. 

 The central bank said it would also call for details of cancellations of forward contracts above $500,000 since the beginning of the month. 

 It said it would monitor such cancellations in future to prevent speculation by firms which booked forward sales and cancelled them to take advantage of market turbulence. 

 "This will have a salutary effect on curbing volatility," said the chief foreign exchange dealer at a state-run bank. 

 "Many corporates, including some big names, have been speculating through cancellation of forward contracts." 

 In a related measure the RBI increased the interest rate on export credit to make it costlier for exporters to hold on to their foreign currency earnings. 

 The RBI also announced it would conduct repurchase auctions at a fixed rate of interest to mop up excess liquidity. 

 The RBI further said it would delay forthcoming cuts in banks' cash reserve ratio (CRR) requirements which it had announced in October. 

 Higher money market rates could further delay a revival in India's industrial growth, bankers said. 

 And they were unconvinced the package would rescue the rupee. 

 "I don't think they've done much to help the rupee, not after the government has fallen," said a dealer with a major foreign bank. "I think it will come under a fair amount of pressure on Monday morning." 

 Other bankers said the RBI had not exhausted all options. 

 "This is a shallow market and not a very developed one," said a dealer at a private bank. "If things go out of hand, the RBI will resort to its last option - massive intervention." 

India's foreign currency reserves stood close to $26 billion on November 13. 

 Analysts estimate the reserves are enough to cover over seven months' imports and provide sufficient buffer to the central bank to beat back speculators.

title: Indian rupee's floor seen set by RBI  intervention .
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 28 (Reuters) - The rupee's fall was checked at 38.60 to the dollar level on Friday by repeated central bank interventions, dealers said. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) came in three rounds, selling dollars after the rupee breached the 38.60-level, they said. 

 "I see a 38.30/60 range for some time," said Ravi Pai, chief dealer at HDFC Bank in Bombay. "People are a little nervous but there is no panic buying (of dollars)," he said. 

 On Thursday, Indian commerce minister Bolla Buli Ramaiah said the "rupee would take its own course." 

 "Right now what is happening is due to political reasons," Ramaiah told Reuters in New Delhi. 

 "People are theoretically connecting politics with the rupee," said a dealer, referring to political uncertainties affecting the survival of the ruling United Front government. 

 But foreign exchange dealers said the impact of politics on the currency market was grossly exaggerated. 

 "Personally I don't consider them (politics) as relevant," HDFC Bank's Pai said. 

 The rupee hit an alltime low of 38.85 in early morning trade, triggered by a newspaper report which suggested the government was thinking of a five percent trading band around 38.40 within which the rupee should trade. 

 An RBI official later denied the report. 

 The rupee has fallen by about 8.0 percent against the dollar since August.

title: India rupee weakens vs forward dlr, RBI stays away.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 28 (Reuters) -  The Indian rupee weakened further against the forward dollar in afternoon trade Friday as central bank intervention failed to materialise, dealers said. 

 They said the Reserve Bank of India was expected to intervene through swaps, a regular feature of its intervention in the past few days, but had not done so on Friday. 

 "Their (RBI) absence is driving premiums up," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "There is some dollar demand -- mainly interbank and some from corporates." 

 At 2 p.m.(0830 GMT), the annualised premium on six-month forward dollars was 6.75 percent against Thursday's close of 6.02 percent. 

 "Normally there is some demand from banks towards the end of every month when they roll over swaps, particularly on their foreign currency deposits," said a dealer. 

 "But it also looks like some banks are taking fresh positions besides squaring off existing ones." 

 Dealers said repeated RBI intervention in the spot market had helped the rupee settle down after high volatility in the morning when it hit a record low of 38.85 minutes after opening. 

 At 2 p.m. (0830 GMT), the rupee was quoted 38.58/62 per dollar against its previous close of 38.60/63. 

 "The market is moving up and down with the RBI," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "Volumes are thin and there is nothing much other than RBI to move the market today."

title: Indian call money ends easy amid good liquidity.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 26 (Reuters) - Indian call money ended Wednesday easier at 4.0-5.0 percent amid good liquidity compared to the previous close of 5.0-5.5 percent, dealers said. 

 They said call money rates eased in afternoon trade on good funds supply while demand petered out.

title: Indian rupee should fall further - economists.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Already six percent down in the last three months and saddled with a government in danger of falling any day, the rupee needs to depreciate further to fit into the changed Asian currency landscape, economists said on Sunday. 

 Ashok Gulati, chief economist at the National Council for Applied Economic Research in New Delhi said officials at both the World Bank and International Monetary Fund privately advocated a substantially weaker rupee. 

 "The feeling in Washington is that the rupee has to go down more," Gulati said. 

 IMF and World Bank economists believed a depreciation against the dollar by a further seven to eight percent was warranted, he said, adding that the greater part of the move could happen as early as the next 15 days to one month. 

 "Political instability is a contributory factor, but it is the economics around the world that are driving the depreciation in the rupee," Gulati said. 

 S.P Gupta, director of the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations, said the rupee should be nearer 40 to the dollar and "the sooner the better." 

 The rupee fell to a 21 month low of 37.75/80 to the dollar on Friday, dropping 30 paise from the previous close. 

 But it is still high, if not spry, compared with the devastated currencies of Asia's wounded Tiger economies, which have suffered falls anywhere between 10 and 40 percent in the last 10 months. 

 Gulati and Gupta are far from being isolated voices, but others are more wary about sticking their necks out publicly. 

 A number of economists at foreign brokerages here see the rupee falling but because of sensitivities over being guests in the country are wary of saying so openly just yet. 

 Two privately forecast a rupee at 40 per dollar by the end of March, while a third said he would like it to fall beyond that in the next eight to 10 months. 

 Others like the Peregrine India brokerage saw it going to 38.5 and recovering to 37.40 by March. While Sandeep Nanda at NatWest Markets said he was sticking by a forecast of 38.30 by March, but added it was under review. 

 The Reserve Bank of India has said it will intervene to curb any exchange rate volatility, and sold more than $1 billion in just over a week doing just that. 

 The RBI has heeded IMF advice that the market should be allowed to determine the rupee's level, but it seems the market is moving too fast for comfort. 

 Chakravarty Rangarajan, who handed over governorship of the central bank to Bimal Jalan on Saturday, told the market last Tuesday it had taken the rupee down far enough when it hit 37.50, but by the end of the week the slide had resumed. 

 The RBI, with close to $30 billion in foreign exchange reserves, has the ammunition to dominate the shallow market for a rupee which is only convertible on the current account. 

 Whatever the rupee's short term outlook, the very short term looks as precarious as Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's minority government. 

 Gujral said on Saturday an election was "just around the corner." 

 His United Front (UF) alliance was set on Sunday to formally reject a Congress party demand for the UF to remove a coalition partner from government or lose Congress support. 

 One side may yet pull back from the brink, as a common perception is that the Hindu nationalist opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has most to gain from a mid-term poll. 

 The constant concern that the minority government lacks power to follow through on reforms, and fear that it could fall whenever Congress chooses, along with worries about the rupee's future have all contributed to a slowdown in foreign direct investment. 

 FDI, in the first half of 1996/97 (April-March) was only around $1.5 billion, well under the $2.7 billion registered in the corresponding period last year, and monthly inflows have dwindled to just $100 million, analysts said. 

 An early decision on the currency at least will reassure foreign investors, and will also help exports give impetus to an economy lacking domestic demand to fire up sluggish industrial growth, Gupta said.

title: India rupee quiet, unmoved by political turmoil.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee was trading quiet at 37.39/41 per dollar in afternoon trade Thursday, little affected by political developments, dealers said. 

 They said forex market players were looking for direction more from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which intervened actively in the morning, than from the emerging political scenario. 

 "With the RBI looming large today, no major flare-up is likely," said a dealer at a private bank. 

 "I think corporates are waiting to see what really happens," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "Some people are talking of a compromise and the stock market has rallied on this hope." 

 "As far as we forex market players are concerned, I think it is RBI who will move the market and they have given a clear indication in the morning that they want the rupee to stay around current levels," he added. 

 Analysts had predicted turmoil for markets after the Congress party decided to ask the ruling coalition to expel one of its members. Congress is not part of the minority 15-party United Front coalition but supports it from outside. 

 The rupee opened steady at 37.46/49 and weakened to 37.49 before rallying on RBI dollar sales. While no precise figures of the quantum of the central bank's intervention are available, dealers estimated it could be around $100 million.

title: India  RBI Sells -2: Small  Intervention  Has No Impact On Mkt
text:
BOMBAY (AP-Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of India sold dollars in the spot market just before the close of trading Wednesday, dealers said. 

 Dealers at two foreign banks confirmed the central bank sold them the U.S. currency around 1015 GMT (0415 am EST). 

 The RBI sold dollars around 37.45 rupees, dealers said. 

 As reported, a dealer at one foreign bank had confirmed the RBI sold him dollars in late morning trading, but no other dealers could confirm that intervention. 

 At 1024 GMT (04:24 am EST) the dollar is trading between 37.42 rupees and 37.45 rupees. 

 'They are selling in small lots, so it has no impact on the market,' one of the dealers who transacted business with the central bank said. 

 But most other dealers said the RBI hadn't approached them for trades. Several dealers said the RBI inquired about price-levels which caused the dollar to fall back a bit. 

 'There is no RBI,' a dealer at a state-owned bank said. 'People who are long dollars are selling now, that's why it's falling.' 

 One dealer estimated the RBI sold around $50 million to $70 million. 

 The dollar opened Wednesday between 37.43-.46 rupees, up from its close between 37.39-.41 rupees Tuesday. 

 The rupee fell to a new 21-month low Tuesday at 37.52 to the dollar, but recovered on a statement by the Reserve Bank of India Governor C. Rangarajan that he believed 'the adjustment that has taken place in the value of the rupee is adequate.' 

 The RBI governor also said there wasn't any ground for a further weakening of the rupee in view of the strong fundamentals and added the central bank wouldn't hesitate to intervene to prevent any 'overshooting.'

title: India Rupee's Fall Seen Arrested For Now, Traders Say
text:
BOMBAY (AP-Dow Jones)--A strong statement from the Reserve Bank of India Tuesday seems to have arrested the rupee's recent plummet, but foreign exchange traders are divided about how long it will be before the Indian currency starts testing new support levels. 

 Although the Reserve Bank has indicated it believes India's economic fundamentals, in particular its narrow current-account deficit, are sound, there is still a net demand for dollars, traders said. 

 The rupee has slipped steadily since the end of October on a combination of foreign investors selling shares to repatriate funds and importers buying dollars. But Tuesday it went into - by local standards - a freefall. It opened at 36.925 rupees to the dollar and had tumbled 1.6% to an intraday low of 37.52 by midday. 

 In contrast to recent sessions, in which the RBI is estimated to have spent several hundred million dollars in a largely unsuccessful effort to halt the rupee's descent, the central bank opted Tuesday to communicate its views via words not deeds. 

 'We believe that the adjustment that has already taken place in the value of the rupee is adequate,' Reserve Bank Governor C. Rangarajan said in a brief press statement. 

 'In view of the fundamentals, there is no ground for a further weakening of the rupee. Reserve Bank of India won't hesitate to intervene to prevent any overshooting,' he added. 

 Within minutes, the rupee had jumped back to 37.22 to the dollar. It retreated lightly in the afternoon and ended at 37.39-.41, still well down from a Monday close of 36.88-.89. 

 Traders said the statement was more concretely worded than other comments from the central bank in the last few months, in particular the remark that there's no need for further rupee weakening. 

 'They have defined the cap at 37.50 rupees,' said Sunil Sharma, chief dealer at ANZ Grindlays Bank. 'But that statement and (recent) intervention will have to be further intensified if (the dollar) has to go below 37.20' rupees. 

 Other dealers said the current levels are likely to hold for a while. 

 'I think we will now see some consolidation for two weeks,' says K. Jayaram, senior dealer at Credit Lyonnais. 'We might see a revisit to 37.50 rupees, but that will be protected.'

title: India: Bombay Shrs Down At Midday; IPCL Dn 6.0%
text:
BOMBAY (AP-Dow Jones)--Shares recovered slightly from early lows on the Bombay Stock Exchange around midday Tuesday due to a statement by the governor of the Reserve Bank of India that the central bank will intervene to prevent a further depreciation of the rupee, dealers said. 

 They said remarks Tuesday by the Indian Prime Minister I.K. Gujral that 7% growth in Gross Domestic Product is still feasible have also helped trading sentiment. 

 The BSE Sensitive Index (Sensex) of 30 companies, which stood at 3544.27 in early trade, plunged to a low of 3494.80 points in late morning trade but recovered slightly when the rupee recovered from early lows.  Foreign funds sold shares in a panic in early morning trading because of concern over the weakening of the Indian rupee. 

 The dollar touched a new 21-month high of 37.50 rupees but fell later to 37.35 rupees on the RBI governor's statements that the adjustment in the value of rupee is 'adequate' and there is no ground for further weakening of the currency. 

 A dealer at Pranav Securities Ltd. said the stock market moved up slightly on the RBI statement as well as the comments by Gujral at a meeting in New Delhi. However, the market is still bearish on increasing foreign fund selling because of volatility in other Asian regional stock exchanges. 

 A dealer at Mafatlal Securities Ltd. said most of the blue chip stocks are trading lower on selling pressure from foreign institutional investors and local traders. 

 Shares of Hindustan Lever Ltd., tobacco company, ITC Ltd. and Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (BHEL) declined sharply on foreign fund selling.

text:

 The dollar opened Tuesday between 36.91-.94 rupees, up from its close between 36.88-.89 rupees Monday. 

 The U.S. currency has been traded at a high of 36.95 rupees Tuesday, dealers said. 

 But dealers said the Reserve Bank of India hasn't been seen in the market yet Tuesday. The central bank hasn't even inquired on prices, as it generally does when the market turns volatile, a dealer at a foreign bank said.

 The U.S. currency has been traded at successive new 20-month highs in the previous three sessions. The dollar rose above 36.30 rupees on Oct. 29 and has been rising continuously after that. 

 That rise has been fueled by the increasing belief that the RBI wants the rupee to depreciate slowly in order to lessen the impact of Southeast Asian devaluations on Indian exports. 

 On Monday, the Reserve Bank of India is estimated to have sold between $100 million and $150 million in outright forward contracts and swaps for six months forward, dealers said. 

 That intervention was over and above its sales of $360 million Wednesday and another $200 million Tuesday last.

title: Indian rupee succumbs,  central bank  draws line.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee buckled on Tuesday, sinking to a 21-month low, and looked to be on a one-way street until the Reserve Bank of India intervened to arrest the fall. 

 The rupee ended the day at 37.40/42 to the dollar, sinking 1.4 percent from its close at 36.87/89 on Monday. 

 "It has been a hell of a move... And the rupee is not out of the woods yet," the head of treasury for a major international bank in Bombay said. 

 The rupee hit a low of 37.52, after which heavy central bank intervention and a warning from RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan that the selling should stop prompted a half-hearted rally. 

 "We believe that the adjustment that has already taken place in the value of the rupee is adequate," Rangarajan said in a statement. 

 "In view of the fundamentals, there is no ground for a further weakening of the rupee. 

 "The Reserve Bank of India will not hesitate to intervene to prevent any overshooting." 

 Dealers say the RBI has spent close to $1 billion trying to slow the rupee's slide since the beginning of last week. 

 At its low, the rupee was five percent below early August levels of 35.70, which marked the start of pressure on the rupee after a year of stability. 

 The central bank action restored calm to a feverish market, but failed to wipe out bearishness toward the currency. 

 "It could go down a few percent more,"said Sandeep Nanda, head of research at NatWest Markets. NatWest's forecast of a rupee at 38.30 by March is unchanged but under review, he said. 

 Eyes will be on Bimal Jalan, who takes over from Rangarajan on Saturday as RBI governor, to see what stance he has toward the currency, dealers said. 

 The RBI has espoused a policy of allowing the market to set the rupee's trend, while intervening to smooth any volatility. 

 "The outlook depends a lot on investor confidence and there are some signs of portfolio inflows dwindling, in which case the rupee could fall a lot further," said Mark McFarland, regional economist for Peregrine Securities International Ltd in Hong Kong. "At the moment there is a loss of confidence," he said. 

 The international bank treasury head said uncertainties were hanging over the rupee during the next two months. 

 The political fallout from a report into the 1991 assassination of former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi is threatening to destabilise the minority government. 

 The report, due to be released in parliament later this week, could lay some blame at the feet of United Front coalition members, endangering Congress party support for the government. 

 And the ongoing turmoil in other Asian markets will continue to rub off on India. 

 Collapsing currencies elsewhere in Asia in the last few weeks heightened concern that the rupee was too strong, and when the Hong Kong market led a worldwide dive in stock markets three weeks ago, the rupee began a steady decline. 

 Rangarajan, whose five-year term is ending, said the rupee has been adjusting to the changing circumstances, but after Tuesday morning's precipitous move the necessary adjustment was complete. 

 He said India's economic fundamentals remained strong. 

 India's current account deficit as a proportion of gross domestic product is likely to be 1.4 percent in 1997/98 (April-March), up from 1.0 percent last year -- both very low levels for a developing country. 

 The rupee's strength was built on two pillars: high foreign capital inflows -- as investors streamed in after the economy began liberalising six years ago -- and low import demand. 

 The turn in sentiment against emerging markets after Asian markets imploded meant inflows would slow, economists said. 

 Foreign institutional investors have begun withdrawing funds from India, and an overvalued currency would be a deterrent to money coming in, given the cheaper valuations available elsewhere, economists said. 

 There are also growing expectations that India's economic growth will soon start rising, prompting growing demand for imports and for dollars to pay for them.

title: Indian rupee dips 1.4 pct, ends at 37.40/42 a dlr.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee closed at 37.40/42 against the dollar ON Tuesday, registering a 1.4 percent compared with Monday's close after a day of volatile trading, dealers said. 

 The rupee opened at 36.90/93 compared with the previous close of 36.87/89 and started weakening fast. 

 Bank dealers and forex brokers attributed the rupee's fall to a rush for dollars by Indian corporates, but corporate treasurers and stock market analysts said inter-bank speculation played a complementary role. 

 "The market overreacted," said N.S.Paramasivam, head of forex at Essar Group, a leading Indian private business. 

 "It was a combination of inter-bank (covering) and moderate dollar demand (from corporates)," he said. 

 He said the rupee's sharp movement on Tuesday was more panic-driven than volume-driven. 

 Dealers said the fact that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) did not intervene until the rupee breached the 37.50 level at noon signalled that the central bank was happy with its fall. 

 The RBI intervened in small lots and immediately followed it up with a verbal intervention which cooled the markets. 

 In a statement, RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan said he believed the rupee's adjustment was adequate. 

 "We believe that the adjustment that has already taken place in the value of the rupee is adequate," Rangarajan said. 

 "In view of the fundamentals, there is no ground for a further weakening of the rupee," he said. 

 "The Reserve Bank of India will not hesitate to intervene to prevent any overshooting," the statement warned. 

 Dealers said the State Bank of India (SBI), a major dollar buyer in recent days, who bought on Tuesday morning, revisited the market in late afternoon, buying dollars at 36.40-plus levels. 

 They said the Indian Oil Corporation (IOC), India's largest refiner and monopoly importer of crude oil, has started buying dollars from the domestic market through IOC. 

 IOC has for over a year been raising dollars through offshore debt issues. 

 "It could be due to volatility in the foreign markets that IOC is buying dollars from the SBI," an official of the petroleum ministry told Reuters in New Delhi on Tuesday. 

 There have been reports that IOC has exhausted its ECB (external commercial borrowing) limit of over $3.0 billion but the ministry official said he could not confirm this. 

 Most dealers expect the market to test the 37.50 level on Wednesday, but were divided on whether RBI will defend the rupee with all the resources at its command. 

 RBI's foreign currency reserves exceed $26.0 billion. 

 "RBI seems determined to keep the rupee at this level," said Rohit Malhotra, dealer at ABN-AMRO Bank N.V. in Bombay. 

 But some dealers were not sure. 

 "RBI does not seem to have sold much today," said a dealer at a leading foreign bank, referring to comments from some dealers that the central bank sold over $200 million on Tuesday. 

 "But market participants will be nervous at 37.50 levels," he said. "We will see this level tomorrow itself." 

 Frederick Castellino, chief dealer at brokers Mecklai & Mecklai said importers did not seem to be reassured by RBI's statement. 

 "They think further depreciation is in store. The market is still bearish on the rupee," he said. 

 A dealer at a European bank said he saw the rupee dipping to 38 to the dollar by this month-end. 

 Forward premiums fell in tandem with recovery of the spot rupee but today's action was focused in the spot market, dealers said. 

 R. Balakrishnan, president of Dil Vikas Finance Ltd, said foreign institutional investors (FIIs)'s selling of shares in the local market had little to do with the rupee's fall. 

 "Their (FIIs) net sales are less than $60 million -- it could not have caused today's sharp movement," he said. 

 "There has been no unusually large selling by FIIs in recent days," he told Reuters.

title: Indian rupee buckles,  central bank  says low enough.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee buckled in early trade on Tuesday, sinking to a 21-month low, and looked to be on a one-way street until the Reserve Bank of India intervened to give some support. 

 The rupee slumped in brisk trading to 37.52 to the dollar after opening at 36.90/93 and closing on Monday at 36.87/89. 

 But the Indian currency steadied immediately on RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan's warning to stop selling rupees and heavy central bank intervention. 

 By two p.m. (0830 GMT) the rupee stood at 37.35/38. 

 "We believe that the adjustment that has already taken place in the value of the rupee is adequate," Rangarajan said in a statement. 

 "In view of the fundamentals, there is no ground for a further weakening of the rupee. 

 "The Reserve Bank of India will not hesitate to intervene to prevent any overshooting." 

 Dealers say the RBI has spent close to $1 billion trying to slow the rupee's slide since the beginning of last week. 

 The central bank intervened around midday, just before Rangarajan's statement, as the rupee's decline gathered momentum. 

 "They really hammered the market at 37.50 so I think this should hold for some time. We are looking at 37.50 holding until March end," said Shekhar Sathe, senior vice-president at Kotak Mahindra Capital Company. 

 Earlier, Indian corporates rushed to buy dollars and banks began speculating against the rupee while the RBI held to the sidelines. 

 "Corporates are panicking and with RBI keeping away, it has become a one-way market," said a dealer at a private bank at the height of the action. 

 At its low, the rupee was five percent below early Agust levels of 35.70, which marked the start of pressure on the rupee after a year of stability. 

 "The market is slightly comforted now after the governor's statement that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will not hesitate to intervene to prevent any overshooting of the rupee," said N.S. Paramasivam, head of foreign exchange at the private Essar Group. 

 Collapsing currencies elsewhere in Asia heightened concern that the rupee was too strong, and when the Hong Kong market led a worldwide dive in stock markets three weeks ago the rupee began a steady decline.
