 Foreign institutional investors have begun withdrawing funds from India, and an overvalued currency would be a deterrent to money coming in, given the cheaper valuations available elsewhere, economists said.

title: India/Rupee Closes -2: Dlr Seen Close To 37.00 Rupees Tue

The Reserve Bank of India's interventions Monday come on the back of sales of $360 million Thursday and another $200 million last Tuesday.

title: Indian rupee sinks as firms rush for dollar cover.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee sank to a new 21-month low on Monday as firms rushed for cover amid signs of a slowdown in foreign capital inflows and indications that the central bank will not intervene in a big way, dealers said. 

 The rupee ended Monday at 36.875/895 compared to a previous close of 36.75/76 on Thursday -- most banks were shut for a religious holiday on Friday. Dealers expected the rupee to breach the 36.90 level on Tuesday. 

 "Indian firms are covering their unhedged exposures," said a dealer at a leading Bombay bank. "The realisation has dawned on them that the dollar has only one way to go," he said. 

 The head of foreign exchange at an American bank agreed. 

 "There is widespread corporate buying today," he said. "And dollar supply appears to be drying up." 

 India's capital market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), said on Monday net portfolio holdings by foreign institutional investors (FIIs) fell by $58.4 million between November 1 and 14. 

 SEBI said cumulative FII investments dropped to $9.05 billion from $9.10 billion on November 10. 

 Foreign funds have been under pressure to send money home after taking losses on other Asian markets. 

 But some brokers said there was a growing perception among fund managers that India had no alternative but to allow its currency to depreciate following the collapse in other Asian currency values. 

 The rupee is now just over three percent below its early August levels, when a comment by RBI deputy governor Y.V. Reddy that it appeared to be overvalued in trade-weighted terms triggered pressure on the currency. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI)'s intervention strategy has also unnerved Indian firms which believed the central bank would mobilise its $26.27 billion foreign currency reserves to draw a line under the rupee's fall. 

 "Last week they vigorously defended at 36.75 level, today they intervened in a small way but allowed it to slip further," said a corporate treasury executive. 

 "It is clear they only want to smooth the (rupee's) fall, not arrest it," he said. Indian exporters have been clamouring for a weaker rupee, saying their exports have become uncompetitive after a sharp devaluation by their Asian neighbours. 

 Most dealers said political worries had little to do with the rupee's weakening. Historically, the Indian rupee has been immune to political crises. 

 India is bracing for the presentation of a report on an investigation into the 1991 assassination of former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, which could undermine the United Front coalition government's stability. 

 The minority government led by Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral depends on Congress party support for survival, and Congress has already threatened to reconsider support for the government over the report into the killing of its former leader. 

 Arbitraging between the local forex market and the overseas non-deliverable forward (NDF) market has been keeping the local forward dollar premiums on the higher side, dealers said. 

 Foreign funds are not allowed to hedge their equity investments in India and can hedge only in the NDF markets. 

 Some Indian and foreign entities are selling forward dollars in the NDF market, taking advantage of higher overseas premium and buying cheaper forward dollars at home, dealers said. 

 Indian firms which borrowed cheap offshore loans are also seeking cover. 

 Many Indian firms borrowed overseas when the rupee was steady and the local six month annualised forward dollar premium was at six percent or lower, dealers said. 

 "With six month premium now ruling at over seven percent and spot rupee weakening, most of these firms are scared and rushing for cover," said a company executive. 

 The fact that forward dollar premiums have not traced a fall in domestic interest rates reflects the demand-supply mismatch, dealers said.

title: India  RBI's verbal  intervention  slows rupee's fall.
text:

title: Indian  central bank  races to support falling rupee.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 12 (Reuters) - India's central bank intervened, in its own words, "aggressively and repeatedly" on Wednesday to support a fast-weakening rupee. 

 The rupee at one stage touched 36.75 to the dollar -- its weakest level since February 1996. 

 But persistent Reserve Bank of India (RBI) dollar selling, countering mounting demand from importers and firms needing foreign currency to repay offshore debt, helped the rupee recover slightly by the close . 

 "We intervened aggressively and repeatedly today," an RBI spokeswoman told Reuters. 

 Dealers estimated the central bank sold more than $400 million on Wednesday, over double the amount it threw at the market on Tuesday to cushion the rupee's slide. 

 "Today's intervention should be some sort of record," one dealer said. 

 The rupee has depreciated by nearly 1.5 percent since markets in Asia began plunging three weeks ago. 

 While the scale of the decline pales beside other Asian currencies, Indian importers, anticipating further falls, scrambled for dollar cover as the weakness became manifest. 

 "The RBI is intervening to avoid (India becoming) another victim of the Asian markets contagion," said a senior dealer at Societe Generale bank in Bombay.

title: Indian rupee ends weak despite large RBI dlr sales.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee ended at 36.69/71 against the dollar on a volatile Wednesday marked by aggressive and persistent central bank intervention to arrest the fall in the local currency, dealers said. 

 The rupee opened the day at 36.65/67 to a dollar compared to the previous close of 36.63/65 and quickly began losing ground. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which has been intervening since Monday, stepped in only after the rupee breached the key 36.70-barrier, dealers said. 

 Thereafter, the RBI hit the market repeatedly, selling dollars every time the rupee flared up, dealers said. 

 "They began selling at 36.70/71 and continued upto 36.74," said the chief dealer at a Bombay bank. 

 After the market closed, an RBI spokeswoman confirmed the aggressive intervention. 

 "We intervened aggressively and repeatedly today," she told Reuters, but declined to quantify. 

 Dealers conservatively put today's intervention twice Tuesday's estimated intervention of $200 million. 

 "They must have sold $150 to $200 in the spot and over $200 in the swaps market today," said the chief dealer at a bank. 

 The spot rupee saw a low of 36.75 after the State Bank of India (SBI) entered the market as a dollar buyer. 

 After SBI left the market, the rupee rose briefly to 36.66 before weakening again to 36.72, dealers said. 

 RBI was more aggressive in the forward dollar segment, pulling down premiums by as much as 20 to 25 paise for far-forward maturity dollars, dealers said. 

 October 1998 dollars closed at 2.32/2.35 rupees compared to Tuesday's close of 2.57/2.62 rupees. 

 "Their main aim appears to be to bring down forwards," said Sharukh Wadia, chief dealer at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 "Premiums are expected to come down," he said. 

 The six month annualised premium closed Wednesday at 7.15 percent compared with the previous 7.47 percent, dealers said. 

 A dealer said dollar sales from Indian exporters have shrunk after some of them started selling dollars in the overseas non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets. 

 Foreign investors are not allowed to hedge exchange risk for their Indian investments, especially in the stock market. The overseas NDF market allows them to hedge currency risks. 

 The rupee had weakened in the NDF market following Asian stocks and currency crisis but the gap between premiums in the NDF market and the Indian market has narrowed since last week. 

 Most dealers are looking forward to further, though staggered, depreciation of the rupee. 

 "There is enough corporate demand (for dollars)," said Sunil Sharma, chief dealer at ANZ Grindlays Bank. He said RBI will have to continue its intervention to control the pace.

 "But they are happy with the 36.70 level for now," he said.

title: Indian gov't will not interfere in rupee--Ramaiah.
text:
NEW DELHI, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The Indian government will not interfere in the value of the rupee, Commerce Minister Bolla Buli Ramaiah told Reuters on Wednesday.

title: FOCUS-India rupee seen under pressure vs dollar.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Dollar demand from importers will keep the Indian rupee under pressure this week but sharp falls in the currency's value are unlikely, dealers said. 

 "We expect the rupee to touch 36.60 (per dollar) before the end of the week," said a dealer at a private bank. 

 "Corporate demand (for dollars) remains fairly strong but we do not see the rupee weakening below that," he said. 

 The rupee has been dropping at a rate of about 10 paise (0.1 ruppee) a week since the recent convulsions in East Asian financial markets began just over two weeks ago, but it is still only about one percent lower against the dollar, while other Asian currencies have plunged. 

 The rupee closed Friday at 36.53/54 against the previous week's close of 36.37/38, a fall of 0.4 percent after the government postponed a mega-issue of global depositary receipts (GDRs). 

 The government last week decided to defer a GDR issue by the state-run Gas Authority of India Ltd (GAIL) after it ran into pricing problems. The issue was expected to raise around $800 million. 

 "Basically, the rupee was due for a correction," said a dealer at a European bank. "It is certainly overvalued." 

 The dealer said he expected the rupee to weaken to 37 per dollar by the end of 1997. 

 "I think at some time or the other the turmoil in other Asian markets was bound to affect us," the dealer said. 

 The rupee had remained largely unshaken through the current crisis in Asian markets, which began last summer with the devaluations of several regional currencies. 

 "The decision to defer the GAIL issue triggered the fall in the rupee but there were a number of events which contributed," he said. 

 Besides the GAIL GDR postponement, a statement by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor that the central bank will intervene in the market only to check high volatility also contributed to the rupee's weakening, dealers said. 

 "We will intervene only if there is a high degree of volatility," RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan told reporters on Thursday. 

 "Market players have decided the RBI will not intervene unless the rupee weakens very sharply," said a dealer at a state-run bank. 

 "We will probably see the rupee close weaker by say 3-5 paise (0.03-0.05 rupee) every day for the next few days," he said. "We expect the RBI to start defending the rupee as it weakens past 36.70 levels." 

 Dealers said demand from importers was strong but there were no indications of panic covering which could spark a free fall. 

 "If you look at the movements in the (exchange) rate, volatility has not really been much," said a dealer at a private bank. "A drop of a few paise is nothing great." 

 "There are signs the market is maturing," he added. 

 On Friday the rupee fell nine paise, but later recovered as exporters nipped in to sell dollars. 

 "In earlier days, there used to be one-way movement which would be reversed only by RBI intervention. This time we saw exporters were quite willing to sell at higher levels," the dealer said. 

 Dealers, however, expect the rupee to strengthen against the forward dollar. 

 "I think current levels of forward premiums do not reflect interest rates differentials (between India and the U.S)," said a dealer. "They should be much lower...say around 4.5 percent." 

 The annualised premium on dollars for six-month forward delivery closed on Friday at 7.27 percent against 6.36 percent the previous week. 

 "But premiums may not fall at once," said the dealer. "There will continue to be some covering (by importers) although current levels favour exporters more than importers." 

 The dealer said he expects the RBI to sell forward dollars if the rise in premiums is not checked.

title: India sells dollars to brake rupee's fall.
text:
BOMBAY, Nov 10 (Reuters) - India's central bank intervened in the country's foreign exchange markets twice on Monday to halt the currency's slide which dealers said would continue to be fuelled by corporate demand for dollars. 

 The rupee closed on Monday at 36.58/59 to the dollar, forced unrelentingly down by purchases of dollars from a handful of the country's banks, chief among them the largest commercial bank, the State Bank of India (SBI). 

 "The rupee fell to 36.58/59 at close mainly on SBI's demand," said a dealer at a public sector bank. "This indicates rising corporate demand (for dollars) which will break the 36.60-mark." 

 Earlier on Monday, two bouts of intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had helped stop the rupee from hitting the 36.60 level, dealers said. 

 The rupee opened steady at 36.52/54 a dollar and began retreating immediately, they said. 

 Dealers said the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) started selling at 36.58 levels, after the rupee slipped to 36.59 a dollar. 

 "They began selling at 36.58 and later at lower levels," a dealer said. 

 Some dealers said they had expected RBI intervention as the rupee approached the 36.60-mark, but others said they were surprised since there had been no sharp swings in the exchange rate on Monday. 

 "The rupee weakened much more on Friday, but they were not around," said a dealer at a European bank about RBI. 

 After RBI's intervention, the rupee stabilised at 36.55/56 until about 3.30 p.m. (1000 GMT), when dollar demand from the State Bank of India (SBI) and a handful of other banks dragged the rupee to its earlier lows, dealers said. 

 The rupee, trading in a 36.30/40 band in recent weeks, breached the 36.50-level on Friday on the back of an RBI statement on its intervention strategy, dealers said. 

 RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan told reporters the central bank would intervene only in case of "a high degree of volatility". 

 Dealers said the use of that phrase was interpreted by the market to mean that the RBI was willing to see faster depreciation of the Indian currency. 

 Rangarajan's remark followed closely after the government deferred an $800-million issue of global depositary receipts (GDR) by the state-run Gas Authority of India Ltd (GAIL) because of poor investor response. 

 The deferral of the issue along with other offshore debt issues by Indian firms following the turbulence in Asian markets prompted importers and borrowers to rush for cover on fears of a slowdown in foreign capital inflows, dealers said. 

 Analysts said several other proposed overseas equity issues could be adversely affected by a weak global capital market. 

 "A weak global stock market is likely to have adverse effect on the Indian stock market and may have wide ramifications on the future of the rupee," Societe Generale said in a report. 

 Recent trends suggesting a reversal of a slowdown in Indian industrial growth could spur import demand, adding to the pressure on the rupee, dealers said. 

 The rupee has been dropping at a rate of about 10 paise (0.10 rupee) a week since the recent convulsions in East Asian financial markets began just over two weeks ago, but it is still only about one percent lower against the dollar, while other Asian currencies have plunged. 

 This has rendered many Indian exports uncompetitive and the RBI will have no alternative but to let the currency weaken further, analysts said.

title: India  RBI Deputy Governor: Bank  Intervenes  For Orderly Mkt
text:
BOMBAY (AP-Dow Jones)--Y.V. Reddy, Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank of India, Wednesday said foreign institutional investors account for a large supply of dollars in the Indian foreign exchange market, forcing the central bank to buy and sell foreign exchange at its discretion to ensure orderly market conditions. 

 In a speech at the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade in New Delhi, Reddy said that until recently, 'the foreign exchange market was dominated by trade-related flows and wasn't driven by financial market expectations because the arbitrage opportunities between the Indian and offshore money (financial asset) markets were highly restricted.' 

 But because of major initiatives taken by the RBI to broaden the foreign exchange market in recent years, this has begun to change, he said. 

 Market-makers are now better-placed to give quotes with narrower spreads than before, he said.

title: India Rupee Marginally Up On Early Dlr Sales, Seen Steady
text:
BOMBAY (AP-Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee opened little changed against the U.S. dollar Monday then rose marginally on early dollar sales by a few banks, dealers said. 

 The dollar opened Monday between 36.36-36.38 rupees, then fell slightly to trade between 36.34-36.35 rupees. It had closed Friday between 36.365-36.375 rupees. 

 Dealers said they don't expect much demand for dollars Monday. 'The month-end demand is over,' a senior dealer at a state-owned bank said. 

 As reported, the dollar had risen sharply Friday on the back of usual end-of-the-month demand from local companies. That buying, led by the State Bank of India, the country's largest commercial bank, took the dollar up from its Thursday close of around 36.32 rupees. 

 The State Bank deals on behalf of several large companies, including state-owned oil companies. Its actions often set the trend for the market. Later Friday the State Bank was also reported to have sold the U.S. currency at higher levels. 

 '(The dollar) will come off a bit initially, but there should be some demand later,' a dealer at a large foreign bank said. 

 Most dealers said demand for the U.S. currency will be modest at best, which would rule out any intervention by the Reserve Bank of India. 

 'I don't think (the dollar) will reach a level where the RBI will need to intervene,' the dealer at the foreign bank said. 

 On Friday, dealers said they expected the RBI to sell dollars to cap the dollar's rise at around 36.42 rupees. 

 Those expectations were based on an unusual statement from the central bank on Tuesday. In that statement, the RBI noted the rupee should remain stable in the backdrop of the global stock market meltdown and said it 'will ensure orderly conditions in the foreign exchange market.'

title: Indian rupee bends on dlr demand in holiday market.
text:
BOMBAY, Oct 31 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee closed for the weekend weaker against the dollar after brief fluctuation early on Friday, baffling bankers' expectations that activity would be dampened by the holiday season, dealers said. 

 "We are so used to a static rupee that small volatilities make headlines," said a dealer at a public sector bank soon after the nation's largest commercial bank bought dollars aggressively in early trade. 

 He said Indian firms and banks should get used to two way movements depending on day-to-day factors. 

 The rupee opened Friday steady at 36.31/32, but large purchases by the state-run State Bank of India (SBI) caught the market offguard, and dragged the rupee to 36.41 -- a drop of 0.10 rupees. 

 Throughout the recent turmoil in East Asian currencies, the Indian currency has been relatively stable, losing roughly half a percentage point to 36.40 from 36.20 over the last ten days. 

 That it maintained this level without central bank intervention is widely seen as an achievement, analysts said. 

 Dealers said there was little demand on Friday from any source besides the SBI. "The rupee recovered only after SBI dropped its purchase price below the 36.40 level," one dealer at an Indian bank told Reuters. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) checked prices but did not intervene in the market by selling dollars, dealers said. 

 Yet the rupee failed to entirely make up its losses in a thin market, since inflows from corporates were blocked by the holidays to mark Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights. 

 "Banks were long on dollars," said a senior dealer at a foreign bank. "They went and offered (dollars) to SBI (after SBI had stopped bidding)," he said. 

 Some dealers attributed SBI's demand to month-end dollar payments on behalf of public sector companies. 

 Fund managers who have invested in Indian stock markets said the rupee's stability was a source of comfort. 

 "It's very consoling that the rupee has remained virtually unmoved throughout the crisis," said an official with an overseas fund manager. 

 The inter-bank foreign exchange market saw minor convulsions but the rupee recovered quickly when fears of repatriation by foreign funds proved unfounded, bank dealers said. 

 Despite the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) recent assurance that it was watching the situation and would ensure that orderly conditions prevailed in the forex market, dealers saw the rupee weaken gradually over the next few months. 

 "India's plan to liberalise gold imports should lower the premium on the yellow metal in the country and boost imports, simultaneously boosting forex demand," said one dealer. 

 India's appetite for bullion is among the world's largest. 

 Another factor is Indian firms' increasing preference for domestic debt compared to offshore debt, facilitated by falling domestic interest rates, dealers said. 

 Offshore debt has been one of the important sources of foreign currency in recent months. 

 But falling interest rates have prompted some of India's leading firms to fund new projects through domestic issues instead of the offshore loans they originally envisaged.

title: India Rupee Closes Dn Vs Dlr; Banks Cover Earlier Dlr Sales
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee closed weaker against the dollar Friday on dollar-buying by banks covering earlier dollar sales, dealers said.

title: India  rupee ends steady, RBI in token  intervention .
text:
BOMBAY, Sept 29 (Reuter) - The rupee closed Monday steady against the dollar as a token intervention by the central bank towards the close went largely unnoticed, dealers said. 

 The rupee opened steady at 36.19/20 and moved in a narrow range thorughout the day, dealers said. It closed at 36.18/19. 

 The opening quote was the rupee's lowest point on Monday. 

 It touched a day's high of 36.17 in the afternoon. 

 Moderate dollar demand from the State Bank of India (SBI) and a few others sustained the dollar at this level, a dealer at a public sector bank said. 

 The rupee would have ended around the same level even without Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervention, he said. 

 The RBI stepped in near the close and bought very small amounts - estimated at about $10 million - from a handful of public sector banks in Bombay, dealers said. 

 "They bought $3.0 million from us at 36.19 at closing time," a dealer at a public sector bank in Bombay said. 

 Foreign and major Indian public sector banks which are normally hit by the RBI were spared today, dealers said. 

 "If they hit foreign banks, it will be easily absorbed," said the chief dealer at a foreign bank. 

 He said RBI wanted to achieve its objective -- that it wanted the rupee to continue at the current level -- through relatively cheaper intervention and hence the selection of low profile public sector banks. 

 RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan said in a television interview on Saturday the rupee can and will continue to remain stable at the current levels. 

 "Maybe they (the RBI) wanted to pre-empt (the effect) of any month-end (spurt in dollar) demand," said a dealer. 

 The foreign exchange market will be largely inactive on Tuesday as banks are closed for customer transactions. 

 Banks are again closed on October 2 for a holiday. 

 But dealers said there was no doubt about the rupee was set to extend its gains over the dollar in the coming days. 

 Foreign funds continued to be net buyers on Indian stock markets and there were good dollar inflows from other channels, dealers said. 

 "The RBI is controlling the market very well," said Sharukh Wadia, chief dealer at Standard Chartered Bank, referring to the central bank's double-edged intervention strategy designed to check a sharp rise as well as fall in the rupee's value.

title: Indian  central bank  buys dlr to stem rupee's rise.
text:
BOMBAY, Sept 26 (Reuter) - The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened on Friday to halt the rupee's steady rise against the dollar and dealers said it may need to continue buying dollars in the weeks ahead as fears of a rupee depreciation had abated. 

 The rupee closed Friday at 36.19/20 against the dollar, slightly weaker from its 36.18/20 opening, on the back of two rounds of dollar purchases by the central bank, they said. 

 "The move was gradual, there was no sharp volatility, but they stepped in nevertheless to stop the rupee's rise," said a dealer at a foreign bank. 

 The central bank and the government said earlier this year that RBI interventions aimed to check excessive volatility and that the exchange rate would be determined by the market. 

 But many dealers were unsure whether this was the case. 

 "They did not buy (dollars) yesterday when the rupee rose by ten paise," one dealer said. 

 Dealers had been speculating about RBI intervention since the rupee breached the 36.30-mark, the level at which the central bank bought dollars last Friday. 

 The rupee opened Friday at 36.18/20 compared to the previous close of 36.16/17, dealers said. 

 The morning session saw mild dollar demand, with some trades at 36.20/22 per dollar levels. 

 Dollar sales by some Delhi-based banks, notably a Japanese bank, triggered an appreciation in the rupee which was only arrested by the central bank's intervention, dealers said. 

 The RBI stepped in when the rupee hit a high of 36.175 and stepped up its purchases up to 36.20 levels, dealers said. 

 The rupee began rising again in the afternoon session and towards the close RBI bought dollars from a string of public sector banks in Bombay, dealers said. 

 Continued foreign direct and portfolio investment and foreign equity issues planned by public sector Indian firms would exert upward pressure on the rupee in coming months, dealers said. 

 U.S. investment firm Merrill Lynch said on Friday currency risks in India were lower given the Indian rupee's resilience and stronger fundamentals. 

 "We expect that any weakening of the currency will be limited given that the Indian rupee at 36.2 rupees to a dollar is already close to our fair value estimate of 37.2," it said. 

 Merrill Lynch said low inflation and declining interest rates make the Indian stock market a favoured destination for investment in the Asian region, excluding Japan. 

 Merrill Lynch has recommended increasing its asset allocation in Indian markets. 

 "In India, our views on sharply declining long term interest rates, benign inflation, continued economic reform and attractive valuations underpin our overweight stance," it said. 

 "With expectations of earnings growth of 15 percent in FY98 (financial year ending March 31) and 18 percent in FY99, India is a favourite market in Asia, ex-Japan," it added.

title: Price Stability Key To Floating Asian  Currencies : India RBI
text:
HONG KONG (AP-Dow Jones)--Price stability achieved through adjusting interest rate policies will be the key to ensuring the new floating rate regimes in Southeast Asia succeed, India's central bank chief said Saturday. 

 'With price stability, you can kill many birds with one stone,' Chakravarthy Rangarajan, governor of the Reserve Bank of India said. 

 While the currency depreciations in other Southeast Asian countries will have an impact on India's exports, the country isn't planning on devaluing its currency, the rupee, he said. 

 'We would like the foreign exchange rate to be determined by market forces, but we will intervene quite heavily' to quell volatility, he said. The problem India is having, however, isn't so much depreciating currencies, but an appreciating one, he added, noting the central bank recently had to enter the foreign exchange market to buy foreign currency against the rupee.

title: Exotic  Currency  Focus: India Rupee Seen Calmer After Fall
text:
BOMBAY (AP-Dow Jones)--A swift response by monetary officials to a recent fall in the Indian rupee and continuing foreign investment inflows are likely to keep the currency steady in a relatively narrow range over the coming months, economists and analysts say. 

 After the rupee fell to an 18-month low of 36.72 rupees against the U.S. dollar Sept. 9, down nearly 3% from mid-August, India's Finance Ministry moved rapidly to talk up the currency, while the Reserve Bank of India intervened aggressively to steady the market. 

 Analysts now say the aggressive action has helped to damp concerns that the rupee could be hit by the same speculative selling that has hit Southeast Asian currencies in recent weeks. Foreign investment continuing to flow into the stock market will also help the rupee hold its ground for the near future. 

 Traders and analysts say they expect the rupee to trade in a range between 36.35 rupees and 37.25 rupees to the dollar for the next few months because the fundamentals are strong and foreign inflows are expected to continue. 

 The Reserve Bank of India is also expected to remain vigilant, effectively preventing any further sharp and sudden depreciation of the rupee. 

 Abheek Barua, economist at S.S. Kantilal Inshwarlal Securities Ltd., says the central bank is likely to buy dollars if it falls to around 36.35 rupees, so that the rupee doesn't strengthen too much and hurt export competitiveness. 

 But analysts also note that the the central bank is likely to sell dollars if any major rupee weakness emerges, preventing any climb by the dollar to 37.25 rupees. 

 'A two-way movement in the rupee is more likely than a gradual depreciation,' Barua of SSKI says.

 The rupee dipped to an 18-month low of 36.72 rupees to the dollar this week despite heavy dollar-selling by the Reserve Bank of India to prop up the Indian currency. 

 Comments by key officials Wednesday brought on a rebound, but some analysts question its sustainability. 

 'What we want is orderly conditions in the market,' Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said Wednesday at a conference for economic editors. He noted that India had a much smaller current account deficit - about 1.3% of gross domestic product - than many Southeast Asian countries hit by currency speculation in the past month. 

 And earlier Wednesday, RBI Governor C. Rangarajan issued a statement to the market saying 'the Reserve Bank of India will continue to intervene in the foreign exchange market to reduce volatility and to ensure orderly conditions.' 

 But some economists think the central bank and Ministry of Finance are sending mixed signals to the market because both have also recently noted signs of a widening budget deficit, a possible upswing in inflation, high interest rates, and diminishing growth prospects because the country's poor infrastructure is holding development back.

title: India  RBI to continue  forex intervention -governor.
text:
BOMBAY, Sept 10 (Reuter) - The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will continue to intervene in the foreign exchange market to check volatility, central bank governor Chakravarty Rangarajan said on Wednesday. 

 "The Reserve Bank will continue to intervene both in the spot and forward markets to reduce volatility and to ensure orderly conditions in the foreign exchange market," Rangarajan said in a statement. 

 "The recent volatility seen in the exchange rate has been caused in a large measure by the rush to cover unhedged positions. There has been no basic change in the fundamentals of the economy which continue to remain strong." 

 "Market participants both in the spot and forward markets are, therefore, advised to take note of the basic trends," the governor said. 

 He said the fundamentals of the economy, especially in relation to the external sector, were unchanged and are strong. 

 "The current account deficit has remained low and it is estimated to be at 1.4 percent of GDP for 1996/97. It is not likely to exceed 1.5 percent in 1997/98," he said. 

 He said capital flows under various routes -- non-resident deposits, portfolio investment, direct investments and external commercial borrowings -- are steady and strong. 

Foreign exchange reserves increased by $5.2 billion in 1996/97 and by a further $4.0 billion in the current financial year till the end of August 1997, the governor said. 

 He said the rupee had depreciated against the dollar in the last two weeks after a prolonged period of stability. 

 "The depreciation is of the order of 2.5 percent. At the present level, the rupee depreciation in relation to the dollar is far less than in the case of East Asian currencies which have experienced unusual turbulence," he said. 

 The RBI later clarified that the current account deficit during 1996/97 is estimated at 1.0 percent of GDP and not 1.4 percent as earlier stated.

title: FOCUS-India says won't tolerate rupee volatility.
text:
NEW DELHI, Sept 10 (Reuter) - Indian financial authorities led by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram and the central bank governor on Wednesday threw their weight against currency speculators and vowed to defend the rupee. 

 Their words appeared to have the desired effect. On Wednesday the rupee rose smartly to around 36.475/495 to the dollar at 0730 GMT after closing on Tuesday at 36.59/61. 

 On Monday it ended at a 19-month low of 36.685/95 to the dollar, but recovered on strong RBI intervention on Tuesday. 

 Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor C. Rangarajan said in a statement issued in Bombay that the country's economic fundamentals were strong and the central bank would continue to intervene both in the spot and forward rupee markets to reduce volatility. 

 "While the exchange rate is market-determined, the RBI will not allow volatility and excessive speculation," Chidambaram told an annual meeting of economic editors in New Delhi. 

 "What we want are orderly conditions in the foreign exchange market," he said. "We want orderly conditions in the market and let the market determine the exchange rate." 

 Chidambaram said Southeast Asian exchange markets had been extremely volatile. "It is naive to think that some of that volatility has not spilled over. It has spilled over to the Indian market." 

 After trading at a sedate 35.70 to the dollar for several months, the rupee has been hit by major turbulence over the past few weeks. 

 "There has been no basic change in the fundamentals of the economy which continue to remain strong," Rangarajan said. 

 But Chidambaram was not equally optimistic, saying India's fiscal deficit was under severe pressure. 

 "This year we hope for a further fiscal correction but I am afraid there are severe pressures," Chidambaram told reporters. 

 Chidambaram said the government had estimated the 1996/97 (April-March) fiscal deficit at 5.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) but added: "It may end up at 5.1 percent." 

 "I think it still has not been inscribed on the consciousness of the Indian political and economic leadership that fiscal correction is the single most important goal we must pursue," Chidambaram said. 

 On Tuesday the International Monetary Fund in its annual report urged India to aim for an accelerated reduction in its large fiscal deficit, adding a delay in fiscal adjustment would leave the economy vulnerable to adverse external developments. 

 India aims to reduce its fiscal deficit as a proportion of GDP to 4.5 percent in 1997/98. "The too large fiscal deficit still needed to be tackled decisively," the IMF said. 

 Chidambaram and his chief aide, Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia, were at pains to stress that India was unlikely to be affected by the currency crisis in Southeast Asia because its own economic fundamentals were stronger. 

 "I have said there is some turmoil in the Southeast Asian markets," he said. "I am not of the view that we are affected by the same degree as Southeast Asia." 

 Ahluwalia, the highest-ranking civil servant in the Finance Ministry, said India's current-account deficit as a share of GDP had been hovering between 1.3 and 1.4 percent and noted that in Thailand it was eight percent when that country was hit by the baht crisis. 

 He said Indian banks have reduced their short-term borrowing as opposed to Thai banks which relied heavily on short-term borrowing. "India's situation is hugely different from Thailand's," he said.

title: India must allow rupee to respond to market - IMF.
text:
NEW DELHI, Sept 10 (Reuter) - The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Wednesday urged India to allow its exchange rate to respond to market signals. 

 The annual report of IMF's executive board for the financial year ending April 30, said that its directors had stressed the need for India to have a flexible exchange rate management in close coordination with other macroeconomic variables. 

 A senior IMF official in New Delhi also said that India must move in a phased manner towards full rupee convertibility. 

 "They stressed that the exchange rate should be allowed to respond to market signals and that in managing intervention policy, the authorities should avoid a too mechanical reliance on indicators of the real exchange rate," the IMF report said. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervenes regularly to smoothen any fluctuations in the foreign exchange market. 

 The Indian rupee ended on Monday at a 19-month low, but the RBI cushioned the fall by selling dollars before the market moved too fast, dealers said. 

 The rupee closed at 36.685/95 per dollar on Monday, after opening unchanged at 36.57/59. Spot rupee on Tuesday closed at 36.59/61 against the dollar compared with 36.60/72 opening and 36.68/69 closing, dealers said. 

 The rupee had held steady against the dollar at 35.70/85 for nearly a year until the mid-August watershed. 

 But it had appreciated on its real effective exchange rate index -- which takes into account inflation differentials against a basket of major currencies -- prompting central bank concern. 

 Deputy RBI Governor Y.V. Reddy told a meeting of foreign exchange dealers last month that the rupee is overvalued in light of an analysis of Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) data. 

 IMF would focus on including capital account convertibility in its articles of agreement at its annual meeting to be held later this month in Hong Kong, the IMF official said. 

 "The Fund has decided that capital account convertibility in appropriate circumstances can add to world economic growth and an individual country's prosperity," the IMF official, who asked not to be identified, told reporters. 

 "It has benefits for India but has to be in a phased manner," he said. 

 A panel appointed by the RBI in June submitted its recommendations to make the rupee convertible by the turn of the century. 

 But the IMF official said India must restructure its state-owned banks before getting to capital account convertibility. 

 "There are many weak banks and it is difficult to see how they survive under competition," he said.

title: RBI  intervention  slows Indian rupee depreciation.
text:
BOMBAY, Sept 9 (Reuter) - The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) daily intervention in the currency market aims to ensure its overvalued rupee depreciates smoothly rather than to turn the tide, dealers said. 

 The rupee has fallen by over two percent since the central bank labelled its currency overvalued in mid-August. 

 On Tuesday, the currency hit a 19-month low of 36.72 per dollar, but rallied after the RBI sold up to $120 million and closed at 36.59/61 rupees. 

 Some bankers said it was a correction. "The rupee was falling too much and too fast," said a foreign bank dealer. 

 "The RBI is probably not averse to seeing the rupee further down - maybe around 37.50 by end March. But the problem is, the market is looking to take it there straightaway," he said. 

 "So the RBI is just cooling things down by dollar selling." 

 "The interbank market was long on dollars," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "When RBI sold early in the morning, stop-loss limits were breached and longs were quickly unwound." 

 He said the overall view on the rupee remained bearish. 

 The rupee had held steady against the dollar at 35.70/85 for nearly a year until the mid-August watershed. 

 But it had appreciated on its real effective exchange rate index -- which takes into account inflation differentials against a basket of major currencies -- prompting central bank concern. 

 However, having given the green light to sell rupees, the central bank has had to act to stop a precipitous fall. 

 Some dealers said they expect the central bank aims to pilot the rupee to around 37 rupees per dollar. 

 "I think RBI is helping a soft-landing to 37 (rupees to a dollar) level," Ravi Kumar, chief forex dealer at ABN-AMRO Bank N.V. in Bombay told Reuters. 

 This week, RBI began selling dollars at 36.65 rupees on Monday before stepping up the price to 36.685 and on Tuesday sold at 36.72. 

 Dealers said many Indian exporters had cancelled forward dollar sales, increasing nervousness among Indian firms needing to cover forward dollar commitments. 

 A horde of Indian firms who raised offshore loans and did not take forward cover as the rupee held steady against the dollar until August have now rushed to cover, dealers said. 

 Indian exporters have been complaining that the overvalued rupee was one of the main reasons for the deceleration in India's export growth in 1997/98 (April-March). 

 HSBC Markets said a weaker rupee would act as a deterrent for imports. The government has been seeking to kickstart corporate activity - a weaker rupee would not help it. 

 A strong rupee has been blamed for a deceleration in Indian export growth this year. But latest numbers show April-July exports rose 1.81 percent to $11.03 billion from a year earlier, and July exports rose 6.64 pct to $2.77 billion from a year earlier.

title: HSBC sees RBI  intervention  stabilising  India  rupee.
text:
BOMBAY, Sept 9 (Reuter) - Continued central bank intervention will help steady the Indian rupee in the short term but it was expected to depreciate to around 37.5 per dollar by June 1998, HSBC Markets said on Tuesday. 

 "If the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) continues to defend the rupee at 36.50-70 (which we believe it can and will) over the next few weeks, the apprehensions of importers would subside and the demand-supply situation will revert in favour of the rupee," it said in a commentary on the Indian rupee. 

 On Tuesday the rupee dropped to 36.72 per dollar within minutes of opening before RBI intervention and unwinding of long dollar positions helped it recover to close at 36.59/61. The Indian rupee ended Monday at 36.685/695. 

 "Looking ahead, we expect a depreciation of 4.0-5.0 percent over the next year would find favour with the government and the rupee would move to 37.50 per dollar by June 1998," it said. 

 The commentary said a change in sentiment has triggered the current spell of weakness in the Indian currency. 

 "Importers and borrowers in foreign currency have started to hedge their payables," it said. 

 HSBC Markets said central bank data showed that there had been no drop in supply of spot dollars from corporates but there had been a pick-up in demand for forward dollars. 

 The Indian rupee has weakened by more than than two percent from mid-August when an RBI official said the rupee appeared overvalued. 

 HSBC Markets said it did not rule out skittishness in the foreign exchange market in the short term. 

 "However volatility in the immediate future cannot be ruled out as both importers and exporters try to find out the right level for the rupee."

title: India Rupee Weakens Further Vs Dollar In Midday Trading
text:

 At 0650 GMT (2:50 a.m. EDT), the dollar is trading between 36.6750 rupees and 36.6925 rupees.

 Last Friday, the dollar rose to close at 36.59 rupees, from 36.37 rupees a week earlier despite the RBI selling an estimated $650 million.

An expert committee of the RBI headed by former Deputy Governor S.S. Tarapore on June 3 recommended that the central bank fix a trading band for the rupee of 5.0% on either side of the currency's neutral real effective exchange rate, adjusted for inflation and trade. 

 The panel had suggested that the RBI shouldn't intervene when the rupee was trading within the band except to curb speculation and volatility.

text:

 In the spot section, there was little demand for dollars except from the central bank.

title: India/Rupee -2: Shift In Strategy Seen Aiding Exporters
text:
The Reserve Bank of India has shifted strategy to buy forward dollars to contain the economic effect of its foreign exchange interventions, dealers said. 

India's M3 measure of broad money supply has grown at 16.30% year on year as of July 4, according to the latest data available from the central bank. 

 That growth is way above the RBI's own target of an M3 growth of 15.00%-15.50% for the financial year that began April 1. 

 The RBI's dollar purchases in the spot market add to broad money immediately as it releases rupees into the system. However, its forward market purchases will add to money supply only if and when its takes delivery of its purchases. 

 The RBI also has the option to roll over or even reverse its trades in the forward market before or when the contracts mature. 

 By pushing up the rupee premiums for forward dollars, the central bank also probably hopes to entice exporters to sell their receivables forward, dealers said. The exporters' earnings by way of the premium for their forward dollar sales are expected to at least partly compensate them for the loss the strong rupee has brought on. 

 The premium for January-end dollars closed Tuesday between 0.85 rupee and 0.88 rupee. 

 The Indian rupee has been under tremendous upward pressure for the past few months in the face of continued strong inflows from international investors.

title: =India: RBI Seen Continuing Forward Dlr Buying: Analysts
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of India will continue to buy forward dollars in an effort to keep the Indian rupee from appreciating against the U.S. currency in the spot market, foreign exchange dealers said Monday. 

 But the success of the strategy is difficult to predict, they added. 

 Forward-market intervention probably isn't the central bank's preferred, or most effective, mechanism for trying to affect the spot value of the rupee, but concerns with India's ballooning money supply mean intensive spot market intervention isn't an attractive option at present, dealers said. 

 'They seem to be confused about what to do,' said a dealer at a private-sector bank. 'Their spot dollar purchases don't seem to be having the desired effect on the exchange rate,' he said. 'And they have the monetary impact of the spot-buying to consider,' he added. 

 Monday, the Reserve Bank is estimated to have purchased around $125 million, most of it in the forward market, in three rounds of intervention intended to stop the rupee from appreciating. 

 But despite these forward-market purchases, the rupee gained on the day. The dollar closed around 35.7400 rupees, down from its Friday close between 35.7750 rupees. 

 The intervention wasn't fruitless, traders said. The U.S. currency probably would have sunk below 35.7000 rupees Monday if the RBI hadn't intervened at all. 

 The less-than-successful outcome of intervention Monday stood in contrast to the central bank's actions Friday. A surprise round of forward dollar purchases by the RBI then had sent the U.S. currency shooting higher in the spot market.

title: India's  central bank  knocks rupee to one-month low.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 1 (Reuter) - India's central bank rode a wave of changing sentiment towards the rupee on Friday, buying dollars in the open market to knock the currency to one-month lows. 

 Traders said the rupee dropped briefly below 35.82 to the dollar after heavy intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) combined with import-related dollar buying and covering of short positions in the interbank market. 

 By the close of business it was at 35.78/79 against the dollar after starting at 35.705/710. 

 "It's a combination of factors...RBI buying, import covering, some interbank short-covering," one dealer at a foreign bank in Bombay. "It looks like sentiment has changed, we saw some import covering today for the near months after quite some time." 

 The RBI, unlike beleaguered central banks in Southeast Asia, has been struggling for the past year with a strong local currency due to heavy inflows of foreign funds and weak import demand. 

 In the past 12 months it has appreciated by around seven percent. 

 In recent days the central bank had successfully capped the rupee at 35.70 per dollar, dipping into the market openly or -- to keep the traders guessing -- simply buying the U.S. currency from banks whenever they offered them for sale. 

 India's authorities are worried that persistent rupee strength could dent exports, which tend to be price-sensitive. 

 The Commerce Ministry reported on Friday that exports fell 0.95 percent in the first quarter of the financial year beginning April from the same period a year earlier. 

 Analysts said the drop could be linked to depressed global markets and infrastructure bottlenecks which hold up industrial growth shared the blame along with the rising rupee. 

 "With the appreciation of the rupee and depreciation of the currency in the surrounding countries there will be some anxieties among the exporters," said V. Raghuraman, Secretary General of the Associated Chambers of Commerce.

title: Indian rupee strength bucks regional trend.
text:
NEW DELHI, July 15 (Reuter) - The Indian rupee is bursting with strength, undaunted by either the dollar's supremacy against other major currencies or a domino-effect collapse among south-east Asian currencies, dealers and analysts said on Tuesday. 

 Waves of portfolio investment have poured into Asia's best-performing stock market in 1997. 

 The Bombay stock index is up almost 30 percent from January 1, striking 33-month highs last week, and because of the rupee's strength the profile looks even stronger. There has also been a regular stream of foreign direct investment (FDI). 

 "The reason the rupee's been so strong is the steady inflow of foreign funds and weak import demand," said Nupur Joshi, economist at Jardine Fleming (India) Broking Ltd. 

 "And the central bank has not been intervening as actively as it can." 

 While other central banks around south and south-east Asia are either actively devaluing or battling against tumbling currencies, the Reserve Bank of India has struggled to keep the rupee on a tight rein. 

 The RBI, along with India's largest state-owned commercial bank, State Bank of India, dominates India's currency market. 

 But the cost of intervening is causing a growing problem for the RBI, which has to neutralise the growth in money supply caused by selling rupees for dollars. 

 India's foreign currency reserves totalled $25.4 billion in June, compared with $17.3 billion a year ago. 

 Portfolio investment inflows and FDI amounted to $5.0 billion in 1996/97 (April-March). And since April portfolio investment inflows have totaled around $700 million. There are no reliable figures for FDI inflows this fiscal year. 

 Add to this the herd of Indian corporates raising foreign currency loans abroad. The flood of money coming in will test the RBI's ability to contain the rupee for much longer. 

 About $50 billion is traded in rupee-dollar transactions each month, according to RBI estimates. 

 The power of inflows is likely to get greater as India moves towards a capital account convertibility. The rupee is presently convertible on the current account. 

 An unexpected absence of RBI intervention allowed the rupee to break below 35.70 to the dollar on Friday, marking its strongest level for seven months. It finished Tuesday around 35.71, after the RBI came in again to sell rupees. 

 On its real effective exchange rate (REER) the rupee has appreciated by around seven percent in the last 12 months, analysts said. The RBI does not publish its REER index on a daily basis, so uptodate, precise calculations are difficult. 

 India's rung further down the development ladder puts the rupee in a different cycle from south-east Asian currencies. 

 "India is an emerging market, not an Asian market," said Mark McFarland, economist at Peregrine Brokerage Ltd in Hong Kong. 

 South East Asian countries are well established on their development paths, while India is coming from a lot further back, analysts said. Liberal economic reforms began in India in 1991, but have regained impetus in the last year under the stewardship of Finance Minister P.Chidamabaram. 

 "India is different because it is just liberalising. The inflows of foreign capital are linked to the changes in policy it is nothing to do with arbitraging interest rates or anything like that," Mcfarland said. 

 That drive towards reform have put India further along the track than its South Asian competitors, Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. All three countries currencies have weakened either through pegged devaluations or slowly guided depreciation. 

 The currency divergence with its neighbours will hit India's exports, which are, software sector apart, low value added and price sensitive, analysts said. 

 Ravi Kumar, chief dealer at ABN-AMRO Bank in Bombay said a strong rupee to pay for capital imports and to build the home market made abundant sense, even if the export sector suffered.

title: India Strong Rupee Seen Chance For Liberalizing Imports
text:
NEW DELHI (AP-Dow Jones)--Stubborn strength in the Indian rupee could provide the government an opportunity to move quickly to dismantle its remaining barriers to imports and spur economic growth, but only if it can overcome daunting political obstacles, analysts and officials say. 

 While countries in South-East Asia have seen their currencies tumble in recent weeks, Indian monetary officials have been faced with the opposite problem: a currency becoming so strong than many fear the country's exports will be priced out of world markets. 

 As foreign investment pours into the country, some of it apparently redirected from bleak markets elsewhere in Asia, the Reserve Bank of India has been forced to repeatedly intervene in the market to buy dollars to prevent the rupee from rising too far. That in turn has pushed money supply well above the central bank's targeted level. 

 But some observers - including India's main trading partners - argue that this problem could be solved if the country opens its markets to more imports by scrapping remaining quotas and other restrictions. 

 'Given the level of inflows, one has to start taking these steps. Otherwise the rupee will remain highly overvalued,' said Anindya Chatterjee, an economist with Natwest Markets in Bombay.

title: Strong global dollar bends before the Indian rupee.
text:
BOMBAY, July 14 (Reuter) - The U.S. dollar, surging against major global currencies, was fighting a losing battle against the Indian rupee on Monday, dealers said. 

 The rupee ended the day a shade weaker after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened in the market, buying dollars to push the rupee to close at 35.72/73 against a 35.71/72 opening. 

 The dollar had closed at the latter level on Friday after the RBI intervened when the Indian currency broke through the crucial 35.70-mark to trade at 35.69. 

 The market was looking to the RBI from early Monday morning but dollar purchases by the State Bank of India (SBI), India's largest bank, helped hold the dollar at the 35.71/72 level. 

 SBI's dollar purchases usually move the thin Indian foreign exchange market. 

 After SBI withdrew from the market, the rupee eased to 35.7050/7100, threatening to test the 35.70-barrier, provoking RBI's entry, dealers said. 

 RBI bought unspecified amounts of dollars upto the 35.73 level, dealers said. On Friday too, RBI purchases had pushed the rupee to 35.72/73 before closing at 35.71/72, they said. 

 "The (dollar) supplies were heavy today," said the treasurer of a European bank in Bombay. 

 India's leading truck maker Tata Engineering and Locomotive Company is raising $200 million in overseas debt and two Indian telecommunications firms are about to begin road shows to tap the global capital market. 

 Foreign institutional investors (FII) continue their purchases on Indian bourses. On July 10, FIIs' net purchases on the Bombay Stock Exchange alone amounted to 80 million rupees, according to latest data released by the exchange. 

 "The RBI has decided to put the dollar on 'intervention oxygen' only in extreme cases," said a dealer.

 "The forex market has become a graveyard for dealers," said a dealer at a European bank in Bombay. "If the fundamentals are so strong, they should allow the rupee to strengthen," he said. 

 "Otherwise the RBI should open a dollar purchase window," he said. He said the central bank's current unannounced interventions left most banks groping in the dark.

title: Indian  central bank  brakes rupee's rise vs dollar.
text:
BOMBAY, July 11 (Reuter) - The Indian rupee softened on Friday after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened to cap the currency's gains but it remained around its strongest level for seven months against the U.S. dollar, dealers said. 

 They said the RBI bought dollars after the rupee broke through the 35.70 per dollar barrier, pushing the rupee down to 35.725 in afternoon trade. 

 "The whole purpose of today's trade was to find at what level the RBI will show its hand," said Ravi Kumar, chief forex dealer at ABN-AMRO Bank. 

 "It was a classic market versus RBI situation. And show their hands they did." 

 But the rupee recovered once the RBI went off the market to end at 35.71/72 against its previous close of 35.735/745. 

 Dealers said Friday's trade was crucial in determining whether the RBI was prepared to defend the dollar. 

 Lack of central bank intervention was largely responsible for the rupee hitting a seven-month high on Thursday, dealers said. Opening at 35.755/765, the rupee hit an intraday high of 35.735 as the RBI kept to the sidelines. 

 The RBI's absence from the market on Thursday triggered speculation on whether the central bank would check the rupee's gains or let market forces determine the exchange rate. 

 Dealers said the RBI has been constrained by the impact intervention has on the domestic money market. The RBI's dollar purchases cause an injection of rupees into the banking system, boosting money supply growth.

 The decision was made after a meeting between RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan and finance minister P. Chidambaram last Saturday, the newspaper said. 

 An RBI spokeswoman declined to comment on the report. 

 The spokeswoman said RBI's intervention policy was guided by the demand-supply situation in the market and it sought to even out any mismatches. 

 The other objective was to keep the value of the rupee close to the real effective exchange rate, the spokeswoman added. 

 Indian exporters have recently complained about the exchange rate, saying the rupee was overvalued and its strength had hurt their competitiveness in international markets.

title: Reining Indian money supply growth seen tough job.
text:
BOMBAY, July 2 (Reuter) - India's central bank has a tough job trying to keep money supply within targets with foreign capital inflows continuing unabated and the government delaying a long-pending hike in petroleum prices, analysts said on Wednesday. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor C. Rangarajan on Monday reiterated the central bank's commitment to maintaining the money supply growth in the 15.0-15.5 percent target. 

 The M3 money supply growth rose to 16.6 percent on June 6 compared with 16.4 percent on May 23, according to latest figures released by the RBI. 

 "The key to both (controlling) money supply as well as rupee's depreciation is in the oil price hike," Chetan Ahya, analyst at Caspian Research said. 

 He said state-run oil firms have been raising offshore loans to pay for oil imports as the government has not reimbursed billions of rupees it owed these firms for the oil subsidy. 

 The oil price hike will raise revenues for oil firms who could then buy dollars from the local inter-bank market to fund imports, Ahya said. The resultant spurt in dollar demand will also help depreciate the overvalued Indian rupee, he added. 

 The RBI has been conducting regular repo auctions in recent months to mop up excess liquidity with banks but this is not sustainable over a long period, Anindya Chatterjee, economist at NatWest Markets, said. 

 Large capital inflows combined with RBI's dollar purchases from the market to arrest the rupee's appreciation have been fuelling money supply growth in recent months, analysts said. 

 India's foreign currency reserves rose to $24.88 billion on June 20, 1997, from $17.13 billion in June 1996. 

 Banks, flush with funds because of growing deposits and poor credit offtake, have been investing heavily in government securities and parking funds with RBI through repo auctions. 

 RBI's decision last week to cut the benchmark bank rate and the one-year deposit rate will also help to push down yields and reduce speculative inflows into the debt market, money market dealers said. 

 The RBI could control the money supply growth through several measures -- but each of them will be a difficult choice, French bank Societe Generale said in a India commentary. 

 It said the RBI could suspend its intervention in the foreign exchange market, but it would not be in the interest of Indian exporters. 

 The government could issue fresh bonds to mop up liquidity, but over 50 percent of the budgeted borrowing programme is already over in the first quarter of 1996/97 (April-March). 

 The RBI could impose cash reserve requirement on expatriate Indians' foreign currency-denominated deposits, the bank said. 

 This may lead to a slowdown in expatriate Indians' deposits but such a move will not be welcomed by overseas Indians or banks, analysts said.

title: INDIA RUPEE - India hitting  currency  pain barrier.
text:
BOMBAY, June 19 (Reuter) - As India moves toward capital account convertibility the country's central bank must decide whether it can pay the price of a rampant rupee. 

 The Reserve Bank of India bought around $5.0 billion in 1996/97 ended March 31 and around $2.0 billion in the first two months of this fiscal year to try and halt the rupee surfing higher on a wave of foreign capital inflows. 

 But bigger waves are on the horizon as India moves further toward convertibility, and managing the consequent increase in broad money supply will become an acute problem, analysts said. 

 "The big danger is on the rupee. Already we are seeing more and more pressure on it. The RBI has to make a big policy decision on what kind of currency it wants," said Nupur Joshi, economist at Jardine Fleming (India) Broking Ltd. 

 Exporters have already hit the pain barrier. 

 The rate of export growth in April went into fast reverse, clocking a negative 10.8 percent compared with a positive 13.7 percent in April last year, according to data from the Federation of Indian Export Organisations. 

 Exporters say the trend began in 1996/97 when export growth slumped to four percent from 21.4 percent the year before. 

 "India faces a very well defined problem," Mark McFarland, economist with Peregrine Brokerage Ltd in Hong Kong said. 

 "It exports low value-added products to the world market, and their competitiveness is very much tied to the exchange rate. Allowing the currency to appreciate will only make it worse." 

 South Asian neighbours' currencies have all fallen against the dollar in the past year, to add to Indian exporters' woes. 

 India is losing market share for high value basmati rice to Pakistan, tea to Sri Lanka, and jute and garments to Bangladesh, warned one banker. 

 The Pakistan rupee has fallen around 15 percent against the dollar over the past 12 months, and the Sri Lankan rupee is down 5.5 percent on a year ago. 

 Meantime the Indian rupee has stayed stubbornly strong against a dollar which has surged against other international currencies, making the rupee's trade weighted performance even stronger. 

 The rupee was trading at around 35.82 to the dollar on Thursday, virtually unchanged from a year ago. 

 The lack of diversity in India's export sector increased the vulnerability of the trade performance, analysts said. 

 Anindya Chatterjee, economist at NatWest Markets in Bombay, believed official expectations of 15-20 percent growth in exports this fiscal year were overblown. 

 "India's exports, which are non-oil and non-electronics are not going to grow by more than eight percent in 1997/98," Chatterjee said. At the same time imports will head higher. 

 That spells some hard work lowering India's debt service ratio from 25 percent to 20 percent, after successfully whittling it down from 35 percent when the country embarked on its liberalisation programme in 1991. 

 Aggressive central bank intervention has helped build India's foreign exchange reserves to their highest levels ever, at $28.22 billion in early June compared to $21.62 billion a year ago. 

 But the RBI has to face a stark choice on whether to let the rupee firm, when its strength is already damaging exports, or miss its monetary target of 15.0-15.5 percent for M3. Data for late May showed M3 growing at 16.4 percent. 

 The worst case scenario would be a rising rupee and rising inflation, setting the scene for a future currency shock. 

 Under the timetable proposed by an expert committee earlier this month, India will relax barriers on outflows of funds before lifting the boom on inflows to try to offset the impact of the incoming funds on the monetary base. 

 So far the RBI has neutralised the monetary impact of extra rupees in circulation from forex intervention by selling government paper to take the rupees out of the system. But this so-called "sterilisation" is only a short term answer.

title: India money supply gets priority over rupee - RBI.
text:
BASLE, Switzerland, June 9 (Reuter) - Controlling money supply growth is more crucial to India's central bank than the exchange rate, but intervention to hold back the strong rupee can be sustained, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) deputy governor Y.V. Reddy said on Monday. 

 Asked where the RBI's priority lay between money supply growth and the rupee rate, Reddy said the former held the key. 

 "Money supply is naturally the dominant factor that we have to keep in view," he told Reuters Financial Television while attending the annual meeting of the Bank for International Settlements in Basle. 

 "If the money supply goes out of hand then it will ultimately result in inflation and exchange rate distortions -- so they are not separate in that sense," he said. 

 The RBI has a 15.0-15.5 M3 monetary growth target. Latest M3 data, on May 9, showed growth running at 16.3 pct year on year. 

 Heavy RBI intervention in the currency market, buying dollars and selling rupees, has raised worries that domestic monetary growth could surge unless the central bank sterilises the inflow of rupees through sales of government debt. 

 Reddy said the RBI had managed to do this successfully in 1996/7 (April-March) and could do so again if needed. 

 "Last year actually we intervened and mopped up more than $5.0 billion and managed with a money supply of just 15.6 percent." 

 "And in the first two months of this year (April-May) we have already intervened...(to the tune of) $2.0 billion," he said. 

 "It just shows that we can do that and we may have to continue to do that," he added. 

 The rupee was trading at 35.78 to the dollar on Monday morning in Bombay. 

 Reddy said the RBI had a large enough stock of government debt to sell, but this would have to be combined with other measures to sterlise any sustained intervention. 

 He said India was on the right track for capital account convertibility, as mapped out in a report by a committee appointed by the RBI which was published last week. 

 He also said he did not see any particular reason for a rapid moderation in foreign capital inflows into India after they doubled to $6.5 billion in 1996/7.

title: India seen facing macro maze on convertible rupee.
text:
BOMBAY, June 4 (Reuter) - India's plan for a fully convertible rupee by the turn of the century poses the problem of stopping an overvalued currency getting stronger, analysts said on Wednesday. 

 Rajan Govil, economist at HSBC B & K, reckons the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will have to engineer a weaker rupee soon, helped by a slowdown in capital inflows. 

 "Exports were down 10 percent in April and and the strong rupee is a major reason," he said. 

 He expected the RBI to drag the rupee back to 37.8 to the dollar by March 1998, compared to Wednesday's rate of 35.77. 

 But India will pay for its more competitive exchange rate with higher inflation, Govil said. 

 A committee headed by former central bank governor S.S. Tarapore, which on Tuesday presented a report commissioned by Finance Minister P. Chidamabaram on how to make the rupee convertible on the capital account, was quite clear on the exchange rate risks involved. 

 "The international experience has shown that liberalisation of the capital account induces large capital inflows, which can cause a real appreciation of the exchange rate and erode the effectiveness of certain domestic macroeconomic policies," the report said. 

 The committee recommended that an inflation rate of three to five percent was one prerequisite for full convertibility. 

 It also said the Reserve Bank of India should be given more independence to pursue this goal. 

 Deregulation of interest rates and a reduction in banks' cash reserve ratio (CRR) to three percent by 1999/2000 from the current 9.5 percent were also on the committee's wish list. 

 Somehow the RBI must balance these goals with managing the exchange rate. 

 Most analysts reckon the rupee should be shedding three to five percent of its value annually, based on purchasing power parity criteria which take account of inflation differentials between India and major convertible currencies. 

 And Chidambaram, while leaving the RBI to do the job, said last month he would not like the rupee to strengthen further. 

 The RBI has intervened heavily to stop the rupee appreciating. 

India's foreign exchange reserves, including gold and special drawing rights, have shot up to $27.79 billion, covering seven months' imports, from $21.6 billion a year ago -- which is a positive by-product for a country pursuing convertibility. 

 But the sale of rupees for dollars increases the domestic money supply, which will lead to inflation unless the RBI sterilises the surplus rupees through sales of government debt. 

 That is exactly what the RBI has done. 

 It has sold government paper covering around one-third of the central government's 1997/98 borrowing requirement in the first two months of the fiscal year. 

 Economists wonder what the RBI will do if the rupee is still straining at the leash at the end of the year, when there is little debt left to sell. 

 The authorities will be left with a stark choice of either letting the rupee rise or allowing inflation to rise, Sanjeev Sanyal, analyst at Bombay brokerage SocGen-Crosby, said. 

 "We're expecting the wholesale price index to average eight percent in 1997/98 against 6.4 percent last year," said HSBC's Govil. The WPI is running at 6.0 percent. 

 The Tarapore committee has pitched for an ideal, where all targets are achieved and the rupee can make a soft landing into the world of full convertibility. 

 But analysts are sceptical that the macroeconomic targets can be achieved. 

 A currency analyst at a major U.S. investment bank said India should press ahead with convertibility even if the targets are missed, as the markets could then force the monetary and fiscal discipline wherever the authorities fail. 

 "If you do not have a credible policy you should go ahead with capital convertibility because the markets will force one on you," he said. 

 The rupee has remained stubbornly strong, backed by heavy capital inflows, against the dollar, which itself is strong against other major currencies. 

 The U.S. banker said the rupee is currently overvalued by 10 percent on its real effective exchange rate index (REER) using 1993 as base year. 

 The Tarapore committee has recommended that the central bank try to hold the rupee in a plus or minus five percent band on its REER index. 

 It also said the index should be published to provide the market with a guide to the authorities' intentions. Currently, only an out of date REER index is published by the RBI, which releases the data infrequently. 

 "I think there is a real risk. You have to sterilise that intervention. The RBI has to resolve what it wants to target - money supply or REER," the U.S. investment banker said.

title: Indian rupee ends up on aggressive RBI dlr buying.
text:
BOMBAY, June 2 (Reuter) - The Indian rupee closed at 35.8050/8150 after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened aggressively on Monday to arrest the rupee's rise, dealers said. 

 Spot rupee opened steady at 35.78/79 and was mostly firm until noon in the absence of major demand. 

 As an expected dollar demand from the RBI did not take place until early afternoon, the rupee started rising, touching a high of 35.77, triggering RBI action, dealers said. 

 The RBI started buying in lots of $5.0 million at 35.78 and continued its buying upto the 35.80 level, dealers said. 

 "It was aggressive and they must have bought a large amount today," said a dealer. 

 "RBI's action was better today (compared to its dollar buying in recent days)," said a dealer. "The market was caught short and rupee touched 35.810 because of short-covering." 

 Towards the close, dollar demand from cities outside Bombay pushed down the rupee to the day's low of 35.815, a dealer at a state-run bank said. 

 RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan told the Indian Merchants Chamber on Monday the central bank sought to arrest the appreciation of the rupee and to keep the exchange rate "fairly stable." 

 He said RBI wanted a proper integration of the forex and money markets and and sought to achieve the twin objectives of inflation control and a competitive exchange rate through its day-to-day operations. 

 Forward dollar premiums continued to soften as exporters, resigned to a strong rupee, continued to sell their dollar receivables, a dealer said. 

 The six month annualised forward premium fell to 4.36 percent compared to the previous close of 4.47 percent. 

 "Premiums may go down to 4.25 percent but that may be the bottom for now," said a dealer. 

 "A government auction may appear next week and there would be tax outflows (from the banking system) on June 15," he said. 

 "But after all is said and done, the upside is absolutely limited, and 4.8/4.9 percent should be a safe cap."

title: India Rupee Steady Early Despite Selling Pressure On Dollar
text:
BOMBAY (AP-Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee opened little changed against the U.S. dollar in a thin market Wednesday as players sought to push the U.S. currency lower in an effort to test the market's downside, dealers said. 

 'There was a bit of selling pressure on the dollar, but not much business was transacted,' a dealer at a state-owned bank said. Only a couple of small trades were reported, following the first 10 minutes of dealing, which saw no trades at all, dealers said. 

 The dollar-selling, however, was cautious, because most players fear the Reserve Bank of India might intervene to prevent the rupee from appreciating against the dollar, dealers said. 

 The dollar opened between 35.83 rupees and 35.84 rupees and is currently trading between 35.835 rupees and 35.840 rupees, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed Tuesday between 35.835 rupees and 35.840 rupees. 

 'I think the dollar should bottom out around 35.825 rupees,' the chief dealer at a private sector bank said. 'If it gets buying support from the Reserve Bank (of India) or the State Bank, it will top around 35.865 rupees.' 

 State Bank of India is the country's largest commercial bank and it trades in the market on behalf of several large companies, including state-owned oil companies. Its dollar purchases Tuesday pushed the dollar up from its intraday low. 

 Dealers said the RBI was unlikely to buy dollars Wednesday, because current exchange-rate levels are thought to be within the range viewed as acceptable to the central bank. 

 'The RBI will step in only if the dollar falls below 35.83 rupees,' a dealer at a foreign bank said. The central bank wasn't seen in the market Tuesday, dealers said. 

 The RBI is estimated to have bought $450 million last week and an estimated $30 million to $50 million Monday. Those purchases were aimed primarily at setting a floor for the dollar against the rupee, dealers said. 

 In the fiscal year ended March 31, the RBI is reported to have bought $7.8 billion to keep the rupee from appreciating against the dollar and thereby hurting India's exports. Of this, $1 billion worth of purchases are estimated to have been made in March alone.
