title: India says market can set rupee rate, within limits.
text:
BOMBAY, May 12 (Reuter) - Judging by Indian monetary authorities' words and action currency traders can play with the rupee anywhere between 35.75-90 per dollar, albeit under the watchful eye of the central bank, dealers said on Monday. 

 The Reserve Bank of India has intervened on a daily basis within that range, but as soon as the 35.75 level is neared the central bank dollar buying become heavier, they said. 

 Both the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor Chakaravaty Rangarajan and Finance Minister Palaniappen Chidambaram have said the market should set the exchange rate. 

 But only regular central bank intervention has stopped the rupee firming sharply. Chidambaram spelt out the RBI strategy in an interview with Reuters Financial Television on Sunday. 

 "The RBI is not intervening indiscriminately," the Finance Minister said. "Within a band it allows the rupee to fluctuate and it's only when it goes beyond the band does the RBI intervene." 

 The RBI's recent forays into the market have signalled how far the market can go. 

 "I think a 35.75-35.90 range seems to be indicated if you look at the two levels of intervention," said a dealer. "They (RBI) stepped in when the rupee looked like breaking 35.75 but allowed the market to find its own level back from 35.89." 

 In late trade Monday, the rupee was quoted 35.835/842, against 35.840/845 at Friday's close. 

 RBI intervention is one-way at the moment. Poor dollar demand and strong supply will keep the rupee buoyant in the near term and only the RBI can stem its rise, dealers said. 

 "At the moment the only demand is from the RBI," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "Left to itself, the rupee can only appreciate." 

 Dealers also said the situation was ideal for building up foreign exchange reserves, currently equivalent to seven months imports at $26.65 billion, ahead of an end goal of full convertibility. 

 Exporters have been asking for a depreciation in the rupee against the dollar, complaining that its strength is undermining their competitiveness. 

 Analysts also reckoned that the rupee should depreciate by anywhere between three and six percent annually to reflect inflation and other economic fundamentals. 

 But Chidambaram said on Sunday the rupee was currently at the right level and the market should set the rate. 

 "No, I do not think we should induce a depreciation just to boost someone's confidence," Chidambaram said in reply to a question whether the rupee should be weakened. 

 "Once you say the rupee will find its level in the market, then you must leave it to the market," he said. 

 The rupee has traded in a broad 35.75-35.90 per dollar range since last July. In recent weeks it has threatened to break through the 35.75 barrier but was blocked by RBI intervention. 

 Dealers said the RBI bought $400-500 million last week to push the rupee down to its current levels from last Monday's opening of 35.75. RBI purchases weakened the rupee to 35.89 on Wednesday before it rallied to current levels.

title: Exotic  Currency  Focus: India Rupee Seen Set For A Fall
text:
NEW DELHI (AP-Dow Jones)--Currently considered overvalued against the dollar, the Indian rupee is poised to fall about 3% to 5% later this year, economists and analysts said. 

 Some predict the rupee may drop sharply, as it did in late 1995 and early 1996, when speculative forces hit the currency after two years of stability. 

 Others suggest that the fall may be more gradual, with the central bank taking the lead in nudging the Indian currency lower toward its fundamental level, seen by some around 36.5 rupees per dollar. 

 But there's a general consensus the rupee will fall, as the current overvaluation is unsustainable in the longer term. Economists say the rupee needs to weaken against the dollar to make exports more competitive - exports in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1997 grew by around 4%, well down from growth of almost 21% in the previous fiscal year. 

 The dollar currently trades around 35.865 rupees, down a touch from 35.89 rupees at the end of 1996. 

 A recent report by DSP-Merrill Lynch warned of a heightened 'probability of a sharp depreciation in the future. 

 The report argues that the Reserve Bank of India will intervene less actively in coming months to prevent the rupee's appreciation. Without active central bank intervention, the rupee is expected to remain overvalued in the near term, setting it up for a sharp fall later in the year, the report stated, as an overvalued rupee isn't sustainable over a longer period. 

 'In such a scenario, the currency is likely to fall below the fundamental levels on speculative pressure, before recovering on active RBI intervention,' it predicts. 

 Despite annual inflation of 6%-8% over the past few months, the rupee has held steady against the dollar in recent months, even as the dollar rose sharply against many other world currencies. 

 That suggests an overvaluation on an underlying real exchange rate basis. The rupee has been supported by large capital inflows from external commercial borrowing, by issues of Global Depository Receipts by Indian companies and foreign investment inflows.

title: Daewoo, W.I. Carr analysts views on Indian markets.
text:
BOMBAY, April 2 (Reuter) - Following are the views of two analysts interviewed by Reuters Financial Television on Wednesday on how India's political crisis could affects its financial markets and the future course the markets could take: 

 -- 

 Tushar Sarda, President and chief executive officer at Daewoo Securities in Bombay AND Dilip Rathore, senior economist at W.I. Carr in Singapore: -- 

 Q. Foreign investors seem to have been caught unawares by those political developments over the weekend. Do you think the markets have over-reacted somewhat? 

 SARDA 

 "I think the markets over-reacted on Monday, but since yesterday they have started recovering and I expect the recovery to continue over next couple of days." 

 Q. What kind of specific levels are you looking at? Do you see support rather strong around the current level it holds? 

 SARDA 

 "I would expect all the losses to be recovered. On Monday, the market had fallen by about 300 points. I expect the entire losses to be recovered. The markets had gone down on the expectation that the government would be dismissed and the budget may not be passed in parliament. 

 But, what has emerged in the last couple of days is that there is a broad consensus amongst all political parties that it was a good budget and all efforts must be made to pass the budget. That should boost the confidence of foreign investors in India." 

 Q. Do you think that any other surprises are out there for investors or is most of the bad news out of the way and the focus will be on just passage of the budget? 

 RATHORE 

 "No, the focus will be on the passage of the budget, there is no doubt about it. But, I don't think all the bad news is out of the way yet. Because, we still don't know what the political outcome will be, which means there might be a delay in finally getting the economic management acts together finally. 

 It could take about three months or maybe even four months before they can really start implementing the reforms program... but I don't see any major threat to the new economic reforms program that were announced in the budget which was very pro-market and...I would say very good." 

 Q. What kind of investor strategy would you recommend towards India? 

 RATHORE 

 "I would recomend actually buying on the dip right now, because long term and medium term, India does offer very good earnings prospect... The growth in particular, GDP (Gross Domestic Product) is going to take off and people are now talking about an eight percent growth. 

 In that set-up, I would think investors should just set aside political considerations as long as they can hold onto their investments for maybe, a year. 

 Q. How would you describe the recent investor flow into India? Has it been investors with -- that kind of year outlook or more medium term outlook or has it been...people look for a quick market ride and to get out just as quickly? 

 SARDA 

 "I think the money which has come into India since 1992, initially it was short-term money, when investors were looking for a quick ride on the market. But, what has happened over the past 1-1/2 years is that we have seen money flowing into the country from investors who are really committed to India and who are investing over a longer time frame. 

 I would think that their time frame would be a minimum of five years. They would really not be disturbed by what has happened over the week-end. In fact on Monday and Tuesday, we saw very strong buying from these long-term committed investors." 

 Q. Again, the confidence vote coming up in the next few weeks, do you expect the market to bounce back significantly. 

 RATHORE 

 "Not in the next few weeks. I would think that the market would wait for a while. It all depends on how the political event shapes up during the course of this week itself. But, I do not expect any major improvement in the market. For example, coming back to the same level as the last week in the short-term." 

 Q. Staying with that, the currency has been rather untouched by the political situation. Do you think it could become vulnerable or do you think the central bank would dampen any speculation.? 

 RATHORE 

 "The central bank is going to intervene as they have intervened always in the past, and now of course, they are backed by huge foreign exchange reserves. Since you know, one of the reasons why imports of consumer goods were liberalised was because the rupee was under buying pressure, for a change... 

 But, even if there is an outflow of capital and there is selling of rupees. I think the Reserve Bank of India has enough reserves to defend it and they will intervene in the market. So, I would expect the rupee to remain stable against the US dollar. 

 Q. In terms of the size of the budge and its passage, what is key to further investment growth into India from here." 

 SARDA 

 "The crisis has given a message that there is a political consensus on the reforms and I think that would be the key to the further growth of investment into the country. Whether it is the Congress party or the United Front or the Bharatiya Janata Party, everybody is agreed that the reforms must continue. 

 And therefore, the political risks of investments into India comes down significantly. 

 The only worrying factor is that there should be some government which continues with announcement of policy measures and implementation of these things. We should not lose too much time on that." 

 RATHORE 

 I think.. economic reforms are the most important, guiding factor for foreign investors right now and if there is some chance of political stability, that should be positive for the foreign investment inflows... 

 I think all political parties are now agreed on the course of reform, that the economy has to become pro-market and they have to go for economic liberalisation. That is in the positive direction. 

 The only problem is in implementation of the policies for which political stability is important. And, we do need to see a stable government, otherwise we will continue to see some sort of fluctuation in the market mood. 

 The other important point..is that they have to do something about the infrastructure sector which is always causing some long term worries for investors.

title: Political drama seen leaving Indian rupee untouched.
text:
BOMBAY, April 1 (Reuter) - India's unfolding political drama is unlikely to infect the rupee as the central bank possesses more than enough muscle to dampen any speculative fever, foreign exchange dealers said. 

 India's currency markets were shut on Tuesday as banks finalised their year-end accounts. 

 But there little worry among dealers that they were missing any of the torrid action that has gripped the country stock markets since the Congress party withdrew support for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority coalition government. 

 A shortlived blip weaker on Monday morning was the rupee's sole reaction to political upheavals that could culminate in a confidence vote by April 11. 

 Dealers said the central bank may not even have to sell a dollar to brake any impending slide in the rupee. 

 "The RBI (Reserve Bank of India) can manage that even without actively intervening," said a foreign bank dealer. 

 The RBI has been the key factor influencing the dollar-rupee movement in recent months. 

 Dealers say the RBI's long-term strategy was a gradual depreciation of the exchange rate to reflect inflation trends. 

 But in recent months, it has had to buy dollars as the rupee threatened to appreciate on the back of large dollar inflows stemming from foreign direct investment, portfolio investment and overseas equity issues of Indian firms. 

 "Yesterday (Monday) was the ideal day the rupee could have fallen sharply, but nothing much happened," said Ravi Kumar, chief forex dealer at ABN AMRO Bank in Bombay. 

 The rupee quickly recovered back to opening levels around 35.92 a dollar after initially weakening to 35.99. 

 Forward dollar premiums were attractive for companies to book their near-term requirements, but there was little demand, dealers said. 

 "Indian companies don't see the dollar rising above 36.10 level in the near term," said the treasury head of another bank. 

 "They don't think the current (forward dollar) premiums are justified. And that is why they don't want to book forwards." 

 Last week, the RBI said its foreign currency reserves were at an all-time high of $21.16 billion as on March 21, which covers around seven months imports. 

 "Building up reserves is crucial in RBI's plans to move towards full convertibility on the capital account," said a dealer. "I doubt they'll be too keen to sell dollars." 

 Even if the rupee suddenly skidded beyond the 36 a dollar level, the RBI will only have to check prices for the market to calm down, a dealer said. 

 "The market is so tentative and nervous at such levels," said a dealer. RBI in the past has said the objective of its intervention is to prevent sharp volatility in the market. 

 Some dealers said the RBI will be happy to see the rupee touch the 36 mark. 

 "I don't think RBI will sell at 36, They may, at 36.20, to arrest the (rupee's) fall," said Moses Harding, vice president and head of forex at the private IndusInd Bank. 

 NatWest Securities said in a recent report India sought to restrict the current account deficit to a sustainable level. 

 "This could keep the rupee slightly overvalued in the long term, as that would encourage both imports and capital flows," it said.

BOMBAY, March 12 (Reuter) - The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will continue to intervene to stop the rupee from strengthening but a resulting boost to monetary growth was a constraint, the central bank chief said in a newspaper interview on Wednesday. 

 "We have to look at the monetary impact of the intervention and also look at the real effective exchange rate and try to achieve some balance," the RBI governor C. Rangarajan told the Financial Express daily. 

 He said the central bank was intervening in the currency market in response to a question whether the RBI would help exporters by encouraging a gradual depreciation in the rupee. 

 "I think this is one action we are taking," he said. 

 Rangarajan also said a medium term target for the central bank was to reduce banks' cash reserve ratio (CRR) further below the current 10 percent. 

 "We will have to see what is warranted in the present circumstances," he said. "On the removal of CRR on interbank borrowings, these are all matters under consideration," he said. 

 The central bank chief said the dollar has gained substantially in the last 15 months against other major international currencies, while the rupee/dollar rate has been been very stable for the last nine months. 

 The rupee traded at 35.84 to the dollar on Wednesday. 

 "Therefore, we certainly look at the real, effective exchange rate," he said. 

 The trade-weighted real effective exchange rate index stood at 63.05 in September 1996, according to lates RBI data, compared to 63.58 in September 1995. 

 "We do not have a target for the level of foreign exchange reserves," he said. Currency reserves stood at 20.09 on March 6.

title: India RBI says buying dollars to stabilise rupee.
text:
BOMBAY, March 6 (Reuter) - The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is intervening in the foreign exchange market to stabilise the rupee's exchange value, an RBI official told Reuters on Wednesday. 

 "Why should people say we're buying dollars to recoup our reserves?" asked a RBI official, who declined to be identified. "Intervention is to stabilise the exchange rate." 

 The official was referring to comments that RBI could be buying dollars to replenish its foreign currency assets. Another explanation was that RBI could be buying dollars against rupees to inject liquidity in a tight domestic money market. 

 According to official figures, India's foreign exchange reserves have fallen to $20.65 billion as on February 23, 1996 from $23.95 billion a year ago. 

 Following its intervention in the foreign exchange market by selling dollars after the rupee began a free fall in mid-1995, the RBI has started selling dollars since last week. 

 It bought an estimated $10 million dollars each on Friday and Monday and on Wednesday, purchased around $15 million, dealers said. 

 The RBI does not comment on the quantum of intervention. 

 "Any large-scale buying of dollars would help replenish the reserves for battles ahead while adding to the domestic rupee availability," ICICI Securities said in a commentary. 

 It said rising forward premia on the dollar and the falling spot rate are at a divergence that suggested a weakness in the current rally. 

 "The trade deficit in January against expectations of slight surplus, large oil payments ahead due to rising consumption and oil prices and subtle signs of a slowdown in FII (foreign institutional investor) buying could portend tough times ahead for the rupee," it said. 

 But it added that a revival in the GDR (global depositary receipts) markets and sustained FII buying would render most supply-deficit calculations meaningless and reverse the role of the central bank to capping the gains of the rupee, it said. 

 Treasury managers with banks said the relatively firm forward premia on dollar at 19 percent did not reflect genuine demand for dollars from importers. 

 "Importer-covering has virtually stopped since February 5," said a leading dealer. 

 He said the high forward premia reflected the high swap costs incurred by private and foreign banks which are very dependent on expatriate FCNR (foreign currency non-resident) deposits. 

 "High forward premia is the result of compulsions of bank treasuries to raise rupee resources," said the vice president, treasury at a private Indian bank. 

 The high forward premia would continue as long as the liquidity crunch in the domestic money market continued, forcing banks to convert their dollar assets to rupees at high cost, dealers said. 

 The Indian rupee started falling against the dollar in mid-1995 after remaining steady at 31.37 for almost two years. 

 In the first week of February, the rupee touched a historic low of 38.35 per dollar. 

 The rupee has revived suddenly during the last two weeks on the back of remittanaces from foreign institutional investors and Indian firms which raised equity from overseas markets. 

 A slow-down in importer covering aided the rupee's rally.

Tarapore also noted that it is essential that India's economy respond to changes in the external accounts, and said one aspect of that response was in the exchange rate.

title: FOCUS--Indian rupee gains vs dlr after 6-mth fall.
text:
BOMBAY, Feb 27 (Reuter) - The Indian rupee has recovered from a six month-long battering on the back of rising foreign investments and steps by the central bank to strengthen the currency, dealers and analysts said on Tuesday. 

 "What is interesting (about the rupee's recovery) is that it did not require massive intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)," said T.T. Ram Mohan, head of research at Birla Marlin Securities. 

 The rupee began to fall by August 1995 after holding steady against the dollar for almost two years at 31.37 to a dollar. 

 "The drop was too fast, and now the recovery has been fast," said the chief forex dealer at a newly-established Indian bank. 

 He said Indian importers were desperately buying dollars in the first week of February, when the rupee touched an all-time low of 38.50 to a dollar. 

 The scenario had reversed by this week, with importers no longer in a hurry to cover their imports and exporters beginning to worry about the appreciating rupee. 

 The rupee recovered to 36.50 level by mid-February and was widely expected to stabilise at this level. But on Monday, the rupee breached the 36 per dollar barrier to trade at 35.87/92. 

 The dollar was traded at 35.65/68 rupees on Tuesday. Several bankers said they expected the dollar to trade in the 35.50-36.50 range until the fiscal year ending on March 31. 

 Analysts said the trend reversal was triggered by the combined impact of a spurt in foreign portfolio and direct investment and a package of measures by the RBI to brake the free fall in the rupee. 

 "FII (foreign institutional investors) investments and positive comments from the government made an impact," said Moses Harding, chief forex dealer at Indusind Bank in Bombay. 

 The chief dealer at a European bank in Bombay said RBI's abolition of concessional dollar-denominated credit to Indian exporters made their funding costlier and dealt a blow to the practice of giving longer credit to their overseas clients. 

 The RBI on February 7 also freed interest on rupee credit to Indian exporters above 90 days with a view to forcing them to repatriate their earnings earlier. 

 "The RBI was for long accused of not telling the market the (exchange) range it wanted," said a dealer. The RBI measures and subsequent statements by its top officials signalled that it would not tolerate a weak rupee, he said. 

 But what really tilted sentiment was the spurt in FII investment on Indian bourses estimated as high as $500 million in February, analysts said. 

 According to official figures for January, FII investment up to January 25 totalled $233.4 million. It was $121 million in December, 1995. 

 "It's the opposite of what happened in Mexico," said a dealer at a private Indian bank. "When their currency fell, FIIs withdrew. Here they have been investing." 

 "But one should bear in mind that capital flows, either way, can have a disproportionate effect on the exchange rate," said Ram Mohan of Birla Marlin Securities. 

 The RBI on Monday said India's foreign exchange reserves rose to $20.63 billion as on February 16 from $20.56 billion a week ago.

title: Indian rupee could fall to 40 per dollar - industry.
text:
NEW DELHI, Feb 7 (Reuter) - The Indian rupee could tumble to as low as 40 per U.S. dollar before coming general elections, triggering a slowdown in domestic investment, industry analysts said on Wednesday. 

 "It looks to me that probably it will touch 40," said M. Roy, a senior official at the Confederation of Indian Industry. 

 "This way, it is bound to affect project viability and many, many of our industries are going to postpone fresh investment because a lot of machinery and equipment are imported." 

 The rupee touched a record low of 38.35 per dollar on Tuesday, more than four percent below its opening level on Monday and 10 percent lower than at the start of the year. 

 The currency recovered some ground on Wednesday on news Finance Minister Manmohan Singh and Reserve Bank of India (RBI) governor C. Rangarajan were meeting in Delhi to discuss the rupee's plight. 

 At mid-morning on Wednesday the rupee was trading at 37.55/65 per dollar, slightly stronger than Tuesday's close of 37.70/37.80. 

 Roy told Reuters the rupee's volatility was fuelled by speculative trading. 

 "Importers are bunching their demands while exporters are holding back their remittances, and such aggressive buying is causing a paucity of dollars," she said. 

 The Economic Times newspaper said Indian exporters failed to repatriate foreign exchange earnings amounting to more than 70 billion rupees ($1.85 billion) in calendar 1995. 

 A rift between the Commerce Ministry and the RBI emerged on Tuesday when a senior ministry official accused the central bank of failing to do its job of checking the rupee's slide. 

 "Obviously, when the market is so volatile, the RBI should intervene more aggressively to ensure stability," said Roy. "Industry would like to operate in a situation of stability." 

 But V. Raghuraman of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India (ASSOCHAM) said central bank intervention could only be a short-term solution. 

 "Unless we are able to improve our own productivity, the rupee will depreciate," he told Reuters. "Right from September, the industry has understood we have to look after our own interests and stop relying on the RBI as a crutch." 

 Until last August the rupee had held steady for two years at about 31.40 per dollar. But higher inflation in India than the United States took its toll, triggering a selloff in rupees. Between August and October, the currency fell about 12 percent. 

 "The RBI cannot intervene in a big way for a lasting solution," Raghuraman said. "The only way to stop it is to beef up exports and attract more foreign investment to India." 

 He said Indian shares were currently selling at throwaway prices. "It's a very good buy for foreign investors," Raghuraman said. "When the rupee depreciates, it attracts foreign investment as our scrips are very cheap. 

 "But we must be prepared for the slide. It should settle maybe at 40 or even at 37, but there can be stability only after the elections," he added, referring to general elections which must be held by mid-year and are expected in April. 

 "The slide is a temporary phenomenon," Roy agreed. "It will continue for some time, for a month or so perhaps, until the elections." 

 Lehman Brothers analyst Arup Raha said the rupee could touch 40 per dollar if the U.S. currency rose to between 108 and 110 yen. On Wednesday the yen was at 105.75/85.

title: Indian rupee ends at record low despite support.
text:
BOMBAY, June 2 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee ended at new closing low on Friday amid dollar demand from corporates, but dollar sales by state-run banks and exporters helped the rupee to recover from intra-day lows, dealers said. 

 The Indian currency ended at 44.625/635 off mid-morning lows of 44.65 per dollar. It had opened steady 44.5625/5725 compared to its previous close of 44.56/57. 

 Dealers said state-run banks which had protected the rupee from slipping past the 44.60 mark on Thursday, reportedly sold dollars at 44.65 level. 

 These state-run banks are considered the central bank's proxy and often sells dollars to keep the rupee stable. 

 Dealers said the bank had quoted along with the market in morning trade before the Indian rupee hit 44.65. 

 Demand for dollars on Friday was mainly corporate driven, they said. Earlier in the day, large corporates, including a large petrochemical firm bought dollars triggering the slide in the rupee. 

 "It looks like the central bank wants to defend the 44.65 level now," a dealer in a private sector bank said. 

 Last week the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened verbally when the rupee fell to its weakest level of 44.75, and warned against speculation and imposed fresh measures to contain volatility. 

 It also said it will sell dollars through the State Bank of India to meet foreign exchange needs for oil imports and some government debt payments. 

 Forwards premia rose despite easy call money rates on reporting day amid paying pressure from a large state-run bank after the spot rupee weakened. 

 The six monthly forward premia annualised was at 2.62 percent compared to the previous close of 2.50 percent.

title: Indian rupee ends at new low, SBI checks slide.
text:
BOMBAY, May 30 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee ended at a record low on Tuesday amid sustained dollar demand from importers during the day, but its slide was checked by the State Bank of India's (SBI) dollar supplies, dealers said. 

 The rupee ended at 44.565/575 per dollar, its lowest close. 

 It has been ending at new lows in the past three days after last week's dip to an all-time low in intra-day trade and the central bank's measures stirred a lot of importers out of complacency. 

 The rupee opened Tuesday at 44.49/51 before sliding on heavy dollar buying by importers, including a state-run oil firm's $40-50 million requirement, dealers said. 

 "The SBI was there protecting the 44.58 level...except for a brief minute when the SBI was off the market, dollar demand was taken care of," a dealer with a foreign bank said. 

 Dealers said the SBI's continuous presence indicated the central bank probably did not want the rupee to weaken beyond current levels. 

 "Now the exporters who are holding back sales will slowly emerge," a dealer with a state-run bank said. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened when the rupee hit lows of 44.75 last week with a warning against speculation. 

 The RBI also imposed a 50 percent surcharge on the import finance rate and raised the interest on overdue export bills to 25 percent. 

 It said it will continue to sell dollars through the State Bank of India (SBI) and will meet foreign exchange needs towards oil imports and some government debt payments. 

 The RBI said it was not considering monetary tightening immediately. But on Tuesday it placed on its open market sale list the 10.95 percent 2011 bond auctioned on Monday, which devolved heavily on the central bank. 

 It also placed several 364-day treasury bills on its sale list. 

 Dealers said forward premia however moved lower amid receiving across most maturities. 

 "Call rates are easy, the bond auction did not take any liquidity out of the market and the central bank has assured liquidity will not be tightened...why should the market be paying," the chief dealer at a private bank said. 

 The six-month premium ended at an annualised 2.63 percent compared with Monday's 2.79.

text:
BOMBAY, May 29 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee traded in a weaker range in Monday afternoon deals amid persistent light dollar purchases by banks and corporates. 

 Dealers said import demand was a trickle, yet kept the rupee from firming. 

 Purchases by foreign funds through custodian banks was also adding to the dollar demand, dealers said. 

 The rupee was quoted at 44.47/48 per dollar at 2:35 p.m. (0905 GMT), having slipped from opening levels of 44.36/39.

 Exporters waiting for the rupee to stabilise to sell dollars at peak levels may soon show interest, dealers said. 

 The rupee's slide last week forced the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to intervene with a warning against speculation. 

 It also imposed a 50 percent surcharge on the import finance rate and raised the interest on overdue export bills to 25 percent to speed dollar inflows and prevent bunching up of demand. 

 The central bank said it will continue to sell dollars through the State Bank of India (SBI) and will meet foreign exchange needs towards oil imports and some government debt payments. 

 Forward premia in far maturities were stable in afternoon deals but there was receiving interest (buy-sell swaps) in the near-term following the dip in call rates, dealers said.

title: UPDATE 1-Indian rupee recovers as market weighs next move.
text:
BOMBAY, May 11 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee settled into a wide and slightly firmer range on Thursday morning as the market waited for the central bank to signal a direction a day after the currency fell to its lowest levels ever. 

 Traders said sentiment was still a little bearish, and the market would be jittery until the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) either indicated its intention or stayed away from the market for a reasonable period. 

 The central bank often intervenes through the State Bank of India (SBI) and other state-run banks, and the market believes Wednesday's sharp fall was a move engineered by the central bank to weaken the rupee. 

 "All eyes are on the RBI. Sentiment is still slightly negative for the rupee," said V. Ravikumar, chief dealer at ABN Amro Bank. 

 The rupee fell 0.85 percent to a record low of 44.08 per dollar on Wednesday, largely because SBI, India's largest commercial bank, bought dollars continuously. 

 It was quoted in a wide range of 43.94-43.98 in noon trade, firmer than the opening 44.03/06 per dollar on Thursday morning. 

 Trade was quiet, partly on account of a nationwide strike by bank employees to protest against privatisation which dampened cash market transactions. 

 ADJUSTMENT FOR STRONG DOLLAR, INFLATION 

 The market speculated the RBI may have wanted a weaker rupee for several reasons, including the need to adjust the real effective exchange rate and keep it on par with other Asian and global currencies which have been falling. 

 "...it's just a one percent adjustment after a year of stability, it's quite tiny. If you look at it as a weakening against a very strong dollar, it's really an adjustment for dollar strength rather than rupee weakness," Sanjeev Sanyal, regional economist at Deutsche bank told Reuters Television. 

 India has strict capital controls and curbs on speculation, and the rupee has lost just three percent in 12 months, inclusive of Wednesday's sharp slide. 

 In the past few months, major currencies like the Japanese yen and the euro, as well as Asian currencies like the Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah, have weakened. 

 The baht has lost 3.7 percent and the rupiah 15 percent since the end of the previous year. 

 Local inflation is rising, with wholesale prices at a 70-week high of 6.1 percent, but core inflation is still low. 

 "They (the RBI) are likely to keep it here, watch what happens on inflation, the dollar and then, should anything move on those fronts, they will adjust again. This is going to be small discreet moves," said Sanyal. 

 WILL MARKETS TAKE OVER? 

 By noon on Thursday, the market was veering to the view the planned weakening for the rupee had ended and the central bank's efforts would be to ensure the new band is maintained. 

 The rupee, technically a gradually depreciating currency, has been very strong in the past year amid large foreign investment. This has boosted confidence in it, with most importers choosing not to hedge payables. 

 Bankers said Wednesday's move had unsettled some corporates, but if they perceived the rupee would stabilise soon, the current demand for dollars would subside. 

 Flows into India have been positive so far. Portfolio flows have crossed $1.6 billion until now, compared with just $1.5 billion in all of 1999. Direct investment flows could also be strong with corporates having lined up overseas issues, provided the technology sector's current slump does not last. 

 Flows could dwindle if the United States hikes rates to counter inflation and foreign investors cut down on Asian assets. ((Bombay Newsroom +91-22-265 9000; fax 91-22-264 1708; vidya.ranganathan@reuters.com)).

title: India Rupee Ends At Record Low INR44.04/Dlr (INR43.6775)
text:
BOMBAY -(Dow Jones)- Dollar-buying by companies, driven by the absence of support from the Reserve Bank of India pushed the Indian rupee to a record closing low against the dollar Wednesday, dealers said. 

 The dollar ended Wednesday at 44.04 rupees, up sharply from the INR43.6775 at Tuesday's close. 

 The previous record low hit in August 1998 was INR43.6950. 

 The absence of direct intervention as well as aggressive indirect intervention from the central bank also hurt sentiment on the rupee, dealers said. 

 State Bank of India, seen as the Reserve Bank's proxy in the currency markets, bought dollars in early trade and that set the trend for the rest of the session, dealers said. 

 The dollar opened steady, but began its ascent when State Bank bought dollars at INR43.6950, the highest bid in the market at that time. This pushed the dollar to INR43.75. At this level State Bank sold a token amount of dollars to support the Indian unit. 

 The dollar however continued to rise on dollar-buying by State Bank of India and other banks. 

 The weakening rupee also attracted a lot of companies, who covered their near-term positions and bought aggressively. 

 A few large Indian companies also bought dollars, when the rupee continued to weaken. 

 The dollar rose all the way to INR44.08, the rupee's record traded low, by the end of the session.

 The Reserve Bank didn't intervene directly in the market Wednesday. Although State Bank of India, perceived to be its surrogate, did step in to protect the Indian rupee. It sold merely a token amount and then continued to buy dollars on behalf of its clients. 

 "There was no direct intervention and indirect intervention was ineffective," a dealer at a foreign bank pointed out. 

 This has led the market to believe that the fall wasn't just with its tacit approval, but was probably engineered by the central bank, dealers said. 

 The dollar is expected to rise further Thursday, unless State Bank sells dollars to protect the Indian unit.

text:
BOMBAY, April 17 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee	    opened Monday little-changed from its previous close against the dollar and dealers expected it to come under pressure after the early crash in Asian stockmarkets on the tails of Friday's sharp fall in U.S. markets.



The rupee was quoted at 43.645/6525 per dollar against the previous close of 43.645/65.


 "The open is definitely steady. But with the stockmarket crash, the dollar will be well bid today," a dealer at an American bank said. 

 "The (dollar) shorts will get covered, people will look to remain long and those with dollar supplies will prefer to wait and watch." 

 Asian stockmarkets fell sharply and regional currencies were weak on Monday tracking the fall in the technology-laden Nasdaq index and the blue-chip Dow Jones index on Friday. 


The technology-laden Nasdaq index	   plunged 355.49 points or 9.67 percent on Friday at 3,321.29 - a level not seen since November.

"In the the normal course they may have let it meandered down. But today, I don't think, they will let it slip much," a dealer said.



The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) rarely intervenes directly in the foreign exchange markets and mostly does it through a clutch of state-run banks, mainly the country's largest bank the State Bank of India , dealers said.



They said SBI offered dollars at 43.65 levels in early trading, but were unsure if it was on the central bank's behalf.



Dealers said dollar sales could be expected during the day as banks offload dollar stocks accumulated over the long weekend.



Banks and financial markets in most centres were closed on Friday and Saturday for festival holidays.

title: Fitch-IBCA Executive Says India Reform Process Has Slowed  Down
text:
Bombay (Dow Joens)--Global investors are beginning to fear that India's reform process has slowed down, Pauk Rawkins, senior director of sovereign ratings at Fitch IBCA, said Wednesday. 

 Rawkins comments come ahead of an announcement by the ratings agency on India's foreign currency rating. The announcement is due Wednesday at 1100 GMT (7.00 a.m. EST). 

 "Investors feel that reforms have slowed down" and that is why India is missing out on foreign direct investment, he said. 

 Rawkins added that there is a "need to invigorate the reform process on the broad front." 


He was speaking at the seminar on "Sovereign and Financial Sector Risk
Assessment - India and Global Perspectives," organized jointly by Indian
ratings agencies CARE and Fitch-IBCA.
- - 08/03/00 06-12G



One of India's strengths is that its exchange rate is competitive
vis-a-vis other Asian countries, said Rawkins. "The Reserve Bank of
India has managed it (exchange rate) very well," he added.



India's exchange rate has been relatively free from sharp
fluctuations, with the currency falling by 12% to 15% versus the dollar
every year, largely thanks to the intervention policy followed by the
Reserve Bank of India, India's central bank.



He also noted that the cost of bank restructuring as a percentage of
the gross domestic product is lower in India than in many Asian
countries.



Recounting the strengths and weaknesses of the Indian economy, Rawkins
said that India's strengths are the improved external debt position, and
the unblemished external debt-service record.



He noted that for a foreign currency rating, rating agencies look at
the country's willingness and ability to pay. India, when faced with a
balance of payments problem in 1991, indicated its ability to take tough
decisions, he said.



Also, he said, a matter of concern is India's low share in world
trade, which discourages the flow of foreign direct investment into the
country.



Other weaknesses of the country, relevant to the foreign currency
rating, are its huge fiscal deficit, high government debt, poor human
capital and its narrow tax base.



The strengths include India's long record of established democratic
institutions, and low cost labor.

title: India Defense Spending Hike Absolutely Unavoidable-Sinha
text:
NEW DELHI -(Dow Jones)- Indian Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha said Wednesday that his proposal for increased defense spending in the budget for the financial year 2000-01 was "absolutely unavoidable." 

 Sinha proposed to increase defense spending by 130 billion rupees ($1=INR43.54), 20% higher than the revised figures and 28% higher than the original estimate for the coming year. This is the largest ever increase in the defense budget in a single year. 

 He also said that he expects to exceed the INR100 billion targeted level of receipts the government hopes to get from the sale of its shares in state-owned companies. 


Sinha also reiterated that the government had the "strongest
determination," to proceed with its privatization target. He was
speaking to industrialists Wednesday about his budget proposals
presented to Parliament Tuesday.
- - 01/03/00 05-42G



Sinha also said that he had created the right conditions for an
interest rate cut, which was the best he could do, given that the actual
signal should come from the country's central bank.



"I have stubbornly refused over the past two years to intervene with
the Reserve Bank of India" in its decisions on interest rates, he said.



"My responsibility is to create the necessary conditions" for interest
rate cuts, he said. "So what have I done. I have reduced interest rates
on General Provident Fund by one percentage point. Those who criticize
me for not doing enough to reduce the interest burden should take note
of this fact," Sinha added.



The government reduced the interest rate on the General Provident Fund
for government employees to 11% from 12% as part of the budget
proposals.



On the local currency, Sinha said the fall of the rupee against the
dollar over the past year has benefitted exporters significantly. When
combined with no tax on export earnings, it represents too much
favoritism for the export sector.



The rupee has fallen 2.5% from INR42.51 over the past 12 months.



"I hope you'll agree with me that there is no reason anymore to treat
the export sector differently," Sinha said. "Export income has to be
taxed."



"I have tried to do my best...we have taken the reform process very
strongly forward in this budget," Sinha said.



-By Denny Kurien; Denny.Kurien@dowjones.com



Sinha also said the time was not yet ripe for full capital account
convertibility. The rupee is currently partly convertible on the current
account, but not for capital account transactions.



"The time has not come for full convertibility," Sinha told
industrialists.



"As for corporates, the RBI is working on it and will come out in due
course with rules for capital account convertibility for the
corporates," he added.



The exchange rate is market-determined and the only thing the Reserve
Bank of India can do is to watch the market and check any undue
fluctuations, Sinha said.



He declined to comment on the rupee-dollar level.



Sinha's Chief Economic Adviser Shankar N. Acharya said in a
post-budget press conference Wednesday that the government has assumed
an "average" rupee-dollar level at 45 rupees. The Indian rupee was
trading at INR43.61 against the dollar in late morning trading.



"We have taken it at 45 rupees at the average" for computing what the
total import bill will be, Acharya said.



The foreign exchange market is stable now because of the confidence of
investors in the Indian economy. If there is any volatility in the
market, the RBI will step in to curb it, Sinha said.



The minister also said he wasn't overly concerned about the fall in
India's stock markets following his budget speech, and expected the
market to "bounce back" once players get a chance to examine his tax and
spending proposals in more detail.



The Bombay Stock Exchange Sensitive Index, or Sensex, fell 5.1%
Tuesday after the budget revealed higher taxes on dividends paid by
companies, some taxes on the export earnings from the services sector
and raised excise duties on a range of products.



However, the Sensex was up 1.76% midday Wednesday to 5542.68 points
from Tuesday's close.

title: FOCUS-Indian rupee at 13-mth low despite cbank.
text:
BOMBAY, Sept 29 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee fell slightly on technical factors on Wednesday, but enough to notch a 13-month low despite some central bank support. 

 Underlying dollar demand from importers and technical factors caused the fall, and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened through state-run banks to curb the fall. 

 The weakness was anticipated and largely due to month-end factors, but the latest decline brought the rupee within striking range of a 43.70 all-time low hit in August 1998. 

 The rupee has been showing signs of weakness and in the past two weeks it has lost 10 paise (0.1 rupee). It ended at a record closing low of 43.59/595 per dollar on Wednesday after hitting an intra-day low of 43.61. 

 "There is a lot of underlying dollar demand and 43.60 is a psychological level," said Ravi Pai, treasury vice-president at HDFC Bank. 

 The chief dealer at a foreign bank said: "Although the state-run banks supplied dollars in the afternoon, the way it was lapped up by the market and the rupee still ended weak shows how much more of dollar demand there is." 

 A market holiday on September 30 for banks' half-yearly closure of accounts led to large demand for dollars from banks and corporates reaping benefits of high swap differences over the month-end. 

 ANXIETY OVER RBI SUPPORT 

 Bankers say corporate import remittances are picking up because of fears the RBI will relax its hold on the rupee once elections are over. 

 The last stage of India's five-phase election is to be held this weekend and results are due to be announced on October 6. Exit polls project a victory for the alliance the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is leading. 

 The RBI had in August announced it would bridge any dollar supply gaps in the market through intervention and keep most of the country's oil imports and defence payments out of the market. 

 That safeguard for the rupee is expected to remain in place until a new government is formed. 

 Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) have shied away from Indian markets in the past two months, but there is hope inflows will pick up once the elections give the BJP a clear mandate. 

 "After the elections, we could even see upward pressure on the rupee if FII inflows pick up," said Pai. 

 FIIs have sold close to $200 million in Indian equity and debt markets since August after being net buyers of close to $1 billion in the April-July period. 

 Besides shrinking foreign investment, analysts point to a host of factors the currency market has to contend with soon. 

 Crude oil prices, still close to $24 per barrel, are a cause for worry, and gold prices at 16-month peaks above $300 are also expected to hurt the trade balance. 

 The country's oil imports are expected to cross the $10 billion mark in 1999/2000 (April-March) from close to $6 billion last year. ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, vidya.ranganathan@reuters.com)).

title: India bonds stable on lower call, seen cautious.
text:

 Dealers said bonds were cautious on market expectations of the central bank intervening in the foreign currency markets after it made statements in the morning about its plan to increase dollar supplies in the market. 

 "Obviously the central bank expects the rupee to turn weak and in case of an intervention by it, rupee funds would leave the market," a primary dealer said. 

 Minutes before the currency market opened for trading on Monday, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said it was prepared to intervene directly or sell dollars through the State Bank of India (SBI)  in order to augment dollar supply in the market. 

 Bond prices had firmed up in morning deals as call money rates opened at 8.75-9.25 percent after ruling around ten percent for most of last week.

title: Indian rupee ends firm on  central bank  statement.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 23 (Reuters) - Verbal intervention by India's central bank early on Monday helped the rupee end firmer after it dipped to an all time closing low at the weekend, dealers said. 

 The rupee ended at 43.50/51 per dollar after mostly trading in a range against Friday's all time closing low of 43.565/57, but off early highs of 43.49. 

 Minutes before trading commenced on Monday, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said it was prepared to intervene directly or through the State Bank of India (SBI)  in order to augment dollar supplies in the market. 

 The RBI said it would meet either fully or partially, the foreign exchange requirements for the import of crude oil by Indian Oil Corporation  and added it was also prepared to meet the country's debt service obligations directly. 

 The central bank's statements vaulted the rupee, weighed down at the weekend by rising importer dollar demand amid concerns of reduced flows into the country, to a firm start at 43.49/52 per dollar. 

 The rupee was traded in a tight range amid SBI dollar sales, which dealers said, were executed mostly through brokers. SBI's dollar sales were maximum in the last hour of trading. 

 "SBI did not hit banks directly. Most of its sales were through brokers," a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 The rupee hit an all time closing low on Friday on newspaper reports the G-8 countries could stall loans to India in reaction to its draft nuclear deterrence policy and speculation of a yuan devaluation. 

 Dealers said corporate demand for dollars remained good, despite the central bank's statements. 

 "Inspite of the central bank's statements which seem to suggest the rupee will not fall much from these levels, there was good demand for dollars," the chief dealer at a European bank said. 

 Dollar supplies seemed elusive with no foreign flows into the country. 

 Data released by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) on Friday showed foreign funds sold nearly $80 million worth of debt and equity in Indian markets in August after having invested nearly one billion dollars in the April-July period.

title: RBI statements propel India rupee to firm open.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 23 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee	    started stronger on Monday as the country's central bank issued a statement minutes before the market opened saying it was taking steps at cutting any demand supply gaps that may emerge.



The rupee opened at 43.49/52 per dollar against the previous close of 43.565/57, and dealers reported early deals upto 43.50.


 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said on Monday it was prepared to intervene directly or sell dollars through the State Bank of India (SBI)  in order to augment dollar supply in the market. 

 "Arrangements have been made by the Reserve Bank of India, to meet fully or partially, the foreign exchange requirements for the import of crude oil by Indian Oil Corporation," the central bank said in its statement. 

 The RBI said it was also prepared to meet the country's debt service obligations directly. 

 Dealers said while the statements helped the rupee open firmer, bids for the U.S unit had reappeared in early trade. 

 "Banks are sitting long dollars. A major sell-off now would mean hurting themselves. They will probably wait to see how corporates behave. Chances are the rupee may firm before the end of the day," a foreign bank dealer said. 

 The rupee was quoted at 43.505/52 per dollar at 9:20 a.m. (0350 GMT) and dealers said they were surprised by the central bank's moves. 

 "Probably they see some major demand supply gaps which the market does not know about. Otherwise, these statements are most unexpected," the chief dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 Dealers said the central bank had probably stepped in following the rupee's fall to an all-time closing low on Friday and the sharp drop in the country's foreign exchange reserves in the week to Agust 13. 

 The RBI on Saturday said India's foreign exchange reserves dropped to $33.115 billion on August 13, down from $33.410 billion in the previous week. 

 The head of currency trading at a foreign bank said the central bank's moves were aimed at halting the slide of the rupee. 

 "Without these statements, the rupee would have tested 43.60 levels and moved very swiftly to its all time low of 43.70. This (the RBI's sattements) will apply the brakes," he said. 

 The rupee's all time low of 43.70 was hit on August 19 last year. 

 "They probably expect uncertainty ahead of the elections. And the fact is that dollar supplies have come down sharply lately." 

 Dealers said foreign institutional investors (FIIs) have been lying low in the run-up to the elections which has resulted in a sharp decline in portfolio inflows into the country. 

 Foreign funds sold nearly $80 million worth of debt and equity in Indian markets in August after having invested nearly $1 billion in April-July. 

 Dealers said forward premiums were expected to open lower tracking the spot rupee's gains and easier call money rates. 

 The six-month premium ended the weekend at five percent against the previous close of 4.90 percent. ((Santosh Menon, Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: India call money above nine pct, rupee weighs.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Indian call money was traded in in higher ranges in opening deals on Wednesday, with sentiment affected by heightened tension with Pakistan after the downing of a Pakistani military aircraft, dealers said. 

 Fighters of the Indian air force shot down a Pakistani maritime reconnaissance aircraft on Tuesday saying it intruded into its airspace, a claim denied by Pakistan which accused its neighbour and arch-foe of downing the plane without any provocation. 

 The tension affected sentiment, already hit by reduced liquidity in the past few days, dealers said. 

 Call money was traded at 9.10-9.40 percent compared with Tuesday's close of 8.8-9.10. 

 "Most of the deals are getting done at 9.20 percent," a dealer with a private bank said. 

 Liquidity was strained by outflows of 30 billion rupees into a 10-year bond auction last week and a further 20-25 billion into the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) open market operations since Friday, dealers said. 

 "The pressure on the rupee is complicating matters further. The market feels state-run banks, which normally intervene in the currency market on the RBI's behalf, will lend less," a dealer with a foreign bank said. 

 The rupee was quoted at 43.485/495 per dollar at 10:05 a.m. (0435 GMT) after it opened at 43.45/50, weaker than Tuesday's close of 43.425/43. 

 Dealers said the rupee could weaken further if the tension with Pakistan escalates. 

 Pakistan's Foreign Minister Sartaj Aziz told Reuters Television on Wednesday his country's armed forces were on full alert and said India should apologise for its action. 

 On Tuesday evening, Aziz had said Pakistan reserved the right to make an appropriate response to the Indian action. 

 Money market liquidity would be further hit if the RBI sells dollars through state-run banks to defend the Indian currency, as it has done in the past, dealers said. 

 "The spot date for today falls on the reporting Friday, so even if there is intervention there should be no major impact on liquidity," a dealer with a state-run bank said. 

 Banks report two-weekly positions to the RBI on alternate Fridays and maintain cash reserve ratios over the two-week period. The next reporting day is August 13. 

 "But it is likely the availability of funds has been affected by their intervention on Monday, the spot date for which falls today," he added.

title: FOCUS-Suspected  intervention  halts rupee's slide.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 9 (Reuters) - Suspected intervention brought the rupee's accelerating slide to a juddering halt on Monday, but analysts say the currency is set for further falls. 

 Dealers said leading public sector banks, probably at the behest of the central bank, sold dollars prompting a sudden recovery in the rupee as the currency headed toward all time lows set a year ago. 

 While the rupee has stabilised for now, most analysts still foresee the currency gradually weakening. 

 Several factors are conspiring against the rupee's stability. 

 Global oil prices have surged, Indian gold imports have ballooned and an expected hike in U.S interest rates could reduce investment inflows from foreign funds. 

 On Monday, the rupee was fast nearing its all-time low of 43.70, struck last August, when dollar selling by the country's largest commercial bank, State Bank of India (SBI), stopped the rot at 43.585. 

 It closed at 43.395/405 per dollar, firmer than Friday's close of 43.47/475. 

 Dealers said the rupee's sudden slump from around 43.30 a week ago had gathered pace due to large demand from state-run firms and oil importers. 

 Bankers and corporates who had predicted the rupee would slip to 44 or 45 per dollar by March 2000, have not revised forecasts and some believe the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will be content to let the market weaken the rupee slightly. 

 The rupee, only partially convertible, is protected by RBI curbs on speculation although the central bank stresses the market can set the rupee's trend so long as it does not move too fast. 

 "They (the RBI) will leave it to the market to determine what should be the right level for the rupee. That is what they have been saying all the while. What they are worried about is the volatile swings in the exchange rate," S.Anand, Senior Vice-President, IDBI Bank told Reuters Television on Monday. 

 Economic indicators have turned favourable in recent months, exports have recovered and the approaching mid-term elections have largely been discounted. 

 India reported 6.5 percent growth in exports in the first quarter of the year (April-March). But a 53 percent rise in oil imports, driven by global oil prices surging to 20-month highs over $20 per barrel, has cast a cloud. 

 "If international oil prices remain over $20 a barrel for another two to three months, it will be a real cause for concern," Chetan Ahya, economist at BNP Prime Peregrine India said. 

 Gold, India's second biggest import item may be out of favour in world markets but the cheap price has only fuelled appetite here, according to local newspaper reports. 

 The Business Standard daily said there was a 32 percent rise in gold imports in the first quarter of the year to 187 tonnes. But the world gold price, now around $256 per ounce, is much lower than last year's level of over $300. 

 India's foreign exchange reserves climbed to nearly $33.5 billion on July 30, around $6 billion more than the year before, with the buildup in recent months helped by dollar inflows from foreign funds investing in Indian stock markets. 

 Those funds invested close to one billion dollars in April-July but turned sellers in the first week of August. 

 A likely hike in U.S. interest rates, the second in as many months could further dampen funds' interest in emerging markets, including India. 

 "Even though the intervention has cooled the market, the sentiment has shifted and the rupee will suffer due to lack of flows," V.Ravikumar, Chief Dealer, ABN Amro said. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: Slight India rupee rally seen once Kashmir cools.
text:
BOMBAY, June 30 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is unlikely to recover much ground once the Kashmir crisis ends, after losing around 1.4 percent against the dollar since the conflict began in mid-May, currency dealers said on Wednesday. 

 Comments by a Pakistani emissary that he expected India and Pakistan to soon draw up a schedule for the withdrawal of infiltrators from the Indian side of Kashmir failed to affect the currency market. 

 If a diplomatic solution does bear fruit, the rupee will certainly react bullishly, but dealers said the gain would likely be limited to 10 to 15 paise. 

 Technical factors, scarce dollar supplies and the restricted trading environment would muffle the reaction, they said. 

 "Technicals seem to be the dominant resistance factor for the rupee," said V. Ravikumar, chief dealer at ABN AMRO Bank. 

 "We've seen four daily closes above 43.33, which is a key chart point. Even if the rupee firms beyond 43.33, it may not breach 43.20. Overall, it is a dollar bullish trend." 

 The rupee stayed in a steady 43.35/36 range on Wednesday, compared to 42.75 on May 26, when India first launched air strikes against the militants it says are backed by Pakistan. 

 "In markets, it is our experience that anything that goes up does not normally come down fully," said Kalyan Mukherjee, treasury head at Credit Agricole Indosuez. 

 "Besides, there is a perception that a weaker rupee is preferable to boost exports. A fall is desired but it should be smooth," he added. 

 The Reserve Bank of India has denied market speculation that it is seeking a weaker rupee. 

 The central bank's official policy toward the rupee is that the market should determine the trend, so long as trading conditions remain orderly. 

 The rupee's month-long descent has not been one-way, which is one of the reasons why the authorities appeared fairly comfortable with the move, although there has been sporadic intervention through state-run banks. 

 One reason why India's currency markets cannot react more strongly is a central bank ban, introduced when the rupee hit an all time low of 43.70 per dollar last August, on importers re-booking cancelled import contracts. 

 The Kashmir confrontation prompted several corporates with dollar payables, who had stayed on the sidelines during the rupee's 10-month stable trade, into increasing hedging ratios. 

 But because of the ban on re-booking cancelled import contracts, they will be unable to exit those positions. 

 "I don't see much of importer cancellations in event of peace in Kashmir, since they cannot rebook," Ravikumar said. 

 "Besides dollar supplies are not what they used to be and the rupee's appreciation will not be much," he said. 

 Most exporters had cashed in on the rupee's slide in the past few weeks, dealers said. 

 Investments by foreign funds in Indian equities, which were $578 million in April and May, slowed to $77 million in June. 

 Overseas investors have also sold close to $35 million worth of investments in Indian debt instruments so far in June. 

 Governor Bimal Jalan said last week the central bank was keeping a vigil on the market's reactions to events in Kashmir and would do whatever was necessary to maintain orderly markets. 

 He said the RBI added $2.5 billion to its foreign exchange reserves in March, April and May but had to sell dollars through the State Bank of India (SBI) in the second week of June to defend the rupee.

title: Central bank intervention  dents  India  reserves.
text:
BOMBAY, June 26 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves fell by $200 million in the third week of June, reflecting the central bank's intervention to cool the currency market hit by the Kashmir crisis. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) said on Saturday that foreign exchange reserves were $33.289 billion on June 18, down from the week-ago level of $33.489 billion. 

 Dealers said the drop was expected after RBI Governor Bimal Jalan said on Friday that the central bank had sold dollars to the state-run State Bank of India , the country's largest commercial bank, last week. 

 In a statement released at a conference on rural development, Jalan said the central bank had deliberately followed a policy of keeping reserves at a very high level and the RBI bought dollars from the market in March, April and May. 

 "In fact, we bought as much as $2.5 billion during these three months. Last week, however, RBI sold dollars to SBI (State Bank of India) in order to meet some extra demand," a central bank statement quoting the governor said. 

 The statement rescued the rupee from its 10-month lows of 43.43. It closed at 43.315/33 per dollar on Friday. 

 The rupee has weakened by more than one percent since late May when news of the conflict in Kashmir first hit financial markets. 

 India has been fighting what it says are Pakistani infiltrators and Islamic guerrillas on its side of the military control line in the Himalayan territory of Kashmir for the past one month. 

 The situation put investors in a cautious mood and increased corporate demand for dollars. 

 "The Kashmir conflict is driving importers to increase their hedging horizons and cover ratios. The RBI's decision to sell dollars is to curb any excessive volatility or undue bearishness on the rupee," said Vasan Shridharan, Treasury Economist at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 Jalan was quoted as saying the central bank would continue to keep a watch on the markets. 

 "Except for some temporary hiccups, financial markets are functioning normally and overall conditions are satisfactory. RBI will continue to monitor the position and as in the past take appropriate measures when necessary," the RBI statement said. 

 "Our policy is to keep forex markets orderly and meet as necessary temporary demand-supply gaps that emerge from time to time," it said. 

 While the depletion in the foreign currency assets was $200 million, dealers said it was likely the central bank had sold a lot more and adjusted the spot position by receiving forward dollar premiums (buy-sell swaps). title: WRAP: India Rupee, Bonds Seen Dn Next Wk; Shrs Steady
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The conflict in Kashmir weighed on India's financial markets this week and will continue to cast its shadow, traders said Friday. 

 The markets had hoped that a U.S. diplomatic mission to Pakistan and India would be a step towards an early settlement of the border dispute between the two countries that started May 26. 

 But with no positive news from Pakistan and reports of northeastern Indian states declaring security alerts Friday, funds and other market participants sold shares ahead of the long weekend. The same sentiment also prompted banks to go long on the dollar. 

 The Indian rupee (INR) and bonds are expected to fall next week, as companies are expected to buy dollars and banks will try to offload their bond holdings, traders said. 

 However, shares are seen little changed next week, with market participants reluctant to take on large positions while the situation in Kashmir continues, dealers said. 

 India has been engaged in a border conflict with its neighbor Pakistan after launching air strikes on the border May 26 to flush out what it called Pakistan-backed infiltrators. 

 While events on the border initially didn't affect market sentiment too much, the situation is beginning to take its toll on the market as it's over a month since air strikes were first launched. 

 The rupee slipped steadily against the dollar through the week, propped up only by dollar sales by State Bank of India. The rupee, which began the week at INR43.12 against the dollar, ended at INR43.32 - down 0.46%. 

 A further fall was prevented only by a statement from the Reserve Bank Governor Bimal Jalan Friday, that the central bank sold dollars to the State Bank of India to meet the dollar demand in the market, confirming that State Bank's dollar sales this week were only at its behest. 


          Further Decline In Rupee Seen



However, dealers see corporate dollar demand continuing next week and
only active intervention from the Reserve Bank of India can prevent a
further fall in the rupee, they said.



The rupee is expected to trade between INR43.30 and INR43.40, traders
said.



Indian bonds also saw some selling by market players as banks tried to
"lighten their positions," a dealer at a private bank said. Though most
market participants are long of government securities, there is a
feeling of unease as players are trying to offload positions, dealers
said.



"The only reason for this uncertainty is the border situation," a
trader said. "Logically there should be buying," he added. Liquidity has
returned to the market once again, he said, and the rupee's fall in the
foreign exchange market has also been smooth.



Although money was tight earlier this week after tax outflows and a
bond auction in the previous week, the situation has eased in the past
couple of days. However, bond prices haven't had a major rally yet.



In contrast with the nervousness in the money market, the mood in the
stock market is buoyant as foreign institutions continued to buy shares.



However, there is a reluctance to take on huge positions as long as
the border conflict continues. Also, traders said domestic players have
begun to offload positions as border tensions are taking a toll on
sentiment.



India's benchmark stock index, the Sensex, has been very steady,
ending the week at 4111.77 compared with 4109.89 last week. Traders said
the index hasn't risen too much because of the Kargil issue. Volume,
however, has fallen significantly, dealers noted.



Next week, the stock market is expected to see lack luster trading,
dealers said. "Even if the market doesn't fall, it definitely won't
rise," Vivek Mahajan, vice president, IIT Investrust said.

title: WRAP:India Rupee Dn On Border Worries, Oil Cos
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--Fears of protracted border tensions with Pakistan and dollar buying by oil companies caused the Indian rupee to suffer its largest single-day fall Tuesday. 

 Bankers are now anxiously waiting to see if the Reserve Bank of India, which had been surprisingly quiet Tuesday, will intervene to support the currency Wednesday. 

 The rupee fell 0.4% Tuesday to close at INR43.32. This is still well above the all-time low of the rupee of INR43.70 which it hit on August 1998. 

 Market participants said they won't be surprised if the dollar inched close to the INR43.50 level in the current week. Continued reluctance of the central bank to support the rupee and bad news on the India-Pakistan border conflict will be enough to push the rupee to that level, they said. 

 "Everyone is wondering what will happen next on the border. The possibility of a protracted war is worrying the market," Ravi Vasantraj, vice president, Mecklai Financial Ltd. said. 

 Besides hurting the economy, bankers said continued border clashes will further force foreign institutional investors to slow down purchases of Indian shares, reducing immediate dollar inflows into the system. 

 Foreign investors who had bought shares totaling $405 million in May and $224.6 million in April have become wary in June. They have bought a mere $3.7 million in the first half of June. 

 These dwindling inflows have a direct impact on the country's foreign exchange reserves which after rising all through May fell by $99 million to $33.433 billion in the week ended June 4. A treasurer at a leading construction company pointed to this reversal of trends as the key reason for sentiment turning against the rupee. 

 Dlr Buying By Oil Companies Hits Rupee 

 Given that the rise in oil prices and border clashes aren't news, the sudden dramatic fall of the curreny Tuesday certainly took many corporates and banks by surprise. 

 What triggered the fall say brokers was some aggressive buying by the State Bank of India, the country's largest state-owned bank, presumably on behalf of oil companies. 

 Analysts point out that oil prices rose by about 50% in the eight weeks ended May 31, and oil company Indian Oil is probably paying for oil which it bought weeks ago, presumably on suppliers' credit. 

 Neither Indian Oil nor State Bank officials were available to confirm these guesses. 

 "There wasn't any other reason for the rupee to fall this sharply," Punit Bhatia, deputy manager at Credit Agricole Indosuez in Bombay said. 

 Bankers said these dollar-remittances are expected to continue for some more days and thereby create pressure on the rupee. 

 Many banks had gone short on the dollar on the expectation the Reserve Bank will intervene to protect the rupee once it crossed INR43.20. But with Reserve Bank not making any attempts to shore up the rupee, many banks were caught short and had to cover their positions. 

 Market participants said the movement of the rupee Wednesday and thereafter will depend largely on what action Reserve Bank mulls and when it chooses to act. 

 A senior monetary policy official told Dow Jones Tuesday that the fall of the rupee doesn't worry the central bank. 

 "Our target isn't a number. We are more concerned whether the market is volatile," he said asking not to be named. 

 In a similar vein, last week the deputy governor of the Reserve Bank was quoted saying that the central bank won't stand in the way if the market wanted to push the rupee lower. 

 Although the Reserve Bank subsequently denied that this statement was intended to push down the rupee, bankers insist the central bank won't mind a gradual depreciation of the rupee. 

 "The market may have already tested the RBI's patience too far," said a dealer at a state-owned bank. 

 If the central bank decides to sell dollars, the rupee could stage a smart recovery. But if it doesn't, there will be continued weakness in the rupee, a dealer at a U.S-based bank said.

title: Indian rupee at risk as Kashmir tension escalates.
text:
BOMBAY, May 27 (Reuters) - Flows of foreign money into India will shrivel and the rupee will weaken if the current tension with Pakistan over Kashmir escalates into war, dealers said on Thursday. 

 The rupee, which fell to an all-time closing low of 43.04 to the dollar on Thursday, was expected to hit 43.20-43.30 on Friday and 43.50 if the war clouds did not dissipate, they said. 

 The rupee has weakened 0.67 percent since its close on Tuesday, falling on Wednesday on news India had launched airstrikes against infiltrators in Kashmir and on Thursday as Pakistan shot down two Indian jets. 

 "The dollar looks fairly well bid tomorrow," said Janak Desai, treasurer at Standard Chartered Bank. He said it could hit 43.25 unless the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervenes. 

 Dealers said the RBI, the central bank, would act to control volatility. 

 "We should see 43.30 tomorrow," said Sunil Sharma, head of foreign exchange trade at ANZ Grindlays Bank. "But RBI will come in to dampen any sharp moves so there should not be any undue volatility." 

 The currency market is largely closed and controlled by the central bank, which has record foreign exchange reserves of $33.250 billion. 

 Curbs on speculation imposed after the rupee hit a record low of 43.7 last August have resulted in the currency firming, and the RBI has had to buy dollars in recent months to stem its rise. 

 War fears would hit foreign investor sentiment and foreign inflows would be affected, putting pressure on the rupee, dealers warned. 

 Surging inflows from portfolio investors and direct investments have been a major reason behind the rupee's recent strength and helped the rise in foreign exchange reserves. 

 "Dollar supplies will be affected as foreign fund flows will decelerate," Desai said. 

 Some dealers said the rupee's fall on Thursday was in a thin market. 

 "I think quite a few banks were sitting short and when the news hit the screens, they panicked and looked to cover positions," said a dealer at a foreign bank. 

 "There was very little corporate interest and we really need to see what corporates do tomorrow. I feel what will happen now is the exporters will start to hold back their remittances while importers may start covering more, so there may be pressure on the rupee." ((Giri Venkatesan, Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Fears of Indian Ctrl Bk Action Seen Limiting Rupee Fall
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--Fears that the Reserve Bank of India will intervene to stem any dramatic slide of the Indian rupee (INR) will likely limit the fall of the currency Friday, dealers said. 

 "The Reserve Bank of India will support the rupee through the State Bank of India," a dealer at a foreign bank said. 

 On Thursday the Indian rupee (INR) slipped sharply in late trade to close at a new low of INR43.025 to the dollar compared with INR42.83 at Wednesday's close. 

 The impact of political developments on the rupee is of concern as the reaction of the bond market is directly linked to this market as well. 

 Wednesday, Indian forces began air strikes in the northern province of Kashmir, close to Pakistan, against what it called Pakistan-backed infiltrators in the region. Thursday, Pakistan said it shot down two Indian aircraft. 

 Since recent tensions on the border between the two countries began Wednesday morning, the rupee has fallen 0.64% while the Sensex, India's benchmark stock index, has fallen 4.9%. 

 The central bank has on two separate occasions stemmed the slide of the Indian currency by withdrawing facilities to banks and companies and raising short-term interest rates. 

 In fact, conviction that the central bank won't allow the rupee to slip sharply has prompted smaller importers to stay unhedged in the market. 

 Senior central bank officials have also reiterated from time to time that they will ensure orderly conditions in the market without targeting a specific level for the rupee. 

 Dealers said they see the State Bank of India selling dollars in early trade to prevent volatility. " I see the RBI (the central bank) selling when the rupee touches INR43.50, not before that," the chief dealer at an American bank said. He added that there were corporate dollar sales late Wednesday and early Thursday which helped the rupee recover, but said that it wasn't likely to happen Friday. 

 "In fact, the same guys who sold this morning (Thursday) will be the first ones to buy back their dollars," he said.
