title: India  Rupee Opens Steady; Ctrl Bank  Intervention  Seen
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee opened steady against the dollar Tuesday and is expected to continue to trade in a narrow range on lack of both corporate and interbank interest, dealers said. 

 The dollar opened Tuesday between 42.735-42.745 rupees, unchanged from Monday's close. 

 Dealers said dollar supplies continue to flow into the market only to be absorbed by one or two large state-owned banks acting at the behest of the central bank. The central bank is said to be holding the rupee steady by mopping up these excess dollars through large state-owned banks. 

 This intervention is expected to keep the spot dollar in a narrow range. With importers preferring to stay unhedged, demand for the dollar is expected to be dull. And as is always the trend in a stable rupee market, there are more exporters looking to sell dollars than there are buyers of the U.S. currency. 

 According to the latest available figures from the Reserve Bank of India, the central banks' foreign exchange reserves touched a record high of $33.25 billion May 15. 

 Dealers put the range for the dollar Tuesday between INR42.73 and INR42.76 during the day.

title: ANALYSIS-India RBI policy must factor in govt fall.
text:
BOMBAY, April 18 (Reuters) - The goverment's fall and the daunting prospect of yet another shaky coalition means India's central bank will have to build in checks to ensure the currency does not slide and interest rates remain stable, bankers said. 

 Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Bimal Jalan is due to present the central bank's monetary and credit policy for 1999/2000 (April-March) on Tuesday. 

 Bankers have been low-key in their expectations ahead of the policy, but the government's fall on Saturday and prospects of new elections that could trigger populist spending by any government in power will put an additional burden on the RBI. 

 "We can safely kiss good-bye all promises of controlling government expenditure and fiscal deficit," the treasury head of a European bank said. 

 "Politicians will now be out to woo the electorate...there will be all kind of populist programmes and promises made and I expect spending to be out of control by the year-end." 

 But Jalan is no stranger to piloting India's currency and money markets through turbulent waters. One week after he took over as RBI governor in 1997, the government led by I.K. Gujral fell and the Asian crisis began to buffet India's currency market. 

 When he presented his first credit policy in April 1998, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) had been in power for around a month and had yet to get its budget passed. Last year, he also had to contend with pressures on the rupee, following economic sanctions after India's nuclear tests and a credit rating downgrade. 

 Bankers say Jalan's pragmatic policy-making and responses to changing market conditions have been instrumental in ensuring ralative calm in India's markets. 

 Saturday's confidence vote brought down Prime Minister Atal Behari Vajpayee's government by just one vote and with such a slim margin the opposition Congress will find it very difficult to run a stable government. Prospects of fresh federal elections, India's third since 1996, therefore loom large. 

 Analysts said apart from the risk of populist spending worsening the fiscal deficit, the RBI would also have to provide safeguards for the rupee. 

 "RBI has to maintain the rupee's stability," said T.R. Sridharan, chairman and managing director of state-run Canara Bank. 

 "The current political situation could put some pressure on the rupee and the RBI's main concern will be to check this." 

 The currency's stability against the backdrop of a volatile political situation was underscored by others too. 

 "The single most important factor on policy-makers' minds right now must be currency stability," the treasury head at a foreign bank said. 

 "I think the RBI will maintain the status quo on interest rates as they would not want to give even a slight scope for people to pull the rupee down." he said. 

 In any case, a rate cut did not necessarily translate into a boost to the economy, said A.T. Pannir Selvam, chairman and managing director of state-run Union Bank of India. 

 "We saw last year that cuts in lending rates did not have any impact of credit disbursals by banks. So I do not expect any rate signals," he said. 

Foreign exchange dealers say the RBI has been intervening through state-run banks, particularly the State Bank of India (SBI) , in the currency markets to ensure there is no undue volatility in exchange rate movements. 

 "From Tuesday, the fall in the rupee was cushioned by a steady stream of dollar offers from the State Bank of India," former RBI deputy governor R. Janakiraman wrote in the Hindu Business Line daily on Saturday.

title: India rupee seen weak on politics, RBI to guide.
text:
BOMBAY, April 14 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is likely to open weaker on Thursday on political uncertainty, but a sharp fall is unlikely in a currency market largely controlled by the central bank, dealers said on Wednesday. 

 Indian President K.R. Narayanan on Wednesday asked Prime Minister Atal Behari Vajpayee to seek a parliamentary vote of confidence in his Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) led government after a meeting with opposition parties. He specified no timeframe for the vote. 

 The move came after the ruling coalition's second biggest partner, the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam, formally withdrew support for the government, after having kept the BJP on tenterhooks for some two weeks. 

 "Initially, the dollar will be bid tomorrow and we may see a test of 43 but that should be the limit," said P.H. Ramaswamy, country treasurer at Credit Lyonnais. 

 He was speaking after the opposition parties' meeting with Narayanan, but before the President announced his decision on the holding of a confidence vote in the government. 

 The rupee ended Tuesday at 42.74/75 per dollar, down from its previous close of 42.685/695 on dollar demand spurred by political uncertainty. 

 The foreign exchange and money markets were shut on Wednesday for a local holiday. 

 "There should be no significant impact on the money market which is mainly driven by liquidity of which there is plenty at the moment," Ramaswamy said. 

 "But looking beyond tomorrow, where the rupee goes depends whether some other party or group is able to form the government. If no one is able to get the required numbers and we need fresh elections, then we may see some significant volatility," he said. 

 "Otherwise, the market seems to have largely discounted the currrent uncertainty." 

 The rupee has weakened some 31 paise (0.31 rupee) or 0.73 percent over its fiscal year-end bid close of 42.43 on March 31. 

 Dealers said they expected the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to intervene in the event of excess volatility. 

 "The RBI is sitting on huge forex reserves and should easily be able to handle any volatility," said a chief dealer at one state-run bank. India's foreign exchange reserves stood at a record $32.535 billion on April 1. 

Foreign exchange dealers say the RBI intervenes indirectly, through state-run banks, to regulate dollar supply in the market. 

 "Further, many corporates have hedged their exposures and I think we will not see the kind of panic buying we saw last year or during the Asian crisis," the chief dealer said. 

 "There is hardly any scope for speculation in our market and I cannot see inter-bank trades driving the rupee down very much," Ramaswamy said. 

 The central bank has kept a tight rein on currency speculation since the rupee struck an all-time low of 43.70 per dollar last August.

title: Indian rupee seen weak as ally to quit coalition.
text:
BOMBAY, April 12 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee is expected to come under pressure as a key partner in India's ruling coalition said its withdrawal of support was inevitable, but the central bank was expected to provide a safety net, dealers said. 

 "The market has been biddish since the political uncertainty began and there will certainly be dollar bids tomorrow (Tuesday)," the chief foreign exchange trader at a private bank said. 

 "The rupee could take a dip tomorrow, but it will not be much, maybe around 20-30 paise (0.20-0.30 rupee) at the most," said P.H. Ramaswamy, country treasurer at Credit Lyonnais. 

 On Monday, Jayaram Jayalalitha, leader of the regional All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) told reporters her party would withdraw support to Prime Minister Atal Behari Vajpayee's coalition government. 

 The AIADMK would also work towards bringing a no-confidence motion against the government, she said. 

 Bond prices could open lower on political worries but dealers said the domestic money market was largely inured to politics and liquidity would be the principal factor in driving price movements. 

 "There could be a drive by speculators to drag it (the rupee) lower. But I don't expect too much as importers are fairly well covered and the RBI will be there. They (RBI) have the market firmly in their grip," Ramaswamy said. 

 Ramaswamy said much of the move had already taken place last week, when the rupee broke from a range around 42.30-42.50 per dollar where it had traded since recovering from a record low of 43.70 last August. 

 The AIADMK's support is crucial to ensure that the minority Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which leads a motley coalition of 19 parties with support from two more from outside, stays in power. 

 The rupee ended Monday at 42.685/695 per dollar, off early lows of 42.71/72, but slightly weaker than the weekend close of 42.67/69. 

 "I don't think anything will happen for the next few days so long as the ruling party maintains it has got the strength for a majority in parliament. The pressure will be there, but the market will watch for the next move," said Satish Nayak, Head of Treasury, Barclays Bank. 

 Dealers said the record foreign exchange reserves with the central bank gave it sufficient ammunition to intervene directly if required although most expected it to continue intervening passively through state-run banks. 

India's foreign exchange reserves sttod at an all-time high of $32.535 billion on April 1, compared to $31.586 billion a week earlier. ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: India Rupee Ends Flat; Lower Co Demand, Ctrl Bk Sales Rumors
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee ended steady and regained early losses against the dollar on long selling by banks and reduced demand from importers, dealers said Wednesday. 

 The dollar ended at INR42.67-42.6850, around its Tuesday close of INR42.67. The dollar touched a high of INR42.76 in early trade Wednesday. 

 Rumors that the Reserve Bank of India had intervened by selling forward dollars deliverable in June also helped ease the pressure on the rupee, dealers said. The Reserve Bank of India declined to confirm or deny the rumor. 

 Bankers said it wasn't clear yet whether the central bank had intervened to steady the Indian currency. "We are asking around but haven't been able to get a confirmation from any bank," the chief dealer at a large U.S-based bank said. 

 The foreign exchange market was less apprehensive Wednesday of the political threats to the federal government, bankers said, explaining the rupee's recovery. 

 The rupee lost 0.6% of its value against the dollar Tuesday when banks and importers bought dollars heavily on political concerns. 

 The All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam, a key ally of the ruling coalition, recalled its ministers Monday and threatened to withdraw support from the government when the parliament reconvenes next week. The AIADMK had demanded the resignation of the defense minister, who belongs to another party in the coalition. The Bharatiya Janata Party, which leads the ruling coalition, has so far shown no signs of compromise. 

 Exporters also took advantage of the dollar's rise and sold dollars, bankers said. 

 Rupee premiums on the forward dollar ended lower because of the stronger rupee and lower interbank overnight call rate. 

 The premium on the six-month forward dollar closed unchanged at 7.1%. 

 Overnight call money rates slipped to 5.50%-5.75% after the market saw inflows to the tune of INR47 billion. Most of the trades on Wednesday were done at 7.00%. 

 Looking ahead, dealers said the rupee is expected to trade between INR42.65-42.75 unless there are further political developments.

title: Political fears send Indian rupee to 7-month low.
text:
BOMBAY, April 6 (Reuters) - The rupee hit a seven-month low on Tuesday as fears India's coalition government will collapse prompted importers to cover their dollar needs, dealers said. 

 The currency lost just over 0.5 percent, but in a market used to intra-day moves of less than five paise (0.05 rupees) the 25 paise drop to a close of 42.68/70 per dollar was a jolt to the system. 

 "A lot of corporates were caught uncovered and unprepared by the political developments," said Munish Saigal, controller of forex operations at Ranbaxy Laboratories . 

 The All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK), the second largest partner in the coalition, said late on Monday that its two ministers would resign from the government and it would decide later whether to withdraw support for the coalition. 

Central Bank measures introduced when the rupee struck an all time low of 43.70 last August have eradicated inter-bank speculation, but the cloud over the government shook importers out of their complacency, dealers said 

 Dealers saw the currency stabilising under the watchful eye of the central bank, but also expected a gradual weakening to keep the rupee competitive against other Asian currencies. 

 "I expect a period of consolidation for the rupee. It may however slide to 44 by mid-May," Saigal said. 

 Some believed the decline had been set in train. 

 "Importers have been shaken out of their inertia. The rupee will be in a 42.80-43.0 range against the dollar soon," said N. Venkatramanan, country treasurer of American Express Bank. 

 There was no sign of Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervention as the rupee dropped, but dealers were watching closely to gauge the central bank's attitude to a weaker currency. 

 Traders said stock market movements could provide clues to the rupee's trend, as dealers watched the ebbs and flows of foreign portfolio investment in the wake of the coalition crisis. 

 The benchmark Bombay index slumped 4.53 percent on Monday, but recovered 1.42 percent to end at 3,569.47 on Tuesday as the market corrected. 

 The rupee had remained rock solid on Monday but caught a bearish backlash on Tuesday which at one point relegated it to a low of 42.78. 

 The decline accelerated on dwindling prospects that the Hindu nationalist government's estranged partner would decide to stay in the coalition after a lawmaker allied to the AIADMK said the party would vote against the government if a vote of confidence was called. 

 "A good indicator of where the rupee is headed is the stock market. Today the stock market has already recovered some of Monday's losses," said Alok Nandi, director at Delhi-based Apex Forex Consultants. 

 Bond prices rose ahead of a bond auction later in the day, impervious to the turbulence in the currency market. 

 Liquidity tightening has been the RBI's favoured weapon to check rupee depreciation, but while traders expect it to hold back interest rate reductions, the situation did not warrant a reversal of the recent cut in rates, they said. title: India rupee ends weaker, shaken by politics.
text:
BOMBAY, April 6 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee ended Tuesday sharply weaker as importers rushed to buy dollars, shaken by a deteriorating political situation, dealers said. 

 The rupee ended at 42.68/70 per dollar, off an intra-day low of 42.78 but much weaker than its Monday close of 42.43/435. 

 Dollar demand spurted as corporates took fright after the All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagham (AIADMK), which controls 19 seats in parliament, said on Monday its two ministers would resign from the federal cabinet, traders said. 

 This triggered fears the fragile coalition government could fall, they said. 

 The AIADMK said it would take a decision on cutting off all support to the government later. 

 Dealers said forward premiums were less volatile, reflecting less forward hedging and more inter-bank demand. 

 Earlier the cabinet, led by the Bharatiya Janata Party, decided not to concede the AIADMK's demands which included a change of defence minister and reinstatement of a dismissed naval chief. 

 "I am not ruling out another fall later when the parliament session begins and the actual position is known. But, the reaction to current developments should end at current levels," said a foreign exchange consultant. 

 The fall was aggravated by dollar purchases by the State Bank of India , the absence of central bank intervention and a short-dollar position in the market, dealers said. 

 A lawmaker, close to the AIADMK, said the southern ally would vote against the government if there was a trust vote, and added to the market's concerns. 

 Forward premiums ended at an annualised 6.22 percent for the two-month dollar against Monday's 5.87. 

 The Bombay stock exchange's benchmark index ended 1.42 percent higher on Tuesday, recovering from a 4.53 percent fall the previous day, and this had led to hopes the rupee would also consolidate in current ranges. title: FX  Asia:  India  Ctrl Bk May  Intervene  To Counter Oil Prices
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Reserve Bank of India is concealing a couple of aces up its sleeve, ready to counter any adverse impact high oil prices may have on the value of the rupee. 

 Of all Asian currencies, the Indian rupee is the most vulnerable to higher oil prices, offshore analysts warn. A sustained rise in the price of oil threatens to inflate India's import bill, widen the country's already sizable current account deficit and put additional pressure on the rupee, they reason. 

 The Indian government itself has acknowledged the threat. In its Economic Survey released in February, the government warned that the country's growing appetite for imported petroleum products could cause a serious balance of payments crisis, should prices start to rise. 

 With the price of WTI blend crude oil currently trading at a 12-month high of $16.80, up from its near 13-year low of $10.35 hit in December, offshore analysts may be forgiven for thinking that crisis may be looming. But although more expensive oil imports will undoubtedly aggravate India's record trade gap, it would be wrong to assume this automatically translates into rupee weakness, counter analysts in the onshore market. 

 The Reserve Bank of India still has two cards to play, they say. For one, the central bank is expected to be prepared to deploy its substantial reserves to intervene in the market to prop up the rupee. In addition, the authorities may also cut a deal with the country's main oil importer - state-run Indian Oil Corp. (P.IOL) - directly providing it with a supply of dollars and bypassing the foreign exchange market altogether. 

 In drawing up contingency plans to cope with the effect of higher oil prices, the central bank is merely being prudent. 

 According to the most recent data, India logged a record $7.79 billion trade deficit in the first 10 months of the current fiscal year, up from $5.58 billion in the same period the previous year. 

 Oil imports in those ten months amounted to $4.91 billion - some 14% of total imports. With official government projections showing that the economy will need to import around 78 million tons of crude oil in fiscal 2001-2002, nearly double the 39.37 million tons imported in 1998-99, India can little afford any hike in the crude price. 

 Given the recent rise in the price of oil, however, "the country's total import bill should rise by $500-600 million in the next fiscal year," says to Sandeep Dhingra, a petroleum analyst with Jardine Fleming Securities. 

 "If industrial activity picks up next year, then we will see an increase in demand for oil, which in turn will push up our import bill," agrees Vasan Shridharan, an economist with Standard Chartered Bank. 

 An increased demand for imported oil will naturally bring an increased demand for U.S. dollars, putting pressure on the rupee. But market participants say the central bank is watching the rupee closely and is prepared to intervene to prevent any abrupt slide. 

 "The rupee is undervalued by 2% against the five-country real effective exchange rate that the central bank is said to use. In such a situation, I doubt if it will allow the rupee to depreciate further," says Shridharan. 

 Most market observers feel that if a fall in the value of the rupee is unavoidable, the Reserve Bank will intervene in the market for the first time since August 1998, to engineer a gradual depreciation. The central bank does not lack the resources, they note: India's foreign exchange reserves hit a record high of $31.24 billion for the week ending March 19. 

 Although market watchers expect the rupee to remain steady at around INR42.42 to the U.S. dollar in the near term, they will be watching closely to see if the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries can enforce its recent agreement to cut back crude production. 

 If it can, there may be cause for concern later in the year, according to some. 

 The central bank may also cut a special deal with Indian Oil Corp. to ensure that the rising oil import bill does not hit the market directly. 

 Market players suggest that the Reserve Bank may be prepared to enter into a series of cross-currency swaps contracts with the State Bank of India, which conducts most of the company's crude oil purchase business. Under the arrangement, the State Bank of India would be able to access U.S. dollar funding without entering the market directly, which would avoid putting additional downward pressure on the rupee.

title: Indian Rupee Opens Slightly Weaker; Seen Range-Bound
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee (INR) opened slightly weaker against the U.S. dollar Monday, with dealers predicting range-bound trading. While some dollar supplies are expected this week on unwinding of long-dollar positions by banks, the month-end demand from customers is expected to balance the market, dealers said. 

 The dollar opened Monday at INR42.29-.31, slightly stronger than Friday's close at INR42.28-.29. 

 The rupee is expected to trade in a tight range for a few days, mainly on fear of intervention by the Reserve Bank of India. The central bank has, on two occasions, raised short-term interest rates and withdrawn facilities to companies to halt a run on the rupee. Because of this, market players will think twice before pulling the rupee down, dealers said. 

 State Bank of India, the country's largest commercial bank, has also been keeping the rupee in a range over the past few weeks. State Bank's actions are significant because the market perceives them to be on behalf of the Reserve Bank of India. 

 Some participants are holding long-dollar positions, dealers said. The rupee weakened considerably, to INR42.41, Friday as banks took long-dollar positions, anticipating heavy corporate demand. They expected their customers to buy dollars in reaction to the lowering of India's sovereign rating by international credit-ratings agency, Standard & Poor's late Thursday. 

 However, State Bank of India came in selling dollars and pulled the U.S. currency down to INR42.28. As a result, some banks held on to their long positions over the weekend. The unwinding of these positions is expected to bring in some dollars, dealers said. 

 These supplies can be expected to prop up the rupee, they added. However, it is not clear if the State Bank of India, under the central bank's instruction, will allow the rupee to move up too much, bankers said.

title: India  Monetary Measures For  Forex Intervention  Welcome -Exec
text:
HYDERABAD, India (Dow Jones)--India's Vysya Bank Chairman K. Ramamoorthy said Friday that the Reserve Bank of India's recent measures using monetary policy instead of direct foreign exchange intervention to control a fall in the value of the rupee (INR) ($1=INR42.46) versus the U.S. dollar was a welcome change. 

 He said that the central bank must at some point put a stop to the use of an increase in rupee resources by market participants to engage in arbitrage in the foreign exchange market. 

 The RBI in August reduced liquidity and raised interest rates to restrict the rupee's fall against the dollar when the Indian currency breached record lows, touching INR43.70. The RBI's measures stabilized the rupee at around INR42.50 against the dollar, and the Indian currency has remained around that level since. 

 The central bank's market intervention is like "riding two tigers," Ramamoorthy said, adding that it's a tough job to simultaneously stabilize the foreign exchange level and maintain liquidity at a comfortable level.

title: Indian Rupee Trades Slightly Higher Late On Gulf Dlr Inflows
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--In late trading Monday, the rupee (INR) is slightly firmer on good dollar inflows from Gulf countries, dealers said. 

 The Gulf countries have a large population of Indians working and their dollar remittances normally rise at the start of the week, dealers explained. 

 At 0933 GMT, the dollar is trading at INR42.51-.52, slightly lower than Friday's close at INR42.51-.53. The dollar opened Monday at INR42.51-.54. 

 Dealers said that there isn't much dollar demand in the market because of the Reserve Bank of India's indication to Treasury heads of banks Saturday that they are concerned about the dollar-rupee exchange rate. 

 The central bank asked for suggestions from bankers about how to manage liquidity and disallow any arbitrage between the money and the foreign exchange market, which could lead to speculation against the rupee versus the dollar. 

 But "the market is very quiet," said a dealer at a state-owned bank adding that the effect of dollar inflows on the rupee "isn't worth speaking about." 

 The dollar-rupee exchange rate is moving in a "tight range" and "I expect it (the dollar) to trade between INR42.45-.55" for the rest of the trading session Monday. 

 The rupee premiums on forward dollars too are at their earlier levels "on fears of Reserve Bank of India intervention," he said. 

 The annualized premium on the 6-month forward dollar is around 10.8%, and would continue between 10% and 12%, dealers said.

title: India  RBI  intervenes  in  forex  market through swaps.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 25 (Reuters) - The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened in the foreign exchange market in late morning trade on Tuesday through sell-buy swaps, dealers said. 

 "They (RBI) paid in September and October," said a dealer. 

 Dealers said forward dollar premiums which had opened sharply lower edged up after the central bank's intervention. 

 "Premiums were lower in the morning on easier call money and some receiving," said a dealer at a private bank. "But maybe RBI does not want premiums to fall too sharply for fear there will be a surge in import demand." 

 Premiums on September dollars rose to 0.56/0.6 rupee after the intervention from the day's open of 0.54/0.56 and compared to Monday's close of 0.59/0.64. 

 October dollars were quoted at 0.93/0.98 after opening at 0.86/0.91 and compared to the previous close of 0.95/1.00. 

 Dealers said the rupee weakened slightly in spot deals from opening levels but trade was light. 

 "Supply in the spot segment remains limited and less than demand so there is always a downside risk for the rupee," said a dealer. "The rupee will trade in a range for some time before dollar demand pushes it down." 

 At 12.15 p.m. (0645 GMT), the rupee was quoted at 42.49/51 after opening at 42.42/45 and compared to Monday's close of 42.45/48. ((Giri Venkatesan, Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: India rupee ends sharply firmer on RBI support.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 20 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee ended firmer on Thursday after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened directly in the spot and swap markets and also announced a package of measures in support of the currency. 

 The rupee ended at 42.80/90 per dollar against its previous close of 43.47/53 and after volatile trade ranging between a record low of 43.70 and an intra-day high of 42.60. 

 Dealers said the rupee's slide to its lifetime low of 43.70 was first halted by RBI enquiries about rates, followed by direct intervention through spot dollar sales. 

 A series of measures announced by the central bank later accelerated the rupee's rise and helped it reverse a three-day losing patch earlier this week. 

 At its lowest on Thursday, the rupee had lost around 1.4 percent from its weekend close. 

 The RBI announced a 100 basis point increase in banks' cash reserve ratio (CRR) to 11 percent from August 29 and hiked its repo rate to eight percent from five. 

 Other measures included a warning to exporters not to delay their remittances and a requirement that banks report their end-of-day positions and intra-day peak positions. 

 "Overall the measures reversed sentiment to a large extent and should keep the rupee stable for some time to come," said a dealer at a private bank. 

 "People are now going to be more careful about taking the rupee up or down. We should see only back-to-back covering of trade transactions for some time now," he said. 

 Dealers said the RBI's moves came when dollar demand had picked up on statements by Commerce Minister Ramakrishna Hedge that the rupee could weaken further by around one percent and that India was unlikely to reach its 1998/99 (April-March) exports growth target of 20 percent. 

 Forward dollar premiums flared up sharply after the central bank paid (bought dollars in the swap market), dealers said. 

 "RBI paid in September," said a dealer. Some dealers said the central bank also paid in October-dollars. 

 The annualised premium on six-month dollars ended at 12.43 percent against Wednesday's clsoe of 9.08. Premiums for other months also rose although they dipped slightly towards close, dealers said. 

 "The uptick was particularly sharp for near months," said a dealer. "It looks like RBI wants forward premiums to be a bit firm to prevent a rush for cover by importers." 

 "Current levels are also attractive for receiving and we may see exporters coming in now," he said. "Premiums should start easing in a couple of days." ((Giri Venkatesan, Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: India  RBI  intervenes  in  forex  market - dealers.

title: India Commerce Min/Barter Trade -2: Address In Singapore
text:
NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--India favors barter trade to lessen its dependence on the U.S. dollar for key imports, Commerce Minister Ramakrishna Hegde said in Singapore Wednesday while addressing an India Day seminar. 

 In a report carried on Press Trust of India, Hegde was quoted as saying Southeast Asian nations should encourage barter trade as a way of avoiding dollar dependency. 

 "Members of the ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) family should be able to have benefit of increased mutual trade with interference and over-dependence on one currency," Hegde said. "For this, India would like to encourage trade on a barter basis." 

 Hegde's suggestion comes amid a steep fall in the rupee Wednesday with the Reserve Bank of India intervening in the currency markets and restricting foreign exchange dealings. 

 In a bid to tighten rupee liquidity, the central bank has raised the cash reserves that banks must maintain as a ratio of their liabilities to 11% from 10%. This will become effective on Aug. 29. 

 It has also raised the rates at which the central bank will sell repurchase agreements of government bonds to 8% from 5% currently. The Reserve Bank didn't say when the new RP rate will take effect. 

 The rupee is currently trading at INR42.85 to the dollar, compared to a new record low level above INR43.00 to the dollar before the announcement. The currency has weakened from INR42.50 in the last two weeks.

title: India Rupee Closes Dn Despite Reserve Bank Gov Comments
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--Dollar buying by State Bank of India, the country's largest commercial bank, created panic in the foreign exchange market Wednesday, pushing the rupee (INR) to new lows and forcing the Reserve Bank of India governor to verbally intervene and support the rupee, dealer said. 

 Reserve Bank of India Governor Bimal Jalan said Wednesday the central bank is closely monitoring the foreign exchange market and will take appropriate steps, including monetary measures, when necessary. 

 However, the nervousness in the market continued when State Bank of India asked for dollar quotes from several banks in late afternoon trading. Banks - assuming State Bank will buy dollars - panicked and bought dollars to cover short positions. 

 Their dollar-buying pushed the rupee to new lows, albeit briefly, leading the dollar to trade at a high of INR43.66 in intraday trading. 

 The dollar ended at a record closing low of INR43.50-.51, up from its previous close of INR43.36 on Tuesday. 

 "When State Bank along with others actually sold (dollars) near close of trading, the rupee quickly regained part of its losses," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 He said the State Bank dollar selling near close of trading could be have been prompted by the Reserve Bank of India's dollar sales directly to them. 

 Sometimes the Reserve Bank doesn't like to intervene directly by selling dollars in the market because it creates panic and the central bank is keen on avoiding a volatile market, dealers said.

title: India Fin Adviser -2: Speaking At Govt Meeting
text:
NEW DELHI (Dow Jones)--The recent fall in the Indian rupee to record lows below INR43.40 in early trading Wednesday doesn't reflect a sharp depreciation of the currency, said the government's chief economic adviser who was attending a meeting of customs officers. 

 Since August 1997, the rupee has depreciated around 17.5%, and in the past two weeks has dropped from INR42.50 to INR43.43 currently. 

 "I don't think the fall in the rupee has been sharp," said Finance Adviser Shankar Acharya, who is also acting Finance Secretary, following the transfer of Montek Singh Ahluwalia from that position last week. 

 He noted the Reserve Bank of India is mandated to intervene in the market at any time it feels the value of the rupee should be supported. 

 He also said the devaluation of the Russian ruble won't hurt Indian trade. 

 "There will be no significant" drop-off in exports to Russia because of an agreement with Russia to fix the rupee-ruble exchange rate, Acharya also said. But he noted that the devaluation of the Russian ruble affects markets worldwide and does increase uncertainty in that regard. 

 Russia's Central Bank on Monday cut the lower limit of the ruble (RUR) band to RUR9.5 to the dollar from RUR6.3 to the dollar previously. 

 In 1992, India and Russia agreed to a rupee-ruble rate at 19.1 rupees to the ruble for the repayment of INR310 billion, about $7.14 billion, in debt accrued by India for the purchase of defense equipment and other items from the former Soviet Union. The debt is auctioned by the Russian central bank to Russian importers who can obtain letters of credit and buy goods denominated in rupees from Indian exporters. The Indian exporters then receive payment from the Reserve Bank of India.

title: FEATURE - India rupee braces for more pain.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 17 (Reuters) - A mood of uncertainty and unease 

 is palpable among India's currency market players as they brace 

 for the next likely burst of volatility to hit the rupee. 

     The rupee hit its lifetime low of 43.35 to the dollar on 

 August 12 before paring some of its losses but traders say 

 further falls lie in store. The rupee was quoted at 43.20/21 on 

 Monday morning. 

     "Basically, we have to realise that India is a 

 dollar-deficit country," said the corporate treasury head of a 

 western-India based textile firm. 

     The rupee's trend will therefore always tend to be bearish. 

     "What happens is that events - political uncertainty, 

 regional market developments, bad news in general such as the 

 ratings downgrade - these determine how bearish this sentiment 

 gets to be and this will determine the rupee's rate of fall." 

     SHARP FALL IN PAST YEAR, MORE PRESSURE SEEN 

     The wheel has turned full circle for the Indian rupee and 

 its central bank in the past year. 

     On August 15, 1997, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) deputy 

 governor Y.V. Reddy said the rupee appeared to be overvalued 

 based on real effective exchange rate data. 

     The RBI was then buying dollars to prevent the rupee 

 appreciating and analysts were concerned over how the central 

 bank would manage strong capital inflows. 

     A slowing economy also hit domestic dollar demand and 

 helped the rupee. 

     One year later, the rupee has fallen more than 17 percent. 

     And the central bank has sold dollars a number of times to 

 check speculative attacks on the rupee. 

     On Friday, the RBI again warned rupee bears not to 

 speculate against the currency. Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha 

 also stressed that the central bank would intervene to check 

 speculation. 

 Poor exports and foreign investor unease, particularly 

 since India conducted nuclear tests in May, mean that a country 

 which has traditionally relied on foreign capital flows to 

 bridge its current account deficit must brace itself for 

 pressure on its currency. 

 NUCLEAR-BLASTS, SANCTIONS HAVE MORE IMPACT THAN ASIA CRISIS 

 "If you look at the rupee's fall, it lost about 10 percent 

 between August 1997 and May 1998," said K.N. Dey, senior 

 vice-president at Mecklai Financial & Commercial Services, a 

 risk management advisory firm. 

     "But it has fallen more than seven percent in the 

intervening period," he said. 

India carried out two sets of nuclear tests in May, after a 

 24-year gap, triggering major economic powers to slap 

 sanctions. 

     Investor worries over the country were not helped by a 

 sovereign credit rating downgrade to junk bond status in June. 

     And it is these two factors which have concerned analysts 

 most. 

     "Actually, despite political uncertainty the rupee was 

 pretty steady till May," Dey said. 

     General elections earlier this year in the world's most 

 populous democracy were inconclusive and analysts had feared 

 that currency markets would react negatively to the uncertainty 

 inherent in a fragile minority coalition. 

 FALL CUSHIONED BY GOOD MANAGEMENT BY RBI, CAPITAL CONTROLS 

 While the rupee has fallen, it has been shielded from the 

 steep falls of other regional currencies thanks to fairly 

 strong external account indicators, the presence of capital 

 controls and some deft exchange rate management by the central 

 bank. 

 India's current account deficit for 1997/98 (April-March) 

 was around 1.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) while 

 the short-term component in its total external debt was less 

 than 20 percent. 

     India's foreign exchange reserves, at $27.09 billion on 

 July 31, are enough to cover six months' imports, analysts say. 

     The rupee not being fully convertible on the capital 

 account has also made it less susceptible to speculative 

 attacks. 

     "Speculative attacks could be more severe if the currency

 is fully convertible," Dey said. "But in India there is a limit 

 to the speculative positions that traders can take." 

     But poor exports are a cause for concern and the central 

 bank has said it expects the current account deficit to widen 

 to two percent of GDP this year. 

     Exports declined by almost 8 percent between April-June 

 1998 from the year earlier period. And RBI's Reddy said on 

 Friday a poor forecast for global trade for the year reduced 

 the scope for Indian exports to grow. 

 JAPAN SNEEZES, CHINA CATCHES A COLD, INDIA SHIVERS 

 The headline in a local daily last week sums up India's 

 current predicament. 

     The latest plunge in the rupee comes as fears over regional 

currencies grow after the yen hit eight-year lows. 

     Analysts say local sentiment remains nervous as the 

 Japanese yen holds weak and amid uncertainties over a possible 

 devaluation of the Chinese yuan. 

     But analysts say capital flows remain the main concern for 

 the Indian currency. 

     "Sentiment of course will be affected if the yuan is 

 devalued but for me the biggest worry is over capital inflows," 

 said Vasan Shridharan, treasury economist at Standard Chartered 

 Bank in Bombay. 

 ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, 

 Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: India spot rupee off lows, dollar premiums up.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 13 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee recovered from an intra-day low but the currency remained under pressure on Thursday, dealers said. 

 Players were cautious about likely central bank intervention, political and regional developments, they said. 

 The rupee was quoted at 43.15/18 per dollar in dull trade in the afternoon, off its intra-day low of 43.25. 

 Dealers said the undercurrent was still very bearish for the rupee. 

 "We've been advised to buy dollars by the banks who are all very bearish," said the head of a corporate treasury. 

 Heavy corporate demand led to the rupee's sharp fall on Wednesday when it touched an all-time low of 43.35 in volatile trade, and it took several rounds of intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to help it to a firmer close at 42.95/05. 

 "After Wednesday's hectic trading and wild movements, the market is slightly calm today," said a dealer with a local foreign exchange brokerage. 

 The forward premiums on the dollar were higher at the short end with the one and six month levels at 9.28 and 9.30 respectively against the previous close of 8.11 and 9.02. 

 "Near-term paying interest (buying of dollars in swap market) has emerged on fears that the central bank will resort to tightening of liquidity to support the rupee," said a dealer with a private bank. 

 In the overseas markets, the dollar was stronger against most other currencies on concerns about the Russian economy, the rouble's possible devaluation and Hongkong's falling stock markets. 

 "The rupee is unlikely to be influenced by the rouble since our trade ties with them are minimal and restricted to the escrow account," said a dealer. 

 Dealers said some of the concerns on the political front had eased after reports that a key ally of the ruling coalition had deferred its decision to withdraw support. 

 The ally had been upset that a regional river waters dispute had not been setlled as per their wishes. 

 Offshore, the rupee was at 46.30/50 for the six month non-deliverable forward (NDF) dollar, unchanged from Wednesday. 

 Dealers said much of the corporate forward dollar demand on Wednesday had been fuelled by the high spreads between onshore and offshore rupee markets. ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: India rupee ends weak, off record low on RBI sales.
text:
BOMBAY, Aug 12 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee ended weaker against the dollar on Wednesday in volatile trade, but was off its record low of 43.35 on central bank intervention, dealers said. 

 The rupee ended at a record low of 42.95/05 per dollar against its previous close of 42.88/91. 

 Dealers said the rupee weakened sharply to hit an all-time low of 43.35 during the day on heavy corporate demand in the spot and forward markets, but several rounds of intervention by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) helped it cut part of the losses. 

 The previous low was on June 23 when the rupee briefly crossed the 43 level after Moody's Investors Services downgraded India's rating following the May nuclear tests and subsequent imposition of economic sanctions. 

 The rupee's fall on Wednesday was on account of heavy bidding for the dollar from local corporates and a spillover of public sector demand which has been seen for the past few days, dealers said. 

 "Initially it was one large corporate buying dollars and after some time even the smaller ones joined in," said a treasury-marketing executive. 

 Dealers said the fall in premiums on regional currencies in overseas non-deliverable forward (NDF) markets could have triggered some local forward demand. 

 "Despite Asia's economic woes, traders felt that offshore premiums were slightly overdone," said a dealer at an overseas bank. 

 Regional markets have been affected in the recent past by Japan's economic and banking woes, the falling Japanese yen and fears of devaluation in China and Hongkong. 

 "Indian corporates would have started buying onshore and selling offshore on the view that the rupee NDF premiums would come off," he added. 

 The rupee was quoted at 46.30/50 for the six month NDF dollar - a spread of 1.35 rupees higher than the domestic rupee on Wednesday morning. 

 Another factor fuelling the rupee's fall was the political instability, dealers said. 

 India's ruling coalition is facing problems with two of its regional allies having threatened to withdraw support if their demands were not met. 

 Dealers said the RBI came into the market several times today, and intervened both verbally and by selling dollars themselves and through the State Bank of India (SBI). 

 Dealers said the SBI sold dollars in the first half of the day at 42.98, but after the 43 level was breached the SBI turned a buyer of dollars and this led to a sharp fall in the rupee. 

 "The SBI was selling (dollars) again at 43.20 but only the RBI's enquiries could check the rupee's decline," said a dealer at a local forex brokerage. 

 The rupee recorded a historic low of 43.35 before the retracement, dealers said. 

 The forward premium on the dollar ended up at 8.11 percent and 9.02 percent for the one and six months respectively against the previous close of 5.64 and 8.20. 

 Dealers said enquiries by the RBI and receiving (selling dollars in swap market) by the SBI guided premiums to a lower close from their intra-day highs hit after the rupee's sharp fall.

title: CMIE sees India 98/99 capital inflows down to $1bn.
text:
BOMBAY, July 10 (Reuters) - Net foreign capital inflows to India are seen falling to $1.0 billion in 1998/99 from $7.7 billion in the previous year, the Centre for Monitoring the Indian Economy (CMIE) said on Friday. 

 The CMIE expected foreign funds to make net sales of $1.0 billion in 1998/99 after making net purchases of $752 million in 1997/98. 

 Foreign direct investment was seen lower at $3.0 billion, down from $3.2 billion the previous year. 

 Deposits by non resident Indians were expected to rise to $1.5 billion, up from $1.14 billion. 

 CMIE foresaw net repayments on external commercial borrowings of $500 million in 1998/99 after inflows of $1.0 billion from this source in 1997/98. 

 Repayments on foreign assistance were seen at $1.0 billion after an inflow of $1.5 billion in the previous year. 

 The CMIE expected zero receipts from global depositary receipt issues of Indian companies abroad, after inflows of $500 million from GDRs last year. 

 Net repayments to the International Monetary Fund were expected to be $500 million, the same as 1997/98. 

 Rupee debt servicing outflows were expected to be smaller at $500 million, down from $800 million in 1997/98. 

 As a result of the fall in inflows India's foreign currency reserves were seen falling around $5 billion to $21 billion by March 1999 from $26 billion at the end of March, 1998. 

 The estimate on reserves excluded the impact of any currency market intervention undertaken by the central bank during the year. 

India's trade deficit was expected to rise to $15.8 billion in 1998/99 from $15.0 billion last year. 

 Exports were forecast to rise to $35.7 billion from $34.0 billion and imports were seen rising to $51.5 billion from $48.5 billion. 

 Net invisible earnings were seen little changed, rising to $9.8 billion from $9.7 billion. 

 The current account deficit was expected to widen to $6.0 billion in 1998/99 from $5.3 billion, and as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) it was expected to rise to -1.7 percent from -1.4 percent. 

 CMIE also forecast growth in industrial output to slow to 4.5 percent in 1998/99 from 6.6 percent last year. 

 And agricultural ouput was expected to post 0.7 percent growth in 1998/99 after a fall of 3.2 percent in 1997/98. 

 GDP gowth is expected to continue its slower trend, the rate dropping to 4.5-5.0 percent in 1998/99 from 5.0-5.5 percent in 1997/98 after averaging seven percent growth in the previous three years. ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: India Sinha says ready to check market volatility.
text:
NEW DELHI, June 23 (Reuters) - Indian Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha said on Tuesday that the financial authorities were ready to take whatever steps required to calm volatility in the markets. 

 "If it is needed, we will take whatever steps are required to calm down volatility in the markets," Sinha told reporters after a meeting with Communications Minister Sushma Swaraj. 

 "We are not in favour of volatility. I have repeatedly said that we are for orderly conditions and if we feel that undue volatility is taking place, then the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) will take whatever steps are needed," Sinha said. 

 Replying to a question at what level there would be intervention to support the rupee, Sinha said: "It's not a question of at what level. If there is a feeling at a point of time that there is too much volatility, that the market is being disturbed, that will be the point of time when the RBI intervenes." 

 On Monday the minister had said the government would not 

 defend the currency. 

 "There is no question of defending the rupee... If we were defending the rupee we would not have stopped at $1 billion," Sinha told reporters on Monday in Bombay. 

Central bank currency market intervention along with investors taking their money home resulted in India's foreign exchange reserves dropping by just over $1 billion in the first two weeks of June to stand at $27.57 billion on June 12. 

 The rupee has lost some seven percent of its value against the dollar since bearish sentiment hit the currency after India conducted a series of nuclear tests last month. 

 It ended on Tuesday at a new closing low of 42.90/93 per dollar, but off a record 43.02 hit in stray deals earlier in the day.

title: India Rupee Dn Midday; Pft-Taking Pares Early Gains

 Reserve Bank either intervenes directly or else through the State Bank of India, the country's largest commercial bank, of which it owns 68%. 

 At the moment State Bank isn't supporting the rupee at any particular level, bankers added.

 TOP STORIES 

 Indian Express 

 INDIA, RUSSIA SIGN NUCLEAR POWER DEAL 

 Russia and India have signed an accord to build India's first large-scale nuclear power station. Russian atomic energy minister Yevgeni Adamov and chief of India's Atomic Energy Commission R.Chidambaram signed a pact to cooperate in building two 1,000 megawatt nuclear power reactors at Kudankulam in Tamil Nadu. With this, the nearly two-and-a-half decade of ban imposed by western countries limiting India's access to atomic energy cooperation have come to an end. 

 - 

 The Pioneer 

 STATE GOVERNMENTS WON'T BE SACRIFICED: ADVANI 

 Federal Home Minister Lal Krishna Advani ruled out the dismissal of any state government merely to ensure survival of the coalition government at the Centre. But Advani justified his decision to send fact-finding teams to Bihar and West Bengal. Advani's statement comes in the wake of a threat by ruling party's key ally All India Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam to withdraw support if the Tamil Nadu government was not dismissed. 

 - 

 The Economic Times 

 COGENTRIX TO REPLACE U.S. FIRM WITH EUROPEAN 

 U.S. power developer Cogentrix has initiated moves to replace the U.S. firm with a European firm for handling the boiler contract at its power plant at Mangalore. The switch-over was being done to work around the U.S. sanctions and, according to sources, could be the first U.S. casualty in infrastructure sector. Several U.S. companies' projects in India are backed by U.S. Exim exposures. Cogentrix is developing a 1,000-megawatts Mangalore plant, one of the seven fast-track power projects. 

 - 

 RUPEE DIP: FOREIGN DEBT UP 

 India's external debt burden has moved up by around 440 billion rupees in the past eight months due to the 15 percent depreciation of the rupee against the dollar. But the movement of other major currencies against the U.S. dollar has reduced the country's external debt burden in other currencies. A finance ministry status report on India's external debt put the external debt at $92.880 bilion as of end-September 1997. 

 -. 

 Financial Express 

 INDO-OMAN REJECTS UHDE'S LOWER OFFER FOR UREA PROJECT 

 Indo-Oman Fertiliser Co. has rejected Uhde GmbH's offer to lower its bid for the 32-bilion-rupee ($800-million) turnkey tender for urea-ammonia project by 3.2 bilion rupees. Uhde's offer was seen as a last-ditch attempt by the German multinational to wrest the project from Italy's Snamprogetti which has been shortlisted for the contract. The reduced offer would have improved on Snamprogetti's leveraged bid by over 2.4 billion rupees. 

 - 

 RESERVE BANK MAY STEP IN TO STEM RUPEE SLIDE 

 The Reserve Bank of India is likely to intervene in the foreign exchange market to check any slide of the rupee in the aftermath of Moody's downgrade. The central bank has already discounted the downgrade. Banking sources said the the market was nervous and Moody's two-notch downgrade was unexpected. Exporters have already decided to hold on to dollars after the new downgrades, they added. 

 - 

 Business Standard 

 GOVERNMENT WORKS ON TWO-PRONGED STRATEGY 

 The government will go in for more political dialogue, particularly with the G-8 countries, and a series of new policy initiatives to bolster foreign investor sentiment. India is also expected to play down its belligerent approach and opt for more behind-the-scenes negotiations. The diplomatic offensive will seek to persuade members of the Group of Eight to soften their hardline stand on multilateral loans to India, which, at present, have been deferred. 

 - 

 INFLATION RATE COMES DOWN TO 6.54 PCT 

 The annual rate of inflation came down marginally by 0.13 percentage point to 6.54 percent for the week ended June 6, despite increase in prices of petrol and urea in the Budget. The inflation, based on the wholesale price index (WPI), stood at 6.54 percent (provisional) for the week compared to 6.67 percent in the previous week and 5.63 percent in the corresponding week of the previous year. Surprisingly, the hikes in petrol and urea prices, which were later rolled back, did not influence the WPI. 

 - 

 The Observer 

 GOVERNMENT TO CONTEST EU DECISION 

 India will contest the European Union's decision to levy contervailing duty on imports of broad-spectrum antibiotics originating from India. India's case would be presented at the Brussels during the bilateral meet scheduled for end-June. Officials said the European Union has not taken into account all the facts provided by the India while arriving at its decision.

title: India reserves to show small drop in 3rd week June.
text:
BOMBAY, June 22 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves will only show a small decline in the third week of June after registering a $1.19 billion drop in the first two weeks, a central bank source told Reuters on Monday. 

 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has been intervening to moderate the rupee's slide against the dollar, largely operating through State Bank of India, the country's largest public sector comercial bank, dealers said. 

 "There will not be much depletion seen when figures are released for that period," the RBI source said on Monday, referring to the week through June 19. 

 India's foreign exchange reserves fell by $1.19 billion to $27.57 billion in the two-week period to June 12 after the central bank spent $909 million during the second week of June. 

 The reserves had fallen by $258 million during the first week to June 5. 

 The sources pointed out the reserves were still $215 million higher than December 1997 levels, when the rupee was reeling in the wake of the South-East Asian crisis. 

 The rupee lost over 60 paise in value after it weakened to 42.85 per dollar in Monday mid-morning deals in reaction to a fresh wave of bearish sentiment after Moody's Investors Service demoted India's credit rating by two notches to below investment grade on Friday evening. 

 There was little sign of any intervention in Monday morning trading, dealers said. 

 Over 6.5 percent has been chipped off the rupee during May and June after the Indian unit was lashed by a wave of bearish sentiments following India's nuclear tests carried out last month. ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: India call ends higher, bond down on weak rupee.
text:
BOMBAY, June 9 (Reuters) - Indian call money rates ended higher on Tuesday on a slight squeeze in funds supply, dealers said. 

 Call money was traded at 6.5-7.0 percent in closing deals on Tuesday against the previous day's close of 6.0-6.10 percent, they said. 

 Stray deals were reported even up to eight percent. 

 "It (rates) opened around 6.0-6.10 and moved steadily after that. Probably, banks are covering excess amounts as sentiment is building up that money could get scarce later," a private bank dealer said. 

 Banks had over 50 billion rupees outstanding in central bank repo agreements, which also put pressure on available liquidity, they said. 

 Dealers said nearly 30-40 billion rupees would leave banks early next week as they paid advance tax payments of their corporate clients to the Reserve Bank of India. 

 "There is enough money in the system... Rates should hover around 6.0-7.0 percent, but there could be occasional spurts on technical factors such as money being locked up in repos," a primary dealer said. 

 Dealers said the foreign exchange market volatility had not yet impacted call rates, but they could get affected if the Reserve Bank of India decided to intervene to stabilise the rupee. 

 The Indian rupee clocked a fresh low of 42.26 per dollar on demand from importers and foreign institutional investors (FIIs) paring exposure to Indian stocks and debt markets. 

 Dealers said the bond market bore the brunt of the volatility in the currency market and bond prices were down across the board. 

 The 13.05 percent 2007 bond was traded at 105.60 rupees against the previous close of 105.75 rupees. 

 The 12.69 percent 2002 bond was traded at 103.60 rupees against the previous close of 103.70/75. 

 "There is simply no trading sentiment. There may have been some arbitrage as people sold bonds to reinvest in dollars," a foreign bank dealer said. ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: India call up in mid-morning deals,bonds seen down.
text:
BOMBAY, June 9 (Reuters) - Indian call money was traded at 6.75-7.0 percent in Tuesday mid-morning deals against the previous close of 6.0-6.10 percent on slightly reduced funds supply, dealers said. 

 Dealers said the weakening of the rupee as it burst through 42.00 per dollar in early trade stoked anxiety but had no real impact on rates. They were watching for Reserve Bank of India intervention for clues to strategy. 

 "It all depends whether there any intervention by the RBI in the currency market. If that happens, call rates will move up," a foreign bank dealer said. 

 Call rates opened low at 6.0-6.25 percent but started moving up soon after, they said. 

 "It is the third day of the fortnight and there is good covering. The locking up of funds in central bank repos has also made an impact," a primary dealer said. 

 Banks funds worth 50.91 billion rupees were locked up with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). 

 The rupee hit a new low of 42.10 per dollar in early deals on Tuesday after closing Monday at 41.785/795. 

 Dealers said the bond market was quiet and also closely watching the currency movements for RBI support. 

 "Banks are not giving bond price levels. The market looks headed down as banks arbitrage in the currency market," a bond broker said. 

 The 13.70 percent 1999 bond was dealt at 102.85 rupees against the previous close of 102.95. This bond was dealt up to 103.15 on Monday. ((Santosh Menon, Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: India  forex  reserves edge up after fall week ago.
text:
NEW DELHI, June 1 (Reuters) - India's foreign exchange reserves rose slightly in the week ended May 22 after a sharp fall the previous week and bankers said it was an indication the currency market had stabilised after initial panic. 

 India's foreign currency reserves stood at $25.52 billion on May 22, a $53 million increase over the May 15 figure. 

 Foreign currency reserves had fallen by $526 million in the week ended May 15, largely on account of central bank action to prop up the rupee, dealers said. 

 Support for the currency became necessary after it came under pressure on fears of foreign capital inflows slowing down after the United States and some other nations imposed economic sanctions against India for its nuclear tests on May 11 and May 13. 

 Bankers said the Reserve Bank of India did not intervene directly in the market, but supported the rupee through dollar sales by the State Bank of India. 

 "It is good that there has been an increase even if marginal," said an official at a state-run bank. "After the sharp fall in the previous week, even a slight increase should boost the sentiment." 

 The official said it was too early to predict the rupee's fortunes. 

 "A good deal depends on the budget and whether it revives foreign investor confidence," he said. 

 Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha will present the federal budget for 1998/99 (April-March) on June 1 at 5 p.m. (1130 GMT). 

 The rupee hit a record closing low of 41.72/75 per dollar on Friday. 

 It has fallen some 4.5 percent from its pre-nuclear test levels on a combination of factors - fears over the impact of economic sanctions, a ratings outlook revision to negative from positive by Standard & Poor's and tit-for-tat nuclear tests by Pakistan last week. title: Dubai gold down on India rupee, direct imports.
text:
DUBAI, May 31 (Reuters) - Dubai gold re-exports to India have been checked by a weaker Indian rupee and a move to direct imports, Dubai-based bullion traders said on Sunday. 

 Imports of U.S. dollar-denominated gold have become more expensive for Indian buyers as the rupee lost ground against the dollar on renewed tension between India and arch-rival Pakistan over nuclear testing. 

 The Indian rupee was last quoted on Saturday at 41.62/69 to the dollar, compared to a year-on-year 35.70/80 rate. 

 The rupee touched an all-time low of 41.77 this week, prompting verbal intervention from the Reserve Bank of India and direct dollar sales by the State Bank of India in an attempt to bolster the currency. 

 "The rupee situation is squeezing trade, the margins and absolute demand," said one Dubai-based gold trader. 

 India's decision to free up gold imports has also continued to cap trade. 

 Dubai's often lucrative link between European and South African bullion suppliers and Indian consumers has been challenged since last year by direct imports of the yellow metal by Indian banks and agencies. 

 The Indian government in October freed up bullion import rules, authorising three state-run agencies and eight banks to import and sell gold freely in the Indian domestic market. 

 Since then one more nominated agency and bank have been added to the list, raising the number of Indian importers who have turned directly to European banks and bypassed Dubai. 

 Traders at Dubai's market have said Indian demand has ebbed by more than 50 percent year-on-year because of the growing impact of direct imports to India. 

 Dubai customs figures showed that Dubai imported 32.2 tonnes of gold in April, down from a record 61.9 tonnes in January and the 54.4 tonnes recorded in April last year. 

 Figures for May imports, expected to be released by mid-June, are also expected to be below the 52.2 tonnes recorded in May 1997. 

 "The trend for less imports continued this month (May)," said one wholesaler in the Dubai gold trade, pointing to the growing impact of last year's liberalisation. 

 Dubai has been the main feeder market into India, the world's largest gold consumer, with 80 percent of the Gulf Arab emirate's total imports of 660 tonnes last year going to India. 

 Sellers continued to point to forecasts of double-digit gold demand growth in India this year. Gold purchases could also be boosted as a refuge against a falling currency. 

 Other factors dampening short-term trade between Dubai and India were the coming Indian budget and a traditional slowdown in import demand in the June and July monsoons, traders said. 

 India's government is scheduled to unveil its federal budget for 1998/99 (April-March) on Monday. 

 "Gold can be affected by the budget's impact on the currency and by any new laws on duties," said one Dubai trader. 

 Dubai's benchmark ten tola bar (TT) gold bar - 3.746 ounces of 24 carat gold - was trading on Sunday at 4,048-4,050 dirhams ($1,102-1,103) in line with weaker international bullion. 

 Spot bullion was last quoted on Saturday at $292.70/293.20 an ounce, down from the London Friday afternoon fix of $293.60 on the back of speculation of further central bank selling. 

 Silver was last quoted on Friday at $5.09/5.12 an ounce, down from a week-on-week $5.28/5.32. ($1 = 3.67 dirhams). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: India Rupee/Early -3: Reserve Bk Statements Stabilize Rupee
text:
Dealers said State Bank of India, the country's largest commercial bank, is selling dollars at INR41.50 and this has resulted in the rupee remaining stable. 

 Market participants said the Reserve Bank of India's statement that the Pakistani nuclear tests won't have any impact on India's financial markets and that it would take steps to ensure stability in the foreign exchange market has also quieted the market. 

 The Reserve Bank issued the statements early Friday, reacting to the unoffical dollar trades that took place at INR40.80-.90 on Thursday evening after close of official trading. 

 The movement of the spot rupee is determined by the direct intervention of the Reserve Bank of India and the dollar sales and purchases of State Bank. 

 Reserve Bank owns 68% in State Bank. The market believes that State Bank sometimes operates in the market on behalf of the the central bank. 

 Dealers said they expect the rupee premiums on forward dollars to rise if there is panic buying from companies. 

 The forward market opens at 0500 GMT (1 a.m. EDT).

title: India rupee ends at record low of 41.72/75 per dlr.
text:
BOMBAY, May 29 (Reuters) - The Indian rupee notched a new record closing level of 41.72/75 per dollar on Friday on nervousness following Pakistan's retaliatory nuclear tests, dealers said. 

 In intra-day trade, the rupee touched an all-time low of 41.77. 

 "The nuclear tests were only the latest in a string of bad news hitting the markets," a dealer said. 

 On Thursday, the rupee closed at 41.37/40. 

 Dealers said most of the trading was in the inter-bank segment - corporate volumes were marginal which took some of the edge off speculation. 

 "Or else, the rupee would have definitely tested 42 (to a dollar)," one dealer said. 

 The rupee opened at 41.60/42.00 but dealers reported only quotes and no deals at those levels. 

 It stabilised in morning trade - holding in the 41.45 to 41.50 range upto noon - supported by verbal intervention from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and direct dollar sales by the State Bank of India (SBI). 

 The RBI, in a statement, said the Pakistan tests had no financial implications for India and the central bank would monitor the markets to ensure orderly conditions. 

 "Yesterday's (Thursday's) developments have no financial implications for us. Financial markets are expected to continue to function normally. 

 "RBI will closely monitor market developments, including foreign exchange markets and take such action as may be necessary to ensure continued orderly conditions," the statement said. 

 The government echoed the RBI's statement - Indian finance minister Yashwant Sinha said on Friday that it was government policy to prevent excessive volatility in the rupee's value. 

 However, a lull in dollar supplies in afternoon trade pushed panic buttons - and the rupee plunged to a historic low of 41.77. 

 But continued dollar sales by the SBI saw it recover, only to weaken again on renewed corporate buying, dealers said. 

 The rupee cut losses against the forward dollar also on nominal corporate covering, and increased receiving (forward dollar selling). 

 The six month dollar premium ended at 9.11 percent, higher than the previous close of 8.61, but off its intra-day high of 9.69 percent. 

 "Some corporates are covering positions for the near term, but demand is not much," a dealer said. 

 "Besides, some exporters are receiving as premiums are at attractive levels," he said. 

 Dealers were unsure of the rupee's position on Monday ahead of the budget. 

 "Unless there is some unexpected trigger, trading on Monday should be ranged - volumes will be low as all eyes will be on what the budget offers," a dealer said. ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: India rupee, bonds to draw fire on Pakistan N-tests.
text:
BOMBAY, May 28 (Reuters) - India's currency and bond markets were likely to feel the heat from Pakistan's nuclear tests when they opened for trading on Friday, senior bankers said. 

 Pakistan on Thursday conducted a series of five nuclear tests to match those carried out by India two weeks ago. 

 "There will be a reaction tomorrow morning. The first hour will be crucial, the rupee will test 42 (to the dollar) levels immediately," P.H. Ramaswamy, country treasurer at Credit Lyonnais told Reuters. 

 There were strong expectations the Reserve Bank of India will have to intervene overtly to cool the market if the bears run too fast. 

 Stray quotes for the rupee at 41.90 per dollar, after the market closed at an historic low of 41.37/40, showed some banks were poised to react to Islamabad's nuclear tests, news of which surfaced after market hours here. 

 The rupee's previous record intra-day low was struck on Wednesday at 41.52. 

 The rupee has fallen around four percent since India conducted the first of its own tests on May, sparking international fury and U.S and Japanese sanctions. 

 "This will spoil an already bad sentiment. Every bit of news in the last two weeks has been bad," the chief forex dealer at a leading foreign bank said. 

 Dealers said if the rupee tumbled on Friday, it would pull down bonds with it and prematurely abort a fledgling rally in prices seen on Thursday. 

 "The market is already nervous. Prices began falling after news of the blasts. If the rupee goes down tomorrow, bond prices will also fall," Ashish Parthasarthy, chief dealer for money markets at HDFC Bank, said. 

 "All eyes are on the rupee-dollar rates. Every other variable including interest rates, will have to adjust based on what happens to it," J. Moses Harding, forex head at IndusInd Bank, said. 

 Indian bonds hit the recovery path late on Wednesday after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) sent signals it did not view interest rates moving up while fixing the cut-off yield at an auction of nine-year government bonds. 

 Parthasarthy said a rally in any case appeared aborted irrespective of the rupee's behaviour. 

 "Even if the rupee is stable, it will take time for bonds to shed their nervousness," he said. 

 Bankers felt the central bank may be forced to directly intervene in the markets if the rupee continued to fall. 

 The RBI had refrained from directly intervening in the market but had put subtle pressure on the market by checking banks' dollar positions. 

 The task of calming the markets by selling dollars was left to the public-sector State Bank of India. But bankers said the RBI may have to step in on Friday. 

 "The central bank has (verbally) intervened in the last few days occassionally. They may step in if the situation warrants it," Martin Fish, chief executive officer of Standard Chartered Bank said. 

 "It may be one of those days when the RBI will have to take things head on," a foreign bank dealer said. 

 Bankers said the outlook for the rupee depended on how the corporates reacted. 

 "Corporates will have to keep their cool. Panicky corporates fuel inter-bank speculation. If corporates keep their heads, inter-bank speculation cannot be sustained," Harding said. 

 ((Bombay newsroom, +91 22 265-9000 fax +91 22 264-1699, 

 Bombay.newsroom@reuters.com))

title: India Rupee Ends At New Low On S&P Cuts But Pares Losses
text:
BOMBAY (Dow Jones)--The Indian rupee (INR) ended lower on hectic dollar-buying by banks and companies after rating agency Standard & Poor's downgraded the outlook on India's sovereign rating to negative from stable late Friday. 

 The rupee ended at 40.96, down from Friday's close of 40.66. The rupee touched an intraday low of INR41.20 on Monday but recovered on some profit-taking by banks and exporters. 

 The previous low of INR40.80 was touched on May 14 after the U.S. imposed economic sanctions on India following its nuclear test explosions. 

 As reported, Standard & Poor's have retained India's long-term foreign currency issuer credit rating of double-B-plus and its local currency issuer credit rating of triple-B-plus, but changed the outlook on both ratings to negative from stable. 

 State Bank of India, the country's largest commercial bank, gave some early support to the rupee but withdrew once it realized that dollar demand was heavy, dealers said. 

 "State Bank was buying dollars when it touched 41 but started selling at 41.20," a dealer at a European bank said. 

 The movement of the spot rupee is determined by the intervention of Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank or sales and purchases of the State Bank. 

 The Reserve Bank owns 68% in State Bank. The market believes that often the State Bank operates in the market on behalf of the central bank.

title: Indian Rupee/Budget -2: S&P Should Have Waited For Budget
text:
Measures expected in the budget to attract foreign investments include a range of tax benefits for foreign investments in infrastructure projects and in Indian shares. 

 Some bankers said the government may also provide incentives to banks to raise interest rates on deposits held by expatriate Indians. 

 Some traders also said that S&P should have waited for the presentation of the government's budget before deciding on its change to the country's rating outlook. 

 "S&P's decision has come a little too early; it could have at least waited till the budget," said Sharukh Wadia, chief foreign exchange dealer at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 Meanwhile, the Reserve Bank of India, which said on Saturday it will closely monitor the rupee following S&P's rating move late Friday, was "intriguingly" absent from the market Monday, one dealer said. 

 Wadia said that the "RBI perhaps wants the rupee to depreciate slowly, given the pressure from exporters." 

 Looking ahead, dealers said they expected the rupee to remain in the INR40.90 to INR41.50 levels against the dollar until the budget's presentation. 

 Wadia of Standard Chartered said he expected the rupee to fall by INR0.10 every day until the budget is released. "There isn't any panic from importers. They have covered nearly 50-70% of their dollar requirements," he added. 

 Bankers said they expect the Reserve Bank of India, the country's central bank, to intervene in the market only if the rupee falls sharply and suddenly. "I see intervention only if the rupee drops suddenly to INR42," Abheek Barua strategist at SSKI Securities said. 

 Until then, the Reserve Bank is expected to support the rupee by selling dollars through the State Bank of India, the country's largest commercial bank. 

 In India's foreign exchange market, the movement of the spot rupee is determined by the intervention of Reserve Bank of India or by sales and purchases by the State Bank. 

 The Reserve Bank owns 68% in State Bank and the market believes that the State Bank often operates in the market on behalf of the central bank.
